# I’ll Build You a Temple

## Foreword

I'll Build You a Temple transports us into one of the great events of our time. It is a story of surrender on the path of pure love—an incomparable story that many have tried to relate but which no one will ever be able to tell like His Holiness Giriraj Swami. He was there, intimately involved, from the beginning to the end.

Giriraj Swami gives us personal witness into the life of Srila Prabhupada at a time when Prabhupada faced insurmountable odds against him at every step. The story reveals Prabhupada’s unwavering faith, indomitable courage, and profound humility. As we turn the pages, absorbed, we find that these virtues expand from Prabhupada’s unconditional love and all-encompassing compassion.

In Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Srila Prabhupada writes, “One’s greatness has to be estimated by one’s ability to tolerate provoking situations.” In this extraordinary book we discover how Prabhupada personified this quality.

In 1971 devotees were eager to build a temple in prosperous downtown Bombay. Instead, Srila Prabhupada chose a site on an undeveloped property infested with rats, infectious mosquitoes, and hostile opponents in a swampy fishing village miles away from the city and foresaw that it would soon be a place of pilgrimage. He welcomed the Deities of Radha-Rasabihari into a small shack and promised to build Them a wonderful home.

As the story unfolds, powerful, corrupt politicians conspired with the local mafia to cheat, exploit, and evict Prabhupada and the devotees. Intimidated by threats, violence, and disease, almost everyone lost hope and was ready to give up—except Srila Prabhupada. He inspired the handful of inexperienced young Western devotees to follow him as he personally led the charge.

There are two types of Bhagavatas: the book Bhagavata (sacred scripture) and the person Bhagavata (one who embodies the scripture). This book opens a door to understanding the goal of life and how to achieve it. It shows us how a great soul interacts with the world of dualities, with all of its struggles, while remaining fixed in remembering

Krishna (God). Herein, Prabhupada teaches us how to see every situation as a blessed opportunity to serve with compassion and devotion.

I'll Build You a Temple is a contemporary narration that shares the emotions, excitement, and message of sacred texts such as the Ramayana, Mahabharata, Srimad-Bhagavatam, and Bhagavad-gita, whose conclusive teachings are revealed through the lives of great souls, such as Srila Prabhupada, who battle and ultimately vanquish powerful enemies against seemingly insurmountable odds.

Appreciating the sincere dedication of young Giriraj dasa, Srila Prabhupada entrusted him with the leadership of this most complex and difficult project, and to carry things on whenever Prabhupada was away from Bombay. Giriraj—and all the devotees who sacrificed so much in the course of their service—deserves to be honored with gratitude and affection.

Srila Prabhupada said that his project in Bombay was his heart. We are sincerely grateful to His Holiness Giriraj Swami Maharaja for dedicating years of research, writing, and praying to authentically reveal Srila Prabhupadas heart to the world, as only he can do.

Radhanath Swami

## Reflections

Srila Prabhupada introduced Krishna consciousness in the West in an unprecedented, inconceivably extensive manner and then, in 1970, with several of his chosen disciples—including young Giriraj dasa—began his activities in India. Right from Giriraj’s early days in the International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON), Srila Prabhupada engaged him in many important services, and in 1972 he appointed him president of ISKCON Bombay.

Ever since I have known Giriraj Swami, he has manifested an intensity of determination that is very rare. He is a devotee who displays enthusiasm at an exceptional level. With very few facilities, he helped Srila Prabhupada in several key projects, sacrificing his own personal comforts and priorities for Srila Prabhupada’s pleasure. He became renowned for his tireless efforts, for the austerities he accepted, for his loyalty and dedication to Srila Prabhupada’s mission, and for his ability to raise funds and cultivate important members of society, especially in Bombay.

Hare Krishna Land in Juhu, Bombay, was, as Srila Prabhupada often observed, his “dearmost project.” When we started the excavation work on the land for the temple area, as we were digging, we found a plaque that a scholar dated at five hundred years old, and on that plaque was an inscription in Marathi, establishing that there had been a Hanuman temple at the location, almost exactly where the Sita-Rama altar is located today. Srila Prabhupada was extremely happy about the discovery.

I had the good fortune of working closely with Giriraj Swami in Bombay for many years, beginning March 1975, when he and I used to go to Sachivalaya, the administrative headquarters of the state government of Maharashtra, in South Bombay, to meet with different government ministers and officers.

In the words of Giriraj Swami, “By the strength of Prabhupada’s desire, an overgrown plot of land in what had been a remote fishing village became a place of pilgrimage and devotional service. And in the process—a long one—he engaged so many of us—his disciples and so many others—in devotional service.”

On December 22, 1971, Srila Prabhupada wrote to Yamuna Devi, “Here in Bombay we have got good prospects to purchase a very large land in Juhu for very cheap price, just in the middle of a rich neighborhood. We shall build our camp there and begin constructing a temple immediately, and later on we shall develop a large hotel and school. There is also a chance of getting a nice bungalow in Bombay city also. So in general we shall make our headquarters in Bombay, and also build up Vrindaban and Mayapur.” It’s truly extraordinary that Srila Prabhupada could visualize it all.

During a lecture in Bombay on February 25,1974, Srila Prabhupada said, “A devotee sees: ‘Oh, this land is so nice. Why not construct a nice temple for Krishna?’ This is Krishna conscious vision. ‘Oh, there are so many skyscrapers. Why not construct a nice skyscraper temple for Krishna?”’ He could see a temple when others could see only an uncleared jungle.

Srila Prabhupada would say, “Vrindavan is my home, Bombay is my office, and Mayapur is where I worship the Supreme Personality of Godhead.” He described Bombay as the gateway to India; he started his spiritual movement from Bombay, and it was from Bombay that he initiated the vision and directions for the management of his international endeavors as well as set up the Indian yatra.

I wasn’t in India during the early days of Hare Krishna Land; I started serving as GBC in March 1975. When I arrived, the first thing Prabhupada told me was that he wanted the Bombay temple built in six months. This was an impossible target, but wherever he was, whether in Hawaii or Los Angeles or London or Manila, Srila Prabhupada meditated deeply on Hare Krishna Land in Juhu to ensure that there would be a world-class temple for the worship of Sri Sri Radha-Rasabihari, a temple which would bring great repute to ISKCON’s name.

He promised Their Lordships, “My dear Sir, please remain here, and I shall build You a beautiful temple.” Even though his disciples were against moving to Juhu, he persisted and was victorious. And in the end, by Srila Prabhupada’s mercy, the project was completed. Over time, ISKCON Juhu became known as Heaven on Earth, and the temple will always remain the symbol of Srila Prabhupada’s struggle and triumph— in many respects a true Prabhupada institution.

Srila Prabhupada spent more time in Bombay—554 days—than in any other city in the world. And that indicates the significance of the Juhu project—and of this book. In I'll Build You a Temple Giriraj Maharaja has translated his long years of commendable involvement in the leadership of ISKCON Juhu as well as his intense desire to serve Srila Prabhupada’s instruction to him to write into a riveting, thoughtful, and inspiring book.

I welcome you all to take a dip in the nectarean pastimes of Sri Sri Radha-Rasabihari in Juhu, which glorify Their pure devotee Srila Prabhupada. Srila Prabhupada ki jaya! Sri Sri Radha-Rasabihari ki jaya!

Gopal Krishna Goswami

Governing Body Commissioner, ISKCON

Trustee, Bhaktivedanta Book Trust

## Preface

Srila Prabhupada’s struggle to build a temple and establish Hare Krishna Land in Juhu, on the outskirts of Bombay, was perhaps the greatest effort of his preaching movement. In fact, from the time he returned to India in August 1970, he spent 554 days in Bombay, more than any other place in the world. It took six years—from 1972, when he took possession of the land, to 1978, when the temple opened—and after the conveyance was signed, he declared, “It was a good fight. Someone should write a book about it.”

I served in Juhu as temple president and later as Governing Body Commissioner between 1972 and 1999, raising funds and overseeing every aspect of the project—the only devotee to be closely involved throughout that period—and Srila Prabhupada had already told me, in 1971, “You should write. This is your first business,” and repeated this instruction over the years. So despite my limitations and disqualifications but with the encouragement and assistance of many well-wishers, I took up writing about him and Juhu.

It was an illuminating experience. I became absorbed in Prabhupada’s divine qualities, activities, and words, and I came to understand him and the history of the project—even events to which I had been party—in new, deeper ways. I felt like I was mining a limitless reservoir of precious gems. And I came to appreciate him—and his servants—and those who have supported me in my efforts to write—even more than I had before.

In his purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.13.50, Prabhupada explains, “The word svakarthanam refers to great desires. As mentioned in this verse, the glance of Lord Visnu creates the desires of the devotees. A pure devotee, however, has no desires. Therefore Sanatana Gosvami comments that because the desires of devotees whose attention is fixed on Krsna have already been fulfilled, the Lord’s sidelong glances create variegated desires in relation to Krsna and devotional service.” Thus, in “a place where there was no temple ... a devotee desired, ‘Let there be a temple and seva, devotional service.’ Therefore, what was once an empty corner has now become a place of pilgrimage. Such are the desires of a devotee.”

By the strength of Prabhupada’s desire, an overgrown plot of land in what had been a remote fishing village became a place of pilgrimage and devotional service. And in the process—a long one—he engaged so many of us—his disciples and so many others—in devotional service.

Throughout, in spite of so much opposition and so many obstacles, Prabhupada remained perfect in Krishna consciousness—an ideal sadhu: “tolerant, merciful, and friendly to all living entities. He has no enemies, he is peaceful, he abides by the scriptures, and all his characteristics are sublime.” (SB 3.25.21) And after his departure, by his mercy, we were left with great challenges of work and responsibility, both for our own spiritual benefit and for the benefit of all those who would associate with the temple.

It was our greatest good fortune to be able to associate with Srila Prabhupada, and through this book, I want to share with you that good fortune and give you his association.

‘sadhu-sanga’, ‘sadhu-sanga—sarva-sastre kaya  
lava-matra sadhu-sange sarva-siddhi haya

“The verdict of all revealed scriptures is that by even a moment’s association with a pure devotee \[sadhu\], one can attain all success.” (Cc Madhya 22.54)

Writing this book describing Prabhupada’s monumental efforts has been a humbling endeavor but one with great rewards. In Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, Krishnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami, after enumerating some of his superiors, writes, “It is by the mercy of all these Vaisnavas and gurus that I attempt to write about the pastimes and qualities of Lord Caitanya Mahaprabhu. Whether I know it or know not, it is for self-purification that I write this book.” (Cc Adi 9.5)

Prabhupada explains, “This is the sum and substance of transcendental writing” and directs that “\[o\]ne should write transcendental literature to purify oneself,” since “\[b\]y writing about the pastimes of the Lord, one associates with the Lord directly.” I have tried to follow Srila Prabhupada’s and his—our—predecessor acharyas’ instructions and examples.

The benefits of reading about such an empowered pure devotee are incalculable. I think of Srila Rupa Gosvami’s statement (Vidagdha-madhava 1.6, Cc Antya 1.139):

abhivyakta mattah prakrti-laghu-rupad api budha  
vidhatri siddharthan hari-guna-mayi vah krtir iyam  
pulindenapy agnih kim u samidham unmathya janitor  
hiranya-sreninam apaharati nantah-kalusatam

“O learned devotees, I am by nature ignorant and low, yet even though it is from me that \[this book\] has come, it is filled with descriptions of the transcendental attributes of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Therefore, will not such a literature bring about the attainment of the highest goal of life? Although its wood may be ignited by a low-class man, fire can nevertheless purify gold. Similarly, although I am very low by nature, this book may help cleanse the dirt from within the hearts of the golden devotees.”e vacana mora nahe, sarva-sastre kaya

## Prologue

In 1970, when I was serving at the Boston temple, I submitted my first article, entitled “The Genuine Spiritual Master,” to Back to Godhead (BTG), “The Magazine of the Hare Krishna Movement,” which Srila Prabhupada had founded in India in 1944. “With confidence in this relationship \[with the guru\],” I had written, “the student, out of love, agrees to serve the spiritual master. There is no question of force. Where there is force, there is no love ... \[and\] the service rendered by the student to the bona fide spiritual master is performed out of love. Anyone who sees His Divine Grace Srila Prabhupada with his disciples is seeing the perfection of family life.

“The mother, the Vedas, directs the child to the father, the bona fide spiritual master, as illustrated so personally in the Gita. Arjuna, who had very great spiritual qualifications as well as material qualifications, still confessed to Krishna, the supreme spiritual master: ‘Now I am confused about my duty and have lost all composure because of miserly weakness. In this condition I am asking You to tell me clearly what is best for me. Now I am Your disciple, and a soul surrendered unto You. Please instruct me.’ (Gita 2.7) ‘By nature’s own way, the complete system of material activities is a source of perplexity for everyone. Vedic wisdom therefore advises us that in order to solve the perplexities of life and to understand the science of the solution, one must approach a spiritual master, for a bona fide spiritual master is supposed to know everything.’ (Gita 2.7 purport)”

The qualifications of the bona fide spiritual master were spelled out in the Vedas, I had continued—he had to come in disciplic succession, have realized knowledge, and never present himself as God or promise his students that they could become God. I had contrasted Srila Prabhupada with “fake spiritualists,” some of whom I described, and, quoting from Srimad-Bhagavatam, presented Krishna’s list of qualifications for a disciple to hear from the guru:

“‘This instruction should be imparted by the spiritual master to persons who have taken Me, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, as moredear than anything, and who are not envious of anyone, are perfectly cleansed and have developed detachment from everything outside the purview of Krsna consciousness. Instruction in Krsna consciousness should be given to the faithful devotee who is respectful to the spiritual master, non-envious, friendly to all kinds of living entities, and ready to render service with faith and sincerity? (SB 3.40-41)...

“The student takes the spiritual master as his spiritual father and follows the teachings of the spiritual master to his full capacity. Jesus Christ said, ‘Unless you become like little children, you cannot enter the kingdom of God? Only to one who has full faith in the spiritual master will all knowledge be revealed. The word of the spiritual master is the life of the student, and everything else is secondary. Then there is contact. If one touches electricity, even if the source is thousands of miles away, the current is there, and one who follows the instructions of the spiritual master can always feel the blissful association of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

“Everyone now has all facility to become happy by the mercy of His Divine Grace A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, our spiritual master. He wants everyone to be happy in Krishna consciousness, and he is offering us all transcendental opportunities.” He had translated and provided commentary on the Bhagavad-gita, Srimad-Bhagavatam, and other Vedic texts; had opened temples devoted to Krishna consciousness; and, “greatest of all, he is offering Krishna Himself directly, in His holy name—the greatest benediction for the conditioned living entities.”

The following February, in Gorakhpur, India, Srila Prabhupada received the issue and asked to see me.

The long temple room was only dimly lit by narrow shafts of sunlight filtering through the wooden shutters on his right. Sitting on his asana, a simple raised cushion, at the far end, Prabhupada was the very image of the eternal spiritual master.

Alone with my guru maharaja, I sat at his feet, my eyes and ears wide open.

“I saw your article in Back to Godhead” he said. “It was very nice. You should write.”

My attention was focused on his every word.

“This is your first business. Go on writing. We require many, many articles about Krishna consciousness. So you should devote yourself to writing.”

“I will try, Srila Prabhupada,” I said. “But why are you asking me? I have no special qualification.”

“We require many to do this work, and we need you also. So, you travel with me and I will guide you. You come and stay with me.”

I felt thrilled and honored—and a little intimidated. Prabhupada had never given me an instruction directly, in person. In fact, we hardly ever spoke personally, or privately, and now he was inviting me to stay with him.

I didn’t know how it would work. I had always served under other devotees, and I wondered who would tell them about Prabhupada’s instruction. I asked, “How will we decide whether I should travel with you or what I should do?”

“By mutual consultation,” he replied.

Srila Prabhupada was at Sri Krishna Niketan with a dozen disciples, including myself, Kausalya, Hamsaduta and Himavati, Tamal Krishna, and a few others, at the invitation of the estate’s owner and former resident, Hanuman Prasad Poddar, the head of the Gita Press, the largest publisher of Hindu religious books in India. It was a grand old house surrounded by fields, and the whole time there, I kept thinking of Srila Prabhupada. Sometimes I couldn’t even sleep at night—I would stand on the balcony near his room and look out over the fields and up at the moon and stars and think of how wonderful he was. I was in ecstasy that he had read my article and invited me to travel with him, and I felt a new kind of love in my heart.

Hamsaduta, who was one of the authorities in India at that time and wanted to start a world traveling sankirtana party, asked Prabhupada if I could join him. Since Prabhupada had suggested that I accompany him on his travels, I was surprised and disappointed when he agreed to Hamsaduta’s appeal. Still, I thought, Prabhupada knows best. So I became a member of Hamsaduta’s party.

After two weeks on the road, we received a telegram from Prabhupada directing us to go to Bombay for a big pandal program. When we got there, Shyamasundar, who was the temple president and in charge ofthe program, told me, “We’re going to have a big pandal program, and you should raise funds for it.”

I’d really had it in my mind to start writing. I had my sheets of paper and my pencils, and I was constantly thinking about Prabhupada’s instruction. So I said, “Srila Prabhupada told me I should write.”

“You can write anytime,” Shyamasundar pointed out. “But this is the one time we can walk into the office of any big man in Bombay and ask for money. You should do it.”

I thought what he said made sense. It was easier for businessmen to place advertisements in a pandal souvenir book than to give straight donations; they could deduct the cost as a business expense. As it turned out, that is exactly what happened, and I became successful at raising funds by selling ads for the book. I really liked the Indian gentlemen I approached, and they liked me. I loved Indian culture, and, to greater or lesser degrees, they all still had some. Especially in the old part of Bombay, where I went first, they would receive me as a sadhu and offer me milk, fruit, sweets, savory Indian snacks, and other refreshments. And I was convinced that they would benefit if they gave to Krishna. Many of them became long-standing friends and supporters, and we developed deep, affectionate relationships. Later, Prabhupada commented, “Giriraj can make friends with any man, become his son, and take his money.”

Every morning, in preparation for the pandal program, the devotees would meet and discuss the previous day’s activities and the upcoming day’s plans. We each had our specific tasks: Gurudas was getting permits, Shyamasundar was doing the publicity, Yamuna was collecting and arranging for the Deities’ paraphernalia, and I was soliciting ads.

When Prabhupada arrived in Bombay, all the devotees there sat down in his room, and he led a short kirtan. He was radiant, beaming and smiling and casting glances everywhere. “So, Giriraj,” he asked me, “how is your writing going?”

“Well, Srila Prabhupada, I haven’t done any writing.”

“Oh, you haven’t done any writing? Why not?”

I was completely flustered; I didn’t know what to say.

“All right, we will speak later,” he ended.

I left the room with the other devotees but then went back in. “So, you are not writing?” Prabhupada asked again.

I explained what had happened and said, “I considered that you wanted us to work cooperatively, and I thought what Shyamasundar Prabhu said made sense, so I agreed to what he asked. Did I do the right thing?”

“Yes, that’s all right,” Prabhupada said. “One may temporarily suspend the order of the spiritual master, but one should never neglect it. Just like my guru maharaja gave me the order to write, but I am so busy traveling and preaching in India now, I have no time to write. But I am always thinking of his order, and when the opportunity arises, I will take it up again.”

## Chapter one

Arriving on the Scene— A Good Fight

OCTOBER 1970-OCTOBER 1973

IN AUGUST 1970, AFTER FIVE YEARS in the United States, Srila Prabhupada prepared to return to India with some of his American disciples. When he was asked why he was going to India when his guru maharaja had ordered him to preach in the West, he replied, “I have already done that”—spread Krishna consciousness in Europe and America. “Now I want to revive the spiritual culture of India.”

One of the first things Prabhupada did when he got to Calcutta was introduce life-membership—a program meant to distribute books, generate funds for his projects, and engage important people in Krishna consciousness. By the terms of the program, a life member would contribute Rs. 1,111 and receive in exchange, for the duration of his or her life, all of Prabhupada’s books, present and future; a subscription to Back to Godhead; and free accommodations in any of our centers and guesthouses throughout the world.

Before leaving for India, Prabhupada had asked that each of our fourteen or so temples in America send the best man they could spare— generally the second in command—to join him. Pretty much every devotee wanted to get to be with Prabhupada in India, and I was chosen to go from Boston.

So, that October, I was on my way to India, and in Brussels I first met three of Prabhupada’s earliest and most prominent disciples: Yamuna, Shyamasundar, and Shyamasundar’s wife, Malati (with their two-year-old daughter, Saraswati). Gurudas, Yamuna’s husband, whom I had met in Boston, was also with them. He had arranged a cheap flight on a small airline, and that evening eleven of us—without Shyamasundar, who stayed behind to escort four more devotees from America the following day—boarded an old converted dual-propeller cargo plane, bound for Bombay with a stop in Cairo.

In my mood of single-minded Krishna consciousness, I was practically oblivious to things around me. I wanted to avoid maya—anything that could distract me from Krishna—and didn’t pay much heed to anything that didn’t relate directly to my service. I was focused on chanting and hearing every word of the Hare Krishna mantra and on always thinking about Krishna and never forgetting Him. I had heard that Prabhupada had said that if you had trouble hearing, you should chant loudly, and sometimes, to avoid any possible lethargy while chanting, Iwould jump up and down. There was some anxiety in the group about how people iri Egypt might react, but I was fixed.

There was unrest in Cairo—President Gamal Abdel Nasser had recently died—and when we landed, we were met on the tarmac by soldiers and armed security guards with bandoliers of bullets strapped across their chests and machine guns slung over their shoulders. As we deplaned, they followed us with their machine guns. Stepping down the mobile stairway, Yamuna noticed the guards shifting their aim behind her, the muzzles of their guns pointing up, then down. When she turned to see what they were aiming at, there I was behind her, jumping up and down as I chanted.

On the tarmac, Cidananda set up an altar on a table and we began kirtan. Crowds of onlookers surrounded us and watched from the terminal’s windows and balconies, leaning over the railings to smile and wave at us below. I was elated; not only were we on our way to the holy land of India, but now we were chanting and dancing in exotic, Muslim Egypt, and all these people were getting the benefit of hearing the holy names. After leading the chanting for some time, I addressed the soldiers and other people gathered around us. Then I took two of the soldiers by the hand and pulled them into the kirtan, and they sang and danced and laughed in enjoyment.

Nanda Kumar had been playing kartals, but feeling anxious about the potential dangers of the situation, he had circled around the plane to chant by himself and pray for protection. “When I came back,” he later described, “the first thing I saw was two machine guns leaning against the bus and Giriraj holding one guy in each hand, and these Egyptian military guys were jumping up and down and chanting Hare Krishna with big grins on their faces!”

When we arrived in Bombay, we didn’t know what to expect. We were filled with excitement and expectation. We were finally in the holy land of India and would soon be meeting up with Srila Prabhupada and embarking on great adventures in Krishna consciousness.

At the airport, while we were wondering what to do and where to go, we were met by a man wearing a brown fedora, who asked us to come with him. For some reason, Gurudas thought he was a detective, so he asked for the man’s identification. In response, the man showed Gurudasa telegram from Prabhupada addressed to “Gurudas, in charge,” telling Gurudas to go with the man to his home and wait for Prabhupada to join us there in a week’s time. The man was Kailash Seksaria, with whom, through his uncle, the wealthy Calcutta Marwari businessman Ram Niwas Dandharia, Prabhupada had arranged for us to stay.

So, we all got into Ambassador cars and headed in a caravan to Mr. Seksaria’s house. Cars, buses, and motorbikes all sped down the streets, horns blaring, barely avoiding crashing into each other or knocking into the bicycles and crowded rikshaws drawn by skinny, sinewy men through the traffic. I was intrigued, but also a little fearful. And amidst all this chaos were cows—sacred cows, our mothers. When I saw them, my heart was filled with joy.

Mr. Seksaria’s residence, Seksaria Bhavan (House) was a seven-story creamy-beige stone mansion facing the Arabian Sea on a corner of affluent Marine Drive, “The Queen’s Necklace.” The entrance, flanked with vines and bushes, had dark-green marble facing the front and lighter green on the sides, with gleaming white marble front steps. One entered a foyer through two carved wooden doors, and beyond that was a small marble entry way with a stairway and two elevators (the first I’d seen in a private residence), on top of one of which stood a two-foot-square clock.

Almost immediately upon entering, I could feel—and was touched by—the devotional culture in the entire household. Hired brahmans cooked for the whole extended family in a huge white-tiled kitchen, next to which was a Deity room where all the food was offered. Other than Srila Prabhupada’s disciples and followers, I had never met anyone who offered his or her food to Krishna before eating.

Throughout the building elderly ladies sat performing puja for Deities of Krishna housed in small temple structures less than three feet tall— ringing bells; offering incense, lamps, and flowers; and reciting prayers.

Mr. Seksaria had arranged quarters for us on the ground floor. “The windows had white bars arranged in a pattern that resembled a key,” Yamuna Devi later recalled, “the top of the key round and coming down to a half moon at the bottom. I envisioned it to be the key with which Srila Prabhupada would unlock India for me, as he had promised years earlier in San Francisco.”

A couple of days later, we received a telegram that Srila Prabhupada would be arriving in two days, and our group was buzzing with excitement.

His coming, Tamal Krishna described, was like a comet approaching the earth—a luminous heavenly body being awaited with great anticipation.

Mr. Seksaria arranged a procession of cars to receive Prabhupada at the airport and for Prabhupada’s car to be covered with yellow marigolds. We greeted Prabhupada with a large kirtan, after which he rode with Mr. Seksaria to Marine Drive.

When Prabhupada arrived at Seksaria Bhavan, he was met by a tumultuous reception of thirty devotees who had been waiting in eager anticipation. After acknowledging everyone with nods and smiles and loving glances, he was whisked into one of the elevators and brought up to a bedroom on the fourth floor, though eventually he moved down to the ground level, where he was given another bedroom, with an attached bath.

Prabhupada was pleased with his quarters at Seksaria Bhavan, with its large rooms overlooking the sea. But personally, I was experiencing some anxiety about all the facilities we were being offered. I felt uncomfortable accepting the rich, opulent prasada and costly varieties of sweets and nuts. Even the elevator seemed a great luxury. I saw other, more senior devotees avail themselves of the facilities, but I was uneasy, and when I did accept something, I sometimes felt guilty afterward, so 1 often refrained. I would climb the stairs instead of taking the elevator, and I tried to limit my eating to the most basic, simple prasada.

Soon after Prabhupada’s arrival, Mr. Seksaria arranged a press conference for him on the fifth floor. Sitting on a large mattress with a few of his disciples, Prabhupada spoke about his work, focusing on New Vrindaban, and then, when reporters asked about his disciples becoming sadhus and leaving their countries, he called on me to speak. Although I was a little nervous, I was also enlivened and inspired in Prabhupada’s presence, and I told the story of how I had come to Krishna consciousness. The next day, the press was full of stories about Srila Prabhupada and his mission, and The Times of India ran a story referring to my talk, under the heading “U.S. Millionaire’s Son Seeks Solace in Krishna Society,” recounting how I had renounced my father’s wealth to join Prabhupada’s movement.

Although the news coverage and public response was generally favorable, some reactionary Hindus wrote letters to the editor(s), raising objections to Prabhupada’s making foreigners into brahmans and

Vaishnavas and accusing us of being faddists and sentimentalists. In response, Prabhupada dictated points for a reply that, on his instruction, I submitted in my name. “The main point is that our Society is teaching, ‘Here is God,’” I wrote, “and some people do not like that. Generally, people are trying to kill God, push Him out of the picture. But we are advertising for God: ‘Here is Krishna.’ Therefore, persons who are envious of God, who want to be God, become our enemies. They see that we are publishing books, acquiring property, and gaining members, and they find fault. But our movement is authorized, scientific, and practical, and it will continue to grow no matter how many speculators raise arguments against us.”

Srila Prabhupada, I stated, was simply passing on the knowledge that Krishna had imparted to Arjuna in the Bhagavad-glta, which had been passed on unadulterated through an authorized disciplic succession. It was a non-sectarian philosophy that had “nothing to do with any of the faiths that have some historical beginning or end. Krishna is God; God is God; He is not ‘Hindu’ or any other faith.” No matter one’s “religion,” as Krishna had instructed, the only way to realize God was through devotional service, and the recommended form of devotional service in our age was the chanting of God’s holy names.

Addressing some people’s objection that Srila Prabhupada’s Western disciples were not true brahmans, I countered that Lord Chaitanya had taught that one was a brahman by qualification, not birth. And we were serious in our endeavor. We were Vaishnavas, I wrote, “because we act like Vaishnavas, not because we have taken to wearing saris and churning butter.... this is not a sporadic fad of sentimentalists, as has been suggested. How can our movement be sporadic when this science was taught in the Gita five thousand years ago and instructed to the sun-god millions of years before that? How can it be called sporadic when our activity is sanatana-dharma, the eternal occupation of the living entity? Would faddists give up all meat-eating, intoxicants, illicit sex, and gambling for over five years now? Would faddists give up friends, family, and money and get up at 4:00 a.m. daily, ready to go to any country in the world and preach in any conditions immediately on the request of their spiritual master?”

I quoted Rupa Gosvami, who, citing the Padma Purana, had stated that Vaishnavas, who were transcendental, actually surpassed ordinarybrahmans, who could be conditioned by the mode of goodness. “But,” I emphasized, “we accept the proposal of Lord Chaitanya: ‘I am neither Hindu, nor brahman, nor sannyasi—I am the servant of the servant of the servant of God.’”

“To become a devotee of the Lord is a rare thing,” I encouraged readers, “and everyone knows that there will never be a problem of too many people taking to Krishna consciousness. Actually, there can be no scarcity in God’s creation; the only scarcity can be of Krishna consciousness. Therefore, we urge people to change their consciousness, not their occupations.... We are working, each person according to his natural capacity, for the pleasure of the Supreme Lord. Thus some are running our printing presses and some teaching university courses in Krishna consciousness; some are operating an ideal farm community modeled after Vrindavan and sheltering hundreds of cows in the U.S.A., while others are preparing the Krishna prasadam we serve to thousands of persons daily; some are on sankirtana and circulating five hundred thousand Back to Godhead magazines per month in six languages, and still others are maintaining our fifty centers with Radha-Krishna Deity worship all over the world. Actually we are working harder than anyone, but because we are working for Krishna, and not maya, our work is joyful and free from anxiety. Thousands of new Vaishnavas, who are considered already liberated, are doing the work of India, which is to present the gift of Krishna consciousness, and thereby save the world from gliding to hell. Not only can everyone do this, but they must do it. For this reason we are traveling to all countries of the world and begging all people to revive their love of God and sing the glories of His name.”

Prabhupada liked my submission, and the skeptics and critics, at least for the time being, seemed to have been silenced.

Prabhupada’s first preaching engagement in Bombay was at a gathering of sadhus in a pandal in a vacant plot some blocks from Mr. Seksaria’s house, organized by the Bharat Sadhu Samaj. Several other disciples and I went to the pandal a few hours before Prabhupada, and I was startled to see the exotic array of Indian sadhus sitting in rows on long tables. Some of them were bearded, some shaven-headed; some had long matted hair and held tridents; some were covered with ashes, some adorned with beads and clay markings; some had sacred texts open before them.

I was amazed, and I imagined that many of them, seeing us fair-skinned Vaishnavas, were equally astonished.

I had been curious about the holy men of India and how they would compare with Srila Prabhupada, but seeing this assembly of what seemed to me somewhat bizarre-looking fellows, I could see that Prabhupada was a distinct cut above the rest. He was clean, effulgent, and looked grave and dignified. And more than anything else, I could see without doubt, he was full of love.

When I had joined the Boston temple, devotees told me that if you looked at Prabhupada’s eyes, you could see that they were always wet with tears of love for Krishna. And that was true—I could see it and feel it when I looked at him. Years later, when the Caitanya-caritamrita was published, I read something similar about Minaketana Ramadasa, a great devotee of Lord Nityananda—that his eyes were always brimming with tears.

Seeing the motley crew of sadhus sitting on tables at the pandal, I had a realization of Srila Prabhupada’s immense stature as a spiritual master. Even though I viewed the others as sages, saintly persons, and yogis, I could see that none of them were like Prabhupada: so effulgent, so compassionate, so full of grace.

We were invited onstage, and when we performed kirtan the audience responded by chanting and clapping in rhythm. And when, on Mr. Seksaria’s advice, we took our kirtan onto the streets, many in the audience followed, and the people outside too responded enthusiastically and joined us in singing and dancing.

That evening, we returned to the pandal with Prabhupada. He sat on a raised platform, and we sat around him, at his feet. After having three of his disciples speak in English, he spoke in Hindi, and the audience of more than five hundred listened in virtual silence. After his lecture, he stepped down from the platform, and a crowd gathered around him, touching his feet and following him to the car.

The next day, when Prabhupada heard about the success of our public kirtan, he said that we should go to the busiest areas and chant daily. So every day after that, wherever large numbers of people gathered, we would go and chant for three or four hours while Prabhupada was in his room translating or writing letters or doing other service.

I was enthralled by Bombay. Everything felt new and exotic, and from the way people looked at us and how they responded, I think they were enthralled by us, too. They would look out from their windows and balconies and rooftops and line the streets, sometimes causing big traffic jams.

Prabhupada knew that the people of India wanted to imitate the West, and especially America, so if they saw that Americans took to Krishna consciousness, they would want to do that, too. And his strategy worked. Seeing us, Indians reevaluated their own traditions, their own culture and practices, and considered that there must have been more there than even they themselves had thought. Otherwise, why would Americans and Europeans, who had every chance to enjoy material facilities and sense gratification, be chanting Hare Krishna and dancing, studying Bhagavad-gita and preaching? Why would they come to India? So, they were thrilled, and sometimes, when they saw us doing sankirtana, tears would come to their eyes and they would be moved to join.

I was thrilled to see how Krishna conscious the people were—how traditional their culture and surroundings remained; I’d never seen anything like it. I saw men wearing dhotis and kurtas, and most of the women wore saris. Cows roamed the streets and lazed on the sidewalks and medians, and many of the names of buildings and businesses included names of Krishna and Rama. We were captivated by it all, but at the same time we were filled with the sense that we were pioneers in Srila Prabhupada’s mission to revitalize Krishna consciousness in India, working to serve him and please him according to his superior guidance and vision. And we had faith that the whole process would culminate in wonderful results.

We didn’t have to go far to create a sensation; all we had to do was step out of the door of Seksaria Bhavan, which we dubbed Krishna Mahal, and people would gather around us. They were so eager to see us that sometimes we would just go out front and they would gather around to hear us chant, and then one of us might speak to the crowd. Sometimes we would do that while waiting to leave for a program, or upon returning. We were all so full of enthusiasm to chant the holy names and preach.

As I wrote in an article for a special All-India Issue of BTG, under the heading “Krishna Returns to India ” “When the Hare Krsna chanters first appeared in America five years ago, Americans were surprised. Dressed in ‘Indian’ dhotis and saris and chanting ‘Hindu’ chants in Sanskrit, they were a novelty, but when they braved the winter snow and freezing temperatures to perform their sankirtana, people had to take them seriously.

“Now it is time for the Indians to be surprised. For the first time in many years, Indians in the downtown sectors of \[India’s\] major cities are seeing this same performance of sankirtana, as taught and popularized by Lord Caitanya Mahaprabhu, who advented Himself in India, in West Bengal, 480 years ago. Yet instead of seeing Indians chanting, as one would expect in India, the Indians are astonished to see that the chanters are actually Americans and Europeans, dressed in the traditional garb of Indian sadhus, or holy men. These American and European devotees are following the Vedic system even more strictly than the Indians. By dint of their determination and eagerness to chant the Lord’s praises, Indians are beginning to understand the purpose of their chanting. No longer are the devotees viewed as curiosities or public entertainment, as they were taken to be when first appearing in the West. The serious purpose of the Krsna consciousness movement is a wonderful and welcome surprise to all.

“These surprises are the mercy of His Divine Grace A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, who came to America five years ago from India and just recently has returned to India from the West.”

One evening we had a program on the roof of Seksaria Bhavan, with the elite of Bombay, invited by Kailash Seksaria. Although he had expected the guests to number only two hundred at most, many more came. After kirtan, Prabhupada spoke about his work in the West and then quoted Caitanya-candramrta 8.90:

dante nidhaya trnakam padayor nipatya  
krtva ca kaku-satam etad aham bravimi  
he sadhavah sakalam eva vihaya durad  
caitanya-candra-carane kurutanuragam

\[“Taking a straw between my teeth and falling at your feet a hundred times, I humbly submit, ‘O great personality, please give up all mundane knowledge that you have learned and just submit yourself at the lotus feet of Lord Caitanya Mahaprabhu.’”\]

“Ladies and gentlemen,” he said, “you are all so highly qualified. You are all so much devoted, and you have such good qualities in all respects. You are all intelligent, learned, and educated. You are all very great persons. I beg you—I take the straw of the street between my teeth, and I beg you, ‘Just chant Hare Krishna. Please chant Hare Krishna?” He was begging them, on the spot. I was moved and humbled by Prabhupada’s earnestness, humility, and compassion.

After his talk, Prabhupada left, and we gave a slide show of ISKCON’s activities around the world. That night, several of the guests, including the prominent industrialist G.D. Somani—and Kailash Seksaria—became life members and received a collection of Srila Prabhupada’s books.

A few days later, there was another gathering of sadhus and spiritual leaders, on Chowpatty Beach. Prabhupada and his disciples were seated on a stage that had been erected right on the sand. Prabhupada sat with the twenty or so sadhus; the rest of us were in rows toward the back. Two prominent Mayavadis expounded impersonal philosophy, and then came Prabhupada, the last scheduled speaker. But instead of addressing the audience, he told us, “Begin chanting.”

When we began the kirtan, little Saraswati, Shyamasundar and Malati’s two-year-old daughter, stood up and began to dance. Following her, the rest of us devotees rose and danced as well. As the kirtan grew, with mridangas and kartals, one by one the sadhus onstage rose and left. The audience, however, responded enthusiastically, many of them standing and clapping, and after five minutes, we jumped down onto the sand and headed toward them. Thousands in the crowd rose to their feet and began to move backward and forward, singing and clapping. So moved were they that many began crying in happiness, overwhelmed by our ecstatic devotion. They had never seen anything like it. Even policemen and press reporters joined in the chanting and dancing. Chowpatty Beach was in an uproar of Hare Krishna kirtan.

After the kirtan, the crowd took some time to settle back down. Then Prabhupada’s voice boomed over the public-address system. “Ladies and gentlemen,” he began, “I was requested to speak in Hindi, but I am notvery much accustomed to speaking in Hindi. Therefore, the authorities in this meeting have allowed me to speak in English. I hope you will follow me, because it is Bombay and most people speak English. The problem is, as this evening’s speaker His Holiness Swami Akhandanandaji said, how we can make everyone accustomed to take up good habits—sad-acara?, In this age, Kali-yuga, there are many faults.”

He went on to explain the power of Lord Chaitanya’s movement to clean the hearts of everyone and referred to the two great rogues whom Lord Chaitanya had delivered—Jagai and Madhai. “Now we are saving, wholesale, Jagais and Madhais. Therefore, if we want peace, if we want to be situated on the sad-acara platform, we must spread the hari-nama maha-mantra all over the world. And it has been practically proven. The American and European Vaishnavas who have come here, who have chanted Hare Krishna mantra, they were cow-flesh eaters, they were drunkards, they were illicit-sex mongers, they were all kinds of gamblers. But having taken to this Krishna consciousness movement, they have given up everything abominable. Sad-acara has come automatically. They are no more meat-eaters, they are no more gamblers, they are no more illicit-sex mongers, they are no more intoxicators. They do not even take tea, they do not even take coffee, they do not even smoke, which I think is very rare to be found in India. But they have given up. Why? Because they have taken to this Krishna consciousness.”

“I do not feel that I have to say very much,” he concluded. “You can see what is the result of Krishna consciousness. It is not something artificial. It is there in everyone. I have not done anything magical. But this Krishna consciousness is present in all of us. We simply have to revive it.”

The audience responded with cheers and applause. Prabhupada had shown the essence of spiritual life—ecstatic chanting of the holy names—and had presented us as living testimony. It was wonderful to feel of use to his mission.

The Times Weekly's coverage of the Bharat Sadhu Samaj highlighted Srila Prabhupada and his disciples’ participation: “A group of twenty Americans, members of the Hare Krishna delegation, took over the dais. The air was filled with the beating of mridangas, the clash of cymbals and the music of the maha-mantra. Swaying from side to side, their tufts of hair tossing in the breeze they chanted: Hare Krishna ...

“One greying reporter whom I had always regarded as a particularlyunsentimental person said to me in an emotion-choked voice: ‘Do you realize what is happening? Very soon Hinduism is going to sweep the West. The Hare Krishna movement will compensate for all our loss at the hands of padres through the centuries.’”

“Srila Prabhupada’s interplay with us at this time was truly wondrous,” Yamuna Devi recounted. “I can only describe him as being like a conductor with many devotee ‘instruments,’ watching each of us carefully and directing the rhythms and tenors of our individual services. He knew our strengths and weaknesses, tried to bring out the best in each of us, and protected us. We felt that we couldn’t have figured out anything regarding the day-to-day adjustments to being in India, without his constant guidance. He set the example of how to live and how to behave, and he allowed us access to him nearly twenty-four hours a day.

“Srila Prabhupada’s energy level at this time was also beyond description. Here he was in his seventies, while we were all in our twenties or less, and yet he worked circles around us. He was present, alert, and up each night until after midnight, translating. Then he had a full day of activities, including instructing us, writing and sending letters around the world, meetings with important men and aspiring devotees, doing preaching programs, and, of course, his daily personal sadhana. It was simply inconceivable, and yet he did this every day, regardless of where he was.

“I was only in Bombay for under two weeks, but those two weeks were two of the most powerful in my life because Srila Prabhupada allowed us to taste kirtan in Lord Chaitanya’s Bharata-varsa—Lord Krishna’s. The effect of the enthusiastic and powerful chanters of the sankirtana party was immediate and extraordinary. We were all like a tight family, with each person playing a specific role. Malati’s ‘Prabhupada’s World Sankirtan’ banner, along with one bearing the maha-mantra, announced, or introduced, us to the thousands who heard us in the streets. We were shoulder-to-shoulder, just like godbrothers and godsisters, with so much affection and respect for each other. We felt like Srila Prabhupada was our father and we were all his spiritual children, and there was such a nice mood. It was really burning hot for us in India, but we chanted until we almost couldn’t chant anymore. And then our host, Kailash Seksaria, would come with big urns of cold nimbu pani \[lime- or lemonade\] and we’d get rejuvenated.

“From the very beginning of our programs in Bombay, Srila Prabhupada became known as one ‘who is startling India with kirtan.’ Ourkirtans were full of so much excitement—they were so thrilling—that we were like one throbbing heartbeat, the heartbeat of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s mission of Krishna consciousness. It is difficult to describe how much potency we felt in the kirtans—not just in the chanting itself, but in how the chanting was being received by others. It was amazing how clearly we could see the chanting changing the hearts and psyches of so many people, and this spurred us on even more. Like a holistic circle—the dynamic circle of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s sankirtana movement—we took to heart the process our guru maharaja gave us, practiced it, gave it to others through hari-nama-sankirtana, and then saw it act on their hearts. It was truly a magical, wonderful thing, and I felt so privileged to be part of it.”

Practically from the time I had joined, our lives had revolved around sanklrtana—and at no time, nowhere, had that been more true than during that period in Bombay. Then suddenly one day Prabhupada told us, “No more street sankirtana. In India, if we chant on the streets, people will think that we are beggars.” We were shocked, stunned—and dismayed. We had been taught that this was the sankirtana movement.

“By 1970,” Tamal Krishna remembered, “active street sankirtana— chanting Hare Krishna on the streets and distributing Back to Godhead magazines—had been going on for a year or a year-and-a-half, and when we arrived in India that year we applied the same formula. We chanted Hare Krishna on the streets. But some people ridiculed us, and there were newspaper articles in the same mood. When Prabhupada heard this, and he heard that people were throwing coins at us, he told us to immediately stop doing daily street kirtan because people were taking it cheaply.... Prabhupada was willing to completely adjust the fundamental strategy of street chanting if it didn’t have the desired effect.”

Srila Prabhupada explained that we must approach the higher sections of society—with his books and especially through life membership. And he led the way, personally enrolling life members and presenting them his books, or arranging for us to do so, as he had on the terrace of Seksaria Bhavan. Whenever and wherever he had a program, he wanted his books displayed, and he would almost always speak about them or have one of us do so.

Prabhupada also spoke at Prem Kutir, which consisted of not only a hall for satsangas, religious meetings, but also guest facilities for sadhus. Prabhupada had stayed there before going to America. The facility wasrun by an industrialist, Hari Krishna Das Agarwal (I was thrilled that someone could have the name Hari Krishna Das), who greeted us warmly when we arrived and later gave us a tour of the premises, showing us where Prabhupada had translated Srimad-Bhagavatam, There was another sadhu already speaking on the platform, with a large build, long black hair, and a beard. He was sort of a devotee of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. He had huge kartals, which we call whompers, and he would chant, “Haribol! Haribol!” and clash the whompers together. His name was Vairagi Baba, and Prabhupada took a liking to him and tried to engage him.

After we had been in Bombay for ten days, Mr. Agarwal invited Prabhupada and his party to Amritsar for a Vedanta Sammelan conference, at which people would gather to hear sadhus speak on—or speculate about—Vedanta. Prabhupada accepted, and on October 20 he and a party of disciples—seven men and two women—were on a train headed north to Amritsar.

The Vedanta Ashram was dedicated to the propagation of impersonal Mayavada philosophy, and the buildings and walkways displayed signs with popular Mayavadi slogans such as tat tvam asi (“you are that”) and aham brahmasmi (“I am spirit”)- We were provided two small rooms and the use of the common courtyard. Prabhupada occupied one room and Yamuna and Kausalya the other, and the men slept either in the courtyard or in a large hall for sadhus.

We had programs in the evening, and every morning we would go into Prabhupada’s room and sing the Gurv-astaka prayers in front of his Radha-Krishna Deities, after which he would speak with us. One morning he explained the different Mayavadi slogans. The organizers knew that he did not agree with their philosophy, he told us, but they had invited him and his disciples because they had known that the “foreign” devotees’ kirtan would attract people.

“They will talk and talk about Vedanta,” he commented, “but it is simply mental speculation, and they never come to any conclusion.” Just then, one of the ladies removed the food offering she had made to Srila Prabhupada’s Deities and put the plate in front of him. He continued, “They will go on speculating for many lifetimes,”—he popped a maha sweet in his mouth—“but we will realize God simply by eating.”

In Amritsar, Gurudas was our main preacher. One evening, when, to refute the impersonal philosophy, he told the audience, “If it’s allone, then why don’t you give me your wife to enjoy?” Gurudas’s example offended the Indians’ sensibilities. So the organizers asked Prabhupada to assign another disciple to speak in the evenings, and Prabhupada chose me.

So, every evening I would speak, and one morning, when I happened to pass Prabhupada while he was getting his massage outside his quarters, he said, “I heard your talk last night. You spoke very nicely.” And from then on, while we were traveling, he would sometimes ask me to speak at public programs. Whenever he did, I would always pray that my words would be pleasing to him, because I knew that if he was pleased, Krishna would be pleased, and the audience would progress in Krishna consciousness. And I would pray to the Paramatma, the Lord within the hearts of all the people listening, to inspire them to receive my message—Srila Prabhupada and Lord Krishna’s message—favorably.

From Amritsar, we returned to Bombay by train. At the Delhi station, a lawyer named D.D. Gupta, who had been corresponding with Prabhupada and had been informed of his stopover, came to meet him. While they were speaking, Mr. Gupta requested Prabhupada to leave some disciples in Delhi to start our activities there. Prabhupada turned to Gurudas, who was riding in the same compartment, and said, “This man is inviting us. Get down and see what you can do.” Gurudas asked for some devotees, and he and Srila Prabhupada agreed on a team: Yamuna, Gopal, Bhakta Bruce (later Bhanu Swami), and me. And so the preaching in Delhi began.

From Bombay, Prabhupada wrote that he wanted us to meet “many government members and ministers and other important men”—and to get our picture taken with Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. He wanted to counteract the propaganda that we were CIA agents or otherwise disreputable and considered that a photo of us with her would show that we were all right. So, with the help of some influential friends we had made in Delhi, we met her and got our picture taken. In the photo, I held the large volume of the Krsna book we had brought to present to her, with the back cover facing the camera, so Srila Prabhupada was in the image, too.

Prabhupada also suggested that we meet some of his old friends in Delhi, most notably the pious industrialist and philanthropist Jaidayal Dalmia, who not only became our life member but also introduced us to many of his important friends, who also became life members and introduced us to other influential people.

Prabhupada also wrote Gurudas that “a big temple and compound belonging to the Maharaja of Bharatapur on the bank of the Yamuna at Kesighat is for sale. Therefore I would like you to go immediately...” Gurudas went, and when after several days we received no word from him, Yamuna and the rest of us followed, and thus I experienced Vrindavan for the first time. And as I later told Prabhupada, “I felt Krishna’s presence.”

After a month in Bombay, Prabhupada proceeded to Indore for the Gita Jayanti Mahotsava, the celebration of the date on which Lord Krishna spoke the Gita to Arjuna, and soon after his arrival, our group joined him there.

Prabhupada was staying in a house provided by the organizers. When we entered his darshan room, he looked up from his desk. “Srila Prabhupada,” Yamuna remarked, “you look just like a picture I have seen of your guru maharaja looking up from his desk.”

“All that glitters is not gold,” he replied. “My guru maharaja was like gold; I am like iron.” Of course, we knew that he was pure gold—just like his guru maharaja.

From Indore, Prabhupada and his party traveled to Surat, in Gujarat, where we received an extraordinary reception from the large population of Krishna devotees and were joined by John Griesser (who would later be initiated by Prabhupada and named Yadubara dasa), and, soon after, his wife, Jean (later initiated as Visakha dasi).

One afternoon, John came into Prabhupada’s room while Prabhupada was preaching, advising a local man that the government of India should form a Department of the Bhagavad-gita to present the message of the Gita—as it is—globally. After John had been sitting for some time, Prabhupada offered him some prasada. John refused to eat in Prabhupada’s presence, but Prabhupada insisted: “No, no. Take prasada. The spiritual master is pleased when the devotees take prasada.” And he quoted a verse from Sri Sri Gurv-astaka (4):

catur-vidha-sri-bhagavat-prasada-  
svadv-anna-trptan hari-bhakta-sanghan  
krtvaiva trptim bhajatah sadaiva  
vande guroh sri-caranaravindam

\[“The spiritual master is always offering Krsna four kinds of delicious food. When the spiritual master sees that the devotees are satisfied by eating bhagavat-prasada, he is satisfied. I offer my respectful obeisances unto the lotus feet of such a spiritual master.”\]

After Surat, Prabhupada visited Bombay for two or three days and met with the few devotees based there. We were all staying at the Sea Palace Hotel, a pure-vegetarian establishment that belonged to our friend Sri Ramchand Chhabria, who knew the devotees from England and was himself vegetarian. While we were there, a new issue of Back to Godhead arrived, and the first article was Srila Prabhupada’s poem "Markine Bhagavata-dharma” which he had written when he had initially come to America, in Boston. We had never seen the poem before; it had never been published. Gurudas, Yamuna, and I got together to look at the magazine, and Yamuna read the poem out loud. It was written in a mood of deep humility and dependence on Krishna. And when she got to the end—“Signed—the most unfortunate, insignificant beggar, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami”—she could no longer contain her emotions; she just burst into tears.

Prabhupada then proceeded to Allahabad for the Ardha-kumbha-mela, “half Kumbha-mela,” the world’s largest gathering of humanity, a spiritual festival attended by millions of pilgrims. After working with some of the senior devotees to arrange a meeting in Bombay to gain support for our activities and eventually start a center there, I joined him there. Our program at the mela was austere and rigorous—it was bitterly cold at night, and we were expected to get up at four in the morning to bathe and attend mangala-arati A few steadfast devotees, such as Tamal Krishna and Hamsaduta, got up early, by three or three-thirty, and walked all the way from our camp to the Ganges to take an early-morning bath. But those of us in the men’s tent were not as staunch, and generally when it was time to get up at four, it was so cold out that we preferred to stay in our sleeping bags.

Prabhupada knew how important mangala-arati and the rest of the morning temple program was for us, and when he noticed that some of us were coming to mangala-arati late and some were not coming at all, he became very upset. So, one morning, even though he was somewhat frail in health, he got up at four o’clock and came out in his gamcha, a thin cotton towel wrapped around his waist, sat down under the hand pump, and took an ice-cold bath—just to encourage us to get up, bathe, and go to mangala-arati. His action had a profound effect on all of us, and we felt so ashamed that from that morning on, we just couldn’t sleep late anymore.

Still, it was freezing out, and most of us continued to struggle with rising early, taking bath with the cold water from the pumps, and reaching the pandal in time for mangala-arati. Our pujari, Nanda Kumar, struggled along with the rest of us. He wore gloves to keep his hands from going numb, but one morning, no matter how hard he tried, he just could not light the ghee lamp to offer to the Deities. Cold gusts kept blowing out the matches before they reached the wicks, and when a lit match did manage to reach them, the wind would blow out either the match or some of the flames before all the wicks were lit. Nanda Kumar tried again and again to shield the matches and wicks with one hand while lighting them with the other, but he just couldn’t manage to do it.

Watching the futile exercise, Prabhupada urged Nanda Kumar to execute the task. One or two other devotees came forward to help, but they too were unsuccessful. Finally, in a mood of resignation born of frustration, but with profound spiritual realization, Prabhupada uttered,

harer nama harer nama  
harer namaiva kevalam  
kalau nasty eva nasty eva  
nasty eva gatir anyatha

\[“In this Age of Kali there is no other means, no other means, no other means for self-realization than chanting the holy name, chanting the holy name, chanting the holy name of Lord Hari.” (Brhan-naradiya Purdna 38.126)\]

We all knew how seriously Prabhupada took Deity worship. He understood that the Deity was Krishna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Himself. And he was strict that his followers maintain the proper standard of worship as defined for us by guru and shastra. Still, in Kali-yuga, ultimately, harer namaiva kevalam.

In Indore, reading from his volume with Sanskrit commentaries, Prabhupada had begun speaking on the history of Ajamila, glorifying the holy name. Later, when his translation of the Sixth Canto of Srimad-Bhagavatam was published, we found the same conclusions that he had presented to us then:

“Especially in this age of Kali, sankirtana alone is sufficient. If the members of our temples in the different parts of the world simply continue sankirtana before the Deity, especially before Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu, they will remain perfect. There is no need of any other performances. Nevertheless, to keep oneself clean in habits and mind, Deity worship and other regulative principles are required. Srila Jiva Gosvami says that although sankirtana is sufficient for the perfection of life, the arcana, or worship of the Deity in the temple, must continue in order that the devotees may stay clean and pure. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura therefore recommended that one follow both processes simultaneously. We strictly follow his principle of performing Deity worship and sankirtana along parallel lines. This we should continue.” (SB 6.3.25 purport)

From the Ardha-kumbha-mela, we traveled with Prabhupada to Gorakhpur. There, for the first time, I took the opportunity to go to newspapers and magazines to persuade them to publish articles—about Prabhupada’s visit and about Krishna consciousness in general. Enlivened in my service, I mentioned my efforts to Prabhupada on a morning walk. “You are a very good public-relations man,” he responded, which made me feel elated.

After a while, the discussion turned to humility, and I remarked that sometimes I felt that I wasn’t really doing anything for Krishna or Krishna consciousness. “That is good,” Prabhupada responded. “That feeling is humbleness.”

“But sometimes that feeling is turned into maya,” I added, meaning that sometimes I felt discouraged about myself and lost my enthusiasm to preach.

Prabhupada stopped walking and looked me straight in the eyes. “Turned into maya?” he asked. “You are always in maya.”

His words hit me hard. As he and the other devotees continued their walk, I placed my forehead on the ground in obeisance. By Srila Prabhupada’s mercy, I understood my actual position—and had gained a glimpse of his position as my spiritual master. He not only spoke about the importance of humility; he also knew how to humble us—all for our benefit.

In Gorakhpur, Prabhupada instructed me to write as my “first business.” “See that my books are accepted in the universities by the scholarly class,” he also told me. Then he asked, “Do you ever think of getting married?”

“No,” I replied, but after a moment I added, “The only time I ever thought of getting married was when I saw that all the GBCs were married.”

“You will never be GBC,” Prabhupada said. “It is best to avoid marriage. Sex desire is like an itch. If you have an itch and you scratch it, it just becomes worse. Similarly, sex desire is there, and if you try to satisfy it, it becomes worse. So it is better to tolerate. Not only sex desire—all the demands of the senses—eating and sleeping also. Better to tolerate.

“So, you remain brahmachari, and after two or three years I will give you sannyasa.”

In a matter of twenty minutes Srila Prabhupada had given me my whole life’s program in Krishna consciousness.

From Gorakhpur, a small sankirtana party led by Hamsaduta went by train to Agra and Aligarh, where we received a telegram from Prabhupada calling us to Bombay for a big pandal program.

In Bombay everyone knew about the program, scheduled over eleven days, March 25-April 4, entitled “Bhagavata Dharma Discourses: A Hare Krishna Festival,” featuring “World Preacher of Bhakti Cult, His Divine Grace A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami,” to be held at Cross Maidan, downtown. As a climax to the publicity, Shyamasundar had fixed a giant balloon to the site, announcing from high over the city, “Hare Krishna Festival—Cross Maidan.”

Twenty thousand people attended daily—thirty thousand on weekends. Prabhupada spoke strongly, and people responded favorably. One evening he performed initiations and the wedding of Vegavan dasa,from Sweden, and Padmavati dasi, from Australia, with a full Vedic fire ceremony. “This is the real United Nations,” he declared, and the entire audience—twenty thousand people—clapped and cheered.

Madhudvisa was in charge of the stage program; Tamal Krishna was the general manager, and he made me the pandal temple commander, putting all the responsibility and work on my shoulders. So I was at the pandal all afternoon while the other devotees were back at our rented premises—a temple and ashram—in the Akash Ganga high-rise with Srila Prabhupada. Nobody stayed to help, and I didn’t know what to do.

Prabhupada would come late in the day and, before going on the stage for the program, sit behind it in one of several rooms formed with cloth attached to bamboo poles. One afternoon when he came, the room was a mess—the rented sofas were out of place; used, dirty cups were left around; and the tables had not been dusted or washed.

As I was practically the only devotee there, Prabhupada asked me, “What is this? Why is everything so dirty?”

“I don’t have anyone to help me,” I replied. “I have to do everything myself.”

Prabhupada looked at me and said gently but firmly, “It is better to control five asses than to work like an ass yourself.”

In addition to my other, general duties, I was responsible for the book table: actually several long wooden tables placed together in a line. I knew from distributing magazines in Boston that the crucial point was to put the literature in the hands of the potential customers. They would hold it and page through it, glancing at the pictures and text, and become attached to it—and then I would ask for a donation. I tried the same approach at the pandal, but I was dismayed to find that people would simply walk away with the magazine without paying anything. I explained the situation to our advisor, Sadajiwatlal, and he told me, “Oh, you can’t do that here.”

“Then what do we do?” I asked.

“You have to poke a hole through the corner of the magazine and thread a string through it and tie the string to the legs of the tables,” he said. “Then people can hold the magazine but won’t be able to walk off with it.”

It seemed like a good solution, so I decided to try it. There was a young American man with matted hair, wearing faded white cloth, whom I had noticed around the pandal, and when I asked him if he would like to do some service, he agreed and took up the job of poking holes in the magazines and attaching them to the tables. At the start of the evening program, I suggested to him, “Why don’t you sit in the audience and hear the lecture.” And when Prabhupada spotted the boy at the back of the crowd, he had Gurudas bring him onto the stage.

“Every now and then Prabhupada would look at me,” the young man remembered, “and something that had never happened took place in my heart. I was thinking, This is my eternal father and spiritual master. But my mind rejected it: You should not accept just one man; you should learn from everyone. And my heart was saying, No, no, this is your guru. Cant you see? You should surrender. And while I was going through this intense inner conflict, during his lecture, Prabhupada looked right at me. He stopped speaking for a few seconds and looked into my eyes—so serious—and I could actually hear his eyes speaking: ‘Give up your nonsense and surrender.’ After the lecture, as Prabhupada was leaving the stage, he affectionately rubbed my head and smiled and said, ‘You come up and sit with us every night, and every morning too.’ So, I did that.” And almost exactly two years later, the young man accepted Prabhupada as his spiritual master and was initiated by him as Radhanath dasa, later to become Radhanath Swami.

On the last day of the program, Prabhupada spoke about devotees and the movement and invited his audience to join.

“Ladies and gentlemen,” he began, “I thank you very much for kindly participating in today’s meeting. We are known practically all over the world as the Hare Krishna people. Wherever we go, they immediately recognize us as the Hare Krishna people. So, I’ll try to speak something about the Hare Krishna people.

“I started this movement in New York. I went there in 1965, and for one year I had no shelter, nor any means to maintain myself. I had some books only—Srimad-Bhagavatam—and some way or other, I pulled on.

“In 1966 I started this movement after incorporation in New York under the state religious act, and I began to chant the Hare Krishnamantra in a park in New York—Tompkins Square. And these young boys and girls began to assemble and chant and dance. This was the beginning.

“And when one well-known poet . . . Perhaps you know him— Mr. Allen Ginsberg—he was also coming and joined with us. In this way, first of all we started our center in New York, Second Avenue, and then gradually expanded to San Francisco, Montreal, Boston, Buffalo, and Los Angeles. Now we have got fifty-two branches all over the world, including one in Tokyo, one in Hong Kong, one in Sydney, Australia.

“Now, try to understand what is this Hare Krishna movement. This Hare Krishna movement was started recently, about five hundred years ago, by Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. He appeared in Bengal, in the district of Nadia, about sixty miles north of Calcutta, and He started this movement.

“Of course, it is not to be understood that Chaitanya Mahaprabhu started something new. No. It is the oldest, in the sense that five thousand years ago Lord Krishna spoke about this Krishna consciousness movement in the Bhagavad-gita. And if we go further, then from the statement of Bhagavad-gita we understand it was started about forty million years ago.”

Prabhupada spoke at length about the science of Krishna consciousness. Then he concluded, “Now, what is this Krishna consciousness movement? The Krishna consciousness movement means the essence of all religious principles. What is religious principle? Religious principle means to abide by the laws given by God. That is called religious principle, simple word. Dharmam tu saksad bhagavat-pranitam: ‘Dharma means the codes and the laws given by God? That is dharma, or religion.

“This is a long subject matter. It is not possible to explain everything that is the Krishna consciousness movement. But the actual fact is, this Krishna consciousness movement means to bring one to his original consciousness. That is the sum and substance. That original consciousness can be achieved by a simple method. What is that? Chanting this Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare/ Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. It is a fact.

“Just like we have got so many European and American boys and girls. How have they come to this platform? How have they given uptheir old habits? Naturally, these boys and girls were taught from the beginning of their life so many things which are not accepted in Vedic civilization, but they have now given them up. There is no illicit sex life amongst our students. There is no meat-eating, there is no intoxication, including coffee and tea and cigarettes, and there is no gambling. And they are practiced to chanting Hare Krishna mantra, as you have seen some of the samples. We have got fifty-two branches. In every branch we have got not less than twenty-five devotees, up to a hundred.

“So, this is the brahma-bhutah stage. It is not story; it is fact. How it is attained? It is attained by Krishna consciousness.

“This Krishna consciousness movement is neither a new movement nor is it a concocted philosophy. It is based on authorities such as Bhagavad-gita and other Vedic literature. And practically you see how it is effective. Simply by chanting this Hare Krishna mantra, these boys and girls have become elevated. And they have taken the matter very seriously. They are preaching this cult all over the world.

“Our request to everyone is—whatever you are doing, it doesn’t matter—please take to this chanting of Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare/ Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. That is our only request. You will not lose anything, but you will gain very much, simply by chanting. It will cleanse your heart....

“I do not wish to take much of your time. This Hare Krishna movement is very nice—authorized, spiritual, simple, and sublime, all at a time. If you kindly take this, you will be benefited and your life will be successful. Thank you very much.”

After the pandal program, Prabhupada revealed his desire to establish a permanent center in Bombay for training and the distribution of books and prasada. He wrote an open letter to our supporters:

“My plan is to establish in this most auspicious city a unique International Krishna Conscious Training Center, where hundreds of persons from abroad may be educated in the Vedic way of life, while at the same time Indian boys and girls may be trained up for pracara \[preaching\] work in foreign countries. We will construct classrooms, workrooms, dormitories, a kitchen for large-scale public prasada distribution, a lecture hall, a library, and a beautiful temple for the glorification of Radha and Krishna.

“We are on the threshold of bringing this important project to fruition, and we are very excited to inform you about the progress made in this respect....

“Your active participation and your direct involvement in this is most essential, and hence I appeal to you to spare your valuable time for Krishna and make it a point, in spite of your extremely busy life, to extend your unstinted cooperation. It is proposed to hold a meeting ... to discuss and to finalize plans to channel our united energies to achieve the goal. It will also be a great opportunity for like-minded Krishna devotees to meet, to have darshan of the Deities, and to exchange views and suggestions to make rapid progress in spiritual life. I very much want to meet you again.”
