Building on the success of the Bombay pandal, Prabhupada sent Tamal Krishna and me to arrange a similar program in Calcutta, and a few days later the two of us embarked on the long train ride.

Our temple in Calcutta was in a large rented house in an aristocratic area in the south-central part of the city, near Camac Street, overlooking a square manmade pond surrounded by a park. One night, after the other devotees had gone to sleep, Tamal Krishna and I were still awake, talking on the balcony. Srila Prabhupada had a few disciples, including himself, Tamal Krishna said, with whom he was especially close and in whom he confided. This was a revelation to me. I had never before distinguished among the senior devotees; I saw them all as my superiors, as devotees whom Prabhupada loved, and I did not make any further distinctions.

Tamal Krishna glorified Shyamasundar, saying that he was one of the biggest preachers in the movement.

“What do you mean ‘one of the biggest preachers’?” I asked. “I don’t think I have ever heard him give class.”

“Preaching doesn’t just mean speaking about Krishna,” he replied. “Preaching ultimately means engaging people in Krishna’s service.” Shyamasundar was the one who had conceived of the Bombay pandal and organized us all in its execution. He had been instrumental in developing the life-membership program and had designed themembership form and written a brilliant appeal, the best I’d ever seen. But the whole time I was working with him, I had never seen him give a class or address the public.

Tamal Krishna explained that through activities such as developing the life-membership program and staging the first pandal, and through so many other efforts, Shyamasundar had engaged thousands of people in Krishna consciousness—and that those too were preaching. This was, for me, an important instruction.

Then, returning to his relationship with Srila Prabhupada, Tamal Krishna told me about an incident in 1970 when Prabhupada had felt that some of his disciples were trying to wrest control of the movement from him, and how Prabhupada had called him to Los Angeles and confided in him. Some of the temple leaders were preoccupied with collecting money and were engaging devotees to collect even when it was at the expense of their other devotional practices. And the spiritual lives of the devotees were being hampered. When Prabhupada had become aware of what was happening, he had discussed with Tamal what to do. And they had arrived at ways to reform the situation. For the first time, I understood how much Prabhupada valued him as a confidant and trusted him to help make decisions.

“The essence of spiritual life,” Tamal Krishna told me, “is service to the spiritual master.”

That point really impressed me and entered deep. We chanted the holy names, read the scriptures, worshipped the Deities, and rendered service—that much I knew. But the essence of spiritual life being service to the spiritual master? I had never thought of that. The process of bhakti-yoga was all there, and I knew we had to follow all of it, but I did not see how the different practices related to each other. And Tamal Krishna’s realization, which I accepted, was that service to the spiritual master was the essence.

From then on, my approach to devotional service—even chanting— changed. I still liked to chant, but I began to chant more in the mood of service to Srila Prabhupada. Sometimes when we were in Calcutta, Tamal Krishna would get annoyed because I wouldn’t want to go out for preaching until I had finished at least twelve rounds. “Oh, you just wantto avoid work,” he would say. “That’s why you are standing in front of the Deities and chanting.” Still, he let me. Sometimes he would get more annoyed than other times, but he let me, because I needed that.

But now my mood was a little different. Yes, I was chanting, but now I was also thinking, I need to chant to do my duties for Srila Prabhupada. If I chant, my consciousness will be purified. Krishna will guide me what to do. And I will be better prepared to deal with people. I will be able to preach more effectively if I chant and purify my consciousness.

After the Calcutta pandal, devotees from throughout India gathered in New Delhi for the first pandal program there, a big ten-day festival in November at the prominent and prestigious LIC grounds near Connaught Place, downtown. As in Bombay and Calcutta, tens of thousands of people came daily, and as a new, special feature, every evening a distinguished person was invited as chief guest and spoke before Prabhupada, and in his talk Prabhupada would often directly or indirectly address statements the person had made. Among the guest speakers were Hanraj Gupta, the mayor; Harivansh Rai Bacchan, a respected Hindi poet; Shyam Charan Gupta, the chairman of the Delhi Metropolitan Council; С. B. Agarwal, a famous orator; Bipin Chandra Misra, a judge of the Delhi High Court; Dr. Atma Ram, a renowned scientist; Colonel B.R. Mohan and L.N. Sakalani, prominent industrialists; Aditya Nath Jha, the lieutenant governor; Jagjivan Ram, the Indian defense minister; and James George, the Canadian high commissioner. It was quite an illustrious group.

Many political leaders came forward to help and support us, and they were visible at the pandal and often made announcements from the stage. As one devotee pointed out to Prabhupada, the politicians were not selfless in their service—they were hoping to get votes from the pious Hindus in attendance. But Prabhupada was not fazed. “If they take advantage of us and we don’t lose,” he said, “then we don’t mind. We are not envious.”

The Deities at the pandal were the white-marble Sri Sri Radha-Gokulananda, who were later sent to Bhaktivedanta Manor, outside London. With help from experts in Vrindavan, Yamuna made the most spectacular outfits, and all the guests—and devotees—were thrilled by the new standard of worship she set. The first night’s outfit was dazzling, with shiny gold sequins on opulent white cloth, and Prabhupada’s oldfriend Jaidayal Dalmia, one of India’s leading industrialists and philanthropists, came onto the stage at a quiet time and just knelt before the Deities, gazing upon Their divine beauty.

From Delhi, Prabhupada planned to proceed to Vrindavan, and all the devotees were excited about accompanying him. But he had also received an invitation to visit Madras, and he wanted some disciples to go there in his stead. Although none of us could imagine missing being in Vrindavan with Prabhupada, Achyutananda, Bhavananda, and I volunteered to go to Madras, accompanied by a new Indian brahmachari.

In Madras the three of us got to speaking about how things were going in India and how they could be organized in a better way, and somehow, although I did not have as much regular interaction with Prabhupada as the others, they wanted me to write him the letter.

“Achyutananda Maharaja, Bhavananda Prabhu, and myself have met and collectively decided upon a plan,” I wrote, “based on our limited and imperfect senses and limited knowledge of what has happened in India since we left Delhi, and we humbly put forth those ideas for Your Divine Grace. ... I know that I am a great fool and that the errors of judgment, perception, and logic in this letter are very great. But somehow or other things must go on, and I shall take it as a blessing if you reply to me with your desires, which are coming from the perfect platform, free from illusion, mistakes, and cheating, unlike mine, so I can immediately try to execute that divine will. Still, I felt it my duty to offer these ideas on behalf of my godbrothers, in the hopes that some lasting solution can be made for the problems in India.”

Although in retrospect many of our ideas may have been impractical or inappropriate, Prabhupada praised our efforts. “I am very encouraged by your thoughtful plan to organize very nicely all our men in India,” he replied from Bombay. “I can understand that you are very eligible to be among the biggest leaders, so I have all confidence in your Madras programs. There appears to be some feeling of dissatisfaction with the way things are being managed in India, so I have simply said that if you all get me at least two life members daily in India, then I shall do the rest. So, I am pleased to hear from you that you are making many life members there—that is the proof of our preaching strength. Wherever there is preaching strength, there is also success, no matter it may be pandal show or making members or traveling sankirtana party or whatever itmay be—just maintain our strong position of purity of routine work and preach and distribute literature, that’s all.

“So far as our program for India, at present we are trying seriously for a nice house in the aristocratic section of Bombay . . . Otherwise, when funds are there we shall construct very nice centers in Vrindavan and Mayapur, that’s all. Let many foreign students and disciples come to India for staying with us in these places. We shall be content to sit down there, chant, and have kirtan very vigorously twenty-four hours, and if anyone calls us we shall go for a few days and have a program. Our real interest is in the Western countries. The trouble in India is we cannot preach. There are language difficulties, and the people think they already know everything. But now many foreign tourists are interested to come here to taste the spiritual life, so we shall concentrate on that field. Recently we have received one letter from Cox & Kings, one of the world’s biggest travel agencies, requesting us to kindly assist them by providing facilities for all the tourists coming from foreign places who are interested in seeing the real spiritual life of India. So in this way we shall work here.”

In the same letter, Prabhupada informed us of his plan for the first international Mayapur festival and emphasized the distribution of his books: “After the Madras program, we shall all go to Mayapur. I think that Bhavananda and Nara Narayan are organizing a very nice festival there....

“I am most pleased especially to hear that you are distributing many books. Go on increasing books, and go on increasing my pleasure. You are doing very, very nicely in Madras, and except for you I think there is hardly any devotee so hardworking and with such good ability to persuade men to help us.”

And so, from Madras I proceeded to Calcutta and Mayapur for the first Gaura-purnima festival and the cornerstone-laying ceremony for the Mayapur temple.

Mayapur then was mainly rice paddies, with a few temples along the single-lane main road. Prabhupada was living in a simple straw hut near the main entrance to our property, and beyond that stood a pandal, where the festival and ceremonies would take place.

Prabhupada’s room had a cement floor covered with straw mats. When I entered, he was clearly in a grave mood. In a choked voice, with tears in his eyes, he said, “Krishna is giving us everything now. Everything is the mercy of Krishna.”

He called me to his room again later that day. After offering my obeisances, I sat at his feet, and he explained that when the British were ruling India, they divided the country into three provinces—Bombay, Madras, and Calcutta—each ruled by one governor. Prabhupada had never spoken to me about Indian politics or history, and I did not know where this was all going, but I was fascinated—spellbound—and hung on every word, waiting to find out where he was heading.

“Which one do you want?”

Prabhupada’s question left me speechless. I had never made an independent decision about my service. I told him that I would do whatever he wanted. But he did not accept my answer; he wanted me to decide. So I asked if I could have time to think about it, and he agreed.

I thought and thought, but I just couldn’t decide. The preaching in Calcutta was good, but Madras also had potential. And I already knew people in both places. Then again, Bombay was the biggest field. Actually, all I really wanted was to please Srila Prabhupada. But how?

After a few days, Prabhupada drove from Mayapur to the Calcutta temple, and the rest of us followed by bus and train. Once there, I felt that my main service, my assignment, was to determine where I should serve. Whenever I could, I would stand before the beautiful Deities of Sri Sri Radha-Govinda and chant and pray to Them for guidance.

I soon realized that Prabhupada was forcing me to come to a higher level of Krishna consciousness. As he sometimes explained, there are three classes of disciples. The third-class receives an instruction from the spiritual master and then forgets it, or neglects to act upon it—or argues. The second-class disciple receives an instruction from the spiritual master and executes it perfectly. And the first-class disciple knows what the spiritual master wants and does it even without being told. To obey the order of the spiritual master requires some basic submission, but to know the desire of the spiritual master without being told requires much more spiritual advancement. I was being compelled to become sincere enough and pure enough to hear the guru in the heart.

But although I thought and thought and prayed and prayed, no answer came. Where did Prabhupada want me to serve?

Not knowing what else to do, I devised a plan to get Prabhupada to reveal his desire. So, one day, sitting before him in his room, I ventured that I had decided to go to Bombay.

Prabhupada’s response was noncommittal: “That’s all right.” His face was inscrutable.

“But then again, the preaching potential in Madras is very good,” I continued, hoping that either by word or gesture or facial expression he would indicate his approval or disapproval.

Once more, he simply replied, “That’s all right.”

“But then again,” I said, “I was thinking of staying in Calcutta.”

“That’s all right.”

How could I try to trick Srila Prabhupada? I felt so ashamed, trying to cheat my spiritual master. But I also felt exhilarated: my spiritual master was so great and perfect that he could not be fooled.

When, after five days in Calcutta, Prabhupada left for Vrindavan and Bombay, I continued to ponder my situation. If I go back to Madras, I considered, I can preach on my own, but if I stay in Calcutta, I can help teach others to preach also. That was better. So I crossed Madras off the list.

Finally, after many days of thought and prayer, the answer came: I should go to Bombay. The most important program in India was life membership. Srila Prabhupada had written, “If you all get me at least two life members daily, I shall do the rest.” And he was pleased that I was making so many life members. But many members were up in arms against us because we had not given them everything we had promised.

We were making life members, I reasoned, but were we taking care of them? If we took nice care of them, they would be so pleased that they themselves would make more members. But if we neglected them, they would feel cheated and speak ill of us. Then, even when we ourselves approached people, they would not agree.

I felt that I should go to Bombay and organize the life-membership program on an all-India basis. I wrote Prabhupada my conclusion: since Bombay had the most life members and was our head office, I should come and, if required, take care of the life members and attend to other affairs related to the head office.

Prabhupada seemed pleased. “I am very glad to inform you that today we have laid down the cornerstone for our Bombay center here in Juhu,” he replied, “and the ceremony was very wonderful, with many important people attending. I am very much glad that you are doing so nicely in Calcutta by making many life members daily, so now I think you should join me in Bombay immediately as soon as you are free, after training up a competent replacement there. We have also a few days back laid the cornerstone for our Vrindavan temple, and they have given me many more rooms at Radha-Damodar Temple for our use. The program now in India is an immense task, so I am very much encouraged that you feel yourself enthusiastic to help me in this way, by taking a bold lead for pushing on this movement here.

“Now Brahmananda is in charge here, and there is a huge land and we are occupying it in tents and small cottages like the Mayapur cottage, and the work is immense. Gargamuni is collecting also not less than two life members daily, but his collection goes toward our Vrindavan construction work. Things are not going very nicely in Nairobi, because Brahmananda has left, so I shall have to send him back there tomorrow. Therefore I wanted that you should come here to assist Madhudvisa by collecting profusely, and I think there will be no difficulty here because there is such rich population. Madhavananda \[whom I had been training\] can go from Mayapur to Calcutta to help Bhavananda collect there, and you shall come here at the earliest possible ... at the latest by the 27th March 1972."

Bhavananda arranged for my ticket, and within a couple of days I reached Bombay.

I rode from the train station with eager anticipation, but the suburb of Juhu seemed far away. As we got closer, the area struck me as remote—covered with trees and poorly lit. But when I saw posters stuck on tree trunks and lampposts advertising our Hare Krishna Festival and Prabhupada’s talks, my heart leaped. And when I saw signs with arrows pointing the way to the site, my excitement increased. But the long lonely lanes in Juhu seemed to never end, and I wondered when we would ever get there.

Suddenly, we came to a green, lush expanse of land dotted with coconut palms and other trees. Toward the front of the property was alarge, festive pandal decorated with blue-and-white trim, with a stage holding a set of Deities facing away from the street. And in the back, beyond the open land, was a cluster of two-story apartment buildings.

As much as I was looking forward to meeting all the devotees and getting settled, I wanted to see Srila Prabhupada as soon as possible. I was told that he was staying with Mr. Padmanabha Acharya on the ground floor of one of the buildings at the back of the property. The devotees were living in tents, and I put my trunk and other things into one and went to see my spiritual master.

When Prabhupada saw me, he opened his eyes wide, smiled broadly, and set everything else aside. He was excited about the whole Juhu project and, wanting me to see the property, stood up and personally escorted me around, walking next to me but leading the way. He pointed out all the coconut palms—there were one hundred forty of them—and told me how desirable the location was, being so close to Juhu Beach.

Even after seeing everything, however, I still couldn’t quite visualize what the place would become. But Prabhupada said, “One day this property—this land with the buildings—will be worth a crore of rupees.” In those days, one crore (ten million) rupees was unimaginable for us; all we had in the bank were a few thousand—at most two or three lakhs (hundred thousand)—and that was the result of one and a half years of work.

Returning from a walk with Prabhupada and a small group of devotees one morning, Madhudvisa pointed to the property and exclaimed, “Oh, Srila Prabhupada! They have Disneyland, so we should call this Hare Krishna Land!” And that’s how the Juhu property got its name: Hare Krishna Land. Like the famous American theme park, we too had a major center of attraction, but instead of the central figure being a cartoon character, it would be Krishna—the chanting of Hare Krishna.

Prabhupada had asked me to come to assist Madhudvisa, but when I arrived I heard that Madhudvisa was not doing well; he was sleeping late, going to the beach, and generally not performing his duties as temple president. Finally, Prabhupada concluded that Australia would be a good field for him; he would have more opportunity to perform sanklrtana there, and, Prabhupada expected, he would regain his enthusiasm.

With Brahmananda soon returning to Africa and Madhudvisa proceeding to Australia, Prabhupada had to find someone to fill the position. He called a meeting with his senior disciples. I was present, but more, I thought, as an observer. I was not among the most senior or important devotees, and I had never had a say in such matters.

To begin, Prabhupada raised the question: “So, who will take charge?”

No one said a word. The atmosphere was charged with anxious uncertainty.

From behind his low table, Prabhupada looked up at the group and then directly at me. “So, Giriraj,” he said, “you will take charge?”

I was stunned, silent; I didn’t know what to say. This was not at all what I had been expecting; in fact, it was the last thing I could have imagined. I had come to Bombay to preach and develop the life-membership program and had neither the inclination nor any special ability to manage. This project was on a whole other level, and the responsibility seemed too much for me.

Still, I knew that obeying and pleasing the spiritual master was the secret of success in Krishna consciousness. So somehow I managed to stammer, “Well, Srila Prabhupada, if you want me to, I will.” I didn’t feel comfortable with the idea, but I couldn’t refuse Prabhupada.

“Yes!” he exclaimed with a bright smile.

A day or two later, I went into Prabhupada’s room and sat down in front of his desk. “So now, Giriraj,” he began, “the whole responsibility is on you.” I winced, and he chuckled.

I couldn’t understand why Prabhupada was laughing. Didn’t he know how I felt? He seemed to be rubbing it in.

I rarely had such thoughts about the spiritual master. Why am I thinking like this? I asked myself. But I was also wondering, How could Prabhupada be so insensitive? I am reluctant to take this responsibility, and he is rubbing it in by saying, “Now it's all on you”—and on top of that, he is laughing.

At the same time, I understood that the spiritual master could discern what was best for his disciple, and based on all my experience with Prabhupada, I knew that he must have foreseen that my taking responsibility for the project would be good for me, even though that was hard for me to imagine.

I just had to surrender. I had heard that whenever the spiritual master gave an order, he also gave the potency to execute it. And I knew that for the project to be successful, Prabhupada would have to empower me to act on his behalf.

Every evening, we performed an arati for our Radha-Krishna Deities on the stage of the pandal. Attracted by the dancing lights and the kirtan booming from the speakers, people would come from throughout the surrounding areas and park their cars around our property and alongside the road, and Prabhupada would speak to an assembly of about five hundred.

On Prabhupada’s last night at the pandal, he spoke about the Six Gosvamis and their feelings of separation from Krishna. I could tell that he was addressing the devotees and that the visitors would not be able to understand, but he had spoken to them for half an hour, and now he was speaking to us. He quoted the last verse of Sad-gosvamy-astaka:

he radhe vraja-devike ca lalite he nanda-suno kutah  
sri-govardhana-kalpa-padapa-tale kalindi-vane kutah  
ghosantav iti sarvato vraja-pure khedair maha-vihvalau  
vande rupa-sanatanau raghu-yugau sri jiva-gopalakau

The Gosvamis “were chanting very loudly everywhere in Vrindavan, shouting, ‘Queen of Vrndavana, Radharani! О Lalita! О son of Nanda Maharaja! Where are you all now? Are you just on the hill of Govardhana, or are you under the trees on the bank of the Yamuna? Where are you?’ These were their moods in executing Krsna consciousness.” (Sad-gosvamy-astaka 8)

As Prabhupada spoke, I began to see what he was doing. He would soon be leaving Bombay, and, knowing that we would be feeling separation from him, he was preparing us to enter the mood of service in that state. Powerless to stop myself, I began to cry.

From Bombay, Srila Prabhupada was going to Australia. Before leaving for the airport, he paid his obeisances to Sri Sri Radha and Krishna and stood before Them for some time. Then he walked out to the car, and I opened the door for him.

I got into the back seat next to Prabhupada, and devotees crammed into the front seat with the driver. The rest of the devotees rushed to catch rides with life members, who followed behind.

At the airport Prabhupada was given a VIP room, and we all crowded at his feet, eager for a last darshan before he departed. Accompanied by the ringing of kartals and rhythmic thumping of mridangas, Madhudvisa led an ecstatic kirtan, and the rest of us rose, held our arms in the air, and danced with abandon, jumping wildly up and down. The outside world ceased to exist.

“If you go on having kirtans like this,” Prabhupada said when we ended, “our Bombay project will be a success.”

Mrs. Nair, a middle-aged Maharashtrian lady in whose name the land in Juhu stood and who had attended the pandal program every night, was there to see Prabhupada off. “Oh, Mrs. Nair, you are also here,” he said when he saw her. “You are becoming one of us.” The devotees all smiled at her, appreciating that Prabhupada was drawing her toward Krishna consciousness.

When the time came to board the plane, Prabhupada stood up and distributed the garlands hanging around his neck. We offered our obeisances at his lotus feet, and with passport, boarding pass, and immigration form in one hand and his white plastic case in the other, he walked toward the passport-control booth. We followed him as far as we could and then watched his saffron-clad golden form disappear from sight. We again offered our obeisances, then stood, paralyzed, as if the world had come to an end, until we could pull ourselves together and walk away.

How, I wondered, would we manage in Juhu without Srila Prabhupada there with us? His words—“If you go on having kirtans like this, our Bombay project will be a success”—were encouraging, and I knew he would be present by his spiritual potency and instructions, but we had also depended on his personal presence. The gravity of the situation and the weight of the responsibility felt overwhelming.

Back in Juhu, I offered my obeisances in front of the Deities. More than ever, I felt dependent on Their mercy. Not knowing what to donext, I sat down before Them and prayed for guidance—for the ability to help fulfill Srila Prabhupada’s vision of a beautiful marble temple for Them and a Krishna conscious training center for devotees and others. Reflecting on how enthusiastic Prabhupada was about the Bombay project, I took heart. Even though we were neither experienced nor qualified, his pure desire would surely prevail.

I was also heartened by what I learned about Srila Prabhupada’s history with the Juhu land: When Prabhupada had first seen it, in 1965, before going to America, he had thought, This would be a nice place to have a temple. And then, six years later, having returned to India with thirty or forty of his disciples, he had been offered the same land. He had been staying in Bombay, in Akash Ganga, an upscale apartment building near the sea which had been serving as our temple. It had been close to most of our supporters’ offices and residences, and the devotees had been making life members one after another. They’d had only one telephone—all that was allowed for a private residence—and Gargamuni, Guru Kripa, Madhudvisa, Mahamsa, and Tusta Krishna would sit in a circle on the floor, with the phone in the middle, and take turns making calls. When one of them put the phone down, another would pick it up, and then the next. That had gone on for hours every morning—just making appointments to meet people. And in the course of meeting people, Tusta Krishna had encountered Mr. A. B. Nair—the former sheriff of Bombay and editor of the Free Press Journal, one of the city’s three English dailies—and, after speaking with him and visiting him in his office, had brought him to Akash Ganga to meet Srila Prabhupada.

One of the first things Mr. Nair had said to Prabhupada at their initial meeting was, “I have a nice piece of land in Juhu that you might be interested in.” Yadubara had noticed that he’d been nervous—sweating and practically shaking.

“You would think that Mr. Nair would have checked Prabhupada out,” Yadubara later commented, “checked out the person that he was offering the land to. But it seemed like he offered it immediately, right after he met him.” Yadubara hadn’t trusted Nair from the start. But Prabhupada, always gracious, had said, “All right,” and arranged to see the land.

The next morning, after taking a walk on Juhu Beach, Prabhupada and a party of devotees had gone to see the property. Prabhupada had liked it very much. “Look at all these coconut trees,” he pointed out. “There are a lot of coconuts, and we can sell them and drink from them.” “This is the most important land in Bombay,” he had said. “We are going to develop it.”

But his leaders—Madhudvisa, Shyamasundar, and Tamal Krishna— hadn’t agreed. To begin with, the land was far from the city, where most of our life members and friends had their homes and offices. The devotees had been thinking of somewhere like Malabar Hill—some nice place nearby.

“Juhu was beyond the suburbs,” Brahmananda later said. “It was a place where no one went.”

“A fishing village,” Gargamuni called it. “That’s what it was—a fishing village.”

In other places, the devotees had always rented or bought a house and converted it into a temple; they’d never bought land and built a temple from scratch. And the land was rough—overgrown by jungle and brush and full of junk, with old two-story apartment buildings, occupied by tenants, in the back. Locals were distilling illicit liquor in the thickets. Even staying on the land, what to speak of developing it, would be a challenge.

“The stench,” Madhudvisa later recalled. “And the mosquitoes. Cockroaches that could knock you over. Rats, snakes. Mangy dogs picking through the garbage, sniffing around.... I was dead set against it.”

“We’re Westerners,” Tamal Krishna had objected. “We can’t live like this.”

“Don’t you want to be purified?” Prabhupada had questioned.

No one had wanted to take responsibility for the project.

The life members had resisted as well. Most of them lived in central Bombay and we would hold programs there, so when they’d heard that Prabhupada was considering buying land in Juhu, a delegation of them had gone to try to convince him not to go through with the purchase. “We will never go there,” they had told him.

“They were our only supporters, and very influential, wealthy people,” Brahmananda recalled. “If we were going to build a temple, wewould go to these people to help us, and right from the very beginning they didn’t want it to happen.”

But Prabhupada had been determined.

On December 1 Mr. Nair had written Prabhupada in Delhi:

Dear Respected Swamiji: I am writing this letter to you in connection with my estate called “Nairwadi” at Juhu, Bombay-54.1 The price of land at Juhu in the said spot is about Rs. 175 to Rs. 200 per square yard. We are selling the land at a dead cheap price of Rs. 70 per square yard. It will be thus seen that there is a wide margin which can be profitably utilized for big purpose, as yours.

Pranams,

Yours ever

A. B. Nair

Ten days later, Prabhupada had replied, “I thank you very much for your kind letter dated Dec. 1, 1971, offering your nice property to our Society. I have received one letter from Tusta Krishna das Adhikary from Bombay, and he told me that you are so sympathetic with our movement that you will accept whatever money we have got just now and the balance may be paid as we collect.”

Prabhupada had gone to meet with Mr. Nair and his wife on December 21, accompanied by Madhudvisa, Shyamasundar, and Tusta Krishna. Their home was near the beach in the Theosophical Colony, a private enclave with lush lawns, flower gardens, and exotic birds. The living room had been filled with chairs and leather sofas, with newspapers strewn around—not, Madhudvisa thought, a Vedic kind of house.

Mr. Nair, a short, stocky, South Indian man in his fifties with a darkish complexion, pockmarked face, and receding hairline, had greeted his guests in a lungi-like dhoti. He had seemed to Madhudvisa kind of highbrow, intellectual, and Madhudvisa, like Yadubara, had distrusted him from the start. “I got a weird feeling from him,” he remembered. “He was a very Westernized Indian—a newspaper publisher. He had been to America various times and was aware of world politics. He was practically an atheist, but he knew shastra and everything like that.”

1 As far as practical, all letters and other documents are quoted verbatim, spelling and formatting intact.

Mr. Nair’s wife had been of fair complexion and worn her hair short, unusual for an Indian woman.

Prabhupada had offered the couple maha flower garlands and prasada, and he and the other devotees had sat with the Nairs on their front porch, facing the garden.

Prabhupada had been forthright in his appreciation of the Juhu land but had explained that he didn’t have much money. Mr. Nair had acted friendly and solicitous, and it hadn’t taken long before they had reached an oral agreement. Basically, Mr. Nair had agreed to everything Prabhupada proposed. They had settled on a total price of 14 lakhs rupees, with a down payment of 200,000 rupees, by which ISKCON would receive the conveyance. ISKCON would mortgage the property from Mr. Nair and pay the balance of 1,200,000 rupees later, in specified installments. Prabhupada had offered—and Mr. Nair accepted—a similar arrangement for the down payment: 50,000 rupees at signing and 50,000 later, at which time ISKCON could move onto the land. And when he’d been paid the remaining 100,000 rupees, Mr. Nair would hand over the deed, though since the property had actually been in Mrs. Nair’s name, she would have to sign all the documents. She’d thought the price was too low and the terms too liberal, but she had been overruled by her husband.

“Nair is a shrewd businessman,” Prabhupada had later told Madhudvisa, “very intelligent, so you must be very careful when you deal with him. He is clever, and if you are not careful, he may take advantage of you.” But Prabhupada had been determined to proceed with the land and the project, and the next day he had written Yamuna and Palika, “Here in Bombay we have got good prospects to purchase a very large land in Juhu for very cheap price, just in the middle of an \[important\] neighborhood. We shall build our camp there and begin constructing a temple immediately, and later on we shall develop a large hotel and school.... In general, we shall make our headquarters in Bombay.”

Six days later, he had written me, “At present we are trying seriously for ... a large plot of land of several acres near Bombay, to establish our India headquarters. Bombay is the richest city, the gateway to India, and in all respects the most important city. So we must have something here.”

At Akash Ganga Prabhupada also met with P. L. Sethi, a successful Bombay builder. Mr. Sethi had heard about some foreign devotees doing kirtan in the city, and he had seen a picture in the newspaper. So he had gone in search of them to the building where they were staying, and after meeting them and hearing their kirtan, he was convinced that ISKCON was a spiritual organization—the best.

Madhudvisa, who was serving as temple president, informed Mr. Sethi that Prabhupada had just come from America and brought Mr. Sethi to meet him.

“What work do you do?” Prabhupada asked. “What business?”

“I am in the construction business, constructing buildings and selling them,” Mr. Sethi replied.

“What time do you get up?” Prabhupada asked. “And what do you do first?”

Sethi said that he was getting up at seven, having a cup of tea, and then washing up and going to work.

“And when do you pray to Krishna?” Prabhupada asked. “When do you chant His name?”

“Not any time I am praying to Krishna,” Sethi replied. “I am only waking at seven, drinking tea, taking bath, tending my clothes, and going to work.”

“Then what is the difference between your life and animal life?” Prabhupada questioned. “You are just like an animal, just like a pig. The pig is also sleeping, the pig is also eating, and the pig is also having children. There is no difference between your life and the pig’s life. You must think of Krishna. This is the purpose of human life.”

“But I have no satsanga” Mr. Sethi replied, “no one who can direct this life to Krishna, krsna-prema.”

“If you want,” Prabhupada said, “I will send my devotees to your house and you do nagara-sankirtana with them and you will feel the effect.” So, Prabhupada sent the devotees, and Mr. Sethi went out with them and they did nagara-sankirtana, street sanklrtana—chanting, selling Back to Godheads, and attracting hundreds of people— early every Sunday morning, from five to seven, for the next year. Mr. Sethi would feed them sumptuous prasada, and he soon became a life member.

In Nairobi, Brahmananda wanted to attract Prabhupada to come by arranging a large pandal program like the ones in India. But Prabhupada did not want to be diverted from Juhu, so he set a condition: he would come only if Brahmananda arranged for him to meet Kenya’s president, Jomo Kenyatta. Brahmananda tried, and he actually met Kenyatta’s right-hand man, the minister of state, but he was not prepared to offer the “gift” necessary to obtain a meeting with the president. Still, he proceeded with arrangements for the program, in the hope that Prabhupada would come anyway.

Finally, Prabhupada did decide to go to Kenya, but the program did not go well. “I was never a very good organizer,” Brahmananda later admitted, “so the program I arranged was a total failure. Not many people came. We rented a football stadium, because they didn’t have pandals in Kenya then. But the stadium was in the African area, far away from the Indians, who were our main supporters, and the stage we constructed was half falling down. It was a disaster. But Prabhupada was happy—because he had some other plan.”

One day Prabhupada walked into Brahmananda’s room in the modest house that served as the Nairobi temple. Brahmananda was shocked. Why has he come to my room? he wondered. He never does that. Why didn't he call me to his room?

Prabhupada sat down on the bed and started talking about Juhu. He explained that he had found a nice property with many palm trees, situated near a prominent beach where people went to walk and where the elites of Bombay came to spend weekends and holidays. He said that he had plans to build a huge white-marble temple, a skyscraper, a hotel, a restaurant, and an auditorium, and to create an international religious and cultural center for people from all over the world. “Our Madhudvisa could not do it,” he said, “so I want you to do it.”

Brahmananda agreed. “My only qualification was that I would do whatever Prabhupada asked,” he later recalled. “I would always say yes. Even if I couldn’t do it, I would say yes. So I said, ‘Oh, yes, Srila Prabhupada.’”

But Brahmananda was also inspired by Prabhupada’s vision of the project, and he took him to see the Hilton Nairobi hotel, a landmark in the center of the city, famed for its round tower. When Brahmanandaand Cyavana, who was assisting him, later returned to the hotel for a tour and advice on how to construct a round building, they learned that the plumbing and electrical installations had to be done differently and that a round building was generally more costly and difficult to construct. Still, it was both distinctive and attractive, and Prabhupada accepted the concept for Juhu.

With the promise of Brahmananda’s support, Prabhupada returned to Bombay for a week and then proceeded to Madras, Visakhapatnam, Calcutta, and Mayapur, for the first international Gaura-purnima festival.

A month later, Brahmananda showed up in Mayapur. “What are you doing here?” Prabhupada asked.

“You invited everyone for the festival,” Brahmananda replied, “for chanting and dancing and prasada”

“The festival is not important for you.” Prabhupada said. “Your business is in Bombay.”

“But all the devotees are here. Lord Chaitanya ...”

“No—no festival for you,” Prabhupada insisted. “You must immediately go to Bombay. And take Nara Narayan with you; he is a builder. Go immediately.”

“Yes, Prabhupada, well go.”

“Go now!”

And so Brahmananda and Nara Narayan left for Juhu.

Their first task was to clear the property—pull up the brush, clear out the snakes and rodents, clean the area, and level the land. It was, Brahmananda said, “a huge, backbreaking job.”

For digging deeper and doing heavier work, Nara Narayan went early one morning to the labor market in nearby Vile Parle. “Well clear the land,” the laborers there told him, “but you have to supply the powra and gamela'" Nara Narayan didn’t know what a powra or a gamela was. When he came back and told a local friend, the friend said, “That’s reasonable”—and eventually Nara Narayan found out that a powra was a hoe-like tool for chopping the dirt and that a gamela was a wok-like metal bowl that the workers balanced on their heads to carry the dirt. So, he went down to Bhuleshwar and returned by train loaded with powras and gamelas. And the next day, he returned to Vile Parle and hired the men, who seemed happy with his purchases.

Men with machetes were hired to cut down the jungle, and to encourage them and speed progress, Brahmananda joined them in the work, along with Mr. Sethi and other devotees. Although Mr. Sethi was a contractor with many laborers under him, he came and worked personally, seeing the endeavor as devotional service. And with everyone working together, all the brush, jungle, garbage—everything—was soon gone.

The workers and the devotees clearing the land naturally attracted the attention of the tenants. While one of them, Padmanabha Acharya, was working in his garden, he saw Brahmananda and other devotees cutting bushes and clearing the front, vacant area of the property. He hadn’t heard anything about the devotees, but they seemed to work hard and without stop, from morning till night, and he wondered what they did for food. The first day, he was curious, but he didn’t say anything. The day after that, he asked one of the devotees, “What’s going on here? And what about your food?”

“We don’t take food unless it is first offered to Krishna,” the devotee replied. “We take early in the morning and then when we go back in the evening.”

Mr. Acharya offered them tea, but they said they didn’t drink tea. Then one day he had three or four of them at his home and gave them milk, and that was the beginning of his relationship with the devotees. The next day, more devotees came, and being from Karnataka, in South India, he gave them upma, a soft savory suji preparation. It went on like this for a few days. Then he noticed one devotee eating the chilies cooked in the food for flavor but not actually meant to be eaten. When he asked about it, the devotee explained, “It is prasada; we can’t leave anything.”

After about ten days, Prabhupada arrived in Bombay. He had told the devotees that he wanted them to occupy the land immediately. This was crucial, he said, since under Indian statutes, possession really was nine-tenths of the law: if you lived on the land, you practically owned it. This was a bit of a conundrum, however, since you couldn’t construct any buildings until you owned the land. According to the agreement with Mr. Nair, with the money the devotees had paid to date, they could live on the land but they could not begin any construction.

“What do we do?” Brahmananda asked Prabhupada. “How do we live in a place where there’s no building?”

“You make a pandal” Prabhupada told him. “You can always make a pandal. It is not a construction, so you don’t need a permit. But make a permanent pandal.”

The devotees had never heard of a permanent pandal, but Brahmananda had the idea to make an elaborate one, with many rooms, of corrugated tin roofing sheets—tin sheds, or “hutments,” which we came to call simply “huts.”

“We’ll live in these,” Prabhupada said.

Meanwhile, the devotees told Prabhupada about Mr. Acharya, who turned out to be a follower of Krishna, and Prabhupada decided to pay him a surprise visit.

When Prabhupada arrived at Mr. Acharya’s apartment and Mr. Acharya invited him in, Prabhupada saw a photograph of Sripada Madhvacharya and bowed in respect. “Mr. Acharya,” he said, “are you a Madhva?”

“Yes,” Mr. Acharya replied, “I was born in the place where Madhvacharya was born—Udupi.”

“Oh, you are fortunate,” Prabhupada remarked. Then, seemingly out of nowhere, he asked, “Can I stay with you?”

Mr. Acharya was taken aback but also pleased. “Swamiji,” he replied, “it will be a great blessing. Whatever I have, you can share with me.” Mr. Acharya had been impressed with Prabhupada’s disciples, and he was filled with wonder that Prabhupada had been able to turn people born as Christians into devotees of Krishna. He felt proud that an Indian could do what Prabhupada had done.

Prabhupada soon came back to stay. “He always had a triangle of devotees standing behind him,” Nara Narayan later remembered, “because everyone wanted to see what he was doing and hear him in case he said something. So, Srila Prabhupada came swooping up to the Acharyas’ house, with some disciples, and all the Acharyas were standing on the open front porch, on either side of the way Prabhupada would enter. It looked grand: they were standing there as though they were Jaya and Vijaya, the gatekeepers in Vaikuntha. Prabhupada swooped up and stood on the porch, then turned elegantly and said, ‘Finally I am taking shelter of the Acharyas.’”

Brahmananda and Nara Narayan undertook to put up the pandal. Brahmananda went down to Bhuleshwar, in Old Bombay, to the office of a contractor, Mr. Bhuther, a Parsi, who was very accommodating. “Oh, yes, sure,” he said. “Anything you want, we’ll do.” When Brahmananda asked about the cost, Mr. Bhuther just said, “Don’t worry about it.” So Brahmananda had him build the pandal with tin sheets, with a stage and a kitchen and separate quarters for the men and women. There was no flooring, only dirt, which was fine for the dry weather then.

Whenever Brahmananda asked Mr. Bhuther about the cost, the contractor said, “Don’t worry about it.” Brahmananda’s experience in Kenya was with pious Gujaratis, and he’d never had to pay for anything. They controlled the retail trade and had given him everything for free—gas, cloth, electronics, food, flowers . . . anything. So when Mr. Bhuther said, “Don’t worry about it,” Brahmananda thought that the work might be done for free, or at most for a nominal sum. But when the work was complete, he later recalled, “I was shocked when he presented a bill for an extraordinary amount, which we couldn’t pay. He demanded his money and threatened to remove everything if I didn’t pay. In a panic, I informed Srila Prabhupada, who said I had been tricked, cheated, and didn’t know how to manage. He told me to go right back to Nairobi. This coincided with devotees in Nairobi needing my help. So, I left, according to Prabhupada’s order.”

Thereafter, Mr. Bhuther had to deal directly with Prabhupada. When he came for payment, asking for Brahmananda, Brahmananda was gone. Mr. Bhuther claimed he had agreements with him for the amount billed, but Prabhupada said, “Brahmananda has left the country, so we will have to review those bills.” Then, after finding out the fair cost from Mr. Sethi, he told Bhuther, “This is what I will pay you—not more,” and Bhuther had no choice but to accept.

Later, Prabhupada commented, “Brahmananda made a contract with a man for that camp—forty thousand rupees. I settled up for ten thousand rupees. So, our work is going on in India and money’s spent; fifty percent is spoiled by this American brain. What can be done? The Indians, they’ll loot. They cheat like anything. Just like this camp. Brahmananda and Madhudvisa combined together made acontract—forty thousand rupees. Then I said, ‘I am not going to pay you. You go.’”

One day during the last week of March, the doorbell at Akash Ganga rang, and when Madri dasi, the only devotee present, opened the door, she found a young Westerner with long hair. ‘Are there Radha-Krishna Deities here?” he inquired.

Madri invited him in. “Please sit down,” she said. “The Deities are here; you can sit here with Them. The other devotees will be back soon.”

The large white marble Deities, ordered from Jaipur and paid for by a donation from R. D. Birla, had first been worshipped at Chowpatty Beach on the last night of the 1971 Bombay pandal at Cross Maidan.

One hour passed, and then another, and the young man just sat there while Madri attended to her service. Suddenly the doors swung open, and Nara Narayan burst in, followed by other devotees, exclaiming, “Haribol! Haribol!”

Shyamasundar approached the young man and said, “It’s great that you came today; this is our last day in Akash Ganga. We are all going to Juhu tomorrow. We have some land, and it has a well, and it’s near the beach. There’s a pandal there, and Prabhupada will be speaking. Would you like to come with us? We’re all going by taxi.”

“Well, I have nowhere else to sleep tonight,” the man said. His name was Hans, and he was a Dutch architect who had been wandering around Bombay for over a week, looking for a Radha-Krishna temple. He had seen devotees in Amsterdam and had come to India to see if their worship had its roots in India or was just a movement in the West.

The next day, Hans accompanied the devotees as they piled into three taxis and rode to Juhu. Three devotees sat in the back seat of each taxi—in one with the marble deity of Rasabihari laying across their laps and in one of the others with the deity of Srimati Radharani. Hans was surprised when on their arrival Shyamasundar asked if he would pay for all three taxis, but he did.

The pandal was decorated with flowers and featured a large stage with a vyasasana for Srila Prabhupada. As the devotees prepared for Prabhupada’s talk, Hans just stood around in the back, not knowing how to act or what to do. Then Shyamasundar came up to him and said,

“We forgot our tape recorder—do you have one?”

“I do,” he replied.

“Can you record Prabhupada’s lecture?”

“Yes, sure.”

“Great—just take the little microphone and stick it on the big microphone, and sit next to the vyasasana, and then when the tape finishes, turn it around.”

While Hans was attaching the microphone, Prabhupada walked in and sat on the vyasasana. He looked at the longhaired young man and gestured to a devotee as if to say, “Who is he?” But then, apparently satisfied, he began.

Hans recorded the lecture and gave the cassette to Shyamasundar. And Dinanath invited him to sleep with the devotees on the roof, where they had set up mosquito nets.

At three-thirty the next morning Hans was awakened by the net being pulled off him. The other devotees had already risen. “Get up! Get up!” Brahmananda was shouting. “Go to mangala-arati and chant Hare Krishna!”

At first Brahmananda thought the reclining figure was one of the devotees trying to sleep in. But when he saw that it was Hans, he said, “Oh! That’s okay—but you can still go and chant.” So Hans went to the pandal for the arati and chanted.

During japa, Brahmananda again approached Hans. “Prabhupada wants to see you,” he said, “but first you have to shave your head. Here’s one rupee. Across the street is a barber; he opens at seven.”

So, Hans went to the barber, and the barber shaved his head, leaving a small but long sikha. A devotee escorted Hans to Mr. Acharya’s place, and Shyamasundar took him inside the building, repeating, “Prabhupada wants to see you.”

For what? Hans wondered.

When Shyamasundar brought Hans into Prabhupada’s room, Prabhupada looked up at Hans. “Oh, now you look beautiful,” he said. “Please sit down.”

Hans sat on the floor, and Prabhupada asked him just one question: “What is the use of decorating dead bodies?”

“There is no use,” Hans replied.

“Exactly,” Prabhupada said. “So Krishna sent you here to design the temple, and you can start right now?

Prabhupada asked Shyamasundar to bring paper and pencils, and then a set of photos. Hans could sense the other devotees in the room reacting—that something extraordinary was happening. “And that,” he recalled, “was the beginning of my involvement with the Bombay project. It was like my life changed in a few moments. I had no idea what was going on.”

Prabhupada also told Hans, “Tomorrow we will have the ceremony”—the consecration of the land. “And you will take initiation.”

“I was already totally confused about everything,” Hans said later. “It was all really very funny. They were digging this hole, and I was standing there, trying to figure out how kartals worked, with a shaved head, next to a Japanese man near a big hole in India, and an Indian guru was giving us both initiation!

“The process, of course, was that you got a new name. So, I was there, and Prabhupada put the beads on my neck, and I was waiting, and he said, ‘Your name is Saurb.’ I said, ‘Zorro?’ I was a little bit shy to ask the name, and when, afterward, the devotees inquired, I said, ‘Zorro.’ This was really something, I thought; everyone wanted a name with ‘Krishna’ or ‘Vishnu,’ and here I was, Zorro.

“So, I went to Shyamasundar and said, ‘There’s probably some mistake.’ ‘Why?’ he asked. I said, ‘I think Prabhupada said “Zorro.”’ And he said, ‘No, that can’t be—don’t worry, I’ll ask him.’ When he came back, he said, ‘No, your name is Saurabha.’

“Saurabha, I thought. What does that mean? Someone said it was a famous Muslim poet, so I thought, Oh my goodness; now I'm coming from the Middle East. I could never figure out why he gave me that name; it was just totally confusing.”

Saurabha had been trained as an artist and decorator at Amsterdam’s Institute for Applied Arts, but his experience had been with alternative, contemporary architecture, and, as he put it, “I had just come ‘off the streets.’ I was not clear what Prabhupada meant by ‘design a temple.’ So, I got paper and pencils, and he gave me photos, and I said, ‘Oh, I can design.’”

Saurabha drew for two or three days. Every few hours or so, Prabhupada would come out of his room, look over Saurabha’s shoulder,and say, “That’s nice. That’s nice.” Saurabha was working from pictures of Vrindavan’s new Govindaji temple, drawing it from different angles and perspectives. “It had a sort of Italian-Indian mix of style, which Prabhupada liked,” he later said. “The European and the Indian together made it sort of international looking.”

So, Saurabha was allocated a place to work, and he started making drawings for the temple. “There was something that gave me the energy,” he remembered, “something that allowed me to do this work that normally I probably wouldn’t have been able to do.”

Two weeks later, before leaving Bombay for Australia, Prabhupada instructed us to build a residential hut in the middle of the open space between the buildings at the back of the property. He said we should consult Dr. Indira Shringi about how to proceed, and she recommended a building contractor named Mr. Mehta. Since an abandoned structure with completed plinth and R.C.C. columns was already there, Mr. Mehta suggested that we build upon it. Although we had not yet applied for permission from the municipality, we had some donated materials, and we felt that we should start construction right away, before the onset of the monsoons. Mr. Mehta estimated that the work would cost five thousand rupees, to which we agreed, though it ended up costing much more.

The walls were brick up to three feet and then chatai (slit bamboo rods woven together, crisscross, in sheets) up to the roof, which was also chatai but which we later covered with tarpaulin. On that rough foundation of a building—apparently meant to be another tenement—which was never completed, there were concrete columns reinforced by metal bars sticking out in all directions. Inside the now-covered structure, our workers laid concrete floors, added a maroon finish, and polished the finish until it was quite smooth. But the workmanship was shoddy: the floors’ cement covering kept crumbling, leaving holes, and the tarps over the roof leaked when it rained. We even couldn’t clean the floors; the cement would loosen or break up.

To make matters worse, the hut proved to be a haven for rats. Bombay rats were notorious—unlike rats anywhere else. Not only were they huge—the size of cats, eighteen to twenty inches long, with big teeth—but they bit into your skin so stealthily that you wouldn’t knowit; you would keep sleeping but then wake up and find yourself in a pool of blood. The hut was also infested with flies, cockroaches, and ferocious mosquitoes. So we were constantly being bitten, stung, and harassed by all sorts of vermin and insects.

“Devotees were living in this terrible hut,” Narayani dasi recalled. “One little part was the kitchen, and the drinking water was kept in a large clay pot, and when you opened the lid, swarms of mosquitoes would fly out. Many of the devotees were completely sick with dysentery and things, and they told me, ‘Oh, you 11 get it, too’—and judging from the water, I believed them.

“The first day I ate prasada in the hut, I noticed rats running across the roof. I was wondering if they would fall in my plate. It didn’t happen to me, but it happened to Dravida \[a devotee from America\]: one of the rats that was scampering around the hut fell right in his plate. There was no meal at night—just milk and reading Krsna book. But before we drank the milk, we would have to remove the bugs and mosquitoes.”

When Dr. S.K. Poddar, a surgeon with a small clinic in nearby Andheri, introduced to us by our early supporter in Juhu Dr. К. H. F. Singhal, visited, he found that devotees were suffering from fever, amoebiasis, diarrhea, dysentery—various tropical and subtropical diseases—not surprising, given that we were sleeping on the floor, eating little, and living in poor, unhygienic conditions. In fact, we were sick so regularly that at some point we practically stopped taking notice. “At one stage,” Narayani remembered, “Giriraj was so sick with fever or something that he was just lying under a table. Somebody suggested, ‘Why don’t you take care of yourself?’ but he replied, ‘It’s okay, it doesn’t matter.’”

Dr. Poddar assisted Dr. Singhal in caring for us and gave us vaccines against cholera and typhoid. He would help in whatever way he could, he said, and appreciated that the devotees, “rather than demanding, did not demand anything.”

While we were living in the hut, another medical doctor from Andheri, Dr. С. P. Patel, heard about us and came to meet us. Dr. Patel was somewhat proud—he had been born into a Vaishnava family and followed the Vaishnava principles of purity, knew Sanskrit and couldrecite many verses, and had gone to London to study medicine (quite a big thing then) and even there had never eaten meat, smoked, or drank. So he considered himself to be a Vaishnava, although he often spoke like an impersonalist. But he took a liking to us foreign devotees, and when he saw our circumstances—that many of us were sick, some with malaria—he was inspired to take up a collection to help. He went stall to stall through Mulji Jetha Market, an enormous cloth market in Bombay, begging for cotton and cloth to make pillows and mattresses—and to obtain blankets, sheets, and mosquito nets. Because of his pride, it was a big thing for him to beg; he had never begged in his life. But he did it, and he presented each devotee with a set of basic items—a mattress, pillow, sheet, blanket, and mosquito net.

When Prabhupada returned to Bombay, Dr. Patel came to meet him, and he soon became Prabhupada’s constant companion on his morning walks. He would usually come to Prabhupada’s room at about six and either walk with him to Juhu Beach or drive him there. Then they would walk and talk for about an hour.

We also received assistance and encouragement from other Bombay residents. One day an aristocratic gentleman came to the land in a vintage black limousine. He was stately and noble, and elderly—just under eighty, three years older than Srila Prabhupada—and seemed to be from a bygone era. He introduced himself as Bhogilal Hargovindas Patel and presented us a large basket with many varieties of luscious fruit. We had been eating pretty much just boiled rice and dal, and apart from the little fruit we got from the afternoon Deity offering, we never had any. But he came every week with a large basket and ended up being one of our closest friends and biggest supporters.

Another helpful person was Mr. Patil, a neighbor just across our southern boundary wall, who was kind enough to let the ladies reside in his small place during the rainy season.

Even though the conditions in the hut were primitive, every Sunday the large partitioned room where the Deities were housed was packed for the arati and program. Dr. Singhal and his wife came every week. And people were quite sympathetic, impressed that we foreigners had come from such a great distance, leaving our opulent country, and were living in such poor conditions and worshipping Radha and Krishna. Soeven though during the week it was quite a struggle, on Sunday many friends and visitors would come, and we would get encouragement from them too.

Mrs. Singhal wrote about this period in her article “Krishna Lila at Hare Krishna Land,” which Srila Prabhupada said should be published in Back to Godhead:

“After some time, the season changed—the monsoons came, the sky covered with dark clouds, sometimes dusty winds blew, and sometimes it drizzled. So the devotees shifted the Deities to their hut because they had no other place. The hut was not in good condition: no pukka flooring, no proper rooms, no light, no proper ventilation. But Lord Krishna and Radharani chose that place for Their temple.

“Devotees made a small temple inside the hut, and with all their might they got everything done: flooring, lighting arrangements, and some other improvements. Adjacent to the hut was a beautiful garden made by Nara Narayan and his associates.

“The devotees were performing all their regular activities and services for the Supreme Lord Krishna and Radha. Daily, they got up early for mangala-arati, and after finishing their other duties many of them used to go to different parts of Bombay for preaching, distributing books, making life members, and collecting funds. The whole day they used to work hard and take food again only in the evening.

“There were always special programs on Sundays. They used to play nice transcendental dramas. And people used to come in great numbers for Sunday arati.

“This hut reminded me of Lord Rama and Sita’s hut in Danda-karanya. It became a pilgrimage place for all of us. We always went there and offered whatever help and services we could. Monsoons are terrible in Bombay. Sometimes they played havoc, but these foreign devotees never neglected their service towards Lord Krishna and Radha. Sometimes they used to suffer bodily too, but they never grumbled or complained or demanded anything. If we said something, they always used to say, ‘No, this is our testing period.’ There were some neighbors, Mr. Acharya and Mr. Patil, who helped them, sometimes giving accommodation to the women devotees. And Mr. and Mrs. Warrier always stood by them to help them. But other surrounding people were uncooperative.

“Devotees celebrated many festivals inside the hut temple. When Jhulana-yatra came, Radharani and Lord Krishna wore dresses I stitched for them. Oh, how happy I was to have their darshan in that dress! They were looking very beautiful and nice. Many days passed like this.”

Srila Prabhupada was aware of the austere conditions we were enduring, and he expressed his appreciation for us on a morning walk with Dr. Patel. “These European, American boys, they gave up their smoking habit, drinking-tea habit, all habits, meat-eating, immediately,” he said. “But if we ask any Indian, he has to consider for three generations.”

“That is because they have been trained from childhood,” Dr. Patel suggested.

“No, no. They have been trained from childhood in meat-eating, drinking tea, drinking wine, smoking, and illicit sex, but they gave up immediately.”

“But in hygiene also they have to learn our way.”

“They are observing hygienic principles as far as possible; the only thing is that they require a little guidance.”

“This kitchen behind is too small—”

“No. We can make a big kitchen; we have got enough room.”

“I told them, maybe we must have a small room attached to it where these boys can ...”

“They are thinking, ‘I am not this body.’ They tolerate. Actually, they tolerate because they factually think that ‘I am not this body. Let the mosquito bite my body.’ Narottama dasa Thakura says, deha-smrti nahi yara, samsara-kupa kahan tara. When a person fully realizes that the material body and world are temporary, he is not concerned with the pains and pleasures of the body. One who is beyond the conception of the body has no obligation for these material things. Just like there are many sadhus, they simply remain naked, even in severe cold. They are practiced.”

“They have reached that avadhuta-vesa?

“So, this is also avadhuta-vesa.”

“But that stage you must reach.”

“Somehow or other, they have gone to some extent. ‘Never mind the mosquito. Let it bite. I am not this body.’”

“You have hypnotized them,” Dr. Patel said, laughing.

“No, actually they are doing. Although we see that from bodily point of view they have become weak, they don’t care about it. If they had been weak, how are they chanting and dancing sankirtana? They are not weak at all.”

It was true: we were weak in material energy but strong in spiritual energy. And despite the austerities, we were ecstatic to be with Srila Prabhupada, serving him and his mission and desire to erect the Juhu temple. As Manasatita dasa, from Italy, later commented, “We were living in bad conditions, but inside our hut we were happy because Prabhupada was there, and we were safe from materialistic life. When he was present, he would give lectures two times a day, and we could see him all day long. From the brahmachari ashram, I could see him chanting his rounds. We didn’t care that we were sleeping on the ground or in a place where rain came in—we were very happy, really very happy. Whenever I remember those days, I weep.”

A month after leaving Bombay, Prabhupada wrote to Cyavana and me with a photo of an artist’s sketch of a skyscraper—a proposal for an ISKCON world headquarters in Los Angeles. “Simply add Govindaji’s temple, as you and Saurabha have drawn it,” he wrote, “and add it onto this skyscraper in the enclosed photo.”

Saurabha sketched and drew for almost a year and then put together a prospectus with Visakha dasi, who was working with him and taking photographs. There was a pause in his work then, and he would come with me to promote the life-membership program. “I couldn’t understand that program,” he recalled. “Giriraj would sit there and then tell all sorts of stories and impress them, and those people were rich, but they wouldn’t listen really; they would just look away or be busy on the phone, or somebody else would come in. But Giriraj had the patience to just sit there and sit there and sit there until he got somebody to become a member.”

During Srila Prabhupada’s first stay at Hare Krishna Land, one of his disciples complained to him that the tenants’ children were runningaround making noise and asked how we could keep them quiet. “That is not possible/’ Prabhupada replied. “But you can engage their propensities in Krishna consciousness, in kirtan.” And that was the beginning of the gurukula, the children’s classes, at Hare Krishna Land.

With his youthful enthusiasm and charismatic charm, Madhudvisa was the natural leader for the program. “I was living upstairs on the roof,” he later recalled. “Prabhupada had said, ‘Yes, that is very good, live up on the roof,’ so I kept all my clothes and books and things in a metal trunk with a lock, and I set up a piece of cloth for shade.

“I soon made friends with the Warriers. One morning while I was doing tulasi-arati, dancing around, the children came up to the roof. I asked them if they knew tulasi, but they didn’t. They were real Bombay Hindus; they didn’t know much. So I explained how we worshipped tulasi, and I showed them how to offer obeisances and dance around tulasi and everything. I gave them pieces of paper with the prayers to read. They learned the words and offered the prayers, and gradually the whole family became devotees. We actually started a little training program there. The children would come up after school, and I taught them prayers and how to do tulasi-arati, and we had a little Bhagavad-gita class. They were the first family on Hare Krishna Land. The mother and the kids—the girl and her two older brothers—all became devotees just from coming up on the roof. And after them, children from the other buildings on the land also started coming on a regular basis.”

At the age of six, Smriti “Baby” Warrier was the youngest. “Madhudvisa Swami, Gargamuni Swami, and Brahmananda Swami were our gurukula teachers,” she remembered years later. “The three of them did it. And it was so much fun. We used to do all kinds of things—little projects, learning slokas, chanting, putting on dances for Srila Prabhupada when he came. My brothers and I used to go. Of course, they were older than me, so they were quicker in learning the slokas. I was slow. The system was that if you learned the Isopanisad, you would get a plate of the Deities’ maha-prasada. It took me a long time to get that.

“Madhudvisa Maharaja and others were living on the rooftop. At night he would carry a bucket of water to the roof, and he would bathe there. In the early morning we would look up, and from where we were,all we could see were these white soapy lathered heads. It was austere, but it was a lot of fun?

Srila Prabhupada considered the gurukula program important, and before he left Bombay he told us that we should develop it. As it was, many of the children would attend the evening program in the pandal with their parents, and some would attend mangala-arati. Prabhupada even had us schedule mangala-arati a little later than in our other temples, to make it easier for the neighbors to attend. He said that the whole area surrounding Hare Krishna Land was “a pious quarter” and that he wanted us to do whatever we could to maintain a school for the local children.

The children learned our regulative principles and how to offer food to Krishna. And at home, if their parents prepared any of the forbidden items, some of the children would ask why and tell them that it was not good. Some parents were embarrassed by this, however, and it became a source of tension with the tenants.

Sumati Morarji, Srila Prabhupada’s old friend and the head of the Scindia Steam Navigation Company, who had contributed funds for the printing of Prabhupada’s Srimad-Bhagavatam in India and later had given him free passage to America on one of her ships, and who lived nearby, was running her own school not far from us, but she was not attracting a sufficient number of students, so she sent a representative from her school to ask if they could distribute circulars to friends and visitors at our pandal and to invite me to meet with her to discuss various matters. I agreed to meet her, and I wrote Srila Prabhupada about her proposal.

But Prabhupada envisioned establishing our own proper Krishna conscious school. A week later, he wrote me from Sydney: “As soon as possible we should open our own school and teach children Krishna consciousness through English medium—that is one of our programs. Our school will not be government recognized, because we cannot follow the government syllabus. We want to teach only Krishna consciousness. . .. I know many parents are eager to educate their wards through English medium. If we can introduce this system, our girl disciples may be engaged for teaching them: a little English grammar, reading and writing, geography, arithmetic, history, Sanskrit, but all of them should be Krishna conscious—that is the Bhagavata program:kaumara acaret prajno  
dharman bhagavatan iha”

I replied, “Madhudvisa Swami and Gargamuni Swami have been leading classes for children from 5 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. daily. About 50-100 children come daily to learn prayers, kirtan, japa, and philosophy. They can be seen with tilak, neck beads, and their hands in their bead bags, not only in class but also outside?’

“I am very much pleased about the children’s classes,” Prabhupada wrote back. “These are very, very important programs, so let it go on nicely, even if Madhudvisa leaves there.” He wrote to Gargamuni, “In the absence of Madhudvisa, you take charge of the school.” And ten days later, he wrote to Gargamuni, “If you leave Bombay, make sure the school is in very capable hands such as yours, because this program is very, very important—not that you shall go away and things will stop.”

Eventually, Sumati Morarji considered turning her school over to us, and I wrote Srila Prabhupada, “Srimati Morarji wants to turn her school over to us when our building is ready; she will give us whatever funds, paraphernalia, and students she has. She has also volunteered to have the children’s meals cooked in her kitchen and sent to us for offering to Radha and Krishna and then distributing. Meanwhile she invited us to lead her present students in kirtan and other programs in her building.”

The following month, on July 11, Sumati Morarji met Srila Prabhupada in London. She had been used to dealing with Shyamasundar, who then was serving as Prabhupada’s secretary—not with me—but Srila Prabhupada steered her in my direction.

“His father is a very rich man,” Prabhupada said.

“Is he?” she replied.

“His father is a very big lawyer, and mother and father both came to me in Calcutta. His mother—after all, a mother—was crying, ‘Give me back my boy? So I replied, ‘You can take away your boy? So, anyway, they are very good gentlemen. And he’s a graduate in psychology. He’s learned.”

“No, no, he’s a very nice man. I asked him just now—I’m running a school—I said, ‘You come and give lecture, tell some stories to the children?”

The next day, Prabhupada wrote me, “Sumati Morarji wants us to come to her school and give classes in Krishna consciousness, so you go there with others as often as possible and give instruction to the children, bring them to our temple, distribute prasadam—like that. More and more, she will become favorably disposed as she sees us that we are performing the best welfare activity. Kindly inform me how these matters are making progress.”

I replied immediately: “We have already been going to \[Sumati Morarji’s\] school, as she wants the students and their parents to gradually accept being taught by us. Naturally the students prefer our methods to the ordinary ones, so they are very responsive.”

Despite his busy schedule and other priorities and important projects, Prabhupada was so enthusiastic to help the children—and encourage his old friend and benefactor, Sumati Morarji—that he too wrote back immediately, on July 30: “So far as the school of Sumati Morarji, make the children into Vaishnavas through English medium of learning. We are not going to abide by the government schedule. They should be taught our books as soon as they can read and write. The idea is that those who will later on accept service \[outside employment\], they cannot be accepted by us for schooling; we cannot help them. They must be the sons of rich and important men who will not be taking education simply to use it for eating and sleeping. They should be taught just to do like the elders—that is, rise early, cleanse, attend mangala-arati, read our literatures, chant, go for sankirtana, like that, and besides that, a little ABC, mathematics, geography, and history; that’s all. And teach the small children to play Krishna games: one child is a cow, another is cowherd boy, they go to the forest, there are demons there, Krishna kills the demons—like that. In this way, let the children play Krishna games, then attend arati, then learn some ABC, then play some more, have kirtan, a little ABC, and by keeping them always diversified, they shall not lose interest and will keep their attention always focused around Krishna.”

Prabhupada was not only explaining how to engage the children in Sumati’s school nearby—he was telling us in general how to engage all children in learning in Krishna consciousness.

In our glossy brochure, we advertised a gurukula as part of the Juhu project. The section began with two quotations from the Bhagavadgita (5.16, 9.2): “When one is enlightened with the knowledge by which ignorance is destroyed, then his knowledge reveals everything, as the sun lights up the daytime. This knowledge is the king of education, the most secret of all secrets. It is the purest knowledge, and because it gives direct perception of the self by realization, it is everlasting and joyfully performed?

It continued, “People of all castes and creeds are welcome to participate in ISKCON’s gurukul school. They will get a complete education in English medium on various subjects and at the same time be trained as men of character and good qualities who are equipped to deal with the material world and at the same time be versed in the science of God.”

And it highlighted the classes that were already being taught, with two photos of the children with their teacher Gargamuni. “Even as the construction is going on,” the brochure read, “young girls and boys are eagerly attending daily classes in our temporary quarters and some have become knowledgeable Vaishnavas overnight, as tilak and japa beads now pervade the neighboring communities and at schooltime singing and dancing fills the air as the neophyte devotees circumambulate Srimati Tulasi Devi and then sit down to become absorbed in hearing about Govinda’s unique pastimes and playful activities with Yasoda, Nanda Maharaja, and His multitude of friends and enemies in Vrindavan.”

From one perspective, the history of the Juhu project can be viewed as the story of Srila Prabhupada’s personal service to Sri Sri Radha-Rasabihari. “My dear Sir,” he told Sri Rasabihari—and Them both— “You just stand here and I will build You a temple.” Yet at the same time as he was serving Their Lordships, he was also training us, his disciples, in the process of Deity worship.

In Calcutta, he had raised the question, “What is the duty of the spiritual master, and what is the duty of the disciple?” Then he had given the answer: “The duty of the spiritual master is to serve Krishna, and the duty of the disciple is to assist the spiritual master.” He had given theexample that it was his duty to see that the temple floor was clean, and so the disciple washing the floor could think, “It is my spiritual master’s duty to keep the floor clean, and I am assisting him by cleaning it?

In his eight stanzas glorifying the spiritual master, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura states,

sri-vigraharadhana-nitya-nana-  
srngara-tan-mandira-marjanadau  
yuktasya bhaktams ca niyunjato 'pi  
vande guroh sri-caranaravindam
