“The spiritual master is always engaged in the temple worship of Sri Sri Radha and Krsna. He also engages his disciples in such worship. They dress the Deities in beautiful clothes and ornaments, clean Their temple, and perform other similar worship of the Lord. I offer my respectful obeisances unto the lotus feet of such a spiritual master? (Sri Gurv-astaka 3)

Srila Prabhupada explains, “Sri-vigraha is the area, or suitable worshipable form of the Lord, and the disciple should be engaged in worshiping the Deity regularly by srngara, proper decoration and dressing, as also by mandira-marjana, the matter of cleansing the temple. The spiritual master teaches the neophyte devotee all these kindly and personally to help him gradually in the realization of the transcendental name, quality, form, etc., of the Lord.” (SB 2.3.22 purport)

So, when we, his disciples, made mistakes in our service to the Deities, he corrected us.

Because of our material conditioning and atheistic tendencies, we may tend to neglect the Deity—to think the Deity is merely a stone or metal statue, not the Supreme Personality of Godhead. This tendency is acknowledged—and criticized—in shastra:

arcye visnau sila-dhir gurusu nara-matir vaisnave jati-buddhir  
visnor va vaisnavanam kali-mala-mathane pada-tirthe 'mbu-buddhih  
sri-visnor namni mantre sakala-kalusa-he sabda-samanya-buddhir  
visnau sarvesvarese tad-itara-sama-dhir yasya va naraki sah

“One who thinks the Deity in the temple to be made of wood or stone, who thinks of the spiritual master in the disciplic succession as anordinary man, who thinks the Vaisnava in the Acyuta-gotra to belong to a certain caste or creed, or who thinks of carandmrta or Ganges water as ordinary water is taken to be a resident of hell.” (Padma Purdna)

Done in the proper mood, with faith and veneration (sri-murtira sraddhaya sevana), worshipping the Deity is one of the five most potent processes of devotional service. As stated in Srila Rupa Gosvami’s Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu (1.2.90), sraddha visesatah pritih/ sri-murter anghri-sevane: “With love and full faith one should worship the lotus feet of the Deity.”

But if we mistake the Deity for a stone, metal, or wooden statue, or idol, we are doomed. Referring to the Deity of Krishna, Srila Krishna-dasa Kaviraja Gosvami, the author of Sri Caitanya-caritdmrta, states,saksat vrajendra-suta ithe nahi ana  
yeba ajne kare tanre pratima-hena jnana

“Without a doubt He is directly the son of the King of Vraja. Only a fool considers Him a statue.” (Cc Adi 5.225)sei aparadhe tara nahika nistara  
ghora narakete pade, ki baliba dra

“For that offense, he cannot be liberated. Rather, he will fall into a terrible hellish condition. What more should I say?” (Cc Adi 5.226)

Commenting on this verse, Srila Prabhupada states, “Those who are actually very serious about devotional service do not differentiate between the form of the Lord made of clay, metal, stone, or wood and the original form of the Lord. . . . The statue of Lord Krsna and Krsna Himself, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, are not different, because the Lord is absolute. . . . Even if one has not developed this consciousness, one should accept it theoretically from the instructions of the spiritual master and should worship the arca-murti, or form of the Lord in the temple, as nondifferent from the Lord.” And thus he kindly trained us in the course of, and as part of, his service to the Deities.

To accommodate the Deities without the large hired pandal, Nara Narayan and his wife, Dinadayadri, constructed a small and simple yet festive pandal-like structure. He went to Bhuleshwar and bought bolts of red and yellow cloth, and she sewed it with her special sewing machinefrom America. He had observed that when Indians built a pandal, they dug holes, put in bamboo poles, and repacked the dirt around them. Then they built a framework, and over that they laid the covering of interlocking pieces laced together. One could make a pandal with just a single piece, or it could be hundreds of yards long. The bamboo was usually covered with striped cloth sleeves, but we didn’t have a way to make them, so our bamboo was just bare. With help from a couple of devotees, Nara Narayan dropped in the poles, packed in the dirt, and put it all together with his own hands. We had almost no money, so there was no hired labor; the devotees built the whole thing themselves. And on a wood-plank platform were the Deities.

To protect the Deities and Their paraphernalia, a devotee stood guard all night, but one night in April the devotee on duty fell asleep and some thieves slipped under the canvas and stole the Deities’ crowns and flute. There was no door—the pandal was really just a tent—so the robbers had just walked in, stepped over the sleeping brahmachari, taken the flute and crowns, and left.

When Prabhupada heard about the incident, he wrote me, “I have got some reports that the Deities in Bombay are being much neglected. This is most abominable affair. Radha and Krishna should not ever be neglected or left unprotected, so I am wondering what you have done to rectify this situation. I have heard that Madhudvisa intervened to get the Deities a better place, so he has done nicely.”

My mind was reeling. I was shaken to the core that Prabhupada had criticized me so severely, saying that the Deities were neglected and calling the situation abominable. Still, I tried to maintain my spirit and formulate a proper reply. “You are so merciful to take the time to chastise this useless soul,” I wrote. “My sluggishness and thoughtlessness are very shameful, and worst of all, before receiving your letter, I was so unconscious of them. But your absolute mercy is such that your chastisement is as good as your blessings. So I pray that my determination and enthusiasm shall not be shaken in trying to follow your instructions.

“As far as the Deities are concerned, from what I heard from Madhudvisa Maharaja, at the time of shifting the Deities the finishing touches on Nara Narayan’s pandal had not been completed, plus the pandal throne itself was not very pukka. But now highly decorative cloth has been puton the sides of the Deities’ house, and for Their protection we have had all-day watch by devotees, and three men sleeping around the Deities at night. Soon the new structure should be up, and until then we shall have all-night awake watch for the Deities, beginning tonight. The Deity room in the Khandelwal structure will be pukka, brick and sheets, with locking door. Right now there is problem of dust dirtying the Deity house, because the sides are open to wind, but the pujaris are very devoted, and in addition to big sewing work I have given a list of prospective donors for Deity things to one of our ladies.” (The Khandelwal structure was to be constructed with Khandelwal steel tubes, manufactured by a dear friend and supporter, the pious and prominent industrialist Biharilal Khandelwal.)

Prabhupada replied later that month: “I am glad to see that all of the programs are going on nicely, especially that the Deities are being cared for again properly. Now you give our ladies full facilities and help them by giving them money and other things wherever required by them so that our Deity program will not be lacking.”

I wrote back, “The Deity program is expanding, and nearly every day a new item appears on the altar. The Deities’ lotus has returned, dipped in silver. And the girls have arranged to purchase marble for the altar. Madri Dasi and others have already got three nice donations for Their Lordships. When the Deities are moved into Their new home, we will feel very relieved and encouraged.” And a week later I added, “1 think when Radha and Krishna move into Their new house, nobody will be able to resist Them.”

Along with the external arrangements, we were also working on our consciousness. “We are eagerly awaiting the completion of Their new home,” I wrote, “and meanwhile are trying to instill in the devotees more awareness of the Deities, meaning Radha and Krishna, the object of all of our service and love, Themselves in fact.”

Worshipping the Deities in the pandal was difficult. Narayani remembered, “Sometimes I would help with the Deity worship, and it was very austere, because the Deities were in a tent in an open field and there were big, huge winds. I would try to do arati, and the ghee wicks were always blowing out. It was hard to get through offering the lamp to all the Deities without having to light the ghee wicks at least five or six times.”

Sometimes the whole pandal swayed in the wind. Once, when Hari-kesa was alone watching the Deities, a strong gust blew the curtainsinto the ghee lamp, and the curtains, which were synthetic and highly flammable, caught fire. But it just so happened that Harikesa had been a New York fireman for five years, and he jumped up and ripped down the burning curtains and threw them on the ground.

For the monsoon season, we moved the Deities into a room we made for Them in the hut, with curtains opening into a small indoor pandal that served as our temple hall. I wrote Srila Prabhupada, “We had an ecstatic kirtan procession, with the blowing of conchshells and the throwing of flowers and grains, along with rosewater, for Their Lordships, to move Them to Their temporary pandal indoors.”

But with the crumbling floor and the rats and mosquitoes and other bugs, serving Them in the hut was also challenging and austere. Once, when rain came through the roof, Harikesa had to hold his raincoat over the Deities to protect Them. So having a proper, “semipermanent” place for the Deities was most essential.

“We often hear of devotees performing austerities for the sake of Deities,” Tamal Krishna said, “but on Hare Krishna Land the Deities performed austerities for the sake of the devotees.” And years later, Narayani made the same point: “Radha-Rasabihari performed more austerities than we did. It was like having the general out there on the battlefield: Krishna Himself was there with us to encourage us. He had to suffer the same as we did. That’s how you get encouragement—when the leaders stay there with you, doing everything you do. Prabhupada was like that, too.”

Srila Prabhupada encouraged me to proceed with the Deity program, but he also cautioned me to be careful. “If you have crowns dipped in gold for the Bombay Deities,” he wrote me, “you must keep them very carefully. I understand that some time ago one crown was stolen from Krishna’s head despite the presence of one brahmachari who was sleeping there and did not even hear the thief coming. So we must take very great precaution to always protect the Deities from all kinds of danger.” And a couple of weeks later, he added, “You should purchase one iron safe and keep the Deities’ jewelry or any valuables in that, or an iron closet, a little heavier, and you may keep either in my room or in some special room.”

It wasn’t for another week, until July 14, that I could finally write Prabhupada, “The Khandelwal structure is finished, and we are soon expecting the permits for the Deity house to be built attached to the Khandelwal... Behind the Deity room shall be the pujaris’ room, where we shall keep the Deities’ heavy iron closet cum safe, which we purchased yesterday.... Within a month the Deities’ house should be ready. At that time we shall move the Deities in a big celebration, with publicity, celebrities, and feasting.”

While we were struggling in the hut, Prabhupada was envisioning a grand future for Deity worship at Hare Krishna Land, in which we served Radha and Krishna with sincere and focused attention, thus attracting large numbers of people to Their lotus feet. “The Deity program must be improved very gorgeously,” he wrote. “Flower garlands should be expanded, and all expenditures for the Deities must be expanded without any miserly contemplation. Our temple should be so gorgeously decorated that we shall excel all Bombay temples. This is my idea. Try to fulfill it. When they hear that we decorate our Deities so gorgeously, people will throng, especially on festival days, like Janmastami, Jhulana Yatra, etc. So, four or five devotees should be always engaged in Deity worship.”

“\[I\]f we make our Deity worship program extremely opulent and gorgeous,” he had begun, “and if all of the devotees are always attending arati and holding kirtan in front of the Deities, that will be the best program for attracting the Indian people to Krishna Consciousness Movement. So, you try to give the pujaris all assistance to improve the standard of Deity worship and always render Radha and Krishna the most sincere attention.”

Shortly after the pandal program on the land (and Prabhupada’s departure to Australia), a young man came looking for me in the hut. He presented me a typed letter, addressed to the President of ISKCON, Bombay:

I have attended almost all the days of your dazzling display of aratik ceremonies, pravachans, kirtans, and transcendental dramas. It is all-attractive and all-effective, which has power to cleanse the heartsof the patitam (fallen) and remove all the dust accumulated for years together.

Your wonderful movement, Hare Krishna Movement, is meant for purification of hearts and leading the inhabitants of this planet towards the fulfilment of the goal of human life i.e. back to their natural home, back to Godhead, back to Krishna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

I wish to be a pure devotee of Krishna and develop my dormant love for Him. I want to be Krishna’s servant, because a valid life is a life of loving service to Krishna, and engage 24 hours a day in His devotional service.

But in this troubled age of Kali it is impossible to be a pure devotee by living in association with worldly, godless people, nondevotees, people who are interested in extracting happiness from matter, which is nothing but impossible. It is simply due to ignorance they are missing the center of seeking pleasure, Krishna.

In Bombay, Hare Krishna Land is the only place where the predominance of the mode of goodness is very easily felt. Of course, it is natural, because in the Hare Krishna Land, Krishna, the reservoir of pleasure, personally resides with His most dear servants, the devotees, who are non-different from Himself. And the land is just an external manifestation of Vaikuntha dhama, the Kingdom of God.

I wish to join you and make my life sublime. I know your four things which you abstain from, viz., no eating meat, fish or eggs, no illicit sex life, no intoxication including coffee, tea, pan, etc., and no gambling. Nowadays I am chanting the Mahamantra:

Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare  
Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare.

So I want to know the pre-qualifications and procedure how you make a new devotee and how he can get admission in your ashram. I expect admission at the earliest moment because, as you know, the moment which is not used in Krishna consciousness is a mere wastage of so valuable life time.

Excuse me, if while reading such material words it has created disturbance in your chanting.

Thanking you,

Hare Krishna,

Yours obediently,

Patil, R. B.

I was delighted by what I read. Perceiving how genuine—how humble and gentle and submissive—the man was, I waved the letter above my head, announced, “Hey, we’ve got a new bhakta!” and embraced him.

The “R.B.” stood for Raghunath Bhagwan. He had attended our pandal program at Cross Maidan and our most recent one, at Hare Krishna Land. In fact, he had taken many of the phrases in his letter from our publicity for the programs.

Bhakta Raghunath took naturally to the lifestyle of the devotees. As he later recalled, “I had a new home, a new uniform, new associates, a new program—almost everything was new to me. Nonetheless, I immediately embraced all of it and liked it. Although the devotees were mostly foreigners, I felt completely at home. I was determined to make this my life’s commitment.”

Raghunath had been a chemistry student at Kirti College in Dadar, Bombay, rooming with other young men from his village of Aravade, in southwest Maharashtra. A year earlier, he had tried to join Vinoba Bhave’s ashram, but he had never made it. His family had been aware of his inclination to join a spiritual community, so they had asked the young village men to keep an eye on him. During the pandal program, Raghunath had commuted between Dadar and Juhu, and his roommates hadn’t noticed anything different, but eventually, when he hadn’t come back after visiting the temple, they had looked for clues, found a handbill with our address, and alerted his family.

A week after Raghunath arrived, his older brother, with one of his previous roommates, came looking for him. His brother wanted him to visit the family, especially for the sake of their mother. If Raghunath didn’t go, he said, she might die. He assured Raghunath—and us—that the family would have no objection to Raghunath’s returning after the visit.

I was apprehensive. I suspected that Raghunath’s family would try to keep him with them, and I wasn’t sure how he would respond. Still, seeing Raghunath’s sincerity and also his respect for his older brother and concern for his mother, I gave him permission to go for one week.

Several days passed, then several weeks, and when Raghunath still hadn’t returned, my anxiety peaked. Finally, after a month, he came back, and we were jubilant. Many Indian devotees had come and gone, promising to return, but hardly any had actually come back, as family attachments in India were very strong.

When we asked Raghunath what had happened, he explained, “After I arrived in my village, people began saying that although I used to be such a nice boy, now something had gone wrong with me. I was wearing dhoti and kurta, chanting Hare Krishna, and avoiding the association of nondevotees, which the villagers considered strange and abnormal.

“My parents tried everything in their power to dissuade me from returning to the devotees. They even went to astrologers to learn some way to ‘cure’ me or to find out how long I would continue living this ‘strange type of life.’ They were really concerned.

“More than a week passed, yet no plans had been made for my return to the devotees, as per the original agreement with my brother. My parents kept telling me that some relative or other still had to come see me and that it wouldn’t be proper for me to leave without meeting him. My family planned to enlist the relatives to talk me out of becoming a sadhu. My parents tried everything on me, but my mind was fixed on going back to the devotees.

“When my family realized I wouldn’t give up the life I had embraced, they came up with the proposal that I could continue the life of a sadhu but do it in our village. They promised to build a small temple where I could do my devotional practices. I rejected this idea too, however, because I wanted to associate with the devotees. There was no question of leading a spiritual life without proper association, without the association of devotees who are practicing Krishna consciousness full-time. I didn’t want to be just another bogus sadhu. India was already overcrowded and overburdened with them. I wanted to engage in the service of Krishna in the Hare Krishna movement. I had sold my heart to Srila Prabhupada and Lord Krishna; Srila Prabhupada had already given me my life’s mission. So, finally, my family accepted the inevitable.”

Raghunath confided that since he had stayed in the village for such a long time, he wasn’t sure how I and the other devotees would respond to his return. So he was happily surprised to find himself so welcome, as welcome as before. “By the causeless mercy of Srila Prabhupada, my spiritual master, and Lord Krishna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead,” he declared, “my return to the devotees became possible.”

“ISKCON was the first institution I ever joined,” he reflected years later, “and Srila Prabhupada was the first and last spiritual master Iaccepted. And having joined ISKCON, the thought of leaving has never occurred in my mind?

To provide flowers for the Deities, Srila Prabhupada wanted us to cultivate a garden. He wrote me, “You can have the gardeners decorate the whole land with flowers and if possible some fruits also. Have a boundary fence so that everyone cannot enter it.” And a week later he added that he wanted Nara Narayan to take charge of the gardening. “Sometimes he may be difficult to live with,” he acknowledged, “but good manager means he is able to satisfy everyone and live in cooperative manner with all the devotees, so if you manage things nicely he can do tremendous work. Practically no one has more energy than Vishwakarma” (the demigod architect and master builder after whom he had nicknamed Nara Narayan).

When I wrote Prabhupada that the “Rose King” of India had offered us one thousand rose plants for free, he replied, “Utilize them nicely. There will be flowers for the Deities; it will be a great service.”

Nara Narayan engaged up to a dozen laborers daily and directed them in laying beds of manure and red soil and planting rose bushes, champac, jasmine, a kadamba tree, and various other flowers. He and Dravida planted a small forest of tulasi. And winding from shrub to shrub was an inlaid brick pathway, with benches on which devotees could sit and chant japa. I later reported to Prabhupada that Nara Narayan had “planted bushes, creepers, and flowers in a wonderfully attractive array of flowerbeds, bushes, and paths. In addition, he put up fence posts all around the garden, cleared wild brush from various places, and put up necessary walls and fences.”

Again Prabhupada instructed me, “Please give him all facility so he can make a good garden on all the vacant land on our property.”

In time, however, the difficulty of dealing with Nara Narayan did lead to conflict. I was in the hut one day with Jagat Purusa and Raghunath when Nara Narayan approached me for funds to make purchases for the garden. The temple was financially strapped, I told him, and there weren’t funds available at that time.

But Nara Narayan would not accept my response. Prabhupada had personally given him the service of creating a beautiful garden, he argued, and he needed money to carry out the service. He becameangry and accused me of obstructing him from carrying out his service to Prabhupada.

I tried to explain that there was nothing I could do until funds were available, but while my peaceful demeanor lessened the chance of Nara Narayan becoming physically violent, it also increased his frustration. His anger, spinning out of control, turned to rage—he seemed like he wanted to rip me apart—and he reared back and spat in my face.

In response, I simply wiped myself off and started chanting the maha-mantra as loudly as I could.

Raghunath, who was of a humble and sensitive nature, was so shocked to see this kind of hostile, aggressive behavior from a devotee that he fainted to the floor, at which point Jagat Purusa and I rushed over to revive and pacify him.

Nara Narayan was still fuming, but the tension in the room had eased, the atmosphere transformed by our concern for an innocent witness. And I bore no grudge against him. I knew that he was intent on his service to Srila Prabhupada and that he was dear to Prabhupada and Prabhupada was dear to him.

The life-membership program was one of Prabhupada’s most important programs in India and served as a means to distribute his books and engage leading people in devotional service. The first appeal was designed and printed by Shyamasundar. It featured a photo of Prabhupada’s face superimposed on a picture of the globe and expressed the mood and intention of the program: Become a member of Srila Prabhupada’s worldwide family. Our homes are your homes.

When Prabhupada first introduced life membership, Tamal Krishna pointed out to him that the value of the books we gave the members would eventually exceed the 1,111 rupees members were committing to pay. Prabhupada replied, “The devotees will keep going back to them, and in their lifetimes they will give five or ten times more than the membership subscription.” We would continue to make new members, he said, and thus we would always keep ahead. He had devised the program as a way to distribute his books. If we just piled them on a prospective member’s desk, he told us, the person would agree to become a member.

Many life members went on to become our biggest supporters in India, financially and in other ways. Still, Gargamuni complained to

Prabhupada that we were not making devotees in India—we were just making life members, who gave their money, but not devotees, who gave their lives.

Prabhupada encouraged him not to feel depressed. Making someone a life member, he assured him, was practically as good as making him a devotee:

“Our business is to chant, so the time that Indian \[people take\] to come to hear our chanting and arati and take prasada means that your preaching work is actually successful. For the time being we should be satisfied with that. And if they become devotees, that is very nice. The only difficulty is the Indians think, What we have to learn from the Americans? So the best thing is to somehow or other make them members and raise funds for our activities. When someone pays, it means he is converted. Somehow or other he has to render some service, so if you can collect money from him, that means practically they are becoming our disciples. So do not become spiritually depressed. Actually these things are going forward very progressively there in India, and I am very much thankful to you all my sincere disciples, especially the elder disciples and sannyasis like your good self, for assisting me in this great mission of reviving the original Krishna Consciousness atmosphere in India. Do not worry, in time we shall be completely successful.” (Letter dated June 8,1972)

The membership program was a practical application of the fourth verse of Srila Rupa Gosvami’s Upadesamrta, for reciprocating with the members in exchanges of love:

dadati pratigrhnati  
guhyam akhydti prcchati  
bhunkte bhojayate caiva  
sad-vidham priti-laksanam

“Offering gifts in charity, accepting charitable gifts, revealing one’s mind in confidence, inquiring confidentially, accepting prasada, and offering prasada are the six symptoms of love shared by one devotee and another.”

In his purport, Prabhupada applied the verse directly to life membership: “The International Society for Krishna Consciousness has been established to facilitate these six kinds of loving exchanges betweendevotees. This Society was started single-handedly, but because people are coming forward and dealing with the give-and-take policy, the Society is now expanding all over the world. We are glad that people are donating very liberally to the development of the Society’s activities, and people are also eagerly accepting whatever humble contribution we are giving them in the shape of books and magazines dealing strictly with the subject matter of Krsna consciousness. We sometimes hold Hare Krsna festivals and invite life members and friends to participate in the feasting by accepting prasada. Although most of our members come from the higher rungs of society, they nonetheless come and take whatever little prasada we are able to offer them. Sometimes the members and supporters inquire very confidentially about the methods of performing devotional service, and we try to explain this. In this way our Society is successfully spreading all over the world, and the intelligentsia of all countries is gradually appreciating our Krsna conscious activities. The life of the Krsna conscious society is nourished by these six types of loving exchange among the members; therefore people must be given the chance to associate with the devotees of ISKCON because simply by reciprocating in the six ways mentioned above an ordinary man can fully revive his dormant Krsna consciousness.”

Making someone a life member was practically as good as making him a devotee. The more care and affection we gave the life members, the more they would reciprocate and want to support our cause. And the more they engaged in devotional service, the more they enhanced their spiritual lives.

The first of the six kinds of loving exchanges is dadati: giving gifts. The greatest gift is the holy name, which at first many people were unable to accept, but we also gave them other, more tangible gifts. I would carry maha-prasada sweets and tulasi leaves in a silver box, and I would always bring a Krishna conscious book, cassette tape, or picture. The Back to Godhead (BTG) subscriptions also served to both enliven and impress our members, and Prabhupada said that the whole purpose of the magazine was to get people to chant Hare Krishna. In Bombay he also instructed us to send a monthly newsletter to the members,informing them of developments in the movement, “so they don’t think we’re dead,” and we developed a regular local publication with news, announcements, advertisements, and our yearly audited accounts.

Sometimes we would also give members specially selected gifts. And I tried to enlist the help of devotees in America to arrange a steady supply and to ensure that members were nicely cared for when they visited our centers abroad. As I informed Srila Prabhupada by post, “I have written Rupanuga, Karandhara, Bhagavan, and Satsvarupa Prabhus that they could help get donations for Indian projects indirectly by providing first-class treatment for life members who visit USA, as the grateful members will certainly express their satisfaction with our movement when they return to India. Life members and others are or will be mad after our gramophone records and art posters, so if they could be sent free, like the books, the members will be enthusiastic to give more by donation and we can make money also on direct door-to-door sales. So I have written Jayatirtha Prabhu in LA to send posters, and if you confirm that a quantity of them be sent here, I am sure they will be useful for selling. Similarly, the life members love our Radha-Krishna ‘postage stamps,’ and I hope they could be sent also.”

The entire basis of our relationship with the donors was our encouraging them in Krishna consciousness. If we had had any other motive, they would have perceived our duplicity and the sublime quality of our relationship would have been spoiled.

The next exchange is pratigrhnati: accepting gifts. When I engaged in dadati, giving gifts, I tried not to be too anxious about pratigrhnati, accepting gifts in return. I was convinced that if we helped people advance spiritually, Krishna would be pleased, and that if Krishna was pleased, others would also be pleased—and our mission would be successful. Pratigrhnati would follow automatically when the relationship was sufficiently developed along the other five principles of loving exchanges.

As a rule, after giving someone a gift I would never accept any payment or donation on the spot, even if the person offered. I asked only later, when we needed substantial help for some major project. And by then most people were already eager and glad to help.

The approach worked, and I saw it work elsewhere as well. One young congregational devotee from Bombay went to a rural ISKCON community in America and took over the management of the temple’s guesthouse. When, instead of charging for the rooms, he focused on caring for the guests and then asked for donations at the end of their stay, the guesthouse revenues went up four-fold.

The next exchange is bhojayate: giving prasada. Prabhupada taught us to hold feasts on Sundays and other special days and to make a special effort to invite our friends and members. He personally organized the first life-member feast in Juhu and had his disciples, who were acting as hosts, perform all the services for the members, whom we treated as honored guests.

Later, whenever Prabhupada received special guests, he would insist that they take full prasada. Sometimes the guests protested, “We cannot take prasada in front of you, Srila Prabhupada,” but he always insisted, “No, I will be happy to see you take prasada!"

“If you give a man full prasada!" he once said, “he will do anything for you.”

In his absence, when special guests came for a feast, I would often sit and talk with them, direct the serving, and try to see that they were satisfied in every respect.

The next two exchanges are guhyam akhyati prcchati: inquiring about and explaining confidential topics. While giving gifts and prasada, I always tried to explain the confidential science of Krishna consciousness and give donors a solid philosophical background for further devotional service. And when the time came to engage a person in some particular service, I would present the rationale for the service on the basis of reason and philosophy and disclose the request in a straightforward manner. I would endeavor to present our philosophy intelligently, without compromise, but keeping in mind the understanding of the individual whom I was addressing.

From my seniors, I learned to detect prospective supporters’ doubts even without their expressing them—and then speak in such a way as to remove them. During my initial training in Bombay, I went with Madhudvisa to meet a wealthy businessman who had promised tobecome a life member, but when we were in the man’s office, he reneged. I had expected Madhudvisa to say, “You promised to give. You can’t refuse now.” But instead, he just talked with the man for twenty minutes. Then, almost mystically (to me), the man opened his desk drawer and wrote out his check.

When I first went out on my own and approached an industrialist to become a life member, the man said, “First I have to ask my brothers.”

When I reported this to Shyamasundar, who had given me the industrialist’s name and sent me, he told me, “That’s just an excuse. You have to be intelligent enough to understand the person’s doubts and address them without him even bringing them up.”

After visiting someone many times with gifts and inviting him to Juhu for prasada, which naturally involved his or her seeing Hare Krishna Land, I might feel that the time had come to engage them in some particular, substantial service.

Whenever I did make a request, I would keep in mind Prabhupada’s instructions on how ISKCON supporters could engage in dadati. During one of our first meetings with life members in Bombay, he quoted Srimad-Bhagavatam (10.22.35):

etavaj janma-saphalyam  
dehinam iha dehisu  
pranair arthair dhiya vaca  
sreya-acaranam sada

“It is the duty of every living being to perform welfare activities for the benefit of others with his life, wealth, intelligence, and words.”

He explained that first of all, as individual living parts and parcels of the Supreme Lord, people had a duty to give pranair, their life. But if someone was unable to give his life, at least he should give his wealth, because next to our life we most valued our wealth. The combined effort of one’s intelligence, words, and time produced wealth, so by giving his wealth, the person would automatically be giving his intelligence, words, and time—in a concentrated form. And if the person gave his wealth to Krishna, we could also say that the entire effort that produced the wealth was purified and spiritualized.

When we asked people to contribute, Prabhupada told us, some might challenge, “How can you sell God?” In reply, he said, we should quote the Bhagavad-gita (9.27):

yat karosi yad asnasi  
yaj juhosi dadasi yat  
yat tapasyasi kaunteya  
tat kurusva mad-arpanam

“Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give away, and whatever austerities you perform—do that, О son of Kunti, as an offering to Me?

“And if you have no wealth?” Prabhupada advised that we should say, “Then you can give your intelligence. You can advise the devotees, Approach such-and-such person; he can help.’ In this way you can serve by dhiya, intelligence.

“And if you have no intelligence? Then help by vaca, words. You can request whomever you meet, ‘Please chant Hare Krishna. Please visit the temple.’”

Shyamasundar told me that the wealthy were accustomed to people coming to them for their money, so naturally they were on the defensive. I didn’t want them to feel that way with me. And when they saw that I actually cared for them, they became more open and relaxed. With the close ones, whenever there was a death or wedding or other major event, I was always there.

Once, I approached one of our friends for a large donation for Juhu, but he was hesitating. Finally I said, “So many people are coming to visit you, but who is thinking of you? They are simply thinking of their own benefit—how they can exploit you, what they can get from you. Perhaps we are the only ones in the world who actually care for your spiritual well-being.”

And as soon as he heard these words, he agreed: “Yes. I will give.”

When we reciprocated in these exchanges of love with our members, both they and we made spiritual advancement. We had only to be concerned for their spiritual well-being, how somehow or other they could be engaged in service to the lotus feet of Krishna. In reciprocation for our sincerity and love, they responded.

Prabhupada once said, “When you speak to people and by your speaking they are convinced that by giving to Krishna they will gain, they will volunteer some service.” Later, I considered that in some cases people were seeking spiritual benefit and in other cases they were hoping for material blessings through pious deeds—or both. People came to Krishna for different reasons. Although we didn’t encourage the concept of getting material results for devotional service, people did sometimes come with that mentality, and we engaged them too.

Prabhupada emphasized that when we went to preach or collect, we should be humble, and he often quoted Sri Prabodhananda Sarasvati:

dante nidhaya trnakam padayor nipatya  
kaku-satam krtva caham bravimi  
he sadhavah sakalam eva vihdya durad  
caitanya-candra-carane kurutanuragam

“Taking a straw between my teeth and falling at your feet a hundred times, I humbly submit, ‘O great personality, please give up all mundane knowledge that you have learned and just submit yourself at the lotus feet of Lord Caitanya Mahaprabhu.’” (Caitanya-candramrta 8.90)

In a conversation in Juhu Prabhupada elaborated: “You have to create faith. That is preaching. . . . Padayor nipatya kaku-satam krtva caham bravimi: ‘I fall down on your feet, and I am flattering you with folded hands.’ ‘Why? Why? What do you want to say?’ ‘Yes, I have to say something.’ ‘What is that? Say it! Why you are becoming so humble?’ ‘Yes, I have something to say.’ ‘What? Say it!’ ‘He sadhavah. You are a very nice sadhu. But now you please forget all nonsense. He sadhavah sakalam eva vihdya durad. Whatever nonsense you have learned, forget.’ ‘Then what to do?’ 'Caitanya-candra-carane kurutanuragam. You just become a devotee of Lord Chaitanya. I am flattering you, I am falling down on your feet’— this is preaching.”

“If you approach people and say, ‘Everything belongs to Krishna, and I am Krishna’s representative, so give everything to me—otherwise, you are a thief, and you will be punished,”’ Prabhupada told us. “They may become angry: ‘What do you mean? I have worked hard for my money. It belongs to me.’ But if you approach them humbly and say, ‘Dear sir, I have come begging at your doorstep. Kindly give some donation forour temple', they will respond, ‘Oh, a beggar has come. Let me give him something? ”

Some people were so averse that we had to be very tactful and induce them to engage in devotional service without their being aware that they were serving Krishna. Still, they would benefit. Prabhupada told the story of a young student who stubbornly refused to learn arithmetic. So instead of asking the boy what 4 + 4 equaled, the teacher drew a picture of two cows and asked how many legs the two cows had. And through pictures and stories she gradually taught the boy all the arithmetical processes. When a classmate of the boy told him, “Hey, the teacher is teaching you arithmetic!” the boy replied, “Arithmetic? I hate arithmetic. No, I shall not learn!”

My task was, somehow or other, to engage people in Krishna’s service and help them to advance in Krishna consciousness (yena tena prakarena manah krsne nivesayet).

In ISKCON, members and donors became part of a spiritual family and got the association of devotees, which was essential for their spiritual development. Unfortunately, some life members took undue advantage of our generosity, and Prabhupada, ever vigilant, made a few adjustments to the rules. “The following scheme should be followed henceforth,” he wrote to me from Vrindavan in 1975. “We have Guest Rooms and Devotee Rooms. The Guest Rooms can be used by anyone who pays the fees, in advance. Any Life Member can live in a Guest Room for a period not exceeding three days free of charge. If he wants to stay with us longer for any reason, then he may move to the Devotee Rooms, where he must live as we do, following all devotional practices as we do.” Or he could pay the fees to stay longer in a guest room.

Prabhupada also saw life membership as a way of engaging his disciples. As stated in the Padma Purana and quoted in the Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu, the basic principle of vaidhi-sadhana-bhakti is to always remember Krishna and never forget Him:

smartavyah satatam visnur  
vismartavyo na jatucit  
sarve vidhi-nisedhah syur  
etayor eva kinkarah

“Krsna is the origin of Lord Visnu. He should always be remembered and never forgotten at any time. All the rules and prohibitions mentioned in the sastras should be the servants of these two principles.”

Prabhupada explained in his purport to the verse (quoted as Cc Madhya 22.113):

“One may sell books or enlist life members or render some other service, but these duties are not ordinary duties. These duties serve as an impetus for remembering Krsna. When one goes with a sankirtana party or sells books, he naturally remembers that he is going to sell Krsna’s books. In this way, he is remembering Krsna. When one goes to enlist a life member, he talks about Krsna and thereby remembers Him. Smartavyah satatam visnur vismartavyo na jatucit. The conclusion is that one must act in such a way that he will always remember Krsna, and one must refrain from doing things that make him forget Krsna. These two principles form the basic background of Krsna consciousness.”

Thus, in conjunction with chanting sixteen rounds and following the regulative principles, going to enlist life members and speaking about Krishna consciousness was a way of remembering Krishna.

Understanding the importance of cultivating relationships with donors, when we enrolled life member number 1,000 in Bombay, I decided to stop making new members and just concentrate on maintaining the ones we had (though things did not work out exactly that way). I understood that the principle of care and cultivation was what was truly important and always remembered how Prabhupada welcomed and encouraged us, despite our coming from wretched conditions and being full of bad habits. He listened patiently to our trials and tribulations, sympathized with us and appreciated us, and tactfully engaged us in the six exchanges of love.

Now I was in a position to help people in their spiritual lives. And they could contribute so much to the mission. I would remember my own fallen condition and try to please Srila Prabhupada by caring for our special friends in the same way as he would have cared for them— the same way he cared for us. I felt that I had to be ready to give myself to the members in the way Prabhupada had said: “To make one devotee, we must spend gallons of blood.”

Prabhupada gave strict instructions that the membership contributions should be deposited 50 percent in his book fund and 50 percent in his building fund—and not spent on maintenance. Thus there would always be funds to print and supply more books and to build temples. Once, I met a very intelligent gentleman in his home in the Juhu Scheme—he had been with Gandhi in the freedom movement—and when I mentioned Prabhupada’s 50-50 policy, he said that it was brilliant, perfect. He mentioned some other party that had applied a similar 50-50 policy and gotten tremendous results. I felt gratified to hear that such a wise elder had appreciated Prabhupada’s genius.

One of the activities that Srila Prabhupada emphasized most for Juhu was the distribution of prasada. In the Bhagavad-gita (9.26), Lord Krishna explains:

patram puspam phalam toyam  
yo me bhaktya prayacchati  
tad aham bhakty-upahrtam  
asnami prayatatmanah

“If one offers Me with love and devotion a leaf, a flower, fruit or water, I will accept it.”

According to the Gita (3.13), if one eats food without first offering it to Krishna, one must suffer reactions, and if one eats food offered to Krishna, one is released from reactions.

yajna-sistasinah santo  
mucyante sarva-kilbisaih  
bhunjate te tv agham papa  
ye pacanty atma-karanat

“The devotees of the Lord are released from all kinds of sins because they eat food which is offered first for sacrifice. Others, who prepare food for personal sense enjoyment, verily eat only sin.”

Soon after Prabhupada left Juhu, I wrote him, “Progress here has been encouraging. On Sunday we began the prasada distribution program, and over a hundred children, and many poor adults, partook. Daily our friends are bringing ten to twenty small bags of rice, etc., andbesides, Dravida Prabhu and others are collecting larger quantities from merchants. On the weekend we go to the nearby apartments to collect the weekly ‘biksha, alms.’”

Prabhupada replied, “This prasadam distribution item is very, very important, and it is so much pleasing to me that in the beginning so many children are coming for taking prasadam, and that supply of rice has come automatically. Please continue this program rigidly. By prasadam distribution you will do service to the Lord, and the public will be pleased upon you as well. Gradually increase the number of guests, and don’t deny anyone. Continue in this way: Whatever is there, distribute equally—it may not be very sumptuous, but no one should be denied equal portion.... Anyone is open to take our prasadam free.”

And in his next message he again stressed the program’s importance: “This food distribution program is to be done very, very nicely, as I have already written in my last letter. Generally people make a plea that why are there so many hungry and naked. So we invite all hungry and naked people to come to us and we will give them food and clothing and Krishna consciousness as well. This will attract the general public and there will never be any shortage of foodstuffs, so continue regularly. In Bombay there are many generous persons who like food distribution programs, and actually, our temple should be the via media for feeding the poor with food and spiritual knowledge. Our Bombay program should be based on giving Krishna consciousness through the English medium and distribution of prasadam without any discrimination. This will enhance our prestige and will accelerate our spiritual life as well. The temple program of arati, kirtan, bhoga offerings, discourses, etc., should continue. There should be no neglect of that program.

“So far as your hired Brahmin cook, since we have our prasadam distribution program this may be necessary, but he must be clean, no smoking, and he must wear kunti \[neck\] beads. As far as possible he must follow our principles.”

When Jagat Purusa came through Juhu on his way to Mayapur to help with the construction and saw the situation, he asked me why we had a hired cook. When I told him that we did not have devotees willing to do the service, he replied, “If you like, I could stay for a month or twoand learn how to cook in this situation, and once I do that, I could try to encourage some other devotees to come in to help.”

So, for about two weeks Jagat Purusa was trained, in his words, “by this person who had a very sweet personality but just didn’t have the standard of cleanliness that Srila Prabhupada insisted upon in cooking for the Deities, and it was quite a grueling schedule. We would come into the kitchen at about seven in the morning and wind things up at about ten-thirty at night. We were cooking seven offerings a day for the Deities, with one extra offering for the prasada distribution. After a couple of weeks, I felt that I could handle the service, and Subal Prabhu, a devotee who was mostly confined to a wheelchair, assisted, especially in rolling chapatis. From that time onward, from what I thought would be maybe a month or two, I was in the kitchen. It was a very austere service—not only were the conditions austere, but the heat! I arrived in April, and April, May, and the beginning of June mark the hottest time of the year, just before the monsoons. It could be 120 degrees outside, and you can imagine inside the chdtdi hut, where we had the pilot stove and the open fire for the chapatis—it was unbelievably hot.”

And yet, within the external agony, there was internal ecstasy. “Once,” Jagat Purusa described, “the heat was so incredibly intense that it was unbearable. I didn’t know what to do; there were no fans, and there was no place to go to get out of the heat. I had been in the kitchen and had just finished the noon, raja-bhoga, offering, so it was the height of the day—it was just unbelievable. When I came out of the ten-foot-by-ten-foot cooking area after cleaning up, dripping with sweat, I sat down in the main area of the hut and was trying to chant my rounds. I was probably nodding off, I was so exhausted, and I was lamenting because I was suffering, and then suddenly I admonished myself, ‘What’s wrong with you, feeling sorry for yourself? You are thinking just about yourself. You should think about the little picture of the Deities here in the hut.’ I told myself, ‘Don’t worry about yourself! Think about Their comfort! They are also here.’ So, with that thought, I picked up a peacock fan, or maybe a bamboo fan—some kind of fan, something I found—and I was fanning this picture of Radha-Rasabihari, and though there was no breeze, within a few minutes I experienced thisunbelievable coolness—this wonderful, wonderful coolness—come over me. I wasn’t hot anymore! The temperature had not changed—nothing had changed—just my consciousness, by Srila Prabhupada’s mercy.”

As it turned out, Jagat Purusa, who thought he would stay in Juhu for only one or two months before going on to Mayapur, remained for ten years.

As eager as Prabhupada was for us to do prasada distribution, he also wanted us to do it in the right way, with the proper understanding. In my next letter to him I presented some mistaken ideas: “The kirtan, food distribution, and English-medium school programs are going on. There are not so many poor people in Juhu, so I suggested that we could build a bigger clientele if we distributed daily, and now we are feeding about 200 people daily but not more. Otherwise, we can try an ad campaign for free prasada on the weekends or take food into poor areas.”

Prabhupada immediately clarified, “So far as prasada distribution, it is not a question of rich or poor. That will be karma-kanda. Our program therefore is that we offer prasada to everyone. Make our temple so nice that everyone who comes is offered some prasada. Not that we are after poor men. It is nice that we are feeding 200 daily, but gradually try to increase. But do not advertise, we shall be self-advertising. And do not go to poor areas, this is not our philosophy. Our philosophy is prasada distribution, without discrimination of rich or poor.”

He wanted us to collect and distribute profusely, but he did not want any prasada wasted. “Waste not, want not,” he sometimes quoted. He wrote to Mahamsa, “If you continue this prasada distribution and keep yourselves as good Vaishnavas, you will be overflooded with foodstuffs. One thing, don’t prepare excess, you must have some idea in advance. We should not spoil anything, better to give to poor men or to animals. Suppose I give you something and you throw it away—I will not be very pleased. So if God gives us our daily bread and we throw it away, that is not very pleasing to Him.”

Dravida was tireless in going out and collecting grains and other ingredients for prasada distribution. He would go out after breakfast— sometimes even before—and return late in the afternoon. After some time, we made Raghunath, who by then had been initiated as Lokanath,his assistant. Lokanath would accompany him to the grain and spice market and translate for him, and sometimes Dravida would send him door to door.

“Dravida Prabhu took me downtown to the Bombay grain market to get dal and other ingredients donated,” Lokanath later remembered. “There was one important ingredient they didn’t sell in the markets, for which we had to go door to door—rice. Somehow there was a shortage of rice in India at the time, and it was not available in the open market. It was being rationed to families a few kilos at a time, so the only way for us to get it was by doing madhukari, begging a little from each home, and that became my service.” (In his purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 5.1.17, Prabhupada explains, "Madhukari . . . literally means ‘the profession of the bumblebees.’ As bumblebees collect honey from many flowers, a little from each, so a \[mendicant\] should beg from door to door but not accept very much . . . from any particular house; he should collect a little bit from every house.”)

“I took a shoulder bag and went knocking on doors and ringing bells at all the houses and apartments in the Juhu area. Madhukari means that at some places you will be honored and dishonored in others. At some houses they opened the door and I could make my appeal. But at some houses they would just look through the little hole in the door, and I would have to shout out who I was and what was my business. Sometimes they gave a quarter, half, or even a full kilo of rice; other times they would slam the door in my face as soon as they saw I was a sadhu begging. Sometimes I had the opportunity to preach and invite them to the temple for kirtan or prasada, and even to sell a few of the small books I brought with me. A few times they set their dog on me, or called their chowkidar (guard), to get rid of me. If it were not for Srila Prabhupada’s pleasure, I never would have done such a thing. It was a traditional, glorious, and purifying experience for me in my new status—beggar in Bombay.”

Prabhupada wrote Mahamsa, “You may give Dravida as much help as he may require to canvas big men in Bombay for collecting the foodstuffs. It is very important that important men in Bombay cooperate with us in this prasada distribution, and they will be always very glad to give for our worthy cause.”

I expressed my appreciation of Dravida to Prabhupada in a letter: “Dravida Prabhu has matured very greatly by taking on big jobs as temple commander and in charge of prasada distribution. Even life members attend regularly.” And in my next letter I wrote, “I have given two men to help Dravida Prabhu in the food distribution program, as Doug and George alternate, one going out with Dravida Prabhu for collecting foodstuffs, and the other Prabhu remaining to help in the kitchen and oversee the actual distribution to the people. (After a brief slump, the attendance for noon prasadam is again up to 50-60 daily.) Jagat Purusa Prabhu is the head cook.” (Three weeks later, Doug was initiated as Dhumrakesh, and George was initiated as Gokulachandra.)

Prabhupada replied, “So far as foodstuffs, you should collect profusely. If you collect more, distribute more, and if you collect less, distribute less, but only distribute what you have collected. If there is no food, do not contribute our own funds for this purpose. Try to collect more.”

A Christian neighbor, Anita, who later joined our staff, was a fortunate recipient of prasada. “Actually,” she recalled, “we used to come here for prasada. They used to have prasada distribution, and we were staying in this village, and this used to be on our way to the Juhu beach. Then, whenever they used to be distributing the chira (flat rice) or suji, halavah, we used to come and take. Once,” she added, “I had a glance of Srila Prabhupada.”

Brahmananda recounted, “One evening Prabhupada was giving out prasada to all these kids. I said, ‘Oh, Prabhupada, let me do it,’ and I went to take the plate from him. Prabhupada looked at me and said, ‘I will do it.’ He was actually giving mercy. That was his mission. This is our program—to worship Krishna and take Krishna’s prasada. In New York in 1966, it was an apple, a cut apple, and here it was just some fruit and halavah. But this was Prabhupada’s program—very simple but very deep. And Prabhupada gave it his full attention. He wasn’t doing it in some offhand, quick way; he was very deliberate.”

Visakha added, “Prabhupada pointed out in his talks that even wellto-do people would come to get this prasadam. They didn’t need it, they weren’t in need of food, but they valued it as something spiritual, something that could help them in their spiritual life. And this, Prabhupada said, was the purpose of prasadam. It’s not just an altruistic activity that we give prasadam to poor people or destitute people. We can do that,but prasadam is for everyone, because spiritually we are all poor, we are all destitute. We need this mercy from Krishna, and Prabhupada was very generous about it. The children would sometimes come two or even three times, and Prabhupada would smile and wag his finger at them, but he would give them again and again.”

As Smriti Warrier remembered, “In the temporary temple, after his lecture, Prabhupada used to give prasada. He’d give it once, and I would still stand there, and he would motion, ‘Go away,’ and I would still stand with my hand—‘I want more.’”

“We like everyone,” Prabhupada explained on a morning walk. “We do not reject anyone. A dog cannot understand the philosophy; therefore we call him and give some prasadam. Therefore prasada distribution is one of our programs—for everyone. Yes. We are not neglectful—‘Because he is dog, therefore he should be neglected.’ No. He should be given.”

In our glossy brochure, we advertised prasada distribution as part of the Juhu project: “There is this specific statement in the Padma Purana: ‘A person who honors prasadam and regularly eats it, not exactly in front of the Murti, along with caranamrtam, immediately can achieve the results of pious activities which are obtained through ten thousand performances of sacrificial rites.’

“Whoever comes to Hare Krishna Land, whether curious, distressed, in need of money, or wise, one and all are invited to sing, dance, and feast on sumptuous prasadam. This process of Krishna consciousness is so sublime that just by partaking of prasadam it is possible to make advancement in spiritual life. Our massive prasadam distribution programs are being continued regularly for any hungry living entities. In this way thousands of people, regardless of their position, are being joyously fed. Muslims, Christians, and Hindus, rich and poor are sitting side by side and accepting the remnants of foodstuffs from the Lord.

“‘The whole material world is full of hungry living beings. The hunger is not for good food, shelter, defense, or sense gratification. The hunger is for spiritual atmosphere. The foolish leaders cannot see that even the people who are most sumptuously materialistically satisfied are still hungry; and what is that poverty? This hunger is actually for spiritual food, spiritual shelter, spiritual defense, and spiritual sensegratification. Such things can be obtained in the association of the Supreme Spirit, Lord Sri Krishna? Srimad Bhagwatam, purport to 1.12.6 by A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada.”

After appointing me temple president of the Juhu project, Srila Prabhupada was also, while contending with many other formidable challenges, faced with the task of training me on the job to be a manager, even though it wasn’t really my nature. For me, dealing with so many devotees was a challenge. Many were senior to me, many were more materially qualified than I, many were new to me (and to India), and many had natures, backgrounds, conceptions, and moods that were much different from mine. And being as inexperienced and unqualified as I was, I was unable to engage and satisfy the devotees as Prabhupada would have wanted.

And so, within a month of his leaving Bombay, Prabhupada was endeavoring, by letter, to train me to actually lead and manage—to mold me into a more useful instrument in his and Krishna’s hands. He sometimes said that the first duty of the leader, or manager, or government, was to see that everyone was engaged (Nara Narayan being one example).

Three days after his directions to me about the gardening, Prabhupada wrote again, chiding me and instructing me how to manage and engage the devotees. And after explaining my duty as a leader, he also delineated the followers’ duties. He knew our natures, and he was simultaneously engaging and training us all. “I have received reports from Mahamsa and Cyavana,” he wrote, “and it appears they are doing nicely. Some of the men, however, are complaining they have no sufficient engagement. Two girls have already left Bombay, and their complaint was that they had no sufficient engagement. Similarly, I have received letters from Puranjana, Vardhana, and Atmarama, and either they are not willing to work according to direction or, otherwise, how do they complain there is no sufficient engagement? I think there is more than sufficient engagement for everyone. We have got so much to do. We have to deal with so many men with different personalities. So kindly utilize their energies and at the same time keep them satisfied. That is leadership. If one man is appointed as leader, all must follow him and beobedient. ‘Obedience is the first law of discipline? They are pointing out irregularities, but they themselves are not doing their duty, so they are pointing out the irregularities in others. They came to serve; now they don’t want to serve, so there is some excuse. Oh, irregularity, let me go away. The workers should not suggest irregularities.”

Above all, he reminded me—and all of us—of our greater mission, our higher responsibility: to reclaim the fallen souls on behalf of Krishna. “So actually we have taken a very responsible task on behalf of the Supreme Personality of Godhead,” he wrote. “At the present moment, to speak the truth, the whole population of the world are demons and animals. It may be a very strong aspersion on the people of the world, but this is the fact. But still, because they are part and parcel of the Supreme Lord, so originally they were pure, and therefore it is the mission of Krishna to get back His parts and parcels to home, exactly like a father likes to get back his son at home because this son had gone out of home for false happiness. But the people are so mad, they are talking so many nonsense things—nonsense philosophy, nonsense science—and our task is to meet all of them and at the same time pacify them in their lunatic condition. So I am sure you are a very good soul to act on behalf of Krishna, and do it nicely. Krishna will give you the proper intelligence. He is sitting in your heart. Simply, He wants to see us working sincerely.”

Still, I was affected by all the criticism—from the other devotees and most of all from Prabhupada himself. And Prabhupada, understanding my heart, in his next letter explained his service to me in such a way that I could appreciate his criticism, which was clearly meant for my benefit. “Actually,” he wrote, “it is the duty of the spiritual master to find fault with his students so that they may make progress, not that he should always be praising them. So if you find some criticism, kindly accept it in that spirit. I am only interested in that you along with all my other students should become Krishna conscious.”

His words and sincere desire acted upon my heart and influenced me to improve my efforts, and I reported to him about some of the progress I—we—had made. In his next letter he expressed his appreciation for my efforts and reinforced his earlier statements about management, encouraging me to continue in the same spirit: “I am glad to hear your explanation how the men are being engaged there in Bombay. Thatwill be the test of your management, how well the men are satisfied by their engagements. I am very glad to hear that Nara Narayan is doing so much work and that Puranjana has decided to remain there. He has decided rightly.”

Seeing things from the perspective of shastra and reminding us of our highest goals and the means to attain them, through parampara, in his next letter he wrote, “Yes, by Krishna’s grace we have a very responsible task before us, so combinedly we should do it nicely so that everything goes on systematically. Rupa Goswami says that the things are enthusiasm, patience, conviction, acting exactly to the order of the sastra and guru, and always keeping oneself in the society of devotees, and this makes our devotional service successful. So our serious students should follow Rupa Goswami’s advice.”

One day in early May, Mr. Nair came in his car to take me to meet our solicitor, K.M. Diwanji. He was in the back seat on the right, I ended up in the middle, and he had arranged for a woman to sit next to me on my left. I didn’t really want to sit next to a woman, but I was so intimidated by the whole situation—I was new, and Nair was a big man in Bombay as well as the owner of the land—that I just went along with it.

Soon after I got in, however, the woman put her hand on my leg, then my upper leg, making her way higher. I didn’t know what was going on, but I was twenty-four years old, and my mind and senses were in a tizzy. I thought I might just give in. But then I considered that when news of the incident got out, our position as a movement would be weakened and Srila Prabhupada’s mission would be compromised. I thought, I can't hurt Srila Prabhupada like this. So, even though for myself I was ready to throw caution to the wind, for the sake of Srila Prabhupada, I couldn’t. Then I realized how powerful Prabhupada’s mercy was, that I actually loved him more than I loved myself, because I was ready to do something that would hurt me personally but wasn’t prepared to do something that would hurt him. Srila Prabhupada invested so much trust and love in us, his young disciples, and gave us so much responsibility, that we wanted to rise to the occasion and not disappoint him. (Later I found out that the woman was a well-known prostitute in Juhu, and thereafter I was careful to stay away from her, though she sometimes came to the Juhu land looking for me.)

At the solicitor’s office I was surprised to see how friendly Nair and Diwanji were with each other. After all, I was Diwanji’s client—not Nair. Then Diwanji advised me to pay more money to Nair, which at that stage was not required, and timid or simple as I was, I paid an additional Rs. 7,500.

When I informed Srila Prabhupada about the payment, he wrote, “What is the Rs. 7,500/- paid to Mr. Nair? On what account that is paid?”

“The Rs. 7,500/- paid to Mr. Nair is on account of final payment for the property,” I replied. “Mr. Diwanji said, ‘When you are paying lakhs, what is that?’ when I mentioned I actually did not have to pay until the conveyance.” The combination of Diwanji’s friendliness with Nair and his cavalier attitude toward our unnecessarily paying Nair another Rs. 7,500/-, a significant amount for us, should have alerted me to the fact that they were in cahoots, but I was too intimidated by the situation to formulate, what to speak of express, that idea.

One of the conditions for the purchase of the land was that we obtain permission from the charity commissioner. As stated in Clause 11 of the sales agreement, “If the Charity Commissioner does not grant the said consent, then this agreement will stand terminated and the Vendor shall return to the Purchaser the earnest money without interest cost or any other compensation, loss or damages.”

The first time I visited the charity commissioner’s office, I was astonished by how little work was being done. The commissioner had a private chamber, and the rest of the staff sat at desks in a large open room, but I hardly saw anybody doing anything. Mainly, the staff was sipping tea, reading the newspaper, or distracting themselves in other ways.

I thought of Prabhupada’s statement that when it came to material advancement, Indians were lazy but that when it came to spiritual emancipation, they could make tremendous sacrifices and go to great lengths. I came to learn that the inefficiency was selective: if an office or officer wanted to help someone, they could be very efficient, but in our case, they showed no interest.

Eventually I came to suspect that Nair had his hand in the matter, and I began to see a pattern: In his agreement with a previouspotential buyer of the same land we were now in the process of buying—S. Chhaganlal and Brothers—Nair had made a condition that the purchaser obtain permission from the Bombay Municipality to subdivide the plot, and then had used his influence—and perhaps money—to make sure the permission was not granted. Then he had claimed that he had grounds to cancel the agreement, and after the cancellation he had kept the purchaser’s earnest money. In our case, he had embedded a condition in the agreement that we obtain permission from the charity commissioner, and even if the permission was not denied—if it was delayed past the six-month deadline for the execution of the agreement (“The sale shall be completed within a period of 6 months from the date hereof or within 3 months from the date hereof. The time fixed for completion of sale as sanctioned above shall be of the essence of the contract.”)—he could say that we had failed to meet the terms of the agreement in time, cancel the agreement, and keep our money. But although that may have been his plan, he still faced the obstacle of removing us—and the Deities—from the property.

While living on the rooftop of one of the buildings on the land, Visakha, sitting on a small piece of wood, wrote an article entitled “Prabhupada: India’s National Hero” for The Hare Krishna Monthly, a publication I had started and which I usually edited, and sent it to Srila Prabhupada. “I am very grateful to you for your kind words about me,” he replied, “but I do not think that I have done anything, but I am only delivering the best message as it is. Actually, anyone who is a sincere devotee of Krishna and who is rendering service by preaching His message is to be considered as hero. So you are all heroes of your country and humanity. Hero means someone whom others want to follow as example of the best type of person. So you all become like that, perfect examples of Krishna Consciousness heroes and heroines, and preach the message exactly as I have taught it to you very seriously and being fully convinced, and others will automatically come forward and join us. We shall all be like one great army of heroes for Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.”

On May 24 the К-Ward of the Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay sent us two show-cause notices, one for the hut and one for the temple, calling upon us to show cause, give reasons, why those structures should not be removed. Our architect, Motilal Khanna, in his letter dated May 29, asked the Municipal Corporation to regularize the structures, and on June 12 the temple structure was granted a year’s permission, which could be renewed.

On June 5 I wrote Prabhupada, “I received a letter from Shyamasundar Prabhu dated May 14, 1972, asking about GBC, and I replied to him directly in a letter dated May 25, 1972, that I am pleased to accept the post.”

Prabhupada wrote to Jayapataka in Mayapur, “I have appointed Giriraj to be the GBC zonal secretary for India zone, and I am sure that he meets your requirements of being equipoised and considerate of all the needs of all the branches under his control or jurisdiction. Simply all you leaders there in India must cooperate with him nicely and give him confidence and advice how to manage the things in the best manner. So I suggest you address your ideas for managing to Giriraj and co-operatively make arrangements. Bombay should be the headquarters for India. You send all money there and when you require you take and they should keep all accounts nicely. Whatever you need, they will supply.”

Prabhupada wanted Bombay to function as the head office for India and for the finances to be managed from there, but being both the GBC for India and president in Bombay proved to be too much for me, and after a short time I went back to focusing on Bombay.

In Juhu, without Prabhupada’s personal presence, with “the whole responsibility” on me, I struggled to deal with many of the devotees, some of whom were proficient in various ways and also quite strong-willed. Some of them could not relate to my style and were critical, speaking against me and sometimes openly challenging and defying my authority. And I did not know what to do about the situation, how to function.

Tensions increased, and finally relationships and communication broke down. Harikesa proposed the ultimate solution—that we phone

Srila Prabhupada. I had never thought we could do such a thing—and I questioned whether we should. But Harikesa thought that the situation was serious. Prabhupada was the only one who could solve the problem and had to be informed. “You are the temple president,” he said. “Srila Prabhupada has put you in charge, and the devotees must follow you. What they are doing is wrong. You must inform Prabhupada immediately.”

“But how?” I asked. I had never approached Prabhupada except by letter or in person.

“You must phone him.”

That was another problem—we did not have a telephone.

“You have to go to the homes of our life members in the Juhu Scheme and explain that you have an urgent need to phone Srila Prabhupada, until one of them agrees to let you use their phone.”

I had made many members in the Juhu Scheme and had affectionate relationships with them. If I asked, they would probably help. But we almost never made overseas calls, and the idea of phoning Prabhupada was intimidating; I didn’t feel I could do it on my own. So I asked Harikesa to accompany me, and he agreed.

That evening, after several unsuccessful attempts at other homes, we were invited in by Sri Daulatram G. Valia, one of three Valia brothers who had all been very supportive. He could tell from the urgency of my tone that the matter was important, and he let us use his phone to call Prabhupada in Los Angeles.

International connections were unreliable in those days and I was nervous and unsure of what to say, but I got through to one of Prabhupada’s secretaries, and with Harikesa by my side encouraging and prompting me, I explained the situation as well as I could, and the secretary promised to relay the message to Prabhupada.

Prabhupada’s response came in a letter, dated June 19:

My dear Gargamuni, Mahamsa, Nara Narayan, and Giriraj,

My dear boys, kindly accept my blessings, and I hope by Krishna’s grace you are doing all well. This morning I received one telephone message that there is some misunderstanding between yourselves and Giriraj, who is in charge of Bombay center. I may inform you in this connection that what I am doing to push on this great movement in the world is all with your cooperation. It is not possible for me alone to execute this great responsibility. Kindly, therefore, abide bythe direction of the man in charge of the center. If there is lack of obedience, then there cannot be discipline, and without discipline we cannot manage a huge world organization. I shall be returning by September next. Kindly therefore do not make any fracture during this period at least, and when I return if you all don’t like the man in charge surely, 1 shall replace him out of you. But for the time being, please do not make any rupture, and please obey by the direction of Giriraj Brahmachari.

So far as Gargamuni is concerned, I have already given him permission to go to Ahmedabad and other places in Gujarat state. He is a sannyasi and his main business is to travel and preach as I am doing in this old age, and that will please me very much.

So far as Nara Narayan is concerned, he is engaged in gardening work, so please give him all facility so he can make a good garden on all the vacant land on our property.

Mahamsa and Cyavana may act by the decisions of Giriraj, so Cyavana may transfer his building supervision work to somebody else, according to Giriraj. I have heard the building work is not going on satisfactorily, but that is our main business there, so if it is not being done nicely, the proper experienced man must be put in charge of the construction work.

So in conclusion, it is my request that even you do not agree on some points, Giriraj is in charge so please follow his direction and that will please me. I am very much anxious to see the progress at Bombay center, and I want it to become the first-class preaching center in the world. Please help me in this ambition. If we can manage successfully, we will be attractive for the whole of India. Our task is very heavy, do not neglect by paltry disagreement. I hope Krishna will bless you to understand my heart and oblige.

The day after he wrote me, Prabhupada sent a letter to Yadubara, with whom I worked closely:

I am in due receipt of your letter from Bombay dated June 14, 1972, and I have understood its contents. Today I have received one telephone call from Giriraj and he has informed me that there is some disagreement among you leaders there in our Bombay Center. This is not at all a pleasant situation for anyone. I am entrusting this huge task to all of you for working together cooperatively for doingsomething wonderful. I can understand that you are responsible and cool-headed along with the others, so you take the hand in reconciling all differences.

I have just now written to Gargamuni, Mahamsa, Nara Narayan, and Giriraj as follows: “It is my request that even you do not agree on some points, Giriraj is in charge so please follow his direction and that will please me. I am very much anxious to see the progress at Bombay center, and I want it to become the first-class preaching center in the world. Please help me in this ambition. If we can manage successfully, we will be attractive for the whole of India. Our task is very heavy, do not neglect by paltry disagreement. I hope Krishna will bless you to understand my heart and oblige.”

You state in your letter that everything is going on nicely there in Bombay, and I suppose that in general things are all right, but this today’s news disturbs me, and so I have ordered that Gargamuni shall immediately leave Bombay for his Gujarat tour and that Nara Narayan be given full assistance for extending the garden to all vacant areas of our property. Kindly assist me for seeing that these plans are carried out immediately and that our main task, namely the construction work, shall not be neglected. This is very important matter.

And the following day he wrote to me:
