Please accept my blessings. I am in due receipt of your letter dated June 13,1972, and have appreciated its contents very well. I am happy to hear that the men are engaged nicely, especially in the matter of distributing our books. Take any number of books without paying any price, and engage the whole amount for our building work there in Bombay, but the building work must be very superb. Now I have sent you one letter yesterday which I hope by now has cured the situation amongst you all leaders there in Bombay....

Somehow or other, all of our tenants should be our devotees, and we can give them concession rents, but they should be devotees and at least in our colony there should be no violations of our rules and regulations. Actually make it a Hare Krishna land or a pilgrimage for Vaishnavas and the Indian people in general.

I am very much especially pleased that you have had such a nice meeting with Sumati Morarji. She is our old friend and benefactor from long years back, and always she has desired for us to live as herclose neighbors. She used to tell me in Bombay two years back that she wanted we should build our temple somewhere nearby to her place. She also assisted Tamal Krishna and Shyamasundar to try to find one house in Juhu for our headquarters several times. So you can mention this fact to her that now we have fulfilled her desire and we are living in close proximity to her, so she should take advantage of Krishna’s blessing her with such an opportunity for serving the Lord by herself building our Juhu temple. Encourage her to attend the meetings every day, and if you make the Deity worship very, very opulent and gorgeous, she will automatically be attracted to them. She has no children of her own, so why not she should take Radha and Krishna as her Children? So you can propose gradually and tactfully that she can alone build up a wonderful temple in our property and we shall name it “Sumati Temple” or “Sumati Hall”. So encourage her in this way, and I am very much engladdened that she is so much willing to help us, now you apply yourself to the matter very diligently and think always of Krishna and it will come out very auspiciously. ... It is a unique temple in the world, and if you show your wonderful abilities as American and European boys and girls to manage everything superbly, she will not hesitate to entrust you in every way. Therefore, there must always be good will and cooperation amongst yourselves for this huge task ahead. I always think of our Juhu place, and I want that it shall be the model for all the world to emulate and respect as the perfect example of a Krishna conscious community.

Prabhupada was so earnest in his desire to engage us—and all others—in devotional service to Lord Krishna, and so caring and loving, that he inspired us to at least try to rise above our weaknesses and conditioned natures and work together, cooperatively, exclusively for the pleasure of guru and Krishna—for the benefit of all the world. We had no choice but to surrender.

Previously, disciples would live with the guru in the ashram and the guru would be there to guide them at all times. The life of the disciples with the spiritual master was simple, consisting mainly of studying the Vedic scriptures and collecting firewood. But Prabhupada envisioned such a huge undertaking. For at least several hundred years, no one had attempted anything on such a grand scale. Prabhupada himself had said,

“I can never think of anything small; my plans are always big—that is my disease.” Further, he had to guide us from so far.

He was training us in the same spirit of surrender as gurus had imparted to disciples for thousands of years: brahmacari guru-kule vasan danto guror hitam/ acaran dasavan nico gurau sudrdha-sauhrdah. “A student should practice completely controlling the senses. He should be submissive and have an attitude of firm friendship for the spiritual master. With a great vow, the brahmacari should live at the gurukula, only for the benefit of the guru.” (SB 7.12.1) Although externally the lives of Prabhupada’s disciples were different from the lives of brahmacharis in the past, the basic principle remained the same. The brahmachari was to serve the spiritual master dasa-vat, humbly, like a servant, and nicah, submissively. He was to live only for his guru, not for any personal benefit, and remain sudrdha-sauhrdah, firmly fixed in friendship with him. “The brahmacari should go out morning and evening to collect alms, and he should offer all that he collects to the spiritual master. He should eat only if ordered to take food by the spiritual master. Otherwise, if the spiritual master does not order, he may sometimes have to fast.” (SB 7.12.5) By such unconditional surrender to the guru, the brahmachari, disciple, would receive all spiritual benefits.

Mr. Nair adopted various strategies to drive us from the property. Our only accommodation was the chatai hut, and Nair sometimes cut the electricity, so the devotees had no lights, the fans we had recently purchased didn’t work, and the mosquitoes were eating us alive. Sometimes he would also cut the water supply.

He also hired a strongly-built ruffian named Ramu, the coconutwallah, who ostensibly was there to cut the coconuts from the hundredforty palm trees on the land, and he kept him in an outhouse at the rear of the property. Especially during the temple’s evening programs, Ramu would position himself near the front of the property and brandish his machete, looking menacingly at our devotees, insulting women, and trying to intimidate and scare away people who might want to come for prasada or aratis, talks, or other functions.

Another of Nair’s agents had printed a handbill ascribing scandalous behavior to the American Hare Krishna devotees and was having it distributed at the nearby Vile Parle train station.

Mr. Nair’s campaign of harassment had some effect. A few devotees left and others wanted to, but about thirty devotees stayed to serve Srila Prabhupada and Sri Sri Radha-Rasabihari, resisting the opposition and tolerating the hardships.

It was the tradition on Nair Wadi that on Indian Independence Day, August 15, the tenants would gather at the statue of Mahatma Gandhi in the garden, hoist an Indian flag, garland the statue, sing the national anthem, and distribute sweets.

The statue, however, was at the center of Nara Narayan’s garden, and he was concerned that the tenants might disturb or destroy his plants. In the midst of the ceremony, in his typical gruff way, he asked the tenants why they were worshipping Mahatma Gandhi when he was nothing but a demon. And, of course, they were offended by his remark, and that evening they held an emergency general-body meeting, and K. Devasan, the general secretary of the Nair Wadi Tenants Association, wrote to Mrs. Nair.

The next day, Nara Narayan and another temperamental devotee, Dvija Hari, had a fight. Both could be difficult to work with, often thought their way was the only way, and were passionate, headstrong, and physically powerful—and they didn’t get along. This time, their smoldering conflict erupted into a major altercation.

According to Nara Narayan, he didn’t like the way Dvija Hari was talking to him, and, brandishing one of the machetes he used to cut coconuts, threatened, “You better get out of my face or I’m going to chop you into pieces.” Dvija Hari left, but he returned shortly thereafter with a hatchet and went after Nara Narayan. Nara Narayan escaped into one of the tenants’ flats and then rented a room in a lodging house for a few nights, until things had settled down, but news of the incident spread quickly throughout the community.

In response to the two incidents, Devasan wrote to Mrs. Nair, under the subject heading “Derogatory Remarks about the Father of our Nation”:

I have been directed by the . . . General Body ... to convey the following matters to you in writing with a request to take suitable steps.

In the year 1946 your husband and you took the initiative to install a statue of Mahatma Gandhi, in the middle of Nairwadi, as a mark of respect to the Father of the Nation and both of you were taking leading part in the flag hoisting ceremonies ever since in front of the statue.

Since the beginning of this year a group of Hare Krishna Movement have moved into the Wadi, who claim to be lessees of this property. They have been going about erecting temporary structures, lavatories, etc. in the compound.

In addition to this they have built up a garden around Mahatmaji’s statue and have fenced the same, presumably to keep the cattle away. One of their members, Sri Nara Narayan, has been mainly instrumental in laying out the garden which the digging implied for inconvenience to the tenants, and whenever such inconvenience was brought to his notice, he has been quarrelsome and abusive, ready to start a full-fledged quarrel, using abusive language and threatening violence. On all these occasions we had tactfully avoided matters found so far, and their overall in-charge had in these occasions apologized to us at the time of such incidents.

Sensing the nature of this man, we had notified their chief regarding our intention to carry out flag hoisting ceremony in front of the statue in advance and we received a verbal assurance from the latter that we could go ahead with this purpose on the Independence Day.

However, when some of the tenants started bathing the statue of Mahatmaji, Sri Nara Narayan came forward saying as to why they wish to bath the statue of this fool. It was explained to him that Mahatmaji is the Father of our Nation, and also made clear to him that we resented this national insult.

When they wanted to plant the flag post this man obstructed them from doing so. He even threatened that he will not permit such a thing and if necessary shed blood to this end.

As arguments were getting heated and violence was anticipated, some of the elder tenants intervened. In the meanwhile, his superiors also came in and pacified him, but he still tried to tell us they would permit this flag hoisting only for this time and that by the same evening the flag and the flag post will have to be removed and in futurethis ceremony will not be permitted by them. We strongly feel that foreign internationals have no right to dictate us for performing a ceremony which have been a practice in this wadi for the past 24 years. Even if they are full-fledged owners of the property, do we wish to tolerate such insults to our nation, by an individual foreign national?

As long as you are, as we understand, still the owner of this wadi, we wish to know what you propose to do about such incidents. To give you a further idea of the violent nature of this individual, there was quite a commotion in the wadi on 16th Aug. 1972 evening involving the above-mentioned Shri N.N. and another member of their movement, where they were seen to be using some weapons of day-to-day use to attack each other, openly leading to gathering of the tenants, who were flabbergasted.

We are to bring to your notice that with such persons staying around in the wadi may lead to an assault on our women, children, or gents.

A line in reply from you will be highly appreciated. In the absence of any positive steps from you we will be constrained to approach the Govt, authorities, in the matter.

I wrote Prabhupada about “disturbing incidents” that had taken place. When he learned what had happened, he telegrammed me, “NARANARAYAN IMMEDIATELY RETURN TO USA,” and the conflict was defused.

We were so preoccupied with just surviving, dealing with challenges, and executing the specific tasks that Prabhupada assigned to us that I had hardly thought about the upcoming Janmashtami. But when Harikesa brought it up, I realized that yes, we must do something. We had no funds in reserve, so I went door to door in the Juhu Scheme to collect donations, and people were glad to contribute.

The new, semipermanent temple, constructed with temporary permission from the municipal authorities, was ready. There was a small room for the Deities, and behind it another small room, for the pujaris’ service. In front of the Deities’ room was a darshan mandapa, an area from which to view the Deity, with a roof of asbestos sheets supported by steel tubes, over a raised floor covered by marble-chip tiles.

On Janmashtami eve, the Radha and Krishna Deities were taken in a colorful procession from the hut to Their new temple. Devoteeswere singing, playing mridangas and kartals, and dancing, and many life members and friends came to participate in the festival. And as Radharani and Krishna approached the front of the property, close to the road, They attracted many local people. It was a joyous, landmark event.

Harikesa had taken charge of organizing the next day’s program. “We had a great Janmashtami,” he later recalled, “the best ever! We had ladies churning yogurt, making lots of butter, and when we broke the fast, we drank the buttermilk.

“We had a drama, a play about the appearance of Krishna. Srimati was Mother Yasoda, and Dinanath was in it. I organized the event. We had a huge feast for everybody, and lots of kirtan. It was a wonderful evening.

“Gandiva’s mother, Yashoda, made the flower garlands, and Mrs. Warrier did the other decorations. Mr. Sethi was involved, and Jagat Purusa and Gandiva cooked. Maithili was in the kitchen, and in the temple were Srimati and Tungabhadra and Palika and Malati. Sridhar was doing kirtan with Dinanath and that skinny young Indian boy \[Lokanath\].”

Srimati had made a Baby Krishna, and local people stood in long lines to get a chance to rock Him by pulling a cord attached to His cradle. They were all excited about celebrating the festival.

“Everybody was so happy,” Urmila Johri, one of the neighbors, remembered. “My daughter Vibha helped organize Garbha dances with girls from the area, and there were bhajans by Surdas, Lord Krishna’s blind devotee, and dramas of Krishna Illas. The platform was decorated, and people churned pots of yogurt and butter was taken out. There was a large crowd, and at midnight, with the sounding of the conchshell and ghantds \[bells\], the curtain was drawn and the Lord took birth on Hare Krishna Land. It was a beautiful sight. The priests bathed the Lord with honey, milk, yogurt, ghee, and water.

“Tears came rolling down my eyes—I had never seen such a sight. The pujaris dressed the Lord, and again we had darshan. Everyone was chanting, and we all had carandmrta and prasada, and in the end we all went away happy.”

After the celebration—and the inauguration of the new, semipermanent temple—on September 16, I wrote Srila Prabhupada, “Wehad a wonderful Janmashtami celebration. Over a thousand visitors attended, and they were all very much pleased by the continuous program of aratis and kirtans, dramas and slides, lectures, butter churning, and so many other nice transcendental activities. The semipermanent structure includes a stage, a deity room, a pujari room, and a small kitchen for the deities. The plan was very nice, and the execution was also very competent.”

Prabhupada replied from Los Angeles, “I am glad to learn in detail how the things are going on in Bombay. I am always thinking about that place. It is only a few steps to the Juhu Beach, and there are many nice palm trees overhead with cooling breezes.”

“Juhu Beach is the best in the world,” he told devotees there on a morning walk. “\[It\] is very nice; you can go out \[as far as\] one mile . . . and the waves are not so ferocious in coming. And the whole thing is clean—the whole beach, ten miles long. Therefore so many foreigners’ hotels are there.”

“I am looking forward very much to return there soon,” he continued in his letter. “Only I am always anxious how the things are going.”

In a letter to Yadubara too, Srila Prabhupada focused on Juhu: “This Bombay project is one of our most important projects in the whole world, and I am looking to you and the others there in Bombay to see that it is done very magnificently. I have been very much encouraged to see some advertisement booklet printed by Air India wherein the theme is exclusively dedicated to Krishna and Vrindavan. With this idea the Air India Company is enticing tourists to come to India simply to experience the spiritual life around Krishna. So in the future I expect that our Bombay project will be one of the most important showpieces in the world for foreign tourists to actually come and get actual experience of Krishna consciousness, or the real Vedic culture. So, with this idea in mind work very vigorously and with renewed spirit to do the work very gorgeously and raise up first our temple and later on the apartment houses as you have planned.”

One day a couple of weeks later, a new man came to the temple, wanting to join. When, surprised that he had just shown up out ofnowhere, I asked about his background, he said that his name was Shekher Kumar Ghosh—he was Bengali. He had been in prison for pickpocketing and stealing, and while there he had seen a copy of Back to Godhead. He had been attracted by a photograph of Srila Prabhupada, especially Prabhupada’s wristwatch, and had decided that he wanted to “work for him”—if not, as he later told me, steal his watch. So as soon as he had been released, he had come to Hare Krishna Land. He wanted to meet Srila Prabhupada and become a devotee.

I explained to the man that Prabhupada was not in Bombay and that he would have to wait until he returned. As became policy for new people who walked in off the street (he was the first), I asked him to sleep outside, which he did—one night behind the kitchen, one night in the electrician’s area, one night at the beach, and the last night on the floor of the temple hall.

The man seemed sincere, and when I had seen him attending all the temple programs for those four days, I asked whether he would shave up.

“Yes!” he replied at once.

“Today is a very auspicious day,” I told him, “Haridasa Thakura’s disappearance day. It’s a good day to shave your head.” I gave him a rupee, and he went to the barber. I also gave him japa-mala and taught him how to chant on beads. And I gave him the spiritual nickname “Haridas.”

Haridas was still anxious to meet Prabhupada, though, and since Prabhupada wasn’t scheduled to return to Bombay until late December, I gave Haridas permission to see him for three days in Hyderabad in mid-November.

So, Haridas went to Hyderabad and met Prabhupada and explained his situation—his history and present status in Juhu. He told Prabhupada that I had given him permission to be with him for three days but that he wanted to stay longer.

“No,” Prabhupada replied. “You have given your word to Giriraj, so you must return as promised.”

Later, Haridas told me, “I came to steal Prabhupada’s watch, but instead, he stole my heart.”

## Battling Nair

Sometimes Nair dealt with us in such a friendly—or, at least, ambiguous—way that I became bewildered and couldn’t determine if he was our friend or our enemy. I even wrote Srila Prabhupada, “Nair is always unsteady and tricky, but at least for the last ten days has been very friendly and enthusiastic for helping us, and seemingly most eager to get the conveyance settled before the government passes more laws, which the government is regularly doing at the expense of the industrialists and landowners.” Two days later, I wrote Prabhupada again: “Several questions arise: How far can we give into Nair’s whims for fear that he will break the contract? How far is Nair sincere in asking the 5 lakhs \[he claims he needs to pay his\] back taxes, or is he simply trying to delay things more with a mind to break the contract? My own idea is there is no plot, only Mr. Nair is crazy, and that presently he does want to complete the agreement.” Once, after meeting with Nair, Yadubara and I sat outside his house and discussed whether he was our friend or our enemy, and we could not come to any definite conclusion.

So, I was confused, but Prabhupada took decisive action. On September 29 he wrote me, “You can give public notice in the Public Notices column in the newspaper and send one copy to Mr. Nair, as follows: ‘The International Society for Krishna Consciousness has purchased the land in Juhu, Bombay-54, known as Nair Wadi, plot, under purchase agreement dated, and we have advanced the requisite money under the Sales Agreement. The other party, Mrs. A. B. Nair, has not, however, completed the business under some pretext. Under the circumstances, if someone attempts to purchase the land, he does so at his own risk as we are already in possession of the purchase agreement signed by Mrs. A. B. Nair.’”

Accordingly, on October 7 the following public notice appeared in the Free Press Journal:

This is to inform the public that International Society for Krishna Consciousness has agreed to purchase the land at Juhu known as Nair Wadi bearing Survey No. 2A, Hissa No. 4, 6, 5A, 5B under an agreement for sale dated 8th February 1972 and that the said societyhas advanced the required earnest amount under the said agreement dated 8th February 1972 to Mrs. A. B. Nair the Vendor. The said Mrs.

A. B. Nair is not completing the sale under one pretext or the other.

This is therefore to warn the public not to deal with the said Mrs. A.B. Nair in connection with the aforesaid property and in spite of what has been stated hereinabove if anyone attempts to purchase the said property he shall do so at his own risks and costs.

Dated this 6th day of October 1972.

M/s. Madhukar Munim & Co.,

Attorneys for International Society for Krishna Consciousness.

No. 4A, Alli Chambers, Fort, Bombay-1

As stated in my subsequent report to Srila Prabhupada, Mr. Nair was outraged by our public notice because, he said, “It is spoiling my wife’s name,” and he threatened to file a suit against us for defamation. And although he didn’t say it, he may very well have been infuriated because the notice thwarted any possibility of his selling the land to yet another party. (Around that time one of the neighbors’ children heard Mrs. Nair say that she was going to force us out and then sell the property to someone else for more.) In any case, he was furious, and, accompanied by some other devotees, I went to meet him at his home.

In the meeting, Nair made a big thing of the newspaper notice I had published, and after quietly consulting the other devotees, I put my head on the floor and bowed down and offered my obeisances and apologies to him—but it didn’t seem to make any difference. Rather, it seemed that from the beginning Nair was planning to cheat us and was just looking for an excuse to cancel the agreement—and in the public notice he had found that excuse. But he was upset because the public notice would block him from “selling” the land to anyone else.

Nair also threatened us. “I have files and files of complaints about you people,” he said, “volumes of complaints and evidence and newspaper articles. I have been keeping quiet, but if you go on acting like this, I am going to ruin your society. I’ll go to the government, I’ll go to the press, I’ll tell them that you are spies, you are smugglers, and I will finish you.” He was trying to scare and intimidate us, and to some extent he was successful.

Within days, on October 10, through a letter from his attorney to ours, Nair cancelled the sales agreement. The letter, filled with distortions and falsehoods, concluded, “The said agreement for sale provides that the time fixed for the completion of sale shall be of the essence of the contract. As mentioned above, the time for completion of sale expired on 8/8/72. As the sale could not be completed by 8/8/72 by reason of your client’s defaults, the said agreement stands terminated and our client is entitled to forfeit all the amounts uptil now paid by your client to our client. Please note that our client treats the said agreement for sale terminated and broken by your clients and our client has forfeited all the amounts uptil now paid by your client to our client. Our client reserves her right to claim from your client damages which our client has suffered by reason of the breach of the contract on the part of your client.”

Two days later, on October 12, our attorney replied, “\[O\]ur clients deny that the Agreement stands terminated or that your client is entitled to terminate the same or to forfeit the earnest money for the reasons alleged or otherwise at all. In this connection we have to refer you to our letter of 30th Ultimo which was replied by you only after the lapse of a period of ten days. Please note that the Agreement is still valid and subsisting and that our clients, if so advised, will file appropriate proceedings for specific performance of the same and/or to claim damages from your client and to adopt such further and other proceedings as they may be advised after we take full instructions from our clients.

“In the meantime all the contentions and/or allegations contained in your letter under reply are hereby denied and by our not replying to your letter seriatim, our clients should not be deemed to have admitted any of the statements and allegations contained in your said letter.”

Understanding that we were struggling with Mr. Nair, Srila Prabhupada wrote Tamal Krishna, “The Bombay dealing has been muddled by the tactics of Mr. Nair and Diwanji. Giriraj is in trouble. He is a child in these worldly dealings, so immediately go to help him.”

Prabhupada also sent Karandhara, having briefed him on his strategy of filing a suit in the Bombay High Court for specific performance of the sales agreement. On October 9 he cabled me, “STOP ALL NEGOTIATIONS WITH NAIR.... KARANDHARA ARRIVING

BOMBAY BY OCTOBER 12 FOR FILING SUIT FOR SPECIFIC EXECUTION OF SALE AGREEMENT”

He also sent Bhavananda, but when they all came and saw the situation, the group became convinced that we—not Nair—had failed to meet the conditions for the sale and thus could not yet file for specific execution. We wrote Srila Prabhupada:

Karandhara arrived safely this morning, Tamal Krishna Goswami arrived yesterday, and Bhavananda also arrived, from Calcutta, yesterday. We all, including Giriraj, met this afternoon and discussed the situation. The first point brought out, and the most significant at the present moment, is that we have not yet received approval from the Charity Commissioner for the transaction. In this regards, then, it is we, and not Mr. Nair, who have failed to execute the terms of sale. We cannot instigate any action to force Mr. Nair to make the conveyance until this is done. It was concluded that our mistake has been relying on Mr. Diwanji and Mrs. Morarji to arrange for the Charity Commissioner’s approval as they promised to do, rather than doing it ourselves. We have approached the Charity Commissioner and have been informed that the approval will take time as there is some processing that has to be done. We plan to find out the person who is the superior of the Charity Commissioner (most likely the Chief Minister of Maharashtra) and appeal to him for expedition of the matter. Once we receive the approval from the Charity Commissioner, we then can request Mr. Nair to execute the conveyance strictly according to the terms of the original agreement of sale without any concessions or changes. If he refuses or delays beyond one day after this, then we can begin the specific performances suit as Karandhara and Your Divine Grace fully discussed.

We are now going to seek out a reliable and competent lawyer for legal consultation of the situation and no more rely upon any big friends or whatever to do our business for us.

With all the legal challenges we were facing, we wanted the best lawyers to represent us. So we approached Mr. R. C. Dhruva, secretary to the great industrialist Seth R. D. Birla (the honorific Seth indicating his exalted status), to find out what solicitors the Birlas used, thinking they must be the best. Mr. Dhruva recommended the firm Mulla &

Mulla & Cragie, Blunt & Caroe, and the next Monday, after informing Srila Prabhupada, we visited their offices and began working with them.

We met with Mr. Vasantrao Naik, the chief minister, and he promised to speak personally with the charity commissioner and see what he could do to expedite our matter.

Even before receiving our letter, however, Prabhupada, in Manila, had written Tamal Krishna and me:

1\. We have fulfilled all the conditions as purchaser.

2\. Mr. Nair has purposefully delayed with a motive to cheat us as he had done with some others in this connection.

3\. But this time he cannot cheat us because we are in possession of the land and our deity Radha-Krishna is installed there.

4\. Therefore we must immediately go to the court for enforcing him to execute the conveyance immediately.

5\. Even the court case goes on for a long time, still our business there cannot be stopped.

6\. Without going to the court, we cannot make any compromise with him.

7\. But I think we can arrange the full amount of 14 lacs to get this rascal out of the scene.

8\. But we cannot do it without going to the court, otherwise we shall become a party for breaking the purchase agreement. Therefore we have to go to the court before making any compromise.

9\. In the meantime, take definite information from the bank whether they can loan us 50% of the whole value.

10\. The whole value is 14 lacs. We have already paid 2 lacs. We can arrange to pay further 5 lacs. That means we pay 7 lacs, the bank may pay the balance 7 lacs.

11\. Actually, the bank may not have to pay even 7 lacs because according to the purchase agreement, the last payment of 4 lacs has to be paid upon the decision on the court case pending about Chhaganlal and Company.

So you have to act according to this program on the advice of suitable lawyers.

From Vrindavan Srila Prabhupada sent us several letters in quick succession. On October 19 he wrote, “It appears the Charity Commissioner permission is delayed and not refused, it is not a verygrand mistake, and we can chastise for that the lawyers. I have read the clause 11 in the original Agreement for Sale, and I do not find any mention of there being any six-month time limit for obtaining the Charity Commissioner’s approval... So there is only some delay, that’s all. That will not be sufficient grounds for \[Nair\] to rescind the contract. Rather, our position is very strong so long we are in possession and we have paid him the earnest money and more. So best thing is to consult Mulla & Mulla and proceed accordingly. . . . Try to fix up some arrangement acceptable to Mr. Nair for paying him, but we shall not risk that we may lose everything to Chhaganlal or some other \[victim\] of Mr. Nair’s cheating dealings. So best thing is to follow the advice of Mulla & Mulla and stick to our position very securely.”

Having given further thought to the matter, he wrote again:

Further to my letter of yesterday, I have thought the matter over thoroughly, and without any doubt our position in the matter is very strong. Nair is bluffing. One of my godbrothers who is expert in these things has advised me, and I also know it from experience, that once the agreement of sale is signed that is final, and it will not be very easy, in fact, it will be impossible for Nair to defeat us in the courts if it comes to that.

Now the thing is that Nair has accepted from us two lakhs of rupees, as follows: On February 8,1972, cheque #GT/HS 306871 for Rs. 50,000; on February 25,1972, cheque CHT/A-T492829 for Rs. 50,000; and on March 28, 1972, cheque # CHT/A-T492831 for Rs. 1,00,000. Now according to our agreement, that last one lakh of rupees was not to be accepted by him until the conveyance was completed. So he has taken, that means he accepts that the conveyance has been completed! Now you may go to the bank or somehow or other determine the exact date on which Mr. Nair accepted the cheque as above mentioned for Rs. 1,00,000, and that will serve as legal proof he has finalized the conveyance terms.

Our position is very strong. Possession is nine-tenths of the law. Why you should be afraid of him? We can satisfy any court of law. He has given us possession according to the terms of the agreement of sale, and we have paid him Rs. 50,000 to take possession, and he has acknowledged receipt, that means the transaction is finished. If I have something and I sell you, and you give me money and I give youthat thing, the transaction is finished, never mind there is no receipt. So with Nair our transaction is finished. We have paid him money, he has given us possession, and we have agreed to terms for paying the rest of the money, that’s all. He is simply planning tricks because there is no receipt and he does not want to give us receipt.

Take information from the bank when he took the money. One year from that time, according to the terms of the purchase agreement, we are supposed to pay further two lakhs, that is, one year from the execution of the conveyance. So we have paid Rs. 50,000 as earnest money, according to the agreement, and the agreement then states that we must pay Rs. 1,50,000 “upon the execution of the conveyance.” So he has accepted, that means conveyance transaction is complete, he may give me receipt or not, that doesn’t matter. It is a case of misappropriation; he did not deliver the goods. Once when I was in business I took money from one man for an order of goods and I was bit late in delivering them, so he wanted to sue me in the court for misappropriation. It is the same thing. We have paid Nair, taken possession, and now he doesn’t want to deliver the goods.

According to the clauses 14 and 15 in the purchase agreement, it is our option to rescind the contract within six months, not the vendor’s. But he has accepted the cheque for Rs. 1,00,000 before six months, therefore we consider that he has completed the conveyance and we do not want to rescind but we shall close the deal immediately, finished, that’s all. He is trying to avoid this issue by tricks, and he has dominated you and you are little afraid of him, and he has fooled you to think he is in superior legal position so that you will give him some money. But this is cheating. We shall not give him any more money. Don’t pay him any more. First of all bring a criminal case against him. . . . Make criminal case by consulting lawyer. It will not take much time. It is simple case of his cheating. That any reasonable man can see. So immediately you can file criminal case. He has taken money but he has not executed. So why you should be disappointed and afraid of him? Our position is very, very strong. We have paid money and we are in possession, so what remains for conveyance? As soon as you take money the transaction is finished, you may take receipt or not, otherwise it is simply cheating. So find out a first-class lawyer and apply in the court that the purchase agreement is already done and get it done, that’s all. He is simply bluffing.

Now you purchase that house on the south borderline, repair it nicely, and you can live there for years if we have to. I think he \[Ratnaparkhi\] will take Rs. 15,000 cash if you can persuade him, or if he will not yield, you can pay him Rs. 20,000 and finish the business.

Enclosed find the copy of one letter I have forwarded to Mr. and Mrs. Nair. You may further request them to come and see me here. It will be too much difficult for me to come to Bombay at this time. Otherwise I am coming to Bombay in December, if he wants to wait so long. Another thing is, I do not think it is necessary for Bhavananda to remain in Bombay for this business. Better if Karandhara and Tamala Krishna tackle the matter co-operatively by applying their full attention, and Bhavananda may return to Calcutta for taking charge there as soon as possible.

And four days later, on October 24, after receiving our report, he wrote:

You think your position is rather hopeless. But I say that our position is very strong, just the opposite. Why you say hopeless? When Nair accepted two lakhs rupees of ours, the terms of purchase are finished, simply he has delayed to give us the papers. The transaction is finished when he accepts the money, so by tricks he is delaying. So why you are delaying to make case?... \[I\]mmediately make a criminal case. After the case is decided, he shall be forced to give us the conveyance, and within one year after we shall give him the next installment of two lakhs. Because the transaction is finished, so we can legally occupy all the land, it is not trespass when the transaction has been completed and Nair has accepted the terms of sale by accepting money.

If you are thinking hopeless, then how I can make you hopeful? Our point is, he has accepted the money, that means he has agreed to terms of sale. Take police precaution if he is threatening violence. We are in possession according to the terms of the agreement, simply he has delayed the conveyance. Therefore I say that you boys cannot deal very well in these matters, because you are too timid. Now whatever you like you may do. Immediately criminal case should be taken, but that you are not doing because he is bluffing you. He says big words and makes threats and you believe him foolishly and do like he says. That I shall not do. When we have paid money that means he has accepted....

Immediately an application should be submitted to the magistrate that he has accepted the money and has willfully delayed the conveyance on tricks, and he has threatened to drive away even by violence, what is this?...

And take police precaution that he is threatening us. Go to the magistrate and tell him we gave Nair money and now he is threatening violence to drive us away. We shall go to the court, there is no other way. Criminal court means complaint that we have given money, he has not given conveyance, he is threatening by force to drive us from the place. This is the only settlement possible, that he returns our Rs. 2,70,000 immediately and we vacate, or immediately file criminal case. There is no other alternative. We have finished the business. He is entrapped because he has received the money. Our boys do not understand. Anything, as soon as you receive money the transaction is finished. And even it is six months passed, it is our option to rescind, not his. Charity Commissioner has delayed, that is not very serious for disqualifying us. There is no time limit mentioned for getting permission from Charity Commissioner. Still, try for the permission from Charity Commissioner as quickly as possible, then we shall go on with the terms of the original agreement, either voluntarily or we shall have to force him through the courts. One thing is, you have said that we shall have to pay “entire additional Rs. 70,000 stamp duty,” so does this mean we must pay only an additional 5% of Rs. 70,000, or Rs. 3,500 extra, or again pay Rs. 70,000 plus 5%? That is not clear.

In my opinion if you apply a petition before the magistrate that Nair has taken the money, that he is not giving the conveyance, playing tricks, and that now he is threatening by violence, such petition will clear everything. He is afraid of going to court, that is our favorable point. My clear-cut view is simply to present a petition to the magistrate. It costs only 12 annas \[less than one rupee\]. This complaint should be submitted, take a good criminal lawyer and file, then everything will be clear.

On Prabhupada’s advice, on November 2, considering Nair’s violent, sinister threats, I had Manasvi lodge a complaint against him at the Santa Cruz Police Station.

Of course, Nair never returned our money, so a week later, on November 9,1 filed a criminal case against him, in the Magistrate’s Court in Bandra, in which I presented the history of not only his cheating butalso his violent threats, which themselves were criminal, citing the following instances:

On September 4, in a meeting in the office of his solicitor, Chimanlal Shah, after expressing his intention to take back possession of the land, Nair had said that we if we did not vacate, he could burn the whole place down.

On October 17 Bhavananda, Karandhara, and I had met Nair at his home in the Theosophical Colony, Juhu, and he had been aggressive and hostile and called us trespassers and demanded that we restore possession to him; otherwise, he said, he could shoot every one of us. Although we had pleaded with him not to speak such violent words, he had persisted and appeared so intent on retaking possession that he seemed ready to go to any extent, lawful or not, to achieve his ends.

And the following day, on October 18, again in Chimanlal Shah’s office, Nair had told Tamal Krishna, Bhavananda, Karandhara, and me that he had the “ways and means” to obtain possession of the land.

Based on my presentation, the magistrate concluded, “From the facts mentioned in the application, I am satisfied that there exists within local limits of my jurisdiction, a dispute between the applicant and respondents 1 and 2 \[Mr. and Mrs. Nair\] over the premises referred to in the application which is likely to cause breach of the peace. I therefore direct the parties to appear before this court in person or by pleader on 1.12.72 and put in writing statements of their respective claims as regards the fact of actual possession of the subject of the dispute and produce such documents or adduce by putting in affidavits, the evidence of such persons as they rely upon in support of such claims.”

But as Prabhupada had written, for all his bluster, Nair was afraid of going to court, and a month later, he met with Prabhupada in Hyderabad.

In the midst of all the battles and intrigues, Prabhupada encouraged me to maintain the standard of Krishna consciousness as the basis of our effort and eventual success. “So long the regulative principles are followed,” he wrote, “everything else will follow.”

Mr. Nair had a cordial relationship with Shyamasundar, and both he and his wife liked Shyamasundar’s wife, Malati, and were fond of their daughter, Saraswati. So Shyamasundar and Tamal Krishna arranged for him to meet with Srila Prabhupada in Hyderabad.

Nair agreed to come, but, suspecting that Prabhupada had some mystic powers and might use them to persuade him to act against his will, he brought a guru with him, a yogi, thinking the man would counteract Prabhupada’s spiritual power.

On November 21 Nair, the yogi, and Shyamasundar all went to the home of Pannalal Pittie—the wealthiest, most aristocratic man in Hyderabad and a good friend of the devotees—where Prabhupada was staying. Prabhupada met with his guests, and they conversed over a huge, elaborate feast.

After they had eaten, Prabhupada let out a big yawn, and when he did, the yogi said, “Oh, Swamiji, you must be very tired. We should not disturb you now. You should rest, and we can talk later.”

“Oh, yes,” Prabhupada replied, “I am very tired.”

So, Nair and the yogi excused themselves and retired to the next room, which they were sharing with Tamal Krishna.

When they had left, Prabhupada spoke privately with Tamal Krishna. “When someone asks you if you are tired,” he said, “it actually means he is tired. Go into the other room and you will see that they are sleeping. Very carefully, without disturbing the guru, wake up Mr. Nair and bring him to me.”

So, Tamal Krishna tiptoed into the room, and sure enough both men were fast asleep. He gently shook Nair and whispered, “Mr. Nair, Mr. Nair—wake up. Prabhupada wants to see you.” And Nair, roused from his slumber, got up and followed him to Prabhupada’s room—without the yogi.

Prabhupada talked with Nair for two hours. Nair said that in order to execute the conveyance, he had to get a certificate from the incometax department saying that all his taxes were paid, which they weren’t. The two lakhs we had paid him, he said, were not enough to cover his back taxes—he needed more money so that he could get the income-tax certificate in order to execute the conveyance.

By the end of the discussion, they had worked out a new sales agreement. We would pay another three lakhs, and that, combined with the two lakhs and 7,500 rupees we had already paid, which amounted to more than five lakhs, would be enough for Nair to pay his back taxes, and the conveyance would immediately be executed in our favor.

While Prabhupada and Nair were settling the final legal points, Tamal Krishna and Shyamasundar drafted the agreement and Shyamasundar typed it out. Then, with the yogi still soundly sleeping, Nair signed the document, and Tamal Krishna flew back with him to Bombay the next afternoon.

Prabhupada was very happy that the memorandum of agreement had been signed and that our legal position would be restored. If all went well, the taxes would be paid—and the conveyance executed— by December 1, in less than two weeks. Working with our solicitor, Mrs. Mehta, of Mulla & Mulla, the devotees drafted the conveyance and sent it to Mr. Nair for his approval and his wife’s signature.

On November 25 Prabhupada flew to Bombay to complete the transaction. He stayed at Pranjivan and Jasu Valia’s home in the Juhu Scheme, which, in honor of Lord Krishna and their association with Krishna consciousness, they had named “Hare Krishna.” The house had been designed by a student of Frank Lloyd Wright, was round in shape, and apart from the large glass picture windows had mostly wood surfaces. It featured an expansive lawn and garden with a small temple similar to the house in design, in which stood a beautiful Deity of Krishna, whom Mrs. Valia worshipped devoutly. We were new to Juhu and had only a small shed for a temple and a hut for our residence (and even that could not be seen from the street), and the house was so distinctive and prominent that when people asked taxi drivers to take them to Hare Krishna Land, they sometimes ended up at the Hare Krishna house.

While there, Prabhupada was asked by Upendra (a local middle-aged man later initiated as Vamanadeva), “If a devotee sees a man drowning in a river, should he save him?”

“A devotee engages only in devotional service,” Prabhupada replied. “He doesn’t interfere with people’s karma. But if he doesn’t save the man, people may criticize, ‘Oh, he is a devotee. He could have saved him, but he let him drown. Devotees are heartless.’ So, in consideration of popular sentiment, loka-vicara, the devotee may save him. But otherwise, pure devotees have nothing to do with karma (jnana-karmady-anavrtam).

During the same darshan, another elderly gentleman, Yogindra, asked Prabhupada about peace of mind. He had recently come to stay at the temple and was meeting Prabhupada for the first time. Prabhupadareplied that the mind was material. It could be made peaceful by drinking, or by sleep. But we were not interested in peace of mind; we were interested in serving Krishna. “Just like Arjuna—he wanted to leave the battlefield of Kurukshetra to have peace of mind, but Krishna said, ‘No, I want you to fight.’” Prabhupada said that our goal was to serve and please Krishna and that Arjuna therefore sacrificed his peace of mind for the sake of Krishna’s service.

Tamal Krishna told Prabhupada how Mr. Nair had bluffed me. Perhaps he expected him to reproach me. But Prabhupada replied, “Giriraj is simple. What can be done?”

Actually, I had really been struggling. I had so much responsibility and so many problems, even with the devotees. And living in India and dealing with the enemies was a big challenge. I had been waiting for Prabhupada to return to Bombay so I could feel some relief and become blissful again. But even after he came, I could not shake off my anxiety.

“I have really been suffering,” I confided in Tamal Krishna. “I know I am doing what Prabhupada wants me to do, because he ordered me to do it, but still I am in so much distress. I thought that when he came I would get some relief, but I am still in anxiety. How is this possible?”

Tamal Krishna replied that it was like being in a house on fire. To get out of the house, you have to go through the window. And to get out of the window, you have to break it with your hand. You know you have to do it. When you break the glass with your hand, your hand will get cut and it will hurt, but you have to do it to save your entire body.

I reflected on his comparison. In essence, he was saying that just as the hand is part of the body, we are part and parcel of Krishna, represented by Prabhupada, and therefore part and parcel of Prabhupada’s mission. For the benefit of the mission, we may have to suffer. Like breaking the window—it may hurt, but we do it for Krishna and Prabhupada. And because we are their part and parcel, even though we temporarily suffer pain, ultimately we benefit. It was a perfect answer, I thought—in keeping with Prabhupada’s statement that if necessary for Krishna’s service, we can temporarily sacrifice our peace of mind.

As soon as Prabhupada revived the sales agreement with Mr. Nair, he wrote to Diwanji, asking him to provide the title certificate, which wouldcertify that Nair had a clear and marketable title to the property. Earlier, Prabhupada had cabled Diwanji from Los Angeles but Diwanji had not replied, so Prabhupada had arranged for his lawyer in LA to contact him, and Diwanji had replied that he no longer represented us. So Prabhupada had advised us to find another lawyer, which had led to our appointing Mulla & Mulla. But because Diwanji had already been involved in the transaction, Prabhupada requested that he issue the title certificate: “It is now difficult to change again our attorneys. Therefore kindly be merciful upon us and deliver the Title Certificate so that the whole business may be completed without delay to everyone’s satisfaction.”

“I thought Diwanji was our friend,” Prabhupada told me one night. “I could not know that he was implicated with Nair.” He paused for a minute and then added, “Or, Krishna did not want me to know.”

I thought of Krishna’s words in the Bhagavad-gita—mattah smrtir jnanam apohanam ca: “From Me come remembrance, knowledge, and forgetfulness.”

On November 28 we sent the charity commissioner the new sales agreement and requested that he grant us permission to proceed with a payment arrangement for the purchase—in time to meet the December 1 deadline. “In this Supplementary Agreement,” we wrote, “it is stated that the conveyance must be executed by the 1st December 1972, time being of the essence. In view of these facts, we shall be grateful if you will kindly grant us permission for the payment of the balance of the purchase amount to be statutory charge on the property in fulfilling the noble and charitable objects of the Society.”

On the 29th the charity commissioner requested that I meet him in his office the following day to discuss our application. Meanwhile, Mulla & Mulla, as we had instructed, returned to Chimanlal Shah two draft conveyances approved by them and reapproved by Ambhubhai and Diwanji Solicitors—one for the front, vacant portion of the land and one for the back, built-up portion. They stated that if the two conveyances required that the land be subdivided by the municipality, we would have to insist upon only one conveyance, but that if Nair obtained the required consent from the municipality, we would have no objection to two conveyances. “Please further note that our clients are consulting their Architects as to whether it would mean a sub-division of land ifthe two conveyance deeds are executed by your clients in their favour and as per the Municipal rules it would require prior consent of the Municipal Corporation.” The letter concluded, “Immediately our clients hear from their Architects in the course of the day they will revert.”

Soon thereafter, our architects, Motilal Khanna and Associates, wrote Mulla & Mulla, “It is our considered opinion that only one conveyance should be made in the sale of the above property. Since the vendor appears to be the sole owner of the holding, two separate conveyances will be tantamount to ‘sub-division.’ This in our opinion would be illegal. For your ready reference we reproduce below an excerpt of a circular number CE/42383/II of 5-1-71, from the city engineer of the Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay.”

With so many negotiations in process, Prabhupada had us put up the Rs. 300,000 payable on execution of the conveyance, according to the supplemental agreement dated November 24. And on November 30, the day before the deadline, Mulla & Mulla wrote Chimanlal Shah:

“In order to show their bona fide for completing the sale herein our clients have requested us to inform you that they have deposited a sum of Rs. 3,00,000/- being the amount payable on the execution of the Conveyance Deed herein as per the terms of the Supplemental agreement dated 24th November 1972.

“Also as per the said Supplemental Agreement our clients await from you prior to the completion of the sale the Certificate of title of M/s. Ambhubhai and Diwanji certifying that your clients title to the property is clear, marketable and free from encumbrances subject to the High Court Suit No. 94 of 1968. As your clients have also undertaken to make out a marketable title our clients also await your clients Certificate under section 230A of the Income-tax Act.”

There were many loose ends to be tied up and only one day to do it.

Meanwhile, Mr. Nair claimed that our insistence on only one conveyance made it impossible for him to meet the deadline. Thus, on the same day, November 30, Chimanlal Shah wrote Mulla & Mulla, “It is surprising that when the sale is to be completed on or before 1st December 1972 time being the essence of the contract your clients at the last moment came forward with a suggestion for one Conveyanceand thereby making it impossible to complete the sale on or before 1st December 1972. Such conduct on the part of your clients amounts to a breach of the contract on the part of your clients.” That being said, “without prejudice,” Nair agreed to executing one conveyance on condition that (1) the new draft conveyance be drafted in the course of the day and reach Chimanlal Shah the next day for approval, in order to be executed on December 4, (2) we would be responsible to get the stamps transferred from the two deeds of conveyance to the single conveyance, or (3) if the stamps on the engrossments of the two conveyances were not transferred to the proposed single conveyance, the cost for the new stamps would be entirely borne and paid by us.

On December 1 Mulla & Mulla sent Chimanlal Shah the draft of the proposed single conveyance, writing, “Please return one copy of the draft duly approved by you at your earliest convenience to enable us to engross the same. Please also send us the stamped engrossments of the two previous conveyances deeds.” Later in the day, Mulla & Mulla asked Chimanlal Shah to have Nair return a declaration required for the sale.

The exchanges went back and forth throughout the evening, well past normal business hours, each side demanding certificates and other documents from the other, each side’s lawyers accusing the other of failing to fulfill the requirements of the agreement, and each side making excuses and justifying its behavior. It was complicated and disagreeable—the machinations of corrupt people.

As Prabhupada commented later, “Nair was thinking, ‘This man has no money, so just involve him, and whatever money he gives us, I shall take it.’” But one thing was sure: Prabhupada was sincere in his desire to complete the transaction and ready to do whatever was required legally, according to the agreement, to make it happen.

Prabhupada waited a week for the conveyance to be executed, but then he had to go to Ahmedabad for a pandal program. He departed on December 2, leaving us with strict instructions to pursue the conveyance and secure the land.

But two days later, we asked our solicitors to return the money we had deposited with them, stating that we were no longer interested in purchasing the property:

Dear Sirs:

(For attention of Mrs. K. F. Mehta)

Re: Sale of property at Juhu by Mrs. A. B. Nair to ISKCON.

Due to the inability of the Vendor to fulfill her part of the supplemental Agreement for sale dated 24th November, 1972, the said Supplemental Agreement as well as the original Agreement of Sale of 8th February, 1972 stand terminated. Therefore we are no longer interested to purchase the property. We request you to return to us the sum of Rs. 3,00,000/- deposited by us with you on 28th November, 1972.

Thanking you,

Yours faithfully, FOR ISKCON.

Sd/ -

Secretary.

As the days passed and it became clear that Nair was stalling in an effort to renege, to cheat us, some of the devotees again questioned the wisdom of purchasing the Juhu land. Shyamasundar in particular thought the agreement—and the whole project—was a big mistake.

After Prabhupada had left for Ahmedabad, Tamal Krishna, Shyamasundar, Dravida, myself, and a few others shifted to Mr. Valia’s Heliopolis flat in Colaba, which was conveniently located for our fund-raising, our work on the pandal program, and our efforts to procure the Juhu land. Shyamasundar discussed the issue of Juhu with Tamal Krishna day and night. The tenants might not leave the property, he argued, and the land itself—and its location—was not a good choice. It was just a jungle overrun with snakes and rats and bugs—no place for a temple and hotel. Life there was very austere, and it was too far from central Bombay.

“It was terrible,” Tamal Krishna later described, “far away from the city, and we had to travel by bus and train—two and a half to three hours every day. It was just unbearable.”

Shyamasundar even suggested that Prabhupada was aware that his decision had been in error but was too old and stubborn to admit it. Adding to their displeasure, neither Shyamasundar nor Tamal Krishna wanted to have to stay in Bombay fighting with Nair. If we continued the legal battle, they were thinking, we could be fighting for years andthey wouldn’t be able to go anywhere or do anything else. We would be suffering, and there wouldn’t be any good results. Even if we did get the land, the project would drag on for many years and take over our lives. The best thing, they thought, would be to cancel the agreement, retrieve the money, and get out of the whole thing. That way we wouldn’t be stuck with the Juhu land and they wouldn’t be stuck in Bombay.

I didn’t agree with their thinking, and certainly not with the idea that Prabhupada could be seen in such mundane terms or was not capable of assessing the situation and making a good decision. I didn’t even like hearing things put in those terms. In fact, I was completely opposed to what they were doing, because I knew how much Prabhupada wanted the Juhu project to succeed. But Dravida and I were junior to them, and we weren’t able to change the way things were going. They had the authority, and they cancelled the agreement.

In Ahmedabad, Prabhupada remained concerned about Bombay. He requested Nair and Mr. Diwanji to come there to try and reach a final settlement, but they declined, and he had not heard from or been able to get in touch with Shyamasundar or Tamal Krishna. “I am very much surprised not to hear from you about the Nair affair,” he wrote to them. “I have tried to contact you by phone, but it is understood that you have left Mr. Valia’s place and they could not say where you are. We have sent a telegram today reading as follows: ‘Anxious to know progress with Nair. Call urgent.’”

Prabhupada had a feeling that something might go wrong—and that Shyamasundar and Tamal Krishna might want to cancel the agreement. Visakha dasi had just arrived in Ahmedabad from Bombay to see, hear, and photograph Prabhupada at the pandal program, and he called her into his room. “Tamal and Shyamasundar are in Juhu,” he said, “and I suspect they may cancel our sales agreement with Nair. I’ve tried phoning, but I cannot get through, and telegrams may not reach them. I’d like you to return to Bombay and tell them that under no circumstances should they cancel the agreement.”

Visakha took the next train to Bombay to convey Prabhupada’s instructions. But when she arrived the following morning, it was already too late; what Prabhupada had foreseen had already happened: the sales agreement had been cancelled.

Even then, and even though Prabhupada had personally sent Visakha to speak to them, Shyamasundar and Tamal didn’t want to listen to what she had to say. She was just a woman, they thought—what could she tell them? They thought they knew what they were doing.

Dravida and I had been shocked when we’d heard about the cancellation. We knew that without an agreement we had no legal standing. We had neither gotten back our earlier payments, nor did we have any claim to potential ownership.

But when Visakha delivered Prabhupada’s message and we saw how she had been treated, we became even more upset. I immediately called Prabhupada in Ahmedabad. He rarely spoke on the phone, and I had never spoken with him on the phone before, but the situation was critical.

“Bhaktivedanta Swami here,” I heard when Prabhupada got on the line. To hear his voice was itself a tremendous spiritual experience. For a second, I felt great ecstasy, despite the seriousness of the matter at hand.

“Yes?” he asked when for some moments I did not reply.

His question brought me back to the situation at hand. “Srila Prabhupada,” I managed, trembling, “this is Giriraj dasa. Visakha came and brought your message, but they didn’t want to listen to her because they thought she was just a woman.”

“Yes, yes?” he repeated.

“Srila Prabhupada,” I finally blurted out, “they cancelled the agreement.”

Prabhupada was silent. Then, in a grave voice filled with anger, concern, and resignation, he said, “Then everything is finished.”

He asked me another question, about the money, but I didn’t know the answer. “You are phoning me, and you don’t have all the information,” he said. “You are also useless.”

I told him that Shyamasundar was thinking of leaving Bombay and coming to Ahmedabad to speak to him.

“Yes, that is good,” he replied. “Let him come.”

Then, understanding that I was in anxiety about the whole situation, he said, “Don’t be anxious,” and then he hung up.

When Prabhupada phoned Tamal Krishna to find out what had happened, Tamal Krishna tried to explain that they had seen that there were many defects with the agreement and so had cancelled it.

“You couldn’t cancel it,” Prabhupada said.

“Yes, we did cancel it,” Tamal Krishna replied.

“And then,” Tamal Krishna later recalled, “all I heard was ‘click.’ No further discussion.

“Somehow or other, by the powerful illusory energy, it was in our mind that Prabhupada had given us the right to decide what to do that was needful. And we took that to mean we should decide whether it was better to cancel it or to go ahead with it.”

Without Prabhupada’s knowledge or approval, he and Shyamasundar had gone back and forth with the lawyers, trying to find a way out of the deal. And the lawyers had provided a host of reasons why the sales agreement was not good. If we wanted the money back, they had said, we should cancel the agreement. Unless we did—if we fought the case in court—the funds would be held in abeyance. We would have to file suit, and it might take over a decade to get the money back, if we ever did. We didn’t have much experience in these legal dealings, but we knew we didn’t want the funds to be locked up and possibly lost.

Ultimately, based on this line of thinking and guided by the lawyers, after Prabhupada had worked on the agreement for two years, Tamal Krishna and Shyamasundar had cancelled it—in no uncertain terms: “Due to the inability of the Vendor to fulfill her part of the Supplemental Agreement for Sale dated 24th November, 1972, the said Supplemental Agreement as well as the original Agreement of Sale of 8th February, 1972, stand terminated. Therefore we are no longer interested to purchase the property.”

“It was basically due to our spiritual defect that we did not carry out Srila Prabhupada’s desire,” Tamal Krishna later admitted. “It was so clear and strong a desire, yet we couldn’t see it as such. We thought that Prabhupada had made a mistake. We began to feel, ‘Oh, we’ve got to get out of this agreement. We’ve got to cancel it.’ And our lawyers showed us how we could do it.

“I know it sounds unbelievable. It’s unbelievable to me also, but \[we\] did it. It was very unfortunate. It was one of those things when the disciple has his independent intelligence and independent desires that are separate from the spiritual master. It was a very big mistake.”

As Prabhupada later explained, our lawyers had their own vestedinterests, and although we were ostensibly their clients, they were not actually working on our behalf. The land was worth more than the agreed sales price and the agreement was perfectly sound, but they didn’t want us to get the land. They had, we eventually learned, been in cahoots with the other side.

So, there we were—still on the land but with no legal standing, no agreement, no claim—trespassers. All we could do was go to court and ask for a return of our deposit.

But Prabhupada did not lose his spirit, or hope. “I shall be the last man to give up the Hare Krishna Land to the rogue Mr. Nair,” he wrote to Captain Singhal from Ahmedabad on December 15. “He has taken our money but tactfully has not given us the conveyance.”

And on the same day, he wrote to Mrs. Singhal, “We have neither changed our plan nor have we any intention of changing our plan of developing Hare Krishna Land in Bombay. We shall stick to the place to the last moment and we require your cooperation very much.” He was already planning how to rectify his disciples’ mistake. No money had yet been transferred, so perhaps it was not too late.

Harikesa had made a life member of S.R. Vakil, one of the main lawyers of the entire Tata corporate empire, and when Mr. Vakil heard about our difficulties, he cited a law that gave us protection even though we had cancelled the agreement. The Easements Act dictated that if you leased a property and built a structure on the property, then even after the lease expired, you had the right to retain the structure.

So that was what we would do. Nair had given us permission to build our small, semipermanent temple. And now we would claim that even though the sales agreement had been cancelled, we still had the right to keep the temple, regardless of the status of the sale.

Anyway, that was our argument, though it wasn’t the strongest. Prabhupada would have to return to Bombay. Until then, nothing more could be done.

When Prabhupada arrived in Bombay, there was a rousing reception at the airport, including our friend Biharilal Khandelwal. I had avoided telling Mr. Khandelwal about the difficulty with the land, because I was afraid he would not give his donation of 100,000 rupees until the disputewas resolved. I thought that at least I would let him give his donation first. But when Prabhupada met him at the airport, he informed him about our problem with Nair, told us to give him the legal papers, and asked for his help.

My heart sank. Adding to my apprehension that Mr. Khandelwal might hold his donation until the problem was solved, Tamal Krishna and I were concerned that we were asking too much of him. But Prabhupada said that although the case might be a big thing for us, for Mr. Khandelwal it was small. “He must be having so many cases like this going on.”

Because we did not have a proper place for Prabhupada in Juhu, we often arranged for him to stay with friends in Bombay. In Ahmedabad, Kartikeya Mahadevia, an early life member and supporter, had offered to share his flat at Sea Face Park—five buildings built in a horseshoe formation with the sea at the open end. And after they had spent four days in his own flat, Mr. Mahadevia arranged for Prabhupada and some assistants to move to the flat of his recently deceased brother, Kumudchandra, in another building in Sea Face Park, and the rest of us stayed in Mr. Valia’s flat.

While Prabhupada had been in Ahmedabad, Shyamasundar had shared with me his assessment of ISKCON. He thought that the leaders wanted only yes-men who would follow instructions and go on sankirtana without being independently creative or intelligent. Therefore we were not attracting quality people. He had ideas about how the Society could be expanded in the West, but he didn’t think we had anyone capable of approaching professors or other intellectuals.

Thinking of my own background and inclination, I had told Shyamasundar that I was acquainted with many leading intellectuals—if not personally, at least through their writings. I felt that I could meet and communicate with them and attract them to Krishna consciousness.

He had thought it was a great idea. “Yes, this is what you should do,” he had said. “You are wasting your time in India. You are just rotting here. You should go back to the West and preach to these intellectual leaders.”

The talk had bewildered me. Much of what Shyamasundar had said seemed to make sense. It did seem that I was suffering in Bombay,fighting with Nair, and I had always felt that I should approach the educators and intellectuals in America. And when I had spoken with Prabhupada in Calcutta about my future service, he had mentioned that I should go to the universities and get his books accepted as required reading. So, I wasn’t sure what to do.

Finally, though I did not like to bother Prabhupada with unnecessary questions, I realized that he was the only person who could provide me with an answer. So I approached him at Mr. Mahadevia’s flat. Shyamasundar, I told him, thought I could be better engaged by going to the West and preaching to the intellectuals.

Prabhupada listened quietly while Srutakirti gave him a massage. Then he said, “Suppose you are massaging Krishna’s left leg and you think, ‘Now I would like to massage His right leg.’ That is also service to Krishna. But Krishna may be feeling that actually He wants more massage on His left leg.”

Hearing Prabhupada’s words, I understood that Krishna wanted me to remain in Bombay.

“Actually,” Prabhupada said, “your service here is more important.”

Hearing this, I immediately abandoned my idea of preaching in the West, offered my obeisances, and left the room.

Later, when I considered what Prabhupada had said, I concluded that I had been foolish. Obviously Prabhupada wanted me in India. If he had wanted me to go to the West, he would have said so. And Prabhupada himself was concentrating on India, especially on Bombay. He had already written me that Bombay was “the richest city, the gateway to India, and in all respects the most important city.”

Really, I could have figured it out for myself. But Prabhupada had been kind and merciful; he had given the answer and had not seemed to mind the question.

Also while we were staying at Heliopolis, a letter arrived for Prabhupada from a Mr. Brijratan Mohatta, asking spiritual questions. We rarely replied to such letters ourselves, but because Prabhupada was not in Bombay and Mr. Mohatta seemed to be a substantial person with spiritual interests, I thought I should meet him as soon as possible, so I phoned his office and made an appointment.

Mr. Mohatta was everything I had anticipated: affluent, intelligent, and inquisitive. As it turned out, he was one of the most prominentbusinessmen in Bombay and was married to the daughter of Seth R. D. Birla of the illustrious Birla family, the wealthiest family in India.

Mr. Mohatta was one of the leaders of the Vishva Hindu Parishad, the world’s most famous Hindu organization, whose goal was to unite and strengthen all Hindus. But he was also a staunch impersonalist, and when I began preaching to him about the Bhagavad-gita, he started to give me his Mayavada philosophy. “When Krishna says ‘Me,’” he claimed, “He doesn’t mean Krishna the person. Krishna is not Krishna; Krishna means something else.” Krishna, he said, meant the Supreme Truth, the impersonal One, “the all-pervading Krishna who is greater than the person Krishna” and could come in any form and lived in everyone’s heart.

When I told Prabhupada about the meeting, he said, “First of all, if Krishna is not Krishna, then who is He? Mohatta? And is Mr. Mohatta not Mr. Mohatta? Does Mr. Mohatta also mean something else? Second, even assuming that the impersonal absolute is greater than Krishna, how do I benefit? You should ask Mr. Mohatta, ‘What is more valuable to you, ten lakh rupees distributed with one rupee in everyone’s pocket, or one lakh rupees in your pocket?”’ Even if Mr. Mohatta believed that the all-pervading Krishna was greater, Prabhupada was saying, he would get more benefit from the person Krishna. And again, he gave a perfect analogy according to the mentality of the person.

Another wealthy impersonalist, Dr. N. D. Desai, also lived in Sea Face Park and often came to meet Prabhupada and argue with him. Dr. Desai was both intelligent and educated, but he was a follower of Swami Chinmayananda, a Mayavadi impersonalist, and would present all sorts of impersonal arguments, which Prabhupada would promptly and thoroughly defeat. Then Dr. Desai would approach Swami Chinmayananda and tell him, “Bhaktivedanta Swami said such-and-such,” and Swami Chinmayananda would tell him what to say in reply, which Dr. Desai would do—only to have his argument smashed again. Like this, Dr. Desai went back and forth between them, but eventually he realized that Prabhupada’s arguments could not be refuted, and further, that Prabhupada was of impeccable character, and his heart softened.

“Out of respect, I would offer my obeisances and listen to Prabhupada,” Dr. Desai recalled, “but I was a Mayavadi and I would also arguewith him. I would say, ‘Brahman is supreme, not Krishna. Brahman takes the form of Krishna, Rama, Nrsimha, etc.’ Prabhupada would tolerate my nonsense and give me prasada. He would ask, ‘Who has told you all these nonsense things?’ I would reply, ‘My spiritual teacher is Chinmayananda Swami.’ Prabhupada would say, ‘Oh, that rascal. He’s the biggest Mayavadi. Ask him, “If you’re Narayana, why are you getting old, why are your teeth falling out, why is your hair getting gray? Why are you not looking young like Narayana?” This is all nonsense. God is always God—He doesn’t become God. We are always jivatma, and we’ll always be jivatma. We are parts and parcels of God, and the part and parcel can never be the same as the complete whole.’

“So, I’d go back to Chinmayananda Swami and ask him, ‘Swamiji, why do you get old? If you control Mother Nature, why are you getting old? Can you not control that?’ And he would say, ‘I have to look old so that people respect me more.’

“I’d go back and tell Prabhupada, ‘He has to look old because people will respect him more.’ And Prabhupada would say, ‘That is rascaldom. Nature is under Krishna’s control, not under Chinmayananda’s control. He will always be controlled by nature. You go and tell him that.’ He would usually quote some verse from the Bhagavad-gita, like the verse where Lord Krishna says, ‘I am the seed-giving father.’ How could Swami Chinmayananda be the seed-giving father of everybody? Again I’d go back and tell Swami Chinmayananda.

“Eventually Prabhupada asked me to invite Chinmayananda Swami to come and have a debate. I asked Prabhupada, ‘What point shall we debate?’ He said, ‘We shall debate whether Chinmayananda Swami will lift Govardhana Hill or not. If he’s God, he should be able to do that. God—Krishna—did it. If he knows what’s in my mind and everybody’s mind, then he’s God, Paramatma. But if he only knows about his own body, and that too not fully, he’s just another human being who’s trying to cheat God and trying to cheat everyone else.’

“I asked Chinmayananda Swami, Are you prepared to have this debate? It’ll resolve this awful doubt I have now as to which of you two is the real spiritual master.’ But Chinmayananda Swami refused. I asked Chinmayananda Swami, ‘Can you please tell me whether you can know what’s in the minds of everyone? God knows what’s goingon in everyone’s mind. Can you do that? If I sit down now and think something, would you be able to write down what I was thinking?’ He said, ‘No. I am not a mind-reader.’ I said, ‘No, no. I am not talking about reading minds. If you are really at an elevated level where you are one with God, then it would be like you’ve plugged yourself into a computer that has so many facts. You should be able to retrieve information.’ He couldn’t do it. Then I surrendered to Prabhupada.”

During this time at Sea Face Park, Prabhupada often brought up his disciples’ blunder in cancelling the Juhu agreement. He held Tamal Krishna, his GBC representative for India, especially responsible, and Tamal Krishna underwent continual humiliation. Often, when Prabhupada received a life member or other friend, sympathizer, or supporter, he would show them the agreement, explain what had happened, point to Tamal Krishna, and say, “This is the foolish boy who cancelled the agreement. He is so foolish, so inexperienced—this is what he did.” And he would make Tamal Krishna sit there and hear the chastisement again and again.

“It was a huge blunder on our part,” Tamal Krishna later acknowledged. “There were many more such blunders, but Prabhupada’s wonderful quality through them all was that he never gave up on us. No matter how many mistakes a devotee might make, Prabhupada would see if that person wanted to continue to serve Krishna, and he would stand by that devotee. Prabhupada knew that there would be mistakes, and he would chastise you like anything, but he never gave you the sense that he didn’t love you. Despite all of the grand mistakes that were made, I never got the sense that Prabhupada loved me less because of them. I always felt encouraged, not discouraged, despite our many mistakes. In the instance of the contract cancellation, Prabhupada did not reject me. He gave Giriraj and me the opportunity to go through a hellish year and a half of regularly going to Bombay, sitting in lawyers’ chambers, trying to rectify the situation.”

Tamal Krishna did whatever he could to make up for his mistake, and for months he spent up to eight hours a day in lawyers’ offices. As he later described his and my activities, “On Dalal Street, Bombay, the sight of a Western sannyasi, with danda in hand, accompanied by a bespectacled young man carrying a heavy briefcase became a commonsight to the solicitors and their clients who normally frequented the street. Giriraj and I, as Prabhupada’s representatives, pleaded the case of Radha-Rasabihari, making continuous rounds from the lawyers’ offices to court, in a transcendental drama that lasted for over a year.” Actually, our position seemed hopeless, but we kept trying different strategies.

Every day, all day, I would go out into the city and meet with people. When approaching prospective contributors, if someone didn’t want to become a life member, I would ask him to take an advertisement in a publication. If he didn’t want to take an ad, I would ask him to buy a set of books. If he didn’t buy a set of books, I would ask him to give a donation, or at least buy one book, or at least give something to help. And in the evening I would go report to Prabhupada about my preaching.
