At the end of one day, I felt particularly discouraged. I’d gone to many people, but most of them had refused to meet me and the one or two I had met were not interested in helping. Not one person had contributed in any way. When I explained this to Prabhupada, he said, “Don’t be discouraged. If you sincerely try your best to please Krishna, Krishna will be satisfied—even if others are not.”

I considered Prabhupada’s words. The people I had met may not have been satisfied, and so they had not contributed. And even the devotees may not have been satisfied, since I had not achieved any desired results. But if Krishna was satisfied, what else mattered? I understood that if I sincerely tried to serve Krishna without any other motivation, Krishna would be pleased, regardless of the results.

Mr. Mahadevia ran a cloth business, including some Mafatlal retail stores. His older brother, Kumudchandra, had been the head of purchases for the Mafatlal textile companies—a responsible position, for a trusted person. Arvind Mafatlal was the head of both the family and the group, which was the third-wealthiest in India. His father and Mr. Mahadevia’s father had been in business together for many years, and Kumudchandra had been married to one of Arvind’s sisters. Arvind was also a leader of India’s Gujarati community and a great philanthropist. In fact, the family was renowned for being pious and religious people of impeccable character, with strong connections with the government. They were especially respected for their charitablework. Mr. Mafatlal distributed food to thousands of people in impoverished areas, and whenever there was a flood, drought, famine, or other disaster, he would take a leading role in providing for the victims. They served nutritious vegetarian food to hundreds of thousands in need, and people often spoke of them with the reverence and adulation usually reserved for the gods.

Many times when we met persons to enroll them as life members and get donations, they would ask, “Have you met Arvind Mafatlal?” And we were embarrassed to have to say no, we had not. Finally, after I had tried for many months to get an appointment, Mr. Mahadevia arranged one.

It was with both eagerness and trepidation that I entered Mr. Mafatlal’s office building, Mafatlal House, at Backbay Reclamation, rode up the lift, and entered his office. After Mr. Mafatlal greeted me from behind his large desk, I sat down and began telling him about our philosophy and some of our activities in India. When he described his food distribution and free eye camps and other charities, however, the discussion became somewhat contentious. I objected that feeding needy persons and giving medical relief were karma-kanda, Mr. Mafatlal insisted that such activities were bhakti. We disputed a bit, but I didn’t want to alienate him by arguing, and eventually the meeting ended without a conclusion.

When I returned to Sea Face Park that evening and Prabhupada asked how the preaching had gone, I related the incident. “Is it karma-kanda?" I asked.

Prabhupada replied that Mr. Mafatlal’s activities were in the category of charity. “Charity is recommended for householders,” he said, and he praised the activities of those who served in this way.

I could see from the way Prabhupada was answering that he wanted me to appreciate Mr. Mafatlal’s philanthropic activities, but then, after telling me how good they were, he acknowledged that they did actually fall in the category of karma-kanda. His point, I understood, was that my attitude toward karma-kanda should be sympathetic rather than condescending. We should appreciate the service of those we met, even if they were not on the highest platform, and not feel that we were superior.

Another time, while collecting ads for a pandal-program souvenir book, I met a shipping magnate, Mr. Kotak, at his residence. I had hardly begun to describe our activities, when Mr. Kotak interrupted and asked, “What can I do for you?”

“Actually,” I said, “we have come to do something for you.”

“What can you do for me?” he countered.

“Engage you in the service of the Lord.”

But Mr. Kotak objected. “How is my serving Krishna going to help me?” he questioned. “It is going to help you”

I tried to point out the mistake in his thinking, but he was just too stubborn, and finally I gave up. “Anyway,” I said, “We are having a big festival at Cross Maidan, and we were hoping you would place an advertisement in our special issue.”

To my surprise, Mr. Kotak immediately agreed. “Oh,” he said. “If you want some money for your festival, we can take an advertisement.” But he held to his point. “This is not for my benefit,” he insisted. “You are not doing anything for me; I am doing it for you.”

When I related the incident to Srila Prabhupada, he replied that preaching required humility. “A preacher should always be humble,” he said. “The gentleman knows that by serving Krishna he will gain; otherwise, he would not give his hard-earned money. Businessmen always calculate their profit and loss. If he did not think he would gain by giving to Krishna, he would not give. Only artificially he was posing that he was not getting any benefit, that he was simply doing it for us. Preaching means that people should conclude that by giving to Krishna they will gain and voluntarily they should give. That is preaching. But a preacher should always be humble.”

I appreciated Prabhupada’s instruction. Even though personally we had nothing to gain if donors served Krishna and they had everything to gain, for their benefit—and ours—we should be humble and approach them as beggars.

I was reminded of an incident in Indore, when Prabhupada had gone to see a wealthy man, a leading citizen, and requested him to become a life member. After speaking to him for some time, Prabhupada had shown him the books.

“I already have these books in my own language,” the man had said. “I don’t need any more.”

“I have not come here to sell you some books,” Prabhupada had replied. “I have come here as a beggar at your doorstep.”

At that, the man’s attitude had immediately changed. “Oh, yes,” he had said. “I will become your member, Swamiji; I will become your member.”

Still, Prabhupada’s preaching was strong, and he didn’t hesitate to tell things as they were, without sugar coating. Lokanath had initially been disturbed by this. He had thought, High-class people are coming all the way from the city, and here is a sadhu telling them they are fools and donkeys and hogs and dogs. Can't Prabhupada use more choice terms?

But as the months passed, Lokanath found himself using the same language. And he realized that it was appropriate. Prabhupada was straightforward, without holding back. “Why flatter?” he would often say. He wanted to dismantle people’s false ego and bodily concept of life, and he delivered Krishna’s message undiluted and unadulterated. He was truly representing Krishna, because Krishna too, in the Bhagavad-gita, did not flatter. He used terms such as mudha, rascal, and asura, demon, and Prabhupada was repeating His message—mudhas, naradhamas.

I observed, though, that after speaking like this, Prabhupada would be courteous and friendly. He wasn’t thinking that these people were rascals and that he should avoid them; he always made sure they got prasada and were encouraged in Krishna consciousness. One could see that he hated the sin—the meat-eating, gambling, intoxication, and illicit sex—but separated the sin and the sinner. As he had said in Boston, at Brandeis University, “We admit everyone. Our mission is to elevate persons from the down state of life to the highest state of life. Jesus Christ also said, ‘You do not hate the sinners, but hate sin.’ So, people may be sinners. We raise them to pious life. But we say, ‘Don’t do this. Don’t do this sinful act. Don’t take intoxication. Don’t do this. Don’t do this.’ We hate the sin, not the sinners. If we hate sinners, then where is the possibility of preaching?” He was endeavoring to remove the sin, and at the same time he was extremely affectionate toward all the sinners.

Actually, Lokanath’s reaction to Prabhupada’s strong words was similar to Prabhupada’s initial reaction to Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati’s preaching. When Prabhupada first met his spiritual master, he noticed that Bhaktisiddhanta would criticize practically any person or ideologythat was presented to him. Prabhupada later commented that at first he had been thinking, “Doesn’t he know how to do anything besides criticize?” But eventually he realized that everything Srila Bhaktisiddhanta had said was right.

One day, Lokanath came to Sea Face Park to inform Prabhupada about the activities in Juhu. Fifty or sixty people were attending the evening programs, he reported, which pleased Prabhupada—“Oh,” he said, “that’s very nice.”

Lokanath also received second initiation at Sea Face Park. Because the wooden altar in Juhu had silver-plating that needed polishing and Lokanath was thin and small-bodied (and Maithili, the head pujari, was not), Maithili had him climb onto the altar to clean it. Lokanath started doing aratis, and in time he became the head pujari.

Even with spending much of the day in discussions about legal matters and maneuvers regarding the Juhu land, Prabhupada gave two lectures daily—including speaking in the evening at Kumudchandra Mahadevia’s flat from December 26 to January 11, on The Nectar of Devotion.

His lectures were the highlight of the day for us—one of the highlights of our lives. All day long we would be looking forward to the evening, to being with Prabhupada and hearing him speak. Most of us had never heard him discourse on The Nectar of Devotion, which was meant especially for devotees. Generally he spoke on the Bhagavad-gita, because the knowledge of the Gita, beginning with “I am not this body,” was meant particularly for new people, but since we were in the Sea Face Park flat without outsiders, he was able to speak to our level of understanding.

When Prabhupada spoke, the devotees sat in rapt silence, erect and attentive. And after the lectures, we would go over what he had said and share our realizations.

He lectured on the meaning of pure devotional service:

anydbhilasita-sunyam  
jnana-karmady-anavrtam  
anukulyena krsnanu-  
silanam bhaktir uttama

“When first-class devotional service develops, one must be devoid of all material desires, knowledge obtained by monistic philosophy, and fruitive action. The devotee must constantly serve Krsna favorably, as Krsna desires.” (Brs 1.1.11, Cc Madhya 19.167)

Prabhupada often used the term pure devotional service, or unconditional devotional service. But I wondered what exactly that was. I thought it must mean that one was ready to perform any service for the spiritual master. But I wasn’t sure, so I asked.

“Unconditional devotional service?” Prabhupada replied. “Unconditional means spontaneous.”

Prabhupada’s talks on The Nectar of Devotion were both profoundly philosophical and relevant to issues we were facing. In his first talk, on December 26, he raised the question of black money in relation to Krishna consciousness. Pradyumna opened by reading from the preface: “Sakara Mallika, who was later to become £rila Sanatana Gosvami, took advantage of his brother’s personal money, which had been deposited with a village banker, and escaped from the prison of Hussain Shah. In this way, both brothers joined Lord Caitanya Mahaprabhu.”

Prabhupada commented, “Sometimes it is questioned that Sanatana Gosvami paid the money in black market.” He chuckled and continued, “Yes, actually he paid. When the Nawab Hussain Shah imprisoned him, he was a minister. And the superintendent of the jail had been working under him. So Sanatana Gosvami requested him that ‘I have done so many times your benefit. Now you do me one benefit. You let me go, although the Nawab has imprisoned me. I am going to be a pir \[religious instructor\].’ The Muslims very much respect the pir. And actually he was going to be a pir. He renounced family life and became a gosvami. ‘I am sacrificing my life for God, and you just help me in this service. And not only that; you will get some material profit also.’ So, he offered five thousand gold coins, mohurs.

“Now, the question is whether this kind of black-marketing, bribing, is required for spiritual life. And the answer is that everything is required, provided you can satisfy Krishna. This is the principle, according to time and circumstances. Just like on the battlefield there was fighting and Krishna advised Yudhisthira that ‘You go and tell Dronacarya that your son, Asvatthama, is dead.’ Krishna is advisinghim to speak a lie. And Yudhisthira hesitated: ‘How can I speak a lie? I never spoke lie in my life?

“When there is fighting, they adopt all means. The aim is how to own victory. Although there are so many international laws, they don’t care for them. . . . The point is that as people act by hook and crook, everything—for satisfying the senses, gaining some material profit— any means, if need be, can be accepted for Krishna’s service. Everything can be accepted. Otherwise, how Sanatana Gosvami is bribing? How Krishna is advising Yudhisthira to speak a lie?

“There is a verse, man nimitte krtam papam punya eva kalpate. Sometimes it appears that this is a sinful act, but if it is done for Krishna...”

He was quoting part of a verse from the Padma Purana, which also appears in the Hari-bhakti-vilasa (1.110):

man-nimittam krtam papam  
api dharmaya kalpate  
mam anadrtya dharmo 'pi  
papam syan mat-prabhavatah

“For My sake, even committing sin is understood to be dharma. Neglecting Me, even an act of religiosity turns into sin due to My influence.”

“Our bhakti,” Prabhupada continued, “is anukulyena krsnanu-silanam. We have to satisfy Krishna. Krishna is asking me to tell a lie. ‘Yes, I shall tell a lie.’ That is bhakti. If I consider, ‘Oh, I have never spoken lies in my life. How can I speak a lie?’ that is not bhakti. Because it is pratikula, against the desire of Krishna. Common people cannot understand this. They’ll shudder.”

He was enunciating a general spiritual principle that was especially relevant to his work in India. In general, he advised his disciples to follow the laws of the land and to act in the mode of goodness and exhibit the qualities of brahmans:

samo damas tapah saucam  
ksantir arjavam eva ca  
jnanam vijnanam astikyam  
brahma-karma svabhava-jam

“Peacefulness, self-control, austerity, purity, tolerance, honesty, knowledge, wisdom and religiousness—these are the natural qualities by which the brdhmanas work.” (Gita 18.42)

Prabhupada continued, “They think, ‘Oh, Krishna is teaching Yudhisthira, such a nice man, religious person, and He’s teaching him to speak a lie.’ Avajdnanti mam mudha manusim tanum asritam. \[“Fools deride Me when I descend in the human form.” (Gita 9.11)\]. If sometimes one thinks like that, he becomes a mudha \[fool, rascal\].”

Yudhisthira declined to follow Krishna’s order—though ultimately he agreed—and his hesitation, or reluctance, based on some material calculation, is not appreciated by pure devotees. Before Yudhisthira told his lie, the wheels of his chariot would never touch the ground, because he was so righteous, but after he lied, his wheels did touch the ground. The mundane interpretation is that he fell from his position because of his lie. But the devotional interpretation is that he fell because he had hesitated to follow Krishna’s instruction.

“There are many instances,” Prabhupada continued. “Just like the gopis. In the dead of night, when Krishna played His flute, they left their husbands, fathers, brothers, children—everything—and they went. Now, according to our Vedic system, young women leaving the protection of father, brother, or superiors and going into the forest for another boy—oh, it is very sinful. Socially, it is sinful. And Krishna instructed the gopis, ‘What have you done? You go back immediately.’ And they began to cry. This description is there. So, from the social point of view, this is sin—when the gopis went to Krishna.

“Similarly, Prahlada Maharaja stood without any protest when his father was being killed. And Bali Maharaja rejected his spiritual master when he—Shukracharya—said, ‘Don’t promise. He’s Vishnu. He’ll take everything of yours. Don’t promise anything.’ Bali Maharaja said, ‘He is Vishnu? And you are asking me not to promise to Him? Oh, I don’t want such spiritual master. I reject you.’ To reject one’s spiritual master is a great sin.

“From social point of view, religious point of view, these are irreligious, sinful activities: to reject one’s spiritual master; to see one’s father being killed in one’s presence; one woman is going to another boy, in dead of night. Superficially they are sinful activities. But Chaitanya

Mahaprabhu recommends, ramya kacid upasana vraja-vadhu-vargena yd kalpita (Caitanya-mata-manjusa). There is no better upasana, method of worship, than as it was conceived by the gopis—first-class.

“Superficially it may sometimes appear against the social and religious rules and regulations, but if it is done for Krishna, anukulyena ... Bhakti means Krishna should be satisfied. It doesn’t matter.

“It doesn’t matter the whole world is going to hell, but if Krishna is satisfied, a devotee is prepared to do that. That is called uttama-bhakti: anukulyena krsnanu-silanam bhaktir uttama. You’ll find it in the Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu: anyabhilasita-sunyam. Not to make business with Krishna—'I shall be devotee of Krishna provided my everything is adjusted all right: I shall not be sinful. I shall not do this. I shall not do that. My family will be kept nicely.’ All these conditions. Just like people go to Vrindavan—after all the money is distributed. There are many persons, and they make sure their sons and grandsons are all right, that ‘You send me two hundred rupees per month. And all the two crores of rupees are for you. That is not for Krishna. And simply for my eating, you send me two hundred.’ There are many in Vrindavan.

“Krishna is also very intelligent, that ‘Two crores of rupees you earned, with hard labor, and that is kept for your children. And you have come here with empty hands. And for your food, two hundred rupees.’ Ye yatha mam prapadyante tams tathaiva bhajamy aham \[“As all surrender unto Me, I reward them accordingly.” (Gita 4.11)\].” Prabhupada chuckled. “No. The first principle is that one should be prepared to sacrifice anything, everything for Krishna.

“Everything. It doesn’t matter—my fate, my honor, my money, my prestige. He doesn’t care. Krishna must be satisfied. Take, for example, Arjuna. Arjuna didn’t like to fight, to kill on the other side his brother, his grandfather. No. But when he understood, ‘Krishna wants it. Yes, karisye vacanam tava \[“I shall execute Your order.” (Gita 18.73)\]. That’s all right.’

“This is Krishna consciousness. No consideration for anything else. Simply to satisfy Krishna. Satisfy Krishna or Krishna’s representative—same thing. That is bhakti. Anyabhilasita-sunyam jnana-karmady-anavrtam. Jnana. It should not be tinged by jnana. This is jnana: ‘Oh, I am going to speak lie. I’ll go to hell. I am going to kill my grandfather. I’ll go to hell.’ This is called jnana, knowledge. But the definition is jnana-karmady-anavrtam: it should be untouched by jnana and karma. Untouched. Yes.

“This is pure bhakti. Anyabhilasita-sunyam jnana-karmady-anavrtam. The gopis are not jnanis; they’re ordinary village girls. What jnana they have? No jnana, no karma. They did not know what is karma, what is sacrifice. They did not know. We should be prepared to sacrifice everything, without any consideration of jnana, karma, yoga. No. We have to see whether Krishna is satisfied.

“People have no information who is Krishna, what to speak of satisfying Him. So-called learned scholars have no idea. But a bhakta is always ready to sacrifice everything to satisfy Krishna.”

Prabhupada was not only instructing us in the principles of pure devotion; he was explaining himself to us—his own mood of being ready to sacrifice anything and everything to satisfy Krishna. As he had told us in Calcutta, his motto was, “Everything for Krishna, nothing for myself,” and so he never complained.

“But if one has no idea who is Krishna,” he continued, “then where is bhakti? For the impersonalist, there cannot be any bhakti, because they have no information of Krishna. And bhakti means satisfaction of Krishna. If I know the person, if I know his nature, then I can know how to satisfy him. If you have no information of a person, then where is the question of satisfaction?

“The point here is that Sanatana Gosvami, Sakara Mallika, was so mad after meeting Chaitanya Mahaprabhu that whatever money he had with the village banker, and even if it was sinful to bribe, he didn’t care. He resigned his service as minister. Therefore he was imprisoned. Now to get out of the prison house, he bribed. He was so much ecstatic.

“This is called laulyam. Laulyam means, just like we become very much greedy in achieving some success or receiving something sometimes, we become mad. That is required. Laulyam api mulyam ekalam. To achieve Krishna consciousness perfectly, this ecstatic eagerness or greediness, to serve Krishna, that is the only price to achieve success in devotional service. That is the only price. Not money, not anything. Not prestige, not good parentage, not beauty—nothing. Simply this ecstatic, intense desire: ‘How I shall get Krishna?’ Then you’ll get Krishna. He’ll take you.

“That is the example of the gopis—intense desire. Tatra laulyam api mulyam ekalam. This ecstatic desire, that ‘I, this life, shall getrecognition by Krishna, that I have sacrificed everything for Krishna,’ this is required.”

What a challenge—and what an opportunity!

Word spread that Prabhupada was speaking nightly at Sea Face Park, and new people started to come. And often, when an outsider entered the room, Prabhupada, to the devotees’ disappointment, would shift from The Nectar of Devotion to the Bhagavad-gita.

One evening, a respectable Indian gentleman, В. M. Kamdar, walked in. Mr. Kamdar was a leader of the Vishva Hindu Parishad, and he asked Prabhupada why India, which had such a history of mahatmas and saintly persons, was suffering so many difficulties. “Swamiji,” he asked, “with so many saints in India, how did we come to this stage?”

“First of all,” Prabhupada replied, “you do not know who is a saint. That is your difficulty. You say, ‘so many saints,’ but there is no saint at all. You say, ‘so many saints,’ so what is a saint? What is your understanding of saint?”

Mr. Kamdar could not answer.

“If I say ‘so many rich men,”’ Prabhupada continued, “I must know who is a rich man. So first of all, who is a saint?”

An Indian woman interjected, “They claim that they are saints.”

“They claim,” Prabhupada replied. “Everyone can claim, ‘I am a saint.’ But you must know who is a saint. Everyone will claim that ‘I am a rich man.’ But there must be a standard of who is rich man. At least we understand that one who has got a nice bungalow, a nice car, a few servants, a nice bank balance, then you can say, ‘Yes, he is a rich man.’ But if I do not know who is a rich man, then what is the use of speaking ‘so many’? First you must know who is a saint. And how do you know it? The exact meaning of saint is sadhu. Is it not?”

“Yes,” the lady accepted.

“So, in the Bhagavad-gita you will find who is a sadhu. Krishna explains,

api cet su-duracaro  
bhajate mam ananya-bhak  
sadhur eva sa mantavyah  
samyag vyavasito hi sah

\[“Even if one commits the most abominable action, if he is engaged in devotional service he is to be considered saintly because he is properly situated in his determination ” (Gita 9.30)\]

“Who is mahatma?

mahatmanas tu mam partha  
daivim prakrtim asritah  
bhajanty ananya-manaso  
jnatva bhutadim avyayam

\[“O son of Prtha, those who are not deluded, the mahatmas, are under the protection of the divine nature. They are fully engaged in devotional service because they know Me as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, original and inexhaustible.” (Gita 9.13)\]

“Not that by stamping one becomes mahatma. First of all, know who is mahatma, who is sadhu. Mahatma, in another place, vasudevah sarvam iti sa mahatma su-durlabhah. \[Gita 7.19\] This is mahatma. These are the descriptions of mahatma.

“If I say, people may be angry. If I say the politician is not a mahatma, then people will be angry. But see the standard definition of mahatma. Krishna says,

bahunam janmanam ante  
jnanavan mam prapadyate  
vasudevah sarvam iti  
sa mahatma su-durlabhah  
\[Gita 7.19\]

You can stamp anyone as mahatma, but sa mahatma su-durlabhah \[“Such a great soul is very rare.”\]—that is mahatma. What is his business? Vasudevah sarvam iti: ‘Krishna is everything,’ and he surrenders—he is mahatma. One who is constantly engaged in Krishna’s service, he is sadhu (sadhur eva sa mantavyah).

“So, you must know first of all who is a sadhu, whether he’s devoted to Krishna, devoted to God. But these rascals, so-called saints, say that ‘I am God.’ He’s a rascal. He’s not a sadhu. He’s not a saintly person; he is a demon. We are accepting demons as mahatma and sadhu; therefore it has fallen down. This is the reason.

“Many are preaching, ‘Why you are finding out God? Why you are going to temple? Gods are loitering in the street, daridra-narayana" And you are accepting, ‘Oh, such a nice sadhu? But you do not know. He is a demon, and you are accepting as sadhu. That is the cause of falldown.

“Mahatma, sadhu, has been described by the supreme authority, Krishna: satatam kirtayanto mam yatantas ca drdha-vratah \[“always chanting My glories, endeavoring with great determination” (Gita 9.14)\]. Tusyanti ca ramanti ca \[“they enjoy great satisfaction and transcendental bliss” (Gita 10.9)\]. Their only business is to glorify the Supreme Lord. Not ‘Cut down the Supreme Lord, kill the Supreme Lord, and I become Supreme Lord,’ falsely, and cheat the innocent people. We are accepting the cheaters, that ‘Here is a god, here is a mahatma, here is a sadhu.’ Therefore it is falldown. Cheaters. Demons. Rascals. That is the cause of falldown.

“Mahatma is mahatmanas tu mam partha daivim prakrtim asritah. He is under the control of daivi prakriti, not this material nature, but spiritual nature. And what is the symptom? Bhajanty ananya-manaso— Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare/ Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. He is mahatma.

“Here we are creating all mahatmas, not demons, rascals. That is our business—Krishna consciousness. As you are importing powdered milk from America, now you have to import all mahatmas from America.” The devotees and visitors laughed. “It is a fact. Yes. Four years ago, when I first went, I had some correspondence with my friend. So, I wrote that ‘Now India has finished the milk and so many things, they have to import from foreign countries. Now you have to import brahmans and mahatmas from foreign countries.’ I tried to make mahatmas in this country, but still they are not prepared. They are not prepared.

“But these boys, American and European boys, they are prepared. They carry my orders, as I say. They were habituated to so many bad habits; I said, ‘Give up,’ and they gave up.

“But our Indian boys are not coming. They think, ‘We know Krishna, everything. Now let us learn technology.’ They are not even prepared to become mahatma. Otherwise, everyone can become mahatma. How to become a mahatma? The knowledge is there, the system is there, butnobody is interested. Just like two young men came here, they saw, ‘Ah, what is this arati?' They went away. There is no interest. They will go to cinema, to become cinema actor. That is their progress.

“And the so-called mahatmas and sadhus say, ‘Yes, you can do whatever you like. Yes.’ They have no courage to say that ‘You don’t do this.’ Then he will lose all customers. Just see. He is a duratma; he wants some money: ‘You do whatever nonsense you like, you simply give me my money, that’s all.’ They are publicly preaching, ‘Yes, you can do anything. Oh, why not sense enjoyment? God has given you the senses, you enjoy.’ One famous yogi was speaking in this way: ‘Why the senses should be controlled? God has given you senses—you must enjoy.’ This is his philosophy. Vivekananda’s philosophy: yata mata tata patha—Whatever mata \[opinion\] you have got, that’s all right.

“Mahatma Gandhi was approached, ‘Mahatmaji, why don’t you ask the Muslims to stop this cow killing?’ ‘No, how can I do? This is their religion.’” Prabhupada winced in disgust. “Now see. If you are nonviolent, if in the name of religion somebody says, ‘It is my religion,’ how can you allow it? If you want to introduce nonviolence, religion or no religion, you must stop it. Somebody will go on killing—‘My religion is to cut throat.’ ‘Yes, you can go on, yes, because it is your religion.’ What kind of mahatma? They are advertising—the government is advertising nonviolence, and ten thousand or forty thousand cows are being killed. What is this nonviolence?

“We are so misled, andha yathandair upaniyamana; we are accepting these rascals and fools and rogues and demons as sadhus, mahatmas, leaders, and we are gone to hell. This is the fact.”

A man asked, “So what is the solution to it? How can the average man know that and not be carried away by it? The average man is just led to it.”

Prabhupada replied, “Yes, the average man is ... Now we are preaching this cult, but why they are not coming? You have kindly come, but maybe tomorrow you may not come. They’re not eager to understand. They want to be misled. They want to be cheated. That is their progress. They don’t want the truth. Because if he wants the truth, then his life will be spoiled.”

“Because of restrictions,” the Indian lady offered.

“Yes,” Prabhupada agreed. “He is living an untruth. The whole world is living on meat-eating, drinking, illicit sex, and gambling. And we are restricting, ‘No, you cannot have illicit sex, you cannot have meat-eating, you cannot indulge in intoxication.’ So how many people will come? ‘Oh, Swamiji is very conservative,’ they say. ‘Swamiji is very conservative, primitive. We are now advanced. We must eat three plates of meat and two bottles of wine. That is advancement of civilization.’ What is this nonsense talking? Yes. Even some of my students left—‘Oh, Swamiji is not allowing even the primary necessities of life.’

“So, we cannot make any compromise. We don’t make compromise. Therefore, although we are preaching all over the world, our principles are very strict. . . . Generally, you can come and chant Hare Krishna mantra, that’s all right. But if you want to become my disciple, then you have to give up all these bad habits. One who agrees, then I accept him as disciple. If I would say, ‘Yes, you can do. God has given you senses; you go now, enjoy your senses and chant Hare Krishna,’ then I would have gotten millions and trillions. I don’t allow that, such kind of nonsense.”

“All right. Thank you,” Prabhupada concluded. “Hare Krishna.” And the devotees and guests responded, “Hare Krishna. Jaya!” At the end of one class, Prabhupada regretted the fallen condition of so-called teachers of the Bhagavad-gita and expressed his determination to persevere.

“People have become so fallen,” he lamented, “they cannot understand the instruction of Bhagavad-gita, although they are very much proud of reading Bhagavad-gita daily. What you have understood? Then they cannot say anything. ‘We have understood that Krishna means this black spot.’ Just see. This rascal hasn’t understood Bhagavad-gita, and he’s preaching Bhagavad-gita. Just see the fun. So, this is going on. And our Krishna consciousness movement is a war declared against all these rascals. We have got many enemies, but we don’t care for them. Still, we shall go on. Johnny Walker is still going strong.”

Taken completely by surprise by Prabhupada’s unexpected, seemingly incongruous reference to an advertising slogan for Johnny Walker Scotch Whiskey (Born 1820—Still Going Strong), the devotees laughed uproariously.

Prabhupada often used his Western disciples as examples to encourage people to take up the practice of bhakti-yoga. On the last evening at Sea Face Park (the pandal would begin the following day), he appealed to his audience to chant Hare Krishna.

“These are the statements of great personalities,” he said, and he quoted Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, the first verse of His Siksastaka:

ceto-darpana-marjanam bhava-maha-davagni-nirvapanam  
sreyah-kairava-candrika-vitaranam vidya-vadhu-jivanam  
anandambudhi-vardhanam prati-padam purnamrtasvadanam  
sarvatma-snapanam param vijayate sri-krsna-sankirtanam

“Let there be all victory for the chanting of the holy name of Lord Krsna, which can cleanse the mirror of the heart and stop the miseries of the blazing fire of material existence. That chanting is the waxing moon that spreads the white lotus of good fortune for all living entities. It is the life and soul of all education. The chanting of the holy name of Krsna expands the blissful ocean of transcendental life. It gives a cooling effect to everyone and enables one to taste full nectar at every step.”

"Sri-krsna-sankirtana is so nice,” Prabhupada explained; “Krishna says, man-mana bhava mad-bhakto mad-yaji mam namaskuru \[“Always think of Me, become My devotee, worship Me, and offer your homage unto Me.” (Gita 18.65)\]. Why don’t you always think of Krishna? Where is the loss? If you are walking on the street or going on a bus or in your car, if you chant Hare Krishna mantra, what is your heavy loss? Is there any loss? Why don’t you do it? Try it. There is no loss. And if there is any gain, why don’t you try it—for nothing, without any loss?

“These European and American boys are chanting Hare Krishna. They are more enlightened, so far as material civilization is concerned. But in their country, young men, as a hobby, have taken beads and are chanting. Our George Harrison, the famous Beatle, is supplying beads and bags to his friends: ‘Chant Hare Krishna.’ And he has written in his record that ‘Anyone who is a friend of Krishna, I am his friend.’ What he has written?”

“‘Any friend of Krishna is a friend of mine,”’ Guru Kripa replied.

“We Indians,” Prabhupada continued, “why you are over-gentlemen?

They’re also gentlemen, the Europeans. But why you are afraid? Whyyou are ashamed to chant Hare Krishna mantra, even working, even going ... ? What is the harm? This is the purpose of Hare Krishna mantra movement, that anyone can chant. A child can chant. An old man can chant. A rich man can chant. A poor man can chant. There is no tax. But see the result. Kirtaniyah sada harih.

trnad api su-nicena  
taror api sahisnuna  
amanina mana-dena  
kirtaniyah sada harih

\[“One who thinks himself lower than the grass, who is more tolerant than a tree, and who does not expect personal honor yet is always prepared to give all respect to others can very easily always chant the holy name of the Lord.” (Siksastaka 3)\] This is Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s order: Always chant Hare Krishna?

“And in the Bhagavad-gita also you’ll find:

satatam kirtayanto mam  
yatantas ca drdha-vratah  
namasyantas ca mam bhaktya  
nitya-yukta upasate

\[‘Always chanting My glories, endeavoring with great determination, bowing down before Me, these great souls perpetually worship Me with devotion.” (Gita 9.14)\] Anyone who is chanting, he’s mahatma. So these boys, although they’re very young, because they’re always chanting, they’re mahatmas. mahatmanas tu mam partha daivim prakrtim asritah bhajanty ananya-manaso. Krishna says, man-mana bhava mad-bhakto mad-yaji mam namaskuru. So, this is the process in this age. You can chant. There is no loss, but there is much gain. Why don’t you try it?”

We were always amazed at how in one moment Prabhupada could be so involved in the battle for Hare Krishna Land and in the next deliver a perfect lecture with no hint of his anxiety about the fight.

He also continued to provide leadership for the Society and respond to devotees’ letters, questions, and problems. In reply to a letter from Tusta Krishna asking about pure devotees, he wrote, “We advise everyone to address one another as Prabhu. Prabhu means master, so how the master should be disobeyed? Others, they are also pure devotees. All ofmy disciples are pure devotees. Anyone sincerely serving the spiritual master is a pure devotee—it may be Siddhasvarupa \[a charismatic devotee who brought Tusta Krishna to Srila Prabhupada and Krishna consciousness\] or others, a-Siddhasvarupa \[not-Siddhasvarupa\]. This must be very clearly stated. It is not only that your Siddhasvarupa is a pure devotee and not others. Do not try to make a faction. Siddhasvarupa is a good soul. But others should not be misled. Anyone who is surrendered to the spiritual master is a pure devotee, it doesn’t matter if Siddhasvarupa or non-Siddhasvarupa. Amongst ourselves one should respect others as prabhu, master, one another. As soon as we distinguish here is a pure devotee, here is a non-pure devotee, that means I am a nonsense. Why you only want to be in the spiritual sky with Siddhasvarupa? Why not all? If Siddhasvarupa can go, why not everyone? Siddhasvarupa will go, you will go, Shyamasundar will go, all others will go. We will have another ISKCON there. Of course, Mr. Nair must stay.”

Despite the cancellation of the sales agreement, Srila Prabhupada remained steadfast in his faith that we would eventually get the land and build the temple. In the meantime, he urged us to do more preaching, which, in our focus on the land and construction, we had been neglecting. “My idea was that we would use the land for preaching,” he said, “even if we don’t build the temple. You shouldn’t think that without the temple you cannot preach.”

He told us to go out more, meet more people, make more members, and preach. And he had us organize a second pandal program—another ten-day festival in downtown Bombay, at Cross Maidan. From Vrindavan he had written me, “You and Tamal Krishna arrange the pandal program in Bombay to be a first-class presentation.”

We formed a pandal committee, including Dr. Singhal, Mr. Pandya, and several others, with Dr. S. K. Poddar as head, and Prabhupada wrote to some of his strongest preachers, encouraging them to come or support the program however they could. “Whoever shall come must bring with them as many mridangas and kartals as possible,” he instructed. “At least four drums are required, and ten sets of kartals.”

“My guru maharaja was also inclined toward his bolder preachers,” he wrote Yasodanandana and Guru Kripa in Coimbatore, South India. “Therefore I am requesting that both of you, with your party, join mevery soon at the Hare Krishna Festival in Bombay Cross Maidan... This is our big opportunity to emphasize our preaching strength to the big men of India and population in general. There is arrangement of ‘Questions and Answers’ tents for the general public, just by the main street of the city, wherein we shall conduct throughout day and night preaching by my disciples by answering any and all questions put forward by the public. I think that you will enjoy preaching in that way, and I want to place my best preachers there for that purpose of defeating all challengers.”

“I think last time you were one of the leaders of that first Hare Krishna Festival,” he wrote Madhudvisa, “so you know how much important occasion that will be. Already there are many banners all over the city advertising this movement as the world’s greatest spiritual culture movement.”

There was a set of big Radha-Krishna deities waiting to be sent to Chicago (where they were eventually installed), and because Radha-Rasabihari were already in Juhu, Prabhupada said that the deities waiting to be sent should be used in the pandal. So we brought them— Sri Sri Kishore-Kishori.

Yadubara and Visakha were in charge of the publicity, and they tried to follow in the footsteps of Shyamasundar, who had done such a brilliant job advertising the first Bombay pandal program. Printed announcements covered downtown Bombay, many saying, “Krishna consciousness is the world’s greatest spiritual culture! Second Annual International Hare Krishna Festival, Cross Maidan, January 12 to 25.”

Sri Ravji K. Ganatra was the mayor of Bombay, and even though he had never met us, we kept getting reports that he recognized the value of Krishna consciousness and was praising our Society in his public lectures. In one talk, he had said, “People say many bad things about the Hare Krishna people, but I don’t believe them.”

At a function to honor donors to a new wing of the Nanavati Hospital in Vile Parle, which had been built by our friend Mr. Ratilal Nanavati, Mayor Ganatra was the chief guest and mentioned ISKCON and the wonderful work we were doing. After his talk, I introducedmyself to him, and he was very friendly, so I asked if I could visit him at his office, and he agreed.

I went to see Mayor Ganatra the next day and invited him to be a chief guest at the pandal program and inaugurate the festival on the first night. He accepted, and at the program he spoke very nicely and presented Prabhupada with the key to the city as an offering of honor and respect.

Prabhupada concluded his talk on the first night with a heartfelt appeal:

“This is a very scientific movement—authorized, practical. You chant the Hare Krishna mantra and you will realize that gradually you are advancing to meet Krishna face to face. That is possible. Chant Hare Krishna:

Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare  
Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare

“People are feeling some difficulty or some deficiency in the whole structure, and that deficiency can be fulfilled, can be satisfied, by making people Krishna conscious. This is the movement.

“We have got ample literature. Not only Bhagavad-gita, Srimad-Bhagavatam—others. There are hundreds of literatures, and we have already published about twenty books like this. . . . All the life members have got our books. And those who are not life members, I would request them to become life members, and we will give you more than your money’s worth of books. We want that everyone—every scholar, every thoughtful man—should read these books, Bhagavad-gita As It Is. These books are very much welcome in the Western countries. I have got a report just now from Los Angeles that within the three days of the Christmas holidays, we have sold one lakh worth of books—within three days. So, our books are being very much welcomed in the Western countries, especially the Bhagavad-gita As It Is.

“This movement is a very important movement. It is not fanaticism. It is based on science, philosophy, and authority, and Vedic principles. And all the students are following strictly the Vedic principles. They do not indulge in illicit sex life, meat-eating, or intoxication, up to thedrinking of coffee and tea, and smoking. They have given up. These are Vedic principles. And they do not take part in gambling. They regularly chant Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare— sixteen rounds. In this way we are training. Not only we are training these young boys, but we are training their sons, their children. We have got a very nice school in Dallas, Texas. From the very beginning they are being taught about Krishna consciousness, how to rise early in the morning, how to take part in the mangala-arati, how to take prasadam. Then teachings—they are learning Sanskrit and English especially, a little geography, mathematics. We have started a school.

“So, do not take this movement very insignificantly. Try to understand this movement with all your intelligence. As Caitanya-caritamrta's author says, sri-krsna-caitanya-daya karaha vicara, Vicara—just put your judgment. Try to understand with logic and with philosophy, not as a fanatic. Vicara, Vicara karile citte pabe camatkara. And if you rightly judge this movement, you will find it very sublime.

“We have got 4 branches now in India, out of 102 branches all over the world. But especially this movement is easier for the Indians, because by birth they are imbibed with the Krishna consciousness idea. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu said,

bharata-bhumite haila manusya janma yara  
janma sarthaka kari’ kara paropakara  
\[Cc Adi 9.41\]

Indians are meant for welfare activities for the whole world. And how they will do? Not by begging: ‘Give me rice, give me milk powder, give me money, give me this.’ No. If you spread this Krishna consciousness movement all over the world, then you will be respected. People will like it. They are very hungry for this Krishna consciousness. So, I am struggling alone. I require many Indians to join and spread this movement all over the world.

“Thank you very much. Hare Krishna.”

Every evening, distinguished guests gave introductory speeches appreciating the work of Srila Prabhupada and ISKCON. Although overall the program was not quite as well attended as the first, some people, like Bhogilal Patel, a pious Gujarati Vaishnava businessman, cameto hear Prabhupada practically every night, and by the last night the site was packed with over twenty thousand people. More devotees arrived daily, and the crowd responded enthusiastically.

The main stage area, which held the Deities’ altar and Prabhupada’s vyasasana, was rectangular, but the pandal tent itself, constructed by Mr. Bhuther, was round—a novel concept conceived of by Tamal Krishna. Unlike a circus tent, a pandal was constructed of bamboo or wood poles and cloth, so building it round was more expensive and more difficult, because the wood came in straight boards and the cloth came in straight sections. To make it round, we had to lose a bit on the materials, and it cost more in terms of labor. The stage protruded a little into the audience, and on the side was a narrow extension where Guru Kripa, Yasodanandana, and other devotees sat and performed kirtan. Prabhupada sat on his vyasasana with his disciples gathered at his feet.

Tamal Krishna had arranged through Srimati for copies of paintings from Prabhupada’s books to be made by Indian artists, and eight paintings depicting the pastimes of Lord Chaitanya adorned the site. The people in Bombay didn’t know about Lord Chaitanya, so the images introduced them to what was for them a new feature of Krishna consciousness.

The question-and-answer area, which had been introduced at the Delhi pandal, was a great attraction. We had a large, high platform erected outside the main pandal, with an ornate throne-like seat that Indian decorators supplied for weddings and other functions, upholstered in red velvet, with its back, legs, and other carved wood painted gold.

Over the course of the festival, the main preachers would take turns, challenging the audience that our Bhagavad-gita philosophy was perfect and complete and could defeat any other, and inviting onlookers to come up to the platform with their questions or statements. Sometimes two of us would be there at once, which Prabhupada liked. If one was tired, he said, the other could speak. And because we were sitting on the big throne and the platform was so high, the booth attracted everyone’s attention. People looked up at us sitting above everyone else and thought, You think you are better than us?

We invited people to present their philosophy based on any spiritual or material ideology and offered that if they could show that it wasbetter than ours, we would surrender right then and there and become their disciples. But if they found that our philosophy was superior and had defeated theirs, they should surrender to Prabhupada. No one could actually defeat us, but big crowds would gather, and many people asked questions and put forth challenges.

Achyutananda, Tamal Krishna, and I were the main devotees for giving answers. Generally, Tamal Krishna would answer questions for an hour or two, then I would answer for an hour or two, and then Achyutananda would do the late shift. Achyutananda also added his own challenge—that he would stay up all night answering questions if people would stay and ask them—and he would usually carry on until eleven or eleven-thirty, sometimes midnight. The audience was always astonished and impressed by our answers, and when it was time for Prabhupada to speak in the pandal, we would close the booth and go listen to his discourse.

Another feature of the pandal was the dramatic performances, directed by Achyutananda, which were enhanced by rented costumes and masks. In our production of “Krishna Has a Headache,” Krishna declared that He could be cured only by the dust of the feet of His devotee.

Krishna’s messenger approached many different types of people to ask for the dust of their feet. One of the persons was a karmi, depicted as a Gujarati businessman, played by Manasvi, who had actually been one, another was a yogi, and another was a jnani, played by me.

All the people the messenger approached refused to give the dust of their feet, saying, “Oh, if the dust from my feet touches the head of Krishna it will be a great offense; I could go to hell.”

When the messenger went to Vrindavan, however, he was immediately surrounded by all the gopis. “Oh, you’ve come from Krishna,” they said. “How is our Lord? Please tell us, how is He doing?”

“The Lord has a headache,” the messenger replied.

“Oh, no!” the gopis exclaimed. “How can we help Him? What can we do?”

“The only thing that will cure Him is the dust from His devotee’s feet,” the messenger said.

They replied without hesitation: “Oh, yes—take it, take it all. Take as much as you want. Take everything.”

“Don’t you know that you could go to hell for this?” the messenger asked.

“We don’t care if we go to hell,” they said, “as long as Krishna’s headache is cured.”

Prabhupada wanted to see the play, so for the final performance we brought his vyasasana down from the stage to the front of the audience. When I saw him sitting there, smiling broadly as he watched, I was struck by his expression—sweet and pure, with a childlike innocence. He was completely absorbed in the drama, seeing Krishna’s pastimes being enacted, and at the same time appreciating the efforts of his loving disciples.

Nara Narayan, who was sitting right behind Prabhupada, also noticed Prabhupada’s absorption: “He looked so involved. He was watching each part as though he’d never heard the story. When people said, ‘No, I will not give the dust,’ he would wince. And then when the gopis said that yes, they would give the dust of their feet to Krishna, you could see Prabhupada’s shoulders jump as he leaned forward, and tears started rolling down his cheeks. When the messenger brought the dust of their feet to Krishna and He accepted it, Prabhupada stood up, his mouth agape and his eyes wide open. It was as if he was actually seeing Lord Krishna and His associates.”

Later that evening—it was Sunday, the last day of the festival, and the crowd was enormous—Prabhupada gave his daily lecture from the vyasasana. When he finished, he nodded and said, “All right, have kirtan.”

Achyutananda, playing mridanga, began to lead the chanting. “The kirtan was especially enthusiastic,” Visakha later recounted, “and Prabhupada started to circumambulate the Deities with a very light step. He went around once, and then he went around a second time, and then a third time. And when he came before the Deities, very gracefully he put his arms in the air and began to dance. It was almost as if he were weightless, he danced so effortlessly, and everyone was electrified.

“Everyone in the audience was riveted on Srila Prabhupada dancing before the Deities. I was in the midst of the crowd, photographing, and it felt as if all the sinful reactions of all those people suddenly lifted. It was an extraordinary feeling. There was such a lightness. It’s stated in The Nectar of Devotion that if you clap your hands in kirtan, the sinful reactions leave you just like birds leaving a tree when there’s a suddennoise—they all fly off together. And that’s what it felt like. There was this burden of karma lifting all at one time.”

All the devotees and practically everyone in the audience also began dancing. “Prabhupada was leading us, dancing around the Deities,” Harikesa recalled. “He was holding his hands up, having a huge kirtan. And the whole place went mad, completely mad.”

“It was amazing how Srila Prabhupada controlled us by the movement of his arms,” Srutakirti said. “When he raised them into the air, he picked everyone up with them and deposited us in the spiritual world.”

With dozens of devotees dancing ecstatically in a circle around the Deities, the stage began to shake so hard that two of us had to hold Them down. Prabhupada was dancing with great jubilation, and the audience was amazed and overcome with ecstasy as they watched and danced and clapped. I wanted to run out into the street and call anyone and everyone to come in and see this wonderful sight.

When the kirtan was over, Prabhupada left for his accommodations in Mr. Mahadevia’s flat. “So, the pandal was very nice?” he asked, smiling broadly.

“It was really wonderful,” Srutakirti replied. “When you dance, everyone immediately goes into ecstasy.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada said. “Actually, I could have kept on dancing, but I saw that the Deities were endangered, so I stopped. Otherwise, I would have kept on dancing.”

Prabhupada was happy with the results of the festival. “In Bombay we have just celebrated our Second Hare Krishna Festival and it has come out very successfully,” he wrote Karandhara. “A special feature was the ‘Question and Answer’ booth where ... our sannyasis answered all philosophy questions. So the people were impressed that we are not seemingly sentimentalists, but have substantial philosophical footing.”

As Mrs. Singhal later remembered, “The public saw the Western devotees and their sincere bhakti, and many misunderstandings were removed from their minds.”

Within days after the pandal, Mayor Ganatra came to meet Prabhupada at Mr. Mahadevia’s residence, and Prabhupada gave him the most gracious treatment I had ever seen, beaming and smiling affectionately as he told the mayor about our different activities.

Atreya Rishi was also there, and Prabhupada asked that his wife be called in to meet the mayor. He was proud that even an intelligent young Muslim man like Atreya Rishi had become his disciple. Atreya Rishi’s wife, Vidhi Bhakti dasi, was an attractive American girl with blond hair and blue eyes and wore a sari and tilak, which even further impressed Mayor Ganatra, who was enchanted, captivated, by Prabhupada’s charm. And from that day forward, he was a close friend and strong supporter of our movement.

Near the end of January, Prabhupada again met with Mr. Nair—at Mr. Mahadevia’s flat—to try to settle things out of court. Nair’s leg was swollen; he had difficulty walking, and it was hard for him to sit on the floor. So Prabhupada had someone bring him a chair.

All along, Prabhupada had been gracious with Nair, and Nair had responded politely. But this time there was a marked change. Prabhupada was courteous, but I could tell that he had had enough, and it was clear that Nair, though showing a veneer of civility, was seething inside. “Swamiji hypnotized me when I went to Hyderabad,” he accused. “He made me sign.”

Prabhupada understood the situation and indicated that the devotees should leave him alone with Nair and Amratlal Pandya, who had tried to reason with Nair and had brought him to see Prabhupada. We went next door to Srutakirti’s room, from where we could hear Prabhupada and Nair yelling at each other.

“Simply take the money and give us the land,” Prabhupada told Nair. “Or, if you want us to vacate, then prepare the check. Bring out your check, and we will vacate tomorrow morning. No, we will vacate tonight! Either take your check or give me my check. But we must finalize it.”

“You are a trespasser,” Nair accused. “Get off my property. You people are calling yourselves the owners of the land, but you are just a big disturbance to the whole area.”

“It is not your property or mine,” Prabhupada countered. “It is Krishna’s.” He was “red hot,” Mr. Pandya described—glaring, furious. “You can’t make us move; Krishna is there.”

“I will break your Krishna,” Nair threatened. And then he walked out.

Soon thereafter, Prabhupada left for Calcutta, Melbourne, Sydney, Auckland, and Jakarta, and then Calcutta and Mayapur.

One Sunday, as I was walking through the streets in Dhobitalao, South Bombay, briefcase in hand, on my way to meet someone, I happened to stop for a moment by the Metro Cinema to look at the periodicals on sale along the sidewalk (something I generally never did). Standing on the busy corner, with traffic rushing from all directions, I glanced at the newspaper headlines. Big, black, bold letters jumped out from one front page: “A. B. Nair dead.” And directly under the headline was a photo of Mr. Nair.

I couldn’t believe it. “A. B. Nair dead.” How could it be? The paper was The Bharat Jyoti, the Sunday edition of the Free Press Journal, where Nair had been editor.

I was jubilant—I felt like dancing in ecstasy. But then I wondered if that was the proper way for a Vaishnava to respond. I am supposed to be developing saintly qualities, I reflected. Maybe I should be feeling sorry. Still, I could not contain my exultation, and I rushed back to our flat in Colaba to share the news.

Bali Mardan, the most senior devotee there, suggested that we call Srila Prabhupada and went out to look for a phone. I decided I should go to Juhu. The devotees there had already heard the news and had been rejoicing and celebrating, chanting and distributing sweets. But I was still uncertain—was this the proper way for Vaishnavas to behave?

When Bali Mardan phoned Auckland to inform Prabhupada of Nair’s death, the phone call came during Prabhupada’s morning massage, just before lunchtime. Srutakirti was sitting on the floor behind him, massaging his back, with Tusta Krishna and Siddhasvarupa nearby. Tusta Krishna took the call, and then Srutakirti came to the phone.

After just a few minutes, Srutakirti ran back into the room. “Srila Prabhupada,” he said, “That was Bali Mardan on the phone. He wanted to tell you that Mr. Nair is dead.”

Srila Prabhupada joined his hands together above his head, as if in prayer. “Oh, thank You, Krishna!” he said. “I prayed that Krishna would kill him. He caused us so much difficulty. He gave so much trouble to the devotees. I was praying that Krishna would do something to this demon.” And he quoted a verse from Srimad-Bhagavatam (7.9.14):

tad yaccha manyum asuras ca hatas tvayadya  
modeta sadhur api vrscika-sarpa-hatya  
Iokas ca nirvrtim itah pratiyanti sarve  
rupam nrsirnha vibhayaya janah smaranti

Prahlada Maharaja said, “Even a saintly person becomes pleased when a snake or a scorpion is killed.”

“Nair was a big snake. So it is very good.”

“Since Krishna killed him, is he liberated?” Srutakirti asked.

“No,” Prabhupada replied, “he was not such a great demon. Krishna didn’t come personally to kill him.”

As Srutakirti continued his massage, Prabhupada recounted some of the struggle and revealed more of his inner mood. “The Deities were installed on the property,” he said. “Mr. Nair had insulted Krishna by trying to remove Him, and that I could not tolerate.

“Some of my disciples didn’t understand. They wondered why their spiritual master was so attached to that piece of property. In truth, we had money; we could have bought property anywhere. We didn’t need that piece of property. But Krishna was standing there at Juhu, and therefore I was determined to have it. Even some of my disciples were ready to leave the property, but I promised the Deities that I would build Them a beautiful temple there.

“When Nair came to visit me last time in Bombay, I noticed he was limping. Generally, he was very strong and robust.” He raised his arms like a muscleman flexing his biceps. “He was not at all ill, but he was limping. I thought to myself, Krishna is going to kill him; he is going to die. And now, Krishna has killed him.”

Nair’s downfall resembled Ramachandra Khan’s, as described in Sri Caitanya-caritamrta; both had allowed the seed of offense to germinate. “This seed later became a tree, and when it fructified, Ramacandra Khan ate its fruits.... Ramacandra Khan was naturally a nondevotee. Now, having offended the lotus feet of Haridasa Thakura, he became just like a demoniac atheist. Because of blaspheming the cult of Vaisnavism and insulting the devotees for a long time, he now received the results of his offensive activities.” (Cc Antya 3.144,146,147)

Later that day, Prabhupada wrote to us in Bombay, “This morning Srutakirti received telephonic message from Bali Mardan. It isunderstood that Mr. Nair is dead. So it is good news that Nrsimhadeva has killed a demon like him ... it is a matter of great pleasure for all devotees.”

Srila Prabhupada celebrated Gaura-purnima in Calcutta. We held a festival on our land, which was attended by Mayor Ganatra, featured a drama of Chaitanya Iila, and included a maha-sankirtana along Juhu Beach and through the main streets in the area. A week later, Prabhupada returned to Bombay, where he stayed at Kartikeya Mahadevia’s flat through the end of the month.

I had been tracking down a wealthy industrialist named S.K. Thirani, who was the managing director of Kores India Limited, the leading manufacturer of office supplies and equipment in India, and was married to Ashok Birla’s sister. Mr. Thirani’s house happened to be just up the street on Warden Road, near Mr. Mahadevia’s flat. On the following Sunday afternoon I had a little free time, so I thought, Why not take a chance and go?

When I arrived, Mr. Thirani was sitting out on his front lawn, chatting with his wife and some friends; there was no way he could avoid me. I just walked up, introduced myself, and started telling him about the Juhu land—not mentioning the difficulties and complications—and that we wanted to build a temple there.

Mr. Thirani replied that actually he had been thinking of building a temple but that he didn’t know where to build it.

“Well,” I replied, “we can provide the land, and you can provide the temple.”

“Yes, this is very good,” he said. “I will give five to seven lakhs of my own, plus I will help raise another five lakhs from my friends.”

This is wonderful! I thought. We’d never had anything like this happen. Then I told him that our guru maharaja was staying just down the street, and I suggested we go over and see him.

“Yes, let us go immediately!” Mr. Thirani replied. So, we got in his car, drove to Sea Face Park, and went up to see Prabhupada.

When we arrived, Prabhupada was in his room with Manmohan dasa (Mr. Kejriwal) and other middle-class friends from Juhu. I introduced Mr. Thirani to Prabhupada and told him of Mr. Thirani’s desire to build a temple for us.

Prabhupada was very pleased and started to preach to him. Mr. Thirani was a rather materialistic man—not very bright-faced or joyful; he hardly ever smiled—but Prabhupada put himself into the meeting completely and focused on trying to bring him to Krishna consciousness. And because Mr. Thirani was somewhat mundane, Prabhupada had to tell some rather mundane stories with mundane examples to attract his interest. He described the movement of a car and imitated the sounds of the vehicle. He was doing everything he could, and Mr. Thirani actually started to come to life, to smile and laugh. It was amazing to see the transformation.

Then Prabhupada mentioned that he had to leave for Zurich early the next morning, and Mr. Thirani said, “Really? I am also going to Zurich tomorrow morning. What flight are you taking?” Prabhupada told him the flight number, and Mr. Thirani said, “Well, that’s the same flight I am taking, so I will see you tomorrow morning.”

All the devotees were enlivened by hearing this; we thought it must have been by Krishna’s arrangement that I had met Mr. Thirani and that he wanted to build a temple and had come and met Prabhupada and they would be flying together to Zurich.

Two days later, Prabhupada wrote me from Zurich, “The gentleman Mr. Thirani was met two or three times on planes or in airports and is eager to construct a temple for us immediately. So, this is an opportunity given by Krishna ...”

Whereas my attention during Prabhupada’s initial meeting with Mr. Thirani had been drawn to how Prabhupada had gone all out to engage him, Manmohan had been impressed with Prabhupada’s quality of being equal to all types of people. Later, speaking with someone about him, he described how Prabhupada hadn’t regarded Thirani any differently than he would have regarded any ordinary person who had come off the street. Prabhupada, Manmohan was saying, was completely detached from any glitter or glamour of the material world or a materialistic person.

On another occasion, Prabhupada had spoken strongly to a very rich man and then, after the man left the room, Prabhupada’s friend Indira Shringi had commented, “You spoke very heavily to this man.”

“Why not?” Prabhupada had retorted. “Why should I compromise with these people? Krishna is there; He is taking care of us. We don’tneed these men.” Still, as a humble servant of Krishna, he would try to engage everyone in Krishna’s service, in Krishna’s mission.

On March 30 Mayor Ganatra sent a wonderful appreciation of Srila Prabhupada and ISKCON addressed to Prabhupada at Hare Krishna Land:

Respected Swami Prabhupadaji:

Please accept my respects. My wife and I were so pleased to meet Your Divine Grace here in Bombay. Certainly you must be the representative of Lord Krishna, because you are fulfilling His prediction as Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu that in every village and town in every country of the world His name will be sung. You only went to the Western world a few years ago and already you have established over 102 Sri Sri Radha-Krishna Temples all over the globe. You may know that I personally have met your devotees in Los Angeles, New York, Washington D.C., Buffalo N.Y., and Paris, France. The Deity worship of Radha-Krishna in Los Angeles is gorgeous, clean, and punctual, and your printing press in New York, which I also saw, is doing a beautiful job of printing your books in English editions with Sanskrit and original colour paintings by your disciples. You are working very hard to spread our shastras into English to spread our original Indian culture for the benefit of the suffering world, and you therefore claim the title as India’s greatest spiritual ambassador to the world.

Here in Bombay I had the privilege of being chief guest at one of the big festivals at your Sri Sri Radha-Krishna Temple in Juhu. There too the activities are progressing very nicely and the local people are participating. Under the leadership of Sri Giriraj-ji, your disciples are working very sincerely and enthusiastically, and I want your movement to expand more and more in India, because your society alone is counteracting the degradation of our modern youth who are falling prey to permissive life. You have already surpassed the greatest of saints in propagating Krishna consciousness around the world, and now with your foreign disciples you are helping Indians themselves remember their own great heritage, and so you have practically become a national hero.

You have been kind enough to invite me to stay at your centres all around the world. Although I will not be able to take advantage of your kind offer at this time, I hope that next year I will be your guestand have another opportunity to enjoy the pure spiritual life promoted by your ISKCON institution.

Pranams.

Yours Respectfully,

(Ravi K. Ganatra).

Mayor of Bombay.

Tamal Krishna and I considered that we needed a proper place to stay, work, and store things, and we proposed to purchase a small flat on the ground floor of the nearby Chand Co-operative Housing Society. Prabhupada approved, and on May 8 we made payment and took possession.

We got a phone installed, and I would make calls to set up appointments for Tamal Krishna and me to collect funds for Vrindavan (the work at Juhu was delayed due to the legal complications). Tamal Krishna was insistent that I make a lot of calls. The best time to phone was early in the morning before people went to the office, but sometimes I would want to chant more rounds first and would go to phone later. And Tamal Krishna would always ask how many phone calls and appointments I had made. One day I had hardly made any calls, and when he asked me what had happened, I was afraid to tell him the truth, so I told a few little lies, that I had tried to reach some people but couldn’t get through, and I mentioned some names. Somehow, by Krishna’s arrangement—or my good or bad luck—Tamal Krishna spoke to one of the gentlemen I had falsely said I had tried to reach, and concluded, rightly, that I had lied to him. He became very angry—transcendentally angry—and said, “You pretend to be very pure and innocent, but you are not innocent at all.” He exposed the truth that I was a liar, and I felt purified by the experience—though it took me a few days to fully appreciate the value of what he had said. But eventually I did, and it helped me in my service.

## Dealing with Mrs. Nair

Encouraged by Prabhupada’s presence in Bombay, I was determined to just carry on with the preaching there and not worry about the land. “Ifnecessary,” Prabhupada said, “we can simply make Hare Krishna Land into a bus stop. We can have many buses for distributing our literature, and those buses can go traveling and distributing books, and they can come back to Hare Krishna Land, the bus stop, and the devotees can spend a few days and become rejuvenated and get more books and then go out again.”

The permit we had for our small temple was only temporary; it had to be renewed every year. Near the end of the first year, when we approached the municipality for a renewal, we did not get any reply. So we wrote them another letter—again without response.

Finally, when the permit was about to expire, I took all the relevant papers and went straight to the municipal commissioner at city hall. I explained the situation in less than five minutes, giving the man a concise account, without mention of Mr. Nair or our dispute with him. And based on my explanation and the documentation I had brought, the commissioner granted the year’s extension.

Just as I was coming out of his office, however, I saw one of Mrs. Nair’s agents, and I could tell that something was up. So I went straight into the commissioner’s secretary’s office and induced him to type the permission right then, on the spot, and get the commissioner’s signature. I sat there and waited until he returned with the signed document, and then I took it with me and left. But I knew that Mrs. Nair was trying somehow to get the land back.

We had also heard rumors that the municipality was planning to demolish the temple. In a letter dated April 28, I wrote to the Santa Cruz Police Department, “We are the owners of a Sri Sri Radha Krishna Temple at Hare Krishna Land at Juhu Village. In his letter dated 27/4/73, the Municipal Commissioner of Bombay Sri M. W. Desai has informed us that the permission for the shed of Khandelwal Steel Tube frame, which is the temple, is extended for one year.

“Two days ago a man allegedly from the Municipal Corporation threatened that at 9:00 or 10:00 today morning the municipality would come and demolish said temple. Such an act would be totally illegal, since the Commissioner himself has assured us that the permission is extended and since the municipality has given us until 29-4-73 to show why the temple should not be demolished, which we have done. Shouldthe alleged authorities from the municipality come to demolish the temple, there is likely to be a breach of peace and we request you to be on hand to prevent any such disturbance.” We also alerted the local devotees and our friends about the danger.

Tamal Krishna and his party were traveling in Madhya Pradesh, and I was keeping him informed by post. He would come every now and then, just to see how things were going, and a few weeks later, in mid-May, he came for a visit, enlivened and full of stories about his preaching.

At around ten o’clock on the morning of May 18, Tamal Krishna left to rejoin his party, and less than two hours after his departure, two large trucks from the Bombay Municipal Corporation drove onto Hare Krishna Land and fifty municipal workers carrying crowbars, chisels, and sledgehammers descended on the temple. Following close behind was a big police truck, from which twenty or thirty constables emerged.

I rushed forward to meet the municipal officer in charge and asked him what was happening, why were they there. He said that the structure was unauthorized and that they had come to demolish it. I replied that the temple was authorized and that I had the papers to prove it, that I had just had our permit renewed. “We have permission,” I said. “You can’t do this.”

The officer, however, seemed uninterested, even after I showed him the permit and the letter I had received at city hall, signed by the municipal commissioner himself. “We don’t accept your papers,” he said. And he ordered the demolition to begin.

I approached the policemen for help but was told offhandedly, “We are just here to see that there is no trouble.” Actually, they knew that we would try to stop the demolition, and they were there to make sure it continued without interference. What we heard later was that Mrs. Nair had collected twenty-five thousand rupees on the death of her husband and had distributed the money to the municipal corporation and the police; and the municipal councilor for Juhu, Pushpakant Mhatre, who had been supporting Mr. Nair all along, had arranged for the temple to be demolished.

Some workers put a ladder up against the temple, but when one of them was about to climb up with a sledgehammer to break theroof, I knocked the ladder over. Three policemen grabbed me—one by each arm and one by the neck—and tossed me into the police truck. Other devotees rushed forward to stop the demolition, but one by one each was apprehended and thrown into the truck—maybe twenty of us in all.

The last one left was Maithili, the head pujari. She had locked the doors to the Deity chamber and was standing steadfast in front of them, ready to knock down anyone who came near. “I was carrying the Deities’ raja-bhoga offering,” she later recalled. “When I saw that there were a lot of policemen surrounding the temple, I dropped the plates and started to run towards the temple. I closed, locked, and bolted the Deity-room doors, which were up a few steps, and I stood on the top step with my back to the doors. The workers were knocking down the whole roof of the temple hall, including the long tube lights, as well as the framed pictures of Krishna, and when they turned to destroy Tulasi I left my position with my back to the doors and went to the middle of the temple, where she was standing from the morning—because they were going to hit her—and at that point they grabbed me. I hit one of the officers in the face—then they all came around me and starting to drag me out of the temple.

“On the way, I wrapped my elbow around one of the steel tubes supporting the corner of the temple and held on as hard as I could.” She was a big, strong woman, and they couldn’t pry her off. “They started hitting my elbow with a stick so I would let go, and I fell onto the floor of the temple, and then they picked me up by one foot and one braid of my hair and dragged me across the field, which was now full of people watching the whole thing. They carried me halfway across the field and, as many people watched in horror, threw me face down into the police wagon.”

When Prabhupada heard that Maithili had been kicking and screaming at the policemen as they were dragging her by the hair, he said that she would go back to Godhead kicking and screaming. And he compared her to Draupadi, whose hair, infamously, had been grabbed by the evil Duhsasana.

After Maithili had been dragged from the temple, two women—Jagat Purusa’s mother-in-law, Yashoda, and another local woman—guarded the Deities. And because they were Hindu Indian ladies, the police didnot touch them. But other than them, no one—not any of the hundreds of neighbors, tenants, or passersby—lifted a finger to help us.

When the demolition squad had destroyed or dismantled the entire temple hall except for the steel poles supporting the roof, they called for a blowtorch. Meanwhile, some of the neighbors who opposed us had gathered to watch and were laughing and joking together. Mhatre was standing by the little Shiva temple across the street, and he and his accomplices were enjoying the show.

One man who lived across the street, Krishna Rao Rane, stood quite close and was laughing as he watched the workers cutting the steel rods with the blowtorch. Before we arrived on the land, he had distilled illegal liquor there and hid it in the overgrown weeds and bushes. He was quite influential in Juhu in a tamasic sort of way and didn’t think he would maintain the same power—the same hold on people—with us there.

Yashoda was also something of a mystic, and when she saw the man watching and laughing, she cursed him, “Just as you are laughing now when Krishna’s temple is being burned, one day you will also burn.”

Only one devotee wasn’t arrested during the demolition—Man-asvi. He was crouched behind some bushes watching the whole thing. When he saw us all being carried away, he found a telephone, called Mr. Mahadevia, and asked him to help.

Mr. Mahadevia phoned Bal Thackeray, a staunch Hindu and the founder and leader of the Shiv Sena, one of Bombay’s most powerful political parties, and told him what was happening. If he did not intervene, Mr. Mahadevia told him, the temple would be destroyed and he would get a bad name.

Bal Thackeray phoned the municipal commissioner, informed him of what was taking place, and told him to stop the demolition. The municipal commissioner, being part of the clique that had conspired against the temple, objected, but Bal Thackeray warned him, “Just remember who this city belongs to.”

“Okay, Balasaheb, okay,” the commissioner said, and he called the local ward, which had dispatched the attackers, and told them to halt the demolition.

The ward officer himself came running, reached the site just as the workers were getting ready to dismantle the Deity chamber, and ordered them to stop. They had already completely destroyed thedarshan-mandapa (viewing area) and had removed the first few pieces of the roof covering the Deities.

Those of us in the police truck were taken to the Santa Cruz station and locked up in a holding cell. “I want to phone my lawyer,” I called out.

“No phone calls,” they said. “Stay where you are. You’re not going anywhere.”

When Dr. Singhal heard that we had been arrested, he came to the station and appealed to the officer in charge on our behalf. “They are not sinful,” he said. “Or criminals. And they are not hypocrites. They are genuine people. We know them. They should be released.”
