The police allowed Dr. Singhal to come inside and see us. “The devotees were doing kirtan,” his wife recounted, “sitting and chanting with kartals. They were not sad—except for the Deities and the temple. Otherwise, they were happy there. They had full faith in Krishna.”

Only after several hours were we released from custody and able to return to the site. When we got back from the police station, we came upon a strange scene. In the middle of a vacant lot strewn with rubble and the metal bars that had once supported the temple structure were the beautiful Sri Sri Radha-Rasabihari, dressed in Their green-and-silver outfits and garlanded with flowers. They stood on Their carved teakwood altar amid the fragrant scent of burning incense and warm glow of ghee lamps. Only a few small pieces of the roof over Them had been removed; other than that, They and Their Deity room remained intact. And the picture of Lord Nrsimhadeva over the altar doors, though slightly tilted to the side, had survived as well, as if He was looking down upon us and assuring us that He had been there to protect the Deities.

“It was amazing,” Maithili recalled. “The flower that I had put behind the ear of Radha-Rasabihari was still there and the ghee lights were still burning. The only offering They had missed was the raja-bhoga offering.”

The next morning, headlines broadcast the news of the temple demolition. “UNAUTHORIZED TEMPLE DEMOLISHED BY MUNICIPAL AUTHORITIES,” announced the Free Press Journal. “The makeshift Radha-Krishna temple constructed about a year ago by followers of the Hare Krishna sect at Nairwadi, Juhu, was demolished by thirty municipal officers amidst police security. This resulted in a clash between members of the Hare Krishna sect and the municipal officers.”

Mhatre had arranged for hostile reports about us to appear everywhere, which, as we learned, could be achieved by bribing the newspaper people. He had been paying people off and spreading his false propaganda, telling them that we were hippies, drug users, kidnappers, even CIA agents. He raised questions about our charitable status with the charity commissioner and even more alarming, had approached the Foreigners Registration Office to have us kicked out of India.

When Srila Prabhupada was informed of what had happened, he was, of course, concerned, but he told us not to worry. The episode was part of Krishna’s plan, he said, and if we took it as an opportunity the results would be positive. The demolition of our temple by the municipality would actually strengthen our position.

Still, he told us, the incident showed that we could not manage it all on our own; we needed the help of our life members. We should take advantage of the incident to organize them and get them more involved in our activities and, along with our other supporters and sympathizers, to publicly protest the attack, expose the persons responsible, and begin the rebuilding process. He suggested several who might be of particular assistance. Mr. Sadajiwatlal, who led the Vishva Hindu Parishad, an organization that defended Hindu dharma, could help with publicity, and Mr. Sethi could help prevent further attacks.

We began to approach our friends and life members. Prabhupada himself sent an open letter, which we published in the next edition of The Hare Krishna Monthly. “The Krishna Consciousness Movement is considerably well known all over the world,” he began. “This Movement is meant for the total reformation of the whole human society. It is not a sectarian religious movement, but is a scientific method to awaken dormant God consciousness in every human being. ... In 1965 I went to the States, and for more than one year I had no support there. Later on, by July 1966, some of the younger section of America had joined me, and they supported this movement wholeheartedly. Our basic principle is the Bhagavad-gita as it is. After organizing this movement in America, Europe, Canada, Australia, etc., I came back to India in 1970 with a group of American assistants. . . . With this purpose I took the Hare Krishna Land.”

He then reported the latest development, “that the Bombay Municipality, under the influence of Mrs. Nair, had the audacity tosmash our temple, against the law and principle of religious faith. So, a great clique is going on in Bombay to drive us away from the land, without returning our money or \[compensation for\] damages.

“We have many sympathizers and life members of our society, and I wish they may come forward to help us in this precarious position and save the situation. Our cause is so noble, scientific, and pure, that everyone, irrespective of caste, creed, and religion, should come forward and save us from this position. I hope that my appeal to the people of Bombay will not go in vain.”

As I was busy with other aspects of our effort, Harikesa had volunteered to publish a special demolition issue, with a photo of the demolished temple wrapped around the front and back covers and the heading “Religiosity in Shambles.” Sadajiwatlal put his whole heart into the temple campaign and helped us arrange a meeting of all our Bombay life members—downtown, in Cama Hall. Only twelve or fifteen showed up, but I read Prabhupada’s letter and Sadajiwatlal gave a strong keynote speech and urged members to get involved and to write letters to the mayor of Bombay. “He was a very powerful speaker,” Sridhar recalled. “And I remember him slamming on the podium. ‘The temple must come up; the temple will come up.’ He was fired up. Sadaji was a pretty inspired person—he always supported Hindu causes —and this was a big thing for him.”

Sadajiwatlal gave us the use of his entire downtown office and enlisted the considerable weight of his wide range of friends and associates. Mr. Vinod Gupta, a member of the Jana Sangh political party, which was committed to maintaining India’s Hindu culture, joined with Kartikeya Mahadevia and others to form a Save the Temple committee and published a leaflet declaring ISKCON to be a bona fide Hindu organization. Sri Sarkar Singh, of the Hindu Mahasabha, threatened to go on a fast if the temple was not reconstructed.

For more than twelve hours every day, assisted by Save the Temple committee members, we made phone calls, wrote letters, issued circulars, contacted newspapers, met with influential citizens and government officials, and generally approached as many people as possible.

We also set to work on getting permission to rebuild the temple. “There was a hole in the roof of the Deity room, over where the pujaristood to do the arati” Maithili recounted, “and until we got that part fixed, I had to stand in the rain when offering arati. I remember Giriraj standing in front of Sri Sri Radha-Rasabihari with an umbrella for mangala-arati until the temple hall was repaired?

“Under the circumstances,” Prabhupada had directed, “we should immediately reconstruct the Deity shed. Barbed wire fencing should be immediately done to cover the naked land. And if possible, immediately in front of the Deity shed, a temporary pandal should be constructed, with our materials. If it is so done, then I can go to Bombay and begin Bhagavata parayana \[discourse\], to continue until the court decision is there. This is my desire.”

Until the demolition, we had been at war with the municipality and losing the fight for public opinion. Both the newspapers and the municipal council had been manipulated by Mhatre, and almost all the press was negative, if not hostile. The sensationalist tabloid Blitz, for instance, in an article headlined “Hare Krishna Hoax,” called ISKCON a “ludicrous cult” and the devotees “alien buffoons” and claimed that we were being funded by the U.S. government.

But Sadajiwatlal and I—or he with Yadubara and Visakha if I was busy—went to speak with the municipal councilors individually to explain the true situation and convince them that they should grant permission for the temple’s reconstruction. Between us, we met with practically every one of the hundred and forty municipal councilors, and they began to see who we really were and started showing sympathy for our cause.

Vamanrao Mahadik, a member of the council’s standing committee, the most powerful committee in the Bombay Municipal Corporation, was incensed by the demolition, which he called illegal. He wrote a letter to the chairman urging that the committee adjourn for a short time in protest “against the ruthless action on the part of the municipal administration in demolishing the Radha Krishna Mandir . . . without prior intimation to the concerned persons and even after granting a temporary permission by the Municipal Commissioner on 27th April, 1973, and further that during the course of the demolition operation the persons concerned with the said temple were kept in the police custody for about more than an hour and that they were not allowed even to establishtelephone contacts and that one of the ladies was manhandled? The temple, he argued, should be rebuilt at municipal cost and permitted to stand until the court reached its decision on the land dispute.

“The partial demolition of a temporary steel shed of Hare Krishna temple of the International Society for Krishna consciousness by the civic authorities on Friday has raised a controversy,” The Times of India reported, “and the Bombay municipal commissioner has promised an inquiry into the matter.

“To protest against the action of the civic administration for demolishing the shed for which a year’s permission was granted last month, the standing committee adjourned for five minutes.

“Mr. Mahadik said what surprised him most was that unauthorized structures on municipal and government lands were tolerated by the administration \[and\] asked whether the commissioner had taken action, ignoring all the procedural rules, because of a pressure from someone.... PROBE PROMISED.”

Mrs. Nair and her supporters had acted on the belief that with the cancellation of the purchase agreement, our position was based solely on possession. With their false, negative propaganda, they had expected that they could control public opinion and that if they destroyed the temple, they could easily drive us out. But their plan backfired. They had thought they were dealing with just a handful of young foreigners, but they soon found themselves facing many of Bombay’s most influential citizens. Despite the unfavorable press, many Indians were shocked at the violent acts, and many were concerned that if one Hindu temple were destroyed without any response, without restitution and proper reprisal, others would be vulnerable and could similarly be destroyed.

The tide began to turn. As Prabhupada had predicted, our position was strengthened, and a great wave of sympathy rose in our favor. In addition to the many friends we had cultivated and the almost seven hundred life members we had enlisted—all of whom had developed a deep respect and affection for Srila Prabhupada—scores of Bombay residents, including many influential businessmen and politicians, were opposed to the violence and what they saw as an attack on the Hindu faith.

Some saw that the property of common citizens was being threatened. “Today it is ISKCON temple,” wrote a reporter for the Sandesh

Daily, “Tomorrow it will be a question of some poor man’s hut... If every time there is a tussle between money and justice and money wins every time, then what about citizens’ welfare and what about his security? What about his future? And so let this problem be a people’s problem.”

The reporter had visited the temple alone, he wrote, without anyone from either side, so that he could “gather the true information which I could present before my readers. And the sum and substance of my visit, in short, is that there is a smell of some selfish political instruments being used in this matter.

“Open allegations have been made against the foreign devotees of this temple that they are using and teaching the use of narcotic drugs under the spell of this ‘Holy Place’. But these allegers forget one thing— that these devotees are not hippies. They have not escaped from the society out of fear. They have willingly left their wealth, and they have put on saffron clothes out of their attraction for Krishna and for the purification of the soul.”

The Times article, too, had its effect. “With deep pain and regrets,” wrote Sanjay Khan, a Muslim movie star, in an open letter, “I read in the Times of India of the unprovoked demolition of the ‘Hare Krishna Land Centre’ at Juhu by the Municipal authorities ... In my humble opinion, I regard this act, if not religiously, as inhuman and totally uncalled for. It is very sad indeed that in our great secular Indian society such a barbaric act has come to pass. I am very curious to know what pleasure the so-called custodians of our Municipal area have had to intrude upon the peaceful and sanctified area of religious belief of the Hare Krishna society.”

In his letter, Mr. Khan advocated for “immediate restoration of the demolished shelter and these people to be allowed to co-exist without any future harassment and injustice.

“I find the people concerned at the Juhu Hare Krishna Society totally peaceful and add colour to our area with so many wonderful people from various parts of the world.

“Their contribution may be assessed in terms of propagating message of love and understanding.”

One by one, many of the area residents and all the municipal councilors were convinced—both of the Nairs’ and their agents’ illegal and reprehensible actions, and of our legitimate claim to the land.

And after some discussion, Mr. Mahadik’s proposal was adopted: other than two abstaining members of the Congress Party, with which Mhatre was affiliated, the committee voted unanimously to censure those officials responsible for the attack.

The Standing Committee chairman, Bhagwati Shroff, wrote to M. W. Desai, the Municipal Commissioner of Greater Bombay, “Since the structure was demolished without issue of notice as required under the provisions of B.M.C. \[Bombay Municipal Corporation\] Act, the structure should be reconstructed at Municipal Cost; and the party should be given temporary permission for the shed till the Court decides the dispute about the ownership of the land.”

“The municipality standing committee has condemned the hasty action of the municipality,” Prabhupada wrote Mrs. Singhal, “and has agreed to reconstruct the shed at their cost. Not only that, the temporary construction shall continue to stay until the court decision is there as to who is the proprietor of the land.”

The apparent calamity had served as an impetus for us to meet more new people and present Krishna consciousness, and to organize and mobilize our friends and supporters far beyond what we could have done under ordinary circumstances.

While we had been working with our life members to get permission from the municipal corporation to rebuild the temple structure, Mrs. Nair and her lawyers were busy trying to prevent us. So we continued to hold meetings with our friends and life members, discussing how to proceed.

At one of these meetings, at Sadajiwatlal’s office, one of our friends pointed out that we might not actually need permission after all. We had already been approved to build the temple in the first place, the municipal commissioner had agreed to extend the temple’s permit, and the municipality didn’t have any valid grounds for its demolition. So although we hadn’t specifically been given permission to rebuild, there was no ruling that said we couldn’t—nothing to stop us from just restoring it.

Somehow Mrs. Nair found out what we were planning to do, and the next day, Friday, she went to the high court with a petition for aninjunction to prevent us from rebuilding. It was her property, she argued, and she hadn’t given us permission. She petitioned that “pending the hearing and final disposal of the suit the defendants, their servants and agents may be restrained by an order and injunction of this Hon’ble Court from constructing or reconstructing any structure on the Plaintiff’s said property ... or any part thereof’ and “\[t\]hat pending the hearing and final disposal of the suit the defendants, their servants and agents may be restrained by an order and injunction of this Hon’ble Court from entering into or remaining upon or otherwise committing trespass on or into the Plaintiff’s said land.”

The judge, Justice Nain, had been both Mr. Sethi’s advocate and a chief guest at our second Cross Maidan pandal, so he was familiar with our Society and activities and appreciative of Prabhupada and our movement. He said he would consider granting the injunction only after he had heard both sides. Because it was Friday, he pointed out, the end of the week, he would take up the matter on Monday.

“Just give a temporary injunction for the weekend and then you can decide on the permanent injunction,” Mrs. Nair appealed, but her request was denied. “No,” Justice Nain responded. “Without hearing the other side, I will not pass any judgment.”

When we heard of Mrs. Nair’s petition and the judge’s response, we knew we had to take advantage of the opportunity. If the judge ruled against us, we would be prohibited from going ahead with the reconstruction. But once the temple was up, we understood, an injunction—even if it were granted—would be meaningless. The temple would already be in place, and no rebuilding would be necessary. We figured we had the weekend, until Monday morning, to put up the structure.

So the next day, Saturday, I went to see our friend Susheel Asnani, who was the lawyer for the Bakhtawar Construction Company and had many contacts, and told him what we had to do. We needed materials— asbestos sheets, sand, bricks, and cement. And although Sadajiwatlal’s most visible business was his sweet shops, Punjabi Chandu Halwai Karachiwala—Prabhupada called him the sweet-ball king—he was also a building contractor, and he helped us arrange for some of the materials.

In those days it was difficult to get cement and almost as hard to get bricks. The demand exceeded the supply, and the government hadimposed cement control: to purchase it legally, one had to procure a government-approved quota. And by the time we were ready to proceed, it was the weekend and many shops were closed.

It so happened, however, that Mr. Sethi was in Juhu with his family to check on his house under construction and enjoy a weekend beach outing, and before returning home, he thought of visiting the temple. “When we came,” he recalled, “we saw that the small shed had been demolished. And the description given to us of the demolition was horrifying. Not only was the temple demolished, but they wanted to take away the Deities.”

Mr. Sethi was in poor health, but he declared, “No matter whether laborers are available or not, I will rebuild this temple and will do the labor work myself.”

As it turned out, he was able to bring plenty of laborers and also supplies from his own construction sites. “I got the material from Andheri East, where my work was going on,” he later recounted. “Bricks, sand, cement.” And asbestos cement sheets for the roof. “We got an electric welding machine and a person from a jhopadpatti \[slum\] who knew welding, and welded all the pipes, which the asbestos sheets would go on.”

In the course of the day, Mrs. Nair, Mhatre, and Mrs. Nair’s solicitor, Bhachubhai Shah, all came to the site. “You can’t do this,” they shouted, demanding that we stop. Bachubhai Shah, the son of Chimanlal Shah, came to serve me with what I presumed to be a notice enjoining me from rebuilding the temple and threatening me with consequences if I did. But when I saw him, I ran away as fast as I could. And he came running after me as fast as he could, in his suit and tie. The respectable solicitor Bachubhai Shah is running after me like a child in a playground, I thought. Where is his dignity? He couldn’t catch me, and when I looked back from a safe distance, I saw him, looking frustrated, leave the letter with someone else who just happened to be there—with no proof that I had received it or ever would.

Mhatre too demanded that we halt the construction.

“No,” Mr. Sethi replied. “Why should we stop?”

“You can build it up,” Mhatre threatened, “but I will come in the night with fifty goondas \[hooligans\] and break it down.”

Mr. Sethi turned to his son, who was by his side, and said, “Brijmohan, bring my revolver and my rifle.”

Then he said to Mhatre, “Don’t bring fifty goondas. Bring a hundred. Bring two hundred. I have two hundred and fifty cartridges. You’ll have to bring at least two hundred and fifty-one.” He had a kshatriya side, and he was staunch.

“They did not count on the amazing heroism and bravery of my personal hero, Mr. P. L. Sethi,” Maithili said later, echoing everyone’s admiration.

As Brijmohan Sethi remembered, “So, with the revolver in my hand and the rifle in Daddy’s hand, we started the work. We could do this not because of something in us, but because of the blessings of Prabhupada. Only with his blessings and mercy could we start the construction. The entire night it was raining cats and dogs, but we never stopped the work; it went on.”

As the rain fell, Mr. Sethi recalled how by lifting Govardhana Hill Lord Krishna had protected the inhabitants of Vrindavan from the devastating rainfall sent by Indra. He was unperturbed. Indra wants to test me, he thought. All right, if you want to come down, you can come down more heavily, but I have the blessings of Srila Prabhupada. I have to rebuild the temple, and I will.

They were joined on guard duty by Jagmohan Sursagar, a popular singer; Amratlal Pandya; Bal Krishan Chugh; Mr. Kejriwal (Manmohan dasa); Dr. Singhal; and Bippin Desai—all life members. V.N. Bakshi, also a life member, organized two strong volunteers on motorcycles, and they circled the land and patrolled the road in front of the temple. A few police constables came in a van, but they left around midnight.

I was overseeing the rebuilding, and Tamal Krishna told me, “I want you to stay up all night and make sure the work is done. People will be working all night long, and goondas may come to attack. I want you to stay up and make sure that the work keeps going and that nothing goes wrong.”

A few days earlier, Satsvarupa dasa Goswami, my first temple president, by whom I was greatly inspired, had passed through Bombay. I appreciated his humble and gentle demeanor, and I wanted to emulate him. When Tamal Krishna told me to stay up all night and oversee thework, I mentioned how I wanted to be like Satsvarupa Maharaja—a simple, humble sadhu. Tamal Krishna looked me straight in the eyes and, with a firm intensity and controlled anger, responded, “Your humility will be to stay up all night and make sure this temple gets rebuilt.”

I thought about it, and I had to agree: Where was the humility if I was not ready to surrender to the order, or desire, of the spiritual master? If I would have retired for the evening so I could get up early and be a good devotee and chant my rounds—which wasn’t bad—I wouldn’t really have been humble. It was more humble to submit to the authority and do the needful for Srila Prabhupada’s service. To be humble meant to be ready, without personal consideration, to do whatever the spiritual master wanted, whether or not it conformed to popular conceptions of a humble sadhu.

Mr. Sethi and his son, the friends and life members, and the laborers stayed up all night to protect and complete the construction. “I was there with a gun,” Mr. Sethi recounted. “We started at nine. At eleven, one man came at the road, but I challenged him, ‘If you come inside, I will shoot you,’ and he ran away and shouted to some other men, ‘They are ready to fight—don’t go there.’

“It was pouring rain and the lighting was bad, and when the men were putting up the asbestos sheets, they were slipping on the ground. So we brought around fifty mats and put twenty men on them—one man supporting another so that there was no slipping. Ten masons worked all night, and we completed the walls and the plaster.”

Sridhar was at the site, too, chanting japa in the Jeep. When someone asked him why he was in there, he joked, “If anybody comes, I can make a quick escape.”

“Actually, the whole thing was right in keeping with my nature,” he recalled. “When there is a good chance for a fight for Krishna, I don’t run away from it. It was very exciting. I was ready. We stayed up all night. Miserable night, but we were waiting for them to come. Mr. Sethi had his gun, and I had a knife or some other weapon.”

And the devotees, life members, masons and other skilled workers, laborers, and other friends did it: they put it all up in that one night, finishing around four in the morning, and no one came to disturb the work. And then we had mangala-drati

“It was done overnight,” Amratlal Pandya described. “In order to help, Bal Krishan Chugh, Dr. Singhal, V.N. Bakshi, Bipin Desai, Mr. Mehta, and I came, though Mr. Mehta left, because he was staying nearby and was threatened. We were also threatened, but we didn’t bother for that. For the sake of Krishna’s temple, suppose we become lame—no worry. If the head is broken—no worry. Somehow or other, we had to see that everything was completed. We stayed throughout the night, and ultimately the construction was completed. The temple was reconstructed, and the festivals started—everything began in a regular way.”

Mhatre returned around seven the next morning, but by then it was too late. “It is built,” we told him. “Go to the court.”

Later that morning, we appeared in the High Court and told the judge that the temple had already been rebuilt. “What is built is built,” he said to Mrs. Nair. “No one can destroy the temple.”

When Prabhupada heard the news, he considered it a complete victory. The temple had been rebuilt. “In Bombay we have just been victorious over the party who had torn down our temple and the temple has been completely reconstructed, in addition to our gaining overwhelming new popular support,” he wrote to Gurudas. “I am glad to hear of victory in the matter of Bombay property,” he wrote to Mrs. Singhal. “Now it is rebuilt and people are supporting our cause and finding out more about our great movement. You please help and tell everyone how nice chanting Hare Krishna is.”

Three weeks later, in London, Srila Prabhupada brought up the topic of the demolition with George Harrison.

“In Bombay we are undergoing some tribulation. You have seen this booklet?” Prabhupada asked, showing George the special demolition issue.

“The city, municipal authorities, knocked our temple down,” Shyamasundar explained.

“Why did they do that?” George asked.

“Oh, that’s a long story,” Prabhupada said.

“About the land,” Shyamasundar added. “There was some dispute. We purchased it, and the other owners had tried to dispute it, and they were powerful with the police.”

“They didn’t want you to have the land, or they said you didn’t own the land?”

“They said we really didn’t, even though we paid for it,” Shyamasundar said. “They were powerful friends with the police, and they got the police to come and they demolished the temple.”

“Really? With the Deities in there?”

“They didn’t destroy the Deities.”

“No,” Prabhupada said; “they dismantled the Deity room. In the meantime, another message came—‘Don’t go on further’—so they stopped.”

“You’d expect it somewhere like in America, in the West,” George said. “In India you wouldn’t expect that.”

“No,” Prabhupada agreed, “this is an extraordinary incident. Now the public is on our side.... When one preaches, he must tell the truth. Just like Lord Jesus Christ. The people did not like his preaching, but he did not stop ... But in preaching there is possibility of creating animosity.”

“This temple demolishing?” Shyamasundar asked.

“Yes,” Prabhupada replied. “We are innocent. We are simply worshipping. We have given money. Everything is all right. But \[the opposing parties\] were creating some unwanted . . . Especially in God consciousness such things are possible. We have to pay sometimes. Even Prahlada Maharaja—he was a five-year-old boy, and his only fault was that he was Krishna conscious. His father became his enemy, what to speak of others. Because his father did not like God consciousness, he became the enemy of his child although the child was only five years old. So, there is possibility of such things, yes.”

Prabhupada often quoted the saying “Failure is the pillar of success.” He said that especially in spiritual life, failure was not a discouragement; we just had to try, and try again. And by his and Krishna’s mercy, we were successful and the temple was rebuilt.

During the temple reconstruction, Mr. Sethi had demonstrated his kshatriya spirit, for which Prabhupada expressed his appreciation, also teaching us a lesson, that sometimes a fighting spirit was required. “In this way we have to fight,” he later said. “We should not be afraid for these rascals. Why you should be afraid? If they take to goonda-ism, we shall engage fifty goondas: ‘Come on. Let us see.’ We have to maintainthat spirit. Anydya ye kare prabhu ara anyaya ye sahe. Rabindranath Tagore’s poetry: ‘One who does wrong and one who suffers wrong—he is wrong.’ One should not do anything wrong; one should not suffer anything wrong. That is human. If somebody does harm to me, wrong to me, I cannot suffer it. I shall not do any harm to anyone; that’s all right. But if you want to give me suffering, I must fight you. Why shall I suffer it? That is kshatriya spirit. Yuddhe capy apalayanam. If you are challenging, then ‘All right, come on, I accept this challenge.’ We have to do like that.”

Prabhupada was referring to the verse in the Bhagavad-glta (18.43) describing the qualities of a kshatriya:

sauryam tejo dhrtir daksyam  
yuddhe capy apalayanam  
danam isvara-bhavat ca  
ksatram karma svabhava-jam

“Heroism, power, determination, resourcefulness, courage in battle, generosity, and leadership are the natural qualities of work for the ksatriyas.”

He continued, “If somebody is atatayi, aggressor—‘You unnecessarily attack me; I must first kill you. That is my duty.’ Just like you have done here, Sethiji: ‘I’ll bring my revolver.’ That is argumentum ad baculum. Here they wanted to put us into trouble, and he was in great trouble. So he came and stood: ‘All right, come on. We shall fight. Bring my revolver.’ He did that. So, we have to do like that. Why shall I tolerate unnecessary injustice? Take that spirit.”

In Srimad-Bhagavatam (1.7.53-54), Lord Krishna Himself instructed Arjuna,

brahma-bandhur na hantavya  
atatayi vadharhanah  
mayaivobhayam amnatam  
paripahy anusasanam  
kuru pratisrutam satyam  
yat tat santvayata priyam  
priyam ca bhimasenasya  
pancalya mahyam eva ca

“The Personality of Godhead Sri Krsna said: A friend of a brahmana is not to be killed, but if he is an aggressor he must be killed. All these rulings are in the scriptures, and you should act accordingly.. ..”

“If there’s a fight,” Prabhupada said, “we must be prepared to fight.”

Mr. Sethi mentioned me, that I had supported him, and I responded, referring to him, “He’s very heroic. He was very heroic.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada said. “He’s a kshatriya.”

Then Mr. Sethi told us about his experiences fighting at the time of the partition between India and Pakistan. “In the Pakistan time,” he said, “I fought forty, fifty men.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada confirmed. “That is kshatriya spirit. If you want to fight... You killed?”

“Yes! So many times. So many times.”

“So, you have got experience.”

“Sometimes I have walked on the dead bodies.”

“Really? So many dead bodies.”

“I was with four men at Pathankot. A tonga, a horse-drawn carriage, came with six Muslims, and they challenged us, ‘We will kill you.’ We said, ‘Yes, come. You kill us; we will kill you. We fight.’ We were ready at that time, because revolver was with us, and kulhrari axe, and khunda-sa, curved sword. One, my friend, was from Gujrawala. He showed this khundasa and cut the first one’s head off, and he was running ...

“Accha. Still running?”

“Running! In Mahabharata I heard that a body was running. But I actually saw it. His head was cut off, and the body was running.

“Just see. And then he fell down.”

“Then he fell down. And after that, the other men went.”

“How he was running with his mind, just see.”

“The mind is in the heart,” Hari-sauri added.

“That,” Prabhupada said, “these rascals do not know.”

“The one man got out from the tonga,” Mr. Sethi continued, “and first we cut off his head. Then all the others ran away. We saved all the fellows.”

“That is also Krishna conscious, “Prabhupada said. “You see how many demons were killed by Krishna.”

Referring to the rebuilding of the temple, Mr. Sethi said, “I declared, if they challenge us, I am ready: ‘Come on.’ In the night at the temple Ichallenged, ‘Come on! And you are 150. We are not afraid.’ Then when Mhatre came with that barrister to give Giriraj notice, I scolded and insulted him publicly.”

“Therefore,” Prabhupada said, “Mhatre was so against, that ‘We must stop this.’ Yes. I heard from that doctor that he was insulted by Sethi, ‘Either Sethi should go . . .’ Like that, he has repeated. He gave me a hint, ‘Remove Sethi,’ but I replied, ‘I will not let that happen.’ And that doctor was Mhatre’s man. He also gave a hint, ‘Give Mhatre two lakhs of rupees.’ He was a canvasser on behalf of Mhatre. He wanted two lakhs.”

“‘We will not give you a single paisa,”’ Mr. Sethi concluded. “‘We will fight you. Come on.’”

At the time of the demolition, Tamal Krishna was leading the traveling sanklrtana party—including Achyutananda, Gargamuni, Harikesa, and Sridhar—and feeling enlivened by their preaching. Also, he was reluctant to get involved with the problems in Bombay, but when he heard about the demolition, he returned immediately. Because of the urgency of our situation, he flew, and the others came in the group’s three jeeps.

Thinking that Juhu was too far from the city and that we should be closer to the important people in Malabar Hill and downtown Bombay, Tamal Krishna suggested that we approach life members to see if someone could give us a place to stay in the city.

When we explained our situation to Brijratan Mohatta, he said that we could use his vacant flat at Nepean Sea Road, in southern Bombay. The building, called Shivner, was conveniently situated on the corner of Nepean Sea Road and Narayan Dabholkar Road. The flat was on the second floor and had three bedrooms; a kitchen; a living room, where we put a makeshift altar; and a smaller room off the hall. Tamal Krishna and Achyutananda took the first bedroom, Harikesa and I shared the next, and at different times various other devotees took the one at the end.

We didn’t have a regular temple program in the flat, but in the evenings we often had preaching programs around the city. Generally, we would return late at night and sleep late the next day. Our cook,

Gurudeva dasa, would make a light breakfast, usually a chidwa (flat rice) preparation, and for lunch we ate in vegetarian restaurants, such as Aram, on Marine Drive, or at a rooftop cafe in the Grant Road area. Personally, I felt uneasy eating restaurant food, other than in a small place on Kalbadevi Road in Old Bombay run by a family who cooked rice, dal, chapatis, and vegetables and served the meal just like in a traditional Vaishnava home.

Because the Juhu project was stalled with all the complications with Mrs. Nair, Tamal Krishna and I formed a team to collect for the temple construction in Vrindavan. One devotee suggested that it would be most effective if two preachers went together, one heavy and the other soft. Tamal Krishna and I fit the roles perfectly—he with a strong, dominant personality and I being somewhat soft-spoken—so we accepted the idea, and it worked well.

One day we went to meet Natvarlal Jivanlal Gandhi in the spice market. It was in the old section of Bombay—Bombay-2, Bombay-3, Bombay-9—the cloth market, the spice and grain market, and the iron market. That time of the year was especially hot and humid, and Old Bombay was really congested. We saw men pulling carts—just long platforms on wheels—loaded with sacks of grains and spices and sugar. The streets were so narrow and crowded with carts and cars and people that we could hardly move, and from the beginning Tamal Krishna was annoyed that I had made an appointment there. “You know I don’t like appointments down here,” he told me on the way. He wanted appointments in the newer and more congenial parts of town, such as Churchgate and Flora Fountain.

Eventually we found the address, climbed up the rickety wood stairs in the old frame building, and came to a big bare room with, at one end, sitting at a desk to the side, a simple man in white khadi cloth— Mr. Gandhi.

The room wasn’t air-conditioned, and Mr. Gandhi didn’t even have his own private office. It was very basic. “Oh God,” Tamal Krishna murmured, “why did you bring me here?” We sat down, but I had hardly opened my briefcase before he turned to me again and said, “We’re just wasting our time. Let’s get out of here!”

“We’ve come all this way,” I whispered. “Let’s just take a chance. We’re already here. It won’t take much longer.”

So, we remained seated at the man’s desk and began our appeal. We took out our book of photos and showed him images of our preaching around the world. Then we spoke about Vrindavan—how due to Prabhupada’s preaching, devotees from all over the world now wanted to come to Vrindavan but how there was no proper place to receive them. I told the story of my parents, how they had come to visit me in Vrindavan and there had not even been any place where we could eat. The only restaurants had been filthy, with flies buzzing everywhere— even the place that had been most highly recommended. We had tried Mathura, but we could not find anything there either. Finally we had gone to Agra, and there we had found some decent hotels. “There is no proper place for Westerners in Vrindavan,” we told Mr. Gandhi. “Srila Prabhupada wants to build a temple with a guesthouse and restaurant to international standards.”

It was a strong argument. We also brought out a booklet that we showed prospective donors, published by the tourist association for Agra, Mathura, and Vrindavan, with a list of hotels and restaurants for each place, and pointed out that for hotels and restaurants in Vrindavan, there was nothing. “We could have been like you,” Tamal Krishna said. “We could have gone into business and made lots of money, but then who would preach this message? We need preachers. So we have dedicated our lives to preach, and you, in your position, can help by giving money.” That also made perfect sense. It was a strong presentation. And in the end, when we showed Mr. Gandhi the pictures of the construction and the budget for the different parts of the project, he really surprised us: he donated for the biggest room in the guesthouse, which was twenty-nine thousand rupees—quite a large amount.

Tamal Krishna and I worked well as a team. Later, when Prabhupada came to Bombay, Tamal Krishna showed him our preaching kit and explained how we approached prospective donors, and Prabhupada appreciated our thoughtful and systematic appeal. He smiled at Tamal Krishna and said, “You have made this presentation very intelligently. Whatever intelligence Krishna has given, you must use only for Krishna.”

Eventually, because both Tamal Krishna and I were strong preachers, some devotees questioned whether it was most efficient for the two of us to go out and preach together, but when they raised the issue with Srila Prabhupada, his reply was practical: “If by going together they cancollect more than the combined total of what they can collect separately,” he said, “they should go together.”

Our general strategy was to meet a potential major donor in his office, arrange to have a program at his home, with kirtan, a talk, and often a slide show, and then some days later return to his office to ask for the donation. We presented Achyutananda as “the swami”—he would lead the kirtans and bhajans, give the talk, and maintain the profile of a sadhu, aloof from money and material concerns.

When at one program, at Pesu Aswani’s home, a fabulous, spacious, opulent residence on prestigious Cumbala Hill, with marble floors and gold gilding and a white-marble temple room with life-size Radha-Krishna Deities, our hosts served Achyutananda a silver thali with varieties of tasty preparations made in pure cow’s ghee, he glanced at it, pecked at a few pieces, and sent the plate away—an impressive display of detachment and renunciation. (After the program, as we were driving home, he announced, “I’m famished—let’s stop at Gurudev’s \[a vegetarian South Indian restaurant\].” Later, when Tamal Krishna and I approached Mr. Aswani, he gave a generous donation for Vrindavan.

Meanwhile, Mhatre was continuing to attack us on all fronts. We soon received notices from the office of the charity commissioner and from the Foreigners Registration Office, and some of the devotees, fearing that they may be arrested, took shelter with us in Shivner.

To help deal with all the challenges, Tamal Krishna and some of the other leading Bombay devotees concluded that we should turn the management of ISKCON in Bombay over to life members and supporters, who were more experienced and expert than we and were both affluent and influential, and just preach and give spiritual guidance. So we scheduled an early-morning meeting at Sadajiwatlal’s office with a committee of some of our best supporters—including Sadajiwatlal, Brijratan Mohatta, M. P. Maheshwari, and Bhogilal Patel—with the intention of giving them control.

The night before the meeting, however, Harikesa told me excitedly that he had read something that made him think we shouldn’t go through with the plan. He and I had both been suffering from jaundice, and we were spending much of our time in our beds, convalescing. Hehad been reading Prabhupada’s as-yet-unpublished Nectar of Instruction and had come across a purport that seemed to address our situation.

He read me the relevant verse:

dadati pratigrhnati  
guhyam akhyati prcchati  
bhunkte bhojayate caiva  
sad-vidham priti-laksanam

“Offering gifts in charity, accepting charitable gifts, revealing one’s mind in confidence, inquiring confidentially, accepting prasada, and offering prasada are the six symptoms of love shared by one devotee and another.” (NOl 4)

Then he read Prabhupada’s purport, which explained the other side of the instruction:

“In this regard, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura warns all devotees engaged in broadcasting the Krsna consciousness movement not to speak to the impersonalists, or Mayavadis ... If a snake is given milk to drink, its poison simply increases. For a similar reason, we should not disclose our minds to the serpent Mayavadis and karmls. Such disclosures will never help. It is best to completely avoid associating with them and never ask them about anything confidential because they cannot give good advice.”

Harikesa thought it was too dangerous to hand over management of the Society to Hindus who were closer to being Mayavadis, or materialists, than being devotees, and we resolved to bring the matter up to Tamal Krishna and Achyutananda first thing the next morning. Before the meeting with Tamal Krishna, Harikesa spoke with Achyutananda, who agreed. It was delicate, because we knew how intent Tamal Krishna was to engage these men and get relief from the management himself, but we felt that Srila Prabhupada and Lord Krishna had revealed the purport to us just in time to avoid a possible calamity.

The meeting was set for 7:30. At about 5:30 Harikesa and I went to Tamal Krishna’s room, read the purport to him and the other leaders, and implored them not to hand over too much control to the committee. At first, Tamal Krishna was apprehensive, because he had been telling the members that we wanted to give them responsibility and control,but eventually everyone in the room agreed, because most of the committee members, as pious and as friendly as they were, were not really devotees. They had already tried to involve us in material welfare activities and had suggested that to attract more people we should include famous Mayavadis in our programs. So, we arrived at an explanation for them that was both reasonable and spiritually valid, and at the meeting, all the members accepted, or acquiesced, to our retaining control of the management. They all knew that the movement was Srila Prabhupada’s and understood that they should not try to go beyond the limits we set, or demand control.

In the midst of all the intrigues and conflicts, I sent Srila Prabhupada my Vyasa-puja offering, and on August 23, from Bhaktivedanta Manor, he sent me an encouraging note: “I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter and the nice Vyasa-puja offering you sent. I have sent it to Satsvarupa Goswami for printing in the BTG. Writing is a very important part of our work, and Satsvarupa is always anxious to have new material from the devotees for expanding the BTG. You have a nice talent for writing, and practice makes perfect, so continue. It will be appreciated.”

Eventually BTG published my offering, in which I described my first meeting with Srila Prabhupada and how it—he—had transformed my life:

All glories to you  
Who have given us light  
To open our eyes,  
Which were firmly shut tight.

When we first came to you  
In the darkness of night  
The words from your lips  
Made everything bright.

“What is your goal—  
Godhead to find  
Or God to become?  
Please make up your mind.

“If you want to become God,  
You can’t be God now.  
Can a non-God become God?  
Please let me know how.

“God is within you,  
Sitting there in your heart,  
Just waiting for your  
Loving service to start.

“But if you insist  
That you want to be Him,  
You’re cheating yourself  
And have nothing to win.

“If the seed of devotion  
With chanting you sow,  
Then God will give sunlight  
To help make it grow.

“But if to become God  
Remains your ambition,  
Why then should God Help  
His own competition?

“Krsna is God,  
And God He is always,  
On Yasoda’s lap  
Or in Dvaraka’s hallways.

“Or in Kuruksetra,  
He’s God all the same—  
It’s not that by yoga  
The Lord He became.

“You are a spark,  
And God is the fire:  
You can be Godly  
If you truly desire.

“Your qualities match His,  
But the quantity’s different,  
For God’s nature is infinite,  
Whereas you’re insignificant.

“I cannot be God,  
For I truly am small,  
But He kindly allows me  
To serve Him. That’s all.

“That is His mercy,  
Transcendent and sweet.  
Take it! Be happy!  
That’s all I entreat.”

Thus Your Divine Grace  
We were blessed to meet,  
And thus we were forced  
To fall at your feet.

You poured nectarlike words  
Through the holes in our ears  
To clean out our hearts  
And vanquish our fears.

Arousing within us  
Our love for the Lord,  
Our actual life as  
His servant restored.

Now we beg to remain  
Individual souls,  
Serving the servant  
Of the one Spirit Whole.

All glories to you  
Who have given us this:  
A life that’s eternal,  
Full of knowledge and bliss.

Taking us from the darkness,  
Cold and alone,  
Back to Godhead,  
Back to home.

With the sales agreement cancelled, we didn’t know what to do— the situation seemed hopeless. Several influential life members had tried to convince Mrs. Nair to sell us the property, but she just wouldn’t listen. And so we sent a telegram to Prabhupada, asking him to come to Bombay to settle the matter with Mrs. Nair personally.

I had heard from Gargamuni, who was the first devotee to meet Bhogilal Patel, that when he had told Seth Bhogilal about how Prabhupada had spread Lord Krishna’s message and service in America and throughout the world, Bhogilal had wept with joy and immediately become a life member. I developed a friendship with Seth Bhogilal, who was quite humble and softhearted, and he became one of our best well-wishers and supporters.

Bhogilal had a mansion—more like a palace, with dozens of servants—on Walkeshwar Road, near the sea, and when I approached him with the idea of Prabhupada staying at his home, named Daskot, he happily agreed.

Having received word that Prabhupada would be coming to Bombay, Tamal Krishna had arranged for our entire flat to be freshly painted, and for a proper altar to be set up in the hall. Sridhar cleaned the flat and got it ready, with new cushions and bolsters and nice decorations.

When Prabhupada came, Tamal Krishna and the other leading sannyasis took him through every room. Then they escorted him into the smaller room, where he sat on his asana and spoke to the devotees. Sridhar cut up a plate of fruit and placed it on a small table beside Prabhupada, who paused, looked up, and said, “Thank you very much.” Prabhupada had often been served fruit, Sridhar knew; he wasn’t saying thank you for that. And he couldn’t have known that it was Sridhar who had cleaned up the flat. But he knew that Sridhar was trying to serve him, just like the other, more senior devotees. And he was thanking Sridhar for giving his life. “That was so gratifying—when any devotee got that kind of reciprocation from Prabhupada,” Sridhar remembered. “It made it all worthwhile.”

Brahmananda was in Bombay for some days, to purchase items for the Deities in East Africa. When Prabhupada asked him why he had come—to Bombay, to India—Brahmananda replied, “To get mukutas and everything for the Deities.”

“Oh, you cannot make flower mukutas!” Prabhupada asked. Nairobi was known for its plentiful flowers, and Prabhupada’s Punjabi disciple there, Shakti-mata, had a landscaping business and a nursery with many exotic plants. “You just make a wire framework and then stick flowers in it, and that’s your crown. If necessary, there are Indian jewelers in Nairobi, and they can make flutes and other items. There is no need for you to come to India.”

Prabhupada criticized us for not having a morning program. Were we having regular programs or, he inquired, “is it simply going out and coming back and eating and sleeping?”

“Well,” Tamal Krishna replied, “we want to have morning class, and Monday, Wednesday, and Friday to have evening programs, evening discourse.”

“Were they going on?” Prabhupada wanted to know.

“We just fixed up the place,” Tamal Krishna said. “The day you arrived was the first day it was painted. Until then, it was not fit for anyone to come into. It was very nasty.”

“But you are living there since a long time,” Prabhupada said.

“We have been living, but we have not invited others.”

“No, you may invite others or not,” Prabhupada persisted, “but was your program going on?”

“No, it wasn’t, Prabhupada.”

“Then it was simply a joint mess, that you go and collect and come and eat and sleep.”

“Yes.”

“That is very dangerous. Then you will all fall down. If you make a joint mess, if you go and collect something and then eat and sleep, then everything will be . . . Therefore I do not want you to keep separate. Temple worship means there will be regulative principles, that you will have to rise early in the morning, attend class and kirtan. As soon as you give up all these things—zero. Then it will be like karmis, as they are, hard labor, collecting money, and enjoying senses. That’s all.

“That is the pitfall everywhere. In the church, temple, as soon as they get some nice income, then in the name of ‘priest, ‘sadhu,’ ‘sannyasi,’ they do the same thing. Visaya chadiya, se rase majiya. As soon as we give up this sravanam kirtanam, hearing and chanting, then it becomes visaya. Visaya means materialism. There is no spiritualism. Ksurasya dhara. Ksura means sharpened razor. If you are careful, you cleanse very nicely. But if you are not careful, immediately blood. Immediately. Spiritual life is like that. As soon as you become a little inattentive, immediately Maya captures, ‘Yes, come on.’ Then everything is failure. We have got the tendency to enjoy the senses. The senses are strong. As soon as there is opportunity, the senses will take advantage immediately. Then your whole business is finished. So, if we do not follow strictly our regulative principles, routine work, then the whole scheme will be failure.

“Anyway, that is the danger in keeping a separate department for collecting money. Then it will turn: ‘Collect money, eat nicely, and sleep nicely.’ And to live in the temple, at least one is forced to rise early in the morning, take bath, have darshan. They’ll get regulated life. Therefore this temple worship is needed, because we are so impure. At least in the temple, by following the regulative principles, we can keep ourselves pure. Otherwise, simply chanting is sufficient. There is no need of constructing big, big temple. But we are so impure . . . That is Jiva Gosvami’s recommendation, that as soon as we give up this temple-worship method, regulative principles ... we become victim of maya. Vesopajivaka. As they are working and doing some business, then our dress will be a means of business. This will be another material business. Actually they are doing so. That is the danger in keeping a separate department. What is the use?”

“The danger is very much there,” Tamal Krishna agreed, “I see that—but there is a use.”

“Well, if the danger is there, why should we accept such use?”

“Can we overcome that danger?” Tamal Krishna asked. “We can try to overcome that danger.”

“You cannot overcome, because you are all weak. Daivi hy esa guna-mayi mama maya duratyaya \[Gita 7.14\]. Unless you are very strong, maya is very much stronger than you. How you can avoid it? Only one who is very, very strong in capturing the lotus feet of Krishna can avoid.

Otherwise it is not possible. All these Vile Parle, Juhu gentlemen, are daily coming to their city business. And is it very difficult for us?”

“They have an office, though, that they come to in the city,” Tamal Krishna replied.

“Their business is office. But your business is begging. Your business is not office. They have to direct so many things from there. That we can do. Anyway, even if they have got an office, they come, in Bombay, Calcutta, even from a hundred miles away.

“If there is no such program—Deity worship, regulative principle—then it will be a joint mess. Hotel. Transcendental hotel. And transcendental fraud. This will go on. The business will be transcendental fraud, and life will be transcendental hotel.

“Nowadays, modern civilization, as we are accepting, there is Jeep, there is telephone—everything is there. One can conduct his activities from anywhere.”

“But it didn’t work last time,” Tamal Krishna said. “They stopped their preaching. The last time everyone moved to Juhu, they completely lost contact with all the life members in the city, because they found it very difficult to continuously go back and forth.”

“So, keep it just like a temple. Not that...”

“The Nepean Sea Road flat downtown,” Achyutananda inquired, “it should be kept like a temple?”

“Yes. The temple routine work must go on there.”

“But no Deity,” Tamal Krishna said.

“Deity—there is picture,” Prabhupada said. “That’s all right. Do you think that picture is not Deity? There are eight kinds of Deity. Picture is also Deity. Even thinking of Krishna within the mind is Deity. But we are not so expert that within the mind we can worship the Deity. We are gross men, so we must have Deity worship. Otherwise, you can worship Deity anywhere, sit down and think. But the method must be there. Bhumir apo ‘nalo vayuh kham mano \[Gita 7.4\]. Mind is also a material thing. And if you think of Krishna’s form within the mind, it is as good as you worship the Deity in the temples, made of brass or wood or stone. Because both of them are Krishna’s energy. Krishna’s energy is not different from Krishna. Krishna can accept your service in any of these so-called material elements. Actually, there areno material things. Material means the desire for sense gratification. Atmendriya-priti-vancha—tare bali ‘kama’ \[Cc Adi 4.165\]. That is material. Krsnendriya-priti-iccha dhare ‘prema’ nama. And the desire to please Krishna’s senses is spiritual. So, picture must be kept in a nice altar, and regularly arati and everything should go on.”

While Prabhupada was in Bombay, Tamal Krishna instituted a morning class at Shivner, which was just a few blocks away from Bhogilal Patel’s house. We would go to Seth Bhogilal’s early in the morning to see Prabhupada, hoping to accompany him on his morning walk. Tamal Krishna wanted us to return to Shivner for the class, but when he complained to Prabhupada that it was time for class and the devotees didn’t want to go, Prabhupada replied, “That’s all right; I have just come. They want to be with me.”

We had also arranged outside programs with Prabhupada, for potential donors. When we mentioned to Dr. Mohanlal Piramal, a textile magnate (Piramal Spinning and Weaving Mills) that Prabhupada was in Bombay, he was eager that Prabhupada should come to his home. Prabhupada accepted the invitation, telling us that we should go ahead and begin and that he would follow.

He arrived while Achyutananda was singing bhajans and was ushered to a sofa, on which he sat cross-legged and observed the bhajans and the devotees. After a while, he said, “Chant Hare Krishna,” so we did kirtan, and then he spoke. After the lecture, our host wanted to feed us, especially Prabhupada. Prabhupada left, but we stayed behind to honor prasada and associate with our host, his wife, his mother, and a few other family members.

Later, Prabhupada questioned our method of “preaching.” He said, “This is not preaching—to go to some rich man’s house and flatter him and sing a few songs and take prasada. Do you actually preach?”

“Yes,” Tamal Krishna said, “We preach very forcefully. We don’t just flatter.”

“Well, all right then,” Prabhupada replied. But soon thereafter, he introduced conditions for our having outside programs. He said that we should accept a program only if there would be a large donation, or alarge gathering at which people would take up chanting Hare Krishna. He also said that he didn’t want the programs to take away from our preaching at Juhu. So, although the system we had devised for collecting funds for Vrindavan had been successful, we could understand that Prabhupada wanted our program to be pure.

The gates and entrances to Daskot were emblazoned with the family crest: a crowned pair of wooden sandals flanked by a prancing horse and lion. The front doors opened to a set of stairs and the hallway to Prabhupada’s wing, with marble flooring, gold-framed paintings along the wall, and ornate metal tables on whose marble tops were displayed decorative vases, Ming jades, ivory carvings, and other priceless traditional works of art. There was even an elevator up to the second floor.

Bhogilal Patel had allotted Prabhupada a bedroom and a darshan room for meeting people, and across the way an area for Prabhupada’s assistants, including his servant, Srutakirti, and his Sanskrit editor, Pradyumna. At the end of the darshan room was Prabhupada’s usual low table and asana; the rest of the room was arranged for people to sit on the floor, with chairs available for special guests.

To get from the servants’ area to the hallway, one had to pass by the doorway to the darshan room. When I passed one day, I saw Gargamuni and Tamal Krishna sitting opposite Prabhupada’s desk arguing with him. I was surprised—I had never seen disciples argue so vehemently with him. “We’re just wasting our time in India,” Gargamuni was saying. Prabhupada clearly wanted them to stay.

“We are just like businessmen,” one of them said. “We’re collecting money and making life members.”

Prabhupada was sympathetic to their frustrations but told them, “I want you to stay here. It is the spiritual master’s desire that you stay here, so that is better.”

“Isn’t it service to go to America and preach?” one asked. “In America the preaching is so much better.”

“I was sitting off to the side,” Srutakirti recalled, “amazed at the intensity of my godbrothers. Gargamuni and Tamal Krishna seemed relentless. But the more they were determined to leave India, the more Prabhupada was determined to have them stay. It was evident that Prabhupada considered the preaching work in India to be of the utmost importance.

“Seeing how upset Srila Prabhupada was, I was squirming in the corner of the room. I also understood how hard it was to stay in India. Srila Prabhupada was depending on these men to assist him in this important work, but they felt that they just couldn’t do it any longer. It was a fierce battle. The intensity of the negotiation was something I would have expected among peers rather than between spiritual master and disciple. Prabhupada wanted them to stay, and that was final. They argued that they needed to leave India to preach. At this time, the West was a fertile preaching field. Finally, in apparent disgust, Srila Prabhupada said, ‘All right, you just chant your sixteen rounds, follow the four regulative principles, and do any damn thing you want.’”

With devotees staying in his Shivner flat, Mr. Mohatta, who lived nearby, asked one or two of them to come to his home every morning and teach him about the Bhagavad-gita and Srimad-Bhagavatam. Now, at Bhogilal Patel’s, Mr. Mohatta complained to Prabhupada that when he asked the devotees questions, they could not answer.

Brahmananda, who was one of Mr. Mohatta’s “teachers,” replied, “When he asks questions, we read him the answers in your books.”

Prabhupada curled his lips and shook his head. “He doesn’t want to know what is in the books—he wants to know what you know.”

As I was passing by the door to Prabhupada’s room one day, he motioned to me with his eyes to enter. Baradraj’s singing of Narottama dasa Thakura’s "Gaurangera Duti Pada” was playing, from a new album of kirtans—Every Town & Village—recorded live at the New York temple. When it was over, Prabhupada looked up and said, “When I am no longer present, you can listen to this song and remember your spiritual master.”

It was a poignant statement that entered deep in my heart. I considered why Prabhupada had singled out that song. One verse says, gauranga-gunete jhure, nitya-lila tare sphure, se jana bhakati-adhikari: “If anyone feels ecstasy and cries from appreciating Gauranga’s transcendental qualities, he becomes eligible to perform pure devotional service.” And I was confident that if I, or we, remembered Srila Prabhupada in that mood of appreciation, with such feelings of separation, we would get the same result.

One Saturday morning we had an appointment with Ashok Birla, whom Tamal Krishna and I had been cultivating over a period of months. Ashok was different from the other, more staid Birlas. Once, when he greeted us at the Birla mansion on Mount Pleasant Road, he was wearing a shortsleeved silk shirt covered with American flags. And whereas the most affluent men, including the Birlas, usually rode in large Mercedes Benzes, Ashok drove a smaller, sportier BMW. After many months of cultivating him, we decided that the time had come to ask him for a donation, and we showed him the list of different parts of the Vrindavan project and how much each item would cost.

After looking at the list, Ashok asked us what we wanted him to contribute for. We weren’t exactly sure what to say, but I replied, “We thought that you could build the temple room”—the single largest item on the list, an expense of three lakhs of rupees.

He immediately agreed: “Yes, I will do that.” In fact, he conceded so easily that we were thinking that maybe we should have asked for more. Practically everyone else we approached would offer a lesser figure, and then we would have to discuss and argue with them to convince them to give more. Anyway, he agreed to give three lakhs, and we were quite happy. Then, before leaving, we informed him that Prabhupada was staying nearby, at Bhogilal Patel’s house, and we invited him to come and meet him. It was around nine, and he said that he would come to meet Prabhupada shortly, before lunchtime.

When we returned to Bhogilal Patel’s house, Tamal Krishna informed Prabhupada about Mr. Birla’s commitment for Vrindavan and told him that Ashok would be coming before lunch. Time passed, and after waiting until around noon, we phoned Ashok to see what had happened. It hadn’t been possible for him to come in the morning, he said, but he would come in the afternoon. So Prabhupada took prasada. By evening, Ashok still hadn’t arrived, so we called again, and this time he gave a message that he would come the next morning. “He will never come,” Prabhupada said. “He has given his money—that’s enough.”

Still, the next morning we were hoping that Ashok would come. We phoned his house, and we were told that although he wouldn’t be able to come, his mother could come meet Prabhupada later that morning. Prabhupada was satisfied with that.

Srimati Gopi Kumari Birla arrived right on time. Although she was a member of the richest family in India, one of the richest in the world, Mrs. Birla was very humble and respectful to Prabhupada. Upon entering the room, she bowed down and offered her obeisances to him, and she sat at a respectful distance, on the floor.

Prabhupada immediately began preaching to her, quoting Sanskrit verses from the second chapter of the First Canto of Srimad-Bhagavatam. She was a highly educated and cultured lady who was also spiritually inclined, so she responded by quoting other verses in Sanskrit, and Prabhupada was very pleased with her. Before leaving, she again offered her respects, and afterward Prabhupada commented, “She is very nice lady.”

Three months later, in Los Angeles, where I was recovering from my jaundice, Prabhupada told Brijratan Mohatta, our good friend from Bombay, and his wife, R. D. Birla’s daughter, “Ashok’s mother came to see me in Bombay. Yes, very nice lady.”

“She has arranged for two or three of your programs in her school,” Mr. Mohatta reported.

“We showed the series of slides of Prahlada Maharaja,” I added. “The children enjoyed it very much.”

We also held a Janmashtami program at the school. We were always ready to encourage both her and her students, and she did everything she could to encourage the spread of Krishna consciousness.

Before leaving Daskot for Juhu, Prabhupada asked everyone from Seth Bhogilal’s domestic staff who had been serving him to come to his darshan room. He gave each of them some daksina, a monetary gift in appreciation for their service during his stay.

I was surprised—I hadn’t expected Prabhupada to give “Krishna’s money” away like that. Then I realized how much I had to learn about real culture, traditional Indian culture—and about Krishna consciousness.

Later, Prabhupada wrote me, “Bhogilal Patel is a perfect gentleman. He has got money and also heart. His son is also good.” And in a conversation in Los Angeles the following year, he appreciated the rationale—and culture—behind Seth Bhogilal’s opulent lifestyle.

When Tamal Krishna remarked that Bhogilal had twenty-three cars just for him and his son and his son’s wife, Prabhupada explained, “Yes, they are spending money to save income tax. They have got enough income. So instead of giving to the income tax, they are thinking, Why not provide some drivers, some servants, and repair the house every year? In this way, they spend money. It is a good policy. Money’s distributed to the poor instead of going to the government’s pocket.”

“He’s got at least thirty-five servants, and it is only the father and son and daughter-in-law,” Tamal Krishna pointed out.

“That’s all,” Prabhupada said. “No children even.”

“They gave us so much attention.”

“They are very favorable to us. Especially the father.”

“And his son, Pranlal, is also a nice boy.”

“Yes. He’s very intelligent. He knows what we are doing. His wife also, that young girl.”

“Yes, very nice. They’re actually a little aristocratic, I think.”

“Oh, yes. When I was staying there, that young girl, the daughterin-law, was always taking care: ‘Swamiji, what do you want? What can I serve you?’And Bhogilal was coming daily to talk with me.”

“Pranlal was offering any help that he could. Your secretaries were also treated very nicely. They gave us each a car. That was a wonderful stay. That was when Mrs. Nair surrendered, at that house.”

When Prabhupada had arrived in Bombay, Mr. Vakil had contacted Mrs. Nair’s solicitor, Mr. Shah, who had confirmed that she didn’t want to sell us the land. “She has someone to buy it for twenty lakhs or more,” he said, “but practically she can get any big amount for it.” Still, he felt sure that if we were ready to pay seventeen lakhs in cash right then, she would go for it. “You’re just trespassers,” Shah stated. “You have no claim to be on the land or to buy the land. The court case is coming up, and when it comes up you will be thrown off the land. It would be better if you just paid the seventeen lakhs now and finished up.”

Prabhupada was not happy with the proposal. He could see that the increase in price was the result of so many lawyers being involved, each wanting his cut. As he later explained, they were thinking, “Cancel the agreement and take seventeen or twenty lakhs from him, and the balance should be divided amongst us.”

Our tenant Mrs. Warrier had been visiting Mrs. Nair—along with Mr. Asnani, the lawyer who was our life member and friend—and she had heard that Mrs. Nair was hard-pressed for money. Mr. Nair “had taken money from everybody and spent lavishly,” she said, and his creditors were demanding payment.

Selling the land to us would be mutually beneficial, she had told Mrs. Nair. “You need money, and they want the land. It is better just to finish up the deal. Otherwise, it will be fighting like this for years. Nobody is gaining anything. And if you give it to a temple, at least in your next birth you will be benefited.”

“What are you doing?” Mr. Asnani had asked Mrs. Nair. “You’re not getting any money, and you’re not enjoying the use of the land. Swamiji is very good. He will take care of all your many needs.”

But Mrs. Nair wasn’t convinced. She claimed to have higher offers. “They are offering fourteen,” she had said of us, “but another person is offering twenty-five.”

“What would you do with twenty-five lakhs and only one person?” Mrs. Warrier had asked. “How much money do you require to live in this world? You are the only person. You don’t have any close relatives.”

“Yes, that is true,” Mrs. Nair had replied, “but so much sickness is there, and I really want cash now.”

“Fourteen, then,” Mrs. Warrier had countered. “You can ask more, but don’t expect twenty-five. And everything in one installment. If that is the only condition, don’t worry. If you want tomorrow, they will give you money. So, will you talk to them?”

Mrs. Nair had agreed—at least to meet with Prabhupada.

“Yes,” Prabhupada said when he heard of Mrs. Nair’s willingness to see him. “Bring her to me, and I will speak to her. She is my daughter. Tell her, ‘Prabhupada said that “You are my daughter and I love you.’””

Mrs. Warrier and Mr. Asnani conveyed his message to Mrs. Nair, and it was arranged that she would come and meet Prabhupada the following night. In the meantime, however, Mrs. Nair’s solicitors were demanding an immediate response. “We have to know today,” they told us. “You pay seventeen lakhs and settle up, or we are going to drive you out. You tell us yes or no—otherwise it’s all finished.”

“So, what to do?” Prabhupada asked, but we didn’t know what to say. Finally he told us, “Okay, we will pay. Actually, I don’t even want thisland, but because I have invited Radha and Krishna to come here, it will be a great insult if They are driven away. And I could not bear that.”

We were supposed to give our answer to Mr. Vakil the following day. Prabhupada said that we should prepare a draft of a letter agreeing to take the land for the increased amount, show it to Mr. Vakil, and ask for his advice—but we should put some mistakes in the letter, so that Mr. Vakil would have to ask us to make corrections. And then we would tell him that we had to take the letter back to retype it and would bring it back. That would at least give us one more day to maneuver.

I was struck by how intelligent and diplomatic—how clever— Prabhupada was. And while all of this was going on, he was holding programs and giving lectures practically every night. Bhogilal Patel and his son, Pranlal, had arranged a gathering of aristocratic people from Malabar Hill on the terrace of their home, but that evening, when Prabhupada was on the terrace about to lecture, he was told that Mrs. Nair had arrived and immediately went down to his room to see her, leaving us to continue the program without him.

In his room, Prabhupada sent everyone out except Tamal Krishna, Shyamasundar, Mr. Asnani, Mrs. Warrier, and Mrs. Nair and then closed the doors. Then he spoke to Mrs. Nair with a kindhearted tenderness. “You are my daughter,” he told her. “I will take all care of you.”

Mrs. Nair bowed down at his feet and burst into tears. “I am sorry,” she implored. “Please forgive me. I didn’t intend all these things to happen. Now I just want to give you the land and be peaceful again.”

Prabhupada touched her head gently. “Don’t worry,” he consoled her. “I will see to all of your needs for the rest of your life.”

If she surrendered to him, he was telling her, he would give her all protection. It was an important lesson for me too—that anyone who surrendered to Prabhupada would be completely protected by him. Hearing of this exchange, I asked myself, Why am I hesitating? This woman is just surrendering to him now, and Prabhupada is giving her complete protection, while I have been hanging around in the movement for years and have never really surrendered. It was a good lesson.

Prabhupada told Mrs. Nair that he still accepted the terms she had proposed—that he pay the balance of twelve lakhs, for a total offourteen, plus an extra fifty thousand rupees as compensation for the delay. And she agreed.

Prabhupada was fully prepared. He had already had Tamal Krishna type up a draft of a new settlement, and as soon as Mrs. Nair agreed, he pulled it out. He told Mr. Asnani to go over the terms of the conveyance with Mrs. Nair and make whatever changes they saw fit right then and there.

While the new agreement was being typed up, Prabhupada went back up to the roof and delivered a beautiful lecture. When he was done, he rose from his seat and went back downstairs, and he and Mrs. Nair signed the document, with November 1 as a tentative deadline for the signing of the final conveyance.

The next step was tricky, since we couldn’t inform Mrs. Nair’s lawyers or our lawyers or any of the lawyers serving as go-betweens. They were being cut out of the transaction and would try to stop it.

And Prabhupada was not going to leave Bombay. “Twice he had made the mistake of trying to let us do this conveyance,” Tamal Krishna recounted, “and both times we were unable. This time he did everything himself.”

The next day, sitting on his asana behind his low table, Srila Prabhupada was talking with Gargamuni and Achyutananda, awaiting the arrival of our American bank manager. He was touching on the same themes, warning his disciples of the dangers of working hard simply to get money and enjoy the senses, and explaining our mission, why we were collecting, and how to avoid criticism.

“Our mission,” he said, “is to teach that ‘You are simply wasting your time. Take to Krishna consciousness.’ That is our only business. And the next business is that those who cannot directly take to the process should help this movement. Therefore we go door to door, to connect them with this movement—life member. People are misunderstanding: ‘They have no other good business. Transcendental fraud, giving us some book and taking money and eating and sleeping.’ They are thinking like that.”

“So, we should preach strongly, and they should know that we also preach,” Tamal Krishna said.

“Yes. They should know that it is for their benefit we are making them life members—not for our benefit. And that should be the motive.

We should deal with them so that they may develop their Krishna consciousness. If you simply make it a point, somehow or other, take some money from them and let them go to hell, that is not . . . That is transcendental fraud. What do you think, Gargamuni?”

“Yes,” Gargamuni replied. “We have to preach.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada continued. “If by the dress of a sannyasi you take some money and eat and sleep, then it is transcendental fraud. Just like others are toiling, we are getting money by some dress. That’s all. They are getting money by laboring hard, and we are getting money. In India, mostly the sannyasis do that. The priests also do that. ‘This is our profession.’ My guru maharaja said that instead of earning livelihood by showing the Deity in the temple, it is better to take the profession of a sweeper in the street and live honestly. He said like that. The sweeper is working hard, toiling, and getting some money and living. This is honest living.”

Just then, the bank manager arrived, accompanied by an Indian lady, Bhanu, who worked under him. The manager was being called back to America, and he wanted Bhanu to help us in his absence. After some preliminary discussion of spiritual life, Bhanu told Prabhupada that people might find Juhu far away and hard to reach.

“In Juhu there are many people,” Prabhupada stated. “Juhu people are not coming here, and people here will not go there. Any part of Bombay is itself a big city. But where will we get such big land in the city? Our property is twenty thousand square yards—and by the Juhu Beach. For this facility, yes. And a new town is growing there.”

Prabhupada asked the bank manager if he had been to Juhu, and the man replied that he used to live there, in a large white six-story building on the beach, which Prabhupada passed on his morning walks.

“How do you like that place, Juhu?” Prabhupada asked.

“Very much,” the manager said. “Quiet, peaceful. After a day of work in the bank, it’s a nice place to retreat to. I take the train. It’s thirty-three minutes by train between Churchgate and Juhu.”

“So, where is the difficulty?” Prabhupada turned to ask his disciples. “Such a responsible officer, bank manager, coming and going, and you sannyasis cannot come and go? He has got responsible duties; he has to arrive in the office exactly on time.”

Prabhupada asked the manager if other bank officers might be living in Juhu, and he replied that National and Grindlays Bank officers were there and that several British companies had officers there as well.

Soon thereafter, we all left the Shivner flat for Juhu. Prabhupada moved into Mr. Sethi’s house, which was still under construction in the Juhu Scheme. It was spacious and well built, just not completely finished—the marble wasn’t polished, and the temporary lighting was dim—and Mr. Sethi and his family had not yet moved in.

Prabhupada could receive visitors there, and at his direction I arranged a meeting with Mr. Shantilal Mehta, the shrewd, seasoned businessman who, with his son, ran S. Chhaganlal and Brothers, which had a claim on the Juhu land.
