An elderly Jain, the older Mr. Mehta came dressed in a traditional white Indian suit, vest, and cap. Prabhupada remained seated on his asana. Almost immediately after entering, as if to catch Prabhupada off guard, Mr. Mehta said, “I understand you are in negotiations with Mrs. Nair. So, who will take the land—you or me?”

Prabhupada sat up straight, looked him in the eye, and said, “I will.” “Well, what about my claim?” Mehta objected. “My claim is for six lakhs”—a hugely inflated figure.

“My claim is for twelve lakhs,” Prabhupada countered. If Mehta wanted the land, he would have to pay Prabhupada twelve lakhs to withdraw.

Mr. Mehta could see that he was up against a smart, tough fighter, not just some simple elderly sadhu. His eyes opened wider and his whole demeanor seemed to change, to become humbler and more respectful.

Prabhupada began preaching to him: “We will use the land for a good cause. We will make a temple.”

Mr. Mehta agreed to a meeting with Prabhupada and Mrs. Nair to negotiate how much she would have to pay him to get him to withdraw his claim. According to the sales agreement, Prabhupada could hold back the majority of his payments until Chhaganlal withdrew its claim in the High Court.

Satisfied with the arrangement, Mr. Mehta offered his respects to Prabhupada and left the room. As I escorted him down the stairs to his car, he kept shaking his head and saying, “Your guru maharaja is pukka. He is a real guru maharaja. He is pukka.”

One morning, Prabhupada was sitting in his room on the second floor, absorbed in discussion with friends and disciples about the struggle for the land. Suddenly, a muscular, sinewy laborer appeared at the door, paused, and, with all eyes on him, entered the room without introduction. The man’s complexion was dark, and he wore only a small, faded cloth around his waist. I was apprehensive. He walked toward Prabhupada, placed a bunch of flowers on his desk, bowed down, looked at him, and walked out.

Prabhupada was so moved by the man’s simple act of devotion that for several moments he could not speak. He just looked down and closed his eyes. Finally, with a choked voice, he said, “Such a simple man. Yet somehow he understood that a saintly person is here, and he gathered some flowers to offer. In the Bhagavad-gita, Lord Krishna says, patram puspam phalam toyam yo me bhaktya prayacchati/ tad aharn bhakty-upahrtam asnami prayatatmanah: ‘If one offers Me a leaf or flower with love and devotion, I will accept it.’ Krishna is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and even His heart is touched by such devotion, what to speak of an insignificant living entity like me—how much more I will feel overwhelmed.”

Prabhupada arranged another meeting with Chhaganlal, which was again held in his room at Mr. Sethi’s. He sat behind his desk and was joined by Mrs. Nair with her advocate, and the senior Mr. Mehta with his son.

Right away, Mrs. Nair verbally attacked Chhaganlal, and Shantilal Mehta counterattacked. They fought bitterly, giving vent to years of hatred. Mrs. Nair despised Shantilal Mehta so much that she was ready to let things drag on for years rather than give in to him. And he felt the same way. He didn’t care if his Rs. 50,000 was tied up with her; he wasn’t going to surrender.

Prabhupada let them fight for a while and then said, “Now let’s forget. What’s done is done. Let us forget about it.” He pacified them, and they started talking civilly, but the animosity soon erupted again and they resumed fighting. Prabhupada again had to pacify them and appeal to them to quiet down, and eventually, when their fighting passions came down to a smolder, he said, “Now let us discuss.”

Just then, Mr. Ganatra, the former mayor, walked in and started glorifying Srila Prabhupada, offering obeisances and prayers. He was a well-known and popular figure, and Mr. Mehta knew him. “Swamiji,” Mr. Ganatra said, “I came for your darshan. I had no idea I would be walking into this.”

“Maybe you can help me,” Prabhupada suggested, and he explained the situation.

“Don’t worry,” Mr. Ganatra assured him.” I will take care of it.” And he took Mr. Mehta and his son into another room.

While Ganatra was speaking with Chhaganlal in the other room, Prabhupada spoke with Mrs. Nair. “How much are you willing to pay?” he asked.

“Well, we have to pay the 50,000 he gave us, plus we will give him another 25,000. That’s all. You have to pay the rest. If he has an extra claim, you have to pay.”

“Why should we pay?” Prabhupada questioned. “I am already paying you for the land. This is your problem with Chhaganlal.”

When Mr. Ganatra entered the room, everyone wanted to know how much the Mehtas were demanding.

“He wants four lakhs.” Mr. Ganatra said.

“Four lakhs? Oh, no, that’s impossible,” Mrs. Nair retorted. “We can’t pay that.”

“How much are you willing to pay?” Ganatra asked.

“We can pay 75,000.”

“He is asking four lakhs, and you want to pay 75,000? No, no. You have to do better than that. We have to settle this.”

Prabhupada appealed to Mrs. Nair to offer more, and she said, “All right, one lakh.” Then Mr. Ganatra returned to the Mehtas.

Meanwhile, Prabhupada was encouraging Mrs. Nair to pay more if necessary. The rest of us couldn’t wait to hear what Mr. Ganatra would say when he returned. Finally he came back in and told us, “I have persuaded him to come down to three lakhs twenty-five thousand, but that’s it. I don’t think he’s going to come down any lower. You will have to come up with a lot more than one lakh.”

I thought, Oh no, there's such a gulf, but Prabhupada appealed to Mrs. Nair to offer more.

“All right,” she said, “one lakh twenty-five thousand, but that’s all.” She was starting to get upset.

Mr. Ganatra went back to Chhaganlal. The situation was tense. I was feeling anxious—I didn’t know what Chhaganlal would demand next. It seemed that the negotiations could break down at any moment.

When Mr. Ganatra returned, he said that Chhaganlal would settle for two lakhs seventy-five thousand—either that or nothing. “Otherwise, he says he’ll go to court and either he’ll get six lakhs or he’ll get the land. So, he wants two lakhs seventy-five thousand and that’s it. Now what are you going to do?”

It was intense. Everyone was sweating and squirming. And Mr. Ganatra was coaxing, coaxing, coaxing. Srila Prabhupada conferred with Mrs. Nair. Finally she said, “All right, I will pay one lakh forty thousand, and that’s it.” And Prabhupada told Ganatra to offer two lakhs twenty-five thousand, hinting that he would cover the difference.

“I don’t know what he’ll say,” Ganatra told us, and he went back to Chhaganlal. Some minutes later, he returned with a big smile on his face. “They have agreed.”

The two Mehtas, father and son, followed Ganatra into the room. Everyone was relieved and elated; so much had hinged on this issue. Then I realized that Mr. Ganatra must have been exaggerating their claim and determination with Mrs. Nair, and exaggerating Mrs. Nair’s unwillingness when he met Chhaganlal. It had seemed like there was a huge gulf, but that was to get them to come down, because our offer was so low, and to get Mrs. Nair to come up, because their demand was so high—and eventually we had met in the middle. Chhaganlal came down from Rs. 400,000 to Rs. 225,000, Mrs. Nair came up from Rs. 75,000 to Rs. 140,000, and Prabhupada agreed to pay Chhaganlal the difference of Rs. 85,000.

Anyway, we were all relieved and elated—and amazed by Prabhupada’s expertise and kindness. It was only out of both Shantilal Mehta’s and Mrs. Nair’s deep respect and admiration for him that they were able to even come and sit together in the same room and talk.

With everyone still gathered, Prabhupada spoke about his mission and the philosophy of Krishna consciousness, and he asked me to lead the singing of the Nrsimha prayers. In the end, everyone was happy.

It was decided that there would be another meeting, that we—and Mrs. Nair—would pay Chhaganlal their money and that they would withdraw the suit. And neither side would tell the solicitors.

As a result of the negotiations, Mehta agreed to withdraw his suit from the High Court for a payment of Rs. 140,000 white from Mrs. Nair and Rs. 85,000 black from us. But the transaction was tricky, because if we paid Mehta first, he could keep the money and not withdraw the case, and if he withdrew the suit first, we could just keep the money, especially because nothing could be done legally to enforce a black transaction.

All the principal parties other than Mrs. Nair met in the office of our solicitor, Mr. Bhesania, at Mulla & Mulla. The basic plan was discussed, but there was a major hitch: who would hold the black money. As Tamal Krishna later described, “It was a gentleman’s agreement, but there weren’t any gentlemen anymore, so nobody trusted anyone else.”

With the whole plan threatened, the atmosphere in the office was tense. No one was ready to trust anyone else with the money. Then Prabhupada meekly, almost sheepishly, offered, “I can hold it.” And everyone immediately concurred, because they knew they could trust him.

The senior Mr. Mehta stayed with Prabhupada in the solicitor’s chamber, and the others went to the court to withdraw the claim. Then, when Mr. Mehta’s son and the others returned, he got his money.

Prabhupada later summarized the settlement: “Chhaganlal advanced fifty-one thousand, and when there was question of settlement, he came. He wanted that ‘If you give me three lakhs, then I’ll compromise.’ So that Mr. Ganatra, mayor— I induced him, ‘Just make settlement.’ Then Chhaganlal came down—two lakhs twenty-five thousand. Then I asked Mrs. Nair, ‘Now you’ll pay this ...’ ‘Where I have got... If he takes all money, then what shall I get?’ Then I had to settle with her how much she would pay. She came from one lakh to one lakh forty thousand. So what is the balance? Eighty-five. So I said, ‘Yes, I’ll pay it. Settle up. The balance I’ll pay, eighty-five thousand.’... That Chhaganlal, I paid him extra eighty-five thousand. That is also black. No more white. The black money was paid in this way, that the money was counted and it was put in a handbag, and it was locked by him. The key was with him, and thebag was with me. As soon as court accepted the agreement, then I handed over, ‘Take this bag.’”

At Mr. Sethi’s house, Prabhupada received an invitation from Yogiraj Shanti Swarup, a life member and spiritual activist, to be the guest of honor at the opening night of a series of lectures and discussions to be held at the Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan in Girgaum Chowpatty, South Bombay, on the subject of how the Bhagavad-gita could solve the world’s problems. Founded by Sri Kanaiyalal M. Munshi in 1938 under the patronage of Mahatma Gandhi, Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan was a leading “educational, cultural, and intellectual” institution for Indian culture.

After K.M. Munshi’s demise, his wife, Lilavati Munshi, who herself had been a prominent freedom fighter and was a politician, author, and welfare worker, became president. Mrs. Munshi was eager to meet Prabhupada, and she extended a personal invitation for him to join her for tea in the library of her quarters, also in the Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan building, just before the conference. Mindful of her having used her influence as the governor’s wife to push Prabhupada out of the premises housing his League of Devotees (a forerunner of ISKCON) when he was in Jhansi in 1955, so that she could use it for her Mahila Samity (Women’s Association), Prabhupada, Shyamasundar, Srutakirti, and I went to meet her.

Several other important people and conference presenters—sadhus, swamis, and political figures—were also there to meet Prabhupada, including Sri Gulzarilal Nanda, who had been minister of home affairs in the central government and acting prime minister after the deaths of Jawaharlal Nehru in 1964 and Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri in 1966. He was a celebrated personality in India, revered for his religiousness and promotion of Hindu principles and projects. But within this group of esteemed leaders, everyone accepted Prabhupada as the leader.

When Prabhupada was seated, everyone started praising him for the wonderful work he had done in spreading Indian culture throughout the world. Mrs. Munshi in particular was astonished by his success. “How did you do it?” she kept asking. “How did you get them to shave their heads? How did you get them to wear dhotis and kurtas and tilak? How did you get the girls to wear saris?”

Prabhupada explained that although there had been many editions of the Bhagavad-gita, it had not been presented “as it is” and there had not been any programs to train students to follow its principles. Although there were many branches and institutions of Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan—both within and outside India—and although they were disseminating books, there was no program for training young men and women to become followers of Vedic culture. Books were required, and also training. And he had given both.

Mrs. Munshi brought up a point that was on many people’s minds. “Quite often, when the founder of a mission is present,” she said, “the mission is very successful—it’s flourishing and prospering—but after the founder leaves, things deteriorate. So, what will be the future of your movement after you go?”

“The future of my mission is very bright,” Prabhupada replied, “as long as my disciples follow my instructions. Just like Gandhiji—he had so many programs, but after he left, his followers changed everything. He wanted village organization, he wanted the economy to be based on agriculture, and after he left, Nehru and others changed the whole program. They wanted to industrialize India and imitate the West. So, he had his program, but after he left, his so-called followers changed everything, and everything became spoiled. So, in the same way, if I leave and my followers change what I’ve given, what can I do?” By saying this, I realized, Prabhupada was challenging us, his followers, with the responsibility of remaining faithful to his instructions.

One bearded sadhu said that he had been holding meetings throughout Bombay and teaching people to cure their diseases by chanting God’s names. Thousands of people were attending, and many were getting cured. He suggested that there could be some cooperation between himself and Prabhupada—that together they could hold massive meetings for chanting Hare Krishna, whereby many more people would benefit. “I am gathering people together, and you are gathering people,” he said. “I am getting people to chant God’s name, and you are getting people to chant. We should cooperate.”“No,” Prabhupada replied. “This is against our principles. The name of God is God Himself, and we are God’s servants. We do not use the holy name of God for our sense gratification or material purposes. We chant the holy name without any personalambition, simply to glorify and serve the holy name. So, we cannot participate in any such program.”

Then Mrs. Munshi disclosed another, special purpose of her hosting Prabhupada: she wanted to sell him Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan’s printing press, the Associated Press. It was a big press that had been one of the best in India, printing religious books and phone directories and handling many government contracts, but it was a letterpress operation, and the publishing field had turned to photo-offset, which produced a higher-quality and less expensive product. In fact, Associated Press had lost their government contracts, their primary means of support, and was in financial trouble.

Prabhupada listened to the proposal and asked some questions, but he was already dealing with Dai Nippon, who had the best, most advanced facility, and wasn’t interested in the outdated machinery. “Actually, to purchase your press is no difficulty,” he said. “Money, I have no problem. However, your press has no utility.”

Mrs. Munshi was disappointed. But there was nothing she could do to convince him, and it was time for the conference to begin in the auditorium. Prabhupada actually wanted to return to Juhu to work on the land matter, but everyone insisted that he address the audience. They had even wanted him to lead the entire three-day conference, because his age, wisdom, stature, and accomplishments elevated him beyond the other participants. “Swamiji, Swamiji,” one of them implored, speaking for everyone, “only you can lead us. You are the real leader; you are the only one who can solve our problems.”

“That’s a fact,” Prabhupada replied, “but are you prepared to follow?” And that was really the issue.

Still, the group wouldn’t take no for an answer. Yogiraj Shanti Swarup threw himself at Prabhupada’s feet and begged him to come, saying that the audience would be packed with leading Bombay people and that the press and many important officials would be there. Finally Prabhupada agreed and we all went down to the auditorium.

Baradraj led a kirtan to begin, and then Prabhupada spoke. Indirectly answering Mrs. Munshi’s question about how he had accomplished so much with his disciples, he explained the dharma of the living entity: service to God. “Is there anybody who can say boldly, ‘I do not serveanyone?’” he asked. “Whether you become a Christian or a Muslim or a Hindu or this or that, your real characteristic is that you have to serve. That service attitude, when it is misunderstood, is applied to maya, and we are not happy. When it is applied to Krishna, then we are happy. You must render service. That is your position. You cannot become master.

“For what does Krishna come? Does he come to establish Hindu dharma, Muslim dharma, or Christian dharma? If Krishna is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, why He should be interested in particular type of dharma—Hindu dharma, Christian dharma, or Muslim dharma? No. Therefore after giving instruction throughout the whole Bhagavad-gita, at last Krishna says, ‘The most confidential part of My instruction, Arjuna’—sarva-guhyatamam—‘is this: sarva-dharman parityajya mam ekam saranam vraja' This is dharma.

“If you are not a surrendered soul to Krishna, or God, your dharma has no meaning; it is useless. The definition of dharma is given by Krishna at the last stage of His instruction in the Bhagavad-gita: sarva-dharman parityajya mam ekam saranam vraja, Prahlada Maharaja said, kaumaram acaret prajno dharman bhagavatan iha. Kaumara, from the very beginning of childhood, one should be taught about dharma, especially bhagavata-dharma, the relationship with God....

“And actually it is happening all over the world. Since we have presented this dharma, to serve Krishna, it is working very wonderfully. We have got branches all over the world. Some of the samples you see—those who are chanting Hare Krishna mantra, these Europeans, Americans, Canadians. We have even got a branch in Iran. Mohammedans, Christians, Africans—everyone is taking to this dharma, this Krishna consciousness movement.”

“Take the standard method as prescribed in the Bhagavad-gita," Prabhupada concluded. “Then you will be successful. . . . The example is already there. I am preaching all over the world Bhagavad-gita as it is. There is no fashionable interpretation. No—as it is. And how it is being accepted. So why not in this country? In this country Krishna consciousness is natural. Artificially it is being cut down: ‘Forget Krishna.’ This nonsense dharma should be stopped. Take Krishna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. He is being accepted all over the world. Why not in India? Why do you present competitors of Krishna? Don’t do this.

Take this instruction of Bhagavad-glta, that sarva-dharman parityajya mam ekam saranam vraja. You will be successful. . . . The standard is there, the instruction is there, everything is there. Why should we try to manufacture something new?

“Is there anybody in this world even now better than Krishna, who can give good instruction more beneficial than Krishna? No, there is not. So take this principle, Bhagavad-gita as it is, the instruction of Gita, instruction of Krishna, and try to follow. It will be successful not only in India, but all over the world. That is my practical experience.”

Cameras flashed, and Prabhupada was covered with garlands. The sadhus, swamis, and political leaders all deferred to him with honor and respect. Still, for Prabhupada, working on the Juhu project was even more important than addressing the prestigious assembly, and I felt that my service was being validated.

On the way out from the program, Prabhupada stood at the top of the stairs at the entrance of the building and surveyed the neighborhood. “This is one of the best places in Bombay,” he said. “One day we should have a temple here.”

After his meeting with Mrs. Nair, Prabhupada had worked intensely to deal with pending litigations and get other claimants to withdraw their claims. He shifted from Mr. Sethi’s house to Kiran Kutir, the weekend cottage of one of Bombay’s most prominent industrialists, Sri Chandrakant Khatau. It was a simple single-story structure near the beach, just two blocks from Hare Krishna Land, near Sumati Morarji’s bungalow, with four rooms and a large central hall, enclosed within low brick walls and chatai that extended up to the thatched roof.

On October 14 he wrote to Bali Mardan, “After a great struggle for existence, it appears that I have won over Mrs. Nair. The negotiation started on my arrival and the mediators suggested 20 lakhs. Then it went down to 17 lakhs, but by Krishna’s grace I have settled with her for 14 lakhs 50 thousand and about 1 lakh for compensation to the other claimants.... The charges of the several litigations have all been withdrawn and the preparations for the conveyance are in progress.”

Prabhupada was eager to receive funds from New York, but they had been dispatched by mail order. The date had been fixed for the 19th, and he was getting anxious. Finally, after several phone calls and telegrams, we received a telex from the bank that the money was on the way, and when it arrived, Prabhupada went to the bank with Tamal Krishna to make further withdrawals from fixed deposits and other accounts. On the 18th he wrote to Kirtanananda, “Our Bombay affairs are almost settled ... The conveyance deed is prepared, and it will be signed within one or two days.”

Normally, conveyances had to be signed in the presence of the registrar at his office in the city, but Mr. Asnani had arranged for the registrar to come to Juhu after hours, and the following day, the 19th, was set for executing the contract.

Mrs. Nair had invited her friends, and we had invited ours, and everyone in the area who had helped with the land gathered at Kiran Kutir to witness the momentous occasion. At six-thirty we all crowded into Prabhupada’s room—the registrar, Mrs. Nair and her lawyers, Mr. Asnani and Mrs. Warrier, Mr. and Mrs. Sethi, friends from both sides, and a number of devotees: Tamal Krishna, Shyamasundar, Gurudas, Harikesa, Srutakirti, myself, and a few others. Prabhupada sat on his asana behind his table, centered between two windows, with the rest of us seated on the floor, Mrs. Nair to Prabhupada’s right. The room was packed.

Prabhupada was ready with a check for the full amount and again assured Mrs. Nair, “Don’t worry, you can stay in any of my centers; we will take care of you. Now you just devote the rest of your life to Krishna, chanting Hare Krishna and serving Krishna. Everything will be all right.”

“I really didn’t go along with my husband,” she told him. “I didn’t want him to do that.”

He patted her on the back and repeated, “Don’t worry. You are like my daughter. Never mind. If a man is going on the wrong path in the morning and comes back on the right path in the evening, it’s all right. Now you are on the right path.”

He looked grave as the registrar prepared the papers for signing. It was as if everyone was holding their collective breath. A historic event was taking place, like the signing of a treaty between two great world powers. The room was hushed—silent save for the rustling of papers and the scratching of the pen.

Prabhupada signed the conveyance and presented a check for the outstanding funds to Mrs. Nair. She was full of emotion, weeping as she read, but she pulled out her pen and added her signature, transferring the land to “His Divine Grace A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, founder-acharya of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness,” and the document was handed over to the registrar. The land was legally ours.

The whole process had taken maybe twenty minutes. But it was the fulfillment of years of struggle—of dreams, desires, and hard work. And now it had happened. There were no losers; everyone had won.

Prabhupada spoke about the temple project, visualizing it for those gathered. It would be made all of marble, he described. “How could that be?” somebody asked, but he confirmed that it could be done. The temple would be a major landmark, like one of the Seven Wonders of the World, and people would come from around the globe to visit. “Prabhupada explained the whole project as if he saw it in his mind’s eye,” Mrs. Warrier later remembered, “and he said that after it was constructed it would be more than what we could visualize. It would be fantastic!”

“All right,” Prabhupada announced, not missing a step, “now we will begin the building fund.... Your help is important. I want all of you to help whatever way you can, bodily or whatever.”

Mrs. Sethi was wearing some gold bangles, and she took them right off and gave them to him. “This,” she offered, “is to begin.” Prabhupada said that he was pleased that the fund had started with gold, which is pure—rather than paper currency.

Prabhupada asked that the news be conveyed to the press, and then invited everyone out to the hall for a grand feast. The guests were seated on two long rows of mats and served on leaf plates. “Now let us start,” he proclaimed. At first he stood, supervising the devotees serving all the prasada—pulao (pilaf); potato, cabbage, cauliflower, and eggplantpakords; dal; poppers; two or three sabjis, including potato, mixed vegetable, and cauliflower; tomato chutney; and the sweets: vermicelli kheer (pudding); burfi; laddus; chumchum; and halavah—all cooked in ghee—with lime juice for a drink. Then he sat with everyone and ate. The mood was happy and festive. Afterward, there were fireworks, and then people began to filter out.

When all the guests had left, Prabhupada, leaning back on his asana in his room, put his feet up, laughed, and said, “It was a good fight? He was beaming. Then he added, “Someone should write a book about it.”

I walked back to the land with some of our local supporters. We had never been so happy. It was a great victory.

“It was like a wrestling match,” Tamal Krishna later described, “like Vishnu having dealt with Kamsa and Canura and Mustika—as if Prabhupada had really enjoyed the whole thing. It had been a great opportunity to utilize so much service for Krishna. . . . There is no single thing that we saw in the history of ISKCON that ever absorbed his energy and attention as much as getting this Hare Krishna Land.”

The next day, Prabhupada wrote to Atreya Rishi, “You will be pleased to know that here in Bombay we have now secured the Juhu land from Mrs. Nair. It is a great relief that after such a long struggle, we can now do something very wonderful for Krishna. This land has very good potential, so now let us utilize it in Krishna’s service.”

Later, in a talk in Calcutta, Prabhupada reflected on how Krishna had helped: “Sakhyam, to make Krishna your friend. Krishna can be served in so many ways. Krishna is such a kind friend, even practically. We had a very big struggle in Bombay for our land. They wanted to break our temple to drive us away. It was a great commotion. All Bombay people know it. But I simply prayed to Krishna, ‘My dear Krishna, anyway, You have come here. You have sat down here. It will be great insult if You are removed from this place.’ So, Krishna heard it, and we won the battle. Now the land is ours. The land is ours. It was a great battle. Krishna is so kind.”

## Chapter two

Facing Challenges

OCTOBER 1973 - JANUARY 1977

## Removing Obstacles

THE MORNING AFTER THE SIGNING OF the conveyance, Prabhupada was already proposing beginning construction, but for that, he said, we needed a crore of rupees.

We were sitting with Dr. Patel, who ventured, “You should bring the money from America.”

Prabhupada was disturbed by the suggestion. “I could bring the money from America,” he replied, “but then what will be your credit?” He said that Bombay was such a place that if people were willing, we could collect a crore in one day.

“True, but people are not willing,” Dr. Patel insisted. “Of course, I don’t want to discourage you, but—”

“But you are discouraging me,” Prabhupada interjected.

Then Dr. Patel asked which way the Deities would face, and Prabhupada said that They would face as They currently were.

“No, sir,” Dr. Patel responded. “I don’t agree. According to scripture, that is not the right direction. According to scripture, the murtis should face east.”

Prabhupada knew that given the shape of the land available for construction, the Deities could not face in that direction, toward the tenement buildings at the back—it just wasn’t practical. “Our God is everywhere,” he explained. “Ito nrsimhah parato nrsimho yato yato yami tato nrsimhah"—“Lord Nrsimha is here and also there. Wherever I go, Lord Nrsimha is there.” We were going to have the Deities face the direction most convenient and favorable for our purposes—for preaching.

As the acharya and the empowered representative of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and the disciplic succession, Prabhupada could understand what Krishna wanted and what was more important and less important. He was concerned not with minor details but with overriding principles.

Although the conveyance had been executed, other encumbrances remained. Mr. Nair had been engaged in rancorous disputes with many parties, one of whom still had a claim on the land. And there were still people living there. Prabhupada had to settle up with all the different parties, and he conducted the negotiations himself.

One of those whom Nair had cheated, Mr. Ratnaparkhi, owned a two-story cottage on the front south corner of the property, which was occupied by his sister, her husband, and their two children. His grandmother had made an agreement with Nair to sell him the structure and the land attached to it, and Nair had agreed to pay for the land and the cottage, plus build the family another house in Juhu. But when he paid the money and the land was transferred to his name, he never built the other house. And so the family never vacated the premises.

Mr. Ratnaparkhi himself lived in a two-room shack nearby, with a small garden overgrown by weeds. He was quite a character—a powerful body builder who could be aggressive, even violent—and he spoke in a loud, rough voice. He was charitable but also quite proud. He would donate blood and always got the award for donating the most. With each award, his picture would be published in the newspaper, and he would display the clippings in his home.

The cottage on the land was located right where we were going to build the temple, and Ratnaparkhi knew it. “We’re not leaving,” he told us. “And I am not going to let you get any of your plans passed unless you make arrangements for my family members to live somewhere.”

I had written to Prabhupada previously, when Mr. Nair had still been alive, “The plans we submitted to the municipality cannot be accepted immediately as they are because Mr. Ratnaparkhi who lives down the street claims that the front south corner of Nairwadi belongs to him and his relatives are living in that house, and he submitted a letter to the municipality that our proposed building will be too close. . . . Nair says that we can ... have the police evict the tenants. But \[he\] has been trying to evict them for four years and still has not succeeded. \[Our friend\] Vijay says that even if we establish that the land does not belong to them, we still have to either find suitable alternative accommodations or pay them enough that they agree to leave, and Mr. Diwanji and all others agree. So Mrs. Morarji says we should pay whatever necessary to get them out.”

We invited Mr. Ratnaparkhi to come speak with Prabhupada to settle the problem, but he refused. “No,” he said. “I want him to come to my house.”

“He can come,” we replied. “There is no difficulty. But it would be better if you came to see him.”

“No!” he objected. “Guru Maharaja must come here.” And not only did he require that Srila Prabhupada come to him, but he insisted that His Divine Grace first make an appointment. “If he has to talk to me about the land,” Mr. Ratnaparkhi said, “he must come to my place. You see, if he does not come to my place, it’s not that I will hate him, but I will not talk anything about the land or land price or land dealings unless Prabhupada comes to my place, that too with appointment.”

When we told Prabhupada what Mr. Ratnaparkhi had said, he said, “Yes, I will go.” And we arranged the visit.

Mr. Ratnaparkhi’s shanty was cramped, barely a shed, with hardly any furniture—just a bed and a couple of broken-down chairs, with two big clubs hanging on the wall, for him to lift as weights. But he arranged the chairs and cleaned the floor, and he was happy that a great saint was coming to visit. He was in the mode of ignorance, under the influence of tamo-guna, but he was also a sort of devotee, or Hindu, attracted to serving Prabhupada and his followers. It was a strange combination.

“This man was a bit unusual,” Tamal Krishna later remembered. “He had a little daughter who was about five. And the first thing he said was, ‘My mother recently died, five years ago, and my daughter is my mother incarnated.’ So we could tell that there was something unusual about the man.”

Prabhupada sat in one of the chairs and said, “I came here to talk to you about vacating the property. How much do you want?”

Mr. Ratnaparkhi started talking about how costly housing was in Bombay and how he had to get a place for his family members. He kept going on and on. But no matter how many times Prabhupada asked how much he wanted, he wouldn’t say. “How much will you give?” he asked.

“How much do you want?” Prabhupada countered.

“No, how much will you give?”

And again Prabhupada repeated, “No, how much do you want?”

The situation got pretty tense. Mr. Ratnaparkhi was upset; perhaps he thought Prabhupada was being too blunt. He became angry with Prabhupada, almost offensive, raising his voice. The rest of us were watching anxiously. The man was volatile and dangerous; there was no telling what he would do, and we were afraid he might become violent.

But Prabhupada didn’t flinch. “I am leaving,” he declared, and stood up to walk out.

Mr. Ratnaparkhi leaped up—and we were about to spring forward— but it was only to beg Prabhupada to stay. “No, Swamiji,” he pleaded, “you can’t leave like this.”

“No,” Prabhupada said, “I am leaving. You tell me right now how much you want or I am leaving.”

“Okay, okay,” Ratnaparkhi accepted. “Please sit down—don’t leave.”

“I came here to discuss how you will vacate that house,” Prabhupada insisted. “I just want to know how much you want to get out. Tell me your price. I want you out of the house.”

“He was so heavy,” Tamal Krishna recalled, “that the man just looked at him and said, ‘Thirty thousand.’”

It was an outrageous amount, way more than the cottage and the land were worth, but Prabhupada replied without hesitation: “All right. Accepted. We will give you thirty thousand, and you get out of there. You make the papers and I will sign.” Then he stood up, took his cane, and walked out.

On the way back to Kitan Kutir, Prabhupada commented, “Whenever I really wanted something, I always got it. I didn’t care how much I had to spend, but I always got what I wanted. If you want something bad enough, you can pay any price for it. That house is not worth anything, but he has to get out.”

Then there was a lot of going back and forth. “Tamal would run from the Ratnaparkhi house to the Chand Society office and tell me what to type,” Harikesa recalled, “and then I had to type up the agreement, and then he would run back with the agreement, and then Mr. Ratnaparkhi would reject it and want another thing, and then Tamal would have to come back and I would have to type up another agreement.”

Mr. Ratnaparkhi’s final condition, out of sentiment for his mother and as a matter of pride, was that Prabhupada should carry a large photograph of his mother from the cottage to the family’s new housing, accompanied by kirtan and bhajans. So later that day, we had kirtan and bhajans in the cottage for ten or fifteen minutes, and then Prabhupada handed the photo to Tamal Krishna, and Tamal Krishna, followed by fifty or sixty devotees and local people, led a procession through Juhu to the new place.

“The idea was that all the people should know that we have come honorably,” Mr. Ratnaparkhi later said, “not that we have been thrownout. That people should not think, ‘Oh, the Hare Krishna people have thrown them out? No. We have left with honor; we have come out with honor. And when people saw Prabhupada and Tamal Krishna carrying the photograph, they were all impressed.” It was crucial to Mr. Ratnaparkhi that he be able to maintain his dignity, his pride.

And Prabhupada was willing to do the needful to achieve his goals. He accomplished things quickly, and this was no exception. Mr. Ratnaparkhi had been disputing with Nair for years, but within a matter of hours all the papers were signed, the formalities were completed, and Mr. Ratnaparkhi’s people had moved out.

We—the devotees—had only our chatai hut to live in, so Prabhupada said that we should move into Mr. Ratnaparkhi’s cottage, not only because we needed space, but also because he wanted to secure possession. We should clean it up and move in immediately.

It was such a rotten dirty old place, however, that nobody wanted to live there.

The next day, Prabhupada asked, “Have the devotees moved in?” We hadn’t. And again, the following morning, he asked, “Have our devotees moved in?” And again, we hadn’t. Then he announced, “At twelve o’clock I am moving in, so have it ready. I want to live on our own land.”

“What?” we exclaimed, aghast. Prabhupada was going to come and live in Ratnaparkhi’s shack? “Oh, no!” And, of course, we all got right to work and started cleaning up.

By noon, everything was in the best shape it could be. And Prabhupada said, “All right, now you move in.”

The next day, Prabhupada left Juhu for Vrindavan and Delhi, where he spoke about the value of endeavoring to build a temple:

“In England the castles are there—very old castles, a thousand years, two thousand. Even this Westminster Abbey and palace. But which king has lived there permanently? And now, if the king has, by his work, become something else ... Not necessarily he’ll become a king in that house. He may become a dog there. This science they do not know. And they are proud of their education, culture. Suppose you have constructed this Vrindavan temple or Bombay temple. It is also certain that we shall not live, but our attempt to construct that temple will berecorded by Krishna. . . . ‘Because he has spent his energy for My service? That will be our gain.... That will not go in vain.”

Two months later, in Los Angeles, he spoke about his settling with Ratnaparkhi: “This Ratnaparkhi first of all proposed twenty thousand to sell that house. Then when I went there, he knew that I was settling at any cost. He said, ‘That twenty thousand was proposed formerly. Now things have gone very high; I cannot sell?” So, he knew that we were eager to purchase. Then I said, ‘Then what do you want to do?’ ‘Now I want thirty thousand? ‘All right, yes. Take it? I did not argue. In this way, I settled up. And our Giriraj’s father appreciated that ‘It is better a bad settlement than prolong the case? So, I took this policy.”

At Shivner I had been suffering from jaundice. With care and patience, I had been able to overcome my condition, but within two weeks, after Prabhupada had shifted from Bhogilal Patel’s mansion to Mr. Sethi’s place in the Juhu Scheme, I’d had a relapse, and no matter what I did, I had not been able to recover. Eventually Prabhupada had said that I would not get better as long as I stayed in Bombay. So I had gone about getting the required stamps in my passport to leave the country and, still quite ill, undertaken the flight from Bombay to Chicago. My parents had received me at the airport and taken me to their home, where I had lived from the age of eight until I’d left for college.

A day or two after I arrived, an old family friend who was a psychologist paid us a visit. She came in my room and inquired, “Tell me, Glenn, did you feel that your parents didn’t love you?”

“Which parents?” I asked. “I have passed so many lifetimes, and in every lifetime I have had different parents.” Whatever questions she asked, I answered with Krishna conscious philosophy.

After some time, she left my room, and I could overhear her speaking with my parents. “I am sorry,” she told them. “I did whatever I could, but I don’t think I can help him.” My parents, I suddenly realized, had sent her to “cure” me.

I began to feel uncomfortable at home, so I went to the Chicago temple, in Evanston, and then to Los Angeles to recuperate at the temple there. Prabhupada arrived from India soon thereafter, on November 30. When he asked about my health and my stay in Chicago, I told him howthe psychologist had come to cure me. “You have been infected permanently,” he said. “You can never be cured.”

As I became well enough, I began to accompany Prabhupada on his morning walks. On one, I asked, “We say that Krishna is the original cause of all causes, but some people question, ‘Then who is the cause of Krishna?’ How do we answer them?”

“According to our information, Krishna is the first cause,” Prabhupada replied. “If you do research and find someone who is the cause of Krishna, we will worship him. But until then, you should worship Krishna.”

In his talks in LA, Prabhupada often smashed mundane, godless scientists, and he inspired his devotee scientist Svarupa Damodara dasa (Dr. Thoudam Singh, an organic chemist) to form the Bhaktivedanta Institute to preach the principles of the Bhagavad-gita in scientific language and establish Krishna as the origin of everything, both matter and spirit. I also became inspired by the idea of scientific preaching, and although I was not qualified like Svarupa Damodara, I wanted to participate.

One day I approached Prabhupada in his room during his massage and told him that I was interested in joining in the scientific preaching. He simply smiled and said, “Your field is psychology.” (He knew that I had been a psychology major.) Still, he said I could apply that knowledge in the work of the Bhaktivedanta Institute.

I said that I had noticed that when he spoke about scientists, he used words such as nonsense, rascals, bluffers, and cheaters and often said that we should “kick them in the face with boots.” So, I asked whether we should use such language when we preached to or met with scientists.

“No,” he replied. “You should speak like a gentleman.”

While I was in LA, the latest issue of BTG arrived, with an article by Vishnujana. He had just returned to America after spending months sailing down the Ganges, chanting the holy names and stopping at towns and villages along her banks to chant, distribute prasada, and preach Krishna consciousness. Srila Prabhupada appreciated the article, entitled, “Some Day the Tiny Soul Will Want to Get Out of Illusion,”and commented, “Because Vishnujana has done so much chanting, he has been able to write so nicely.”

It was said of the Six Gosvamis, dhiradhira-jana-priyau priya-karau nirmatsarau pujitau: they were popular both with the gentle and with the ruffians—because they were not envious of anyone; whatever they did, they were all-pleasing to everyone.

Srila Prabhupada demonstrated the same qualities. He reciprocated with scientists, preachers, managers, and book distributors—even my parents—so perfectly that they all were pleased and satisfied. He was gracious with everyone.

A few weeks after I left Chicago, my parents flew out to see me in LA, and they came along on a morning walk in Cheviot Hills Park. My mother was very pleased when Prabhupada greeted her, “Oh, Mrs. Teton, you look so young!”

At the end of the walk we came to the parking lot, and my father began to eye the Rolls Royce the devotees had arranged for Prabhupada. Humbly, almost diffidently, Prabhupada told him, “My disciples got this for me.”

“Oh, no, you deserve it,” my father responded.

“You can come and ride with me,” Prabhupada invited him.

“No, no, we have our own car,” my father said.

After we left, I later heard, Prabhupada’s servant said to him, “Srila Prabhupada, everyone likes you so much.” And Prabhupada replied, “Yes, because I like everyone.”

My return to America after three years away was such a major event for my family that even my uncle, my father’s brother, came out to LA from Chicago, and I arranged for him to meet Prabhupada in his quarters. My uncle was a doctor with high ideals, and he opened his heart to Prabhupada about how disillusioned and disappointed he was with the state of the medical profession. He felt that doctors had become too materialistic and were more interested in money than in the welfare of their patients. As he went on expressing his chagrin, Prabhupada simply listened intently. In the entire half hour of the conversation, Prabhupada didn’t say more than a few sentences; he just listened withgreat sympathy, or empathy. And at the end, as we were leaving the room, my uncle turned to me and said, “My God! Eve never met anyone like him. I must get a picture of him. I have never seen a face like his.”

One afternoon, after dealing with various managerial problems, Prabhupada leaned back on the bolsters of his asana and quoted a verse from Narottama dasa Thakura: visaya chadiya kabe suddha ha 'be mana, kabe hama herabo sri vrndavana—“When will I give up material sense objects? When will my mind become purified? When will I be able to behold Vrindavan?” He said, “Of course, it is not visaya, material; it is Krishna’s service. But still, I wish to be freed. I am hankering for Vrindavan.”

Eventually, responding to appeals from India for me to return, Prabhupada encouraged me to go “back home, back to Bombay.” I got the impression that he was telling me that if I went back and served him in Bombay, I would go back to Godhead. And when I was well enough, I returned.

In Bombay my work was now facilitated by Aditya dasi—a former assistant to a bank vice-president in the US—whom, in my absence, Tamal Krishna had arranged to be my secretary. I wrote Srila Prabhupada, “I am back in Bombay now and am very glad to be actively engaged in your loving service. Regarding the various points which you entrusted to me before I left Los Angeles, I wish to reply as follows.

“Regarding the Municipal sanction, we are still waiting for the No Objection Certificate \[NOC\] from the police. According to Tamal Krishna Goswami, as soon as we get the No Objection Certificate we will be able to get the final approval from the Municipal Corporation. I shall be personally looking into the matter and trying to get it as soon as possible.”

Meanwhile, after the conveyance was signed and we became the legal owners of the property, one of the tenants vacated his flat in the D Block, and Prabhupada finally had a proper place to stay on Hare Krishna Land. Tamal Krishna wrote him, “One tenant at Hare Krishna Land has approached us and desired to move out of the Hare Krishna Land. He is willing to move out of his flat if we pay him . . . This flatwe are going to keep for Your Divine Grace to stay in when you come to Bombay, and we are herewith presenting and offering to you our formal and humble invitation to come to Hare Krishna Land as soon as you can. You will have a nice accommodation right at the temple in this new flat, which we will decorate and paint and clean very nicely.... We are planning to purchase the flat on the 10th of this month, and as soon as we get the flat, I will telegram you. Similarly, if your Divine Grace would bless us with a telegram of your expected date of arrival, that would be very kind and merciful.”

Prabhupada replied, “I am very engladdened to hear you have secured one flat on our Hare Krishna Land. I am planning to arrive in India on or before February 1... Then I can go to Bombay, say about the second week in February, and together we can go to Mayapur in March. Now by your arrangement it will be very pleasing for me to stay in our own land at Juhu. In the past I was a guest while staying in Bombay, but now we have our own place, and this is very engladdening to me. So I will come.”

He arrived on February 16. We had painted his flat, which was on the second (top) floor, and did the best we could to fix it up. It was quite small, less than six hundred square feet, and comprised a small darshan room, a small kitchen, and an even smaller bedroom, with two balconies. Now, however, in Prabhupada’s presence, it seemed like a huge, opulent flat—indeed, it seemed like Vaikuntha.

With its open verandas and gray stone, the flat was always pleasantly cool. Prabhupada liked to sit on one of the balconies and take his massage in the sun. Surveying the Juhu property, with its many tall coconut trees, their long palm leaves rustling pleasantly in the breeze, he said that Hare Krishna Land was a paradise.

“One of the salient features of the apartment,” remembered Dinatarini, who helped fund its transferal, “was a large open terrace on top. Srila Prabhupada would go up there and sometimes cut karelas and dry them on the roof in the sun. Palika and I had an idea to make him a wonderful asana up there, and we arranged to have big white pillows and a big white seat made for him and put them in front of a neem tree on the roof. Srila Prabhupada would go up there every evening, and he loved to sit on that asana in many different poses. Sometimes hewould sit horizontally with his legs over one pillow and his head over another, sometimes he would sit cross-legged, and sometimes he would sit with his knees drawn up. And it appeared to me at that time that he was extremely robust in health and jolly in his mood. Things were progressing nicely in Bombay at that time. He would sit up there, and whoever came was destined to see the most wonderful features of Srila Prabhupada’s personality, his character, his nature, his eloquence, his gracefulness, his aristocratic bearing. So many aspects of him were in full display.”

Mr. Ratnaparkhi’s cottage, Hanuman Kutir, accommodated some of the devotees—women and householders. It had three rooms downstairs and a wooden stairway with a shaky railing leading up. The second floor had two rooms, both quite small, without proper windows—only bars and shutters. It was like a giant birdhouse, with birds flying in and out. And the third story was an attic, with a base of wooden planks with so much space between them that you could see through to the floor beneath.

When Prabhupada returned to Juhu, he wanted to see the cottage. As Jagat Purusa later remembered, “After Deity greeting, guru-puja, and Srimad-Bhagavatam class, Prabhupada got off his vyasasana and came to the edge of the darshan mandapa, the temple hall, and gazed across the land toward Ratnaparkhi’s house. I was in a position where I could see Srila Prabhupada’s gaze, and I was astonished to see the look in his eyes: he seemed to be looking not just across Hare Krishna Land but across the entire world. He was incredibly grave and deep—it was awesome. Then Prabhupada said, ‘I want to see the house.’”

The devotees accompanied Prabhupada from the temple into the house, which had been freshly painted inside and fixed up with electricity and other basics. Prabhupada inspected the premises. Climbing up the stairs, he shook a loose railing and told the devotees, “This has to be fixed.” At the locked door to one of the rooms upstairs, he asked, “Who is staying here?” A devotee replied that it was Jagat Purusa and Gandiva’s room, and Prabhupada said that he would like to look inside. Jagat Purusa opened the door, and Prabhupada walked in. Everything was neat and tidy, and Prabhupada looked approvingly.

“I really like this room,” Jagat Purusa said. “It reminds me of Vrindavan, and it is very airy and bright and sunny.”

Prabhupada looked at Gandiva and asked her, “Are you happy?”

“Yes, Srila Prabhupada,” she replied.

Then he asked to see another room: Aditya’s. She had thought it was clean, but birds had gotten in and made a mess. Prabhupada surveyed it and asked, “Who lives here?”

Oh my, we are supposed to be clean, Aditya thought. But Prabhupada just said that the light bulb should be replaced.

Next Prabhupada approached the stairs leading up to the attic, which were just as rickety as the others. As he was about to climb up, Tamal Krishna said, “No, Srila Prabhupada, those stairs are too shaky; it’s not safe. Please don’t go up there.” But Prabhupada did not heed his warning; he walked right past him and the other devotees and started up the stairs.

At the top was a storage area filled with Srimad-Bhagavatams that had been ruined by being kept in a damp place and were infested with worms. Seeing the books, Prabhupada became livid. “How did this happen?” he demanded. “Who allowed this to happen?” He quickly descended the stairs, and, as devotees moved aside to make way for him, stormed out of the cottage. Years later, Jagat Purusa could still remember the trembling of Prabhupada’s lips— “The intensity of his fury was indescribable.”

Prabhupada strode from the cottage toward the back of the property, in the direction of the chatai hut. On the way, the devotees were silent, devastated that their spiritual master was upset and feeling helpless to do anything about it.

As he approached the front of the hut, Prabhupada saw the cornerstone that he had personally laid two years earlier lying on the ground near the entrance, broken in two pieces. Again he asked, “What is this?”

“Srila Prabhupada’s anger was terrifying,” Jagat Purusa recalled. “It was so intense that one would expect a cloud of anger to remain in the air for the entire day, if not days or weeks.”

The devotees were crestfallen—ashamed and dejected—but Prabhupada’s anger did not last long. “When I went to the roof to havedarshan that afternoon,” Jagat Purusa said, “I was wondering if he would still be exhibiting his anger and continue to chastise the devotees for our carelessness. On the contrary, though, I found him in a very jovial mood, conversing with guests and disciples and never mentioning the books or the broken cornerstone.

“I was thinking that Prabhupada’s Krishna consciousness was so deep that nothing—absolutely nothing—could disturb his devotional service, especially the service of giving Krishna to others. It was amazing to witness his sudden and complete change of mood. The anger he showed was for us; he never carried it with him. It was instructive anger—he had no anger in him other than anger and anxiousness for seeing that Krishna and his spiritual master were served nicely.”

Prabhupada left for Calcutta and Mayapur toward the end of February, and on March 11 he proceeded to Vrindavan, accompanied by devotees who had been in Mayapur for the Mayapur-Vrindavan Festival. Meanwhile, I was pursuing the No Objection Certificate with the police.

While Prabhupada had been conducting the festival, our architect had received a notice from the commissioner of police, dated March 6, denying the No Objection Certificate on the grounds that “the construction of a temple may lead to more traffic congestion” and that “bhajan singing, which had been complained about in the past, is likely to be a nuisance in the future as well” (See Appendix A).

Prabhupada was furious that the police commissioner had called the kirtan a nuisance, and he talked about it every day—on morning walks, in his room, even in class. In a lecture on the 16th, he expressed his chagrin and offered a philosophical perspective: “Those who are impious, sinful, they cannot approach Krishna. Na mam duskrtino mudhah prapadyante naradhamah. Those who are naradhamah, the lowest of mankind, are always engaged in sinful activities, and rascals may be very educated—mayaya apahrta-jnanah—but their educational value has been taken away by maya. Just like nowadays it has become that the more one is educated, the more one is atheist. We have received one report just now, from Bombay, that Hare Krishna singing is a ‘nuisance.’ You see how degraded the human being has become: ‘Hare Krishna singing is a nuisance, and cinema singing is very good.’ Just see. They have become simply rascals—dogs and hogs.”

The next day, he announced his decision to return to Bombay with an assembly of disciples to protest the police commissioners statement. He wanted all the devotees who had come to India for the festival to converge on Bombay and hold massive protests. “This program should be started immediately,” he said. “And so the whole day and night this nuisance will go on.”

When a friend, Mr. Gupta, suggested how we should assemble the protest, Prabhupada responded, “So, do it. Don’t speak; now organize. Now there is no question of speaking. Practical. Everyone should take a leading part, and the sankirtana nuisance should be started from Bombay. So, Balavanta Prabhu, you are taking?”

“Yes,” Balavanta replied.

“Yes,” Prabhupada affirmed. “Take selected assistants, many sannyasis, and do it. You take the leaders. We shall pollute the whole world with this nuisance. The police commissioner has remarked, ‘This bhajan is nuisance.’ So we have to agitate. There are so many Vaishnavas. Bhajan is nuisance, eh?”

“It’s my life,” an Indian lady said.

“There must be some big agitation to drive away this man,” Prabhupada continued. “The demand should be that ‘this man should be immediately removed. He has focused a sarcastic remark on a very pure religious system.’ This movement should be started. He must be removed immediately.”

“We can hold protest marches downtown,” Balavanta suggested.

“Yes, yes.”

“All the Vaishnavas will come with us.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada said. “You have to organize all the Vaishnavas. In the Bhagavad-gita it is said, satatam kirtayanto mam: one has to chant ‘Krishna’ always. Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu says, kirtaniyah sada harih. And this rascal is saying ‘bhajan is a nuisance.’ Is it not possible to invoke an agitation against this? What right he has got to say ‘nuisance’? He could have spoken in sweet language, that ‘The bhajan may be very good for the devotees, but it creates disturbance to the others. Therefore we cannot allow.’ Say like that. But they cannot stop bhajan.”

“That means the whole government is feeling that way,” Gurudas said. “Otherwise, he would not feel strong in saying it.”

“That is a fact,” Prabhupada said. “But we have to become strong. There are many kirtan parties in Bombay. You have to organize them and bring them. Chant Hare Krishna everywhere. Create this nuisance. And Maharashtra is the country of Tukaram. He organized kirtan. The Tukaram kirtan parties are still there. Vitthala. Vitthala means Krishna.” Then, addressing his disciples based in Vrindavan, who would stay behind, he instructed, “An ideal gosvami should remain here to challenge these false gosvamis. But if you also become false, then you cannot challenge.”

Prabhupada addressed the police commissioner’s statement as soon as he got to Bombay, without waiting for his disciples to join him from Vrindavan. He instructed his foreign disciples in Bombay how they could speak to the local Indians and advised the Indians how they should support the temple.

“A disciple has read an article that Iran wants meat,” Prabhupada related, “so our government said that all these skinny cows should be killed and the meat should be exported so we can get oil economically—that people should not think of religious sentiment but should be practical and not object. The government wants to open many slaughterhouses and kill these mischief, loitering cows. Their policy is that religion is an opiate of the people. They think religion is just a sentiment. Their conclusion is that religion has no value. Therefore, their decision is not to encourage these temples and this bhajan. From their point of view, it is useless. So indirectly or directly, they will not patronize this.

“So, under the circumstances, I suggest we make vigorous propaganda. Hold open meetings in big halls so that the public may understand at least that this movement is very important. Let there be advertisements that we will speak on different subject matters, and then I will come and speak.

“In that meeting make a nice gentleman president. Create public opinion so that they will come and sign, ‘Yes, here must be one temple.’ We will prove from shastric evidence, as it is stated in the Bhagavad-gita, catur-vidha bhajante mam janah sukrtino 'rjuna. This word bhajana is used with reference to the very pious men, sukrtinah. And the opposite kind of man is duskrtinah, the miscreants. So, bhajana is for the pious man, recommended in the Bhagavad-gita. And Bhagavad-gita is heldin great estimation all over the world. And yet this man has accused bhajan as nuisance? How rascal and ignorant he is. And he is in one of the important positions. This is government. The bhajana is described in the Vedic shastra as ... a dealing of the most pious men. And he’s talking it as nuisance.

“So far as kirtan, bhajan-kirtan, is concerned, Krishna has said, satatam kirtayanto mam yatantas ca drdha-vratah. These are the symptoms of mahatmas. We have to make it clear that bhajana is so important. Bhagavad-gita is meant for all solution of material problems, but the people of India are not accepting it. Why not try to follow the principles of Bhagavad-gita? And the easiest process, satatam kirtayanto mam: always chanting Hare Krishna mantra.

“My disciples can also speak and say, ‘You please come with us. We are foreigners, but we know Krishna is not for this one or that one.’ Therefore we have taken this seriously. So why are you Indians lacking? You come forward. You are all educated youths, gentlemen. Accept your culture. We have taken your culture. It is not ‘your’ or ‘our,’ but you think that it is your culture. But Krishna is neither for Indians nor for you. He’s for everyone. Therefore we have taken to Krishna.

“‘So, why not try this? As stated, kirtanad eva krsnasya mukta-sangah param vrajet, Simply by Krishna kirtan, one becomes free from all contamination. So why not join with us? What is the wrong there? It is stated in your shastra, and we have adopted it. And we are feeling better. Why are you so callous, you educated youth and gentlemen?’ This kind of propaganda has to be made.

“And let them come, at least Sunday, and let them give in writing that ‘Here the Radha-Krishna temple must be there.’ Take thousands, millions of signatures. Prove that it is not nonsense—it is the most essential thing. And so far as traffic is concerned, there is a big road. Make two gates, one in and one out, and there will be no question of traffic inconvenience. In this way, make a presentation. That is my suggestion.”

“May I submit a matter?” asked a local Indian life member, a lawyer. Prabhupada told him yes.

“This propaganda and collecting the signatures in the lakhs will not only take a lot of energy of the devotees; it will take time also. By writing the police commissioner to reconsider, we lose nothing. They canalways reopen the case and reconsider, because the two grounds which they have mentioned—number one, it is a nuisance. It is to be proved it’s a nuisance.”

“Then you have to go,” Prabhupada interjected. “The public should go. Interested Hindus and Vaishnavas should go to the court and prove that it is not a nuisance; it is essential.”

“There are three things,” the man went on. “Number one, it is a nuisance. Now, the nuisance is always to be proved. Merely by two or five people saying that the bhajans and the kirtans are a nuisance ...”

“People now are drunkards and meat-eaters,” Prabhupada responded. “They may say. And even if they show, that is not authority. Authority is the shastras.” In other words, whether two or five people, or two or five hundred thousand people say the bhajans and kirtans are a nuisance, they are not the authority—shastra is the authority.

“But the government, which is so-called secular . . .”

“No,” Prabhupada countered. “They may be secular, but they cannot neglect your shastra.”

The man’s next point was that in regard to traffic, it was again the responsibility of the complainants to show that there would be a problem. “Without any justification,” the man said. “Merely one sentence that ‘It could be.’ And if you read their letter, they have not committed that certainly it will be a traffic problem. They said, 'may be.’ That means the other option is equally open: ‘May not be,’ also....

“The third is constitutional rights. Under the Constitution of India, every person, body, or organization has the liberty and equal right to propagate any religion. Under the Constitution, I have got a liberty to express my path for any religion. Of course, Krishna consciousness, according to me, is not a religion because it is universal; it is not for any sector.”

“I am conducting all these temples with the help of these foreigners,” Prabhupada said. “There is no Indian.”

“That will come in the way. That I’ve been telling Tamal Krishna also, that you should have some Indians.”

“‘You should have,”’ Prabhupada retorted, “but no Indians are coming.”

“Then you should appoint somebody.”

“We cannot appoint,” Prabhupada said. “That is not possible. Paid man is useless.”

“Appoint does not mean that you pay them. Appointing can also be honorary?

“Who is coming honorary?” Prabhupada questioned. “They are honorary, but who else is dedicating?”

“You should have those people in India.”

“I should have’ means you, if you become that ‘should have.’”

“I don’t mind becoming, or you can have somebody else.”

“No Indian is taking seriously. We have been here so many years. How many educated Indian youths have come? They are not interested.”

“Because in the court of law you require a person who should be Indian citizen, and he should have some—”

“Indian citizens we have got. Just like here, he is an Indian man.” Prabhupada indicated Jasomatinandan. “But in proportion, they are not even one percent. That is the difficulty. And if the government likes . . . Just like I was refused entrance in Africa, Nairobi. So, if the government understands that these Americans making this satyagraha, as you have proposed, then immediately, within twenty-four hours, they will be deported. Then I do not know who will manage my so many establishments. If the Hindus and the Vaishnavas combine together that ‘This is an important proposal,’ they go to the court, they give their signature, they come here—that will be nice. It may take a long time; that doesn’t matter. But it will be a solid thing. And if the government becomes, ‘Oh, these Americans are making this propaganda,’ at any moment they can ask that ‘Within twenty-four hours you get out.’”

“Yes, they can throw them out,” the man said. “No, my intention was not that this movement should be by foreigners, because that will be against them. What I was meaning, they should be—”

“That should be taken. Therefore I say hold a meeting, and the Hindus, the Vaishnavas, they should take action. Not Americans. There may be Americans, but they’ll...”

“Americans may organize it, but the participants should be Indians.” “No, organize,” Prabhupada said. “They have actually come to me. They are attracted with Krishna conscious philosophy. They did not expect that although the money has been paid by them, still, the Indian government is against this movement. They were not prepared for all these things. Unfortunately, these things are happening in India. We have had no such difficulty in any other part. They are ... junglis”

“Uncivilized."

“Uncivilized. They have become so degraded that a responsible officer in the government, he is saying that ‘Bhajan is nuisance? You see. He has no knowledge how much spiritually valuable bhajan is. In the Bhagavad-gita—Gandhi accepted Bhagavad-gita—it is said, catur-vidha bhajante mam janah sukrtino. Gandhi was chanting in temple raghupati raghava—what they are following? Gandhi was against drinking and intoxication; now they’re introducing. This is the position of the government.

“Therefore I suggest that according to the word, so far as traffic, we are diverting it this way and that way. Let people come here, join with bhajan, take prasada, and sign, ‘Yes, there must be a temple here.’ And make propaganda that people may come here. And I am present here, I will speak. The same thing as it is going on: kirtan and speaking from Bhagavad-gita. And after they are convinced, let them sign, ‘Yes, there must be a temple here.’ In this way, gather public opinion that bhajan is not nuisance. It is essential—we want it.’

“And the other thing: we are making gates in and out—two gates. Submit a plan like that, that there may be a small road, lane, but here is a big road. And purchase that land in front and make a gate. Call a good architect and make a nice gate and road. Take this proposition. Our business is there. If we invite people, ‘Come,’ . . . Even without temple, people may come and take prasada, and if they give their consent, ‘Yes, it is nice,’ that is sufficient. Even there is no temple.

“Then, in such a way, if public opinion is created and the sanction is there, immediately there will be temple. It may take some time. It doesn’t matter. So far as satyagraha is concerned, it will be useless. Hungry people, they are making satyagraha, and they are replied with fire, killing them. The government is so rogue that hungry men have come, and they are firing. Their swaraj was obtained by nonviolence, and this is the result. Actually, you cannot expect any justice from this government.”

“One has to snatch the justice from them.”

“Yes.”

Yet even without the temple construction being sanctioned, Prabhupada was prepared to preach on Hare Krishna Land. He said, “We can request the people, ‘You have tried so many ways, but your problems are not solved. Why not take this simple solution? Come with us, chant Hare Krishna mantra, and try to understand a little, one sloka from Bhagavad-gita. What is the difficulty? You have no loss. But if you do it, we assure you that the solution is there—all solutions.’ Let us make this propaganda. Never mind if they do not give us the sanction forever. It doesn’t matter. But this propaganda is wanted. What is a temple? There are many thousands of temples.

“And let the devotees perform sankirtana. And hold meetings. In this way make propaganda. It doesn’t matter if the sanction is belated. ‘Better late than never.’ But this propaganda should be done. Purchase a hundred chairs and place them around the temple so people do not have to stand, so they can sit comfortably, with their shoes. Make some attraction, that people may come. And whoever comes, give them prasada, whatever you can. ‘Please take prasada' Give him a plate. Do it in this way.”

Our life member wanted to pressure the police commissioner to issue the NOC. “Should we now take help from political parties such as Shiv Sena?” he suggested.

“That is very good,” Prabhupada said.

“They were the ones who stopped the police and the municipal commissioner from breaking the temple.”

“Yes, but my fear is that as soon as they know the Americans are agitating this, they may say, ‘You go.’ And I have no Indians to manage these big temples. Neither are they trained up. I have trained up these American boys. They are doing nicely. But the Indians cannot. These boys have taken brahmachari dress, and they will come with pants. And they will argue, ‘Why? What is the wrong there? Why should I give up pants? Why shall I have tilak? Why shall I give up smoking? Why?’ They will put so many whys that my life will be spoiled. Because they have advanced. So many rascal swamis have told them yes.”

“As you rightly say, if we do anything actively, then they may see your boys going out of India—foreigners, Americans. ‘Throw them out.’

They will argue on that ground, and they will say that ‘You are not required. You are nuisance,’ or whatever the reasons.”

“Any reason. No reason. ‘We don’t want you.’”

“But if that’s so, then we may propagate, or try to get another place, but they’ll take the same action, because they’ll know that we are trying to create public opinion against the government. They can again take the same action of removing the boys.”

“No, same action, but that is our propaganda—preach.” We had been preaching and would continue to preach, Prabhupada was saying. We would never stop.

Later, in his purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.3.22, Prabhupada commented on the police commissioner’s statement that kirtan was a nuisance—and on his own internal mood: “Such uncivilized men are not in favor of the Krsna consciousness movement. As public officers, they declare without hesitation that the chanting of the Hare Krsna movement is a nuisance, although Bhagavad-gita clearly says, satatam kirtayanto mam yatantas ca drdha-vratah. According to this verse, it is the duty of the mahatmas to chant the Hare Krsna mantra and try to spread it all over the world to the best of their ability. Unfortunately, society is in such an uncivilized state that there are so-called mahatmas who are prepared to kill cows and children and stop the Hare Krsna movement. Such uncivilized activities were actually demonstrated in opposition to the Hare Krsna movement’s Bombay center, Hare Krsna Land. As Kamsa was not expected to kill the beautiful child of Devaki and Vasudeva, the uncivilized society, although unhappy about the advancement of the Krsna consciousness movement, cannot be expected to stop it. Yet we must face many difficulties in many different ways. Although Krsna cannot be killed, Vasudeva, as the father of Krsna, was trembling because in affection he thought that Kamsa would immediately come and kill his son. Similarly, although the Krsna consciousness movement and Krsna are not different and no asuras can check it, we are afraid that at any moment the asuras can stop this movement in any part of the world.”

When the devotees arrived in Bombay from Vrindavan, Prabhupada wanted strong action. On one morning walk he told us that we shouldcall the members, call the public, and have a sit-in at the police station and refuse to move until the commissioner granted the NOC.

Balavanta and Amarendra had been getting into politics in America—running for mayor in Atlanta and Dallas—so Prabhupada deputed them to approach the government leaders in Bombay. Tosan Krishna was to meet the press and other media people. In this way the work was divided up, with Tamal Krishna as the main organizer on Prabhupada’s behalf.

“Prabhupada took such a strong position that how could the chanting of Hare Krishna be a nuisance,” Balavanta later recalled. “How could it be a public nuisance in a state where Tukaram lived? Tukaram was from Maharashtra, and he told everyone to chant the holy names. And Bhaktivinoda Thakura said that Tukaram was a follower of Lord Chaitanya. So, how could anyone say that chanting the holy names was a nuisance?

“Prabhupada sent me to meet with the different political parties. The Jana Sangha and Shiv Sena were the two prominent ones known for their sympathy for Hindu causes. There was also the Congress Party, with which Mr. Nair had had connections, but the other parties were more Hindu orientated, so that’s where we went. I would go to get the politicians and bring them to Prabhupada for an audience. And Prabhupada would talk to them about the issue.

“Prabhupada had told me, ‘You can have anyone you want, anybody in the movement. You tell me, and they will come and work with you.’ So, I picked Vishnujana, because the idea was civil disobedience. When we first discussed it, we were walking in Vrindavan and Prabhupada was telling us what had happened, and he said, ‘How can they say chanting Hare Krishna is a nuisance? Rather than stop chanting, we must chant more.’ And I said, ‘Yes, Prabhupada, just like Lord Chaitanya and Chand Kazi.’ ‘Exactly!’ he said. He liked that.”

“Just see this man’s intelligence,” Prabhupada had commented when he had heard Balavanta’s proposal. “See how intelligent he is. He has understood.”

“So,” Balavanta recounted, “Vishnujana and a number of devotees came to Bombay. Vishnujana would go out on the streets every day chanting. And eventually Prabhupada was victorious.”

Amarendra was also in Vrindavan, about to leave. “I couldn’t wait to get back to America after my first time in India,” he remembered. ‘All I could think about was Gauranga potatoes and cauliflower pakoras and getting back to America and real food. I was waiting for the bus, and all of a sudden somebody came up and said, ‘Prabhupada said that everybody must go to Bombay. Don’t return home. We’ll change your visas.’ Prabhupada wanted us to go to Bombay to demonstrate and protest against the government. And Balavanta was there, because he had some experience in dealing with politicians.

“So, we took the flight to Bombay. There, Prabhupada was in a darshan, furious, saying, ‘In the land of Krishna they have opposed the teachings of the Bhagavad-gita.' This was inconceivable. He was on a campaign, and he wanted devotees to go out and protest and have kirtan. He sent Vishnujana Swami out to do hari-nama every day, and he wanted Balavanta to meet with politicians to overturn the decision.”

Many Australian, American, European, and African devotees proceeded to Bombay after the Vrindavan festival and early every morning went on hari-nama processions through the neighborhood, led by Achyutananda, Dinanath, Jayasacinandana, Vishnujana, and other expert kirtaniyas. Sometimes they accompanied Prabhupada on his morning walks.

After a day’s chanting, some devotees went to Juhu Beach for a swim in the sea, which Prabhupada said would be good for their health. Vishnujana was wary of sharks and laughed as he said, “Now Krishna will come to me in His form as a shark and say, ‘Here I am.’”

“After longer chanting processions later in the morning led by Vishnujana Swami, sometimes in downtown Bombay and sometimes in nearby Santa Cruz or Vile Parle,” Kurma dasa remembered, “the devotees would return for lunch. Once the heat of the day faded, they would sit in the temple and sing bhajans, then go out to the surrounding markets and shopping areas, advertising Srila Prabhupada’s evening program at the temple.

“In the night, after arriving in his Jeep from the back of Hare Krishna Land, Prabhupada would speak on Bhagavad-gita, Chapter 4, in the mandapa adjoining the temple.”

“After the lecture,” Balarama dasa described, “there would be an arati ceremony, and every one of us danced enthusiastically in front of Srila Prabhupada.
