Immediately after, Prabhupada would personally distribute the entire plate of Radha-Rasabihari’s maha-prasada. We’d squeeze and push and shove forward to get a handful of halavah and fruit that Prabhupada pressed into our eager hands.”

Hare Krishna Land was situated near a large cinema hall, and every evening, both before and after the movie, there were long lines of traffic. The honking horns and hundreds of pedestrians coming and going created a lot of noise and congestion. If the police could allow congestion caused by the cinema, we wondered, why not for the temple?

The real problem, Prabhupada said, was that people were not Krishna conscious. To combat this, to make people aware of the value of Krishna consciousness, we should hold festivals throughout Bombay. Then the people themselves would protest the actions of the police commissioner and insist that the government allow the temple to come up.

Prabhupada was inspired to both protest and preach. But when the time came for the protest, he adopted a more cautious view. On one morning walk he returned to the point that we were in a foreign country—if the government didn’t like us, if they found us too troublesome, they could just ask us to leave. He quoted the saying “Do not pick a fight with a crocodile while in the water.” It was not good for us to pick a fight with the Indian leaders while in their jurisdiction; we couldn’t win such a fight, and it wouldn’t be appreciated. He suggested that instead of having a demonstration through the streets and ending at the police station, we should hold massive kirtan programs and preach so that the people of Bombay would become convinced of the value of Krishna consciousness, that Krishna consciousness was the only hope of saving the world. “Then,” he said, “when the people of Bombay are convinced of the importance of Krishna consciousness, they will see that the temple is built.”

So, even though Prabhupada modified his position on the protests, he still wanted us to remain active. Bhagavata was given the responsibility of speaking with ministers about our prasada program. “We were getting food from America to distribute to the people,” he recalled, “and

I spoke with different government officials to arrange for permits. I also collected donations of food and money for prasada distribution to the public. Every day I went all the way downtown on the train and then came all the way back.

“In the evenings Prabhupada would await my report: ‘What is the news today?’ I would say, ‘I collected 1,500 rupees from this man and sacks of grain from that person,’ and he would say, ‘Very good.’ He was pleased to see any progress.

“He would also ask me about the ministers I had spoken with. One day I had spoken to the chief minister of the state of Maharashtra. Prabhupada was pleased. He beamed. Here his American disciples were speaking with the highest government officials and arranging for so many things. He appreciated how resourceful, adamant, and tenacious we were about serving our spiritual master. He would praise me for my accomplishments, and I always felt good. I was doing my spiritual master’s work.”

We also began to organize preaching programs, but most of the devotees who came from Vrindavan would be back at the temple during the day. Prabhupada was concerned about how the devotees would be engaged, and he asked his managers what the devotees would do. We replied that we would have a program in the temple all day long, alternating readings, kirtans, and discussions about Krishna consciousness. “Very good,” he approved.

After a few days, Prabhupada asked how the program in the temple was going, whether the devotees were enjoying chanting and reading and hearing.

“Well, frankly, Srila Prabhupada,” Tamal had to tell him, “most of the devotees aren’t coming, and the ones who do come—most of them fall asleep.”

“All right,” Prabhupada replied, “if they are sudras, let them work in the garden—but everyone must be engaged. You tell the devotees that if they are actually brahmans, they should sit in the temple and be engaged in kirtan and krsna-katha, and if they are not brahmans, if they are sudras, they can work in the garden. But nobody can remain idle; nobody can sleep.”

Vishnujana was in charge of the temple program. But in spite of Prabhupadas words, the devotees still didn’t come—or work in the garden. One day Vishnujana told them, “Prabhupada is not pleased that we are all so lazy. We should be doing something. He says that if you just sit around, you’ll get sick.”

After two weeks, the Australian devotees became restless and asked me to approach Prabhupada on their behalf. There was little engagement for them in Bombay, they said, and they would have a lot of work to prepare for Prabhupada’s imminent visit to their country.

When I passed along their request to leave, Prabhupada had me deliver them a stern reply: “What is the question of ‘no engagement’? There are so many opportunities to read and chant. Don’t be impatient wanting to go here and there.” So, the Australian devotees resigned themselves to another week in Bombay.

With all the difficulties and challenges, I had a gnawing feeling that I was failing Srila Prabhupada, that he was displeased with me, and I approached Satsvarupa, my first temple president and senior godbrother, who was now Prabhupada’s secretary, with my concern. He replied that he had never heard Prabhupada speak about me in negative terms; the only thing he had heard him say was, “Giriraj has too much to do.”

Eventually Prabhupada drafted a letter to the police commissioner. He wrote that the Bhagavad-gita, which was accepted by every Hindu, recommended satatam kirtayanto mam, that there should always be kirtan, but that some people—he didn’t mention the commissioner directly—considered kirtan to be a nuisance. Who were these people? He again quoted the Gita—na mam duskrtino mudhah, that fools and rascals didn’t surrender to Krishna and didn’t like Krishna kirtan. He told the commissioner that he was in the position of a king, addressing him in the ideal, and asked him to give us protection from such people. He wrote that traditionally the administrators and the government would give protection to the innocent citizens from such fools and rascals, so we were appealing to him as humble devotees to please give us protection and allow the kirtan to go on in the temple—and grant the NOC.

He had us sign the letter and deliver it to the police commissioner’s office. When after some days there was no response, he asked us toagain go. The commissioner was not available, but we met his secretary. “Did you give the letter to the commissioner?” we inquired.

“Yes,” he said. “The commissioner said it was the best, most brilliant letter he had ever received. He was so impressed. He said he had never received a letter like it before.” But he didn’t give the NOC, because he was involved in a conspiracy.

Whatever happened, Srila Prabhupada always remained fixed in Krishna consciousness, with full faith in his spiritual master and Krishna. As he wrote to Pranava dasa on March 30, “In Bombay we are meeting the opposition peacefully, and I hope things will come out successfully.”

Although some devotees found that Dr. Patel could be annoying, I appreciated the service he did for us, and I liked his discussions with Srila Prabhupada. He knew some Sanskrit, and he liked to analyze different verses with Srila Prabhupada. One day he brought up the verse

yatah pravrttir bhutanam  
yena sarvam idam tatam  
sva-karmana tam abhyarcya  
siddhim vindati manavah

“By worship of the Lord, who is the source of all beings and who is all-pervading, a man can attain perfection through performing his own work.” (Gita 18.46)

“I wanted a little exposition on this,” he said. “Sva-karmana tam abhyarcya”

“Yes,” Prabhupada replied. “Sva-karmana.”

“The karma of a man depends upon his position in the society ...”

“Yes,” Prabhupada agreed.

“... whether he’s a kshatriya, vaishya, or sudra, like me. And whether he’s a sannyasi or a grihastha. On that karma. And when he does that karma without expectation of any fruit, that karma is as good as bhakti according to this line, sva-karmana tam abhyarcya siddhim vindati manavah.”

“No,” Prabhupada said. “The result should be there, but tam, unto Krishna. Give the result to Krishna—not self. You earn lakhs of rupees,but tam abhyarcya, give to Krishna. Not take it yourself or distribute amongst your children. Tam abhyarcya. That is service. First of all understand this word tam.”

“Sva-karmana tam abhyarcya, karmana.”

“Yes.”

“How can you object to the karma? That is what I want to know.”

“Karma, karmana, by your work,” Prabhupada said. “Just like you are working as a medical practitioner. So, you earn lakhs of rupees. Give to Krishna. That is tam abhyarcya. Then you become perfect. That is also confirmed in the Bhagavata. Atah pumbhir dvija-srestha varnasrama-vibhagasah. Everyone is working according to varna and ashrama. So, svanusthitasya dharmasya. Anyone who is serving according to his dharma—an engineer, a doctor, or somebody else—he is serving according to his occupational duty, but he has to see, sva-karmana tam abhyarcya samsiddhim labhate. That is Gita. And it is said, svanusthitasya dharmasya samsiddhih—perfection. What is that? Hari-tosanam. We have to see whether Krishna is satisfied. You earn lakhs of rupees and give it to Krishna. Krishna said yat karosi, ‘Never mind what you are doing,’ kurusva tad mad-arpanam, ‘give it to Me.’ And ‘No, no, sir. I’m serving You, but the money is in my pocket.’”

“Everything is Krishna’s. How can you give anything, even a leaf?”

“Oh, yes, yes. Just like these boys and girls are giving. That is the philosophy. These boys and girls are giving everything—whole life. They do not ask even a single paisa from me that ‘My dear sir, please give me four annas. I’ll go to the cinema.’ You see? They are serving. They have given everything. This boy—you like this Giriraj—he’s earning at least 50,000 per month. He does not keep a single paisa. This is service. They are not poor. They’re earning—but everything for Krishna.”

“Giriraj,” Dr. Patel asked, “how are you earning fifty thousand rupees a month?”

“Because fifty members,” Prabhupada answered for me. “Fifty members, eleven hundred rupees. He makes at least two or three members per day. Some days he is absent, so average fifty thousand. Not a single fifty paisa coin does he keep. There are many—all of them. Not that everyone is earning fifty thousand, but even fifty hundred or fifty paisa, everything for Krishna. That is tam abhyarcya. And if youdivide partially, ‘Some percentage for Krishna, some percentage for my sense gratification,’ then Krishna says, ye yatha mam prapadyante tams tathaiva bhajamy aham—proportionately. If you have spent cent percent of your energy for Krishna, Krishna is cent percent for you. And if you have spent one percent for Krishna, Krishna is one percent for you. Responsive cooperation.”

“Responsive cooperation,” an Indian man repeated, which was greeted by laughter, because it was a term that had been used in the Indian freedom movement.

“This institution has advanced so much all over the world,” Prabhupada continued, “because we have got these boys who have dedicated everything for Krishna. Therefore it has advanced so quickly. They do not think of anything as personal. Sva-karmana tam abhyarcya. Samsiddhir hari-tosanam.”

Even though we did not think we were on the platform Prabhupada described when he used us to illustrate a point, we could not discount what he said—and we felt inspired to come to that standard.

Though he often spoke like an impersonalist, Dr. Patel considered himself to be a Vaishnava. And when Prabhupada would call him a Mayavadi, he would object: “No, Sir. I am a Vaishnava.”

In a way, he was a Mayavadi: he accepted Krishna and the Bhagavadgita, but it wasn’t quite clear how he accepted Krishna—as the person Krishna or as something impersonal speaking through Krishna. His position was always a little ambiguous, and the way he spoke, it was hard to figure him out. But he would always insist that he was not only a Vaishnava, but a pure Vaishnava.

During one of their walks together, Prabhupada criticized one of the revered so-called spiritual leaders of India, and Dr. Patel became livid. He was so angry, he was shaking. “You cannot criticize like this!” he shouted.

“I am not saying—Krishna is saying!” Prabhupada shouted back. “Na mam duskrtino mudhah . . .” And like that, they were shouting back and forth.

This time Dr. Patel’s friends—he led a group of cronies, perhaps because he was a little intellectual and outspoken—tried to drag him away, saying, “Swamiji has a heart condition. Don’t upset him so.”

But Dr. Patel persisted. He was shouting at Prabhupada, and Prabhupada was shouting back. In the end, Dr. Patel’s cronies pulled him away.

Later, at the temple, Tamal Krishna asked, “Srila Prabhupada, why do you do it? Why do you put up with him? He is so offensive.”

“It is our duty to engage everyone,” Prabhupada said.

“But what is his actual position?” Tamal Krishna asked. “Is he a Vaishnava? Is he a Mayavadi? What is he?”

In response, Prabhupada told a story about a man who could speak many languages. In whatever language people addressed him, he could respond fluently. No one could figure out where the man was actually from.

After much discussion, a neighbor said, “I will find out.” And one day, when the man was preoccupied, the neighbor came up behind him and gave him a big whack. And when the man started to curse in his native tongue, his origin was disclosed.

“Dr. Patel is like that,” Prabhupada said. “He can speak very expertly. He can sound like a devotee, sound like a Vaishnava, sound like a Mayavadi, sound like anything. But when I gave a slap where it really hurt—this so-called saintly person that he revered—his real language came out.”

Thereafter, Prabhupada restricted talk during his walks: “Now no more discussion. We will only read Krsna book.” And for the first time in years, Dr. Patel avoided him.

Then, one day, Dr. Patel was walking on one side of the beach and Prabhupada was walking on the other, and something made Dr. Patel change course. He just walked up to Srila Prabhupada and bowed at his feet—he came back.

“We have an assembly,” he told Prabhupada, “and they passed by majority vote that I should refrain from coming here. But somehow or other I came.”

Prabhupada reciprocated graciously and with humor: “I saw your motorcar and offered my obeisances. I was thinking that ‘Dr. Patel’s representative, the car, is here.’”

Then Dr. Patel came to the point. “Swamiji,” he said, “we have been taught to respect all the saints of India.”

“And our business,” Prabhupada replied, “is to point out who is not a saint.”

On another morning walk, Dr. Patel brought up the topic of the twelve sets of bedding he had given to the devotees, complaining to Srila Prabhupada that we hadn’t taken care of them. At first there were twelve sets; then, after a while, there was one less blanket and fewer pillows. In time, there were only about seven sets, then three sets, and finally there was nothing left of the gift at all. So Dr. Patel complained that he had gone and begged and organized the gift and now there was nothing left—not a trace, not a thread.

Prabhupada responded, “These boys and girls from Europe and America who have come to serve me, they don’t care for their bodies. They know, ‘I am not this body,’ so why should they care? As long as they can serve their spiritual master and chant Hare Krishna, they are happy. They don’t mind if they have to sleep on the floor or get bitten by mosquitoes. They are detached from the body. All they care about is devotional service.”

“They are already liberated,” he said. “That moksha you so much want—that moksha they already have. That is why there is nothing left of your gift—they don’t care for the body or the comforts of the body. They are liberated, which you so much want to become.”

Prabhupada’s answer was profound, expressed with a wry twist. It was true: devotees were liberated—pure devotional service began on the liberated platform:

brahma-bhutah prasannatma  
na socati na kanksati  
samah sarvesu bhutesu  
mad-bhaktim labhate param

“One who is thus transcendentally situated at once realizes the Supreme Brahman and becomes fully joyful. He never laments or desires to have anything. He is equally disposed toward every living entity. In that state he attains pure devotional service unto Me.” (Gita 18.54) Even a neophyte devotee was beyond a Mayavadi who desired liberation. So, in a subtle, tactful way (this time), Srila Prabhupada put Dr. Patel in his place and exalted the devotees in comparison.

Still, even liberated devotees sometimes took care of so-called material possessions, knowing them to be Krishna’s property, to be used in

Krishna’s service. The highest conception of renunciation, or detachment, was yukta-vairdgya, defined by Srila Rupa Gosvami:

anasaktasya visayan  
yatharham upayunjatah  
nirbandhah krsna-sambandhe  
yuktam vairagyam ucyate

“Things should be accepted for the Lord’s service and not for one’s personal sense gratification. If one accepts something without attachment and accepts it because it is related to Krsna, one’s renunciation is called yukta-vairagya, befitting renunciation.” (Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 1.2.255)

Srila Prabhupada himself perfectly demonstrated the principle of yukta-vairagya. He carefully maintained whatever Krishna sent him. And he engaged not only anything and everything, but also everyone, in Krishna’s service—including Dr. Patel.

Around this time, The Illustrated Weekly of India carried an article by Agehananda Bharati, an Austrian-born Indologist and Advaitan sannyasi, under the title “Hare Krishna vs Shiva Shiva.” In the article, Bharati gave his version of a series of exchanges and debates he had had with “Swami Hridayananda” of ISKCON. I shared my impression with Prabhupada that the Weekly's editor, Khushwant Singh, had run the piece, along with that title, to make us all—believers in general—look silly, bickering over deities and evidence. Prabhupada agreed with my assessment. “Yes,” he said. “Bharati is a fool, but Singh is a demon.”

On March 26 Amratlal Pandya, our old friend and life member from Vile Parle, brought two sadhus from the Swaminarayan temple in Dadar to meet Srila Prabhupada. Swaminarayan followers considered themselves to be a Vaishnava sect, but generally, instead of worshipping Krishna, they worshipped only Swaminarayan, known also as Sahajanand Swami, who was their original guru and had lived from 1781 to 1830. The sect was popular mainly with Gujaratis, and their principles of conduct were similar to ISKCON’s. In fact, on one morning walk, Dr. Patel had brought the Shikshapatri, written by Swaminarayan, and read excerpts to Prabhupada, and Prabhupada had approved of most of them.

Prabhupada was in his room talking with Jasomatinandan dasa and his seventy-year-old mother when Mr. Pandya brought the monks up to see him. When the door opened and the sannyasis saw her, they became disturbed and covered their faces. In their sect brahmacharis and sannyasis never looked at or spoke to women; in their temples the women listened from the other side of a curtain.

Bhagavata had also brought the monks upstairs. “Let’s wait,” he told them. “Prabhupada will finish soon, and then you can go in.” So they went back down and waited.

When Jasomatinandan and his mother had left and the monks went in to see Prabhupada, he treated them with respect. “I am so sorry,” he said, “but one of my leading students’ elderly mother came to see me. I saw her while her son was present in the room. My sannyasi servant was also here.”

“Oh—we do not see a woman under any circumstances,” they said.

“Yes, I understand,” Prabhupada replied. “Lord Chaitanya was also very strict.”

The monks told Prabhupada that if any of them saw the face of a woman, he was considered to be fallen. “Well, I speak to women,” Prabhupada said. “Does that mean that I’m fallen?” They didn’t reply. Then he brought up the question of why the sect worshipped Swaminarayan and not Krishna.

“We believe that you can worship the guru on the same level as God,” the monks replied. “Just like you are worshipping Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, so we are worshipping Swaminarayan.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada told them, “We do worship the guru on the same level as God—but with God. We worship Chaitanya Mahaprabhu but with Radha and Krishna. So if you worship Swaminarayan with Radha and Krishna, that worship will be proper; otherwise not.”

That began the confrontation. They said that Swaminarayan was God. “Where in Srimad-Bhagavatam does it say that Swaminarayan is God?” Prabhupada questioned. “I have not seen. I have seen Rama, Nrsimha, Varaha, and Chaitanya Mahaprabhu mentioned in the Bhagavatam, but where is Swaminarayan?’

“It is in this book,” they replied.

“Who has written that book? Is it the Vedas? Is it written by Vyasa?” “No,” they said, Such-and-such Swami wrote it.

“Oh, that swami? Who is he—what parampara is he from?”

“Prabhupada was going on, hammering,” Bhagavata later remembered. “He wouldn’t let them go. They didn’t understand the philosophy, and Prabhupada smashed them to pieces.”

“Okay, we’re going to leave, Swamiji,” one of the monks said. “We’ve had enough.” And they walked out.

The next morning, on his walk, Srila Prabhupada brought up the question of how to regard and deal with women. “Why should one hate women so much?” he asked Dr. Patel.

“We don’t hate,” Dr. Patel replied. “We want to protect you from sex.”

“Not to see the face, not to ...”

“Because woman is the embodiment of maya.”

“You should be trained up, that in spite of woman, you’ll not be agitated,” Prabhupada said. “That training is required.”

“Now that training is very difficult to get, I am sorry to say.”

“No, no. That training is there. We are training in that way.”

“You must have a sort of a ... between the objects and the indriyas, the senses ...”

“According to Swaminarayan’s principles, I am fallen.”

“No, no, sir,” Dr. Patel objected.

“Because I am always surrounded by young girls.”

“No, no. Swaminarayan was sitting with women, but the sadhus ...”

“Men should be trained up in such a way that in spite of woman they will not be agitated. In European countries, if you restrict in that way, it will be fanaticism. Nowadays, here also. That is not possible. It is simply utopian.”

“That is all right. It is not possible. So you are doing like this.”

“We are training,” Prabhupada stated. “That is the training of Chanakya Pandit: Mdtrvat para-daresu. There may be thousands of women, but you see them as your mother. That’s it. If you become agitated by seeing even your mother, then what can be done?

“To avoid that trap, they avoid association with women. But these women—my disciples—are not ordinary women. They are preachers. They are Vaishnavas. By their association, one becomes a Vaishnava.”

## Laying Foundations

April 1 was Rama-navami, the appearance day of Lord Ramachandra. On his morning walk, Prabhupada noted that many people were bathing in the sea, and he inquired, “Because today’s Rama-navami they’re taking bath?”

Dr. Patel said yes, and toward the end of the walk, he raised the topic of fasting for Rama-navami, suggesting that one should fast throughout the night, until the following morning. A devotee volunteered that we fasted until sunset. Prabhupada agreed but added, “If one can continue until the next morning, that’s all right.”

Later, I asked Prabhupada when we should actually break the fast, and he replied that I should inquire when the local temples broke theirs and then follow their standard. It turned out that they broke their fasts at noon, so that day we did too.

Prabhupada marked the occasion of Rama-navami by again laying the cornerstone for the Juhu temple—after so many delays and complications, he wanted to reaffirm his intention to build the temple. At the ceremony he said, “On this auspicious day of the appearance of Lord Ramachandra, we are taking this opportunity for the foundation stone, the cornerstone, of our temple in this Bombay center. It is very kind of Mrs. A. B. Nair that she has given us this chance, along with her husband.

“As far as we are concerned, we are preachers. We are preaching all over the world. We don’t require any palatial building or comfortable apartment. But because it is a preaching center, in order to invite respectable persons, we require a nice building, a nice temple. Just like Rupa Gosvami, our predecessor acharya, left his ministership, his government post, and became a mendicant. He was living under a different tree every night: tonight one tree, the next night another. But when he was approached by King Mansingh, the commander-in-chief of Emperor Akbar ... In those days big, rich men were God conscious, and they wanted to do something for God’s service. So, King Mansingh approached Rupa Gosvami, asking if he could do any service. Rupa Gosvami was living under a tree, so what service could he expect from King Mansingh? He said, ‘If you want to do some service, do it for Krishna? And he advised him to construct a temple at Vrindavan.”

Earlier in the day, after our regular morning program, Manasvi had announced that people should come in the evening for “Ram dhun”— bhajans for Lord Rama. Prabhupada responded to this in his talk that evening, saying that chanting Hare Krishna was sufficient.

“There is no difference between Rama and Krishna,” he began. “Krishna is param brahma, and Rama is also param brahma. We Vaishnavas have equal faith and obeisance to all visnu-murtis (ramadi-murtisu)—Rama, Nrsimha, Varaha, Narayana . . . But we Gaudiya Vaishnavas, or Madhva-Gaudiya Vaishnavas, are worshippers of Lord Krishna’s murti. There is no difference between Lord Ramachandra’s murti and Krishna’s murti, but Krishna is full-fledged param brahma, whereas Lord Ramachandra, although also param brahma, did not exhibit His full-fledged opulence. These are very confidential things, but still, on Lord Ramachandra’s birthday we offer our respectful obeisances at His lotus feet so that He may be merciful upon us to bestow His bhakti, devotional service.

“So, although there is no difference between Sri Rama and Sri Krishna, one devotee is attracted by one feature of the Lord, and another devotee is attracted by another feature. But factually there is no difference.

“But in the shastras it is said that if you chant the name of Vishnu, visnu-sahasra-nama—chanting one thousand times Lord Vishnu’s name is equal to one name of Rama. And chanting three times the name of Lord Rama it is equal to one name of Krishna. This is the verdict of shastra. So, when we chant Hare Krishna, Rama is already there, three times. It is not that because we are chanting Hare Krishna we are neglecting Rama. No. With each Krishna name there are three times Rama’s name.

“Besides that, we are also chanting Hare Rama. Hare Rama and Sita-Rama are the same thing. There is no difference between Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna and Hare Rama, Hare Rama. This is also rama-nama: Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. In the shastras— Agni Purana, Brahmanda Purana, Kali-santarana Upanisad—it is recommended:

Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare  
Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare.

“So devotees always chant Krishna’s name and Rama’s name together, and when there is question of rama-nama, there is Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. That is rama-nama.

“So there is no partiality, that ‘These people are simply after Krishna.’ Of course, we are a little more attached to Krishna, but that does not mean we do not know who is Lord Ramachandra. We know that He is Krishna Himself in a different feature for pastimes.

ramadi-murtisu kala-niyamena tisthan  
nanavataram akarod bhuvanesu kintu  
krsnah svayam samabhavat paramah pumanyo  
govindam adi-purusam tam aham bhajami

\[“I worship Govinda, the primeval Lord, who by His various plenary portions appears in the world in different forms and incarnations such as Lord Rama, but who personally appears in His supreme original form as Lord Krishna.” (Brahma-samhita 5.39)\]

“Now let us begin our regular class.”

And he proceeded to sing “Jaya Radha-Madhava” and continue with his evening lectures on the fourth chapter of the Bhagavad-gita.

After Nara Narayan left, we didn’t have a steady gardener for almost two years—until Sankha dasa arrived after Gaura-purnima in 1974. “I didn’t know how to do anything,” Sankha later admitted, “but I feel in my heart that I was blessed by Prabhupada to learn gardening. When I arrived, Caitya-guru, the temple commander, took me to see Prabhupada, and I said, ‘Srila Prabhupada, you have asked me to come to Bombay. What would you like me to do?’ ‘I want you to plant a flower in every square inch of Hare Krishna Land,’ he told me. And we offered our obeisances and left.

“The next day, we went back for clarification, and I asked Prabhupada, ‘Would you like me to grow vegetables?’ ‘No,’ he said, ‘our space is limited; it will be cheaper to buy them in the local market.’ ‘What about fruits?’ ‘Yes—guavas, chikus, bananas.’”

Prabhupada passed by the garden every day on his morning walk, and some time after Sankha’s arrival, he noticed that there still weren’t any fruits or flowers growing. “Where are the flowers?” he asked Sankha, but there never were any. “He’s just bluffing,” Prabhupada commented. “He doesn’t know what he’s doing. Simply bluffing.”

Then one morning, after he had returned from traveling in India, Prabhupada went out for his walk and saw that the garden was full of fruits and flowers. He was very pleased with Sankha’s service, and thereafter, Sankha would offer Prabhupada a flower every day and became known as “Prabhupada’s flower boy.”

Sankha grew papayas, guavas, chikus, and strawberry bananas— small and pink inside, and very sweet. “One day at the airport when Prabhupada was about to depart for London,” he recalled, “I brought a big load of ripe bananas and asked Prabhupada if he would like one. He opened his eyes wide and said, ‘You grew these?’ ‘Yes,’ I replied, ‘I have grown them for you.’ He grabbed one, peeled it, and ate it all. ‘These are very good,’ he said. ‘Now pass them out to everyone in the airport.’ And while I was distributing the bananas, Harikesa jumped up on a table and started preaching. Prabhupada really appreciated when we grew our own food.”

One morning in April, having returned to the temple from Juhu Beach and greeted the Deities, Prabhupada sat down to give Bhdgavatam class and Tamal Krishna asked him if we could offer arati to him. At first Prabhupada refused, but Tamal Krishna pressed his entreaty, and ultimately Prabhupada agreed. So Tamal Krishna offered arati, and Achyutananda led the devotees in singing Sri-guru-carana padma (though he was practically the only one who knew the words).

This was the first official guru-puja ever offered to Srila Prabhupada. It was a wonderful feeling for all the devotees to worship him in that way, singing and dancing and jumping in an ecstatic mood. Of all the living entities in the entire universe, I was thinking, we had to be the most fortunate—not only did we have Prabhupada in our presence, but we would now be able to worship him with arati every morning.

In Calcutta to purchase things for the Nairobi temple, Brahmananda had gotten a pair of padukas, the wooden thong slippers worn by sadhus,and had them covered with silver and engraved with Prabhupada’s name and the title founder-acharya. “My idea,” he said later, “was to touch them to Prabhupada’s feet and then bring them back to Nairobi and worship them on the altar. So, one morning at the guru-puja I ceremoniously placed them on the cushion for Prabhupada’s feet, where the devotees offered flowers. Prabhupada saw them and showed his approval, smiling and slipping his feet into them and wearing them as the devotees showered them with flower offerings.”

Guru-puja was a special feature of our experience with Prabhupada in Bombay. But then, “When I went back to Africa,” Bhagavata recalled, “I told the devotees that this was how we were going to have the morning program, with guru-puja to Srila Prabhupada. And similarly, when other devotees went to other temples, they instituted this standard.”

And without our making any effort, the news spread to the other centers, and soon devotees everywhere were offering arati to Prabhupada as guru-puja right before or after greeting the Deities.

The previous year, when Tamal Krishna had told Srila Prabhupada how Mr. Nair had bluffed me, Prabhupada had replied, “Giriraj is simple. What can be done?” His words had stayed in my mind, and I considered my simplicity a fault, a disqualification.

Now, some sixteen months later, the topic of simplicity came up again, while I was reading the Krsna book to Prabhupada during his morning walk on Juhu Beach. I was reading from “The Salvation of Trnavarta,” in which Lord Krishna defeats a demon who has assumed the form of a whirlwind: “After observing such wonderful happenings, Nanda Maharaja began to think of the words of Vasudeva again and again.”

We had previously read how Nanda Maharaja considered Vasudeva a great sage and mystic yogi because Vasudeva had foretold an incident that happened in Vrindavan, where Krishna was living. Prabhupada had remarked, “Vasudeva is a kshatriya, a ruler. With political eyesight, Vasudeva predicted, ‘This may happen,’ but Nanda Maharaja, as a vaishya, a simple agriculturalist, thought, Oh, Vasudeva is a foreseer."

I noticed that Prabhupada was applying the word “simple” to a pure devotee—Nanda Maharaja—and I was surprised. I wondered how a pure devotee could have such a disqualification as being simple. “Simplicity is not considered a bad quality?” I asked.

“No,” Prabhupada replied. “For him it is all right. He is a vaishya, so he should believe like that. And a politician should act like Vasudeva. One should not imitate. For example, a physician does operations, but I should not imitate and take a knife and operate. That is not my business. . . . But as a simple agriculturalist, Nanda Maharaja was thinking of Krishna; and Vasudeva, when he was asking Nanda Maharaja, ‘Go and take care of your children there,’ he was also thinking of Krishna. If thinking of Krishna is there, then whether kshatriya or vaishya or brahman, it doesn’t matter. Everyone gets the same benefit.

“Everyone should understand, ‘Whatever I may be, I am an eternal servant of Krishna.’ If this consciousness is maintained and everyone is engaged in the service of Krishna by his work and by his occupational duty, then he is perfect.”

Srila Prabhupada’s answer really struck me. He was saying that for a person in a certain position, simplicity may be a good qualification, and for another it may not. For a vaishya or a brahman to be simple may be good, but not for a kshatriya, who has to deal with politics and diplomacy. Yet ultimately it didn’t matter whether one was a brahman, a kshatriya, a vaishya, or whatever. What mattered was that one worked in Krishna’s service and thought of Krishna in love—Krishna consciousness.

Prabhupada was concerned that our preaching thrive. “We have to become very strong preachers,” he said on one morning walk in LA. “Then this movement will stay.” He instructed that we send a monthly newsletter to all the life members, informing them of our activities, “lest they think we are dead.” And after his return from Hyderabad on April 29, he introduced the Sunday feast for them at Juhu. He had us invite all the members and even phone many personally just to make sure they would come, and we arranged a feast with nice plates and utensils.

The members started to arrive before the noon arati. Afterward, Prabhupada came down, sat on the vyasasana, and gave a brief talk. Then he asked us to serve the prasada. We offered him the first plate, but he was not interested in eating; he was focused on the members and personally supervised the serving. Devotees placed a plate in front of each of the guests and came around with pots filled with the various preparations. If Prabhupada saw that a member needed more of anything, he would order the devotees to bring it.

When the members had finished their prasada, they started to take their own plates away, but Prabhupada stopped them: “No, no, no. Let the plates remain; my disciples will take them.” The members, as proper Vaishnavas and cultured Hindus, insisted, “No, no, we will take them.” But Prabhupada asserted himself: “No, you leave them. You just go, and my disciples will take and clean them.” And the members left their plates and washed their hands.

The temple room was completely filled with guests. A hundred and fifty must have taken prasada—a large number considering how many members we had then, how far away Juhu was for most of them, and how small the temple was. At the end, everyone gathered for photos, with Prabhupada on his vyasasana, flanked by all the prominent members. Biharilal Khandelwal, Kartikeya Mahadevia, Mr. Sethi, Mr. Asnani, Dr. Singhal, Mr. Pandya, Manmohan—they were all there, and all the members enjoyed a wonderful afternoon in Prabhupada’s presence.

By his own example, Prabhupada had taught us the meaning of real culture, the importance of hosting guests and serving them prasada. And from then on, we served the members prasada every Sunday after the noon arati.

Although our Deities had been in Juhu for more than two years, They did not yet have specific names. One day I mentioned this to a few devotees, and they encouraged me to bring up the topic with Srila Prabhupada.

“Srila Prabhupada,” I requested, “can you name our Deities?”

“Yes,” he replied. “What about ‘Radha-Madana-mohana?’”

“Srila Prabhupada, the Deities in Hyderabad are already called Madana-mohana.”

“Then what about ‘Radha-Govinda?’”

“Srila Prabhupada, the Deities in New York are called Radha-Govinda.”

Prabhupada paused thoughtfully, considering.

“What about ‘Radha-Rasabihari?’ Is that all right?”

“Yes, Srila Prabhupada!” And smiling in bliss, I paid my obeisances and left..

Later, as I was going back over the exchange, I thought about how in Vrindavan the three principal Deities were Madana-mohana, Govinda,and Gopinatha, corresponding to sambandha, abhideya, and prayojana. And in our discussion, we had gone from Madana-mohana to Govinda to Rasabihari, the enjoyer of the rasa dance—prayojana, the goal.

In Delhi, Tamal Krishna discovered that he had a hernia, and when he came to Juhu he informed Srila Prabhupada. Hernias couldn’t be cured by medicine, Prabhupada told him; the only solution was to have an operation. “My guru maharaja also had a hernia,” he said, “but he wouldn’t get operated, because he found out that there was a plot to kill him. So he just tolerated.”

Tamal Krishna went to Nanavati Hospital, which was nearby and was owned by a friend, but for the operation he shifted to Jaslok, in central Bombay, which was considered the best hospital in the city. Both the owner and the surgeon were life members and friends, so he would get special attention and be treated free of charge.

Prabhupada was concerned about the operation, however, and at the last minute he decided that Tamal should have it done in America, where he would get better treatment. But it was hard to make calls in India then and Prabhupada couldn’t get through by phone, so he got in one of our open Jeeps (the only vehicles we owned) and we rushed to the hospital, more than an hour ride, to try to stop the procedure.

By the time we arrived, it was too late; the operation had already been done. As Tamal Krishna had been wheeled into the surgical theater, he had been meditating on Sri Sri Radha-Rasabihari, on Their arati. And when he awoke from the anesthesia, Prabhupada was sitting by his bed. “I came as fast as I could to try to stop the operation,” Prabhupada told him, “but I was too late.”

“Srila Prabhupada,” Tamal Krishna said, “I had a dream while they were doing the operation. I dreamt that you were giving a report to your guru maharaja and Gaurakishora dasa Babaji and Srila Bhaktivinoda and all the members of the disciplic line. You were reporting on your activities here on this planet. They asked you how everything was, and you said that you had studied the people of this planet and as far as you were concerned, ‘They have no good qualities, they are not pious, they are not austere, they are not very capable of studying and learning, and they don’t have many good qualifications. The only thing is that somehow or other some of them have been induced—they have beenable—to take shelter of my lotus feet. Whatever I say, they accept. And in this way they are becoming redeemed.’”

Prabhupada smiled and nodded in approval. “Actually,” he said, “this is a fact.”

Three days after the operation, the hospital decided that Tamal Krishna could be discharged. But Tamal Krishna was adamant that he needed extra rest. “No,” he said, “I’m not leaving,” and he stayed a few extra days before returning to Juhu. There he lived in the chatai hut, in a tin room that had been used to store books. Devotees brought in a hospital bed, and he got proper prasada and personal care while he convalesced.

Prabhupada came to visit every morning after his walk, sitting in a metal folding chair by Tamal Krishna’s side for five or ten minutes and encouraging him before returning to his quarters.

“I had enjoyed good health in India,” Tamal Krishna later recalled, “and to be suddenly bedridden allowed me a lot of time to think. Vishnujana had come and gone before the operation, and the effect of his association in India was really on my mind.”

Soon he regained just enough strength to crawl onto someone’s back and be carried up to Prabhupada’s room. When he was let down, he flopped over weakly and in pain. Still, he offered obeisances.

“Why did you come up?” Prabhupada asked. “You didn’t have to.”

“I didn’t want you to keep coming to me,” Tamal replied.

“Anything to discuss?”

“Srila Prabhupada,” Tamal blurted out, “I was thinking that maybe I should go back to America for some time.”

Prabhupada was thoughtful. “Why?”

“Well, I can probably quote half of the Bombay municipal codes, but I can’t quote nearly as many verses of the Bhagavad-gita.”

“Oh? That is not very good. What will you do?”

“I can preach there. I’m a sannyasi. I’ve been managing too much. This Bombay case has taken so much effort. We’ve been in lawyer’s offices, and I’ve spent hundreds and hundreds of hours like that. I think I need a change.” Actually, he had been considering this since he had met up with Vishnujana in India and Vishnujana had told him how great the preaching was in America. Vishnujana had suggested thatthey go traveling together in a bus, holding festivals, distributing books, and recruiting devotees.

The idea was appealing, and the period of Tamal Krishna’s recuperation served to increase his desire. “The illness gave me an opportunity to drink deeply from Srila Prabhupada’s books,” he remembered, “something I had rarely found time to do at any length since coming to India. This only served, however, to increase my hankering for preaching. Vishnujana’s visit had stirred remembrances of our friendship.”

“I’m out of here,” he told Dhristadyumna. “But Prabhupada will never let me go.” He knew that Prabhupada didn’t want his GBC representatives to leave their posts.

Prabhupada considered this a serious matter. Tamal Krishna was his GBC for India, and great progress had been made in the four years he had held that position. Prabhupada was aware how austere serving in India could be for his Western students, yet without them it would not be possible to develop Lord Chaitanya’s mission on the subcontinent. Before going to America, he had tried, but without success. Now that he had positive results, he was reluctant to change course and kept a tight rein on his disciples’ movements. Tamal Krishna was an authority figure, and anything he did would set a precedent. If he left India, others might follow.

Still, Prabhupada did not make an immediate decision. Tamal Krishna spoke with him several times about the proposal, and finally, after a few days, although he had at first been reluctant, Prabhupada concluded that a brief change might be beneficial. “Yes,” he said, “we can always pay a manager, but preaching is a matter of realization.” He stressed how important preaching was to the movement. Without it, he said, “ISKCON will become rubbish. The management will be at our fingertips if the devotees simply follow the rules, chant, and take prasada. Preaching is first.”

Prabhupada told Tamal about how he too had left home to preach: “I was always thinking how I could benefit everyone. As the Bhagavadgita says, sarva-bhutanam. Unless one has come to this realization, how can he be a representative of God? I never had any national or humanitarian concerns, but concern for all living entities. Even at home as a householder I was preaching and people were coming. But my family members were upstairs taking tea. I was very angry with them. I told mywife, ‘You either give up tea, or lose your husband? She thought I was joking. But I was determined and took sannyasa. The family took it as a great shock. But now I am fully satisfied.”

“It is our good fortune that you had this disagreement with your wife and that she chose tea instead of you,” Tamal said. “Because now we are all saved.”

“Go and preach and remain active,” Prabhupada said, “and when you are old enough you can go and sit down in Mayapur and simply chant Hare Krishna.”

“But Srila Prabhupada,” Tamal said, “what does ‘old enough’ mean?” “That has to be judged by the individual. As for myself, I am not so old.” “Then,” said Satsvarupa, who was sitting with them, “we also will follow your example and never say we are old enough to stop preaching.”

“Prabhupada called me to his room to give me his blessings and final directions,” Tamal Krishna later recalled, “because we would be separated for some time. Now that I would be outside of India, his instruction to me was surprisingly simple: Learn from Vishnujana how to perform traveling sankirtana from city to city, then take a van with some brahma-charis, travel, and distribute books.”

On April 18 Prabhupada left Bombay for Hyderabad, and there too he spoke about the police commissioner’s statement:

“In Bombay our temple construction has been refused by the Commissioner of Police. Why? Because we chant Hare Krishna. They have openly written that ‘bhajan is a nuisance.’ You see? This is our position. Krishna, Bhagavan, says, catur-vidha bhajante mam. This bhajana word is there. ‘Four kinds of people engage in bhajana" Who are they? Sukrtino "rjuna: ‘Those who are pious.’ And now bhajana is a nuisance. The Vedic scriptures say that bhajana is performed by pious men, and now 'bhajana is a nuisance.’ Satatam kirtayanto mam yatantas ca drdha-vratah. These are the statements of Vedic scripture. Who is a mahatma? Mahatmanas tu mam partha daivim prakrtim asritah. Satatam kirtayanto mam yatantas ca drdha-vratah. These are mahatmas. Nitya-yukta updsate. But at the present moment . . . Not at the present moment—from time immemorial this has been going on. As soon as you become a devotee, as soon as you are inclined to take part in bhajana, you will have so many enemies. Therefore Chaitanya

Mahaprabhu has recommended that you tolerate. You cannot give up your bhajana and Krishna consciousness. That is not possible. Tolerate. Trnad api. What is the process of toleration?

trnad api sunicena  
taror api sahisnuna  
amanina manadena  
kirtaniyah sada harih  
\[Cc Adi 17.31\]

\[“One who thinks himself lower than the grass, who is more tolerant than a tree, and who does not expect personal honor yet is always prepared to give all respect to others can very easily always chant the holy name of the Lord.”\]’’

After ten days in Hyderabad and Tirupati, Prabhupada returned to Bombay. On his first morning walk, he explained why he felt that in pursuance of Krishna’s mission, it was his duty to expose false swamis, yogis, sadhus, and all sorts of other religious and political so-called leaders. I had read aloud from the Krsna book that Krishna had “advented Himself just to kill all undesirable elements in the world,” and Prabhupada responded, “Yes. Similarly, this movement is advented to kill all the so-called yogis, swamis, avatars, philosophers, commentators—rascals. We have to kill them. Kill means .. vanquish all these rascals, so-called swamis. People challenge me, ‘Why do you criticize others?’ Because we have to vanquish them. Now these people cannot come up. When there is sunrise, there is no use of these glowworms. This Krishna consciousness movement is Krishna Himself. Therefore they must be finished, all over the world, the so-called religionists, so-called philosophers, so-called avatars, swamis, and yogis—finished. Our program should be like that.”

When Krishna had confronted the Kaliya demon, I had read, His devotees, the Vraja-vasis, had felt transcendental anxiety. “Does the sentiment of anxiety or fear for Krishna’s welfare exist in the spiritual world, in Goloka?” I asked.

“Yes,” Prabhupada explained. “That is separation. The gopis are full of anxiety: ‘Oh, Krishna has gone to the pasturing ground.’ Their anxiety is there. Rukmini was thinking, ‘Oh, Krishna may give me up. He istalking in this way? She fainted. So, anxiety is there—the anxiety that one may be separated from Krishna. That is the anxiety. Actually, there is no separation—only the feeling of separation out of ecstatic love. One who has got love for another person—beloved—always thinks, ‘My beloved may not be separated from me? This is the ecstasy of love. Just like a miser who has much wealth always thinks, ‘My money may not be lost. My money may not be lost? Out of his excessive attachment for the money, he thinks like that. ‘How shall I protect this money?’ To earn money is troublesome; to keep money is troublesome; and when it is lost, that is also troublesome. This is the position. But with Krishna there is no such thing as loss.”

The topic turned to devotees’ sufferings. “‘O Lord,”’ I read, “‘You have descended especially for the purpose of annihilating all kinds of disturbing elements within the world, and because You are the Absolute Truth, there is no difference between Your mercy and punishment?”

“The surgical operation is there,” Prabhupada explained. “The knife is being used on the patient’s body, but that means he is getting relief. It is not punishment.”

“Is that benefit coming in all suffering,” I asked, “or only when it is given by Krishna?”

“When there is suffering given by Krishna. Therefore a devotee does not take suffering seriously. Tat te 'nukampam susamiksamanah: A devotee thinks, ‘It is the favor of Krishna that He has put me into suffering? They never see suffering as suffering. It is Krishna’s favor. That is a devotee’s vision. It is exactly like a son who knows his father well. If the father slaps, the son never protests. He knows that ‘It is good for me? Similarly, a devotee never is disturbed when there is suffering given by Krishna.”

“A karmi’s suffering is just the laws of—”

“The karmi is different. He is suffering like a criminal is suffering. A criminal is given a slap by the police. But that slap and the father’s slap are different. Although they look the same, there is great difference.”

“So, there is no benefit to suffering unless it is connected with Krishna?” Satsvarupa asked.

“Yes. Therefore we should fully surrender to Krishna. As Bhaktivinoda Thakura says, marobi rakhobi yo iccha tohara: ‘Now I surrender.

Now if You want to maintain me, that is all right, and if You want to kill me, that is also all right? This is surrender. It is not business: ‘If You maintain me, then I surrender. If You kill me, then I do not.’ It is not like that. Marobi rakhobi yo iccha tohara. ‘Now, as You like. If You want to maintain me, that is good; if You want to kill me, that is also good.’ This is the devotee’s view.”

Hearing Prabhupada’s words, I felt chastened, that my own lack of surrender was being exposed.

Satsvarupa brought up that “Someone might say, ‘But if one is surrendered, why should Krishna give him trouble?”’

“Yes,” Prabhupada said, “because He is always free. Why do you make Krishna dependent on your so-called goodwill, that Krishna must always give me pleasure’? This is sense gratification, that you approach Krishna for your comfort. That is not bhakti. That is sense gratification. Prahlada Maharaja was given suffering by his father so harshly, but he never said, ‘Oh, I am devotee of Krishna and \[He is\] giving me so much trouble? Oh! Give it up.’ He never said that. Neither he asked Krishna to come and save him. The Pandavas were always with Krishna, and they were suffering. They never asked Krishna, ‘You are the Supreme, so why we are suffering?’ They never said. This is krsna-bhakti”

‘“Because You are the Absolute Truth, there is no difference between Your mercy and punishment,”’ I repeated.

“Yes. This is to be understood. If we understand the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Absolute Truth, then this is the understanding, that either suffering or enjoying, it is all Krishna’s mercy. There must be some purpose. When Krishna puts me into suffering, there must be some purpose. So, we should welcome it, because it is Krishna’s mercy. Tat te 'nukampam susamiksamano bhunjana evatma-krtam vipakam. ‘I should have been suffering more for my misdeeds. It is Krishna’s mercy that He is reforming me with only slight suffering. I would have suffered very greatly on account of my past deeds, but He is kindly accommodating me by giving little suffering. That’s all.’”

I felt humbled. I realized how far I had to go to reach the stage of full surrender, of pure devotional service. Yet I also felt grateful, that I was under the merciful protection of Krishna and His most merciful representative, Srila Prabhupada.

Things had quieted down in Juhu, and every night, I visited Prabhupada in his quarters, reported on my activities, and received his instructions—the high point of my days.

Flushed with enthusiasm one evening after a day of meeting people in Bombay, I told him, “I like preaching very much?

“Not ‘I like preaching,’” Prabhupada replied, “but ‘preaching is my life'”

Another evening, after a long day in the city, having, as usual, traveled there and back in the crowded trains and to and from the train station in a crowded bus and not having had anything to eat since morning, I staggered up to Prabhupada’s room, exhausted.

Prabhupada looked at me and asked, “How are you feeling?”

Only then did I notice how weak and sick I was. “Well, frankly speaking, Srila Prabhupada,” I replied, “I feel a little tired.”

He already knew, and he immediately ordered grapes for me. He said that they were very good for strength and energy. Then he insisted that I eat the grapes in his presence, and after a minute or two he asked if I was feeling stronger. And yes, I was. “To work very hard for Krishna for two days,” he concluded, “and then to recuperate for three days—that is not a very good proposal.”

Another time, he encouraged me to dress better. He told me, “There is a saying: ‘One who is known as a brahman doesn’t have to wear a thread.’ People know you, and they also like you, but still, you should dress more nicely.”

I never knew when he would give me an instruction, and whenever he did, I concentrated with my full attention and tried to commit to memory everything he said. But my method, he could see, wasn’t the most reliable. “To remember,” he emphasized, “means to remember to write it down.” He added, “You should always carry a pen and paper” and then told me something else that he wanted me to remember.

Prabhupada knew my mind. I was always attracted to the Six Gosvamis of Vrindavan, and I imagined that one day I would be like them, roaming the forests of Vrindavan, chanting “Krishna! Krishna!” But he was also concerned that his property be managed properly, and one evening he spoke to me about it. “Raghunatha dasa managed his father’s estate just like an expert businessman,” he told me. “Similarly, you should also manage your father’s estate. Then you go to Vrindavan and become a gosvami”

Another night, he explained to me the purpose of gurukula in Krishna conscious children’s education. “We cannot expect that many of the students will stay in the temple,” he said, “but they should be trained so nicely that no matter what they do later in life, they will never forget Krishna.” Then he told how he and his sister used to fly kites and pray to God to make their kites fly higher. “They should be trained in such a nice way that no matter what they do in life, they will never forget God.”

As the weather became more pleasant, in the early evenings Prabhupada began sitting on his building’s roof. Satsvarupa would bring up Prabhupada’s bolster pillow and a mattress so he could sit comfortably and speak with guests or, if no one came, sit and chant japa as the sky darkened. Prabhupada’s apartment was in the middle of the tenement buildings, so he could hear the children playing below, and sometimes he would comment how he wished they could all become devotees. He said that he would like to propose to the tenants that they could all live on our land rent-free if only they would become devotees, attend the temple programs, chant Hare Krishna, and follow the regulative principles.

Sri Biharilal Khandelwal was our first supporter in India to pledge one lakh rupees for any of Prabhupada’s projects. One day his secretary phoned and gave us the news that Mr. Khandelwal’s mother had passed away; we were requested to come and perform kirtan. So I organized whatever devotees I could, and we went to chant and offer some words of consolation from the Bhagavad-gita.

Haridas, who did not know about the program, was fanning Prabhupada on the terrace above his apartment that evening, and when at seven o’clock Prabhupada noticed that there was no sound of kirtan from the temple, he asked him to find the devotees and send them to the temple for arati.

Haridas soon returned and told Prabhupada that he had looked everywhere and there were no devotees around. “They must have gone to the city to collect and not yet returned,” he suggested.

“This was not my idea, that they should go to the city and collect all day and night,” Prabhupada said. “Our process is to please Krishna. They may go at nine in the morning and return by five in the evening,and then chant in front of the Deities. Otherwise they will become like karmis.

“We are successful because we try to please Krishna and Krishna is merciful and reciprocates with us. Otherwise, Mr. Nair was much more powerful than we. He had money, influence, his own daily newspaper—he had contacts, so many politicians and government officers. And who were we? We had no money, no influence, and no support. Yet we were successful because we were simply trying to please Krishna, following the regulative principles of devotional service—by Krishna’s grace.

“So, we should come and sing and dance in front of the Deities and please Them, and by Their grace we will get all success. We are not successful by our own strength; we are successful by Krishna’s grace.”

In the morning, Prabhupada asked where all the devotees had been the night before, and we explained that Mr. Khandelwal had invited us to perform kirtan after the death of his mother. “Well,” Prabhupada said, “then that’s all right.”

Later in 1974 George Harrison came to Juhu to visit Srila Prabhupada. He was wearing a white kurta and white yogi pants and had a bead bag. I took him around the property, and he expressed his appreciation for our work and encouraged us in our efforts. When at twelve-thirty we heard the conch shell blow for raja-bhoga arati, we went to the temple shed, and George chose a pair of kartals and sang with the other devotees. Puri dasa, originally from Scotland, was doing the arati, and when he turned to offer the ghee lamp to the devotees and saw George, his hand started trembling so much that he thought he might drop the lamp.

After the arati, I arranged a plate of maha-prasada for George and accompanied him to meet Prabhupada in his apartment. Prabhupada greeted him warmly, and I left them together and returned to my office.

“Prabhupada was behind his desk,” Kishor dasa later described, “with George in front of him. I barely remember what was said, but I remember the feeling of love that went back and forth between them. It was tangible. I didn’t really understand what this relationship was. I was young, and here was a big rock star, and a pure devotee of Krishna, and there was me somewhere. But I could just feel this feeling of love that went back and forth between Prabhupada and George.” After theirconversation, George and Prabhupada were served hot prasada and ate side by side on chonkis, small, low wooden tables.

About two hours later, a pudgy twelve-year-old boy with glasses— the son of our friend and supporter Pranjivan G. Valia of the Hare Krishna house—came to my little office at the back of the property. “I heard George Harrison is here,” he said.

“Yes,” I replied, “he is.”

“I want to see him,” he stated.

“Well, you can’t. He’s meeting with Srila Prabhupada.”

He looked me straight in the eye, sizing me up, and, concluding that he wasn’t going to get anywhere with me, turned, dashed to the stairs, and bolted down the steps.

Oh my God, I thought. He’s going to try to find him. And I bounded down the stairs in hot pursuit.

I ran across to the next building, and when I reached the second landing, in front of Prabhupada’s flat, I found the door ajar. The boy stood just inside, and beyond him George sat cross-legged with his back erect, like a yogi—a perfect disciple listening attentively at the feet of his master.

With the boy’s abrupt appearance, Prabhupada and George had ended their meeting, exchanging some final words. George was gracious and appreciative, Prabhupada affectionate and kind. I was upset that the boy had interrupted them, but they took it as a matter of course. Maybe it was time for the meeting to end; maybe they saw it as Krishna’s arrangement.

Shyamasundar and I accompanied George back to the temple shed for darshan of the Deities. George paid full dandavats, lying completely flat on the floor before Them for a long time, and then left.

The next year, on a morning walk in Sanand, Gujarat, Prabhupada spoke about the meeting: “He is very nice boy—George. I have studied. Very good boy. He showed me in Bombay. He came to see me in Bombay, last year. He is keeping Jagannatha within his bead bag and chanting.”

For Nrsimha-caturdasi, a troupe of devotees led by Jagat Purusa organized a drama depicting the appearance of Lord Nrsimha, to beperformed in the temple room. There was an all-male cast, including the young and slender Nava Yogendra as Prahlada Maharaja; Bhagavata, who was quite large, as Nrsimhadeva; and Jagat Purusa, who was very thin, as Hiranyakasipu. The stage was set before anybody arrived, and Bhagavata, wearing a massive lion headdress, was hidden with a microphone in a papier-mache pillar that had been built in the corner of the darshan area. He narrated the drama, but because his voice was broadcast by speakers, nobody knew where he was. Prabhupada sat on his vyasasana, and the play went on all around him, with the temple room itself as the stage and everyone else in the audience outside on the grounds.

Hiranyakasipu was the most powerful man in the universe, so he was supposed to have a big, muscular physique, but the drama opened with him when he was performing his austerities—standing on the tips of his toes with outstretched hands, with all his ribs showing—and afterward Jagat Purusa put on shoulder pads and lots of wadding.

Anirdesavapu had been in the pujari room washing pots, but when the person playing Lord Brahma didn’t show up, the devotees asked him to fill in. All he had to do was respond to Hiranyakasipu when he asked for his boons, they assured him, and they dressed him up with some ornaments and a crown and sent him to the temple room.

From his viewpoint on stage, Anirdesavapu could see how absorbed Prabhupada was in the drama. “When he saw me,” Anirdesavapu described, “he was astonished and opened his eyes wide, as if he was actually seeing Lord Brahma. His eyes got big, his head tilted back, and he was smiling. He wasn’t just seeing some brahmacharis dressed up in makeshift costumes—he was seeing Lord Brahma and the other divine personalities.” At the climax, when Hiranyakasipu called for Prahlada’s lord and pounded the pillar, Bhagavata, as Lord Nrsimha, burst out with a roar, and Prabhupada opened his eyes wide and leaned so far back that his vyasasana almost toppled over.

Decades later, Jagat Purusa still remembered the day vividly: “Over the years, I had done dozens of dramas with various devotees, but I’d never had an experience like this. In one particular school of drama, the Stanislavski School, the actors meditate upon their roles and by doing so transform into the characters they are portraying. I wasn’t really trying to train the devotees in this way, but even without any consciousattempt, by Srila Prabhupada’s presence every devotee in the drama ceased being that devotee and became the part he was playing. It was just unbelievable! Srila Prabhupada was there from the opening scene to the very end, and he was showing all these amazing expressions: surprise, concern, happiness, delight. Some of the devotees could barely watch the drama, they were so transfixed watching Srila Prabhupada watch it unfold. Everything was flawless, because it was not a drama—it was a pastime.”

Afterward, the actors, still in their costumes, sat down where they were for Prabhupada’s lecture. “Today is the appearance day of Lord Nrsimhadeva,” he began. “I am so pleased that within such a short time these boys have nicely learned how to play, and especially I have to thank Mr. Hiranyakasipu,” at which everyone laughed and applauded. “Mr. Hiranyakasipu has played his part very nicely.”

The devotees—especially the actors—were exuberant. “As every devotee knows,” Jagat Purusa recalled, “nothing—nothing—compares with getting the confirmation that Srila Prabhupada is pleased with something that you have done in his service. I was sitting there just two feet from his lotus feet, and I felt myself melting into the cracks between the tiles, and I thought, This is the best time for me to leave my body! It is so fulfilling to know that Srila Prabhupada is pleased.”

Almost exactly a year after the Bombay Municipal Corporation’s (BMC’s) attempted demolition of our temple, our Juhu neighborhood witnessed a horrific repercussion. One person who had joined with Mr. Nair against us was Mr. Krishna Rao Rane, the man who lived in the old mansion across from the temple and had been laughing when the BMC had brought blowtorches to cut through the steel tubes.

Rane held influence over many people in the area, because he had money and some intelligence. His mansion looked like a classic haunted house, and he conducted nighttime seances by candlelight in his garden, with stone seats and an altar, invoking the spirits of people’s dead ancestors and claiming to communicate with them. In India then, one had to be quite wealthy to own a car, but for some of his gatherings, parked cars would line the road, so we knew that even affluent people were coming to him. He was playing on their naivete. And he didn’t like us, becausewe were spreading knowledge, while he was thriving on people’s ignorance. So he joined the clique against us.

Soon after Gandiva’s mother, Yashoda, had cursed Rane for his laughter during the temple demolition, “Just as you are laughing when Krishna’s temple is being burned, one day you will also burn,” Rane contracted cancer and was tormented by pain. And then, one morning at mangala-arati time, we heard shrieks coming from his house, and we saw an ambulance drive up. Eventually we got the news that Mr. Rane had covered his body with kerosene and set fire to himself. He had died before the ambulance arrived. (Later I heard that when a black magician sends a ghost to attack another person and the ghost fails in his mission, the ghost returns to attack and torment the one who sent him.)

“This temple was his forefather’s,” Dr. Patel explained on a morning walk. “They were doing sraddha-puja here. He was a great, roguish sort of man. His grandfather or somebody had some power to know things here and there, and people used to come and worship him and give him money. Parsis were coming often. Parsis are a very simple community.”

“He committed suicide?” a local man, Nara, asked.

“Yes,” Dr. Patel replied, “he committed suicide, rightfully. He burned himself by pouring kerosene on his clothes.”

“He was drinking,” Nara added, “and—”

“What was he not doing?” Dr. Patel said. “He was in all this, a big debauchee—mentally, physically, and sensually.”

In honor of Mr. Rane, the BMC named an open garden between Hare Krishna Land and Sheetal Apartments “Krishna Rao Rane Maidan.”

One of Prabhupada’s visitors at Bhogilal Patel’s had been an Indian devotee from America. He had worn tilak and the white dhoti and kurta of a householder, but his head hadn’t been shaved, and I had not been sure of his position. While he had been talking with Prabhupada, however, I had noted their intimate and affectionate mood. I had rarely witnessed such familiar, affectionate conversations between Prabhupada and any of his disciples. When I had asked one of my godbrothers who the devotee was, he had told me, “Gopal Krishna.”

Gopal Krishna often visited Bombay to meet his mother, who lived in Santa Cruz, not far from Juhu, and about eight months after I first saw him, he joined Prabhupada on a morning walk and told him of a doctor who wanted us to open a small hospital or dispensary as part of the Juhu project. Prabhupada rejected the idea: “No, we cannot divert our attention. You can say that ‘We consulted Prabhupada, and he said, “At the present moment, until our building is there, we cannot accept any other extra business?” ... You can say plainly that ‘For the present, we are not interested. We have got many more important businesses than this hospitalization?”

Bhagavata mentioned that the devotees had recently had kirtan in a hospital and that “immediately all the patients became happier. The whole attitude had been very dull and unhappy and morose, that ‘Oh, we are in the hospital. My body, my body .. ? But as soon as we had the kirtan, they all got out of bed and came and watched, and some were clapping and chanting.”

“Just see,” Prabhupada responded. “Immediately life. Just try to understand how much great responsibility you have got.”

“They all appreciated that we did the kirtan.”

“Even the Russians appreciate. . . . People say that our devotees are bright-faced. They are surprised to see the American boys. ‘Are you Americans?’ Yes. Completely changed. They cannot recognize. Is it not?”

“My parents telephoned last week,” I said, “and at first they couldn’t recognize my voice. They couldn’t believe that it was me. My father said, Are you sure it’s you?”’

Prabhupada laughed, “Just like a lawyer.” And we all laughed at that. “Mother is also very nice. Unless father and mother are nice ...”

With permission to build the temple complex stalled, Prabhupada arranged with Mr. Sethi to build an additional story on the tops of the existing tenement buildings. We needed funds, and Mr. Sethi suggested to Prabhupada that if we held a benefit performance with famous artists, we could make money for the construction. “You can do,” Prabhupada replied.

“Only, Prabhupada,” Mr. Sethi added, “we will need some devotees to sell tickets.”

“Our devotees cannot sell tickets," Prabhupada replied. “They are meant for selling books.” If Mr. Sethi and his friends promoted the program and gave the profit to the temple, he had no objection, but the devotees could not be directly involved.

My dear friend, our generous supporter Damodar Chanrai (who had given Rs. 25,000 for Vrindavan and had built Jaslok Hospital, where Tamal Krishna had his hernia operation), told me that the Sindhi Hindus in Lagos, Nigeria, were making a lot of money, and he invited me to come there and stay with him. Brahmananda was in Bombay then, and I took him to meet Mr. Chanrai. The plan was that Brahmananda and I would meet in Lagos and preach together and that some percentage would go to the African mission and some to Hare Krishna Land. When I told Prabhupada about this arrangement, he said, “Why should a percentage go to Africa?” I could see how serious Prabhupada was to get funds for Juhu—how important Juhu was to him.

I considered whether there was any need for Brahmananda to meet me in Lagos. Instead, I arranged for Bhugarbha and his wife, Annada, who was a Sindhi, to come from France and join me in Lagos, and together we would all proceed to Bombay.

Prabhupada flew to London on May 17, and I left for Lagos two days later, entrusting more responsibility to the Indian devotees: Jasomatinandan, treasurer; Caitya-guru, temple commander; and Manasvi, property manager. Sridhar Swami was the main collector and leader of the preachers as well as a sannyasi and the most senior devotee.

It was the first time I was leaving Bombay by my own choice, though I had been encouraged and sanctioned by Srila Prabhupada. I felt hopeful about going to Africa and preaching and raising funds, but I also felt a little concerned about Bombay, especially since Tamal Krishna had also recently left. But Prabhupada had worked hard to strengthen the management and felt confident that somehow or other things would carry on. He suggested that in my absence the other leaders should meet from time to time to discuss and solve the problems, and they agreed and met at least once a week.

So, I went to Nigeria, and in less than a month I was able to collect two lakhs rupees, which was enough to finish the additional floors on the existing buildings.

On June 8 Manasvi wrote Srila Prabhupada, “Today by Lord Krishna’s grace we began the construction on the E building. In the morning all the devotees assembled there, and some of the tenants also attended the ceremony. In the midst of maha-sankirtana Mr. Sethi laid the first brick, and one municipal corporator broke a coconut, and people helped to put up the first window frame. Prasada was distributed to all the workers and the people assembled there, and also to all the tenants.”

The roofs of the old buildings were flat, with little white ceramic tile chips set in cement, and Prabhupada said that we should keep that flooring and build the walls and roof over it. We did not know anything about construction or local conditions or labor or materials; Mr. Sethi was arranging almost everything.

I wrote to Prabhupada a few days later, after my return from Lagos: “Here at Hare Krishna Land the construction is going on the rooftops of the E and F Blocks. The F Block is already plastered on the inside, and today the plumbing and electrical work will begin. In addition, the tile floor has to be put in, and then the building will be ready for our habitation. Due to heavy rains it is not possible to give a definite estimate of when the work will be finished, but seven to ten working days should be sufficient. The slab on the E Block has also been put up, and in three days the wooden supports can be taken down. Then the process of plastering the walls and installing plumbing and electrical work and tile floors will follow, and that building may be ready in 15 or 20 days of work. When the F Block is ready for habitation we shall vacate the hut and use the materials to build a godown for cement and other construction items on the other foundation. The present hut cannot be retained as the godown, because our master plan shows that area as garden and in order for the master plan to be passed we must demolish the hut. As soon as the hut is demolished the master plan will be approved, and once the master plan is approved we will submit the complete proposal for the main project in Hare Krishna Land. Mr. Sethi is practically handling the construction himself and is very anxious to demolish the hut so that the main plans can be passed and we can begin construction on the temple after monsoons.” The additional floor on the E building was to become the brahmachari ashram, and the additional floor of the F building was to become Srila Prabhupada’s area, with his personal quarters in one apartment and his staff’s quarters in the other.

In the next month, the brahmacharis shifted to one of the new apartments and the hut was nearly demolished. “We have received an allotment of 30 tons of cement from South India,” I wrote Prabhupada, “and as soon as the cement is received by us we can begin construction on the third rooftop.” The plan was that when the second rooftop apartment was ready, the brahmacharis would move from the first rooftop to that one and the grihasthas would move into the first.

On August 16 Prabhupada wrote me, “I was very glad to learn that you had such a nice Janmastami celebration and that even our Mr. Sethi was dancing during the kirtan. Actually it is due only to him that the plans for the residence quarters were approved by the municipality.”

Soon thereafter, we received a telegram from Brahmananda that Srila Prabhupada, in Vrindavan, had become very ill—so weak that he could not walk or stand. He had a 104-degree fever and was diagnosed with malaria. Prabhupada had said that his illness had been caused by the sinful activities of his disciples, many of whom were not strictly following the rules and regulations.

So we began twenty-four-hour kirtan, and many people of the neighborhood joined. Some stayed until midnight; others came before mangala-arati. Prabhupada’s presence in Juhu had touched and transformed the hearts of many of the local residents. Our tenant Mr. Menon had become a Vaishnava and was wearing tilak. He would sit at the foot of Prabhupada’s vyasasana and read “Lord Krsna Fights with Banasura” from the Krsna book, about how Lord Krishna’s Narayana-jvara weapon cooled down Lord Shiva’s Siva-jvara (heat weapon), in the hope that in a similar way Prabhupada’s fever would be reduced.

Mr. Chugh from down the road also came, saying, “Prabhupada’s life on this earth is so precious that I would rather my life be taken so he can remain to complete his work.”

Brijmohan Sethi told us that he had started twenty-four-hour kirtan in his father’s house and was praying that Prabhupada remain to see the completion of the Juhu temple. “Then Prabhupada will be very happy,” he said, “and only then will my father and I be satisfied.”

Dr. and Mrs. Singhal were collecting money door-to-door to pur -chase dhotis and kurtas for the devotees. They too came, and

Mrs. Singhal recounted how kind Prabhupada had been to her in London, taking care of her in all respects. Friends and neighbors were constantly inquiring about Prabhupada’s health and remembering his kindness upon them.

On August 28 I wrote Prabhupada, “I do not really know what to write, on account of your health.
