However, I would like to invite Your Divine Grace to come to Hare Krishna Land as soon as you feel a little better, because the climate here is mild and the atmosphere relaxing. Sankha Prabhu has covered the entire back corner near your quarters with a fruit orchard, including banana, papaya, and guava trees. And we have built a little place where the cows can graze, so the view from your balcony may be very pleasing. Of course, Hare Krishna Land is yours and you are always free to come and go whenever you desire. But we just wanted Your Divine Grace to know that we are eager to serve you here.”

On September 16 I wrote, “Your new accommodations at Hare Krishna Land are nearing completion and as soon as they are ready, I shall inform you.” I added, “We understand that in order to spread this movement to the maximum number of people, we must have the most intelligent and expert organization. We have vastly expanded our propaganda and organizational activities from the office in the Chand Society, and we very urgently require the large room in which the unmarried ladies are staying. Therefore, we request permission from Your Divine Grace to move your belongings from your old flat on Hare Krishna Land into your new block. Then the ladies can shift from the office to your old flat and we can use the additional room for organizational work in the office.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada replied, “you can move my things into the new quarters.”

In September, Orient Longman publishers approached me to contribute a chapter about Srila Prabhupada for a book entitled Gurus, Godmen, and Good People. The book, to be edited by Khushwant Singh, would have one chapter for each person, and the publishers wanted a devotee of each to write the chapter about his or her guru. I first sent my preliminary draft to Prabhupada, then wrote, “If Your Divine Grace has any suggestions or changes you would like to make in the chapter, orany particular message you would like included, you can inform me and I shall do the needful."

Brahmananda replied on his behalf:

“Regarding your letter dated September 27, 1974, Srila Prabhupada requests the following to be included in the article for ‘Holy Men of India.' It should be very nicely written that so far as cultural contribution to the world is concerned, Srila Prabhupada stands first above all other Indian holy men. Many have gone to the West and abroad, but no one has done what Srila Prabhupada has done. He has completely brought the Vedic culture to the West, and they are following completely. He has transplanted it. This simile of transplanting should be elaborated. As we transplant a tulasi seedling and then it becomes a full-grown plant, so Prabhupada has made the Vedic culture flourish all over the world, without harming or changing anything. When transplanting you have to be very careful with the seedling. If you harm it even slightly it will not grow again. Similarly, Prabhupada has not superficially transplanted the Vedic culture.

“Please send the final draft. I hope this meets you in good health.” Eventually the book was published with my chapter about Prabhupada and a picture of his disciples singing and dancing on hari-nama-sankirtana in central Bombay on the cover.

In the meantime, Prabhupada continued looking for a GBC replacement for Tamal Krishna. “I am now in India,” he had written Atreya Rishi, “so in my presence another GBC may not be required, but if required in my absence, my question is whether it will be possible for you to take charge . . . while keeping your occupation intact?” As it turned out, Atreya Rishi did not come, so Prabhupada tried Karandhara and Jagadish, but neither lasted more than a few weeks.

“Life in India was difficult,” Srutakirti later remembered. “When devotees from the West came, they had no idea what to expect; they thought it was going to be like doing things in the West.” Juhu was especially challenging. “The battle went on for years. Devotees would come from the West to battle for the Juhu property, and before long they were licking their wounds, devastated and wanting to leave India. Just being in India was difficult in the early ’70s, and dealing with the problems in Bombay was impossible.”

Prabhupada decided to try Bhagavan, who was the GBC for France. “I understand that you will be coming in about a week’s time,” Brahmananda wrote him. “Srila Prabhupada confirmed my suggestion that you go straight to Bombay. In this connection Srila Prabhupada said the following: ‘So far as I have studied, there is a clique of some enemies to acquire the land and spoil the whole scheme. So we have to save ourselves. Even if there is no sanction to build further buildings, we should maintain what we have got. We should not let anyone infringe on our rights. The book distribution program must be thoroughly organized.’”

On October 22 Prabhupada wrote the letter we were all waiting for, informing us that he would be returning to Juhu: “Regarding the construction, you should immediately begin work on all four of the remaining flats. The work must begin whether you have got sufficient cement or bricks or not. If you have to lay only one brick, then do that. I may be coming there next week, so you can prepare for that.”

The following day, I replied, “Here in Bombay we have so many different departments of activity that it is necessary to depute various devotees to different departments. Mr. Sethi has been in charge of the construction department, but as President I have been meeting with him every day from fifteen minutes to one hour to check step-by-step the progress in all of our construction activities. Mr. Sethi is personally seeing, along with Mr. Sharma, to the passing of the plans and to getting the No Objection Certificate from the Police. In addition, Mr. Sethi is engaging labor contractors and material suppliers from among friends of his who regularly work with him on his projects. We have compared the prices and quality of the goods and services Mr. Sethi is arranging from his friends with the qualities and prices of goods and services available through other life members or in the market. We have found that in almost every case Mr. Sethi’s quality is the best and his price is the lowest. Even after purchasing materials or taking labor, when the particular contractor or supplier comes for his bills, we take the bill to Mr. Sethi and in his presence reduce the bill even further and then only do we pay. The final result is that we are getting very good results for very little money. Mr. Sethi’s devotion to Your Divine Grace and attachment to his service seem to be growing rather than diminishing. Within a family there may be differences of opinions, but the bond of affection between the family members prevails. Similarly,in one or two occasions Mr. Sethi may have been disappointed with the confusion in our office, but his devotion to his work has not at all diminished. You may know that when Manasvi Prabhu left for Los Angeles he did not properly hand over his portfolio. In addition, when he was in Bombay he was not very willing to let the other managers know exactly what he was doing. Therefore, after he left there was a period of confusion. Now, however, we have taken steps to organize all the files and pending matters in a very tight way so that there is no misplacing of papers or losing track of pending matters.

“Mr. Sethi also appreciates the problems posed by Manasvi’s departure, and he is also pleased to see that we have taken steps to rectify the situation.

“The ladies who were staying in one of the office rooms have shifted to your old apartment, and by adding an additional one room to the office, the organization has become even better.

“Regarding the new accommodations, they are very nice. When Gargamuni Swami and Jayatirtha Prabhu visited we were in the process of building an additional staircase from the \[third\] floor up to the terrace. As such, workers were breaking down many of the walls, and naturally dirt was spread in the ashram. However, certain devotees are assigned to clean the ashram every day, and the floors and bathrooms are all washed and mopped at least once a day. We have recently taken delivery of five big cupboards for accommodating the devotees’ personal belongings and bedding. These cabinets will allow us to pick everything off the floor and keep the room neat and clean and ready for use for other activities during the day. We are also getting the necessary furnishings for your personal secretaries and your translating and editing staff so that they may work as efficiently as possible.”

Prabhupada had left Vrindavan for Delhi, Calcutta, and Mayapur on September 22 and returned to Bombay on October 31.

With the first additional quarters ready, Mr. Sethi brought him for a tour. Prabhupada was extremely pleased with the progress. It was, he told Mr. Sethi, the duty of the spiritual master to provide accommodations for his disciples. “And just as you are building these rooms for my disciples here at Hare Krishna Land,” he said, “Lord Krishna is making your rooms ready in Krishnaloka.”

“I am a sinful man,” Mr. Sethi replied. “How I can go to Krishnaloka?” “That I will see to,” Prabhupada assured him. “This is not your duty.

I will see that you will go to Krishnaloka.”

As we were walking with Prabhupada through the building, he said, “Every day you must lift everything off the floor and wash the floors with a wet cloth. Now that Krishna has given us such nice facilities, we must keep them very clean.”

By then, Bhagavan had come to assume responsibilities as GBC, and one day he went to discuss the situation with Prabhupada, to assess the challenges and consider his responses. Afterward, Prabhupada told Gargamuni the story of the thin horse. “In Bengali it is said, Bada bada ghoda gela rasatala, beta ghoda bole kata jala. There was a great, overflowing river. Many big, big horses tried to cross, but they were swept away by the strong current. And one lean and thin horse came and asked, ‘Can you tell me how much water is there?’” In effect, Prabhupada was saying that so many big GBCs had come and been swept away, and this little Bhagavan dasa was asking how formidable the challenges were.

In his talk with Gargamuni, Prabhupada discussed the frailties of all his leaders in Bombay, including me. He said that I was like a traveler—or a coolie—at the train station who very carefully places all his belongings in a cloth but doesn’t tie the cloth properly, so when he picks it up, all the things fall out. “In the same way,” he said, “Giriraj collects profusely, but he doesn’t take care to see that the money is not wasted.”

“And then,” he continued, ‘“Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare,”’ perfectly imitating my loud, distinctive way of chanting.

When Gargamuni related to me what Prabhupada had said, I was astonished. Prabhupada always seemed so pure and innocent, almost childlike; I didn’t imagine that he saw our weaknesses, or idiosyncrasies, so clearly and accurately, and I certainly never expected that if he did see them, he would discuss them with someone else. But later, upon further reflection, I considered that Prabhupada knew that Gargamuni would tell us what he had said and therefore, in a wry, indirect, and thus gentler way, he would instruct and correct us.

Sometimes Bhagavan would accompany me when I met important people I was cultivating to contribute to the Juhu project, and my interactionswith them seemed so smooth and easy that Bhagavan thought he could do the same thing. Finally, one day I let him speak to a wealthy Sindhi businessman, but somehow he said all the wrong things and the gentleman became very upset and angry and I had to intervene to pacify him.

Srutakirti was skeptical about how Bhagavan would fare in Juhu. “He was always dressed nicely in white silk dhoti and kurta, pressed very nicely,” Srutakirti recalled. “And he told Prabhupada, ‘Don’t worry, Prabhupada, I am going to take care of this situation here. I’ll work very, very hard.’ But within a week he didn’t have the same luster anymore ... another war casualty.”

Almost every day Bhagavan and I would go to the city to work on the permission for the temple. We would usually return just in time to take some prasada and attend the class and kirtan.

Prabhupada was so concerned about the work that sometimes he would call us to the vyasasana during the program and ask for the news. But he also wanted us to be happy in Krishna consciousness. So, one evening during the program he announced from the vyasasana, “You must always dance in kirtan—even if you don’t get the permission.”

The new accommodations were complete, but Prabhupada was determined not to leave Bombay until we got the NOC from the police and permission to build the temple. The fourth, final volume of the Third Canto of Srimad-Bhagavatam had just been published, and Prabhupada spoke on it every night, eventually determining that the talks should be compiled into a book, which was published as Teachings of Lord Kapila, the Son of Devahuti.

When the additional stories were being built on top of the existing tenement buildings, Prabhupada had instructed me to retain the white ceramic chip flooring that covered the roofs to serve as the new floors. Unfortunately, the cement in the flooring started to crumble, and in my presence Bhagavan criticized me to Prabhupada, saying that I was so cheap that I had not put in proper flooring and now the cement was crumbling. Prabhupada knew that I would have accepted anything he said or didn’t say; still, he admitted to Bhagavan, “I told him to do that.” I was impressed and heartened by Prabhupada’s forthrightness and integrity.

Another time, Bhagavan said, Prabhupada told him that we should be so expert that when people finished dealing with us they would tell their friends, “Those Hare Krishna people may look like fools, but they’re very intelligent—don’t mess with them.”

There was a “scarcity” in India during that period, and many droughts, and Prabhupada often spoke on Bhagavad-gita 3.14:

annad bhavanti bhutani  
parjanyad anna-sambhavah  
yajnad bhavati parjanyo  
yajnah karma-samudbhavah

“All living bodies subsist on food grains, which are produced from rains. Rains are produced by performance of yajna \[sacrifice\], and yajna is born of prescribed duties.”

“What Krishna says is practical,” he argued in one talk. “Annad bhavanti bhutani parjanyad anna-sambhavah. ‘But how we shall get anna, food grains? There is no rain.’ You see nowadays, there is no rain. Why? Because we do not know how to get rain. Krishna says, parjanyad anna-sambhavah: ‘There will be food grains when there is sufficient rain.’ And how there will be rain? Yajnad bhavati parjanyah: ‘If you perform yajna, then there will be sufficient rain.’ Nowadays people may say, ‘How to perform yajna? It requires so much money, so much ghee, so much food grains to offer as oblations.’ But Krishna has made it very easy. Yajnaih sankirtana-prayair yajanti hi sumedhasah. The shastras know that in the Kali-yuga it will be very difficult to perform the ritualistic yajna ceremony because people will be poor, poverty-stricken. Where they will get ghee, and where they will get grains? No. This is the yajna: kalau nasty eva nasty eva nasty eva gatir anyatha. Harer nama harer nama harer namaiva kevalam. Chant Hare Krishna mantra. This is yajna.”

Prabhupada also emphasized our prasada distribution program. Every Sunday we would feed people at the temple. But because of the so-called scarcity, the government had passed a law that a person or organization could not serve grains to more than twenty people at a time. The intent was to restrict the lavish functions of the rich, so that a few wealthypeople would not be able to spend huge amounts on grand feasts and celebrations while the poor people were suffering for want of grains.

We, being charitable in nature, were feeding people rice and dal and kichari on Sundays, so although we were aware of the law, we never thought much about it. Mhatre, however, arranged for the police to come one evening during our Sunday prasada distribution to arrest us, on the grounds that we had violated the limits.

Bhagavata dasa was in charge of the distribution. Bhagavan and I were also present, but we all decided that it would be more threatening to our work if Bhagavan or I was arrested. The police were demanding someone, so Bhagavata said he was in charge of the program, and they arrested him and took him away, though we were able to get him out on bail within a day or two.

On his morning walk the day after Bhagavata’s arrest, Prabhupada was considering how Mhatre, just one man, could do so much damage. It might have been coming from the communists, he suggested, because Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, or the Indian government, was in close touch with the Russian government—and we were presenting the only combination that could defeat communism: spiritual enlightenment and Krishna prasada. It was possible that the Russian leaders may have mentioned something to Mrs. Gandhi about the threat from ISKCON.

While we were trying to deal with the police commissioner, some friends suggested that we approach the additional police commissioner, Mr. Jog, who was supposed to be more friendly and accessible. Mr. Valia and Mr. Bakshi said that they knew the additional commissioner and that he would help us. As a rule, whatever new information we got we would present to Prabhupada, and he would weigh it all and then guide the strategy. He agreed that we should meet Mr. Jog and appeal to him to help us. Then came the question of who should go. Prabhupada said that Bhagavan and I should go. I suggested adding Lokanath, since he was a Maharashtrian and most of the officers were Maharashtrian, with a strong ethnic identity. At first Prabhupada said that three was not a good number, that it should either be two or four, but when we couldn’t think of a fourth person who could actually help our presentation, he agreed to the three of us.

So, we went and met Mr. Jog, and he was very friendly—but evasive; he didn’t commit to anything.

Every morning in the temple, Prabhupada would speak on Srimad-Bhagavatam 3.25. In one talk, he spoke about our situation in relation to a verse describing the qualities and behavior of a sadhu:

titiksavah karunikah  
suhrdah sarva-dehinam  
ajata-satravah santah  
sadhavah sadhu-bhusanah

“The symptoms of a sadhu are that he is tolerant, merciful, and friendly to all living entities. He has no enemies, he is peaceful, he abides by the scriptures, and all his characteristics are sublime.” (SB 3.25.21)

Although Prabhupada himself perfectly exemplified the verse, he related it to the devotees in Juhu:

“Here all the boys and girls, the devotees, they are concerned with Radha-Krishna. That’s all. Their whole business, day and night, is Radha-Krishna. From early morning, three o’clock, to night, ten o’clock, their only business is Radha-Krishna. That’s all. Therefore they are sadhu.

“And so many people are criticizing. We are not getting the sanction to build, because we have so many enemies. They say we are creating a ‘nuisance.’ We are chanting the Hare Krishna mantra, and that is a ‘nuisance.’ This complaint is going to the police. So, that is very difficult.”

Filled with emotion, Prabhupada exclaimed, “Therefore a sadhu is advised, titiksavah, tolerate! Tolerate all this nonsense! What can be done? We have no other alternative but to tolerate. Nobody’s coming to help us. Our business is so thankless. Because we are trying to create one temple, so many enemies are giving hindrance: ‘You cannot do it.’ Therefore titiksavah. You have to remain sadhu. You cannot become asadhu. You have to tolerate. What can be done?

“At the same time, you have to be merciful. You know what has happened in this place, Hare Krishna Land? So much attack by the police, by the municipality: ‘Break this temple.’ We could have gone, concluding, ‘What is the use of taking so much botheration? We have hundreds of temples outside India. If people here are not liking, let us go away.’

No. Karunikah, We have come to distribute Krishna consciousness. We must tolerate and give this message to the people. Karunikah: very merciful, in spite of all trouble.

“These American boys and girls have come to help me—not that they have come because they are hungry. No. My mission is, ‘You Americans, you chant Hare Krishna so the people of India will see, “Oh, Americans are also chanting. Why not we?’” But unfortunately— such dull brains—that thought is not coming. But still, we have to do it. We have to tolerate, and we have to become karunikah, merciful.

“Why should you want to be merciful? Para-duhkha-duhkhi. Krpambudhir yas tam aham prapadye. A Vaishnava understands, ‘These people are engaged like cats and dogs in sense gratification. They are misguided, and in the next life they’ll be punished. Let us do something for them.’ This is karunikah: out of mercy. There is no question of getting something, money. No. We have got sufficient money. But just to become merciful upon these fallen, conditioned souls, who are suffering on account of becoming animalistic, without Krishna consciousness, the preacher, the sadhus. . . These are sadhus—titiksavah, tolerant: ‘Never mind. Whatever hindrances and tribulations they are offering to us, never mind. Tolerate.’

“And suhrdah. Suhrdah means the heart is so nice.... The Vaishnava is always thinking how a man can be saved from the clutches of maya. He has no other desire. The Vaishnava is so kind that suhrdah sarva-dehinam: he is kind not only to the human beings but to all embodied souls—cats, dogs, trees, plants, insects. A Vaishnava will hesitate to kill even a mosquito. Sarva-dehinam, Not that ‘I shall take care of my brother only. I am good, and my brother is good.’ No. Suhrdah sarva-dehinam.

“And ajata-satravah, When one is living in that way, as a sadhu, why will others become his enemy? The sadhu does not create enemies, but people become enemies out of their own character. How can a sadhu create enemies? Krishna says, sarva-dharman parityajya mam ekam saranam vraja, and we are simply teaching, 'My dear human being, my dear friend, you become a surrendered soul to Krishna.’ So, what is our fault? We don’t create any enemy, but they become enemy. Why shall I create enemy? Suhrdah sarva-dehinam, But they become, out of their own nature....

“We are in this society, human society, and because we are spreading Krishna consciousness, the envious, who are more dangerous than snakes, are putting so many impediments. But we have to tolerate. We have no other alternative. You see? Ajata-satravah santah. Be peaceful. What can be done? Depend on Krishna.

“These are the ornaments of a sadhu: titiksavah karunikah suhrdah sarva-dehinam, You must know what is a sadhu. First, a sadhu is a devotee. And if he is a devotee, then all the symptoms are there. Now, you find a sadhu and associate with him. Then your path of liberation will be open."

For us, of course, Prabhupada was that sadhu. And by his words and example, he was encouraging us to try to become sadhus as well.

Just before six every morning, I would walk up the stairs to Prabhupada’s room to accompany him on his morning walk. But when another devotee and I went on the day after Rama-ekadasi, we were surprised to find the doors—both to his quarters, on one side, and to his staff’s quarters, on the other—locked. I wasn’t sure what to do, but I gently knocked on both doors. After a minute or two, Prabhupada’s secretary, Harikesa, opened the assistants’ door just a little and said that Prabhupada had stayed up all night and completed his translation of Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, that at the end he had written the most beautiful glorification of his guru maharaja, and that he was in an ecstatic mood and had said that we should celebrate by having a feast.

In his Concluding Words, Prabhupada had written, “Today, Sunday, November 10, 1974—corresponding to the 10th of Kartika, Caitanya Era 488, the eleventh day of the dark fortnight, the Rama-ekadasi—we have now finished the English translation of Sri Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami’s Sri Caitanya-caritamrta in accordance with the authorized order of His Divine Grace Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura Gosvami Maharaja, my beloved eternal spiritual master, guide and friend.”

Prabhupada recounted his first meeting with his guru maharaja and receiving his instruction “to preach the cult of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu in English in the Western countries.” At first he had resisted the order. “Because at that time I was a complete nationalist, a follower of Mahatma Gandhi’s, I submitted to His Divine Grace thatunless our country were freed from foreign subjugation, no one would hear the message of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu seriously.... but at last I was defeated and convinced that Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s message is the only panacea for suffering humanity. I was also convinced that the message of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu was then in the hands of a very expert devotee and that surely the message of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu would spread all over the world. I could not, however, immediately take up his instructions to preach, but I took his words very seriously and was always thinking of how to execute his order, although I was quite unfit to do so.”

When in 1950 Prabhupada had retired from family life and then taken sannyasa, he had finally been, in his own words, “completely ready to discharge the order of my spiritual master. ... By the mercy of His Divine Grace, I was able to come to New York on September 17, 1965. Since then, I have translated many books, including Srimad-Bhagavatam, the Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu, Teachings of Lord Caitanya (a summary), and many others.

“In the meantime, I was induced to translate Srl Caitanya-caritamrta” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta’s favorite book. “I think that \[he\] is always seeing my activities and guiding me within my heart by his words. As it is said in Srimad-Bhagavatam, tene brahma hrda ya adi-kavaye. Spiritual inspiration comes from within the heart, wherein the Supreme Personality of Godhead, in His Paramatma feature, is always sitting with all His devotees and associates....

“It is my wish that devotees of Lord Caitanya all over the world enjoy this translation, and I am glad to express my gratitude to the learned men in the Western countries who are so pleased with my work that they are ordering in advance all my books that will be published in the future. On this occasion, therefore, I request my disciples who are determined to help me in this work to continue their cooperation fully, so that philosophers, scholars, religionists and people in general all over the world will benefit by reading our transcendental literatures.”

Srila Prabhupada was like a grandfather to the children of Juhu, affectionate and tolerant. A couple of days after he completed his translation, on Diwali, there were fireworks—both literal and figurative—at Hare Krishna Land. As Smriti Warrier recalled, “On Diwali evening Mother Kanta was in the women’s ashram above our flat and we were outside setting off fireworks. It was around nine, and I guess she wanted to rest, but we weren’t finished playing. So, she started throwing buckets of water down on us. My brothers and I marched up to Srila Prabhupada’s room. Caitya-guru caught us and said, ‘You can’t go in there—he’s resting.’ We must have made a lot of noise, because Prabhupada called, ‘Let them in.’ My brothers went in and pleaded that we wanted to do fireworks, but Prabhupada said, ‘No, it’s too noisy.’ So my brothers gave up and walked out. But I, the youngest, stood there and said, ‘But it’s Diwali—we’ve got to break some firecrackers.’ Then Prabhupada said, ‘All right, until 10:00—but after that, no more.’ So, we got permission and broke firecrackers. And the next morning, Mother Kanta came with a plate of maha-prasada and apologized for throwing water on us.

“Being so close to Srila Prabhupada, at Hare Krishna Land, we got to associate with him in a different light.”

Years later, Kanta dasi remembered, “Throwing water on the Warriers was probably the worst thing I ever did to the neighbors there, and they were so nice. I threw a bucket or two, but I’m kind of a follower; I’m not an instigator. All the women were complaining because we had to get up early, and everybody was tired and grouchy. I don’t even think I threw the first bucket, but I did throw one or two. I felt really bad about that the next day, because I’m all for those kinds of celebrations, especially when you have kids and grandkids. I’d probably participate now. But we were grouchy ladies that time.”

One morning in Bhagavatam class, Prabhupada described the process of attaining love for Krishna—becoming mad for Him. “To understand Krishna,” he said, “is very, very difficult. Out of many, many millions of persons, one tries to make his life successful. And out of many, many such successful persons, yatatam api siddhanam, who have attained siddhi, perfection, one may understand Krishna. First of all, we cannot understand Krishna. Then where is the question of love of Krishna? If you do not understand somebody, how you can love him? Love is far, far away. But Chaitanya Mahaprabhu is so kind that He is distributing krsna-prema: ‘Take, anyone. Come on.’ Krsna-prema-pradaya te.

“Chaitanya Mahaprabhu is very practical: ‘I want to give krsna-prema. One should be ecstatic, emotional in krsna-prema. One should cry for Krishna? And He taught everyone by His practical example how He was mad after Krishna. Govinda-virahena me. Sunyayitam jagat sarvam govinda-virahena me. This is krsna-prema: without Krishna, one should see everything vacant. This is Radharani’s prema.”

Prabhupada was quoting Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s Siksastaka (7):

yugayitam nimesena  
caksusa pravrsayitam  
sunyayitam jagat sarvam  
govinda-virahena me

“O Govinda! Feeling Your separation, I am considering a moment to be like twelve years or more. Tears are flowing from My eyes like torrents of rain, and I am feeling all vacant in the world in Your absence.”

“But that is not possible for an ordinary human being,” he continued. “It might be possible for Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and few devotees. His immediate disciples the Six Gosvamis were following the same principle. The Six Gosvamis lived in Vrindavan, and they were seeking Krishna, becoming mad.

he radhe vraja-devike ca lalite he nanda-suno kutah  
sri-govardhana-kalpa-padapa-tale kalindi-vane kutah  
ghosantav iti sarvato vraja-pure khedair maha-vihvalau  
vande rupa-sanatanau raghu-yugau sri-jiva-gopalakau

They were mad after Krishna: ‘Where is Krishna?’ They never said, ‘We have seen Krishna? And Chaitanya Mahaprabhu said, ‘I was dreaming of Krishna, so why you woke Me? I have lost the chance? In this way they were doing bhajana. This is called viraha-bhajana, separation—the most highly recommended process. So, we should be awakened, awaken our consciousness, Krishna consciousness, in such a way that being separated from Krishna, we shall become mad after Him. This is krsna-prema. That prema was being distributed by Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. And He is still distributing.”

Prabhupada was giving us a glimpse of his own internal mood of Krishna consciousness and inspiring us to follow in his footsteps. Twodays later, when he reached verse 32 of the twenty-fifth chapter of the Bhagavatams Third Canto—“When that service spirit is engaged in devotional service to the Personality of Godhead, without any motive, that is far better even than salvation”—he explained, “A devotee is not very much anxious for mukti because a devotee is always mukti, liberated. If you have got millions of dollars, why should you hanker after ten rupees? Bhakti is such a nice thing. But what is bhakti? Bhakti is animitta bhagavati. Bhakti should be animitta not with a motive that ‘I shall go to the temple and serve Krishna for some purpose.’ Krishna can fulfill any purpose you desire. It is not very difficult for Him, because He is almighty, full with all opulences. So, if you want material happiness from Krishna, it is not very difficult for Him. He can give you even mukti. But to ask Krishna for anything other than bhakti is foolishness.

“My guru maharaja used to give this example: If you go to a rich man and he says, ‘Now, whatever you like, you can ask from me, and I shall give you/ then if you ask him, ‘You give me a pinch of ash,’ is that very intelligent? Similarly, there is a story that one old woman in the forest was carrying a big bundle of dry wood, and somehow or other, the bundle fell down. It was very heavy. So, the old woman became very much disturbed, ‘Who will help me to get this bundle back on my head?’ She began to call God, ‘God, help me!’ And God came: ‘What do you want?’ ‘Kindly help me to get this bundle on my head.’ Just see. God came to give benediction, and she wanted ‘Put this bundle back on my head.’

“So, we are doing the same thing. We go to God and ask Him, ‘Kindly give me the bundle on my head. May my family become happy. May I have a large amount of money to enjoy material things.’ We ask that. That is our foolishness. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu teaches us, therefore, that actually, if you want something from God, that should be only begging for His service.

“This Hare Krishna maha-mantra means addressing God, Krishna, and His energy, Srimati Radharani, Hare: ‘O internal potency of Krishna.’. . . When you address somebody, you want to ask something. So if they respond, ‘Yes, why you are calling?’ then, ‘Please engage me in Your service.’ This is the prayer, not ‘Give me money’ or ‘Give me a beautiful wife’ or ‘many followers.’ These are material hankerings. But

Chaitanya Mahaprabhu says, ‘No: Na dhanam na janam na sundarim kavitam va jagadisa kamaye' He prayed, ‘O Lord of the universe, I do not desire material wealth, materialistic followers, a beautiful wife, or fruitive activities described in flowery language. All I want, life after life, is unmotivated devotional service to You?” (Siksastaka 4)

Hearing Srila Prabhupada’s strong words, by his grace, I felt both chastened and enlivened.

Continuing his talks on Srimad-Bhagavatam 3.25, Prabhupada came to verse 35:

pasyanti te me rucirany amba santah  
prasanna-vaktraruna-locanani  
rupani divyani vara-pradani  
sakam vacam sprhaniyam vadanti

“O My mother, My devotees always see the smiling face of My form, with eyes like the rising morning sun. They like to see My various transcendental forms, which are all benevolent, and they also talk favorably with Me.”

He related the verse to our beautiful Deities of Sri Sri Radha-Rasabihari and the benefit people receive by appreciating Them:

“Here it is said, pasyanti te me rucirani Krishna is so beautiful, rucirani. Rucira means very attractive. Now, fortunately, people in Bombay say that our Deity here is most beautiful. They say there is no such Deity in Bombay city. So, this is our duty, to dress Krishna in such an attractive way that people at least see that it is very beautiful. Then a person becomes a devotee, simply by appreciating. Simply by appreciating, if they say, ‘Now the Deity worship is very nice,’ they go a step forward—immediately, simply by appreciation. Then other things will come gradually. Therefore the temple worship should be exactly to the routine, to the instruction of the shastra and guru and acharya, so that the worshiper as well as the visitor, both of them will benefit. They will be gradually seeing \[the results\].

“Krishna is so kind that He has consented to appear in a way that we can see. At the present moment we cannot see Krishna, as He is spiritually embodied, sac-cid-ananda-vigrahah, because we have no eyesto see sac-cid-ananda-vigrahah. Here is also sac-cid-ananda-vigrahah, arca-murti. It is not idol worship. The atheist class may say so, but it is not so. Those who have got eyes, they can see. Just like Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, when He entered the temple of Jagannatha, immediately He fainted: ‘Oh, here is My Lord. Here is My Lord.’ So, one has to become santah. Then one can see. But it is by culture. Premanjana-cchurita-bhakti-vilocanena santah sadaiva (Bs 5.38). When you develop that culture, when you develop that love for Krishna, then you will see immediately, and you will faint: ‘Oh, here is my Lord.’”

On December 13 Prabhupada wrote to his friend Dr. V. Channa Reddy, the governor of Uttar Pradesh, summarizing our difficulties in obtaining the NOC and permission to build, and asking him to approach the governor of Maharashtra and request him “to do justice to us”:

My dear Shri Reddyji:

I thank you very much for your kind acceptance of our invitation, and I have read your letter dated November 19,1974, with great interest. Your acceptance of the authority of the Bhagavad-gita and Srimad-Bhagavatam through the blessing of Lord Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu has given me so much transcendental bliss that my ecstasy knows no bounds. Very rarely do we find such an ideal devotee like you in the political field. Actually speaking, according to the Vedic conception of life, every head of the state should become rajarsi, which means a king or governor or ruling chief should be as ideal as a great saint or rishi. Therefore formerly saintly kings were many. The Mahabharata means greater Bharata. So we find saintly kings like Maharaj Yudhisthira, Maharaj Parikshit, Maharaj Bharata, and so on, what to speak of King Lord Ramachandra. The whole history of the battle of Kurukshetra is based on this principle of finding out a rajarsi on the throne of the kingdom. Lord Krishna Himself took part in this battle of Kurukshetra to install Maharaj Yudhisthira on the throne of the world empire and to pluck out the usurper king like Duryodhana from the seat of the ruling power. Bhagavad-gita, the essence of all Vedic literature, was firstly being taught to the rajarsis or the saintly kings. That is recorded in the Bhagavad-gita Fourth Chapter: imam vivasvate yogam, proktavan aham avyayam/ vivasvan manave praha, manur iksvakave ’bravit. (4:1)

So at the present moment there is great need of rajarsis on the head of the ruling government. So I am glad to see you on the throne of Uttar Pradesh as Governor, and I expect your administration should be as ideal as the former rajarsis. At least I expect that you should try to give an example of an ideal Governor from the holy place of Uttar Pradesh where is situated such holy places as Ayodhaya, Varanasi, Prayag, Mathura, Vrindaban, Haridwar, etc. In Bhagavad-gita it is stated: yad yad acarati sresthas, tat tad evetaro janah/ sa yat pramanam kurute, Iokas tad anuvartate. “Whatever action is performed by a great man, common men will follow in his footsteps. And whatever standards he sets by his exemplary acts, all the world pursues.”

I wish that your tenure of office may be an exemplary administration with reference to the principles of the Bhagavad-gita and the Srimad-Bhagavatam. I thank you once more for your agreeing to be our chief guest on the day of Sri Rama Navami, the inauguration ceremony of our temple in Vrindaban. I wish that you may come there one day before the ceremony and remain there at least 24-30 hours in Vrindaban, and by the grace of Krishna Balaram I may arrange for your comfortable stay in our ashram house which is completing construction. I want this opportunity so that we may talk a little bit on the principles of Bhagavad-gita and Srimad-Bhagavatam in the matter of political, social, philosophical, religious, and cultural development of the human society.

I am pushing on this Hare Krishna Movement all over the world with an idea of uniting the human society on the principles of Bhagavad-gita As It Is. I have already established many, many temples all over the world. One of the temples you have already seen is our Vrindaban construction, and similarly I want to establish a great center in Bombay because Bombay is the most important city in India. Many foreigners come to Bombay to enjoy the Juhu Beach atmosphere, and there are already many foreign hotels like Sun-n-Sand, Horizon, Holiday Inn, and so on. So in order to attract the foreigners I purchased land in Juhu, 20,000 sq. yards, just one block from the sea beach, and I am trying to get sanction for constructing the temple, but it is being hampered by the dilatory method of the Municipality and the Police Commissioner.

Just after purchasing the land we submitted our plans to the Municipality, and the Municipality wanted the Police Commissioner’s sanction, and thus we submitted our application to the Police

Commissioner on November 15, 1973 ... and we received the reply as follows:

...Dear Sir:

Reference your letter dated November 19th 1973 on the subject noted above.

2\. There is no objection to your digging the allotted space for the temple structure at Hare Krishna Land, Bombay 54.

3\. You are advised to approach this office a-fresh for a “No Objection Certificate\*\* when you decide to construct a permanent structure at this site in question, after plans have been approved by the Municipal Commissioner.

Yours faithfully,

Sd/

For Commissioner of Police, Gr. Bombay

As advised in this letter our engineer and architects applied for the final sanction by the Police Commissioner and we received a surprising letter as follows:

Subject: “No Objection Certificate” for the construction of a Temple for the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, Hare Krishna Land, Gandhi Gram Road, Juhu, Bombay 54

Dear Sir:

Reference to your letter No. 7274/BMC/1731 dated the November 21st, 1973, on the subject noted above.

2\. It is regretted that your request for the grant of “No Objection Certificate” to the construction of a temple on Hare Krishna Land, Gandhi Gram Road, Bombay-54, cannot be granted on the following grounds-

The construction of a temple may lead to more traffic congestion on Juhu Tara Road.

The bhajan singing which had been complained about in the past, is likely to be a nuisance in future as well.

Yours faithfully,

Sd/for Commissioner of Police

The matter is since then suspended, and later on we proved there is no nuisance, neither is there any difficulty to the traffic. It was properly enquired by the Traffic Police, and we gave over land forextending the road, and the Municipality has accepted the proposal in their letter as follows:

...Sir:

You are requested to advise your client to hand over the setback land ... as the work of widening the road is taken in hand by this office. You are requested to remove the fencing etc. and re-erect beyond set back land.

Yours faithfully

Sd/

Asst. Engineer Maintenance

Dated 3 August 1974

So, in this way the matter has been prolonged since November 1973, and no final decision has been made either by the Municipality or by the Police Commissioner. Recently we reminded the police commissioner, the copy of which is enclosed herewith, but still have not received any final decision. According to the permission for digging and according to the Municipality advice, we have expanded the internal road to 30 feet, sacrificing many trees, and have dug the ground in many places, and taken out the barbed wire fences. In this way we have spent Rs. 25,000/-, and yet have not gotten the permission for the construction for the temple on some plea or other, for the past more than one year.

So I am very much perplexed in this connection. Yesterday our men went to see the Police Commissioner. Now he says, not in writing but verbally, that it requires Government permission. I therefore request you to help me in this great perplexing situation. I was to go to the foreign countries, Bangkok, Hong Kong, Tokyo, Honolulu, Fiji, Australia, and South Africa for two to three months, but on account of this situation I have postponed my touring at the cost of my preaching activities, and at last I am taking your shelter. If you kindly help me as a Life Member of our Society, because you know everything about us. We do not belong to any political party or any sectarian religious conception of life. We are just spreading the philosophy of the Bhagavad-gita and the Srimad-Bhagavatam, and we have had no difficulty in constructing temples in every part of the world, except here in Bombay, where we have been choked up.

As you know from the above facts there is no cause for obstructing us. If the temple is a nuisance, there is another temple just in front of us already there. Our temple has never been accused of theso-called nuisance, and I do not know why the Police Commissioner has raised this question.

Anyway, I have dared to take shelter of Your Excellency just to request you to contact the Governor of Bombay and request him to do justice to us, by personally seeing the records and files called for from the Police Commissioner of Bombay. Please recommend our case for constructing the temple, as we are innocent in the matter of so-called intrigues and politics. By this act of your generosity I wish Krishna will bless you, and I shall also pray to Krishna for your long and prosperous life as you will save us from this great unnecessary anxiety.

I hope this will meet you in good health, and with my good wishes and regards I beg to remain,

Yours affectionately,

A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami

Prabhupada had been scheduled to go to Bangkok, but because of the importance of the work in Bombay, he decided to stay on and to send Brahmananda in his stead. I was delighted: we would get more of Prabhupada’s association, guidance, and support, and he was confirming the great importance of the Juhu project.

The day after writing to Governor Reddy, Prabhupada wrote to “the people of Bangkok, Thailand,” “I am sorry I am not able to come but I must remain here in Bombay for some pressing matters. So I am sending my secretary His Holiness Brahmananda Maharaja who will represent me.

“The Krishna Consciousness mission is not sectarian. We want to do what the United Nations has failed to do. The human form of body is an opportunity for solving all the problems of life. Through evolution we come to the human life for solving this problem. The real problem is the repetition of birth, death, disease, and old age.

“But there is another status of life where there is no birth, death, disease, and old age. The Krishna consciousness movement is the means for promoting the human being to that status. This is a great science, and it is elaborately explained in the Bhagavad-gita.

“So our mission is to give this benediction to all humanity. Let us cooperate together on this basis so that it will be a more effective United Nations. We shall be united on the basis of the prime need of human society, spiritual life.”

Under Prabhupada’s guidance, we were pursuing the NOC and the permission to build on all fronts. Prabhupada himself was dealing with Governor Reddy to get through to the governor of Maharashtra; Bhagavan and I were dealing with the police commissioner; and Mr. Sethi was dealing with his friend Mr. Pai, who, like Mhatre, was also a municipal councilor, to try to get the plans approved by the municipality.

Eventually Mr. Sethi told Prabhupada that if we wanted the plans passed, we would have to pay something. We all knew that the officers and politicians in India were corrupt and that practically nothing moved without a bribe, but we had never indulged in such practices and had never proposed doing so to Prabhupada. Although the municipal commissioner was a relatively small officer compared with the ministers, Mr. Sethi told us, his income from bribes was 20,000 rupees a day.

Mr. Sethi explained that initially only the officers were taking bribes but that after some time even the clerks and peons working in the office had started to demand them: they wouldn’t take your file off the shelf unless you paid them something; they wouldn’t process your file from one table to another unless you paid them. When news of this had reached the officers, they had been indignant and had summoned the clerks and peons and told them, “What is this nonsense that you are demanding money for doing this little service?” But the clerks and peons had said, “You are taking bribes for your work, so why shouldn’t we take bribes for ours?” The officers hadn’t been able to reply and thus had been forced to condone the lower-level corruption.

Mr. Sethi explained that a percentage of every bribe was paid higher and higher up, and that at the top, at least in theory, the prime minister herself received a portion of every bribe paid. The ward officer was accountable to the commissioner, the commissioner was accountable to the urban-affairs minister, the urban-affairs minister was accountable to the chief minister, and the chief minister was accountable to the prime minister. So any bribe paid somewhere along the line would have to be distributed upwards, with each person in the hierarchy receiving his or her share, so that the operation could work smoothly.

When our application for the NOC was again refused, Prabhupada and Mr. Sethi concluded that we should apply for municipal permissionwithout the temple, because only the temple required the NOC. And Mr. Sethi felt confident that if we didn’t have to get the NOC from the police, he could get the permission for the rest of the project, the residential quarters and preaching areas, from the municipal commissioner. So Prabhupada agreed that we give Mr. Sethi 5,000 rupees.

As Mr. Sethi pursued the permit, he kept Prabhupada informed on a regular basis. “We are definitely getting it in two weeks,” he would report. “We are definitely getting it in one week.” “We are definitely getting it in three days.” And then something would come up and he would say, “Well, it’s going to take another two weeks.” Eventually he told Prabhupada that he needed another 5,000 rupees.

Prabhupada called for a meeting with Bhagavan and me to discuss the whole affair. He asked whether we thought Mr. Sethi had “swallowed,” kept, the 5,000 rupees, or whether he had given it to Mr. Pai and Pai had kept it—whether we should give Mr. Sethi the additional funds. He discussed the matter with us all evening, from shortly after 8:00 until almost midnight, asking us for our opinions. When we presented the view that we shouldn’t give the money to Mr. Sethi, Prabhupada said why we should—and we became convinced. Then, when we were convinced that we should give the money, Prabhupada would present arguments why we shouldn’t, and again we became convinced. There were so many factors to consider—whether Mr. Sethi would give the money, or the full amount, to the commissioner; whether the commissioner, having taken the money, would give the permission, or whether he might take the amount and then keep asking for more—so many complexities. In this way Prabhupada kept going back and forth. I started to doze off, but Bhagavan continued to listen attentively and respond.

Finally Prabhupada declared, “We will not do this,” and it was concluded that we would not give Mr. Sethi the money. Then he stood up from behind his desk and walked out of the room, leaving Bhagavan and me stunned and exhausted. We looked at each other, offered our obeisances to Prabhupada’s vacant asana, and retired for the night.

The next morning, Bhagavan and I were a little apprehensive about how Prabhupada would present his decision to Mr. Sethi and how Mr. Sethi would take it, and we waited anxiously for Mr. Sethi toarrive in Prabhupada’s room. As usual, he came around 10:00 and sat on the floor before Prabhupada. We all knew that he had come for the additional five thousand rupees.

“So, what do you think?” Prabhupada asked him. “Should we do it?” “Yes,” Mr. Sethi replied, “because otherwise we are not getting the permission.”

“All right,” Prabhupada said without hesitation—just the opposite of the previous night’s conclusion—and he arranged the money for Mr. Sethi.

Bhagavan and I were amazed and somewhat bewildered by what had transpired, but then we considered what lessons we might have been meant to learn from the incident. One was that Prabhupada was training us to evaluate a situation from every angle. He had always said that intelligence means to see the same thing from different angles of vision. We also considered that he was teaching us not to be naive or ingenuous with regards to even our best friends, such as Mr. Sethi, but to always be cautious and careful. Further, we considered that by agreeing to give Mr. Sethi the money, Prabhupada was showing that even though we should be alert to the possibility of cheating, we should give a good friend the benefit of the doubt. We should not offend or hurt him. And then we considered that the Juhu project was so important that even if the money was lost, it was worth taking the chance, because somehow, if we could get the permission, it would be wonderful for Srila Prabhupada’s preaching and service to Sri Sri Radha-Rasabihari.

Ultimately, Srila Prabhupada was teaching us surrender. It is said that if the guru tells the disciple that a rope is a snake, the disciple will respond, “Yes, it is a snake” and that if the guru then says, “No, it is a rope,” the disciple will agree. This is a basic principle of obedience to the spiritual master. And Prabhupada was showing us that, like Lord Chaitanya, he could take any side of an argument and defeat any other.

While working on getting the permission to build from the municipal corporation, Mr. Sethi was also helping us build the additional floors on the existing buildings. But it appeared that some of the work and materials were below standard. Some of the wood was full of holes and defects.

So Prabhupada directed us to oversee the work and materials more carefully. He had engaged Mr. Sethi to supervise the construction and had put his trust in him, but it appeared that none of the work was being done that well, albeit some was passable. When the rotten wood came to the site, Prabhupada became very disturbed and chastised us. He quoted a Bengali saying that a goldsmith, while fashioning some gold his mother gave him to make into a ring, thinks, “Should 1 use all the gold for the ring or put some in my pocket?” This type of cheating was so much a part of the goldsmith’s business, Prabhupada said, that even if his own mother gave him gold to make an ornament, he would think, “Should I cheat and keep some for myself?” Similarly, the construction business was such that someone in it would automatically think, “Should I make some extra money for myself?” You could not engage in the business, procuring materials and paying bribes and getting permits, without some cheating—no matter whose money it was.

On January 19 Mr. Sethi said that he would get the permission to build the project minus the temple in “two or four” days, and on the third day he got it. Prabhupada was jubilant and called for another cornerstone-laying ceremony. He had already held a ground-breaking and cornerstone-laying ceremony when we had first moved to the land in March 1972, and another ceremony on Rama-navami 1974. But he wanted one now to signify the beginning of the main construction. He devised a festival, wishing to invite all our life members and friends in Bombay. “Immediately you make a ceremony tomorrow,” he directed, “and then the next day I will leave.”

We informed whatever members we could, especially the intimate ones like Kartikeya Mahadevia and Mr. Vashist, a retired school principal living in Juhu whom Prabhupada had initiated as Dixit dasa and who spoke at the ceremony; some of the neighbors; and, of course, Mr. Sethi. With his own hand, Prabhupada applied the mortar around the cornerstone and fixed it in the bricks. Then he spoke about his mission:

“I’ll not take much of your time, but I shall try to convince you what is the purpose of this Krishna consciousness movement. The purpose of this Krishna consciousness movement is to save the human society frombecoming animals—cows and asses. People have established, as stated in the Bhagavad-gita, an animal or asuric civilization. The beginning of asuric civilization is pravrttim ca nivrttim ca jana na vidur asurah. In the asuric, demonic, civilization, people do not know in which way they have to guide themselves for attaining the perfection of life, pravrtti and nivrtti, what is favorable and unfavorable. Pravrttim ca nivrttim ca jana na vidur asurah, na saucam napi cacarah: ‘There is no cleanliness, nor good behavior,’ na satyarh tesu vidyate, ‘and there is no truth in their life.’ This is the beginning of demonic civilization.

“Satyam—there is no truthfulness. And the first-class life means the brahman life. Satyam saucarh—the beginning is satyam. The asuric life is no satya, no truth; and the first-class life in human society, the brahmans, is satyam and tapah saucam ksantir arjavam eva ca jnanam vijnanam astikyam.

“Our Krishna consciousness movement is to create a class of ideal, first-class men, with satyam, saucam, tapo, samah, damah, titiksah, This is godly civilization. And this godly civilization can be given to the whole world by India. That is India’s special privilege.

“And we selected this Bombay city. Bombay is the best, most advanced, city in India. The people are very nice, religiously inclined, opulent—they can take up better things very nicely. Therefore I wanted to start this center, Bombay, for spreading this Krishna consciousness movement. Although there have been many impediments in my endeavor, still, ultimately it is Krishna’s business. It will come successful. So, today . .. The foundation and cornerstone establishment was done two years before, but there were many, many impediments from the asuric jana, people. Now, some way or other, we have got a little relief from such impediments. So, we are putting this cornerstone this auspicious day, and I am very glad that you have joined us.

“So, the mission is very, very authorized, and it comprehends a large jurisdiction of activities. Therefore my request is that the inhabitants of Bombay, especially those who are our members, kindly take active part to make this institution successful in Bombay. So many ladies and gentlemen are present here. Whatever we are doing is not whimsical or mental concoction; it is authorized and just to the standard of Bhagavad-gita,

“So, make this center successful, you ladies and gentlemen of Bombay. We have got very nice place. We are building so that you can come and stay here, at least on the weekend. Those who are retired, elderly ladies and gentlemen, can come here and stay. We will have sufficient place. But try to organize these principles of Bhagavad-gita all over the world. That will be the gift of India. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu desired that anyone who has taken birth in India as a human being ...

bharata-bhumite haila manusya janma yara  
janma sarthaka kari’ kara para-upakara  
\[Cc Adi 9.41\]

‘Anyone who has taken his birth as human being in India, Bharata-bhumi, first of all make your life successful.’ Because you have got the standard, how to make life successful. Here is Bhagavad-gita, Try to understand it, make your life successful, and then broadcast this message all over the world. That is paropakara, working for the benefit of others. India’s people are meant for paropakara—not for exploiting others. That is not our mission. But actually that is being done. Everyone goes out of India to exploit. Now for the first time India is giving something to the outsiders—this spiritual knowledge. And the proof you can see. We are giving; we are not taking. We do not go to beg, ‘Give me wheat, give me money, give me this, give me that.’ No. We are giving something substantial, and they are feeling obliged. Otherwise, why these young men and girls are after this Krishna consciousness movement? They are feeling something, that they are getting something tangible. So, it has got potency, very good potency. They are not feeling like Americans or Canadians or Australians. And we are not feeling as Indians. On the spiritual platform we are one.

“So, this is a great culture, Bhagavad-gita as it is. Those responsible ladies and gentlemen present here, make this center very successful and come here and study Bhagavad-gita as it is, without any foolish interpretation. I say foolish again and again because interpretation is not at all required. Everything is clear, from the very beginning. So try to understand Bhagavad-gita as it is, make your life successful, and spread this message all over the world. You will be happy, and the world will be happy.

“I am a very old man now—eighty years old. My life is finished. But I want some responsible Indians and combined with people from other countries . . . Other countries are giving good cooperation. Otherwise, it would not have been possible for me to spread in such a short time, only seven or eight years, to preach this cult all over the world. So, I require the cooperation of the Indians, especially the educated young men. Come forward. Stay with us. Study Bhagavad-gita. We haven’t got to manufacture anything. And what we can manufacture? We are all imperfect. Whatever is there, let us study it and practically apply in life and spread the message all over the world.

“So, today is a very auspicious day. With great difficulty we have got now sanction. Now please cooperate with this attempt as far as possible with your pranair arthair dhiya vaca, four things: by your life, by your words, by your money . . . Pranair arthair dhiya vaca sreya-acaranam sada. This is the mission of human life. Whatever you have got. . . It is not that ‘Because I am poor man, I cannot help this movement.’ No. You have got your life. So if you dedicate your life, that is all-perfect. If you cannot dedicate your life, give some money. But if you are a poor man, you cannot give money, then give some intelligence. And if you are a fool, then give your words. So, in any way, you can help this movement and do welfare activities for India and outside India.

“That is my request. I welcome you.

“And you study. We have got now enough books. There is no difficulty to study our books. We have given in English translation. Every gentleman knows English. And we are going to give in Hindi, Gujarati, and all other languages. Our friends have already begun translating. So, there will be no scarcity of knowledge. Please come here, sit down at least once in a week, study all these books, try to understand the philosophy of life, and spread all over the world. That is the mission of Bharata-varsa. This is paropakara movement, to do welfare to others, not like cats and dogs, simply bring money and enjoy the senses. This is not human life. Human life is for paropakara. People are in ignorance, without knowledge of God, without the ideal of life. They are simply working like cats and dogs and hogs. They should be educated. Human life is the chance for getting such education. And this is the center for educating the human society to become actually human being and make his life successful.

“Thank you very much. Hare Krishna.”

The next day, January 24, after staying in Juhu for almost three months and finally getting permission to build, Prabhupada left for Hong Kong. And afterward, in quick succession, he visited Tokyo, Honolulu, Los Angeles, Mexico City, Caracas, Miami, Atlanta, Dallas, New York, London, and Tehran.

In London, on March 11, he reflected on his efforts in Bombay. Brahmananda, referring to one of Prabhupada’s youthful exploits, said, “You must have been very brave.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada replied, “I am still brave.” And the devotees laughed. “Otherwise, how could I come alone to preach Krishna consciousness? I am still brave.”

“Jaya, Srila Prabhupada!” the devotees exclaimed.

“Some astrologer told that ‘This boy, for executing his purpose, will enter into the fire,’” he continued. “Yes. Recently, in our Bombay affair, it was fight with fire. Is it not?

“Oh, yes,” Brahmananda agreed.

“And we have come out victorious.”

“Yes. All glories to Srila Prabhupada.”

“So many obstacles,” Prabhupada said, “and still going on. Now the governor is cornered. The governor of Maharashtra, in Bombay. If he says yes, that is dangerous for him; if he says no, that is also dangerous.”

Before Prabhupada left Bombay, anticipating getting the permission to build, Mr. Sethi had raised the question of piling, columns of reinforced concrete driven into the ground to support a building’s foundation. Generally, to determine if you needed piles or how strong the piles had to be, you hired a soil-testing company to drill into the earth and see how far down you had to go to reach bedrock. And because the Juhu land was near the beach, it was expected that the soil would be sandy, with water underneath, and that we would need piles, which would be quite an expense—two lakhs rupees. “This is sea area,” Mr. Sethi had said, “and every building has piling thirty to thirty-five feet below the ground. We must put piling in this land to build the temple.”

“No,” Prabhupada had insisted. “We don’t require piles. After a few feet the land is hard, so don’t waste money.”

Still, Mr. Sethi had harbored some doubt, and he hadn’t wanted to take chances, so he had brought in a soil specialist, who tested the topsoil, and an engineer, and he had consulted other experts. They all had agreed: “Oh, yes, you need piling.”

I felt torn. If Prabhupada said we didn’t need the piling, I thought, then we should just go ahead. But all the experts were saying we needed it. Prabhupada had left, and I was feeling pressure to begin the work, because he had said, “Begin immediately, no matter what.” But the issue of the piling was not resolved, and finally we decided to do a soil test, which was quite expensive—about 10,000 rupees. That would be the only way to know for sure.

A company brought out a boring machine, and the machine started drilling, but after only eight or ten feet the drill got stuck—it had hit bedrock. None of us had expected this so soon—except Prabhupada. The test confirmed that we didn’t need piling. In fact, the layer of rock was so strong that it took the company days to get the drill out. We were all delighted, not only because Prabhupada view was vindicated, but also because we would save a lot of money.

“Srila Prabhupada knows everything,” Mr. Sethi said. “From the beginning he said we don’t need piles.” It was one of many incidents that increased his faith in Prabhupada. When he had been extremely ill, Prabhupada had visited him and, according to Mr. Sethi, had pleaded with Krishna to save him. Mr. Sethi had survived the illness and later remembered, “Prabhupada was all-knowing. A person who can see things that are hidden from our eyes, that we cannot see—you think, ‘Oh, he has relation with Krishna.’ What relation do we have with Krishna? From the beginning, I saw that Prabhupadaji has so much intimate relation with Krishna that he came to visit and Krishna helped me, and now 1 am talking with you.”

Prabhupada was also extremely observant and acute, and he had known of another building that had been built even closer to the beach, without piles. I don’t know how he had been aware of that—I was not— but he said, “I knew that if they didn’t need piles, we wouldn’t either.”

Another time, a man greeted Prabhupada walking between the temple and the beach. He’d never met Prabhupada, but Prabhupada addressed him by name, saying, Oh, you are So-and-so, and you do such-and-suchwork. The man was completely taken aback—Prabhupada seemed to know everything about him. But then Prabhupada told us that whenever he walked between the temple and the beach, he would see the same man on his balcony, looking down, and on the balcony was a signboard with his name, advertising his services. Prabhupada said that an intelligent man noticed all his surroundings. He even noticed how many beams were in the ceiling above his head. Once, having been asked how many cars there were in the Punjab Mail train, Prabhupada told us, he had known exactly how many.

On February 5 I wrote Prabhupada with some good news: “We have received the Commencement Certificate for the towers, allowing us to come up to the plinth. We still have not received the sanction for the RCC \[reinforced cement concrete\] plans and Civil Aviation Certificate. Mr. Sethi estimates that the RCC plans will be ready in three weeks and that after Saurabha Prabhu’s approval they can be submitted to the Municipality for their approval.”

Another issue we faced was the setback land. The municipality wanted to widen the Juhu Tara Road, which ran in front of Hare Krishna Land, and so we had to cede them some of our property—the setback land—running along the road.

“The municipal officers have come and demarcated the setback land,” I wrote Prabhupada. “Presently our architect is preparing five drawings of the property according to the new setback line and upon their calculating exactly how many feet have been taken in the setback, the corporation will issue us a certificate giving us that area in FSI \[floor space index, which determined how much floor space we were allowed\] in our new proposals. Then only after receiving that certificate from the municipality will we actually surrender the land and put up the wall.”

We had worked hard to get the permission to build, but Indian permits often included many conditions and were not valid until all the stipulations were met. One of the conditions in ours was that we had to have an internal access road of a certain width. And it just so happened that right where the access road was supposed to go, there were some palm trees. When Srila Prabhupada had returned to Juhu from his tourthe year before, he had noticed that one or two of the trees had been cut down, and he’d been very concerned—even upset. “Why did you cut down the trees?” he had asked.

I had told him that they had been in the way of the road and that we’d had to cut them down to get the permission for the temple—which, I had thought, justified what we had done.

“No,” he had said. “You go to the municipality and tell them it’s against our religion to cut down trees.”

Prabhupada had told us what to do, so we’d done it, but the municipal officers had objected. Now, on March 16, when he returned from his world tour, stopping for three days in Juhu on his way to the Gaura-purnima festival in Mayapur, practically the first thing he said was, “I was just in Tehran, and I have seen they have trees in the middle of the roads. The government allows it. So, we can also have trees in the middle of our road.”

On Prabhupada’s order, we held our ground with the municipality, and they ultimately gave us the permission to keep the one remaining tree. And even today, that tree, which Prabhupada protected, is still standing in the middle of the road.

Later I reflected that if Prabhupada had so much concern and care, even love, for a tree, how much care and love he must have had for us, his followers. And it was entirely due to his care and mercy and protection that we were able to stand in Krishna consciousness—no matter what.

In a later, similar incident, when the devotees had to remove another tree to facilitate the construction, Prabhupada would not allow it to be killed. Twenty-five or thirty men had to uproot the tree, and, using a big crane, relocate it to another part of the property.

Around this time, Hamsaduta came to Juhu to meet Prabhupada. He had been having difficulties with the other leaders of the ISKCON Hyderabad farm project, and he wanted to share his frustrations with Prabhupada, who listened patiently and with sympathy. I was impressed not only by how kind and compassionate Prabhupada was, but also by how much time he had to spend with us to smooth our rough relationships and heal our hurt hearts.

Hamsaduta explained his strategy for the farm’s cows: the devoteeswould create such a superior breed, which would produce such large quantities of milk, that they would have more than enough milk for their own needs and would be able to sell the surplus for a good profit. This way, he reasoned, people would see that keeping cows was profitable and wouldn’t kill them.

Prabhupada responded, “This is not the idea, to keep cows and get milk and produce yogurt and cheese and ghee and by selling them to become fat, rich capitalists. The idea is to please Krishna. That is bhakti. In the Bhagavad-gita (18.44) Krishna says, krsi-go-raksya: ‘agriculture and cow protection.’ We protect the cows because Krishna wants it, for Krishna’s pleasure—whether we make money or not. Even if we lose money, we will still protect the cows—and depend on Krishna. Our interest is to please Krishna. That is bhakti.”

Many different devotees came to serve at Hare Krishna Land during this period, and though some had personal problems that came with them, Srila Prabhupada showed his care for them all. One of the devotees was suffering from paranoid schizophrenia, and I informed Prabhupada of her extreme behavior and asked him what to do, especially because her father had proposed to send her to a psychiatric hospital for treatment.

“I know her,” Prabhupada replied. “She is a devotee. The mind is also part of the body, just like any other part. Just as one’s arm or leg may be broken, but one’s infirmity does not affect one’s position as a devotee, so one’s mind may be ‘broken,’ but one’s mental illness does not affect one’s spiritual position as a devotee. And just as one’s arm or leg can be mended by medical treatment, so one’s mind can also be treated.” In conclusion, Prabhupada approved of her undergoing treatment in a psychiatric hospital.

Soon thereafter, when the devotee was in Ahmedabad, Prabhupada wrote her, referring to her illness, “Anyway we have to depend upon Krishna in all circumstances. As long as the body is there, there will be different degrees of health and unhealth. We have to tolerate these things, just as we have to tolerate the seasonal changes of sometimes hot, sometimes cold.

“You are a devotee, and so Krishna will protect you. Always think that Krishna is with you. He is present in His name, so you are always associating with Him.”

When Prabhupada left for Mayapur, devotees followed him to the airport. Guru-Gauranga, who, with a small group from Switzerland, had stopped in Bombay en route to Mayapur, happened to be on Prabhupada’s flight and ended up with him, his secretary, and just a couple of others in the waiting room. “I was chanting my japa, pacing back and forth,” Guru-Gauranga remembered, “and as I turned, I saw that Prabhupada was calling me over. It was like in the movies: I had to look in both directions to see who he was addressing, because I couldn’t believe he would be calling me.

“Prabhupada gestured for me to come over, and then he tapped the seat right next to him for me to sit down. ‘So, how is the governor of Geneva?’ he asked. ‘Is he still worried about the Swiss economy if everyone joins our movement?’

“I suddenly realized that Srila Prabhupada knew who I was. When we were in his presence, we sometimes wondered, ‘Does Prabhupada really know who I am?’ From that experience I learned that Prabhupada not only remembered me but also remembered the service I had done for him and everything that had been discussed. He could pick up from exactly where we had left off—the same conversation—and knew who was doing what for him. That gave me an enormous amount of inspiration, that no service was unrecognized by Srila Prabhupada.”

Prabhupada was concerned that his foreign disciples were not allowed entry into some Hindu temples, notably the Jagannatha temple in Puri. In April 1974 Syamasundara Brahmachari, a godbrother of Prabhupada’s connected with Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura’s Gaudiya Mission in Puri, invited Prabhupada to visit the Jagannatha temple, but Prabhupada replied, “I have not visited Jagannatha Puri, because my men are not allowed to see the Deity. When you arrange that we can visit the temple with my disciples then I can come immediately....

“It is very regrettable that these European and American boys who are purely Vaishnava and who follow all principles are not allowed bythe rascals to enter the temple. As stated in the Padma Purana, arcye visnau siladhir gurusu naramatir vaisnave jati buddhir.

“I do not know what makes the management take this attitude. If you can remove this restriction you will do a great service to the Gaudiya Vaishnava community. According to shastra, anyone who wears tilak and sikha \[tuft of hair\] and kunti \[neck beads\] over and above Vaishnava dress must be accepted, especially while chanting Hare Krishna mantra with bead bags. Kindly convince them and induce them to allow these Vaishnavas to enter the Jagannatha Temple.”

Later, Srila Prabhupada gave the same arguments to Swami Chinmayananda, who wrote a letter certifying that the ISKCON devotees were genuine Vaishnavas, with all the symptoms, and should be allowed in all Hindu temples.

After seeing Chinmayananda’s certificate, Prabhupada commented, “He has done some service.” And he asked me to present Chinmayananda a copy of the seventh chapter of Srl Caitanya-caritamrta Adi-lila, entitled Lord Caitanya in Five Features, which described Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s defeat of the Mayavadi sannyasis in Varanasi and their subsequent conversion to Vaishnavism.

“One copy of our book Lord Caitanya in Five Features should be handed over to Swami Chinmayananda as our humble presentation,” he wrote me. “If somebody, or yourself, sees him personally, gives him thanks for his letter recommending our admission in the temples and presents this book to him, that will be nice. As far as possible, all big Mayavadi sannyasis should be presented with this book.”

That month, Gopal Krishna became the GBC for India. He landed in Bombay but proceeded to Mayapur, where Prabhupada told him, “Your first task is to complete the Bombay building in six months.”

He attended the opening of the Krishna-Balaram temple in Vrindavan and then came to Juhu, but before he arrived, Prabhupada prepared me. To impress me with Gopal’s competence and stature, he told me that Gopal had his own office in a major company, and his own car.

I was surprised to hear Prabhupada speak about Gopal Krishna in such terms. Did he think that in my association with big men in Bombay I had developed that standard for assessing a devotee? I hadn’t thoughtso, but I was convinced that he knew me better than I knew myself, so his words made me look into my heart.

“I was thinking of making you the GBC for India,” Prabhupada told me, “but then I considered that your service as temple president in Bombay was more important.” I knew I wasn’t qualified to be GBC for India, but I appreciated Prabhupada’s kindness in speaking to me in that way.

In time, I noticed that Prabhupada gave Gopal a lot more freedom than he had given Gopal’s predecessors. I figured that either Prabhupada had decided within himself to withdraw a little from the management or he felt that Gopal was able to function more on his own than the others. In any case, Prabhupada was leaving to Gopal matters in which he previously would have become more directly involved. I also felt relieved that Gopal was carrying some of the burden of Prabhupada’s management responsibilities.
