With the Krishna-Balaram temple open in Vrindavan, Prabhupada sent Saurabha to take charge of the construction in Juhu, which was accelerating. Although Saurabha expressed a desire to remain in Vrindavan and manage, Prabhupada wanted him to come to Bombay.

Saurabha set up his construction office in our flat on the ground floor of the D Block, which we had gotten in exchange for Prabhupada’s upstairs flat in the same building, after we had constructed an entire floor for him in the F Block. Nistraigunya became his site supervisor, Ekanath his treasurer.

Although Saurabha did the main design for the complex, we needed a local architect to submit the plans and get them passed. We decided on Prem Nath, who was dynamic and modern and had done some high-profile projects.

Saurabha sent the proposed design for the temple complex to Prabhupada, and Prabhupada approved it. Early one morning, Saurabha invited Jagat Purusa to his office to see the design, which he had just received back. Murti dasa, who served in the construction office, was also there. Jagat Purusa studied the plan, noting that Prabhupada had signed it. “Where is the theater?” he asked. He hadn’t been involved in any of the planning discussions, so he hadn’t really considered whetherthere would be a theater or not, but it suddenly dawned on him that there should be.

“There is no theater,” he was told. “That’s not part of the plan.” “Why not? Don’t we need one for cultural performances?”

“It was never really considered, and now it’s too late; Srila Prabhupada has already signed off.”

“But I think it’s important—there should be a theater.”

Saurabha and Murti agreed but insisted that it was too late. All the architecture had been carefully planned out, and there was no space for it.

Then Jagat Purusa pointed to the design and said, “Why not just take this and move it over to this side and put this up here and move this over there and put the theater here?” They examined the design and looked at each other and looked at the design again, and then looked at him and together said, “That might be possible.”

So, they redrew the design to accommodate a theater and sent the new design to Prabhupada, and he approved it. As Jagat Purusa later recalled, “It was such an exciting moment for me, because I felt like I was being Krishna’s instrument. I had no architectural background, but I just was moved, I believe, by the Supersoul, and they saw that it was possible, and that’s how the theater became a part of the design.”

I continued to inform Prabhupada of our progress. On May 19 I wrote him, “Regarding construction, the excavation for the two towers has been completed, and today at the office of Prem Nath, the architect, we will finalize the tenders. After careful inquiry about what sort of contractors to use for this building, we came to the conclusion that labor contract is the best. In Bombay there is great difficulty with labor because many are leaving for neighboring countries where they are offered very high rates. Therefore, to take the responsibility ourselves for labor will be very troublesome. Also, today at the meeting with Prem Nath we will discuss the master plan and all other programs we are planning for Hare Krishna Land in the future.

“In stock we have 2,000 bags of cement and 10 tons of steel, sufficient to lay the foundation of the two towers. We are trying to complete the foundation up to plinth level before the heavy rainfall. We will keep close contact with you regarding the progress of the construction.”

Then, unexpectedly, we got a notice from the municipality dated May 17 addressed to A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami, stating that the construction was “being unlawfully carried on under your direction” and concluding, “NOW I DO HEREBY GIVE YOU NOTICE that if, after the expiration of Twenty Four hours from the Service hereof upon you, it is found that the erection of the said building/execution of the said work is still being carried on under your direction/by you, I shall, pursuant to Section 354A of the said Act and in exercise of the powers conferred on me as aforesaid, direct that you be removed from the said premises by a Police Officer.”

Both the order to stop the work and the aggressive tone and threats were shocking. We investigated why the permission had been revoked and discovered that the police commissioner had issued instructions to the municipality that the permission should be cancelled on account of ISKCON’s being a threat to the national security. Although the police were not directly concerned with the building of the guesthouse—their NOC was required only for the temple—the police commissioner had written a letter to the municipal corporation stating that the whole project should be stopped.

We were trying to assess who was the enemy and what was their strength. We concluded that actually we had a stronger standing with the municipality than with the police. Even though Mhatre was opposing us at every step, there was a consensus among the officers in the municipality that he was just harassing us. At first they believed him because they didn’t know us, but as they came to know us better, they realized that we were good and genuine and that Mhatre was just playing his usual tricks. The municipal officers were not against us, but they themselves were subject to harassment by Mhatre. So they couldn’t go out of their way to help us, though within themselves they may have been sympathetic, and they wanted everything they did for us to be approved by the commissioner. The plans for the guesthouse had been sanctioned by the municipal commissioner, but again the construction was stopped by Mhatre through the police commissioner—ultimately, as we later discovered, through the home secretary of the government of Maharashtra.

So, Mhatre was doing his best to stop us. And we wondered two things: Why was he so determined to oppose us and how could a smallfry politician like him have so much influence that he could stop our progress—though we ourselves were working through many channels, with much influence?

After Mhatre got our permission revoked, I asked Prabhupada why the man was opposing us so staunchly, and he answered that because Mhatre had been defeated when he had wanted to get the land and had been opposing us then, and in the end we had gotten the land, he bore a deep grudge against us and was always remembering his defeat and trying to take revenge.

## New Allies

Gopal Krishna was expert at political and diplomatic dealings, and I was impressed with how he systematically pursued the matter of the permission from one politician to another, one officer to another, and back again. “The president of the ruling Maharashtra Congress party, P. K. Sawant, who had been the caretaker chief minister of Maharashtra for some time, was quite pious, quite nice,” he later recalled, “and V. S. Page, the Speaker of the Legislative Council, the upper house in the Maharashtra legislature, was also pious, and a Sanskrit scholar. So, practically every day we would go to these politicians and tell them we were not getting the NOC. We would go to the police commissioner, and he would say, ‘I have no objection; go to the municipal commissioner? We would go to the municipal commissioner, and he would say, ‘I have no problem; go to that man? So we were going all day, from morning to night, from A to В, В to С, C to D.”

Because I knew most of the important people in Bombay, I was able to inform Gopal Krishna about them, and we went around together meeting with the people we thought could help, especially with the permission for the temple—people I knew or who knew people I knew. I would introduce him, and in most cases, especially in dealing with the politicians, he would speak more than I would, explaining our situationand trying to enlist their help. We were afraid to approach the chief minister, S.B. Chavan, though, because he was the highest authority and we didn’t know about him, how he would respond.

One day we met a newspaper reporter who had interviewed Chavan in some other connection, and he had mentioned us to him. Mhatre was getting bad articles about us published in the newspapers, so the reporter had asked the chief minister what he thought of the devotees. Although we didn’t know the chief minister, he had said, “I think they are very good people; I don’t believe any of the bad things being published about them in the press.”

Feeling encouraged, we went to Sachivalaya to meet the chief minister’s personal secretary to try to get an appointment. While we were waiting in the outer room, Gopal Krishna got the idea to just go into the chief minister’s office. Usually the doors were guarded, but somehow there was no one around, and he said, “Let’s just go in.”

Usually, when we entered an important person’s chamber without permission, the person would press a button and call for his secretary to escort us out—or sometimes just shout, “Get out!” So, we weren’t sure what to expect. But when we opened the door and entered, Chavan stood up and received us as holy men, with honor and respect. He offered us seats and asked how he could serve us. When we explained our predicament, he said, “I will help you—I will solve the problem. Don’t worry.”

The Indian government has a two-tier system. There are the ministers, who are political figures, and the secretaries, who are administrative figures who remain in position regardless of any change of ministers. For every minister there is a corresponding secretary, the administrator in charge of that department.

The home department, which is considered the most important and which includes the police, is handled on the state level by the chief minister. Since he deals with both general administration and home affairs, he has both the chief secretary and the home secretary directly under him. In the central government, although there is a home minister as well as a prime minister, at times the prime minister him- or herself takes up the home portfolio because it includes internal security and is so important. On the state level, there is no home minister, but there isa home secretary. So, the most powerful position in the state is the chief minister, and beneath that is the chief secretary and then the home secretary.

It turned out that Mhatre had been meeting with the home secretary and feeding him false stories about us. And the police commissioner was under the home secretary, which is why he had kept refusing us the NOC.

Chavan, who was impartial, could see that we were being harassed. He called for the urban-affairs minister, who oversaw the municipality, and for the home secretary, who oversaw the police, and addressed them in Hindi. “Who is actually at fault?” he asked. “Are they the guilty ones,” Chavan asked, “or are you?”

It turned out that the home secretary, though in a high echelon, being the top administrative figure in the home department, was close to Mhatre, and Mhatre had been systematically brainwashing him against ISKCON. The home secretary didn’t know us personally, but considering that he was a close friend of Mhatre’s, I doubted he had been very pious or religious to begin with. When Mhatre had kept impressing upon him how bad we were, he had believed him and just regurgitated the bad things he’d been fed. All along, it had been he who had been stopping the permission from the police. The governor was actually more of a figurehead; the powerful person was the chief minister. Had the difficulty been only the police department, the governor of Maharashtra might have been able to do something. But because the opposition was coming from the home secretary, the highest authority other than the chief minister himself, practically nothing could be done. And nothing had been done until the chief minister himself took personal interest.

Chavan put his foot down and stopped the whole thing, and the urban-affairs minister and the home secretary issued instructions that the permission for the guesthouse should be reinstated and that the NOC for the temple should be granted.

On May 26, four days after our meeting with Chavan, Gopal Krishna wrote Prabhupada about what had transpired. Prabhupada replied, “It is a great credit that you have met with the Chief Minister and now he will give us all help. Why did you not apply immediately for the NOC? You should do it immediately, if you have not done so already.”

The next day, I met the acting municipal commissioner of Bombay,and the day after that, upon his request, I submitted a letter to him summarizing our situation and the history of Mhatre’s harassment (See Appendix B). We also, on Chavan’s request, gave him a letter describing our mission and the history of our difficulties and officially applying for the NOC from the police (See Appendix C).

The attitude in the government offices throughout the entire city changed overnight. Word quickly spread that the chief minister liked us and wasn’t tolerating any more nonsense. Up until then, no one had been helping us. But when they heard that we had the chief minister’s support, people became friendly, cordial, and cooperative, and wherever we went, without difficulty, we got whatever was due.

On June 13 the legal department of the municipality informed us that the earlier notice, dated May 17, had been withdrawn and that we could proceed with the construction “as per the plans already approved.”

We were jubilant. It was a huge defeat for Mhatre. Not only was his revoking of our permission overturned, but we were poised to get the full plans passed, including for the temple.

On July 3 I phoned Srila Prabhupada in the US to inform him of the developments—that we had gotten the NOC—and he spoke of it on his walk the next day:

Prabhupada: We have got the No Objection Certificate.

Tamal Krishna: Really? For the temple or the ...

Prabhupada: Temple. Bombay.

Tamal Krishna: Really!

Prabhupada: The chief minister has sanctioned. He is a very nice man.

Tamal Krishna: Naik?

Prabhupada: Not Naik. Naik was a rogue.

Tamal Krishna: A new one.

Prabhupada: Yes, Chavan.

Tamal Krishna: So, now we can build two towers and a temple.

Prabhupada: Now bring money.

Tamal Krishna: Srila Prabhupada, what is the plan? To send money or books?

Prabhupada: Money.

Later the same morning, Prabhupada wrote me, “I have received your report via telephone, and it is a very good news that you havereceived the NOC for the construction of the temple. So, you begin the work, and money will come to you by the grace of God. Don’t worry, just finish the buildings as soon as possible and somehow or other money will come. In Bombay you collect as much as you can, and the balance money will be sent, rest assured. I am instructing Ramesvara to send Guru Kripa’s collection to Bombay. So you just finish all the buildings as soon as possible. You must also keep proper account. Not a single farthing should be wasted. I will see the accounts personally when I return to Bombay.”

Those words—“When I return to Bombay”—were music to my ears.

Prabhupada swung right into action. On the same day, he wrote Guru Kripa, “I may inform you that we have received the permission for constructing our Juhu temple. I want that your collection should be sent there so that the buildings may be completed as soon as possible.” And to Ramesvara, “I may inform you that in Bombay they have received the sanction for constructing the temple in Juhu. Until further order, whatever money you collect should be sent to Bombay. You should print books as far as possible, and whatever money you collect should be sent to Bombay. Guru Kripa has informed by telephone that he is sending you almost $75,000.00. This should be sent to Bombay.”

A few days later, he wrote Governor Reddy, “So far as our Bombay temple is concerned, I have received one telegram from my secretary there stating: ‘NOC FOR TEMPLE OBTAINED.’ It is understood that the present Chief Minister, Sri S. B. Chavan, is a kind gentleman who is religiously disposed, and he has kindly given the order of NOC.”

On June 25, acting at the behest of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, India’s president, Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed, declared a national State of Emergency in response to prevailing “internal disturbance” within the country. The order gave the prime minister the authority to rule by decree, allowing her to suspend elections and curtail civil liberties. Most of Gandhi’s political opponents were imprisoned, and the press was censored. In effect, she became a dictator.

Two days later, at a press conference at the Dallas airport, a reporter asked Prabhupada, “Would you comment on the political situation in India now? What do you think about Mrs. Gandhi’s . . . ?” But Prabhupada avoided speaking against her. “Well, we are not very muchconcerned with political situation” he said. “But our proposition is that anything—whether political, social, economical, or philosophical— without Krishna is all zero. So far as Mrs. Gandhi is concerned, she is inclined to some spiritual understanding. So, actually, if she becomes advanced spiritually, then this emergency situation will improve. Otherwise . . .” He went on to say that dictatorship was not bad if the dictator, or monarch, was godly—of high moral character and spiritual qualification.

The Dallas Times Herald covered Prabhupada’s arrival, and Prabhupada was especially interested in the newspaper’s version of his reply to the question about India’s political situation. He liked the favorable statements about Indira Gandhi and asked that the article be saved.

Prabhupada was so concerned about Juhu that he had Brahmananda phone and say that Prabhupada wanted a report. I wrote him the next day, “I am very sorry that I did not report to you earlier. The foundation of the first tower is already ready except for two footings which are to fall underneath the existing kitchen behind the present temple and which require some special support. Today or tomorrow the contractor should begin pouring the concrete for the columns which rise above the footings for the first tower. Since Mhatre had stopped our work for about one week, just before the heavy rains came, the second excavation got filled with water, but now we have finished pumping out most of the water and can begin to lay the foundation there. Saurabha Prabhu and the contractor have explained that the foundation is always troublesome, especially during monsoon, but that once we come above plinth level we can lay one slab every ten or fifteen days provided we have sufficient funds.

“Our architect Prem Nath has prepared the final plans for the temple and will submit the plans along with the NOC from the police to the Municipality tomorrow. He expects that he can receive the IOD \[permit\] and Commencement Certificate for the temple within three to four weeks, and he suggests we begin the work without waiting for the monsoon to end....

“Meanwhile, Saurabha Prabhu has been seeing to minor repairs for the tenants, and Prem Nath also had a meeting with the tenants todiscuss the overall development of the land. At the meeting we agreed to include a common area for the tenants to sit and for their children to play ...

“Prem Nath and I met with the Municipal officials last week to sort out the different pending disputes. The Municipality is ready to renew the permission for the existing temple and to meet all our other requests. The only dispute which was not resolved involves that ten-foot strip of land which the City Survey Dept, has demarcated as public road. Tomorrow Mr. Asnani and I are going to approach the City Survey Dept, with our evidence to convince them that the ‘access road’ is our private property and that they should adjust their present maps according to the documents which show the road as being private. If the City Survey Office does not agree, we can always file a case in court and let the judge decide. Otherwise, the Municipality still agrees that even if the ten-foot strip is declared to be public they are willing to give it to us in exchange for our surrendering our claim for compensation for the setback land which we have already given them.”

I also reflected in my letter on our success in obtaining the NOC for the temple from the police: “You must be pleased that we received the NOC from the police to construct our temple. It was a great fight. Even up to the last moment, Mr. Mhatre was trying everything to stop us, but by Krishna’s grace, he could not succeed. As stated in the Bhagavad-gita:

yatra yogesvarah krsno /  
yatra partho dhanur-dharah  
tatra srir vijayo bhutir /  
dhruva nitir matir mama

Everyone is appreciating how we could overcome such powerful opposition, but we know the secret, that wherever there is Krishna and Arjuna there is automatically victory and opulence.”

A week later, I wrote, “Last week Prem Nath completed a nice portfolio of plans and drawings of the project, and I shall send a portfolio for you with Kuladri Prabhu when he goes to New Vrindaban.”

While Prabhupada was in America, he received a telegram from Tejiyas saying that if he wanted an interview with Indira Gandhi, he would have to come immediately. So he cut short his North America tour and within days was back in Juhu.

On his first morning walk, he reflected on his recent difficulties. “So many obstacles we are facing," he said. “Never mind. Still, we are coming out, gradually. Kuntidevi said, ‘Krishna, may all those dangerous days come again, so that I can always remember You. When we were in dangerous days You were always with us. Now we are prosperous; now You are going away. So, better I call for those dangerous days again so that You can remain with us and we can become surrendered to You."' Then, looking at the Arabian Sea, Prabhupada remembered his voyage to America: “I started on this ocean, thirteenth August, this ferocious ocean.”

One day shortly thereafter, Lalita Bose, the daughter of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose’s brother, came to meet Prabhupada. I knew her from Calcutta, where she used to visit our temple. They spoke mostly in Bengali, Prabhupada telling her about his mission and asking her to help him, specifically in approaching Indira Gandhi.

“We should be supported,” he said. “If she understands, India will develop—I am sure. This is not bogus; this is exactly what Krishna has said. Our mission is уare dekha, tare kaha 'krsna'-upadesa. Bas. If you speak what Krishna has instructed, you become guru. But if you make your own concoction, your own invention, then ... I don’t speak any nonsense—only the instruction given in the Bhagavad-gita. That is my credit. That’s all. People say that I have done wonderful, but I do not know any magic. The wonderful thing I have done is that I don’t speak any nonsense thing. Whatever success we have achieved is due to this.”

“What you say, you act accordingly,” Lalita added.

“What I learn from Krishna, I say. I don’t say independently. That is not my business. That is Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s instruction. Amara ajnaya guru hand tara ei desa. You deliver your village people and become a guru. Everyone is not going to be so big that he can go all over the world. But everyone can teach within his limit—within his family, within his community, within his village, within his town, within his district. As he is capable, he can increase. But everyone can become a guru and deliver the local people. How? Yare dekha, tare kaha " krsna"-upadesa. Then you are guru. As soon as you manufacture anything, nonsense, then it is spoiled. That is going on. So many gurus are there; they are manufacturing. They are becoming Krishna. That is nonsense. You cannot become Krishna. Isvarah sarva-bhutanam hrd-dese 'rjunatisthati. Can you stay in everyone’s heart? You are claiming to be God. This one instance: Isvarah sarva-bhutanam hrd-dese ’rjuna tisthati. He is andantara-stham-paramanu-cayantara-stham. He is within this universe, and He is within the atom. You are claiming to be Isvara, God. Are you within the atom? Are you within everyone’s heart? Then how do you claim that you are Isvara? Practical. Isvarah sarva-bhutanam. Isvara, God, is in everyone’s heart. Sarvasya caham hrdi sannivisthah. If people lead their lives on the basis of Bhagavad-gita, everything will be fine. And as soon as you manufacture something, then it is spoiled. That is going on. The so-called gurus get some mystic power, yoga-siddhi, and they show it and mislead people that they are God. That is the difficulty.”

In Calcutta, before meeting Prabhupada, Lalita had been a leading follower of Satya Sai Baba, who had showed some magic and been accepted by many people as God. But after being enlightened by Prabhupada, she challenged Sai Baba: “Why are you misleading people? By producing and giving them material things you are involving them more in materialism. Bhaktivedanta Swami is performing the real miracle: making pure devotees of Krishna.”

Prabhupada asked for Gurus, Godmen and Good People, with my chapter about him. “They have written about me,” he told Lalita, “and about others as well. They have written about the others that when they were born a light came, and they did some miracle. For me, these things are not there. For me, there is a picture in Dallas. I am taking one child’s hand, and I am teaching how to write a, a, in Sanskrit. This is my miracle.”

He asked Brahmananda to show Lalita the recommendations of professors who had purchased his books, and a Hindi article about New Vrindaban. ‘The people in America are very much appreciating this,” he told her.

“When I meet the prime minister, I will take this,” she said. “You are changing people, actually, transforming them. I just saw your temple in Mayapur—amazing. And the temple in Vrindavan, you can’t even leave. Everyone is saying that the worship in the Hare Krishna mandir is the best. They are saying that the Deities look like They are about to speak, They look so alive.

“People are so impressed, the way the devotees are putting the sankha and then, you know, arati. People say that it is amazing, that they have never seen anything like it. The door opens, and at the same time the sankha sounds.”

“In all our temples in America and Europe we have the same standard,” Prabhupada pointed out.

“You must give me your blessings,” Lalita said. “Indiraji has a strong desire and told me that I must tell you about village development, that the government is ready to give all money but that they need sincere devotees.”

“Immediately,” Prabhupada responded. “Sincere devotees we have. We don’t have the facility. If they are properly prepared, they can genuinely do the work.”

“I told Indiraji that Guru Maharaja has come to us. I even gave her all this literature.”

“This is my prayer: At least a hundred men come. I require. They will not take even one paisa from India. I can show you in the accounts how money is coming from outside for their maintenance. They don’t care about politics. They just need visas. They will not take one paisa from India—rather, they will give... They have no scarcity. They have come here to learn about bhagavad-bhakti, and if India throws them out, it is not a good thing. They have nothing to do with politics. We are trying to unite the whole world, and our platform is Krishna consciousness. This is the United Nations. They, the so-called United Nations, have been working for over twenty years. What work have they done? Only increasing the flags. Hindustan, Pakistan, Vietnam. What is this? This is not unity. Panditah sama-darsinah. Without being a pandit, without acquiring knowledge, how can they have equal vision? Brahma-bhutah prasannatma na socati na kanksati, samah sarvesu bhutesu. Only when one is transcendental can he be equally disposed. Being covered by the darkness of maya, they cannot have equal vision, being envious and competitive of each other. Such a big work—Krishna consciousness—is going on all over the world, and those who are assisting me, if the India government rejects them, it is not good.

“This you make them understand properly. If they do that, it will not be a good thing. Let us be given this concession. And if I have todo this village organization, and for this if I get cooperation, then I will show them a miracle. Just like people are seeing this miracle: the whole world is chanting the Hare Krishna mantra. I will also show this miracle in India: how to organize villages. This is how I will do it.”

“You want one hundred men?”

“Yes. I’m not asking for more. And if they get into any sort of politics, if any fault is found in them, if they interfere in any politics, diplomacy, then immediately they will leave. But this will not happen. I know, because I have prepared them. They consider these things insignificant, like dogs and jackals fighting. We have no interest in them. We want to remove this dog consciousness from them. You bring some dogs together and tell them to live peacefully—is this ever possible?”

“This you can make by your blessings. Let us start the projects.”

“Yes. Many times, when the newspapers asked me, I said that Indira Gandhi is spiritually inclined. If she improves, it will be perfect. And she wants to be improved.”

“‘Barefoot Swami draws admiring Krishna crowd.’” Prabhupada cited from the article, and he directed Brahmananda to read more.

“Asked about the political situation in his native India and the criticized actions of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi,’ Brahmananda read, “the swami replied that ‘Mrs. Gandhi is inclined to some spiritual understanding, and if she fully develops it, the situation will improve. Democracy is not much beneficial if its leaders have no spiritual values. Mahatma Gandhi was practically a dictator, but he was a man of high moral character, so people accepted him. Dictatorship can be good, provided the dictator is spiritually developed.’”

“Stay for some time in India,” Lalita requested.

“I will, if there is cooperation from you all.... This is a very big movement. If intelligent girls like you help us, then I will stay in India. I will give her such advice that all India will be benefited, provided she listens to me.”

“The person I spoke to yesterday told me that ‘She is eager to meet him, so he should talk high level.’ So you tell her that ‘my boys have sacrificed everything and have come for the development of India, and you please do this little thing. We have some problem with tourist visa.’”

“Why tourist visa?” Prabhupada asked. “There is another visa, missionary. With that visa they can stay permanently. In the US, they havegiven me this because I am missionary, so that I can stay permanently—permanent resident... For India’s improvement, I am ready to do anything.” He quoted a Bengali saying: “‘From stitching shoes to reading the Chandi.' I am ready to do anything.”

“She may ask about foreign exchange, for the development of India.”

“I am bringing foreign exchange. Whatever property I have here, the money has come from abroad. Nothing has come from here. Whatever money I require for my work, I bring from abroad. I have brought crores and crores of rupees. I have all the bank details. I have mentioned this to Brahmananda Reddy, the minister of home affairs, and I am also telling you that if you can arrange for their visas, then I will be in peace. Otherwise, I have made this big institution, and if they leave, then how will I manage? Everything will get spoiled and there will be great harm.”

“You have done such an amazing work. We \[people in India\] cannot be like them; we will need some time.”

“Not time—the way they are listening seriously. The reason I came here running is that this science is meant for the executive head of the state. In the Bhagavad-gita, Fourth Chapter, it is stated,

imam vivasvate yogam  
proktavan aham avyayam  
vivasvan manave prahur  
manur iksvakave 'bravit

Evam parampara-praptam imam rajarsayo viduh. Rajarsayo, It is meant for the rajarsis. Indira is in the position of raja. If she becomes a rishi, then it will be successful. This is what I will tell her. I came running here just to tell her this, that ‘You have got the position of royalty. You become a saintly lady. Then your scheme will be all successful.’ That is required. That I can help, how to make her a rishi. Then not only the people of India will be benefited, but also the whole world will be benefited. And you have got that sampatti, Bhagavad-gita guidance. I will not manufacture anything. That is not my business — concoction, hodgepodge, without any knowledge, without any experience. We are not that type.

“We will account for every single penny. They will do it very nicely. They are expert in doing it, and the money they will give us, we will give accounts for every single penny. We just want facility, even if theydon’t give us money. We will bring money by begging abroad. We want the facility to work.”

“If you two get together, what you say orally alone will not work,” Lalita suggested. “You will tell her everything, and after you meet someone else will come to meet her and she will forget about what you said. But if it is in writing, then on that basis ISKCON’s work will be done.”

“So now what shall I write?” Prabhupada asked. And after discussing with Lalita and the devotees present, he dictated the following draft, which he asked Brahmananda to read out:

“Your Excellency Srimati Indira Devi Gandhi: When I was in Toronto, Canada, Srimati Lalita Devi, who is just like my daughter, sent me one intimation that she approached you for a meeting with me and you, and I have come here, postponing all my engagements. I am preaching this Krishna consciousness movement all over the world on the basis of Krishna’s instruction in Bhagavad-gita. Actually this Krishna consciousness movement is called the sankirtana movement and sometimes the Hare Krishna movement, which was inaugurated by Lord Chaitanya in Bengal and throughout all India. His mission is that everyone should become a guru and preach all over the world the instruction of Krishna. So we are doing this very faithfully, and it is becoming effective. I think in India also, if some vigorous activity is done for awakening the Krishna consciousness of the people under your leadership, it will be very effective. We have already eight branches in India, and all development is being done by foreign exchange. It can be continued if I get encouragement by the government. So I shall be very much pleased to see you in this connection. I have written about fifty books of four hundred pages each, such as Srimad-Bhagavatam, Bhagavad-gita, Caitanya-caritamrta, Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu, and these books are very popular in foreign countries such as Europe and America. By the sales proceeds I am bringing foreign exchange.’ ‘Yours sincerely’”

“‘Yours sincerely’ is all right, or ‘Your well-wisher’?” Prabhupada asked. ‘“Well-wisher,”’ Lalita said.

“‘Your well-wisher.’ The word is already there. Sadhu sastra guru vakya, cittete kariya aikya. So immediately type it and give it to her.”

“Where it says that ‘I am bringing foreign exchange’ in the end, ‘by selling my books I am bringing foreign exchange,’ it’s for India’s development?” Jayapataka asked.

“For developing my scheme here,” Prabhupada replied.

“And Gopal Krishna mentioned the point that we’re bringing foreign exchange—whether there should be any word that also signifies that we have local support also?”

“Our ‘books are popular in foreign countries as well as in India.’ We are getting money also from these books.”

“We have quotations from professors in America and also India ” Brahmananda said.

“Yes.”

“You will present one Gita,” Lalita advised. “And write, ‘Lead your life according to these teachings.’ She is full of bhakti, but she needs good guidance.”

“I shall personally teach Bhagavad-gita to her and her most confidential associates or who is governing. That I can do, if she agrees. Imam rajarsayo viduh. I wanted a rajarsi to take up this movement seriously, but I could not get one till now. If she becomes, it will be of benefit for me, for the world, for her—everyone. Because I have no power, I have no money, but if one rajarsi who has got strength, money, intelligence, if she takes, then it will be very quickly successful. Just like Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, His movement became very successful when Maharaja Prataparudra of Orissa took it. Gautama Buddha’s movement was successful when Maharaja Ashoka took it. It requires. And Krishna says, rajarsayo viduh.”

Later, Prabhupada finalized his letter, including a list of points to be addressed with Prime Minister Gandhi:

1\. As it is stated on our letterhead, the Krishna consciousness movement is for the whole human society for reviving its God consciousness. “Mamaivamso jiva-loke/ jiva-bhutah sanatanah.” (Gita 15.7) The living entity and God are intimately related as the part and the whole.

2\. We are preaching this philosophy on the basis of the Bhagavadgita As It Is without any interpretation. This is a cultural and educational movement to understand what we are, what is God, and what is our relationship and how to act upon it.

3\. The basic principle is that people must eat sumptuously and be free from all anxieties to cultivate \[their\] spiritual identity and \[their\]relationship with God. We invite everyone without any discrimination of caste, creed, and nationality, and factually within our Society there are members from all parts of the world, Europe, America, Africa, etc.

4\. In India we have got special interest to distribute prasad to the half-fed or hungry population. For this purpose we are getting money from America and we are getting goods from Australia. We have got already 6 or 7 centers in India and we are distributing prasad in all centers.

5\. The young Indian men are not joining our movement. So for conducting all this business we require 50-100 men, foreigners who are trained up. We have no business to take part in politics. We are bringing money from outside India. Practically we do not eat by spending India’s money. We are therefore requesting to allow our men to work on this mission to distribute prasad without any expenditure from India’s side. Even for our own subsistence we shall bring money from abroad, and the bank will certify.

6\. If we take to politics we can be asked to leave, but we are only interested in this movement of welfare activities. On this basis we ask for 50-100 men.

The following morning, after passing through a formidable security check, Prabhupada met Prime Minister Gandhi at her residence. She stood, greeted him cordially, and offered him a seat, but he sensed that she was anxious and distracted, fearful for her life—possibly the next target after the recent assassination of the president of Bangladesh. She admitted as much and added that this was not, therefore, a good time to meet. Prabhupada felt that she would have preferred not to meet at all but that because she had promised, she did so anyway—which he took as an indication that she had at least some inclination toward spiritual life.

Gandhi complimented Prabhupada for the good work he was doing internationally.

“They are good boys,” he responded.

As Jayapataka learned afterward—he and other devotees had accompanied Prabhupada to the prime minister’s residence but had not been allowed into the meeting—Gandhi had asked Prabhupada how he knew his followers weren’t CIA agents.

“I went to the West and preached,” he had told her. “These people have sacrificed everything. They gave up their bad habits. They aregetting up at four in the morning, attending mangala-arati. If they were CIA, they would live in five-star hotels and have a whole different lifestyle. They wouldn’t be vegetarians and give up all these habits.”

Prabhupada had understood that he would not be able to bring up his entire list of topics, but when he had asked if Gandhi could arrange permanent visas for his disciples, she said she would.

One of our strategies in Juhu was attracting important people from the vast Bombay entertainment industry—Bollywood—many of whom had residences in Juhu. Several months earlier, the Hindi film star Prem Nath had come to Juhu for darshan. Jagat Purusa had greeted him and presented him with some devotional gifts and maha-prasada. And starting from that contact, Jagat Purusa had begun cultivating actors, music directors, and producers and enrolling as many as possible as life members.

After a few months, he’d been able to meet with Raj Kapoor, the “king” of the Indian film industry, at his R.K. Studios in Chembur. After half an hour of conversation, he had presented him with several books, maha-prasada, and other gifts from the temple. His intention had been just to leave a good impression of Srila Prabhupada’s mission; he wouldn’t yet bring up the subject of life membership. When Raj Kapoor had noticed a membership form in Jagat Purusa’s briefcase, however, he had asked to see it and then kept it with the other items he had received.

Several weeks passed, and then, unexpectedly, news came from Vrindavan that Srila Prabhupada had received a letter from Raj Kapoor with a check for life membership. Sri Kapoor had written that the greatest moments in life were those lived with the Lord, “that infinite ocean of divine love—Krishna,” and “With your great blessings I choose to dedicate myself to the International Society for Krishna Consciousness by becoming its Life Member.”

Prabhupada was very pleased that one of India’s most prominent personalities was appreciating and supporting his movement, and on August 26 he replied:

Dear Sri Kapoorji,

Please accept my greetings. I am in due receipt of your letter dated August 14, 1975, with enclosed check for Rs. 2222/- and membership form. Sometimes in the year 1954, if I am correct, I had the chance ofmeeting you in Jhansi. At that time I was trying to organize my movement with the help of some young men at the Bhakti Bhavan, Jhansi.

So after ten years of struggle, in 1965 I went to USA, and by the grace of Krishna it has become successful all over Europe, America, Canada, and Australia. As it is stated in the Bhagavad-gita: yad yad acarati sresthas, tad tad evetaro janah, sa yat pramanam kurute, Iokas tad anuvartate. “Whatever action is performed by a great man, common men follow in his footsteps. And whatever standards he sets by exemplary acts, all the world pursues.” Your donation to this movement and your becoming the Life Member is a very great thing, and it will ensure others who will also follow in your footsteps. So I am very much grateful to you.

Please visit our Hare Krishna Land, Juhu, for Janmastami and Vyasa Puja Day on the 30th instant. I think the Mayor of Bombay will preside over the meeting.

I hope this meets you in good health.

Your ever well-wisher, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami

The day before, on August 25, in Bombay, the municipal commissioner had agreed to issue the permit, the IOD, for the temple, and I cabled Prabhupada in Vrindavan, “COMMISSIONER AGREES WRITTEN IOD TEMPLE WITHIN 24 HOURS."

Prabhupada wrote me the next day, “So this is very good news. Actually Krishna is doing everything. Only we are taking the credit.”

“I am enclosing a copy of the latest ‘Back to Godhead’,” he added, “and I am requesting that in your Janmastami Festival meeting you read the article under ‘ISKCON NEWS’ about the Ratha Yatra Festival. The point is that in the foreign countries they are accepting this as a bona fide religion and making holidays and our Ratha Yatra is regularly established. But in our own country they are giving so many hindrances. Anyway, after all we have got the permission. I am also sending you a copy of the correspondence with Raj Kapoor. This should also be discussed in your meeting: how prominent people are giving us respect, why are others making false propaganda? This correspondence can be published by you along with his photograph. I think you have one publication of Member Lists. It can go in there.”

When the rain subsided, I wrote Prabhupada, “The construction is progressing according to Saurabha Prabhu’s expectations. The first tower is ready for the first slab to be laid. The second tower pillars are complete to ground level and ready for the plinth. All the work is being done departmentally. There is no general contractor. Saurabha Prabhu feels that once the first slab is laid on each tower the work will proceed much faster, since the RCC design for the ground floor is very complicated and the upper stories will be more standard and replicating.” And three days later I wrote, “The digging for the foundation of the temple has already begun and altogether about 150 persons are working on site daily.”

In time, however, I saw that the quality of the work was poor and that the progress was slow. Just looking at the work, even a layman like me could see that it wasn’t the best.

Then we—or, rather, Prabhupada—discovered that construction materials were being stolen. None of us were aware of it except Prabhupada, who was in Africa, three thousand miles away. One of the tenants had understood what was happening and somehow gotten word to him. There was a conspiracy between the laborers, the engineer, the storekeeper, the chowkidars—everyone. Our engineer and storekeeper were father- and son-in-law, and without checks and balances they were working in collusion, and they had enlisted the help of a next-door neighbor whose property was separated from ours by only a low wall. At night the conspirators were stealing large quantities of material, throwing it over the wall onto the neighbor’s property.

Upon receiving word of the thefts, Prabhupada, in Nairobi, practically stopped eating and translating. When Brahmananda, who was serving as his secretary there, asked why, Prabhupada replied, “How can I eat when my money is being stolen?” And within a few days he packed his bags and came straight back to Bombay.

Prabhupada’s flight arrived at one a.m., but even at that hour he was greeted at the temple by a gathering of intimate life members, disciples, and also some of the tenants. In his room, he disclosed that he had been in a serious automobile accident; he even showed us a scar on his knee. He was in a grave mood, and seeing his leg, many devotees wept, but he said that he was relieved to be back.

He wrote a friend, “I went to Mauritius, South Africa, and again Mauritius, where I met with a major motor accident in my car. All my men got slightly injured, and they were saved by Krishna. The accident was very disastrous, but still Krishna saved us. Then I went to Nairobi, and from there I have come to Bombay. Perhaps I may stay here for some time for finishing our temple construction on this land.”

Prabhupada got right to work. He fired the engineer, whom he held responsible for the poor, slow work and stolen materials. He had tried to avoid hiring a construction company by having Saurabha oversee the whole project, assigning work to various subcontractors, but that wasn’t working. He wanted a change, but there was no clear alternative. “We have come to Krishna consciousness for a life of eternal bliss,” he told me. “But instead of eternal bliss, I am suffering eternal anxiety.” He appealed to us to do something.

Hearing kirtan coming from the direction of the temple one day, Prabhupada commented, “This is Hare Krishna Land: Always the sound of Hare Krishna should be heard.”

Another time, when he heard the sound of a child crying in the distance, he quoted a verse from Srlmad-Bhagavatam (7.9.19):

balasya neha saranam pitarau nrsimha  
nartasya cagadam udanvati majjato nauh  
taptasya tat-pratividhir ya ihanjasestas  
tavad vibho tanu-bhrtam tvad-upeksitanam

In this verse, Sri Prahlada prays, “My Lord Nrsimhadeva, О Supreme, because of a bodily conception of life, embodied souls neglected and not cared for by You cannot do anything for their betterment. Whatever remedies they accept, although perhaps temporarily beneficial, are certainly impermanent. For example, a father and mother cannot protect their child, a physician and medicine cannot relieve a suffering patient, and a boat on the ocean cannot protect a drowning man.”

Hearing the child’s crying, Prabhupada said, “The father and the mother want to protect the child and see that it is always happy, but even in their presence, the child may suffer and cry. The only guaranteed protection is Krishna’s.”

Later, I found the same instruction in Srila Prabhupada’s purport to the verse: “Through parental care, through remedies for different kinds of disease, and through means of protection on the water, in the air, and on land, there is always an endeavor for relief from various kinds of suffering in the material world, but none of them are guaranteed measures for protection. They may be beneficial temporarily, but they afford no permanent benefit. Despite the presence of a father and mother, a child cannot be protected from accidental death, disease, and various other miseries. No one can help, including the parents. Ultimately the shelter is the Lord, and one who takes shelter of the Lord is protected. This is guaranteed. As the Lord says in Bhagavad-gita (9.31), kaunteya pratijanihi na me bhaktah pranasyati: ‘O son of Kunti, declare it boldly that My devotee never perishes.’ Therefore, unless one is protected by the mercy of the Lord, no remedial measure can act effectively. One should consequently depend fully on the causeless mercy of the Lord. Although as a matter of routine duty one must of course accept other remedial measures, no one can protect one who is neglected by the Supreme Personality of Godhead.”

“During the construction,” Gopal Krishna recalled, “as we started the excavation for the temple area, while digging we found a plaque with an inscription in Marathi, and it was established that there was a Hanuman temple almost exactly at the location where the Sita-Rama altar is now located. So, we preserved that plaque in Prabhupada’s apartment, and when two Maharashtrian politicians came to meet him, they read that Marathi and concluded that the Marathi script was five hundred years old. When they told Prabhupada, he was extremely happy to discover that there had been a temple at the same location five hundred years earlier.”

One evening Harikesa and Saurabha got to talking about Prabhupada’s plans for the Mayapur project. Harikesa, appreciating Prabhupada’s genius—how, from Mayapur, God-centered cities with temples, educational institutions, and proper social organization would spread around the globe—became so excited that he ran all the way from the construction office to Prabhupada’s apartment. He bounded up the stairsand, without even knocking, burst into Prabhupada’s room and threw himself on the floor and paid full dandavats.

Prabhupada was in the middle of eating a sandesh (milk sweet) and a puri. He looked at Harikesa with big eyes, then went back to eating.

“Srila Prabhupada!” Harikesa exclaimed, “You’re a genius!”

Prabhupada looked up and said, “Oh?”

“Your plans for taking over the world. This is wonderful, this is fantastic—how you’ve made this plan for Mayapur and everything is so perfectly arranged.” Harikesa went on and on.

Prabhupada smiled and said, “Thank you very much.” Then he said, “Come here.” He broke the sandesh he was eating in half, gave Harikesa one half and the rest of his puri, and, still smiling, said, “Thank you very much.”

One morning I had an appointment with a pious, wealthy Gujarati businessman, Mr. Mehta, at his massive mansion near Haji Ali. In the course of our conversation, Mr. Mehta mentioned that in his Vallabhacharya sampradaya they considered Vrtrasura’s prayers in the Sixth Canto of Srimad-Bhagavatam to express the essence of their philosophy, and he read and translated them to me. Both in the prayers’ content and in their significance in the Vallabhacharya line, they reminded me of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s Siksastaka and its position in our Gaudiya Vaishnava line.

Excited by my discovery of these prayers, when I got back to Juhu I went straight to see Prabhupada. I told him about my talk with Mr. Mehta, and he motioned for me to take down the relevant volume of the Sixth Canto and read the verses aloud. I asked if I should read only the translation, but he said I should recite the Sanskrit and then read the translation and purports.

I read from chapter 11, verses 24-27:

TEXT 24

aham hare tava padaika-mula-  
dasanudaso bhavitasmi bhuyah  
manah smaretasu-pater gunams te  
grnita vak karma karotu kayah

Later, I found the same instruction in Srila Prabhupada’s purport to the verse: “Through parental care, through remedies for different kinds of disease, and through means of protection on the water, in the air, and on land, there is always an endeavor for relief from various kinds of suffering in the material world, but none of them are guaranteed measures for protection. They may be beneficial temporarily, but they afford no permanent benefit. Despite the presence of a father and mother, a child cannot be protected from accidental death, disease, and various other miseries. No one can help, including the parents. Ultimately the shelter is the Lord, and one who takes shelter of the Lord is protected. This is guaranteed. As the Lord says in Bhagavad-gita (9.31), kaunteya pratijanihi na me bhaktah pranasyati: ‘O son of Kunti, declare it boldly that My devotee never perishes.’ Therefore, unless one is protected by the mercy of the Lord, no remedial measure can act effectively. One should consequently depend fully on the causeless mercy of the Lord. Although as a matter of routine duty one must of course accept other remedial measures, no one can protect one who is neglected by the Supreme Personality of Godhead.”

So, we preserved that plaque in Prabhupada’s apartment, and when two Maharashtrian politicians came to meet him, they read that Marathi and concluded that the Marathi script was five hundred years old. When they told Prabhupada, he was extremely happy to discover that there had been a temple at the same location five hundred years earlier.”

Prabhupada looked up and said, “Oh?”

One morning I had an appointment with a pious, wealthy Gujarati businessman, Mr. Mehta, at his massive mansion near Haji Ali. In the course of our conversation, Mr. Mehta mentioned that in his Vallabhacharya sampradaya they considered Vrtrasura’s prayers in the Sixth Canto of Srimad-Bhagavatam to express the essence of their philosophy, and he read and translated them to me. Both in the prayers’ content and in their significance in the Vallabhacharya line, they reminded me of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s Siksastaka and its position in our Gaudiya Vaishnava line.

Excited by my discovery of these prayers, when I got back to Juhu I went straight to see Prabhupada. I told him about my talk with Mr. Mehta, and he motioned for me to take down the relevant volume of the Sixth Canto and read the verses aloud. I asked if I should read only the translation, but he said I should recite the Sanskrit and then read the translation and purports.

I read from chapter 11, verses 24-27:

TEXT 24

aham hare tava padaika-mula-  
dasanudaso bhavitasmi bhilyah  
manah smaretasu-pater gunams te  
grnita vak karma karotu kayah

TRANSLATION

О my Lord, О Supreme Personality of Godhead, will I again be able to be a servant of Your eternal servants who find shelter only at Your lotus feet? О Lord of my life, may I again become their servant so that my mind may always think of Your transcendental attributes, my words always glorify those attributes, and my body always engage in the loving service of Your Lordship?

PURPORT

This verse gives the sum and substance of devotional life. One must first become a servant of the servant of the servant of the Lord (dasanu-dasa). Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu advised, and He also showed by His own example, that a living entity should always desire to be a servant of the servant of the servant of Krsna, the maintainer of the gopis (gopi-bhartuh pada-kamalayor dasa-dasanudasah). This means that one must accept a spiritual master who comes in the disciplic succession and is a servant of the servant of the Lord. Under his direction, one must then engage one’s three properties, namely his body, mind, and words. The body should be engaged in physical activity under the order of the master, the mind should think of Krsna incessantly, and one’s words should be engaged in preaching the glories of the Lord. If one is thus engaged in the loving service of the Lord, one’s life is successful.

TEXT 25

na naka-prstham na ca paramesthyam  
na sarva-bhaumam na rasadhipatyam  
na yoga-siddhir apunar-bhavam va  
samanjasa tva virahayya kankse

TRANSLATION

О my Lord, source of all opportunities, I do not desire to enjoy in Dhruvaloka, the heavenly planets, or the planet where Lord Brahma resides, nor do I want to be the supreme ruler of all the earthly planets or the lower planetary systems. I do not desire to be master of the powers of mystic yoga, nor do I want liberation if I have to give up Your lotus feet.

PURPORT

A pure devotee never desires to gain material opportunities by rendering transcendental loving service to the Lord. A pure devotee desires only to engage in loving service to the Lord in the constant association of the Lord and His eternal associates, as stated in the previous verse (dasanudaso bhavitasmi). As confirmed by Narottama dasa Thakura:tandera carana sevi bhakta-sane vasa  
janame janame haya, ei abhilasa

To serve the Lord and the servants of His servants, in the association of devotees, is the only objective of a pure, unalloyed devotee.

TEXT 26

ajata-paksa iva mataram khagah  
stanyam yatha vatsatarah ksudh-artah  
priyam priyeva vyusitam visanna  
mano 'ravindaksa didrksate tvam

TRANSLATION

О lotus-eyed Lord, as baby birds that have not yet developed their wings always look for their mother to return and feed them, as small calves tied with ropes await anxiously the time of milking, when they will be allowed to drink the milk of their mothers, or as a morose wife whose husband is away from home always longs for him to return and satisfy her in all respects, I always yearn for the opportunity to render direct service unto You.

PURPORT

A pure devotee always yearns to associate personally with the Lord and render service unto Him. The examples given in this regard are most appropriate. A small baby bird is practically never satisfied except when the mother bird comes to feed it, a small calf is not satisfied unless allowed to suck the milk from the mother’s udder, and a chaste, devoted wife whose husband is away from home is never satisfied until she has the association of her beloved husband.

TEXT 27

mamottamasloka-janesu sakhyam  
samsara-cakre bhramatah sva-karmabhih  
tvan-mayayatmatmaja-dara-gehesv  
asakta-cittasya na natha bhuyat

TRANSLATION

О my Lord, my master, I am wandering throughout this material world as a result of my fruitive activities. Therefore I simply seek friendship in the association of Your pious and enlightened devotees. My attachment to my body, wife, children, and home is continuing by the spell of Your external energy, but I wish to be attached to them no longer. Let my mind, my consciousness, and everything I have be attached only to You.

Reading Srila Prabhupada’s translations and purports, I was struck by the depth and beauty of the verses. With its examples of the baby birds and small calves, text 26 alluded to the parental, vatsalya relationship, which is prominent in the Vallabha-sampradaya, and the example of the wife to the conjugal relationship, which is the ultimate goal for the followers of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.

Srila Prabhupada had reciprocated perfectly with my enthusiasm for my discovery, out of his love for me (and for Krishna), which filled my heart with love for him. Where else could I find such a merciful benefactor?

But as I was leaving his room, I had another thought: Srila Prabhupada has so much important service to do, I considered. He was kind to me, but in a way, 1 have wasted his time, which he could have spent for other, more worthwhile purposes. And I felt a little ashamed.

On one morning walk, I was feeling especially wretched and miserable, and although so many other devotees were present, Prabhupada began to speak as if he were addressing me personally. He quoted a Sanskrit verse by Sri Yamunacarya from his Stotra-ratna (43), quoted in Sri Caitanya-caritdmrta (Madhya 1.206):

bhavantam evanucaran nirantarah  
prasanta-nihsesa-mano-rathantarah  
kadaham aikantika-nitya-kinkarah  
praharsayisyami sa-natha-jivitam

“By serving You constantly, one is freed from all material desires and is completely pacified. When shall I engage as Your permanent eternal servant and always feel joyful to have such a fitting master?”

He said that there were two words—anatha and sanatha. Natha meant “master,” so anatha meant “without master” and sanatha meant “with master.” The whole goal of life, he said, was to become sanatha, “with master.”

He pointed to a fat and fit gentleman walking an equally fat and fit dog. The man was walking briskly and confidently with his dog on his leash, and the dog was walking equally briskly and confidently with his master by his side. Prabhupada commented that every dog wants a good master. If the dog has a good master, he is happy. He holds his head high; he wags his tail. He knows that his master will maintain and protect him, so he has no anxiety.

But the street dog—“The poor fellow has no master. Therefore he is always suffering.” Prabhupada pointed to some stray dogs. “They have no master. They do not know where they will sleep, how they will get food. Other dogs bark at them; children throw stones at them. They are always in anxiety.”

Then Prabhupada stopped walking and planted his cane firmly in the sand. Although I stood behind many of the devotees who had moved close around him, he looked at me, his eyes filled with love and compassion, and said, “So, we should be sanatha, protected, not anatha—orphan. We should have our master and be exclusively devoted to him. Then we will feel confident in his protection and always be happy.”

Prabhupada explained each Sanskrit word. Mano-ratha: the chariot of the mind. Mental concoction is driving us here, there, here, there. We have no peace. But when we have our perfect master to serve, we become peaceful, prasanta, and jubilant: “I have got my master. I have no cares and anxiety.” This is the ideal of life, to become sa-natha-jivitam, living with hope that “I have got my master who will give me protection.”

I felt that he was speaking directly to me, addressing my present need in Krishna consciousness.

Without my even asking or saying anything, he knew my heart and gave the perfect solution through his instructions, exemplifying the verse from Srimad-Bhagavatam (3.7.36):

anuvratanam sisyanam  
putranam ca dvijottama  
anaprstam api bruyur  
guravo dina-vatsalah

“Those who are spiritual masters are very kind to the needy. They are always kind to their followers, disciples, and sons, and without being asked by them, the spiritual master describes all that is knowledge.”

Several years later, I again came across the verse that Prabhupada had quoted and, reading the purport, found the same instructions that he had given on Juhu Beach: “Just as a dog or servant is very satisfied to get a competent, perfect master, or as a child is completely satisfied to possess a competent father, so the living entity is satisfied by completely engaging in the service of the Supreme Lord. He thereby knows that he has a competent master to save him from all kinds of danger.”

Prabhupada always spoke on the basis of scripture. At the same time, because of his compassion and humanity, he could say just the right thing in the right way to deeply touch the heart of each individual listener. I always tried to remember and follow the instructions he gave me on Juhu Beach. And ever since that day, whenever I have walked there and seen the different types of dogs—those with masters and those without—I have remembered those instructions and prayed that I will always remain Srila Prabhupada’s dog.

On another morning walk, Lokanath asked Prabhupada why he had prescribed sixteen as the number of rounds to chant. “Why not less or more?”

“No,” Prabhupada replied, “We say ‘minimum sixteen? Minimum. If you can chant sixteen thousand, you can do. That is welcome. Haridasa Thakura was engaged in chanting, and a prostitute came and offered, ‘Let us enjoy.' ‘Yes, let me finish. Let me finish this chanting? He refused to have sex with a beautiful young girl, because he had engagement: ‘First of all let me finish my engagement? And we say we have no engagement. How unfortunate we are. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu says, kirtaniyah sada harih. Twenty-four-hours engagement He has given.”

Lokanath continued, “Some devotees have fixed different numbers than sixteen. Some are chanting twenty minimum or twenty-five.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada said, “it should be increased. But don’t decrease; increase. Therefore a number is fixed: ‘At least this much I shall do.’ That is sixteen rounds.”

“But you are recommending sixteen as a minimum,” Lokanath said, “and some devotees are choosing twenty as a minimum.”

“So, who forbids?” Prabhupada asked. “Who says, ‘Don’t do it’?”

“They can chant?”

“Yes. That is wanted. But because you cannot do it, therefore we have fixed up this minimum. Sankhyata asankhyata. Sankhyata means with vow, numerical strength. And asankhyata means there is no limit.”

“If we chant more than sixteen rounds, how can we know whether we are imitating Haridasa Thakura or following in his footsteps?”

“Imitation is also good. If you imitate Haridasa Thakura, that is also your great fortune. Imitating does not mean you are condemned. Even if you imitate, that is also good. But if you have some other business and you say, ‘Now I am imitating Haridasa Thakura; I cannot do it,’ that is very bad. ‘I am busy in imitating Haridasa Thakura.’ That is not good.”

Brahmananda added, “If the devotees are asked for service, they say, ‘Oh, I have to chant.’”

Prabhupada responded, “Yes, ‘I am imitating Haridasa. This is my first business.’ That is very bad.”

As we were walking back from the beach one morning, Prabhupada continued speaking with the devotees. “When we take charge of the government,” he said playfully, “we will go to the people and tell them, ‘Either you chant Hare Krishna or we will kill you.’”

All the devotees laughed, except for me. Prabhupada turned to me and said, “What do you think, Giriraj?”

“Yes, very good, Srila Prabhupada,” I said with as much conviction as I could muster.

He turned to the other devotees and announced, “Our Giriraj is nonviolent.”

And then we all laughed.

Later, I found a passage in Sri Caitanya-bhagavata (Madhya-khanda 13.8-12) in which Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu speaks in a similar way with His devotees. “Go out and preach My order everywhere,” He tellsthem. “Go to every house and beg, ‘Chant the names of Krishna, worship Krishna, follow Krishna’s instructions (bala krsna, bhaja krsna, kara krsna-siksa).' At the end of the day come and give Me your report. I will take up My chakra and cut off the heads of those who will not chant after being requested by you.” And the passage concludes, “On hearing the order, all the Vaishnavas laughed.”

Although Dr. Patel would spar with Srila Prabhupada, he was deeply attracted, even attached, to him. “Do you know why I come so early and all that?” he asked one morning. “Shall I say, sir?

“Yes, yes,” Prabhupada replied.

Dr. Patel quoted,

prasangam ajaram pasam  
atmanah kavayo viduh  
sa eva sadhusu krtah  
moksa-dvaram apavrtam

“Every learned man knows very well that attachment for the material is the greatest entanglement of the spirit soul. But that same attachment, when applied to the self-realized devotees, opens the door of liberation.” (SB 3.25.20)

“That is why I come so early,” he said. “You may explain to them, sir.” “No, you explain.”

Dr. Patel laughed and proceeded: “It is said in Srimad-Bhagavatam that your mind, atmanah prasanga, the sanga. Sanga means ‘attachment.’”

“Prasangam.”

“Prasanga and sanga, the same.”

“No, no—prakrsta-rupena sanga, Prabhupada corrected. “‘Very tight.’” “Sanga. Very tight sanga, very tight attachment of mind is there always.” “Not mind—of the soul. “Atmanah. Because mind and soul, bothare . . . That is always there, ajara, undying. But if that attachment is made to a sadhu, that becomes moksa-dvaram apavrtam, that becomes opening of the door of moksha. So I come here to sadhusu krtah.”

A week later, Prabhupada asked Dr. Patel why he was coming daily.

“I don’t know,” Dr. Patel replied. “I have got some ...”

“We don’t pay you any fee.”

“I feel some sort of attachment to you. That is why I come. I don’t understand why I am attracted to you specially. I don’t understand. I have been thinking about it. I am very much thinking there must be some purva-janma, something from the past life. I don’t know. No sadhu has been able to attract me as much as you have. Not even temples have attracted me, to tell the truth.”

Jasomatinandan chimed in, “There is no sadhu except Prabhupada.”

On a morning walk the following week, Dr. Patel put forward his theory that the Jews were the greatest people on earth, that they were actually the chosen people of God.

“The Jews?” Prabhupada asked.

“Really,” Dr. Patel confirmed. “It is God’s choicest race.”

The devotees laughed, but Dr. Patel insisted: “They have produced wonderful people right from Christ up to Professor Einstein—very bold people, very bold indeed. They are truthful to their convictions. They would die for their convictions; they will not budge an inch.”

“But they’re impersonalists,” Brahmananda objected.

Dr. Patel pursued his point: “Very brave. Very brave race.”

“They are impersonalists,” Brahmananda repeated.

“Today still, very brave. It is the choicest race from God. It’s a fact.” “Brahmananda is very much pleased,” Prabhupada remarked, referring to his disciple’s Jewish family heritage. And again we all laughed.

“I don’t know who are they,” Dr. Patel responded, meaning he didn’t know which devotees were Jewish, “but that is a fact. When you look back to the history, it’s the really choicest race.”

“Giriraj is also from,” Jasomatinandan said.

“Whatever he may be. I don’t know them, who are they. But historically we look back: They are really very brave people. They have died for the sake of their principle. They never budge an inch.”

Dr. Patel’s praise was encouraging to those of us from Jewish backgrounds, and I glanced at Brahmananda, who smiled at me, and I guessed that he was also reveling. And then he again put forth his idea that the Jews were impersonalists.

“Impersonalist or personalist is immaterial,” Dr. Patel countered. “I talk of boldness—very bold people. Truthful to their conviction, sir.”

Then Srila Prabhupada broke in. “They are so bold,'' he questioned, “that Shylock?”

By Prabhupada’s naming of Shakespeare’s fictitious Jewish scoundrel, any of us who had been puffed up by Dr. Patel’s words became both deflated and thankful. With one word, he had rescued us from the trap of false prestige. And, after Dr. Patel’s broad claims and Prabhupada’s reference to a classic stereotypical figure, we were reminded not to accept generalizations based on bodily designations. Prabhupada wanted us to see everyone as individual, spiritual beings—eternal servants of Krishna.

When Prabhupada was settling back into his quarters after returning from Mauritius, I noticed a new devotee taking Prabhupada’s suitcases out of the trunk of the car. He was dressed as a brahmachari, in saffron robes, but had a full head of hair.

I asked one of the devotees who accompanied Prabhupada about him and was told that he was Ambarisa dasa—Alfred Ford, Henry Ford’s great grandson.

“That’s Ambarisa?” I exclaimed. Except for his hair, he appeared like a simple, humble brahmachari carrying Prabhupada’s suitcases.

It was decided that Ambarisa would come out with me. I was meeting top people and getting support for the Juhu project, and having Alfred Ford with me would be a great boon. I formulated a list of all the really wealthy people who had been avoiding me. There weren’t that many, because most of the aristocratic people then were quite pious, but I compiled a list of the most materialistic entrepreneurs in Bombay—the hard nuts to crack—phoned them and said, “Alfred Ford has come from America, and he would like to meet you.” That opened a lot of doors. But although I anticipated that these difficult people would change their minds by seeing Ambarisa, many of them, when they met him, seemed to think, “He is an heir to a great fortune, and he has become a Hare Krishna? What’s wrong with him?” So, it didn’t work quite the way I had hoped.

When we were out, I was really strict. I wouldn’t go to restaurants or juice bars—or spend money on anything. It was hot and humid, and Ambarisa would ask, “Can’t we stop for a few minutes—have a juice or something?”

“No!” I would respond. “No maya. No compromise.” Only once did I agree, when I felt a little compassion, or a glimmer of it, and we went into a snack bar and got some fresh fruit juice.

My room was in the building right next to Prabhupada’s, where Ambarisa was staying. Every morning I would come to the window and call, “Ambarisa Prabhu.” And Ambarisa would think, Oh, we are going to go out and do this again!

Once, I came into Prabhupada’s room when Ambarisa was speaking to him. “Prabhupada,” he was asking, “why does Giriraj have to go out every day and collect like this? I’ll just build the temple for you.” But Prabhupada said no.

Then Ambarisa got dysentery, and on the morning walks on Juhu Beach he’d see planes flying over, some going to America, and think, Oh, my God, get me on one of those planes!

When Ambarisa had been in Juhu for two weeks, Prabhupada inquired, “So, Ambarisa Maharaja, you are feeling all right or not?”

“Yes, I am feeling well today,” Ambarisa replied.

“You are taking yogurt?” Prabhupada asked—and told a devotee, “Give him kichari and yogurt.”

“He won’t eat yogurt,” Harikesa responded.

“I eat it mixed with Sat-Isabgol \[psyllium husk\],” Ambarisa said.

“Take yogurt with black pepper and salt,” Prabhupada advised him.

During one morning walk, Prabhupada spoke about being focused on one goal and related it to his success in establishing Krishna consciousness—and to Ambarisa:

“vyavasayatmika buddhir  
ekeha kuru-nandana  
bahu-sakha hy anantas ca  
buddhayo ‘vyavasayinam

\[Gita 2.41\]

Avyavasayinam bahu-sakha. And vyavasayayinam—one. From practical point of view, from business point of view also, I started this Krishna conscious business with forty rupees. Now we have forty crores. Who has got such business success? Bring anyone. Within ten years. And here is Ambarisa Maharaja. He is ready to give us any amount of money. Ambarisa Maharaja, yes. Whole Ford Company. Who else has got thisbusiness? I think there is no such history in the world, to begin business with forty rupees, and within ten years it becomes forty crores. One cannot even imagine.”

Before Ambarisa left Bombay, he had a serious meeting with Prabhupada about his future. Prabhupada told him that he wanted him to work. Almost all the devotees in ISKCON were full-time: they lived in the temple and were engaged in serving the mission. But to Ambarisa, Prabhupada said that he wanted people to see that one could be a devotee and still be a responsible member of society.

“Must I work with the Ford Motor Company?” Ambarisa asked.

“No,” Prabhupada replied. “That is your choice, but you should do some work. People should see that you are doing some work.”

“If I am working,” Ambarisa inquired, “what will I do for association?”

“If while you are working you are thinking, ‘I am doing this for Krishna,’” Prabhupada said, “that will be your association.”

About those days, Ambarisa later recalled, “Giriraj Swami taught me everything I know about fund-raising. When I first became a devotee, I went to Bombay, and Maharaja was sacrificing himself to get the temple built in Juhu, and he engaged me very nicely. I was a very green devotee, and a spoiled kid from suburban Detroit, so I was in culture shock from being in India, but he had such a nice character and was such a wonderful personality. He had a room across the alley, and every morning he would come to the window and call, Ambarisa.’ I couldn’t get away. So, we worked a lot, but it was really a wonderful experience to be there.

“My function was to get us in and, with Maharaja, to make life members out of people who had been slamming the door in the face of the devotees. But Maharaja had to conceal the truth a little to get us into their offices. He would say, ‘Mr. Ford is in India, and he would like to meet you.’ But as soon as the life membership material came out, they would throw us out of the office. It was a very humbling experience, and I bow down to his feet. He really gave his life to build that temple. And it is so important.

“Radha-Rasabihari were living in a shed, and Srila Prabhupada was so happy to have the temple built. He was very, very proud of that temple.”

When we met again years later, Ambarisa told me, “I want to apologize, because I was kind of a baby back in those days. And I was kindof sick. But I take the dust of your feet because you really taught me so much, and now that I’m engaged in trying to help build the Mayapur project, the example of your laser focus on getting that temple built in Bombay is such an inspiration for me that I am very, very grateful for your association during those days. I remember them fondly.

“When we met the ‘hard nuts’ and they discovered that we were approaching them for donations or to make them life members, sometimes they would throw us out of their offices. So, there were a lot of lessons of humility in those days. But I thank you for your association back then. It was really wonderful. It cut my teeth.”

On my side, I felt bad. I felt that I had been insensitive to Ambarisa’s needs and background and that I had driven him beyond his capacity. In fact, I considered it a wonder, or miracle, that he didn’t leave Krishna consciousness altogether after those two weeks with me.

One morning, two friendly, elderly, pious political leaders, P. K. Sawant and V. S. Page, came to meet Srila Prabhupada, and he preached to them and asked them to join his movement. “No,” they said, “in our positions we can’t do that.”

Then he asked them to support the movement, but again they objected: “No, in our positions, we can’t do that either.”

Finally Prabhupada requested, “Then at least don’t harm our movement,” and they both became very excited and together assured him, “No, no, we will never do that.”

Somehow or other, directly or indirectly, Prabhupada was determined to extract from them some commitment that was favorable to Krishna consciousness.

On November 18 Srila Prabhupada awarded sannyasa, the renounced order of life, to Nava Yogendra, and in a compact talk of hardly more than ten minutes he explained the significance of sannyasa and outlined the duties of a sannyasi.

“Sannyasa means finishing all material desires,” Prabhupada began. “Real sannyasa means no more material desires. Etam sa asthaya paratma-nistha. Paratma, Bhagavan—to completely devote one’s life for service of the Lord.”

He was quoting the verse from Srimad-Bhagavatam (11.23.57) that Lord Chaitanya recited in ecstasy after He accepted sannyasa:
