etam sa asthaya paratma-nistham  
adhyasitam purvaTamalr mahadbhih  
aham tarisyami duranta-param  
tamo mukundanghri-nisevayaiva

“I shall cross over the insurmountable ocean of nescience by being firmly fixed in the service of the lotus feet of Krsna. This was approved by the previous dcdryas, who were fixed in firm devotion to the Lord, Paramatma, the Supreme Personality of Godhead.”

Prabhupada continued, “There are four ashramas: brahmachari, grihastha, vanaprastha, and sannyasa. Sannyasa means sacrificing everything for Krishna’s sake. Anasrita-karma-phalam karyam karoti yah, sa sannyasi: one who is working without any aspiration for resultant action.”

andsritah karma-phalam  
karyam karma karoti yah  
sa sannyasi ca yogi ca  
na niragnir na cakriyah

“The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: One who is unattached to the fruits of his work and who works as he is obligated is in the renounced order of life, and he is the true mystic, not he who lights no fire and performs no duty.” (Gita 6.1)

“Our sannyasis work very hard,” Prabhupada said. “They preach, they collect money—but not a single farthing for himself. First, the brahmachari is trained up. Brahmacari guru-kule vasan danto guror hitam. The brahmachari is trained up to live at the place of guru for the benefit of guru. The same principle, when it is matured and when one dedicates his life for the benefit of Krishna ... Benefit of Krishna means benefit of the whole world. Krishna wants sarva-dharman parityajya mam ekam saranam vraja. A sannyasi should go door to door. Mahad-vicalanam nrnam grhinam dina-cetasam”

Here Prabhupada was quoting the Srimad-Bhagavatam verse (10.8.4) spoken by Lord Krishna’s father Nanda Maharaja to Gargamuni when the sage visited his home:

mahad-vicalanam nrnam  
grhinam dina-cetasam  
nihsreyasaya bhagavan  
kalpate nanyatha kvacit

“O my lord, О great devotee, persons like you move from one place to another not for their own interests but for the sake of poor-hearted grhasthas \[householders\]. Otherwise they have no interest in going from one place to another.”

“A sannyasi is called mahatma,” Prabhupada explained. “Why he is mahatma? Because his atma is now broader. Grhinam dina-cetasam. Mahad-vicalanam. The mahatma travels, or wanders, country to country, door to door—mahad-vicalanam nrnam grhinam—especially for the householders, dina-cetasam, whose consciousness, or mind, is very crippled. They are dina-cetasam. These materialistic persons are simply interested in how to enjoy the senses; therefore they are called dina-cetasam, cripple-minded. They have no other idea. So to enlighten them, it is the duty of the sannyasi to go from door to door, country to country, just to teach them about the aim of life. That is still going on in India. Even now if a sannyasi goes in a village, people will come to invite him, try to hear from him.

“You are taking this pledge for serving, in front of Krishna, Vaishnavas, guru, and fire. So you shall be very much cautious not to forget your duty. You have got good opportunity. You are going to Africa to deliver these persons.

“So, you must become very rigid Vaishnava; then you will be able to deliver them. Sudhyanti. How can they be purified without taking another birth? Prabhavisnave namah. A Vaishnava delivers them by the power of Vishnu—they are empowered. Practically we have seen last time when I went to Nairobi, so many Africans are making progress very nicely. They are asking nice questions.

“And if you work sincerely and if you can deliver even one person by your endeavor, then immediately you become recognized by Krishna. Na ca tasman manusyesu kascin me priya-krttamah. This is the quickest way to become recognized by Krishna—by preaching work.

“So, take it seriously. This business is very nice, and there is goodprospect. Prospect is there everywhere. Prthivite ache yata nagaradi-grama. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu said, ‘In as many villages and towns on the surface of the globe.’ And His word is not a trifling thing. Yes, there is potency in all the parts of the world for people to become Vaishnava.

prthivite ache yata nagaradi-grama  
sarvatra pracara haibe mora nama  
\[CB Antya-khanda 4.126\]

\[“In as many towns and villages as there are on the surface of the earth, My holy name will be preached.”\]

“So, with Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s blessing and spiritual strength, and with the good wishes of Vaishnavas, just proceed and preach and always think of Krishna. He will help. Dadami buddhi-yogam tarn. If you work sincerely—Krishna is within you. He will give you strength, instruction. Simply you have to become ...

“But we should always remember that sannyasa means material activities finished. This is sannyasa: no more material activities—to live only for the service of Krishna, that’s all.”

Prabhupada asked a disciple to give the danda. “In this danda, there are four dandas. Dandas means rods. One rod is body, one rod is mind, and one rod is speaking. Kaya mana vakya. And the fourth rod is the self. So you should always remember that taking this danda means that ‘My mind, my body, and my words—everything is dedicated to Krishna. It will be used only for Krishna and for no other purpose.’ This is called tridanda-sannyasa. Come on.”

Nava Yogendra came forward to accept his danda. “Jaya! Haribol!” the devotees cheered. “Jaya Prabhupada!”

“Chant Hare Krishna,” Prabhupada said. “Chant Hare Krishna.” And the devotees began chanting japa and then had kirtan.

After the ceremony, Nava Yogendra and Brahmananda went to see Prabhupada in his quarters. Brahmananda told him that he was very kind to have given sannyasa to Nava Yogendra Maharaja, and Prabhupada replied, “I am not kind, but very cruel. I gave him sannyasa, and now he cannot gratify his senses.”

Brahmacharya, which is based on devotion to the guru, is the foundation on which sannyasa—and all the other ashramas in Krishnaconsciousness—is built. In a later class, in April, speaking on Srimad-Bhagavatam 7.12.6, Prabhupada focused on the qualities of a brahmachari. He should be daksa, expert, Prabhupada said, and sraddadhanah, faithful. He “should know something of everything and everything of something—everything of devotional service. . . . Not that because he has become Krishna conscious, Vaishnava, he is unable to do anything of this material world. No. One who is Krishna conscious is conscious of everything and knows how to deal with everything. That is daksa, Not that ‘Because I have become Krishna conscious, I have no knowledge of other things? No. You must know something of everything. That is intelligence—to know something of everything and to know everything of something. That is wanted. A devotee should be expert. You know everything of devotional service, but you know something of everything. That is daksa,

“Daksa sraddadhanah: faithful. Faithful to whom? To the spiritual master. Whatever he says, the brahmachari should take it: ‘Yes, it is my life and soul.’ That is the explanation given by Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura. He explains with reference to the verse vyavasayatmika buddhir ekeha kuru-nandana \[Gita 2.41\] ... He has taught very, very nicely about guru. He has written in Gurv-astaka, yasya prasadad bhagavat-prasadah. He is the practical example of guru-bhakti. So, he said that ‘I am not interested in my salvation, going back to Godhead. It may come; it may not come. That I don’t mind. But I am interested only with the words of my guru. That is my life. Whether I will be successful or not successful, it doesn’t matter. I must take the words of my guru maharaja as my life and soul.’

“Actually, that is the secret of success.

yasya deve para bhaktir  
yatha deve tatha gurau  
tasyaite kathita hy arthah  
prakasante mahatmanah  
\[Svetasvatara Upanisad 6.23\]

\[“Unto those great souls who have implicit faith in both the Lord and the spiritual master, all the imports of Vedic knowledge are automatically revealed.”\] That is the secret of success, sraddadhana, to accept the words of guru very, very faithfully.”

Later that day, Prabhavishnu arrived from England. We were looking for a manager to help me; I wanted to be free to preach. Prabhupada knew as much, and also that in some respects I wasn’t such an expert manager. I understood that Prabhavishnu’s GBC authority, Jayatirtha, would want him back, and that generally, outside India, Prabhupada did not do anything independent of the local GBCs or against their wishes, but in this case he told Prabhavishnu that it would be best if he stayed in India and that he would take care of Jayatirtha. I was again struck by how important India—Juhu—was to Prabhupada, that he would make such an exception.

“Within a few hours of when I landed,” Prabhavishnu recounted, “Prabhupada called me to his room and asked, ‘How are things in London?’ ‘Everything is all right,’ I replied. He said, ‘It is nice that you have come to India. Now you manage this temple.’ When I first arrived, I thought I might not stay that long in India and that I’d be going back to England, but Prabhupada said, ‘You are needed here.’”

Prabhupada appointed Prabhavishnu vice-president of Juhu, and shortly thereafter Prabhavishnu and I walked over to Prabhupada’s flat together to ask him some questions. Prabhupada listened patiently and sympathetically and gave us the information we needed. Back in our quarters, Prabhavishnu and I discussed further and realized that we had more questions. So we went back to Prabhupada, and again he patiently replied. Then, again, back in our quarters, we realized that we had still more questions, so again we went back to Prabhupada, and again he answered us. When we went yet again, for the fourth time, however, Prabhupada got angry. “I have appointed you president and vice-president to deal with these matters,” he said, “and you have many other leaders to help you, so you should be able to figure these things out for yourself. I am not a question-answering machine.”

Every afternoon, Prabhavishnu went with a hari-nama party to Vile Parle or Santa Cruz, near the train station, chanting and distributing books, but he found managing in Bombay challenging. “I was fine with the climate and accommodations,” he remembered, “but what I found austere was going on the train into the city every day, packed up like sardines, and then sitting in offices and waiting, and being given excuses, and especially in government offices waiting for hours for some officialto come, then being given the runaround and told to come back the next day. So I became more inclined to go for some preaching activity. I asked Prabhupada if I could get more into book distribution. He said, ‘What do you like better—temple management or book distribution?’ And I said, ‘Book distribution, Srila Prabhupada.’ And he said, ‘All right. Manage the temple for some time, and then you can go on book distribution. I’ll show you how to put the books in colleges and libraries throughout the country.’ I had never imagined that kind of book distribution. The library party hadn’t started in India, but it was like Prabhupada could see what was going to happen, and he said, ‘You stay and manage for now, and you’ll get the chance.’ And after some time the library party did begin and I got the chance to go, and we actually traveled all over India and put his books in the universities and libraries.”

Harikesa could never make chapatis properly; they would never puff up. He was always blaming something—either the stove wasn’t adequate or the flour was no good, or something. And Prabhupada was growing increasingly upset with him. “Big, big brain,” he would say, “but he can’t make a chapati.”

In Mauritius, Harikesa didn’t have the right flour and had to cook in a closet on a weak electric hot plate, and his chapatis were like saucers, completely flat, and with the texture of rubber. Prabhupada was complaining about them, but Harikesa couldn’t seem to do anything about it. This went on for months, in different places, and Prabhupada kept chastising him. Every day, he would say, “Again, no good chapati.”

Finally, in Bombay, there was a gas stove, but Harikesa still couldn’t get it together. “Again it is the stove!” Prabhupada commented.

“Srila Prabhupada,” Harikesa said, “nobody can make a good chapati on this stove.”

“Nobody?” Prabhupada asked.

“Yes, Srila Prabhupada,” Harikesa said, “nobody.”

Prabhupada stood up, walked into the kitchen, and sat on the floor in front of the stove. “Where is the dough?” he asked. And he took the dough, formed a ball, squished it on the board with some flour, rolled out a chapati, put it on the pan, cooked it, flipped it over, put it on the flame, and ... nothing.

“Ha!” Harikesa exclaimed with a laugh. “It didn’t puff up!”

Prabhupada turned slightly and just looked at him. “He gave me one of those looks that could cut you into twenty pieces,” Harikesa later remembered, “and I stopped laughing.”

Then Prabhupada grabbed another piece of dough, formed it into a ball, rolled out another chapati, threw it on the pan, flipped it over, and put it on the flame. This time it puffed up perfectly. He picked it up with a pair of tongs, looked at Harikesa, and threw it right in his face. “No one can make a chapati?” he questioned and then stood up, cast down the tongs, and walked out in triumph.

After the matter of the setback land was resolved, Mr. Sethi, as instructed by Srila Prabhupada, had constructed a compound wall around the property. One morning, as we approached the temple on our way back from Prabhupada’s morning walk, Dr. Patel pointed to the new, five-foot-high wall and told Prabhupada, “Seeing this wall, people are saying you have made a prison inside.”

“Nooo,” Prabhupada responded, elongating the “o” sound. “The prison is outside. Inside is freedom.”

While Prabhupada was in Bombay, I arranged a program for him at the home of the Birlas, the wealthiest family in India. Mrs. Gopi Kumari Birla wanted a title for Prabhupada’s talk, one that would appeal to their exclusive circle of friends. I prepared a list of a dozen titles, and Mrs. Birla chose “How to Become Successful in Life.” It was a telling choice, I thought: the invitees were already successful by ordinary standards, but still they were not satisfied—they wanted to become more successful.

I went ahead with a few devotees to set up the arrangements for Prabhupada and the Deities on the Birlas’ expansive lawn. We had prepared a high vyasasana for Prabhupada and, near it, an altar with our small brass Radha-Krishna Deities.

Prabhupada arrived in the Birlas’ white Mercedes and walked into the garden. When he saw that his seat was higher than the Deities, he immediately had us remove the base of his asana.

Addressing the Birlas’ family and friends, Prabhupada gave a transcendental definition of success. He said that Krishna had two energies:

His inferior, material energy, and His superior, spiritual energy. The material energy was Durga, with ten hands brandishing ten kinds of weapons, and the spiritual energy was Srimati Radharani. We were under the control of the material energy, and success meant gaining release from the material energy and being blessed by the spiritual energy, Srimati Radharani.

“Radharani and Durga,” Prabhupada said, “both are prakritis of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, but one prakriti is meant for controlling this material world and the other prakriti is meant for blessing the spiritual world.

“Radharani—the name has come from the word aradhyate. Aradha means worshipping, beginning from Radharani and her expansion Laksmi in Vaikuntha. Here we worship Mother Laksmiji, the goddess of fortune, to receive some favor, but in the Vaikuntha world there are many hundreds of thousands of Laksmis, and with great respect they are engaged in serving the Supreme Lord.

“So, we, being expansions of the spiritual Laksmi, or Radharani, our duty is to serve Radharani, and through Radharani to serve Krishna. This is the Krishna consciousness movement. We are missing this point. Instead of learning from Radharani how to serve Krishna, we are being controlled by the other prakriti, material energy, Durga, with weapons in her ten hands. This is our position.

“In this material world people do not know what is the aim of life. Everyone is very much expert to see his interest. Two businessmen, they are agreeing, but everyone is trying to see his personal interest first. This is called svartha-gatim. That is natural. But Prahlada Maharaja says, na te viduh svartha-gatim hi visnum. Unfortunately, these materialistic persons do not know what is real interest. The real interest is Vishnu, how to serve Vishnu.”

As Hari-sauri later described, “Prabhupada possessed a unique ability to link anyone from any walk of life to the common goal of spiritual attainment. His preaching was always perfectly suitable for the time, place, and circumstance. To the leaders of this wealthy business community he thus offered a pertinent example.”

“The subject,” Prabhupada said, “was how to become successful in life. Krishna comes to instruct this simple truth—that you are being controlled by the material energy. You give up this business andbecome controlled by the spiritual energy, and your life is successful. Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu has said, jivera ‘svarupa haya-krsnera ‘nitya-dasa. But our disease is, instead of becoming dasa we are trying to become the master of the prakriti. This is called the materialistic way of life. It will not make us happy at any stage of our life. The success of the human form of life is to understand our relationship with God. And we should act in relationship with God. Then our success of life will be achieved. This is the main purpose of Krishna consciousness movement.”

The Birla family was famous for their religious interests as well as their business enterprises, with opulent Birla temples prominent in most major Indian cities, and Prabhupada took the opportunity to invite them and their friends to progress to engaging in munificent transcendental activities. “That is Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s mission,” he said. “He wished especially Indians to take this job of preaching the teachings of Bhagavad-gita all over the world. The mission is they must be very, very merciful to all outsiders. That is India’s mission. People are in darkness, tamasi; bring them into the light: tamasi ma jyotir gamah. This attempt has been done by us individually with teeny effort, but it is becoming successful. But every one of us should become completely aware of this movement and take this mission.”

Prabhupada challenged his audience: “Krishna said, ‘You just offer Me a little flower and water.’ If you think, ‘We have got money, the money is for my enjoyment, and Krishna may be offered a little water and flower,’ that is cheating. That is not good. According to your position you must worship. This is wanted. To become very big businessman is not an ordinary thing; it requires tapasya, very great labor, brain, yat tapasyasi. But the result, Krishna says, kurusva mad-arpanam. He’s asking, ‘Give it to Me.’ So, there is no harm to become a very big businessman, earning money. That is all right. But you give it to Krishna. Then in any position you can remain Krishna conscious. And if you remain Krishna conscious, then you will understand Krishna.”

At the end of his talk, Prabhupada asked several times for questions but got no response.

I addressed the audience: “The process of hearing and then asking questions is the way to clarify our understanding, just like Krishna and

Arjuna. So actually, we must have some questions in our minds; otherwise, we would all immediately surrender to Krishna.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada said. “Either you surrender to Krishna or clear it by question.”

Still, there was no response. So I ended the talk, and while other devotees showed a film on the lawn, Prabhupada and a small group of us were invited inside to have dinner.

Ashok Birla, who had donated three lakhs of rupees for construction of the ISKCON Vrindavan temple, expressed his happiness with the evening’s program. Then Mrs. Birla and her brother-in-law and Prabhupada’s friend Brijratan Mohatta led us upstairs in the lift to a large, beautifully furnished dining room.

When Mrs. Birla offered Prabhupada prasada, he refused. My heart sank, because I feared that he might offend her by not accepting dinner and create an awkward situation. She again offered, and again he declined. Finally, the third time, he accepted, and I could see from the smiles on everyone’s faces that they had both been playing their parts perfectly—she as the gracious hostess and he as the renounced sannyasi. Indian culture was so subtle and elevated.

Sitting at the head of a long, polished mahogany table, Prabhupada chatted with his hosts, complimenting them on the delicious meal and answering a variety of questions.

After a cordial departure, we arrived back at the temple around eleven o’clock. It was a successful preaching engagement, but Prabhupada said to me, “That no questions were asked after the lecture indicated a lack of interest on the part of the guests.”

The next morning on his walk on Juhu Beach, he commented, “Last night I explained at the Birla house that you have to change only your care of. Now we are under the care of the material energy, and you have to transfer yourself under the care of the spiritual energy.”

On December 24, by invitation of the king, Prabhupada went to Sanand, Gujarat, for a week of programs.

Four days later, Om Prakash Dhir came to the temple for the Sunday program. He was the chief engineer of ECO, the Engineering and Construction and Contracts, a division of Larsen & Toubro. Earlier, hehad invited Dhirasanta home for dinner and become a life member, and Dhirasanta had informed him about the construction on Hare Krishna Land and invited him for the Sunday celebrations. The construction site was near our temple shed, and after the feast he took a look. He was appalled by the miserable work, and quite concerned.

“We have to do something about it,” Prabhupada had told me. “You have to do something.” He didn’t want to directly challenge or oppose— or discourage—Saurabha, but he did want change. He had spoken to me about the Vrindavan guesthouse, how poor the work was—the plumbing was bad, the plaster was cracking, this was bad, that was bad—and didn’t want anything similar to happen in Bombay.

“Yes,” I had said, appreciating his concern. “If this happens in Bombay, it will be very troublesome.”

“Not troublesome,” Prabhupada had replied. “Everything will be spoiled.”

So, I knew that Prabhupada wanted change—and wanted me to accomplish it. But Saurabha was opposing my efforts to change the construction arrangements, and I wasn’t able to find anyone else who could do the work. I was exhausted by the whole situation.

When Mr. Dhir said the work was poor, however, I had to inquire further. “Is it really that bad?” I asked. “What do you mean?”

“The construction is the typical substandard work going on in Bombay,” he said. “Within two or three years this type of work starts falling apart. ISKCON is a great institution. This temple should be a monument that will last for hundreds or thousands of years.” He explained that ECC, the leading construction firm in India, didn’t usually take up anything involving less than several crores. He described some of the work they had done—dams, bridges, and other major civil projects. But he said that he would speak to the directors and try to persuade them to take up our project. Even though it would be much smaller than most of their jobs, it was different—it was for Krishna— and it would be a prestigious job for the company.

I immediately wrote Srila Prabhupada:

Today one of our life members came to spend the day at Hare Krishna Land. His name is Mr. О. P. Dhir, the Chief Engineer for Larsen &

Toubro, Ltd., the largest construction firm in Bombay. Mr. Dhir is presently undertaking the construction of the new Council Hall for the Government of Maharashtra as well as the new Stock Exchange Building, which will be the tallest building in Bombay.

Mr. Dhir inspected the site and expressed his opinion that if the work continues in the present manner the building will not stand. He said that the present workmen are obviously accustomed to a very low standard of work, and he particularly criticized the shuttering and casting. He said that the present structural defects would render the entire building defective in the end. I asked if his company would be willing to take up the project, and he replied that they might not be willing but that he could request them. He said that Larsen & Toubro had consented to build an important building at Auroville, and he hoped that he would be able to convince them to take up our work also.

In order to maintain a high standard of workmanship throughout the building, he said that his company would like to supply materials after consulting our architect on the rates to be paid for the materials. He said that the company would probably work for cost plus 5%. He seems very sincere and sober, so I suggested that he meet Your Divine Grace and Gopal Krishna Prabhu when you return to Bombay. Mr. Dhir is also going to think of alternative solutions in the event that his company does not agree to do our work.

Prabhupada liked the idea of our engaging ECC. He knew from experience that there were problems with hiring different contractors. And seeing how our work was going, he concluded that the best arrangement would be to hire one big contractor to take responsibility for everything: the foundation, the structural work, the plumbing, the electricity, the marble, the finishing—all of it. And he thought ECC was the proper organization.

Although Larsen & Toubro’s head office was in Bombay, ECC’s was in Madras, where its managing director, Mr. Ramakrishna, was based. So we asked Mr. Dhir to arrange a meeting with Mr. Ramakrishna and us the next time Ramakrishna came to Bombay.

We met at Mr. Dhir’s residence. Mr. Ramakrishna came from a traditional Hindu family, but he seemed to be quite a tough businessman, and it wasn’t clear to me where he actually stood. Still, he seemed positive about doing the job, and he said that for us he would charge only hiscost price or just 2 or 3 percent above. He explained that their general calculation was cost plus 30 percent, the rate they charged even Larsen & Toubro.

Initially, Saurabha was disturbed. He didn’t like the idea that the construction would be taken out of his hands, and he was skeptical about ECC. “So many people come and talk big,” he said, “but when it comes time to do the work, they never do anything.” He was critical of the whole arrangement. But as he met with Mr. Dhir and others from ECC, his attitude began to soften, and in the end he went along with the change.

Once we agreed in principle to engage ECC, they gave us their cash-flow requirement, which came to seven lakhs per month—a huge amount for us. Mr. Dhir presented a progress chart, detailing each phase of the work and indicating when it would be completed.

“In Bombay we had the best collectors,” Gopal Krishna later recounted. “Giriraj, Sridhar, Citrakara, Jagat Purusa, and others were collecting well, but still the collections were nowhere near the seven lakhs required to get the project completed. I was with Prabhupada in Madras, and I told him, ‘I just spoke to Giriraj, and the contractor is ready to take on the job only if we guarantee seven lakhs a month.’”

We sent the draft of the contract with ECC to Prabhupada in Mayapur. He approved of ECC’s approach; now the work would be done quickly and professionally. The Hare Krishna Land project was so dear to him that he wanted to see it realized at any cost, and he took immediate steps to arrange the funds. He wrote Ramesvara, who was in charge of the Bhaktivedanta Book Trust (BBT), “We have just engaged the best and most experienced construction company in India, Larsen & Toubro, to complete our Bombay project. We have had to guarantee them seven lakhs rupees per month for the next nine months. And thereafter we shall immediately begin the Mayapur temple. So I think $50,000 will not be sufficient. Gopal Krishna Prabhu suggests that in addition to sending this amount, if the Radha Damodara Party is given books at the printer’s cost, then whatever else they collect they can send directly to me in India. In this way we shall be able to meet the Rs. 7 lakhs per month. So please make this arrangement to send $50,000 per month as well as supplying Radha Damodara Party at cost. Begin thisimmediately.” And a month later he followed up, “Regarding the money for Bombay, you may send it by the first week of each month. Following each transfer, please send me a xerox copy of the transfer slip.”

“Ramesvara was a very strong motivator of book distribution,” Gopal Krishna recalled. “He was one of our best sankirtana generals. He started writing sankirtana newsletters to devotees all over the movement, how Prabhupada wanted the Bombay temple built but that it could be built only if we increased book distribution, because unless we increased book distribution, we couldn’t send the required money to Bombay. So the whole world went on a marathon to increase book distribution to generate funds so Ramesvara could send money to Prabhupada in Bombay for the construction. Then ECC started the work. And they really started—they at once put two or three hundred people.”

“At the end of 1975,” Ramesvara remembered, “we had just finished the seventeen-book Caitanya-caritamrta marathon. Now we knew we could do anything. There was no such thing as ‘impossible.’ We got a letter from Srila Prabhupada stating that they had finally gotten permission to build the beautiful Bombay temple, hotel, theater, and cultural center in Juhu Beach. So in 1976 the loans plus the Bombay money totaled almost two million dollars. Again it had doubled.

“When Prabhupada first told me about Juhu Beach and his desire to build a temple and cultural center, I was not just amazed, but I got a glimpse of the magnitude of his vision and how fabulous and overwhelmingly successful the project would be—and the whole idea of this land being so valuable because of its location: the beach in the heart of the film capital of India. It would end up being an amazing opportunity, and Prabhupada just injected me with this enthusiasm, and I was really committed to sending as much money as Prabhupada directed. It was done with no reluctance; it was done with the utmost enthusiasm, that this is going to be something so wonderful for the movement. You just knew it was going to happen.”

After my success in raising funds for Juhu in Lagos, I went to the Canary Islands to pursue more leads from my friend Damodar Chanrai, whose daughter lived there. I developed what turned out to be a compelling strategy for approaching the Hindus there, advising them thatthey had to ensure that their children maintained their Vedic culture and were aware of—and convinced about—the Vedic knowledge. I explained that their children might not accept the tradition solely on faith—it had to be presented to them rationally and scientifically, which practically only ISKCON devotees, many of whom came from the West, could do. I also said that their children, most of whom knew only Spanish, should read the Vedic scriptures, and that only ISKCON could provide Spanish translations. I arranged Spanish books for them, and they were delighted to become life members, but they could not afford to contribute more than the membership fees.

The Sindhis, especially the wealthier ones, were a close-knit group, and friends in the Canary Islands suggested Sindhis in different places whom they thought could contribute. So after the Canaries, I pursued affluent Sindhis in places as far-flung as Italy, Jamaica, and San Diego, California. But none of them gave much.

In America I also received several invitations and suggestions to preach there, and I began to think I should. I had seen the college preaching that devotees were doing in Berkeley, and it seemed like a good field for me. In 1971, in Gorakhpur, Srila Prabhupada had told me that I should try to get his books accepted in universities, by the scholarly class, so I began to put together a whole plan of how I would preach there, write for BTG, and meet with leading intellectuals. Prabhavishnu was in Juhu to manage affairs, and ECC was taking care of the construction, so I concluded that I wasn’t needed in Bombay. I would just let them carry on, and when the building was ready, I would go back and preach. I extended my tour as long as possible before returning to India for the Mayapur festival.

I was still having difficulty surrendering to the idea of being based in Bombay. Bewildered about what course I should take, I consulted various senior devotees in Mayapur. Tamal Krishna, who had already given up his service in India, told me, “You are just wasting your time here. You should come out and do something.” Satsvarupa thought the idea of my writing and preaching in the West was good, as did Ravindra Svarupa. Everyone seemed to agree. The only one who didn’t was Gopal Krishna, the GBC for Bombay. In fact, he was quite upset about the proposal. But the others said that he was just attached to my servingin Juhu because he was the GBC. I consulted Hamsaduta, who had no objection to my leaving Bombay but thought I should travel with him in his bus program in India and do kirtan and preach.

I didn’t know what to do, and my anxiety began to mount. Eventually it reached the point where I couldn’t take it anymore. I confided in Gopal Krishna, and after discussing the situation further, we decided to ask Prabhupada.

In Prabhupada’s room, I began to explain with great earnestness and thoughtfulness (or so I thought) how Prabhavishnu was now in Juhu to manage and ECC was there for the construction—but before I got out three sentences, Prabhupada interrupted and said, “So, you want to change?”

“No, no,” I replied. “I don’t want to change. I just want to do what is right, what is best for the preaching.”

Prabhupada smiled and said, “Best you take up residence in India.”

All my elaborate plans and arguments were shattered. “Yes, Srila Prabhupada,” I said, and I offered my obeisances and walked out.

On the veranda, I turned to Gopal Krishna and said, “I feel like such a fool. I can’t believe I just did that.”

Gopal Krishna was very kind and said, “That’s all right. Prabhupada knows what we are. He understands.”

All this time I had been keeping the conception that I was attached not to Bombay but to Prabhupada: if he wanted me in Bombay, I’d be in Bombay, but if he wanted me elsewhere, I’d go there. I had never grasped that he wanted me in Bombay permanently. But after my meeting with him in Mayapur, I started to consider that my leaving Bombay was not to be taken as lightly as I had been thinking. So, with renewed determination to serve the Bombay project, I returned from Mayapur.

Upon my arrival in Juhu, I found a letter from Prabhupada waiting for me—his reply to my report about my preaching in the Canary Islands. “It is my intelligence and your cooperation that is working,” he wrote. “There is a story of a man who was challenged whether he had any intelligence. He then began to look in his pocket. When asked why he was looking in his pocket, he replied, ‘If there is money, then there is intelligence.’ So, you have gone so far to collect money and intelligently,but if there is no money, where is the intelligence? Both must combine, then everything works out nicely?

Chastened and humbled by Prabhupada’s words, I began to ponder their significance. But Prabhupada encouraged me to go, I considered. He even suggested that I go to East Africa. When I was in Mayapur, however, I had been getting reports that Prabhupada was not pleased with my preaching tour. Gargamuni had approached him with the same idea to go outside India and preach to Hindus in different places, and Prabhupada had told him, “Giriraj’s program of collecting from Hindus in other places is not good, because they are giving their hard-earned money and they will want something local that they can benefit from. They won’t like it that he is coming, preaching for a few days, taking their money, and going to Bombay.”

Also, in Mayapur, when I had met Prabhupada a day or two after I had presented my proposal to him about preaching in the West, he had asked me how much I had collected on my tour. I had told him about a lakh of rupees. “Well,” he had said, “if you had spent the same time collecting in Bombay, do you think you would have been able to collect as much?”

“Probably,” I had replied.

“Then what was the use of your going?”

Reading Prabhupada’s letter in my office in Juhu, I went over it all in my mind. On the one hand, before I had left, Prabhupada had been encouraging me to go, but on the other, while I was gone, he had been criticizing me for going when I could have been collecting in Bombay. Actually, even in the Canary Islands, I had understood that if I wanted to preach to rich Indians, Bombay was the best place. I concluded that Prabhupada had known that I had wanted to go and had encouraged me to go just to teach me this lesson.

I thought about it all day long for several days. Then finally I just surrendered: I accepted the fact that I would be in Bombay for the rest of my life. Earlier, I had been thinking, What am I doing in Bombay? What do I have to do with Bombay or India? I'm an American, I was a college student, and suddenly I'm here in Bombay. I have nothing to do with Bombay or India. I could see being—serving—in Vrindavan or Mayapur, which were holy dhamas, but I had thought that Bombay was just some foreign city.

Now I could see that actually the internal cultivation of Krishna consciousness was transcendental to time, place, or situation. It didn’t matter whether I was in Bombay or New York or Chicago or any other place; the transcendental process could go on anywhere and not be affected by the geographical location. By Krishna’s arrangement, I had been engaged in service in Bombay, and by Prabhupada’s desire I had been engaged in a particular way there. So, I accepted it: Well, my body is going to be given for Krishna's service somewhere, and it could be anywhere, so why not in Bombay?

A couple of weeks later, Kuladri, who was passing through Juhu, perhaps also coming from the festival, told me that New Vrindaban had never really developed until devotees had started surrendering to the project and committing themselves to dedicating this lifetime. When one devotee did that, and then another, and then another, the project really got going.

I saw that this was what had just happened to me, and that from me it would have to spread to others, and then the Juhu project could really take shape. And that was how I ultimately surrendered to staying in India, in Juhu. From then on, I just accepted Prabhupada’s desire for me to be in Bombay. What Kuladri had said about New Vrindaban was true: by actually surrendering and dedicating oneself to a particular project, one could work more sincerely and accomplish more service.

When I accepted that I would be in Bombay permanently, I began to see things in a new light. Whomever I met, I would think, “You are going to be here, and I am going to be here, so we may as well get to know—and like—each other.” If I met someone and asked for a donation or tried to engage him in some other service and he declined, I would always try to leave him with a good impression, because I would think, “I am going to be here for a long time, and you are going to be here for a long time—we may meet again.”

After the Mayapur festival, Prabhupada visited Haridaspur, Calcutta, Delhi, Modi Nagar, Aligarh, and Vrindavan, and arrived in Juhu on April 11. The next morning, before going for his walk on the beach, he made a careful inspection of the entire building site. All the ground-floor construction for the temple, auditorium, and twin-toweredguesthouse was finished. Prabhupada was pleased with ECC’s work. He tapped the pillars with his cane and said, “Very good. There is a big difference between this and the other work that was being done here.”

One thing that Mr. Dhir had been concerned about was the temple’s foundation, and he had promised that when ECC took over the job, they would strengthen the foundations done by the previous contractor, which included both the guesthouse and the temple. And that was the first thing ECC did: they used a sophisticated technical process that employed high pressure to fill in all the holes and gaps in the foundation and added layers of cement on top of that.

With the construction now progressing well, Prabhupada spoke with me about what deities we should install in the new temple. “There are many devotees of Rama in Bombay,” he said, and he suggested that we have Lord Ramachandra. We discussed different possibilities: Sita-Rama, Sita-Rama-Laksmana-Hanuman, Sita-Rama-Laksmana-Hanuman and their associates.

Finally he decided: “Sita-Rama-Laksmana-Hanuman.”

The first altar was clear: Guru-Gauranga, as in Vrindavan. And the central altar would be Sri Sri Radha-Rasabihari.

“What if we have Lalita and Visakha with Radha and Krishna?” I suggested.

Prabhupada’s eyes widened, his eyebrows raised, and his lips spread in a broad smile. “Oh, yes,” he said. “Very good. Very good idea.”

Personally, I didn’t think the idea was so exceptional—Prabhupada had already installed Lalita and Visakha with Sri Sri Radha-Syamasundara in Vrindavan. But he made a big thing of it, as if it was a stroke of genius or inspiration. In times to come, I would think of its significance—that we approach Radha and Krishna through, or with the help of, Their gopl friends and servants, such as Lalita and Visakha.

Six weeks later, Saurabha wrote Prabhupada, who was then in Los Angeles, to clarify the standard of worship in the new temple—whether there should be any change or any special arrangement, such as extra bhajans.

Prabhupada replied on June 7: “For worshiping the Deities in Bombay, including Sita-Rama, there is absolutely no change in worship. Adopt the same method as in our Vrindavan center, with three pujaris, just like in

Vrindavan. They are all Vishnu-tattva: Ramachandra, Radha-Krishna, Gaura-Nitai. No additional kirtans; simply do exactly as in Vrindavan.” In addition to the main temple complex, Prabhupada wanted another building constructed on some vacant land toward the rear of the property, near the southern border. The building would house a godown for storing books, classrooms for a gurukula school, and a vanaprastha ashram, a facility for elderly people to stay at Hare Krishna Land, to “retire from their material responsibilities and take up spiritual responsibilities.” He gave the example of former mayor Ravji Ganatra: “He is just the kind of person we want.” The rooms could be small, he said, but should have all the basic amenities; although these vanaprasthas would be living a simpler life in the ashram, we couldn’t expect them to change their lifestyles completely.

Most evenings, Prabhupada would meet with visitors on the roof. We never took up his subsequent suggestion—that we should have devotees speak on all the terraces in the evenings, preaching in different languages, since whoever presented the message of Krishna would get good results—but his roof talks were a treat for devotees and visitors alike. During one such darshan, he met with five or ten devotees and a few Indian guests, including a famous movie star and his wife. Somebody had brought mangoes for him, and at one point he called for a knife and told a devotee to cut a mango and distribute it as prasada. So a brahma-chari got a knife and sliced the mango, but it was dripping juice all over—it was a mess.

“You cannot cut it?” Prabhupada asked.

“The knife is not very sharp,” the brahmachari replied.

“That is not the way to cut it,” the movie star’s wife interjected. “Give it to me.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada said. “You do not know how to cut. One who knows, let him cut.”

So, the woman took the mango, cut it into two neat halves and scored the flesh into crisscrossed cubes. Then she popped the insides out, and it was a simple matter to pick the cubes off the peel.

Prabhupada laughed at how expertly and neatly she had done it. “Just see,” he said, “even for cutting a mango, one requires a guru.” Then he quoted from the Mundaka Upanisad (1.2.12): “Tad-vijnanarthamsa gurum evabhigacchet”—“To learn the science one must certainly approach a spiritual master.” The guests and devotees all laughed, and Prabhupada told the brahmachari to distribute the prasada, one piece to everyone.

“Everything requires a guru,” Prabhupada repeated. “Otherwise, one remains a fool, rascal—that’s all. In every item you require a guru. And to understand Krishna, or God, everyone thinks they are independent. Just see the foolishness. Yata mata tata patha. ‘Ah, you consider about God in your own way. It doesn’t require any guru.’ This foolishness is going on. For cutting a mango, one requires a guru, and to understand Krishna, he doesn’t require a guru. This foolishness is going on. And Krishna says,

tad viddhi pranipatena  
pariprasnena sevaya  
upadeksyanti te jnanam  
jnaninas tattva-darsinah  
\[Gita 4.34\]

\[“Just try to learn the truth by approaching a spiritual master. Inquire from him submissively and render service unto him. The self-realized souls can impart knowledge unto you because they have seen the truth.”\] Krishna says you have to understand like this. But everyone is thinking, ‘Why shall I go to guru?”’

“The first requirement,” he continued, “is humility, that ‘I have no knowledge; I have to go to somebody who has knowledge.’ This is humility. And if you think, ‘I have got very advanced knowledge; why shall I go to anyone?’ there is no entrance into knowledge. He is finished from the beginning.”

The next day, Srila Prabhupada departed for Melbourne. Soon thereafter, Amogha and his wife came to Juhu from Australia. Prabhavishnu, who had been serving as the Juhu vice-president, wanted to join the library party and travel and distribute books. He had asked Prabhupada several times if he could do some kind of traveling and preaching, but Prabhupada had always told him, “You have to stay; we need you here.” Then, finally, Prabhupada had said that if Prabhavishnu could find a replacement, he could go. We asked

Amogha, and he wrote to Prabhupada, who agreed: “You may remain in Bombay and assist with the temple management in cooperation with Giriraj das?

Soon thereafter, in August, Back to Godhead published a lecture by Srila Prabhupada under the title “What is a Guru?” in which he referred to an exchange between Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and Sri Vallabhacharya:

“The bona fide guru will simply present what the supreme guru, God, says in bona fide scripture. A guru cannot change the message of the disciplic succession. Once there was a gentleman named Vallabhacarya, who was very devoted to Caitanya Mahaprabhu. Vallabhacarya wrote a commentary on Srimad-Bhagavatam, and he presented it to Caitanya Mahaprabhu, saying, ‘Lord Caitanya, please hear my commentary on Srimad-Bhagavatam. You will find that it is far better than Sridhara Svami’s.’ Sridhara Svami was a very ancient commentator. Caitanya Mahaprabhu immediately rejected Vallabhacarya, saying, ‘Oh, are you claiming that you have written something better than Sridhara Svami?’ Caitanya Mahaprabhu then chastised Vallabhacarya, saying, svamike yini na manena, tini vesya. Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu sarcastically used the word svami, which also means husband. He said, ‘I think that one who does not recognize the svami \[husband\] is a prostitute.’ In other words, ‘If you do not recognize Sridhara Svami, then you are a prostitute. How can I hear from a prostitute?”’

Sumati Morarji was a staunch follower of the Vallabhacharya sam-pradaya, and she became disturbed and wrote Prabhupada a long letter, which was delivered to me in Juhu and which I forwarded to him in New Mayapur, France. In my covering letter I mentioned that her secretary had been approaching me almost every day on her behalf but that H. H. Tilkayat Govindalal Maharaja, the head of the Vallabha-sampradaya in Nathdwara, who, as Tilkayat, was entrusted with the sevd of the famous Deity Shrinathji, appeared to be the main person behind the agitation.

“I had a firm belief in your mission of spreading the message of Shri Krishna all over the world,” Sumati Morarji had written, “but reading the above extract of your lecture I was very much disappointed, since thereinyou attempted to portray an incorrect image of Shri Vallabhacharya, based on hearsays. Time has been changing, and when we present the image of our ancient Acharyas to the public today, great responsibility rests in us in preserving their greatness and not in tarnishing them.... Every Acharya is great in his own way and no Acharya is greater than another. Each had come to this world to perform one’s duties and every Acharya has done so in the best possible way.”

She said she could generate wide and adverse publicity against ISKCON but did not feel that doing so would serve anyone’s interest. She ended with a request that things could be amicably resolved: “I sincerely trust that your good self will take my observations in the proper perspective and spirit and publish your clarifications with a view to remove any misunderstanding which may have been created in the minds of the readers of Back to Godhead.”

Prabhupada was concerned that Sumati Morarji not misunderstand his statements or intentions. “I am sorry to learn that you have become a little agitated regarding the publication of an article in our Back to Godhead magazine,” he replied. “It is certainly unpleasant, but the officers who publish the magazine do not know satyam bruyat priyam bruyat, in this material world only palatable truth should be spoken. Unpalatable truth should be carefully avoided. The cause of Lord Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s agitation was much the same as your own. As you are irritated by the criticism of Sri Vallabhacharya, similarly Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was also agitated when Vallabhacharya criticized Sridhara Svami.”

Prabhupada pointed out that Sridhara Svami was accepted as the original and most important commentator on Srimad-Bhagavatam. The parampara of commentators, he stated, “has existed for a very long time. It was also accepted during Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s time, but Sri Vallabhacharya violated the system. Instead of acknowledging Sridhara Svami’s pre-eminent position, he wanted to take it himself. I am enclosing herewith some photocopies of the important verses from the original book Caitanya Caritamrta that specifically deal with the subject matter. These verses are from Antya-lila, Chapter 7, entitled ‘Lord Caitanya meets Vallabha Bhatta.’ I would like to draw your attention to verse 113 on page 55 where Vallabha Bhatta says:

‘“In my commentary on Srimad-Bhagavatam ... I have refuted the explanations of Sridhara Svami. I cannot accept his explanations.’

“Moreover, verse 114 states:

“‘Whatever Sridhara Svami reads he explains according to the circumstances. Therefore he is inconsistent in his explanations and cannot be accepted as an authority.’

“Vallabha Bhatta’s declaration certainly agitated Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu. Consequently, Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu remarked sarcastically that He considered that anyone who did not accept the svami (or Sridhara Svami) as an authority was a prostitute. Prabhu hasi kahe; but he smiled and said this jokingly, because they were friends.

“Although this point is very controversial, it is not based on hearsay, as you have stated, but it is authoritatively documented by the Caitanya Caritamrta. As you have written in a friendly spirit, I do not wish to discuss this point further. If you will kindly take a little trouble to read this chapter ‘Lord Caitanya meets Vallabha Bhatta’ you will understand the whole situation....

“Everything will become clear if you kindly read this chapter with attention. For example, we see that two lawyers in the courtroom may fight vigorously about a law point, but upon returning to the law library, they talk and embrace like friends. So, you should always remember that we have no ill feelings towards Vallabha Bhattacharya. We have full respect for him, so there is no harm if these facts are discussed in the society of devotees. Devotees always humbly offer respect to everyone, but when there is a discussion on a point of shastra, they do not observe the usual etiquette, satyam bruyat priyam bruyat. They speak only the satyam \[truth\], although it may not necessarily be priyam \[pleasing\].

“I hope you will understand the whole situation. If you still have any doubts, I shall be glad to hear from you and shall try to satisfy you to the best of my ability. I am presently not in very good health, nonetheless I hope this meets you well.

“Your ever well-wisher,

A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami”

After Prabhupada’s reply, there was no further argument from Sumati Morarji, and Prabhupada also submitted a testimonial for her later that month:

“Madame Sumati Morarjee is a great friend of our Krishna Consciousness Movement. I first met her in connection with the printing of my Srimad-Bhagavatam, and she was so kind as to immediately pay me 500 Rupees for it. Later on, in 1965 when I wanted to go to the USA, I appealed to this benevolent lady again to carry me aboard one of her ships to New York, and she immediately arranged for it. I was able to start for the USA on account of her kindness, and taking some books with me I safely reached on September 19th, 1965.

“When I returned to India in 1970, she gave me a good reception in her office building. Many nice gentlemen also met me at that time. I feel obliged to this benevolent lady in so many ways for her helping this Krishna Consciousness Movement. I wish that Lord Krishna may give her a long life fully engaged in the service of the Lord.”

Prabhupada was not happy that the editors of BTG had printed an article on such a controversial topic and said that they should be more discreet in what they published and not disturb people who were friends of ISKCON, including our life members in Bombay who were also followers of Vallabhacharya. “There has been some disturbance created by the publishing of a few comments on Vallabhacharya,” he wrote Jagannatha Suta, the editor. “Kindly avoid comments such as these in future publications.”

The head of the Vallabhacharya sampradaya in Bombay was a good friend of Srila Prabhupada and ISKCON. Prabhupada had even mentioned him in Sri Caitanya-caritamrta: “The present head of the Vallabha Bhattacarya sampradaya of Bombay is named Diksita Maharaja. He is very friendly to our movement, and whenever we meet him, this learned brahmana scholar highly praises the activities of the Hare Krsna movement. He is a life member of our Society, and although he is a learned scholar in the brahminical caste tradition, he accepts our Society and considers its members bona fide devotees of Lord Visnu.” (Madhya 19.70)

But Diksita’s son, Shyam Goswami, also in Bombay, had from the beginning been antagonistic to ISKCON, and he took up the cause of criticizing us for Prabhupada’s statements in BTG. I wrote to Prabhupada and enclosed a strongly worded letter written by Shyam, which had been circulated to some of our life members. In it he protested the BTGarticle, condemned ISKCON as a fanatical organization, called for our life members to withdraw their support, and was personally insulting to Prabhupada.

I also proposed a solution: “We were thinking of replying to this incident in the ‘Hare Krishna Monthly,’ sent to all of our members every month. The format would be in terms of a letter to the editor stating that ‘I was very concerned about the article published in Back to Godhead about Sri Vallabhacharya and I would like you to clarify the situation.’ Then we could publish the reply you sent to Smt. Morarji.” Prabhupada accepted my suggestion, and a few weeks later, I was pleased to add, “We received only one letter of protest after Shyam Goswami sent his letter, and now that the Vallabhacharya leader in Ahmedabad has been exposed, none of the Vallabhacharya followers are venturing any criticisms against us. So, except for a few sensitive souls, the matter seems to have died down.”

One criticism that continued was from Sri Govindalalji Maharaja of Nathawara, the head of the Vallabha-sampradaya, who wrote me through his secretary that he had been pained by “the highly disparaging remarks” in the BTG article and accused the author of Sri Caitanya-caritamrta of being biased and ignorant of Sri Vallabhacharya’s commentary on Srimad-Bhagavatam and how it had refuted Sridhara Svami’s. The letter concluded by saying that until ISKCON and Prabhupada made suitable amends and rectified the error of insulting Sri Vallabhacharya, the head and members of the sampradaya would disassociate themselves from our movement.

When I sent Prabhupada Govindalalji Maharaja’s comments, he replied immediately, citing the authority of the shastras and directing his remarks to Maharaja. “We can’t rectify what is written in Caitanya Caritamrta,” he wrote. “We have no bad feeling or disrespect for Vallabhacharya. We consider ourselves the most obedient servants of Vallabhacharya. The exchange between Lord Chaitanya and Vallabhacharya was on friendly terms. This was raised in connection with supporting the position of the acharyas. The real point is that Sridhara Swami is still being criticized by you, and this criticism of Sridhara Swami was as much intolerable for Chaitanya Mahaprabhuas His criticism upon Vallabhacharya is intolerable for you. Such kind of friendly criticism you’ll always find among learned scholars, but that does not mean any ill feeling with one another. So, as you can criticize Sridhara Swami in the above words, what is the wrong if in the same spirit the supporters of Sridhara Swami criticize you? There is an English proverb spoken by Lord Jesus Christ, ‘Judge not others lest ye be judged.’ So, the conclusion is, as we learn from Caitanya Caritamrta, that in the beginning Sri Vallabhacharya criticized Sridhara Swami and then Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu criticized Vallabhacharya. So what can we do now after 500 years? Recently some criticism has appeared in The Illustrated Weekly also. So, such things will go on in this world, but that does not mean we have got any disrespect for any Vaishnava acharya.”

I conveyed Prabhupada’s points to Govindalalji Maharaja, concluding, “We hope that these words will help clarify the situation.”

A few months later, I wrote to Prabhupada that Shyam Goswami’s temple in Bombay had been raided by government authorities. One after the other, leaders of the Vallabhacharya sampradaya in both Bombay and Nathdwara—as well as in Ahmedabad—were exposed, as authorities found hidden caches of gold, jewels, and money and discovered love letters and sex scandals between the priests and ladies in the congregation. Shyam Goswami and Vallabhacharya’s other inheritors were replaced by a new set of trustees. The whole sampradaya was in chaos.

“Perhaps,” I wrote Prabhupada, “their offense at your lotus feet is becoming their downfall.” I thought of Sanatana Gosvami’s quote from the Skanda Purdna in his Hari-bhakti-vilasa:

yo hi bhagavatam lokam upahasam nrpottama  
karoti tasya nasyanti artha-dharma-yasah-sutah  
hanti nindati vai dvesti vaisnavan nabhinandati  
krudhyate yati no harsam darsane patanani sat

“One who derides an exalted devotee loses the results of his pious activities, his opulence, \[and\] his reputation .. . Whoever kills or blasphemes a Vaisnava and whoever is envious of a Vaisnava or angry with him, or whoever does not offer him obeisances or feel joy upon seeing him, certainly falls into a hellish condition.”

Murti dasa, from the construction department, and some other devotees from Juhu went to Nathdwara and met the Tilkayat Maharaja, who received them warmly and graciously and gave them a beautiful large painting of Shrinathji, with gold leaf and stones, as a gift for Srila Prabhupada. Prabhupada was pleased to receive it—especially after the earlier tense dealings with the Maharaja—and he had the framed painting hung on the wall opposite his translating desk, where it hangs even now.

Earlier, in October 1974, Murti dasa had visited the Shrinathji temple, and his warm reception there had prompted Prabhupada to address a letter to the temple:

My dear Sir:

Please accept my best wishes. I have received a report from my disciple Murti das Adhikari of the nice program that was held in Nathawara. I am very thankful for your cooperation for spreading Krishna consciousness all over the world. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and Vallabhacharya were good friends, and Vallabhacharya many times visited Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. We get this information from authorized books. So far as I know, Gopalaji is coming from Madhavendra Puri, the original acharya of Gaudiya Vaishnavas. His disciple was Isvara Puri, and his disciple was Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.

There is a great need for spreading Krishna consciousness all over the world based on the Bhagavad-gita As It Is. We have been successful in this attempt. I am very well known to Dixitji Goswami of Bombay. He likes very much my movement and my books. I am very much grateful for your contribution of so many books on Vallabha Sampradaya and also the framed pictures....

Faithfully yours,

A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami

On August 15, Indian Independence Day, some of the tenants assembled in the garden at noon, stood in silence for a minute before the small statue of Gandhi, and then proceeded with their annual celebration—garlanding the statue, hoisting the flag, singing the national anthem, and distributing sweets.

“Where is the question of independence?” Prabhupada challenged as Hari-sauri gave him his massage on the balcony adjoining his bedroom.

“We are all dependent at every step on Krishna’s mercy. The Indians struggled to become independent of the British, but who is independent of the laws of material nature?”

Prabhupada cited the ongoing drought in England, which was afflicting many people: the vegetation was drying up, animals were being killed prematurely because there was no fodder, factories in Wales were closing, and there was talk of importing water. “No one can do anything about it, and they think it is all happening by chance,” Prabhupada said. “There is not a single person in the whole world who actually knows anything.”

“No one except you, Srila Prabhupada,” Hari-sauri commented.

“Is that just flattery, or do you actually acknowledge that?” Prabhupada asked, smiling.

Hari-sauri assured him that it was not just empty praise and, as he related in his diary, “Prabhupada accepted it with pleasure as a heartfelt submission.”

The following day, during an early-morning conversation on Prabhupada’s roof, some devotees raised the question of other devotees going to Radha-kunda. Those going to Radha-kunda were supporting their actions by citing Srila Rupa Gosvami’s advice in the last verses of the Upadesamrta (9-11) that one should bathe in and reside at Radha-kunda.

Prabhupada challenged whether the devotees going to Radha-kunda had followed the other instructions, beginning with the first verse: vaco vegam manasah krodha-vegam/ jihva-vegam udaropastha-vegam/ etan vegan yo visaheta dhirah/ sarvam apimam prthivim sa sisyat: “A sober person who can tolerate the urge to speak, the mind’s demands, the actions of anger, and the urges of the tongue, belly, and genitals is qualified to make disciples all over the world.” He said that there was a test—whether one was sober and could tolerate these urges (etan vegan yo visaheta dhirah). If so, then Radha-kunda was for him—not that someone kept “three dozen seva-dasis \[mistresses\] and was living in Radha-kunda.”

He said that his guru maharaja had wanted to publish the confidential scripture Govinda-lilamrta and asked Bhaktivinoda Thakura’spermission. First Bhaktivinoda had said, ‘I'll tell you one day.” And when Bhaktisiddhanta had reminded him, he had said, “Yes, you can print one copy—for you. Not for distribution.”

“We are printing all these books for understanding properly,” Prabhupada explained. “Not that ‘Here is Radha-kunda. Let us go? Jump over like monkey. ‘Here is rasa-lila.'”

When Achyutananda added, “Even in Krsna book, rasa-lila should not be told in public,” Prabhupada responded, “No, why? Krsna book must be there, in the book it must be there. But you should go gradually. First of all, understand Krishna, then krsna-lila. If you have not understood Krishna, you’ll think Krishna’s rasa-lila is just like our mixing with young women. And then it becomes polluted—because you have not understood Krishna. The Bhagavad-gita says, manusyanam sahasresu kascid yatati siddhaye/ yatatam api siddhanam—‘Out of many thousands among men, one may endeavor for perfection, and of those who have achieved perfection, hardly one knows Me in truth? Krishna understanding is so easy? If you do not understand Krishna, how can you go to Krishna’s confidential activities? . . . You read all the books first of all. Then you’ll be able to understand. . . . Krishna lifted a hill. Now, how you can become equal with Krishna?”

“They also wear the Radha-kunda mati, tilak,” Achyutananda added.

“There is no harm,” Prabhupada replied, “but they should understand what is Radha-kunda and how to deal with Radha-kunda. Raghunatha dasa Gosvami showed how to live in Radha-kunda. Sankhya-purvaka-nama-gana-natibhih kalavasani-krtau. He was circumambulating Radha-kunda, falling down, making a mark. That is Radha-kunda vasi \[resident\]. He not only counted holy names but also offered obeisances so many hundred times. That is Radha-kunda. So much vairagya \[detachment\] he showed. He can take bath in Radha-kunda. First of all, do this like Raghunatha dasa Gosvami: sankhya-purvaka-nama-gana-natibhih kalavasani-krtau/ nidrahara-viharakadi-vijitau catyanta-dinau ca yau. \[“The Six Gosvamis were engaged in chanting the holy names of the Lord and bowing down in a scheduled measurement. In this way they utilized their valuable lives, and in executing these devotional activities they conquered over eating and sleeping and were always meek and humble.” (Sad-gosvamy-astaka 6)\]

“The Bhagavad-gita is the entrance. Then the Bhagavata is graduate, and then Caitanya-caritamrta. This is the step-by-step. But if one is sincere, everything becomes revealed. He does not commit mistake.”

The conclusion was that we must be sincere. But how would we demonstrate that we were sincere—or how could we become sincere? “You see,” Prabhupada continued, “you can become independent; nobody can check you. Everyone is independent (yathecchasi tatha kuru). But one who wants to be regulated, he has to surrender. That is voluntary. Otherwise, everyone is free to do whatever he likes. And those who are surrendered souls, they will wait for the instruction of guru and do accordingly. That is the proper . . . Guru-mukha-padma-vakya, cittete kariya aikya, ara na kariha. \[“Make the teachings from the lotus mouth of the spiritual master one with your heart, and do not desire anything else.” (Sri-guru-vandana 2)\] That is wanted. Otherwise, all living beings are independent. Even if I say that you do not do it, you are independent, you can do it. Even Krishna gives independence to Arjuna: yathecchasi tatha kuru—‘I have told you everything. Now you do whatever you like? So, that depends on the candidate. Everyone is free to do anything, but if he’s actually serious then he has to do guru-mukha-padma-vakya, cittete kariya aikya, ara na kariha."

To be sincere, serious, surrendered—that, I considered, was our challenge. If we were successful, we would be saved from mistakes, and everything would be revealed, step-by-step.

“What prompts the soul to misuse his independence?” Achyutananda asked.

“Because he has got a little independence. Yathecchasi tatha—he has got this.”

“Why do some misuse it and some never misuse it?”

“That depends on him. If one is determined that ‘I shall only act according to the advice of my guru maharaja? then he’s perfect. One has to submit like Arjuna said, sisyas te "ham sadhi mam prapannam. \[“Now I am Your disciple, and a soul surrendered unto You. Please instruct me.”\] Otherwise, he’ll argue.”

When a disciple offered that even the nitya-siddha, the eternally perfect, liberated soul, had a guru in the spiritual world, Prabhupada replied, “Liberated soul never says that ‘I am liberated? As soon as hesays ‘liberated,' he’s a rascal. A liberated soul will never say that ‘I am liberated.’ That is liberation. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu—He is God—said, guru more murkha dekhi’ karila sasan: ‘My guru maharaja saw Me fool number one, and he chastised Me.’ And He’s God! This is the example. If one remains always a servant everlastingly of guru, then he is liberated. And as soon as he thinks that he is liberated, he’s a rascal. That is the teaching of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. Guru more murkha dekhi’. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu is murkha? Why He’s posing Himself as murkha, ‘I am fool number one’? That means that is liberation. You must be ready always to be chastised by guru. Then he’s liberated. And as soon as he thinks that ‘I am beyond this chastisement, I am liberated,’ he’s a rascal. Why Chaitanya Mahaprabhu says guru more murkha dekhi’ karila sasan? This is sahajiya-vada, thinking, ‘Oh, I have become liberated. I don’t require any direction of my guru.’ Then he’s rascal.

“Why this Gaudiya Matha failed? Because they tried to become more than guru. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura, before passing away, gave all direction and never said that ‘This man should be the next acharya.’ But these people, just after his passing away, began to fight, who shall be acharya. That is the failure. They never thought, Why Guru Maharaja gave us instruction so many things, why he did not say that this man should be acharya? They wanted to create artificially somebody acharya, and everything failed. They did not consider even with common sense that if Guru Maharaja wanted to appoint somebody as acharya, why did he not say? He said so many things, and this point he missed? The real point? And they insisted on it. They declared some unfit person to become acharya. Then another man came, then another acharya, another acharya. So better remain a foolish person perpetually to be directed by Guru Maharaja. That is perfection. And as soon as he learns that Guru Maharaja is dead, ‘Now I am so advanced that I can kill my guru and I become.’ Then he’s finished.”

“They kept fighting,” Jasomatinandan said, “and when the real acharya emerged, they all became wonderstruck. They all became baffled. Now they all know in their hearts. They all know it. I can see. They all know who is the real acharya.”

“Jaya Srila Prabhupada! All glories to Srila Prabhupada!” the devotees said, offered obeisances, and left.

For Janmashtami, we made a stage in the area of the darshan mandapa in the new temple and set out rows of chairs amid the construction work and scaffolding. Prabhupada had heard that the devotees were rehearsing for “The Appearance of Lord Krishna,” and he wanted to see the play before departing for Hyderabad, two days before the festival. Jagat Purusa had organized the drama and played Kamsa; Ananga-manjari played Devaki; Bhaya Hari played Vasudeva; and Achyutananda, plucking the strings of a tamboura (representing a vina), played Narada Muni.

Prabhupada enjoyed the performance and applauded enthusiastically, and as was common in ISKCON dramas, at the end the devotees and audience chanted Hare Krishna together.

When Prabhupada began to leave for the airport, devotees jumped down from the stage and began to chase after him. And although his car left first, some devotees managed to arrive at the airport before him. When he stepped out onto the curb, he found Ananga-manjari and Aditya dasi there, shouting “Jaya Prabhupada! Jaya Prabhupada!” Ananga-manjari was still in costume as Devaki, in an ornate wedding sari. But she was about to leave for America, and, as Prabhupada was both elderly and in fragile health, she thought this might be the last time she would see him, and her makeup was smeared by tears. Prabhupada smiled broadly as the women offered their obeisances, and, as they jumped up and down in bliss, he proceeded into the terminal.

“Prabhupada stood there for the longest time,” Ananga-manjari later recalled, “leaning on his cane and smiling at me, practically laughing. When he had moved on, Aditya said, ‘Did you see how he looked at you and smiled at you?’ And I thought, This is the perfection of my life: I entertained him!"

Two days later, in Hyderabad, Prabhupada asked Saurabha, “What news from Bombay?”

“The Janmashtami festival was a great success.” Saurabha replied. “We counted approximately, for the last two days, twenty thousand people. The place was packed. People were everywhere. They were sitting everywhere, even on the balconies and in the scaffolding.”

“The press and the television people came?” Gopal Krishna asked. “Every year the television comes. They televised this?”

“The film news,” Saurabha answered. “For the abhiseka ceremony,which lasted about an hour, up till one o’clock, and everyone remained. There were thousands of people. They were just everywhere.”

Ten days thereafter, on a morning walk in Delhi, I told Prabhupada, “There’s a lot of enthusiasm for Krishna consciousness in Bombay. Just due to this Janmashtami we made about fifteen or twenty life patron members. They just keep coming, saying, ‘I visited your festival.’ Then they arrange other programs for us and become patron members. And newspaper people also are starting ...”

“Giving some coverage,” Prabhupada said.

“Good coverage,” I confirmed. “The Free Press Journal wants to make a two-page feature with pictures all about our activities.”

As the construction progressed, various platforms were created, and they were sometimes used as stages for dramatic presentations. For Govardhana-puja, “The Lifting of Govardhana Hill” was performed on a semicircular area at the top of the stairs of the main temple entrance, with the audience sitting on the ground level.

With his many contacts in the film industry, Jagat Purusa was able to engage professional set artists to help build and paint the Govardhana Hill. A pulley system was concealed behind an overhead beam, and when Krishna, played by Smriti Warrier (now almost eleven), went to lift the hill, it rose smoothly into the air.

That evening I wrote Prabhupada, “We had a very nice celebration for Govardhana-puja, and about 1,000 persons attended. We prepared a big mountain of prasada and served full meals to all the guests. And we had a full program of Krishna consciousness, including a drama of the story of the lifting of Govardhana Hill.”

In America, ISKCON was being accused of brainwashing and mind control, and devotees were being kidnapped and deprogrammed. I wrote Prabhupada in Vrindavan that with the help of other devotees, I had been busy enlisting the support of our life members and other leading citizens against the deprogrammers and their allies and that many were coming forward to help with statements attesting to the authenticity of ISKCON and Krishna consciousness. I also offered suggestions on how to further the campaign. “Many of our friends in Bombay are helpingto counteract the movement against us in USA,” I wrote. “Sadajiwatlal suggested that Your Divine Grace include Swami Gangesvar Anandji Maharaj in your efforts from Vrindavan. Also, perhaps a delegation of leading citizens and government leaders from Delhi could accompany us to the American Embassy to officially protest the harassment of our devotees and request the Ambassador to inform the authorities in America that this harassment will damage Indo-American relations and should be stopped.” With the letter, I enclosed a decidedly favorable article from a Bombay newspaper.

Prabhupada replied, “That newspaper article was very nice.” “It is good that our friends are coming forward to help in Bombay,” he wrote. “Let them present a statement that it is a genuine movement. All Indians are interested in spreading this movement. Krishna is accepted as the Supreme Lord by all Indians. His birthday ceremony, Janmashtami, is observed by all Indians. In Bombay there is an embassy branch. Our Bombay friends should go there to express their protest.”

He had a meeting with local Vrindavan dignitaries, and they talked at length about how to support our movement. Gopal Krishna had been garnering letters from leaders of Bombay society and had gotten one from the ex-mayor. He was working on the draft of a letter that he hoped would be signed by members of parliament as well as by the prime minister, Indira Gandhi. Three MPs had already written positive letters, and Gopal Krishna was confident of across-the-board support for ISKCON as a genuine representative of Indian culture and religion.

Efforts were mounting in what was becoming an ISKCON-wide effort. In Vrindavan Gopal Krishna spoke by phone with Ramesvara, discussing their requirements. And along with Hamsaduta, Jagadish, Aksayananda, and Hari-sauri, he met with Prabhupada to discuss the fight. Another case had come up in Los Angeles, he informed Prabhupada. One of the top young female book distributors had been kidnapped and held for several days, but she had managed to escape and return to the temple. Now she and the devotees were suing her parents and their hired deprogrammers, and the case was generating favorable publicity. The whole issue was attracting public attention. Articles were appearing in almost every major paper in America, though some in New York were not very favorable, and even overseas publications were carrying the story.

Prabhupada was not worried. “We should not be afraid,” he said. “Mam anusmara yudhya ca”—Remember Krishna and fight. (Gita 8.7) “Krishna advised Arjuna that ‘You fight,' not that we shall not fight. We shall fight to the best.”

He said that as we gained importance, our enemies would try to suppress us. “That is natural. Even Krishna was suppressed. Krishna could not be suppressed, but the attempt was there: Kamsa. So, these things go on. Still, we have to work. If we work sincerely, then we’ll come out successful.”

The attacks were actually a good sign, he said—people were feeling the pressure of the movement. Otherwise, they would not be bothering about us. He was especially pleased to hear that Professor Shaligram Sukla, from Georgetown University, who had written a favorable review of Prabhupada’s Gita, had attended a press conference and declared that the attacks were an insult to his religion. Prabhupada stressed that the devotees should canvass the expatriate Indians to step forward and support their culture: “They should take signatures from all Indians that ‘this is a genuine Indian cultural movement, and it a great fortune for Indians. We were bereft of our own culture, and now we have got this culture again. The Ratha-yatra is going on; we are so much enlivened.’ In this way they should file petition.”

Prabhupada didn’t want just talk; he wanted positive action. He told Gopal Krishna, “You note down; you are simply hearing. Note down and inform them. Yes.
