Give them this direction: Combine the Indian community. There are many thousands of Indians—New York, Canada, London. These are very important places. Yes, many thousands and thousands of important Indians, very rich men. In London there are very rich Indians. They can form immediately a solid association. They should present that ‘This Krishna is our God; in every Indian home we observe Krishna Janmashtami.’ Even though one does not follow Krishna cult, still if he is Hindu he follows Janmashtami. Inevitably, everywhere.

“This Krishna cult is genuine, Vedic, based on Bhagavad-gita, which was spoken long, long ago, before any religion, any religious literature in the world. The Buddha literature or the Christian literature and Jewish literature, they cannot be counted more than two thousand years, or a little more than that. But this Krishna cult is coming from—I havealready explained in the introduction—four hundred million years ago. But even historically, it is five thousand years—beyond all religious literature in the world. We have to present this case in the court. And let it be discussed thoroughly, and see our books, compare any religious books with our books. Present all the opinions of big, big professors how traditional Indian culture is there. You have to fight, organize.”

Prabhupada was in a feisty mood. He wasn’t going to just sit back and allow ignorance and prejudice to stop his mission. “How they can defeat us?” he challenged. “We have got such solid ground. How they can defeat us, these rascals? We consider them simply rascals and fools. And we call them rascals and fools. What do they know of religion? What do they know of God? They know slaughterhouse and killing, and illicit sex and killing the fetus. That’s all. What do they know? They are not even civilized. We have come to make them civilized. They should understand. They are not civilized.”

After seven weeks in Vrindavan, Prabhupada proceeded to Hyderabad, and while he was there, George Harrison returned to Hare Krishna Land for a visit. My overriding impression was how humble, elevated, and kind George was. We exchanged a few words, and I invited him to take a tour of the construction, which was now well underway. He was all praise for the design and workmanship. At 12:30 we heard the conch shell blow and the arati begin. We continued touring the site, but after ten or fifteen minutes we went to the temple. George came before the Deities, offered his obeisances, and joined in the kirtan with the devotees, swaying in a sort of dance. Afterward, we invited him to honor a plate of maha-prasada that had been kept for him from the raja-bhoga offering.

“When the temple opens,” he told me, “I would like to come and stay.”

Srila Prabhupada returned to Bombay on December 23, and on his morning walk three days later, he asked me to explain the opposition to our movement in America.

“We just today got a new package from New York,” I replied. “Some of the parents are charging that we are kidnapping and mentally imprisoning their children by making them devotees. Because from their point of view, their children were lost to our movement. So—”

“He’s a lost child,” Prabhupada said to Dr. Patel and the other devotees, indicating me. “His father and mother came to me, and his mother was crying. I said, ‘So, take your son.’ And the son would not go.”

He was emphasizing, demonstrating, that Krishna consciousness was voluntary—not “mental imprisonment,” which parents claimed he effected by keeping the devotees sleep-deprived, by having them rise at 4 a.m.; undernourished, by having them on an austere, strict vegetarian diet; and exhausted, by having them go out and collect for him from morning to night.

“You are washing away their brains,” Dr. Patel responded.

“They are charging like that. What is the new charge?”

“They are saying ‘mind control,’” Srutasrava said.

Prabhupada laughed. “‘Mind control.’ Yes.”

“So many big scholars in America, all big famous scholars, have put together a petition saying how authorized our Krishna consciousness movement is,” Srutasrava added. “And they are willing to come forward. If any time we want some papers in the courtroom to show how bona fide our movement is, how we are actually not brainwashers and mind-controllers, these scholars in America have pledged their support.”

“There was a meeting of four big scholars at Harvard University, which is like the Oxford of America,” I added. “One was a famous theologian named Harvey Cox—his books are very famous. They brought up this issue of freedom of religion, that this is a bona fide religious movement and we should have freedom to worship. And there’s also a letter from a member of the World Fellowship of Religion, and he is also saying that he takes this very seriously, as very grave, that such a bona fide movement is not being allowed to practice its religion freely. And then there’s one, I think, Professor Sharma at an American university, and he is saying that he has personal experience that this is a bona fide movement, and that the American public in general may not know, but A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami is one of the most renowned writers of Vedic translations and commentaries of Vedic literature.”

Sometimes on his walks Prabhupada would come to the point of calling people, even reputed spiritual and political leaders, mudhas— fools, or asses. The Bhagavad-gita says,

na mam duskrtino mudhah  
prapadyante naradhamah  
mayayapahrta-jnana  
asuram bhavam asritah

“Those miscreants who are grossly foolish, who are lowest among mankind, whose knowledge is stolen by illusion, and who partake of the atheistic nature of demons do not surrender unto Me ” (Gita 7.15) And Prabhupada would say, “Anyone who doesn’t surrender to Krishna is a duskrtina, miscreant”: either a mudha—“fool,” “rascal,” or, in stronger language, “ass”; naradhamah—“the lowest among mankind”; mayayapahrta-jnana—someone who may be knowledgeable or intelligent but whose knowledge has been stolen away by maya; or asuram bhavam—one who has the nature of demons. He would say, “Anyone who is not surrendered to Krishna falls in one of these four categories: fool, rascal, demon,” and so on. And sometimes Dr. Patel would become very upset. But Prabhupada would counter, “I am not saying; Krishna is saying. I am only repeating what Krishna says.”

But the two had an affectionate relationship, and after Prabhupada left this world, Dr. Patel wrote a heartfelt account of their time together. His article, published in Back to Godhead as “My Life’s Most Precious Moments,” was subtitled “A Bombay doctor wins the title ‘big fool’ and loves it.” So, at least in retrospect, he relished being called a mudha by Prabhupada.

## The Gita in Wardha

Among the influential friends I had been cultivating in Bombay was Ramkrishna Bajaj—one of the twenty top industrialists in India, who ran many big companies, including Bajaj Electricals. Under the guidance of Acharya Vinoba Bhave, a leading follower of Mahatma Gandhi’s who had been considered his spiritual successor, Ramkrishna Bajaj had formed the Gita Pratisthan (Gita Foundation), through which individuals and organizations propagating Bhagavad-gita could coordinate their activities, and proposed a conference to bring everyone together. Vinoba Bhave had introduced the Bhoodan movement—bhumeans earth, or land, and dan means gift—and traveled on foot across India to persuade wealthy landowners to give a percentage of their land to landless laborers, who could then settle on it and grow their own food. He had rendered the Bhagavad-gita into a book of Marathi verse known as Gitai and was a great champion of cow protection. He was much respected by Indira Gandhi, who often went to him for advice and blessings.

Although Mr. Bajaj said that he believed in the philosophy of the Gita, he didn’t want to bring in the personality of Krishna; his idea was to preach the philosophy of the Gita without reference to Him.

When Prabhupada came to Bombay and I told him about Bajaj’s idea, he was perturbed. He said that the whole philosophy of the Bhagavad-gita culminated in surrender to Krishna—you couldn’t separate Him out. “This is very nice that Bajaj wants to invite all preachers of Bhagavadgita to work together,” he granted, “but what is their understanding of Bhagavad-gita? First we have to understand what Bhagavad-gita is, what Bhagavad-gita teaches; then we can discuss about coordinating our activities for preaching Bhagavad-gita. What is the use of this conference? There is no use. We should avoid.”

He continued, “We will all get together, and everyone will have a different idea of Bhagavad-gita, and who will be the judge?” He paused and then answered his own question: “Let Indira Gandhi be the judge. This is a very good proposal. We will all come together and present our idea of Bhagavad-gita, and Indira Gandhi and her leading colleagues will hear the arguments and decide what is the real understanding of Bhagavad-gita. Indira Gandhi is very respectful to Vinoba Bhave, and on his invitation, she and her leading colleagues can come, hear the presentations, and decide what is the correct understanding of Bhagavad-gita. And if Indira Gandhi accepts our philosophy, then our whole preaching in India is a success.”

Mr. Bajaj came to Juhu in November and invited Prabhupada to join the Gita Pratisthan’s coordinating committee, and because Bajaj had come personally, Prabhupada agreed. Bajaj was the leader of the effort, and he kept his sister’s husband, Shriman Narayan, former governor of Gujarat, as president, and himself as secretary. Some months later, he wrote Prabhupada, “It has now been decided to hold the first meetingof the coordinating committee... The meeting will be attended by selected prominent persons and representatives of different institutions engaged in the propagation of the Gita and will enable the members to exchange information about their activities, promote closer contacts, and coordinate the work being done in the field of Gita prachar in different parts of the country and abroad. It will also provide an opportunity to the members to consider ways and means of bringing about greater coordination in this work and also to facilitate the furtherance of the cause of Gita prachar, which is dear to all of us, in a more effective and systematic manner.

“In view of the valuable work being done by you, we would be very happy if you could kindly make it convenient to attend and participate in this meeting.”

On May 14, from Honolulu, Prabhupada replied, “As you know, I am trying my best to preach the teachings of the Bhagavad-gita all over the world, and I am experiencing some glimpse of success in this connection. Naturally, I'm inclined to preach the teachings of the Bhagavad-gita very fervently in India. India is the land of spiritual culture. But gradually, India, being influenced by material allurement, its spiritual culture is being forgotten.

“It is the duty of the Indian leaders to note this degradation. There is no harm to become materially advanced, but if simply for material advancement we forget our spiritual basis, it will be a great loss. Therefore, I am also very eager to revive India’s spiritual culture with the help of the Gita Foundation.”

Prabhupada added in a postscript, “The teachings of the Bhagavadgita are so potent that if practiced seriously, it can bring in a new life and civilization. Now you have established a Gita Pratisthan, so do it very seriously.”

The next day, Prabhupada explained to Pusta Krishna, who was serving as his secretary, “That Bajaj is a rich man and the son of a very important man. His father, Jamnalal Bajaj, worked with Gandhi \[he had been Gandhi’s treasurer\]. He was a very rich man, and he joined Gandhi’s movement and was financing it. So, this man is also a very big, rich man in Bombay. He is our life member. He came to see me: ‘Is it not possible?’ 'l am ready.’”

Prabhupada was already propagating the Gita, Pusta Krishna pointed out. “Why don’t they just join our society? Why do they want to develop a separate society, Gita Prachar conference, or their separate work, when they can simply support our work, which is doing it already?”

“He is trying to organize,” Prabhupada said. “But why not combine? Any moment it can be done, but the rascals will not agree. They stick to their own foolishness. It will never be successful. Misinterpreting the words of Krishna—how much offensive it is they do not know, and they want success. They do not take seriously that it is Krishna’s instruction. They think that somebody has written an allegory or mythology. They do not believe there was battle of Kurukshetra and Krishna is God and Krishna instructed ...”

“At the most, they will admit that Krishna was a great personality,” Radha-vallabha suggested.

“That’s all,” Prabhupada agreed. “All this Chinmayananda and Vinoba Bhave and Gandhi and Dr. Radhakrishnan and Aurobindo—all rascals.”

On July 18 the New York media gave our Ratha-yatra parade prominent and favorable coverage under the headlines “Fifth Avenue, Where East Meets West” and “East Meets West in Hare Krishna Fete,” the Daily News dedicating its center photo section. Prabhupada, there for the event, had his secretary include copies of the papers in a letter to Ramkrishna Bajaj. “This title is very nice,” he said. “This is the point. The lame man meets the blind man. Together they do wonderful, but separately they cannot do anything. He is blind, and he is lame. But if they join together, Indian culture and American money, they will save the whole world.”

He felt that the headlines had captured what he had said on a walk before the parade: “America is blind by money. Dhana-durmadandha: when one gets too much money he becomes blind. To get too much riches means he becomes blind. He doesn’t care. So this is the blindness of America. And we Indians have no money, but we have got culture. Combine together, then things will be very nicely done for the good of the whole world. Simply money is not the end; there must be culture. Take that culture, Vedic culture, and use it with American money, then the whole world will be paradise, Vaikuntha.”

In his letter Prabhupada encouraged Bajaj to follow his example in preaching the message of the Gita and doing actual good for the world. “Enclosed please find news clippings of our Rathayatra Festival held on 5th Avenue, New York, last Sunday,” he wrote. “They are taking it seriously now, ‘East Meets West. . .’ This is the real platform of United Nations—spiritual understanding. I wish that the coordinator of the Gita Pratisthan will preach the gospel of the Gita on this understanding.”

In October, in Chandigarh, Hamsaduta read out a stack of mail to Prabhupada and noted down his dictated replies. Ramkrishna Bajaj had written to inform Prabhupada of the new dates for the Gita Prachar conference—December 19 and 20, in Wardha, Maharashtra. He had enclosed a list of about twenty-five other invitees, including some well-known Mayavadis, and expressed his appreciation of Srila Prabhupada. “As you have made invaluable contribution to the propagation of the message of Gita all over the world,” he had written, “the benefit of your mature advice and guidance will be most helpful in planning the future work of Gita Pratisthan and coordinating the activities of different organizations engaged in this work. We earnestly hope that you will be able to join us in this meeting and shall be grateful if you could kindly let us have your early confirmation in this regard.”Prabhupada accepted the invitation. “I will advise Giriraj, my secretary in Bombay, to see you in this connection,” he replied. “I wish to take with me my sankirtan party, if you would like to accommodate them. If not, then only my personal secretaries, all together five, will go with me, so you have to arrange accommodation for them. I am sending a copy of this letter to Giriraj to do the needful.”

On November 1, in Vrindavan, Prabhupada received another letter from Bajaj, acknowledging Prabhupada’s acceptance and finalizing the program. I had been discussing with Mr. Bajaj a proposal to set aside time for us to do sankirtana and show the “World of Hare Krishna” movie, and Bajaj suggested that Prabhupada and his disciples come a day earlier and hold a program on the evening of the 18th.

Prabhupada replied that he was happy to accept whatever arrangements I made. But he had something else on his mind as well. He had toldhis leading disciples to muster as much support as possible for the legal fight in America, and he was eager to show the way himself. Mr. Bajaj was influential both in India and abroad, and so were many of his associates on the Pratisthan, and Prabhupada wanted to seize the opportunity.

“One thing has developed now in the Western countries,” he wrote Mr. Bajaj. “They are feeling the weight of our movement. Therefore, an attempt is being made to suppress or stop the movement in Europe and America. In America the parents of my disciples are combining together.

“On account of the Hare Krishna Movement, people in the Western countries are being attracted. There is now counter-propaganda by the enemies. They are organizing opposition. Will Gita Pratisthan help this Hare Krishna Movement to face the cultural fighting between East and West?

“The idea is that the rapid advancement of the Hare Krishna Movement has threatened the foundation of Western civilization. One American politician has remarked that ‘the Hare Krishna Movement is spreading like an epidemic. If we do not take steps to stop it, it may one day capture the government.’ This is a good certification for our success, but the time has come now when we have to meet strong opposition. After all, this Hare Krishna Movement is Indian culture. If the leaders of Indian culture will take it seriously, then certainly India’s glories will be magnified.

“In the foreign countries India is much advertised as a poverty-stricken country. But if India can give her spiritual culture, Krishna consciousness, she will be glorified everywhere. This should be the aim of Gita Pratisthan.”

Things were taking shape for Prabhupada to attend the conference, and on November 5 I wrote him, “I spoke to Ramkrishna Bajaj the day before he left for Europe, and since then I have met his secretary in charge of Gita Pratisthan. The secretary says that Mr. Bajaj will arrange for accommodations for all devotees in our sankirtana party and in addition he is willing to publicize our program throughout the District. Mr. Bajaj suggested that we have the program in his family temple in Wardha, since Paunar is just a small town about eight miles away. He suggested we could have the program the day before the actual Gitaconference begins, and that day is Saturday. I told Bajaj’s secretary that we would like Vinobaji to attend our program also, and he said that Vinobaji has taken a vow and never leaves Paunar. He suggested that we could arrange a separate program for Vinobaji in Paunar, perhaps on one of the two evenings of the conference itself. The official talks by members of the committee will take place throughout the day and the two evenings are free. Mr. Bajaj wants to arrange a committee meeting on one of the evenings, so we might be able to have our program on the other evening.”

The following week, I wrote him, “Mr. Bajaj has agreed to pay for Your Divine Grace and five secretaries to come, but he did not agree to pay for the sankirtana devotees to come, though he will accommodate them. This is a Gita conference, and the Gita says, satatam kirtayanto mam, that one should always engage in kirtan. So the organizers of this conference should know that sankirtana is an essential ingredient for a Gita conference and cannot be regarded as separate.”

And two weeks after that, I was pleased to write, “I had a very nice meeting with Mr. Bajaj, and he has agreed to pay for Your Divine Grace and ten others to go to Wardha. Mr. Bajaj suggested we all go by train, as he himself usually goes by train.... Mr. Bajaj has also agreed to arrange our program with film at Vinobaji’s ashram during the days of the conference. ... Mr. Bajaj will make wide publicity all over the area for Your Divine Grace’s discourses at the temple .. . \[He\] praised his visit to our Paris temple and was generally very respectful. He said that the Gita Pratisthan is not paying for the conveyance of any of the members of the committee, but since you are speaking at his temple, he is arranging for the temple to pay.”

Prabhupada replied, “After thorough deliberation, it seems much better for us to go straight from Hyderabad to Wardha.” He gave me the details of the train he would take and told me to ask Bajaj to send the money. And he added, “Then from Wardha I would like to go with one assistant to Nagpur and return to Bombay by plane.

“Otherwise, the program as outlined by you is accepted. I am preparing now for the meeting with Vinobaji as you have suggested.”

Mr. Bajaj had told us that Vinoba Bhave was deaf and suggestedthat Prabhupada write his points on pieces of paper and present them to him one by one. So for several hours over several days at our farm in Hyderabad, in discussion with Jagadish, who was serving as his secretary, Prabhupada prepared for the conference and generated a long list of points about the Bhagavad-gita and how its philosophy could be practically applied to solve the worlds problems:

1\. Purpose of reading Bhagavad-gita. Reference: Gita 15.15, translation and purport.

2\. Bhagavad-gita study is essential in human society, as they do not know Krishna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Reference: Gita 7.13, translation and purport.

3\. The process of reading Bhagavad-gita through parampara. (If the parampara is lost or when Bhagavad-gita is not studied through parampara, it is not Bhagavad-gita—it is some foolish mental concoction.) Reference: Gita 4.2, translation and purport.

4\. What is the wrong if one does not read Bhagavad-gita? Reference: Gita 9.3 translation and purport.

5\. What is mrtyu samsara-vartmani—the path of birth and death? Reference: Gita 2.13, translation and purport.

6\. The real problem is to stop transmigration of the soul (people are perturbed by temporary troublesome life and their valuable lifetime is spoiled to solve the temporary problems). The actual problem is to stop the transmigration of the soul. That will solve all the problems. They should be trained up to tolerate the temporary disturbances and should give attention to the serious problem, transmigration of the soul. Reference: Gita 2.14, translation and purport.

7\. The real mode of civilization is as follows. Reference: Gita 13.8-12, translation and purport.

8\. Human civilization begins by the introduction of the varnashrama process, or the division of the orders of life. Without this there is no question of human civilization—it is animal civilization. Reference: Gita 4.13

9\. The purpose of civilization is to develop our love for God, or Krishna. (God means Krishna.) Reference: Gita 7.7, translation and purport.

10\. Krishna is the original source of everything. Therefore, those who are budha, or in awareness of real knowledge, worship Krishna. Budha bhava-samanvitah—this bhava means the immediate previous state of love of Krishna. Reference: Gita 10.8, translation and purport.

11\. The bhava, preliminary loving stage. (This bhava stage can be attained by the following process.) Reference: Gita 18.65, translation and purport.

12\. The simple process of attaining the loving stage. (The mass of people must be given the chance to become devotees of Krishna, which is attainable by the simple process of glorifying the Lord.) Reference: Gita 9.14, translation and purport.

13\. What is the Hare Krishna movement? (For this we have to take help from Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s Movement or the Hare Krishna Movement.) Reference: Gita 18.68, translation and purport. The conclusion is that if our aim is to love Krishna and be recognized by Him, we must take to this sankirtana movement introduced by Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.

14\. Engagement of the mahatmas. (Persons who are engaged in preaching the Krishna consciousness movement are all mahatmas.) Reference: Gita 18.68, translation and purport. Unless one becomes a mahatma, there is no perfection of human civilization. Mahatma means that he has no other business than Krishna consciousness.

15\. “To serve human beings is to serve God” is a fashion of the modern day. (This is not a perfect idea. To serve human beings, although a good proposal, is not perfect service.) Reference: Gita 9.23, translation and purport.

16\. Worship of human beings is fallacious. (To worship human beings in general is never recommended in Bhagavad-gita, except for a few qualified living beings without any deficiencies. In Vedic civilization the acharyas were recommended to be worshiped, acarayopasanam. Even the best of the living beings, the denizens of the upper planetary systems, known as demigods, anya-devata, are worshiped only by the less intelligent. Sometimes in the Vedas there are recommendations to worship the demigods for a higher standard of material comfort.) Reference: Gita 9.25, translation and purport. Addition: So, this worship of demigods is irregular, avidhi-purvakam. That is not the way.

17\. By worshiping the Supreme Lord, Krishna, all living beings are worshiped. (By worshiping the Supreme Lord, Krishna, the demigods are automatically worshiped. Not only the demigods but all living beings. There is no need of worshiping any living being separately. That is avidhi-purvakam. The modern theory of worshiping the general masses of people is fallacious. Every living being is part and parcel of God.) Reference: Gita 15.7, translation and purport.

18\. Every living entity is the son of God. (If we worship one class of living beings and slaughter another class of living beings, that is not at all intelligent. Every living being is a son of God. You cannot please God by worshiping one class of living beings and sending another class of living beings to the slaughterhouse. This is a most unintelligent way of dealing with the living beings.) Reference: Gita 14.4.

19\. The prime objective of human life is to re-establish Krishna consciousness. (The whole purpose of Bhagavad-gita is to give a chance to the people in general for understanding God, or Krishna, and to take to Krishna consciousness. But one who has no sense to understand this Krishna consciousness movement does not get Krishna but returns back to the miserable condition of birth and death.) Reference: Gita 9.3.

20\. Intelligent persons therefore take to Krishna consciousness very seriously with determination. Reference: Gita 2.41.

21\. Spoiled human civilization. (At the present moment the trend of modern civilization is to increase material comforts of the body. This is a very dangerous civilization, or a “soul-killing” civilization. Real humanitarian activities are the Krishna consciousness movement. If people are dragged by so-called education and advancement to the platform of too much material opulence, then their life becomes spoiled.) Reference: Gita 2.44.

22\. Without Krishna consciousness means “wandering in the wilderness.” (Without Krishna consciousness a person remains perpetually a mudha, or rascal, and becomes lost within this material world. He cannot understand the situation of the whole universe and therefore wanders in conditional life without any knowledge.) Reference: Gita 15 verses 3 and 4.

23\. The theory of accidents is fatal. (Everyone is blind. It is an asuric, demoniac civilization. They do not know who they are. They claimthere is not God in control. This is very dangerous.) Reference: Gita 16.8, translation and purport. Addition to purport: They do not accept the creator. They think everything has come accidentally.

24\. Godless civilization means digging one’s own grave. (If we keep human society in the darkness of ignorance, which means godless civilization, its opportunity of human life is lost. There are two kinds of men: The daiva, or theist, and the asura, or atheist. Therefore, if we allow ourselves to remain in atheistic philosophy or godless civilization, we dig our own grave perpetually.) Reference: Gita 16.20, translation and purport.

25\. Darkness of atheistic or godless civilization. (The atheistic civilization does not understand how nature is working, how things are happening in different species of life.) Reference: Gita 13.22, translation and purport.

26\. Difficulty of understanding Krishna. (Without this parampara system, nobody can understand Krishna.) Reference: Gita 7.3, translation and purport.

27\. Devotional service is the only way to understand Krishna. (Krishna can be understood only by devotees, therefore Arjuna was selected to begin the parampara.) Reference: Gita 4.3, translation and purport.

28\. Nondevotees’ wrong way of understanding Krishna. (One who is not a bhakta cannot understand the teachings of Bhagavad-gita. So karmis, jnanis, and yogis should not attempt to explain Bhagavadgita and spoil the whole atmosphere. Krishna and His teachings can be understood only by bhaktas.) Reference: Gita 18.55, translation and purport.

29\. Following Arjuna to understand Krishna. (One should therefore approach a bhakta in the parampara from Arjuna. Then he will understand Krishna and His teachings of Bhagavad-gita.) Reference: Gita 4.34, translation and purport.

30\. Arjuna is the real jnani. (Arjuna is a jnani about Krishna consciousness, and he has seen Krishna, the Absolute Truth, to receive the jnana.) Gita 7.2, translation and purport.

31\. Krishna—the Absolute Truth. (The parampara in the present age has to be accepted from Arjuna. What Arjuna says has to beaccepted. By the pararnpara system Arjuna understands Krishna to be the Supreme Brahman.) Reference: Gita 10, verses 12 and 13, translation and purport.

32\. Krishna consciousness is the practical solution to the world’s problems.

Prabhupada then expounded on how the philosophy of the Gita could be employed to solve specific world problems, though at the meeting Jagadish would read out only the main headings:a - Scarcity of Foodstuffs. Throughout the whole world, so much land is lying vacant. If it is properly cultivated, ten times more food can be produced. That means that instead of scarcity there can be ample \[food\] produced and distributed. The land is being misused, kept fallow, and the world’s population is suffering.

annad bhavanti bhutani  
parjanyad anna-sambhavah  
yajnad bhavati parjanyo  
yajnah karma-samudbhavah

“All living entities subsist on food grains, which are produced from rains. Rains are produced by performance of yajna (sacrifice), and yajna is born of prescribed duties.” (Gita 3.14)

“Food grains and vegetables are factually eatables. Human beings eat different kinds of food grains, vegetables, fruits, etc., and the animals eat the refuse of the food grains, vegetables, grass, plants, etc. Human beings who are accustomed to eating meat and flesh must also depend upon the production of vegetation in order to eat the animals. Therefore, ultimately, we have to depend upon the production of the field and not on the production of big factories. The field production is due to sufficient rain from the sky, and such rains are controlled by the demigods like Indra, the sun, moon, etc., and they are all servants of the Lord. The Lord can be satisfied by sacrifices; therefore one who cannot perform them will find himself in scarcity—that is the law of nature. Yajna, specifically the sankirtana yajna prescribed for this age, must therefore be performed to save us at least from scarcity of food supply.” This is from the purport of this verse. Additions to this: By eatingsufficiently, when the man and the animals are satisfied due to Krishna consciousness, there can be perfect peace. “Krsi-goraksya-vanijyam/ vaisya-karma svabhava-jam.” Translation: “Farming, cow protection, and trade are the qualities of work for the vaisyas.” (Gita 18.44)

Land is being misused for growing coffee and tea and keeping cows for slaughter. The three items mentioned in this verse of Bhagavad-gita can keep everyone supplied with all the necessities of life. Now we have experience how by keeping cows nicely, milk can be had in huge quantities and thousands of nice preparations can be supplied.b - Overpopulation.

sarva yonisu kaunteya  
murtaya sambhavanti yah  
tasam brahma mahad yonir  
aham bija-pradah pita

“It should be understood that all species of life, О son of Kunti, are made possible by birth in this material nature and that I am the seed-giving father.” (Gita 14.4)

If Krishna is the father, He knows how to take care of His children. He is completely opulent. And nature is under His control.

mayadyaksena prakrtih  
suyate sa-caracaram  
hetunanena kaunteya  
jagad viparivartate

“This material nature is working under My direction, О son of Kunti, and it is producing all moving and nonmoving beings. By its rule this manifestation is created and annihilated again and again.” (Gita 9.10)

The problem is that the rascals are creating their own problems. Quote Gita 9.15.mamaivamso jiva-loke  
jiva bhutah sanatanah  
manah sasthanindriyani  
prakrti-sthani karsati

“The living entities in this conditioned world are My eternal fragmental parts. Due to conditioned life, they are struggling very hard with the six senses, which include the mind.” (Gita 15.7)

If every living being is part and parcel of God and a son of God, does that mean that God is imperfect and creates so many living beings without any provision for their food? Then God becomes imperfect. Besides that, He says,

vedaham samatitani  
vartamanani carjuna  
bhavisyani ca bhutani  
mam tu veda na kascana

“O Arjuna, as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, I know everything that has happened in the past, all that is happening in the present, and all things that are yet to come. I also know all living entities; but Me no one knows.” (Gita 7.26)

So, He knows the future, and He knows how to provide for the future population. There is no question of overpopulation. The lower animals are never concerned about overpopulation. The leaders have mismanaged, and then they give some theory of overpopulation.

People are punished due to sinful activity, therefore there must be scarcity. When people are put into jail, it is not due to overpopulation, it is due to over-criminality. Similarly, whenever there is a scarcity of food, it is not due to overpopulation, it is due to over-criminality or over-sinful-activity. Overpopulation is a bogus theory.

tan aham dvisatah kruran  
samsaresu naradhaman  
ksipamy ajasram asubhan  
asrurisv eva yonisu

“Those who are envious and mischievous, who are the lowest among men, are cast by Me into the ocean of material existence, into various demoniac species of life.” (Gita 16.9)

The demons and godless people must be suffering. They cannot make a solution. They cannot surpass the law of nature.

daivi hy esa gunamayi  
mama maya duratyaya  
mam eva ye prapadyante  
mayam etam taranti te

“This Divine energy of Mine, consisting of the three modes of material nature, is difficult to overcome. But those who have surrendered unto Me can easily cross beyond it.” (Gita 7.14)

There is enough water in the ocean, but still we have suffering due to scarcity of water. Why? Unless there is intervention by nature’s law, you cannot use it. Therefore, you are completely under the laws of nature. Nature will punish you, nature will reward us according to our karma.

prakrteh kriyamanani  
gunaih karmani sarvasah  
ahankara vimudhatma  
kartaham iti manyate

“The bewildered spirit soul, under the influence of the three modes of material nature, thinks himself to be the doer of activities which are in actuality carried out by nature.” (Gita 3.27)

You are falsely thinking that we are independent. A slight deviation from the laws of nature will put us into difficulty. If we are dependent on nature’s supply, then overpopulation or no overpopulation, we can be punished if nature’s supply is restricted.c - National Defense. There is no question of national. Everything belongs to Krishna.

bhoktaram yajna tapasam  
sarva Ioka mahesvaram  
suhrdam sarva bhutanam  
jnatva mam santim rcchati

“The sages, knowing Me as the ultimate purpose of all sacrifices and austerities, the Supreme Lord of all planets and demigods, and the benefactor and well-wisher of all living entities, attain peace from the pangs of material miseries.” (Gita 5.29)

So, things should be utilized in that way.d - Taxation. That is our created problem. When we transgress the laws of nature, there is a shortage of supply. On this plea, the government will tax, but on the plea of our miseries they will levy taxes and divide among themselves. This is another way of punishment, because the government is our government. Because we are rascals, we elect other rascals, and they invent ways of rascaldom to mitigate our miseries. To avoid taxation we have to become good men and select as our rulers good men. Then there will be no excessive or false taxation.e - Race Relations. That is also due to ignorance of Krishna consciousness. If Krishna is the original father, where is the question of race? We are all brothers.f - Inflation. This is because in the Government there are all rogues and thieves, and instead of giving real money they print paper and cheat the public. The public are all fools. They accept paper as money. The whole world is an association of the cheaters and the cheated. Somebody is a cheater, and somebody agrees to be cheated. Those who are cheated elect cheaters, so naturally they suffer from artificial inflation, which has no value, artificially decreasing the purchase value. As soon as there is inflation the purchase value is decreased. Gresham’s theory is that “Bad money drives away good money.”g - Water and Air Pollution. That is also our creation. Water coming from the sky is pure, but as soon as it touches the ground where you are living it becomes polluted. It is due to your always being engaged in sinful activities, duskrtina, without Krishna consciousness.h - Fuel Shortage. That is nature again, restricting the supply.i - Student Unrest. They are the sons of demons and not properly educated.j - Crime. When people are in distress there will be crime. Duskrtinas. The atheist class must be criminals because they do not believe in higher authority.

Overpopulation was an especially prominent issue, since Indira Gandhi’s Emergency was still in force and her son Sanjay Gandhi was executing a program of forced sterilization.

Prabhupada had written one or two pages about each topic, the aggregate amounting to a small book in itself. To solve all the problems, he would point out, there had to be a section of men who were brahmans. And all others should consult them and live as kshatriyas, vaishyas, sudras, and so on.

At the end of the discussion, Prabhupada asked Jagadish if there were any more problems to be solved, and Jagadish replied, “No, I think we’ve exhausted them all.”

One of Prabhupada’s secretaries told me that Prabhupada knew every verse in the Gita, or if there were some he didn’t know exactly, he was aware of their contents. This compilation demonstrated to me both Prabhupada’s thorough knowledge of the Gita and his deep conviction that it could answer all questions and solve all problems.

When Prabhupada and his party arrived in Wardha from Hyderabad (I had come with other devotees, from Bombay), he received a royal reception at the train station, with all classes of people and many flower garlands. A leading citizen had distributed a leaflet announcing Prabhupada’s arrival and declaring that he was an incarnation of Lord Chaitanya, and many people had responded. People lined the streets and threw flowers and offered prayers as he was taken on a grand procession to Mr. Bajaj’s Laksmi-Narayana temple in the heart of the city.

Inside the temple we had a rousing kirtan, joined by many of the local residents. Prabhupada was piled high with garlands, and people were throwing flowers and petals into the air. When he spoke, it was as if he was the greatest thing that had ever happened to the town. Then Mr. Bajaj took him to his estate and gave him a nice room and quarters for the devotees.

Before the beginning of the meetings, Prabhupada told me, “When I see you all enthusiastic to distribute my books, my enthusiasm increases.”

I was surprised, because Prabhupada was always unlimitedly enthusiastic, but the Vedanta-sutra says that Brahman—Krishna, or Krishna consciousness—is unlimitedly great and always expanding. And by Prabhupada’s mercy, our little enthusiasm was able to contribute to his great enthusiasm.

Mr. Bajaj arranged for Prabhupada and his party to take prasada on the veranda of the house where Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru,

Sardar Vallabhai Patel, and Jamnalal Bajaj had all taken their meals, pointing out where each of them had sat, as we sat in the same places.

The first afternoon, Prabhupada had a personal meeting with Vinoba Bhave at his ashram in Paunar. There wasn’t enough time to present and discuss the long list of points, but Jagadish was able to present the main points later, at the conference. When Prabhupada showed Bhave pictures of ISKCON’s activities, Bhave said, “Bahut achd kdm kar rahe hain”—“You are doing very good work!”

That night, we had a grand program at Bajaj’s Laksmi-Narayana temple in Wardha. The organizers had erected a large stage and pandal on the grounds, and thousands of people attended. There was an ecstatic kirtan, and then Prabhupada spoke. We showed the movie, and people flocked to buy books. Overall, the program was a great success.

The conference began the next morning, at Vinoba Bhave’s ashram. Srila Prabhupada, Bhave, and Swami Chidananda Saraswati, the head of the Divine Life Society, founded by Swami Sivananda, were on a dais, and everyone else sat on the floor, facing them. The ashram’s residents—all ladies—sang Visnu-sahasra-nama and a Krishna bhajan, and Prabhupada motioned for us to accompany them on mridanga and kartals, which seemed to please them. Bhave spoke for a few minutes, to inaugurate the conference. Then Prabhupada was asked to speak.

Prabhupada gestured to indicate that we should have kirtan, lifted up his kartals, and began to chant. The kirtan wasn’t on the schedule, but it infused the whole meeting with spiritual energy, and he kept it short, ending before the audience became impatient.

When Prabhupada addressed the assemblage, his argument was clear and simple: Krishna had preached the Bhagavad-gita to instruct people to become devotees (man-mana bhava mad-bhakto). And how did people become devotees? By chanting the Hare Krishna maha-mantra (harer namaiva kevalam). Therefore, those who wanted to preach the message of the Gita should propagate the chanting of the holy names of Krishna— Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare/ Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare—because that would fulfill the Lord’s purpose in the Bhagavad-gita. In his half-hour talk, he also emphasized that only those who accepted the Gita as Arjuna did had the right to preach it; otherwise, it was a waste of time. When Prabhupada finished, Chidananda was finally given the microphone. He seemed annoyed thatso little time remained for him, but Prabhupada didn’t seem to care. The meeting ended shortly after noon, and Prabhupada returned to Bajajwadi in a car, with Chidananda and another man sitting with him in the back and Jagadish and Hari-sauri in the front with the driver.

On the way, Chidananda launched into a eulogy of Bhave, describing his plans for spreading the message of Gita to the masses. He spoke about Bhave’s latest attempt at social reform: his creation of the “Women’s Power Awakening” movement, which to Hari-sauri sounded like a Gandhian version of women’s liberation. Chidananda declared that Bhave had understood that the world needed love, compassion, and sensitivity to change it for the good. And because all these qualities were naturally found in women, he said, Bhave had a program to train young women between the ages of sixteen and twenty for a seven-year period in his ashram. There they learned to chant Sanskrit and the Visnu-sahasra-nama and were trained in the shastras, the principles of cleanliness, and how to organize family life. They chose a district in India where they would work and learn the local language, and after the seven-year period they would travel there on foot (vehicular conveyance was forbidden). From there, they would go from one village to another, organizing the women into groups and teaching them by personal example how to be clean, run their families, and so forth. Bhave’s idea was that if there was a good atmosphere at home, the men would naturally be pacified and peace in society would prevail.

Hari-sauri thought the project was “a laudable enough endeavor no doubt, but completely mundane—hardly the real essence of the teachings of the Gita.”

While Chidananda was speaking, Prabhupada, sitting to his left, was mostly looking out of the window. At the beginning of the laudation, Prabhupada pointed out that the Gita was actually for the leaders of human society and only if they took it seriously could society be changed for the good, but Chidananda wouldn’t hear him out and was determined to have his say.

When Chidananda had calmed down a bit, Prabhupada turned to him and said, “The thing is, you can imagine any plan you like, but the fact is stri-sudra-dvijabandhunam—these are the less-intelligent class of human being and they cannot preach Bhagavad-gita. Of course, if the women are devotees then it is different.”

Chidananda replied cuttingly, “Well, of course, the masses are less intelligent, so the path of devotion is naturally the only way for them. Because they have no knowledge, they can only be engaged in bhakti.” It was the typical, envious fault that Mayavadis imputed to the devotees. Prakasananda Sarasvati had leveled the same criticism at Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu five hundred years earlier—that bhakti was only for the less intelligent; one who was more intelligent engaged in the study of Vedanta.

This time Prabhupada replied with labored patience: “I have already explained that the Gita is for the rajarsis, the leaders of the society who are also great saintly persons.” But Chidananda would not allow Prabhupada to continue. He was determined to be heard, and, having been denied the opportunity to speak at the meeting, he now imposed himself on everyone in the car with his praise of nondevotees.

Prabhupada simply turned away to look out the window again.

Late that afternoon, Shriman Narayan escorted Prabhupada and his party to visit Gandhi’s ashram Sevagram. Gandhi had come to Wardha in 1934 on the invitation of Jamnalal Bajaj and stayed for some time in one of the rooms at Bajajwadi, Jamnalal’s estate. In 1936 he established his residence in Segaon, a village on the outskirts of Wardha, which he renamed Sevagram: “Village of Service.”

Sevagram was a simple place out in the countryside—green and hilly. It was large and clean, with thatched-roofed mud houses—all smooth and clean and neat and tidy. The residents came out to receive Prabhupada and took him to see every single room. “When we got to Gandhi’s room,” Srutirupa later remembered, “they said, ‘This is where he used to . . .’—this and that. They asked Prabhupada to sit, so he sat, and we had a little kirtan in Gandhi’s room, and then we all went outside. It was getting dark, and we sat on the ground under the stars, with only lanterns—no electricity. First the followers of Gandhi sang some bhajans, and then we had kirtan. Then Prabhupada spoke with Gandhi’s niece and another relative about the Bhagavad-gita, and we could tell by their expressions that they very much appreciated what Prabhupada was saying.”

When ashram residents brought out a guest book, Prabhupada took his time to sign it and then read aloud what he had written: “Iwas fortunate to come to the Gandhi Ashram Sevagram today. It is so quiet and serene. I have requested them to chant the Hare Krishna maha-mantra.”

During one morning walk, Basu Ghosh dasa turned to Prabhupada and said, “Srila Prabhupada, Mahatma Gandhi—”

“Don’t criticize Gandhi here,” Prabhupada interrupted. “This is his place; they will not understand.” And he changed the subject.

Another morning he told us, “There is an art to criticizing—unfortunately, you do not know that art.”

The conference’s other participants offered all sorts of ideas, or speculations, about how the Gita should be preached. One suggestion was to present it for factory workers, and for farmers. Another, based on Vinoba Bhave’s ashram, was to send as many as two hundred women to go barefoot from town to town and preach. Prabhupada replied that everyone was eligible—vaishyas, sudras, and women as well—but that it was more difficult for women, so men should preach, too.

The entire program was enlivened by Prabhupada’s presence. He was, after all, recognized as the world’s foremost preacher of the Bhagavad-gita. He knew the science of the Gita and had gone all over the world and distributed millions of copies of the Bhagavad-gita As It Is. He had preached the message of the Gita and made thousands of devotees who had become followers and preachers of the Gita themselves. From every point of view— age, learning, success in preaching—he was the natural leader.

Although many other dignitaries also participated—including a representative of Swami Chinmayananda; V.S. Page, the Chairman of the Legislative Council of Maharashtra; and Swami Chidananda Saraswati—everyone gave Prabhupada first importance. He had been the first to speak and been allotted forty-five minutes, whereas the others were given only ten minutes each. Shriman Narayan and Ramkrishna Bajaj—all the organizers—were most respectful of him, and the public was wildly enthusiastic over him and the devotees.

On the last day of the conference, there was to be a meeting of the coordinating committee to discuss practical programs for promoting the teachings of the Gita, but Prabhupada said that he wasn’t feeling well and that they should begin without him. The organizers begged him,

“No, Swamiji, you must come; the meeting wont be complete without you.” The committee members wanted to agree on a list of specific initiatives, and so, to accommodate Prabhupada, they would first prepare the list of proposals and then invite him to come.

When Prabhupada came and spoke, he stuck to one point: parampara. Unless they followed the disciplic succession and presented the Bhagavad-gita faithfully, without personal interpretation, they had no right to preach in its name. “You can preach any philosophy you like,” he told them, “but don’t take the name of Bhagavad-gita.”

He explained that because he was presenting the Bhagavad-gita as it actually was, his efforts were bringing success: “There is no interpretation. Krishna says, ‘I am the Supreme.’ Mattah parataram nanyat. We are presenting, ‘Here is God.’ You are searching after God, Krishna, and they \[foreign devotees\] are accepting. . . . How they are accepting? Because it is the real thing; there is no interpretation.”

He then invited the committee to present its proposals, but after the very first one, he returned to his main point: they had to surrender in parampara, as Arjuna had surrendered to Krishna as guru. Only then could they preach the Bhagavad-gita. And he would not proceed to the next proposal until the group accepted this basic principle for understanding—and properly presenting—the actual teaching of the Bhagavad-gita.

“Imam vivasvate yogam proktavan aham avyayam” Prabhupada quoted. “‘I spoke this science of Bhagavad-gita to the sun-god millions of years ago.’ By calculation it is forty million years ago. Now, who will believe that, that Krishna spoke this Bhagavad-gita forty million years ago to the sun-god? Hmm? Who will believe that? They’ll say mythology. So, where is the faith in Bhagavad-gita and faith in the words of Krishna? Understanding Hamlet without Hamlet. You cannot make your interpretation that whatever is written there, I take instead . . . That is not the way of understanding Bhagavad-gita. Then from the very beginning you’ll spoil it. Then what is the meaning of preaching Bhagavad-gita? If you do not accept the direction of the author, then what right you have got to say that you have understood Bhagavad-gita7.”

“Could it be that there may be different interpretations?” one participant asked.

“No,” Prabhupada replied, “that is not possible. That is not the process. You cannot interpret Bhagavad-gita. If you want to preach Bhagavad-gita, you must preach what Krishna has said. If you have got a different philosophy, you can say. But don’t cheat people that you are speaking Bhagavad-gita and then interpret in your own way—cheat others and be cheated yourself. You cannot do that.”

“Well, for example, Tilak Maharaja ...” the man broke in.

“Tilak, Gandhi, whoever,” Prabhupada said, “but the point is that you have to understand Bhagavad-gita according to the direction of the author. Because you are Mr. Tilak or Mr. Gandhi, you can do anything in the name of Bhagavad-gita?"

“No, no, that is not the idea,” the man objected. “But there are different types of slokas.”

“How you have got different types? The Bhagavad-gita begins, dharma-ksetre kuru-ksetre samaveta yuyutsavah. So dharma-ksetre kuru-ksetre, how you can interpret in a different way? Kurukshetra is already there. How you can interpret, ‘Kurukshetra means this, Kurukshetra means that’? You cannot interpret.”

“Yes, but who decided what exactly is the meaning?”

“Exactly the meaning is there.”

“Literally?”

“Literally, yes. The thing is, interpretation is required when you cannot understand. If I say, ‘This is a stick,’ everyone knows it is a stick. So if you say, ‘No, I do not accept it is stick,’ what is that interpretation? Everyone knows it is stick. Similarly, Kurukshetra means that big place, still existing. And in the Vedic shastra it is ordered, kuruksetram devanam deva-yajanam. You go . . . From time immemorial it has been a place of pilgrimage. Even Krishna, during a solar eclipse, went there with His family—Jagannatha. The ceremony is there, Ratha-yatra, because Krishna, Balarama, and Subhadra came in the same chariot. That is being performed. So, Kurukshetra dharma-ksetra, at least five thousand years ago the system was that people used to come to Kurukshetra as a place of pilgrimage, dharma-ksetra. And Kurukshetra, the place is there. And the two families, the Kurus and the Pandavas, they fought—the Battle of Kurukshetra took place. These things are evident. Then why there is need of interpreting? That is the first point.”

“Those points are very clear.”

“Every point is very clear. In the Bhagavad-gita, every point is very clear, unless you interpret it in the wrong way.”

“Swamiji,” another participant said, “I have a question. We were having a discussion just before you came, whether there is any possibility of coordination of the preaching of Bhagavad-gita.”

“How can there be coordination?” Prabhupada replied. “He is interpreting in his own way, he is interpreting in his own way, he is interpreting in his own way, so where is the question of coordination? First thing is, take Bhagavad-gita as it is. Then there will be coordination. Why should you interpret? You have no right to interpret the words of the Bhagavad-gita.”

“But Swamiji,” another participant said, “you have also written so much literature on this. That is interpretation.”

“No, that is not interpretation. That is explanation. Interpretation— if I change Kurukshetra into something else, that is interpretation. That is being done. Instead of collecting so many hundreds and thousands of literatures on the Bhagavad-gita, why not take Bhagavad-gita as it is? What is the difficulty? Kurukshetra is historical fact. Mahabharata means greater India. It is itihasa \[history\]. If you don’t believe that there was any battle in the Kurukshetra, then you decry even the history. Then how you can approach Bhagavad-gita? Every point of Bhagavadgita is clear. It is clear. There is no need of interpretation. That is the first thing. If you interpret, you spoil the whole thing, because interpretation is required when the things are not clear. If everything is clear, why should you interpret?...

“Take the Sanskrit. Dharma-ksetre kuru-ksetre. You do not require to go to any other language. Take the Sanskrit. Kuru-ksetra is clear, dharma-ksetra is clear, Pandava is clear. Then why should we interpret?... This practice should be stopped. If you want to preach Bhagavad-gita and you actually want to preach your own philosophy through Bhagavad-gita— don’t do this cheating. You preach your philosophy. You are at liberty. You can preach any philosophy you like, but don’t take Bhagavad-gita and do this nonsense. That is being done. Therefore, instead of studying, collecting so many literatures, why not take Bhagavad-gita as it is and preach?

“As evidence to prove this, people all over the world are taking.

Before me, for two hundred years there was preaching of Bhagavad-gita, and not a single person became a devotee. It is the history of devotees of Krishna. Now you see thousands. Why? Because there is no interpretation. Krishna says, lI am the Supreme.’ Mattah parataram nanyat. And we are presenting, ‘Here is God.’ You are searching after God, Krishna, and they are accepting. They do not ask, ‘What is Krishna?’ How they are accepting? Because it is the real thing, there is no interpretation. They are not Hindus; they are not born in India. How they have come to Krishna consciousness? They have given up bad habits—no illicit sex. Because you cannot understand Krishna unless you are free from all sinful activities. And one who is sinful, he cannot understand Krishna. Na mam duskrtino mudhah prapadyante naradhamah. We test him. We test like this, that Krishna says that anyone who does not surrender to Krishna as the Supreme Lord, he is under these four groups: duskrtina, mudhah, naradhamah, mayayapahrta-jnana. That’s it. We are fools and rascals; we have no education. But we take Krishna’s word that ‘Here is a fool, here is a sinful man, here is a naradhamah, here is mayayapahrta'

“So, unless you stick to this point, that we shall preach Bhagavadgita as Krishna says, then there is no meaning of it. You are misled, and you will mislead others. But if you take Bhagavad-gita as it is, as Krishna said, then it will be all right. But if you are not prepared to do that, then however you make combination, coordination, interpretation, thousands of literatures, the result will be zero. This is practical....

“Now, what is the first point?”

Jagadish read, “To collect all available materials and survey all institutions in India and abroad who are doing work based on Bhagavad-gita so that we will have completely up-to-date library.”

“What is the need of collecting?” Prabhupada asked.

“For information,” a participant replied.

“Information,” Prabhupada said, bhagavad-gita—take information from Bhagavad-gita. What others have said, you have nothing to do.”

“Now, for example,” a participant said, “we should have all the published literature available on Gita.''

“Then there will be no limit,” Prabhupada said. “There are so many, 600,000 interpretations. Then your life will be spent collecting.”

“If I want to go to Bombay,” a devotee said, “I must have the correct timetable, not a false timetable.”

Some of the committee members objected that there were many approaches to the Gita, and one of the proposals was to survey all the different institutions both in India and abroad to compile a library of all the work that had been done, but Prabhupada returned to his point. “Krishna directs, evam parampara-praptam imam rajarsayo viduh,” he quoted. “Parampara means to hear the truth from the spiritual master. You take this. Arjuna, when he was puzzled whether to fight or not, accepted Krishna as guru. Sisyas te 'ham: ‘Now I don’t want to talk or argue with You,’ because as soon as you become a sisya, disciple, you have to accept the statement of the guru. That is the relationship between guru and sisya, You cannot talk with guru from the same level. Whatever guru says, you have to accept. Otherwise, don’t accept guru. Don’t make a fashion of taking guru just like you keep a dog.

“First of all, you have to select guru. Tad viddhi pranipatena pari-prasnena sevaya. You have to select such a person where you can fully surrender. Krishna was accepted by Arjuna like that. Sisyas te ’ham sadhi mam tvam prapannam. First of all, ‘I have surrendered to You.’ This is the first instruction. That means whatever He says, as at last Arjuna said, sarvam etad rtam manye yan mam vadasi—‘I totally accept as truth all that You have told me.’ Not that you make cut-cut. This is the process. Here is the parampara. Krishna is speaking to Arjuna, and Arjuna is accepting, sarvam etad rtam manye yan mam vadasi. Not that you make cut-cut. ‘Whatever You have said.’ Param brahma param dhama pavitram paramam bhavan, ‘You have said that You are the Supreme, param brahma, I accept it.’ This is parampara.

“We have not seen Krishna talking, but the words are there. Arjuna accepted Krishna as the param brahma, How we have changed ‘Krishna is ...’? First of all, we have to accept by the parampara system. Sa kalene-ha yogo nastah parantapa, ‘That parampara is now gone,’ Krishna says. ‘Therefore I am speaking to you again the age-old system.’ Not new. Purana, And now you take parampara system, you try to understand Krishna as Arjuna understood. That is bhakti. Otherwise, it is futile. There is no meaning. But if anyone has accepted the parampara system as Arjuna has understood, then he can speak on Bhagavad-gita, Otherwise, he has no right to speak anything. That is parampara.”

One of the participants suggested having an all-India conference for the masses.

“All-India conference” Prabhupada said, “but this is not for mass understanding. Krishna said, yad yad acarati sresthah. Sresthah means the leaders of society, rajarsayo. Not ordinary persons. Raja— he must be just like Maharaja Yudhisthira, Maharaja Pariksit, Lord Ramachandra, Maharaja Ambarisa. They are rajarsi. They are saintly persons, but they are governors. Such persons should understand. Yad yad acarati sresthas tad tad evetaro janah. It is not for the mass of people. Because,

manusyanam sahasresu  
kascid yatati siddhaye  
yatatam api siddhanam  
kascin vetti mam tattvatah

\[“Out of many thousands among men, one may endeavor for perfection, and of those who have achieved perfection, hardly one knows Me in truth.” (Gita 7.3)\] You cannot make a mass meeting and pass resolution and you’ll understand Krishna. It is not like that. And the workers must also be sresthas, not ordinary workers. They must understand Krishna. Then they can preach. So, if you want to preach Bhagavad-gita, find out the sresthas of the country, sit down. Not that at mass conference, big meeting, you pass resolution and everything is done. Select. Just like we are all selected here and we are talking. If you understand, then you can preach. But if you do not understand what is Bhagavad-gita, how to understand Bhagavad-gita, what is Krishna ...

“To understand Bhagavad-gita, one has to become a devotee, pure devotee. Not that because he’s a learned scholar, he’s a big politician, or a big yogi or big jnani. Because Krishna plainly says, bhaktya mam abhijanati yavan yas casmi tattvatah. If you do not understand Krishna tattvatah, in truth, what He is, then it is natural one will interpret in his own way, his own philosophy. That is not the teaching of Bhagavad-gita. If you take jnana, yoga, karma, or other, it is not possible. You have to receive it through the parampara system. The parampara system is clear. As Arjuna understood, you have to take it. Then if you preach, it will be effective.”

“Then what is your idea?” someone asked.

“If you say ‘my idea,’ then I become one of you! So I don’t want that.

I say I am a foolish man. I have no idea. Whatever Krishna says, that isthe idea. Just like a child speaks the words of the father. The child asks, ‘Father, what is this?’ The father says, ‘This is a stick? So if the child says, ‘That is a stick,' that is correct. ... If you accept Krishna as the Supreme, then where is the question of interpretation?... Don’t manufacture. What Krishna has said, you say. Just like a child can say, ‘This is a stick.’ ‘How you have learned?’ ‘Father said.’ That’s all.”

Toward the end of the discussion, Prabhupada spoke in Hindi about his successes—and challenges—in spreading Krishna consciousness in the Western world, and the participants were charmed. And at various points in the conversation, his words drew hearty laughter from his appreciative audience. “At the end,” Hari-sauri said, “he had everyone smiling and laughing.”

By the conclusion of the conference, the hosts were so impressed that they became life members and arranged for friends to take us around to meet other people to become life members. Shriman Narayan’s wife, Madalsa, wrote a favorable article, which was printed in major local newspapers.

Before catching our flight to Bombay, Prabhupada spoke with Jagadish and me. “How did you like my preaching?” he asked. “How did you like the way I spoke to them?”

“I think we have injected our poison,” he said—by which he meant nectar, or medicine—“and now it will act.” Then he took out the Seventh Canto of Srimad-Bhagavatam and read two verses spoken by Prahlada to his father about the blind leading the blind, along with the purports:

“Because of their uncontrolled senses, persons too addicted to materialistic life make progress toward hellish conditions and repeatedly chew that which has already been chewed. Their inclinations toward Krsna are never aroused, either by the instructions of others, by their own efforts, or by a combination of both. (SB 7.5.30)

Purport: “In this verse the words matir na krsne refer to devotional service rendered to Krsna. So-called politicians, erudite scholars, and philosophers who read Bhagavad-gita try to twist some meaning from it to suit their material purposes, but their misunderstandings of Krsna will not yield them any profit. Because such politicians, philosophers, and scholars are interested in using Bhagavad-gita as a vehicle for adjusting things materially, for them constant thought of Krsna, or Krsna consciousness, is impossible (matir na krsne). As stated in Bhagavad-gita (18.55),bhaktya mam abhijanati: only through devotional service can one understand Krsna as He is....

bhogaisvarya-prasaktanam  
tayapahrta-cetasam  
vyavasayatmika buddhih  
samadhau na vidhiyate

‘In the minds of those who are too attached to sense enjoyment and material opulence, and who are bewildered by such things, the resolute determination for devotional service to the Supreme Lord does not take place.’ Those who are attached to material enjoyment cannot be fixed in devotional service to the Lord. They cannot understand Bhagavan, Krsna, or His instruction, Bhagavad-gita.

“As confirmed by Rsabhadeva, mahat-sevam dvaram ahur vimukteh: one must try to understand Krsna by serving a devotee. The word mahat refers to a devotee.

mahatmanas tu mam partha  
daivim prakrtim asritah  
bhajanty ananya-manaso  
jnatva bhutadim avyayam

“‘O son of Prtha, those who are not deluded, the great souls, are under the protection of the divine nature. They are fully engaged in devotional service because they know Me as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, original and inexhaustible.’ (Gita 9.13)... Unless one is properly trained by a mahat—a mahatma, or unalloyed devotee of the Lord—there is no possibility of one’s understanding Krsna and His devotional service.” (SB 7.5.30)

And:

“Persons who are strongly entrapped by the consciousness of enjoying material life, and who have therefore accepted as their leader or guru a similar blind man attached to external sense objects, cannot understand that the goal of life is to return home, back to Godhead, and engage in the service of Lord Visnu. As blind men guided by another blind man miss the right path and fall into a ditch, materially attached men led by another materially attached man are bound by the ropes of fruitivelabor, which are made of very strong cords, and they continue again and again in materialistic life, suffering the threefold miseries.” (SB 7.5.31)

As stated in the purport, “Gurus, teachers, who are simply interested in this material world are described in this verse as andha, blind. Such blind men may lead many other blind followers without true knowledge of material conditions, but they are not accepted by devotees like Prahlada Maharaja. Such blind teachers, being interested in the external, material world, are always bound by the strong ropes of material nature.”

We saw how applicable the reading was to what we had just witnessed: so-called scholars and politicians unable to do any good for anyone, because they themselves were blind. And then the following verse was also applicable, that unless you smear your body with the dust of the feet of the devotee, you can’t be engaged in devotional service— not by your speculation, by the instructions of others, or by joint efforts in big conferences.

Some of the conference participants were on the flight with us from Nagpur to Bombay. I was sitting behind Prabhupada and across the aisle from Ramkrishna Bajaj. Innocently, but foolishly, I told Mr. Bajaj what Prabhupada had said about injecting our poison. Hearing me, Prabhupada turned and glared at me as if to say, “You weren’t supposed to tell that to him.”

Although he could be quite forceful when, he preached and was sometimes blunt in private, Prabhupada was otherwise most tactful and polite. He argued on philosophical principles in debate, but he was always cordial in personal dealings. And because Prabhupada was so genuine, Mr. Bajaj remained friendly even after Prabhupada had taken such a strong position, and later he gave quite a large donation to one of our farm projects. And out of respect for Prabhupada, he held the next Gita conference at the Krishna-Balaram temple in Vrindavan during Prabhupada’s last days.

Despite their philosophical differences, Swami Chidananda also felt blessed by Prabhupada’s affection and Krishna consciousness. Some years later, he met with Radhanath Swami and spoke with him about Prabhupada.

“As we sat close," Radhanath Swami later remembered, “he told me of his deep appreciation and respect for Srila Prabhupada and the wonderful things he had done to spread bhakti throughout the world. Then, with great enthusiasm, he asked me to tell him Prabhupadas life story. So I told him about Prabhupada’s first meeting with Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura, how Prabhupada’s friend Narendranath Mullik insisted that he visit this great sadhu and took him to the Gaudiya Matha in Calcutta, and they went upstairs to the rooftop, where Srila Bhaktisiddhanta was speaking to a group of people. And almost immediately, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta gave him a lifelong instruction: ‘You are an intelligent young man, you should take the message of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu throughout the world in the English language.’

“Before I could speak another word, Chidananda Saraswati, hearing ‘You should take the message of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu to the whole world in the English language,’ became so emotional that he jumped out of his seat, stood up and raised one of his arms in the air, and, tears flooding his eyes, said, ‘That was not just an instruction: that was divine prophecy.’ He said it again: ‘That was not just an instruction: that was divine prophecy. He did it! He actually did it! He spread Lord Chaitanya’s teaching in the English language all over the world. He did it!’

“Then he sat down, and I spoke about Prabhupada for another forty-five minutes, and he was in rapt attention, emotionally listening and appreciating.”

Shortly after we returned to Bombay, I received a copy of Madalsa Narayan’s article and showed it to Prabhupada. The article, which had appeared in the major papers, praised Prabhupada and ISKCON for their work in respiritualizing society. It was especially significant because of all the accusations being leveled against us.

“Where she has sent this article?” Prabhupada asked.

“In some of the newspapers in Wardha, and maybe Nagpur.”

“She has written very nicely,” Prabhupada said. “Good writer. She picked up the essence of the movement.” And he asked Gopal Krishna to publish the article in the next edition of Bhagavata Darsana, the Hindi counterpart of Back to Godhead.

The next day, December 31, a local reporter came to interview Prabhupada.

“When you impart this knowledge to Western disciples,” he asked, “and when you talk to someone who is in India, what difference do you find?”

“Indian men refuse this culture,” Prabhupada replied. “India’s leaders, beginning from Gandhi and all, do not know what is India’s culture. They have forgotten.”

“Would you like to include Gandhi also in that?”

“Oh, yes. Otherwise, how it can be? Andha yathandhair upa-niyamanah—the blind leading the blind.”

“But he was the one who also preached Gita and—”

“But he did not know Gita, actually. Recently I have been in his ashram. They are maintaining the chatai and the lantern in memory. What is that? If Mahatma Gandhi understood Gita, he should have introduced it in that ashram. Where is that? The chatai, food arrangement is there.”

“That is done by his disciples and not by him. He never—”

“That means he could not make his disciples correctly.”

“That is true. That is true.”

“Therefore he did not know. Now see how, within ten years, my disciples are working all over the world. I am sitting here, but still my business is going on. You have to train in such a way. The Deity worship going on. They are now opening different branches, establishing Deity exactly in the way I have trained. It is a question of training. . . .

“Gandhi manufactured. The Bhagavad-gita was spoken in the battlefield, and he wanted to draw the conclusion of nonviolence. What is this? Krishna says, kutas tvd kasmalam idam visame—‘In this battlefield you are talking nonsense, that “I’ll not fight.’” He says so, and Gandhi wanted to make it nonviolent. Just see how from the very beginning he distorted. And people accept it. Yad yad acarati sresthah. He was a srestha, leader. So whatever he will say, people will accept. The whole India became spoiled.”

For weeks after Prabhupada’s visit to Wardha and Paunar, he expressed his chagrin that despite the conference participants’ and local peoples’ claims to accept the Bhagavad-gita, no one was actually worshiping Krishna—not even at Mahatma Gandhi’s and Vinoba Bhave’s ashrams—because their leaders didn’t accept the Bhagavad-gita as it was presented by Krishna.

He quoted the Bhagavad-gita (9.12): moghasa mogha-karmano mogha-jnana vicetasah: “In that deluded condition, their hopes for liberation, their fruitive activities, and their culture of knowledge are all defeated.”

Because Gandhi had not recognized Krishna as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Prabhupada explained to an Indian guest on one morning walk, his hopes and endeavors had been baffled. “His ambition was Hindu-Muslim unity, and that was banned. His ambition was nonviolence, and he was killed by violence. A person so dedicated, so nice, but he followed the wrong path. Recently I had been to his Sevagram in Wardha. There was no Krishna, and he said that he is very fond of Bhagavad-gita. But he understood Bhagavad-gita in his own way. And in the Bhagavad-gita it is said that as soon as you try to understand Bhagavad-gita in your own way, it is finished. Nasta. Yogo nastah parantapa. So, nasta—what is nasta? What is the use of ... ? Suppose if I supply you something which is spoiled, what benefit you will derive? Therefore no benefit is derived by the people in general, either from Gandhi or Vinoba Bhave or Tilak, because it was nasta. Just like if you are hungry, if you get some real food, you’ll understand. The example is these American and European boys. They are simply chanting Hare Krishna, and you see how they are advanced.... But you won’t take. That is your fault. You have manufactured your own way of life. Otherwise, Hare Krishna is India’s gift. But you won’t take it.”

“What is the weakness in the Indian society?” a visiting gentleman asked.

“They have got bad leaders,” Prabhupada replied, “rascal leaders. Just like Mahatma Gandhi—he misled. He did not know how to lead. What to speak of others. They do not know. I saw this Vinoba Bhave; he does not know anything, and he has become a leader. I saw in his ashram about one dozen women, they are reciting Bhagavad-gita. That’s all. For the last forty years he’s working on Bhagavad-gita, and the result is some forty women reciting Bhagavad-gita. This is the result. So, what they will do? They do not know how to lead. And he has written one book on Bhagavad-gita—and that is also not according to Bhagavad-gita—but he has become a great leader. This is going on.”

Prabhupada mentioned that I had told him that Vinoba Bhave had declared that he was going to fully retire and endeavor for moksha. “Thatmeans till now he was not on the liberation platform,” he pointed out.

“Vinoba Bhave is really a brahman,” another man said.

“Yes, I know that,” Prabhupada responded. “That may be. Brahman is sattva-guna. That may be. But that does not mean liberation. But there is knowledge. At least he understands what is liberation and what is not. So if he’s trying for becoming liberated, it is understood that he was not liberated. Now, our point is that if you are not liberated, how you can become leader? That is cheating.”

In a conversation a month later, in Bhubaneswar, Prabhupada said, “Recently I went to Wardha, Mahatma Gandhi’s ashram. Nobody is there. And they are worshipping Mahatma’s lantern and Mahatma’s chaddar. Not a single picture of Krishna.” He chuckled. “There is not a single picture of Krishna. And in Bhagavad-gita it is said, bhajate mam ananya-bhak. This is going on.”

And again, in Juhu in April, he said, “Recently I had been to Vinoba Bhave’s ashram. And there is no Krishna, and he is writing Bhagavad-gita Pravachan or something like that. Even in Gandhi’s ashram, Wardha, Gandhi’s lantern is being worshipped. And where is Krishna? The Bhagavad-gita's instruction is mam ekam saranam vraja \[surrender to Krishna\], and they are worshipping Gandhi’s lantern. ... It is very nice place. How it could be developed as a Krishna conscious center. But they have given up this idea.”

Prabhupada’s disciple Amoghalila dasa, who was assisting me in Juhu, did not have much personal association with Prabhupada, but one morning he joined him for his morning walk. Because Prabhupada wasn’t feeling well, instead of going to Juhu Beach, he walked on the rooftop above his quarters at the back of Hare Krishna Land. And Amoghalila took the opportunity to join him.

“I heard that you quoted a saying that anyone who goes to Lanka becomes a Ravana and that similarly, when devotees come to India they become Ravana,” Amoghalila said to him. “Can you explain what you meant and how we can avoid that happening?”
