“Ask the leaders!” Prabhupada replied. “I was saying that in all our other branches our devotees manage the cooking and kitchen”—there was no question of hiring or paying someone to do work in the temple;the devotees would do everything: cut the vegetables, cook the prasada, wash the pots, clean the kitchen, do the laundry, clean the bathrooms— “but as soon as they come here they become bada sahibs, big masters. That is Ravana. Why do they not do here? Here we have to keep some cook who is neither initiated nor very clean. In all other branches the boys and girls manage everything?

“So, the solution,” Amoghalila proposed, “is to follow your instructions, to chant the holy names and follow the regulations more strictly?”

“That means Ravana,” Prabhupada retorted. “He’s asking. I am repeatedly saying to follow, and he’s asking. That means he’s a Ravana. Why you are inquiring? If you know this is the solution, why don’t you do it? Therefore I say, ye yaya lankaya se haya ravana: ‘Anyone who comes to Lanka, he becomes Ravana.’”

So, Amoghalila started going around saying, “Srila Prabhupada wants us to do all the cooking ourselves. We should get rid of the hired people.” The next morning, our local GBC told Amoghalila that he had informed Prabhupada how Amoghalila was telling devotees that we should get rid of all the hired help and that Srila Prabhupada had said, “Who is this Amoghalila? Why is he creating a disturbance?”

Prabhupada wanted us to know—be convinced—that if we just followed his instructions, the process that he had given, all the problems would be solved. And we should apply such instructions intelligently, according to time, place, and circumstances—as Prabhupada did.

## Chapter three

Preaching in Prayag and Bombay

JANUARY-SEPTEMBER 1977

## Allahabad Maha-kumbha-mela

IN ALLAHABAD, PRAYAG, AT THE CONFLUENCE of the Ganges, Yamuna, and Sarasvati rivers, more than a million sadhus and pilgrims gather every year to bathe at auspicious times, which is said to guarantee relief from the cycle of birth and death. The annual event is called Magha-mela. Mela means “fair” or “gathering,” and Magha is the month spanning parts of January and February in the lunar calendar. Prabhupada told us that the site of the festival was considered very sacred because Mohini-murti had brought nectar there. “Kumbha, he said, “means the waterpot.” Every twelfth year the cosmic arrangement is even more auspicious, and that mela is known as Kumbha-mela. And every twelfth Kumbha-mela is Maha-kumbha-mela, when the star formations and astronomical influences are even more auspicious.

After visiting the Kumbha-mela of 1895, Mark Twain wrote, “It is wonderful, the power of a faith like that, that can make multitudes upon multitudes of the old and weak and the young and frail enter without hesitation or complaint upon such incredible journeys and endure the resultant miseries without repining. It is done in love, or it is done in fear; I do not know which it is. No matter what the impulse is, the act born of it is beyond imagination, marvelous to our kind of people.”

The mela of 1977 was going to be a Maha-kumbha-mela, the first in 144 years. Fifteen million people were to attend, and Prabhupada wanted to participate.

On his morning walk on Juhu Beach on January 8, Prabhupada explained the real benefit of the holy convocation: “Kumbha-mela is sat-sanga. If you go to Kumbha-mela to find out a man of knowledge, then your Kumbha-mela is right. Otherwise, yat-tirtha-buddhih salile ... sa eva go-kharah. If one thinks that this salila, the water—to take bath in the water—is Kumbha-mela, he is a go-kharah, a cow or an ass. The real idea is that ‘Now there is an assembly of so many saintly persons, let me take advantage of their knowledge’—then he is intelligent. It is a congress of highly learned saintly persons; people should take advantage.”

We tried to book Prabhupada’s train to Allahabad for the morning of January 11, but millions of people were going to the mela, and we couldn’tget seats. It so happened, however, that one of our recent friends and life members, Rabindranath Gupta, was a chief engineer in the railway system, and he arranged to get two cars added onto a train—a first-class and a second-class carriage—to accommodate Prabhupada and the devotees and had Prabhupada’s car freshly painted and decorated with garlands.

The day before we left, Ramesvara arrived in Bombay, and he, Jagadish, and Hari-sauri rode to Allahabad in the same cabin with Prabhupada, and I often joined them. The “brainwashing” case was going on in New York, and Prabhupada, eager to preach and fortify us, asked, “What are they saying?” Ramesvara laid out the opposition’s arguments, and Prabhupada refuted them. “What else do they say?” he asked. And Ramesvara gave other arguments, which again Prabhupada defeated. The discussion ranged over various topics, and we were all enlivened by Prabhupada’s preaching.

When we arrived in Allahabad the next morning, several sannyasi disciples and fifty or so other devotees were there to greet Prabhupada. Abhirama and Gurudas had brought Prabhupada’s car from Delhi and drove him from the station to our site on the far side of the mela.

The campsite was out of the way, on an island called Gangadvipa, a twenty-minute walk from the Triveni bathing area and, unlike most of the other sites, was too far from the city lines to get electricity. It had no front gate and was outfitted with only basic facilities: outdoor toilets, running water, and a partitioned area with some bricks and a hole in the ground, for cooking.

Prabhupada was upset about the camp’s remote location and lack of electricity, both of which would limit the number of visitors. There would be no lights for evening programs; no electric heaters in the cold, damp, and windy winter conditions; and no facility for his translation work. He called for Bhagavata and Gurudas, who had been the main organizers. “Who got this land?” he demanded.

“When I got here it was an empty field,” Bhagavata said. “They told me, "We are putting you on this island. The governor is there, Kalapatri Maharaja is there, Maharishi Mahesh Yogi is there.’ I thought you were with all the leading personalities.”

“You are inexperienced, so they cheated you,” Prabhupada told them. “All right, you did not know.” When he heard that they also had notpurchased enough food for mass distribution, however, he again became upset and called for Bhagavata. “Why is there no prasadam distribution tonight?” he questioned.

“I don’t know,” Bhagavata replied. “They didn’t buy any food.”

“Why have they not bought?” Prabhupada asked. “What is the matter with you? You Americans are big spenders—simply wasting money. You have no stock of food. Why did you not stock rice, dal, and wheat? What is the matter with you? You have no brain. You spend five rupees’ cab fare going, five rupees’ cab fare coming back, and you buy one rupee of rice. This is your mentality. You are nonsense! Every time you need something, you go to the store and buy it. You don’t know how to buy sufficiently at one time and then use it. You cannot think like that. And why have you made this location under the elevated train? Why have you done this wrong? The train is making noise. This pandal is a failure. Food is not being distributed.”

Bhagavata finally did get us connected to the electric lines, but, as with other camps, the power frequently went off. Only a few people visited our pandal that evening, and Prabhupada sat in the dark at his desk all night bundled up in sweaters, a heavy winter coat, a chaddar, and gloves. “Prabhupada would sit at his desk and seem not to be doing anything externally,” Ramesvara later remembered. “He would be leaning back, and it appeared that he was resting. It was freezing cold all night in the tent, with raging winds.” Someone got hold of a kerosene heater, but even with Ramesvara staying up to relight it, the wind kept blowing it out, and it did little to warm the tent.

Prabhupada was already quite weak, and by morning his hands and feet were swollen and he had a bad cold, with watering eyes and a runny nose. He was constantly sniffling and did not go to the river for bathing but instead used the icy water from the pump next to his tent.

“For me, every night it was the same routine,” Ramesvara later recalled. “No sleep, and then go outside to the pump—it was freezing, bitter cold winter—and pump the ice-cold water and take your morning bath. And Prabhupada was taking the same kind of baths but in a private area behind his tent. That was our Kumbha-mela. They had no electricity in the tents, no heat—we couldn’t get anything together.”

It was painful for me and the other devotees, especially Prabhupada’s personal staff, to see Prabhupada undergoing such austerities while suffering ill health. Hardly any of us had seen him in such a condition, and we were worried. Many thought that he should leave, maybe to Bhubaneswar, which was warmer and where the water of Bindu-sarovara was supposed to have special medicinal properties.

Kausalya, who was also concerned about Prabhupada’s poor health, had brought him a saffron cashmere sweater. When she gave it to him, he felt it against his cheek and said, “Oh, very soft. Thank you very much, Kausalya.” And then he instructed her to go open a temple in Bangalore.

“By the morning of the 15th, I started asking Prabhupada if we could leave,” Ramesvara remembered. “It wasn’t because I was uncomfortable. I was having an ecstatic time staying up all night, not feeling tired the next day, going out on the kirtans, serving Prabhupada, feeling Prabhupada’s mercy. I was very excited. But Prabhupada was getting sick, and I was really getting worried. I had never seen him so sick. Plus there was no electricity, so he wasn’t able to translate.”

The preaching was picking up, however, and word had begun to circulate that Prabhupada, the guru of the Hare Krishna movement, was there. People were coming to see him—thousands of them—and he was receiving invitations from important personalities. He said that those coming to the mela were expecting all the holy men and spiritual teachers of India to be present, so he felt obligated to stay until the 21st, when he was booked by train to Calcutta. The devotees were suggesting that he leave, but he resisted; he wanted to stay and preach. “We must take advantage of the situation for sankirtana” he said. Kumbha-mela was an opportunity for the devotees to preach, not merely bathe in the Ganga. “My only ambition is that so many people can become enlightened. Our men must go for chanting and book distribution.”

Devotees had come from all over India, and from around the world for the upcoming Mayapur festival. Guru Kripa and his nama-hatta men were the most organized group. He arranged that every morning, the devotees would have rich prasada—French fries and halavah in lots of ghee. It would give them energy and enthusiasm to go out all day, hesaid, and his plan seemed to work: on the third day, the first major bathing day since we’d arrived, fifty of us wound our way through the mela grounds, chanting and distributing books.

Mainly pious people had come for the mela, so we were able to distribute thousands of books—eight thousand on just the first day. And the kirtan party captivated people’s hearts. Many had come from villages or remote places and had no idea that foreigners could become devotees of Krishna. They would bow down when they saw us coming in procession looking like Lord Chaitanya’s sankirtana party—lie down flat on the ground, roll in the dust, pick up the dust, and put it in their mouths.

And they were eager to render service and buy our books. Most of them were poor, so we had one devotee carry a waterpot in the front of each party, and people would throw paisas in the pot, or into the sannyasis’ topcloths, which the sannyasis held out like aprons. If someone gave a rupee, we would give him a book. Many were illiterate, but as Prabhupada had said on the train to Allahabad, “At least they won’t have to hear the false propaganda of the scientists.”

When we returned to our camp, Prabhupada expressed his pleasure over the day’s success and ordered some of the sannyasis and other leaders to stay at the mela until all the books were distributed. And by his grace, the whole effort became a tremendous success. People all over the mela were talking about the Hare Krishna devotees. The books themselves became so popular and famous that people would approach us and ask, “Do you have Sugam Yatra \[Easy Journey\]7.” Give me Janma Mrtyu Se Pare \[Beyond Birth and Death\].” “Can you give me Yoga ki Purnata \[Perfection of Yoga\]?” “I want Puma Prashna Puma Uttar \[Perfect Questions, Perfect Answers\].” They were asking for the books by name.

I liked to be near the hari-nama party and the other devotees while distributing, but sometimes I was so besieged by pilgrims asking for books that I couldn’t move. It was like we were in a sea of people, and every so often I would raise my head above the water, above the pilgrims’ heads, and see the other devotees also engulfed. It was encouraging and enlivening, and in all, we distributed 30,000 books. I would interact with the pilgrims in simple Hindi phrases and sentences and got so much in that mood that when I returned to Bombay and distributed books at the railway stations, I would approach people in Hindi, though almost invariably they would reply in English.

Prabhupada said that he too wanted to bathe in the Triveni—the confluence of three rivers: the Ganges, Yamuna, and Sarasvati—but he did not want to go into the crowd. So at his request, two devotees went at the most auspicious hour, managed to reach the rivers’ confluence and returned with a bucket of water so that he could bathe with it the following morning.

When Prabhupada gave darshan the next morning, everyone wanted to know how his bath had been. He thought for a moment and said that it was like any bath in any water from the tap. Even though many millions of people went to the Triveni during Kumbha-mela to take their auspicious bath, he explained, any service that anyone did anywhere in the world for the pleasure of Krishna was more auspicious.

Outside Prabhupada’s tent was an area of sand covered with straw, enclosed by colorful shamiana-cloth partitions, and when people learned that he was in the ISKCON camp, they started to gather for darshan, especially in the evening. Although Prabhupada felt weak, he allowed us to set up a chair and microphone for him, and even in the cold, the entire area was packed with people, with more people tilting down the cloth walls and looking over them. Even movie, radio, and television people were there, along with the usual newspaper reporters. Everyone wanted to hear Prabhupada.

All the reporters had the same question: “What is the significance of Kumbha-mela?” Prabhupada answered that the heart of the mela was sadhu-sanga—that it was meant to bring the common man in touch with saintly persons. He explained that there were three types of transcendentalists, who were after either Brahman, Paramatma, or Bhagavan, and that Kumbha-mela was the one time when all types of transcendentalists came together to give ordinary people a chance to get their association. “Sadhu-sanga, sadhu-sanga, sarva-siddhi haya”—“By even a moment’s association with a sadhu, one can attain all success.”

As Tamal Krishna later wrote, “Though in India there were many sadhus, gurus, and holy men, no one could come close to equaling Srila Prabhupada. By accompanying him in his travels, the devotees repeatedly observed the uniqueness of their spiritual master in comparison with all others. When they met in Allahabad to observe the Kumbha-mela festival, where all of the saintly persons in India assemble once every twelve years, Prabhupada appeared as a brilliant full moon compared with all the other luminous personalities present. The appreciation hisdevotees felt for him was not exaggerated due to partiality. Whomever he contacted could not fail to be moved by his utter conviction and devotion to serving Krishna. Through lecturing, kirtan, prasada distribution, and the distribution of his books through the life membership program, Prabhupada was able to gain a widespread acceptance for ISKCON throughout India within a remarkably short time.”

In the end, Prabhupada’s illness posed too great a risk, and Ramesvara was able to convince him to leave. “There is something much more important than your giving darshan to these people,” he said, “and that is your writing of your books. Only a few thousand people are going to see you here, but if you go on writing, we will distribute your books by the millions. Millions of people will have your darshan. There is no facility for writing here. The climate is too cold, and your health is weak. Let’s go to Bhubaneswar, where it’s warm and they have healthy water.”

Prabhupada liked the argument that his writing was more important than his giving darshan to the Kumbha-mela pilgrims. “He liked that we had that appreciation of his books,” Ramesvara recalled, “and he liked that we had that spirit of distributing millions of them.” So he agreed to go.

But getting the tickets was not easy. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was expected to arrive soon, so the army was everywhere, and the mela grounds were packed. Ramesvara and Gurudas put a PRESS sticker on the front window and kept honking the horn as they inched through the crowd, but they still couldn’t make much progress. Finally, an army officer sat on the car’s hood and pushed people aside.

When Ramesvara and Gurudas got to the train station, however, they found that every train was fully booked. No seats would be available for weeks. But just when they were about to give up, they happened to run into Mr. Gupta, the same friend who had arranged our passage from Bombay. When they told Mr. Gupta of the situation, he immediately phoned Bombay and had a first-class coach added to a train coming from Bombay to Allahabad and then connected to a train going from Allahabad to Calcutta.

On Prabhupada’s last day at the mela, I went to see him with some questions. He had been traveling throughout the year, and I hadn’t had much of his personal association. Several questions had built up in my mind, but I had felt a little shy about approaching him.

As Prabhupada packed, getting ready to leave, he gave last-minute instructions to devotees. Lokanath asked about Gopal Krishna’s idea for him to leave his bullock-cart program and become a bhakta director in Bombay, and Prabhupada advised him to continue his program and pointed out that there was no need of a separate program for new devotees, because our general temple program was meant for new devotees. Anyone could join, attend the temple program, and make spiritual advancement. And if someone wasn’t able to maintain himself in the regular temple program, he could join Lokanath and travel on the bullock cart.

Encouraged by Ramesvara to present my thoughts and questions to Prabhupada, I approached him. Gopal Krishna kept insisting that I collect money, I said, but I felt I should also preach in the colleges and make devotees. What should I do?

Prabhupada replied that conversion was our first business.

Next I asked about Bombay. Amoghalila had been managing there, and I thought he should continue so that I could be relieved, but he wanted to do something else.

Again Prabhupada encouraged me. “No,” he said. “You must be free to preach. I will speak to Amoghalila and convince him to continue managing.”

I also told Prabhupada that Saurabha didn’t appreciate my involvement in the construction and that it might be better if I withdrew from that area altogether. “No,” Prabhupada replied. “Your presence is required.” His answers were both supportive and reassuring, and I felt closer to him than I had in years.

Prabhupada traveled by train from Bhubaneswar to Calcutta and then, four days later, drove from Calcutta to Mayapur for the Gaura-purnima festival, which was expected to attract more than five hundred devotees from around the world—the most ever. After he left the mela, I stayed back with several other devotees to continue our activities and then break down the camp. I had become attached to the simple life at the mela, with hardly any amenities—just the mode of goodness. In that purified atmosphere, the relationships among my godbrothers became especially sweet and congenial. Sometimes we would lay back on the sand at the site together and talk about Srila Prabhupada and Krishna consciousness. Without the burdens of our regular managerialresponsibilities and the designations that went with them, we felt more relaxed and free—brothers in Prabhupada’s service. In that sense, I did not even want to return to Bombay—I was happy at the mela site.

On the last big bathing day, an incident took place that I thought illustrated the Vedic culture of the festival’s participants. It was cold and rainy, and we needed a rickshaw or taxi to go from the camp to the city, but we couldn’t find any; hundreds of thousands of people had already left and taken all the transportation. We walked in the mist for a few miles until we saw a lone rickshaw by the side of the road. It appeared empty, but when we looked closer we saw the driver hiding underneath, sleeping. We woke him and told him we had to go to Allahabad, but he refused to take us. We offered to pay double the price, but he said, “No, it’s raining and I’m feeling tired.” Even when we offered ten times the price, he refused. He told us that at three that morning he had walked for many miles in the cold rain to take bath in the Triveni. Huge crowds had been pushing and shoving, but he had tolerated everything for the sake of a dip at that auspicious moment. I couldn’t help but admire the man: for mukti he was ready to do great tapasya, but he couldn’t be bothered for the sake of earning money.

## Mayapur and Pandal at Azad Maidan

Back in Bombay, I wrote Prabhupada, “For so long I have been serving so many masters, and my mental chariot has been carrying me from one body to another, but now I have found my perfect master, and I am jubilant to be engaged in your service. After our talks at the Kumbha-mela I really feel that you are my best friend. I feel firmly convinced in my position as Krishna’s servant, and I feel renewed strength and determination in my activities, knowing that so many of the ideas I had for spreading Krishna consciousness are actually Krishna’s ideas, as confirmed by Your Divine Grace.

“My absence from Bombay allowed others to assume responsibility, so I am insisting that they continue as they have been doing. Actually, they have been doing nicely. I will advise them and concentrate on preaching and overseeing your desires in all areas. I learned from the

Kumbha-mela that I have to be prepared to do anything to see that your will is served.”

Three days later, Prabhupada replied, “Yes, train the others in responsibilities in Bombay, and go on as you are doing.”

I thought back to the day at the Kumbha-mela when Prabhupada had been surrounded by members of the media and press, all asking the same question: “What is the significance of Kumbha-mela?”

And Prabhupada had answered that the real purpose was sadhu-sanga:

‘sadhu-sanga, ‘sadhu-sanga—sarva-sastre kaya  
lava-matra sadhu-sange sarva-siddhi haya

“The verdict of all revealed scriptures is that by even a moment’s association with sadhu—a pure devotee—one can attain all success.” (Cc Madhya 22.54)

After two weeks in Bombay, I proceeded to Mayapur to join Srila Prabhupada and the other devotees for the festival. Although Prabhupada had been unwell when he had left the Kumbha-mela, I had hoped that he would recover his health in Bhubaneswar. But in Mayapur I saw how sick he was, and my concern and anxiety over his health increased. His condition had worsened considerably. He was no longer able to climb stairs on his own strength; his disciples had to carry him up on a chair. And one day he collapsed and almost fell off the stage as he was stepping down. He was already more than eighty, and I couldn’t help but wonder what might happen.

Despite his illness, however, Prabhupada carried on with a busy schedule. The GBC members began their annual meetings, and after each day’s session they submitted their proposals to him in his room for his amendment and approval.

When they voted to replace the temple president of Calcutta, Prabhupada said, “So, you have all agreed? If you have agreed, I have no objection.” But when Ramesvara admitted that they hadn’t discussed the decision with the person concerned, to find out his feelings, Prabhupada said, “So, do that.”

“Before posting it, it should be discussed,” Tamal Krishna said. “His feelings should not be . ..”

“No,” Prabhupada agreed. “Everyone should remain in jubilation. That is wanted. You cannot make depressed. That is not good.”

Later that day, a few leading devotees came to see Prabhupada. “So, your GBC meeting?” he inquired.

“They’re going quickly,” Hridayananda replied.

“There was no fight?”

“Just a little fight.”

“Don’t fight,” Prabhupada said, chuckling. “Then everything will be spoiled.”

“Not very much fight this time,” Hridayananda assured him. “It was more peaceful than before.

Prabhupada laughed. “Yes, for Krishna’s business, why there should be? Even if there is fight, it should be mock fight, not real fight. Then it is all right.”

“Most of the fights aren’t personal,” Gargamuni said. “They’re just differences of opinion.”

“That will go on,” Prabhupada acknowledged. “Then majority vote. Then it’s decided. What can be done?” He concluded, “With great force, preach Krishna consciousness.”

When I went to meet Prabhupada the next day, he inquired about various practical matters in Juhu, including the tenants—whether any were vacating and whether any were creating difficulties. I informed him that none were planning to vacate soon and that the pending court cases against the illegal occupants were bogged down in the judicial system. “The tenants are gaining more and more respect for us,” I added.

“After all,” he said, “they are human beings.”

Yes,” I agreed. “They see the book distribution, the construction, and the time factor, that we are still pushing on, not going away. There are many factors. They see that prominent people are also appreciating our activities. Actually, our movement is all-encompassing. I’ve seen from Svarupa Damodara that we can dress up your teachings in different garbs and present them to anyone and they will be convinced, unless they are very envious.”

“Iron-clad demons, they will remain.”

“But innocent people, they can be convinced.”

I broached the subject of the pandal program I was arranging for Prabhupada in Bombay. “One thing I am concerned about for the pandal is that many of these leading personalities would want to meet Your Divine Grace,” I told him. “But at the same time, it might be very strenuous for you to come from Juhu every day.”

“Not every day,” Prabhupada said.

“The other alternative,” I continued, “would be to arrange a place closer to the pandal, but then it would have to be with a member like Kartikeya or someone.”

“That is near pandal—Kartikeya’s house?”

“It’s about a fifteen- or twenty-minute drive.”

“That is also good.”

“If your health permits and if you could come every day, we could arrange leading people for all of those days .. .”

“Yes, yes.”

“.. . and it would enthuse them.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada said. “Bombay is good place for propaganda, for making any movement popular.”

“Yes—people are modern and advanced there.”

Devotees everywhere were concerned about Prabhupada’s poor health, and two days later Tamal Krishna presented him a proposal: “Srila Prabhupada, we were wondering—one time when you were ill in Vrindavan, you requested that the devotees in our temples around the world could chant kirtan all the time, twenty-four hours, till you recovered your health. So, the GBC was wondering whether we could request again for that.”

“Yes.”

“Jaya! Tomorrow.”

“Bhavausadhac chrotra-mano-bhiramat. This is the real remedy for any disease. Very good idea.”

Prabhupada was quoting Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.1.4: “Descriptions of the Lord are the right medicine for the material disease.” He had referred to the same verse in a letter to me when I was sick in Calcutta in August 1971: “If you are feeling tired, you may take rest. Your body is very valuable. It is dedicated to Krishna, so you must take care of the body very carefully. The best medicine is to rest and chant the Hare

Krishna mantra, along with the doctor’s prescription. The Hare Krishna mantra is bhavausadhi, the panacea for all material disease.”

On Gaura-purnima, March 5, Prabhupada gave first initiation to more than two hundred disciples and second initiation to another hundred. He was too ill to give a talk or even chant on the new initiates’ beads, so he had some of his sannyasi disciples chant on the beads for him. Many brahmacharis were begging to be given sannyasa, but, Prabhupada said, it had simply become a fashion to enter the renounced order. In response to his concerns, the GBC drew up guidelines for candidates, including a one-year waiting period and a further one-year proving period.

Huge crowds poured into our site, heard the talks and kirtans, saw the exhibits, and enjoyed the prasada. Some devotees took advantage of the throngs of people to distribute Prabhupada’s writings, and though most of them were from Europe and America and didn’t know Bengali, they managed to hand out many small books.

Prabhupada decided to stay in Mayapur rather than proceed to Vrindavan with the devotees for the second part of the festival. And soon Mayapur was quiet again, with only a few visiting devotees.

Two weeks later, news of the favorable New York court decision appeared across the front page of The Times of India, and Tamal Krishna read it out to Prabhupada in his room.

HARE KRISHNA MOVEMENT IS BONA FIDE RELIGION

Washington, March 18

The Hare Krishna movement was called a “bona fide religion” yesterday by the New York High Court Justice who threw out two charges against the officials of the movement of “illegal imprisonment” and “attempted extortion.”

The charge had been proffered by an angry parent that his son, as well as another disciple, had been held by the movement illegally and that they had been brainwashed.

“The entire and basic issue before the court,” said the Justice in dismissing the charges, “is whether the two alleged victims in this case and the defendants will be allowed to practice the religion of their choice—and this must be answered with a resounding affirmative.”

Said Mr. Justice John Leahy: “The Hare Krishna movement is a bona fide religion with roots in India that go back thousands of years. It behooved Merril Kreshower and Edward Shapiro to follow the tenets of that faith and their inalienable right to do so will not be trampled upon.

“The separation of church and state must be maintained. We must remain a nation of laws, not of man. The presentment and indictment by the Grand Jury was in direct and blatant violation of the defendants’ constitutional rights.”

The Justice said that it appeared to the court “that the people rest their case on an erroneous minor premise to arrive at a fallacious conclusion. The record is devoid of one specific allegation of a misrepresentation or any act of deception on the part of any defendant.”

The Justice said, “The freedom of religion is not to be abridged because it is unconventional in beliefs and practices or because it is approved or disapproved by the mainstream of society or more conventional religions. Without this proliferation and freedom to follow the dictates of one’s own conscience in this search of approach to God, the freedom of religion will be a meaningless right as provided for in the constitution. Any attempt, be it circuitous, direct, well-intentioned or not, presents a clear and present danger to this most fundamental basis and eternally needed right of our citizens—freedom of religion.”

The Hare Krishna movement has been under pressure from various groups and this judgment is expected to stop some of the harassment in which it has been subjected in recent months.

“Now we have got a sound position,” Prabhupada said.

“Yes,” Tamal Krishna agreed. ‘“Hare Krishna movement is bona fide religion?” He laughed and said, “You couldn’t pay for an advertisement this good.”

“Now my mission is successful,” Prabhupada proclaimed. “In 1965 I went there, and this is now recognized after twelve years. I was loitering in the street. Nobody cared for me. Alone carrying the books. Now organize Bombay as our headquarters and New York as sub-office, or headquarters, in America.”

“You can see that the Bombay newspaper is better than these Calcutta papers,” Tamal Krishna said.

“Oh, yes. Certainly.”

Thinking of the Bombay pandal program, Prabhupada asked Sva-rupa Damodara, “So, you are also coming to Bombay?”

“Yes, Srila Prabhupada.”

“But our most auspicious sign is this: ‘Hare Krishna movement is bona fide religion?”

“This is preceding your arrival in Bombay,” Tamal Krishna said. “It’s announcing your coming, practically. Very prominent.” And Prabhupada agreed.

“Yes, I found that in Bombay there is good scope,” Svarupa Damodara added, referring to the potential for spreading Krishna consciousness there in scientific terms.

“Oh, yes,” Prabhupada said. “Organize Bombay as the center of your activities.”

“Especially when our big hall is finished, we can hold several lectures.”

“Daily, or at least twice weekly. We shall hold lectures and call all scholarly people to understand. Do it nicely. . . . Let us go there and organize. At least for one month we shall remain there. Let us organize.”

“A lot of the senior devotees are still there,” Tamal Krishna said. “They’ve gone from here to Vrindavan, and now they’re in Bombay, waiting for your coming.”

“Therefore I am going,” Prabhupada said. “In spite of my so many inconveniences, I am going there.”

“You want to stay in Bombay until ... Is there any date?” Tamal Krishna asked.

“I don’t want to stay anywhere. I want to work. Staying—I have stayed in big, big palaces, big, big cities. That is now complete. I have no other desire.”

“How long do you want to work in Bombay?”

“So long as there is work. There is no end of it. Our Bombay should be organized. Work is our life. There is no question of ‘How long?’ As long as possible. Krishna is giving us good opportunities. Now we should take it seriously. It is not joke—‘Hare Krishna movement is bona fide religion.’”

“Very important decision,” Tamal Krishna said. This judge is a senior man in the courts, very old and conservative.”

“But I think he’s sincere.”

“Yes, he’s God-believing. This statement that he makes at the end, that ‘Any attempt, be it circuitous, direct, well-intentioned or not, presents a clear and present danger to this most fundamental basis and eternally needed right of our citizens.’ ‘Eternally needed right’— freedom of religion.”

“So, we should send him a letter of congratulations. ‘May God bless you for such right judgment. Live a long life to serve God.’”

“Now work very strenuously,” Prabhupada instructed the devotees. “You are all young men, and somehow or other, a dead horse you have given life. Otherwise . . . the last fortnight I was thinking I am dead now. I was thinking like that: ‘Now life is finished.’ Life can be finished at any time. That is not wonderful. To live, that is wonderful. If my life is finished, that is not wonderful. Nobody will lament. ‘Oh, he was old man, eighty-two years old.’ But if I can live for some days more, that is wonderful. If I die, that is not wonderful.”

“Krishna is wonderful,” Tamal Krishna said.

“Krishna is wonderful always.”

“And you are wonderful,” Bhavananda added.

“I am wonderful so long as I serve Krishna. Otherwise, useless; no value. If I can serve Krishna, then I am wonderful, certainly. We don’t want to become cheap wonderful. We want to become really wonderful by serving Krishna. That is our mission. Krishna is wonderful undoubtedly. Who can become more wonderful than Krishna? Mattah parataram nanyat. Always remember, Krishna is wonderful. Don’t take Krishna very slightly, like one of you. That is foolishness. Krishna is wonderful, always. He’s the most wonderful person, and He can do anything wonderful.”

“He can also give wonderful guru,” Svarupa Damodara said.

“Yes. Guru-krsna-krpaya paya bhakti-lata-bija. It is Krishna’s wonderful mercy that one can get guru. Guru-krsna-krpaya paya. Don’t forget for a moment, \[or think\] that Krishna is insignificant. He’s always the most wonderful. He can do anything, whatever He likes.... This is a fact! You may believe or not believe—who cares for you? Fact is fact. And appreciating that ‘Krishna is wonderful’ makes one perfect. You know that story? The cobbler and Narada Muni? Hmm?”

“Yes,” Tamal Krishna said.

“The cobbler believed, ‘Yes, Krishna is wonderful? And Narada Muni immediately certified, ‘Yes, your salvation in this life is guaranteed? The cobbler has his conviction, ‘Yes, Krishna is wonderful. Krishna can do anything. Krishna can draw an elephant through the hole of a needle. Why not? It’s possible? That faith made him perfect. If Krishna is not wonderful, is it possible for me to do all these things? What am I?”

The senior devotees around Prabhupada felt that he was too ill to travel and that he should stay in Mayapur and recuperate. And Surabhi (Saurabha’s name after Prabhupada awarded him sannyasa) wanted more time to finish Prabhupada’s quarters in the new towers in Juhu, so he wired Prabhupada and requested him not to come yet. But I had been arranging the pandal program for Prabhupada at Azad Maidan in central Bombay, and I was appealing to him that he should.

On March 16 I sent him a telegram:

YOUR ROOMS READY PANDAL BEGINNING 23RD EVENING CITY ACCOMMODATIONS ARRANGED CHIEF MINISTER MAYOR HIGH COURT JUDGE OTHER DIGNITARIES ATTENDING EARNESTLY REQUEST YOUR PRESENCE FOR THIS GLORIOUS EVENT HEALTH PERMITTING GIRIRAJ DAS

And two days later I sent him a letter:

Here in Bombay Srimati Radharani has helped us arrange a very nice pandal, and many important persons will be coming. The schedule of Chief Guests who have so far agreed to attend is as follows:

March 23: Sri V.S. Page, Chairman of the Legislative Council of Maharashtra

March 24: Dr. Smt. Anjana Magar, Sheriff of Bombay

March 25: Justice J. M. Gandhi, High Court, Bombay

March 26: Smt. Lata Mangeshkar, Vocalist

March 27: Sri Manohar Joshi, Mayor of Bombay

March 29: (Rama-navami) Sri S.B. Chavan, Chief Minister of Maharashtra

The interest shown by these important personalities suggests a very good opportunity for spreading Krishna Consciousness in Bombay, India and the world. The people in general have been veryabsorbed in the election campaigns, for their political leaders, forgetting the words of Sri Prahlada Maharaja:

sri-prahrada uvaca  
matir na krsne paratah svato va  
mitho ’bhipadyeta grha-vratanam  
adanta-gobhir visatam tamisram  
punah punas carvita-carvananam  
na te viduh svartha-gatim hi visnum  
durasaya ye bahir-artha-maninah  
andha yathandhair upaniyamanas  
te ’pisa-tantryam uru-damni baddhah

These unfortunate persons do not know that the goal of life is to get out of this material world and to serve Vishnu in the spiritual world, and therefore they are mad after political leaders who are equally absorbed in material life. They do not realize that by following either this leader or that leader, they are simply chewing the chewed, repeating the same problems of life under this ‘ism’ or that 'ism.’

Actually, the only leader who can solve their problems is Krishna, or Krishna’s representative. Therefore we have chosen as the theme of this pandal’s discourses: ‘The Real Leader—Krishna.’ Actually the only hope for these unfortunate persons is to smear upon their bodies the dust of the lotus feet of a pure devotee like Your Divine Grace.

Prabhupada considered my desire and the opportunities for preaching and decided to go. As Tamal Krishna wrote in his diary, “Prabhupada was very eager to go to Bombay. He wanted to give the citizens of Bombay a true conception of the essential nature of Krishna consciousness.”

Prabhupada had Tamal Krishna phone me to give me the theme of the pandal: “The modern civilization is a failure—the only hope is Krishna consciousness.” On March 18 Tamal Krishna sent a telegram from Krishnanagar:

PRABHUPADA ARRIVING TUESDAY 22ND IC 273 AT 13:50

HAVE ROOMS READY IN WHATEVER CONDITION - TAMAL KRISHNA

When Prabhupada landed in Bombay, he was too weak to walk down the stairs from the plane, so the airport staff arranged for him to belowered by hydraulic lift. On the ground, the disciples with him assisted him in walking. Responding to Hari-sauri’s surprise that he had even decided to travel, Prabhupada said, “Yes, even up to last night, there was no chance of my coming. But still, somehow or other, we are here." And he was happy to see the devotees waiting to receive him.

On the way to the temple, Hari-sauri informed Prabhupada that his new quarters were not yet ready—there was no toilet or running water, no doors or windows, and the workers were still finishing the walls and floors. Nonetheless, Prabhupada insisted that he would move in, which made the devotees who knew the conditions there quite anxious. They didn’t see how anyone could possibly live in the quarters in the state they were in.

Hare Krishna Land was teeming with activity. Under Surabhi’s direction, two hundred workers plied their construction skills throughout the complex—some cutting redstone slabs to cover the concrete superstructure of the guesthouse, others chipping away with hammers and chisels to make ornate columns and arches for the temple, masons and interior finishers working on the theater area. Although much work had been done, much remained. The guesthouse did not yet have windows or doors, what to speak of curtains or furniture, and the temple itself was pretty much an unfinished structure.

As had been decided earlier, upon arriving Citrakara drove Prabhupada’s car past the twin towers toward his old quarters, at the rear of the property. As they passed the towers, Prabhupada turned silently and watched them go by, then looked straight ahead.

A group of devotees with mridangas and kartals were outside the apartment building performing kirtan, and some of the brahmacharinis, celibate female students, stood ready to throw flower petals before Prabhupada as he walked from his car and up the stairs to his apartment. Other devotees were ready upstairs with paraphernalia to perform his foot-bathing ceremony and arati. Much of the day had been spent cleaning his rooms, which were now decorated with garlands and scented with incense.

When the car pulled up to the old three-story building, the other devotees got out and retrieved the luggage from the trunk and brought it upstairs to the apartment while Prabhupada sat in the car. When everything was ready, one of the devotees opened Prabhupada’s door andinformed him, but Prabhupada wouldn’t budge. “Why have you brought me here?” he asked.

Citrakara repeated what other devotees had already told Prabhupada: “Your quarters aren’t ready yet, Srila Prabhupada. They will take a few more days to finish.”

“This is not my house,” Prabhupada said. “My quarters are there in the tower. I will never stay in this apartment again. Call Surabhi Swami. Take me to my new quarters.” He spoke calmly but firmly, without raising his voice, but everyone could tell that he wasn’t happy. So, the devotees put all the luggage back into the trunk, and Citrakara turned back to the guesthouse.

As they were driving, Surabhi came running up alongside the car. “Why are my quarters not ready?” Prabhupada asked through the open window.

Running to keep pace, Surabhi said that he needed a few more days to finish and asked if Prabhupada could please stay at his old apartment until then.

“You do what I say!” Prabhupada shouted. “If I don’t go there now, it will never be finished. I want to go now!”

“Yes, Srila Prabhupada,” said Surabhi, and he rushed off to see if he could get the elevator working.

Meanwhile, the devotees who had assembled at Prabhupada’s old apartment ran to be with him as he entered his new quarters. Surabhi couldn’t get the elevator to work, so the devotees carried Prabhupada in a narrow palanquin up the five flights of stairs.

The quarters were cluttered, and the floor was covered with a thick layer of greasy, gooey marble polish. There were twenty workers polishing the floors and another forty hammering away at the paneling. And in the midst of it all, the devotees came rushing in with mridangas, kartals, and arati paraphernalia. The workers stopped and just stood there, unsure what to do.

There was no furniture or place for Prabhupada to sit, but he got down from the palanquin, walked into the main room, looked around, indicated a nearby space and said, “I will sit here.” And he began to sit down, right in all the muck on the stone floor, but Surabhi quickly took off his chaddar, found a somewhat drier corner, and threw it downbeneath him. Then Prabhupada said, “Now you can do what you like.”

Surabhi bathed Prabhupada’s feet and then offered arati—though he was so nervous that he kept fumbling with the ghee lamp and the flame kept going out—while devotees sang sri-guru-carana-padma, trying to avoid slipping on the greasy floor.

“It was really ecstatic,” Ambika remembered. “It was so far-out that there we were in Prabhupada’s new apartment in all the slush. We were jumping up and down, slipping and sliding, and we had this ecstatic kirtan for Srila Prabhupada, and he was smiling and throwing flowers at us just as if he had been in a beautiful palace. It was amazing to see Prabhupada sitting there on the floor, in the middle of it all, so nicely.”

Some devotees began washing the floor, and others ran to find serviceable pieces of furniture to provide Prabhupada with a desk, seat, and bed. Prabhupada just sat cross-legged and directed the devotees: “I want the table there and the bed there; this goes over here and the bureau over there; and I want the kitchen things over there.”

“It was really funny,” Vijeta recalled, “because everybody forgot their position in the Society—that ‘I am a sannyasi’ or ‘I am a mataji,' ‘I am the temple commander,’ ‘I am the president,’ ‘I am a book distributor.’ The only thing anyone could remember was, ‘I am Srila Prabhupada’s servant, and he is giving instructions.’ It was amazing. I saw Mother Aditya giving instructions to Tamal Krishna Goswami. She was handing things to him and telling him, ‘This goes over there!’ And he’d run and put it over there. It was really incredible watching all this going on. It was great.”

Surabhi had been saying that it would take at least another two weeks to finish Prabhupada’s quarters, but with all the devotees and the construction crew there—and inspired by Prabhupada’s presence—we accomplished in two hours what might have taken weeks. The quarters were not completely finished, but at least Prabhupada could move in, and very quickly the devotees cleaned the quarters and made them livable for him. I marveled at Prabhupada’s potency—and the devotees’ surrendered service.

Observing the entire scene with a satisfied look, Prabhupada smiled at everyone and said, “Thank you very much.”

Then most of the devotees left, and Prabhupada met with nine or ten of his leaders and personal staff. “We all sat with our heads hangingdown,” Sarvabhavana recalled. “We expected a thunderstorm from Prabhupada, because his quarters were so messy and noisy. Prabhupada had his head hanging down also. We sat like this for several minutes in pin-drop silence. Time lost all meaning.”

Finally Prabhupada raised his head and spoke in a soft and tender voice: “All of you are trying so hard to please this old man who gets irritated so fast. I am old and on top of that I am unwell, so little things irritate me, but all of you are so tolerant.”

“He went on like that for about ten minutes,” Sarvabhavana said. “I thought I was the only one who was crying, but when I looked around I saw that everyone had tears in their eyes, including Prabhupada. It was so sweet, so wonderful. How can you not love such a person?”

Prabhupada was pleased with the quarters—“No one can design like Surabhi Maharaja,” he said—and he spent the night there. But the next day, he agreed to move to Kartikeya Mahadevia’s home for a week, to attend the Bombay pandal program and to give Surabhi enough time to ready the quarters, which he and I promised Prabhupada would be completed by the time the pandal program was over, at the end of the month. I was relieved that he was giving us more time to prepare his facilities and happy that he would be comfortably and conveniently situated at Kartikeya’s place.

I had arranged for large banners to be posted around the pandal with what Prabhupada had defined as the theme: “The Modern Civilization Is a Failure. The Only Solution Is Krishna Consciousness.”

Our two previous Bombay pandals had been at Cross Maidan, which was an ideal location, with heavy foot traffic, especially during rush hours, as pedestrians walked from the Churchgate train station to Flora Fountain and other places in downtown Bombay, and back. This time, however, Cross Maidan had not been available, so we settled for Azad Maidan, which, though it could be reached by car and with some effort by foot, was not on many pedestrians’ usual route.

Also, India had just held general elections, and people were still preoccupied with politics. The Congress Party had been routed at the polls, and Indira Gandhi had lost her seat in parliament and was about to resign. The Janata Party alliance would be choosing a new prime minister in the next couple of days, and some citizens who might other-wise have attended the pandal program were caught up listening to news reports, attending rallies, and talking about national politics and Indira Gandhi’s fall. So in contrast with the crowds of fifteen to twenty thousand people who had attended the first pandal, far fewer—only a couple of thousand each day—attended this one.

Leaving for the pandal from Kartikeya Mahadevia’s flat, Tamal Krishna and Bhavananda would often go ahead, and then Prabhupada and Ksiracora Gopinatha dasa (later Bhakti Charu Swami), who was assisting him, would follow. Prabhupada’s health had deteriorated considerably; he was frail and needed assistance to stand and walk. Devotees would carry him on a palanquin from the flat to the car, from the car to a room behind the stage, and from there onto the stage, where Bhavananda would help him onto his vyasasana and he would sit, hunched over or reclining, almost motionless.

“We were surprised he even came,” Racitambara dasi later commented. “He was so ill and obviously very, very weak. But he was there, and that was already something.”

On the first day, Prabhupada opened by asking Bhavananda to recite two verses from Srimad-Bhagavatam, “which,” he said, “is the theme of our Krishna consciousness movement.”

Bhavananda began with Canto 2, chapter 3, verse 18: “‘Do the trees not live? Do the bellows of the blacksmith not breathe? All around us, do the beasts not eat and discharge semen?”’ He then read the purport, in which Prabhupada criticized the modern conception that life was meant for maximum sense gratification and countered that “the Srimad-Bhagavatam affirms that life is not meant for so-called economic development or advancement of materialistic science for the hedonistic philosophy of eating, mating, drinking, and merrymaking. Life is solely meant for tapasya, for purifying existence so that one may enter into eternal life just after the end of the human form of life.”

The problem, Prabhupada had written, was that “materialists want to prolong life as much as possible because they have no information of the next life. Therefore, they want to get the maximum comforts of life only in this present life, thinking conclusively that there is no life after death. This ignorance about the eternity of the living being and the change of covering in the material world has played havoc in thestructure of the modern human society. Consequently there are many problems, multiplied by various plans of modernized man. The plans for solving the problems of society have only aggravated the troubles. Even if it is possible to prolong life more than one hundred years, advancement of human civilization does not necessarily follow. . . . Prolonged life without spiritual value is not very important.”

Bhavananda followed with verse 19: ‘“Men who are like dogs, hogs, camels, and asses praise those men who never listen to the transcendental pastimes of Lord Sri Krsna, the deliverer from evils.’” Prabhupada’s purport focused on materialists’ animalistic tendencies and training: “Modern university education practically prepares one to acquire a doggish mentality to accept the service of a greater master. Like the dogs, after finishing a so-called education, the so-called educated persons move from door to door with applications for some service, and mostly they are driven away, informed of no vacancy. As the dogs are negligible animals and serve the master faithfully for bits of bread, similarly, one serves a master faithfully without sufficient rewards....

“The human life is so important that even the demigods in the higher planets sometimes aspire after a human body on this earth because in the human body only can one easily go back to Godhead. And in spite of having obtained such an important body, if one does not re-establish his lost eternal relation with Govinda, Lord Krsna, he is certainly a fool who has forgotten his self-interest.”

When Bhavananda had finished reading the verses and purports, Prabhupada delivered his lecture. He explained that we living entities were part and parcel of God but that somehow we had fallen into this material condition and were changing bodies.

Prabhupada continued, “So,

anarthopasamam saksad  
bhakti-yogam adhoksaje  
lokasyajanato vidvams  
cakre satvata-samhitam  
\[SB 1.7.6\]

Anartha. We living entities are part and parcel of God. Mamaivamso jiva-bhutah. Some way or other, we are now fallen in this materialcondition, and we are changing bodies. This is the first instruction in the Bhagavad-gita. There are so many commentators on Bhagavad-gita, but nobody has pointed out what is the real business of Bhagavad-gita. The real business is, as Krishna says in the beginning of His teachings,

dehino ’smin yatha dehe  
kaumaram yauvanam jara  
tatha dehantara-praptir  
dhiras tatra na muhyati  
\[Gita 2.13\]

This is the first instruction, that we are changing body on account of the spirit soul. We are changing our body every day, every moment— kaumaram yauvanam jara. I was a child; you were a child. We have now changed our body. Similarly, now I am an old man. Some of you are also old men. We have changed bodies.

“So, what kind of body are we going to have? What change is going to take place? People have no knowledge. So at least in India this condition should be changed. To keep people in ignorance, in this bodily concept of life—‘I belong to this community,’ ‘I belong to that community,’ ‘I belong to this body,’ ‘I belong to that body’—no. They should be educated to become brahma-bhutah:

brahma-bhutah prasannatma  
na socati na kanksati  
samah sarvesu bhutesu  
mad-bhaktim labhate param  
\[Gita 18.54\]

Sama-sarvesu bhutesu. India’s education is not to distinguish that ‘Here is an Englishman,’ ‘Here is a German,’ ‘Here is a Christian,’ ‘Here is a Hindu,’ ‘Here is a Muslim.’ Samah sarvesu bhutesu. Because India’s realization of knowledge is brahmanubhuti, brahma-bhutah. Then, when one comes to the standard of brahma-bhutah knowledge, he’ll be happy.

“It is not possible, of course, for everyone to realize Brahman. That is not possible. But there must be an ideal institution. Unfortunately, at the present moment it is very difficult to find out where is that ideal brahman, but there must be—Krishna says. Our Krishna consciousness movement includes this: catur-varnyam maya srstamguna-karma-vibhagasah. There must be division. There may be only a small number of brahmans, but there must be ideal brahmans so that people may learn that ‘Here is the first-class brahman. Here is the first-class man. Let us take instruction from him, not from so-called politicians.’ This is Indian civilization. Formerly, even Lord Ramachandra, who was the king—He is God Himself—still, He used to consult learned brahmans, sages, saintly persons, for governmental duties. The divisions in society must be there.

“So, there are many things to be done in the Krishna consciousness movement. Don’t take it that it is simply chanting Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna. Chanting is the prime factor, because if you chant the Hare Krishna maha-mantra, then gradually everything will be clear in your mind. Ceto-darpana-marjanam bhava-maha-davagni-nirvapanam. The whole world is suffering on account of all contaminated things accumulated within our heart. And the Bhagavata process is to hear from the right person.

srnvatam sva-kathah krsnah  
punya-sravana-kirtanah  
hrdy antah-stho hy abhadrani  
vidhunoti suhrt satam  
\[SB 1.2.17\]

“So, our request to all of you is that you take this Krishna consciousness movement, chanting, very seriously. Don’t neglect it. This is India’s gift to the whole world. That is Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s mission.

bharata-bhumite haila manusya-janma yara  
janma sarthaka kari’ kara para-upakara  
\[Cc Adi 9.41\]

India’s mission is para-upakara: not to exploit others but to do good to others. And what is the best thing to do? A human being has got the opportunity to understand his position, but he’s being kept in darkness, like an animal, and his only business now is how to eat, how to sleep, how to mate. This kind of ignorance, at least in India, we should not take up. Let us combine together. That is my request. Take it very seriously. In America they are now taking it seriously. Perhaps you know. Recently there was a judgment by the Supreme Court in New York.

They admitted that the Hare Krishna movement is a genuine religious movement. There was great opposition against this movement—our students were being kidnapped, and so many harassments were going on. But by the grace of Krishna ... I went to America in 1965, and now it is ’77. After eleven, twelve years of struggle ... I was loitering in the street. Who cared for me? But it is now being recognized, that ‘Here is a movement.’ Now we have to utilize it. I always put this logic to my students—andha-pangu-nyaya, that for the benefit of the whole world, American money and Indian culture should combine.” The audience burst into applause. “That will bring benefit to the whole world.”

At the start of Prabhupada’s lecture, his voice had been barely a whisper and he had been practically immobile, not even moving his hand. But as he spoke, he became more animated and increasingly forceful. “His body would become straight,” Bhakti Charu recalled, “and finally he would be sitting as erect as a bolt and shouting, chastising.”

“As it was going on,” Jayadvaita remembered, “Prabhupada was getting more enlivened. Soon he was speaking with full enthusiasm. He had so much energy. By the end, practically he was roaring.”

“He wasn’t pulling any punches,” Aditya dasi said. “He was really giving it to them.”

Lokanath too was struck by the force of Prabhupada’s preaching that day—“how strongly he was preaching, like roaring, scaring his fellow citizens, trying to wake them up, shake them up. I don’t remember any other time Prabhupada was as strongly, forcefully, emphatically making his points, reminding them, bharata-bhumite haila manusya-janma yara, janma sarthaka kari' kara para-upakara. ‘You are born in India. If you want to make your life perfect, don’t lead the life of cats and dogs. Do para-upakara, take to Krishna consciousness.’”

“The opportunity is there,” Prabhupada told the crowd. “Now let our Indian leaders come out. Take this movement very seriously. There will be great advantage to the people of the whole world. This kind of situation, to keep them in darkness, that ‘I am dog,’ ‘I am hog,’ ‘I am American,’ ‘I am Indian’—No: Aham brahmasmi. This is real conception of life. What is the difference if a bulldog thinks, ‘I am a bulldog’ and a man thinks, ‘I am American’ or ‘I am brahman’— what is the difference? The real thing is knowledge. Don’t keep this knowledgelocked up in your books, but spread it. My only request is that the leaders of India should now come forward and join this movement and take advantage for doing good to the whole world, para-upakara” Again the audience applauded.

"bharata-bhumite haila manusya-janma yara  
janma sarthaka kari’ kara para-upakara

“Thank you very much.”

The applause swelled into a thunderous ovation.

“If you have questions,” I announced after a moment, “we request you to ask them now. A lot of information has been presented, a lot of food for thought. This is a very important movement, very important subject matter. So we request any of you who have any question at all to please put that question and we can have further discussion. Who will be the first? Asking questions is a sign of intelligence.”

“What is the most important thing in life?” one woman asked.

“To understand yourself,” Prabhupada answered. “If you misidentify yourself that you are this body, then you are finished. Athato brahma jijnasa. The question should be, ‘What I am? Am I this body or something else?’ That is the most important thing. That is the beginning of Vedanta-sutra knowledge, athato brahma jijnasa. The animals cannot ask, Am I dog, or am I something else?’ And if a man is kept in darkness, that he never questions, Am I this or that?’ then he is an animal. So the most important thing according to our Vedic culture is to understand oneself, ‘What I am?”

The next person asked, “Isn’t such education taxing?”

“Do you think that you are not taxed?” Prabhupada countered. “Why should you not be taxed for the proper gain? You are being taxed for so many nonsense things. Why not be taxed for the proper thing? That is intelligence.”

“What is the importance of health in life?” a gentleman asked. “How do you advise people to maintain health, and how does it connect to your mission?”

“Where is health?” Prabhupada challenged. “First of all, you have to understand that however healthy you may be, you must die. Then what problem have you solved? Janma-mrtyu-jara-vyadhi-duhkha-dosanudarsanam, Krishna says. It is not my manufacture. However you may try to remain very healthy, nature’s law is that you must die. How can you help yourself? After all, you have to meet death. Janma-mrtyu-jara-vyadhi \[birth, death, old age, and disease\]. So long as you have got this material body, there is no question of health. You must suffer. You may be a very great scientist, but nature’s law must act.

prakrteh kriyamanani  
gunaih karmani sarvasah  
ahankara-vimudhatma  
kartaham iti manyate  
\[Gita 3.27\]

Foolish persons—ahankara-vimudhatma—bewildered by false egotism think, ‘I am improving health. I am improving this. I am doing that.’ He is improving nothing. He’s completely under the clutches of material nature. He cannot do anything independently. That is the law of nature.”

“Can we solve political problems with this religious basis?” another man asked.

“Yes,” Prabhupada replied. “All problems will be solved if you become Krishna conscious.”

“What is the simple solution to understand the soul?” another asked. “I would like to understand the soul.”

“This is very simple,” Prabhupada answered, “but we are educated so foolishly that we cannot understand. Krishna says, bhilmir apo ’nalo vayuh kham mano buddhir eva ca, bhinna me prakrtir astadha: Arjuna, there are eight material elements: earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intelligence, ego.’ Apareyam: ‘But these are inferior elements.’ Itas tu viddhi me prakrtim param: ‘Beyond these there is another, superior element.’ What is that? Jiva-bhutam maha-baho yayedam dharyate jagat. The living entity is the superior element. Without the living entity, what is the value of this bhumir apo ’nalo vayuh? This distinction we can experience every day. Here is an important man. Now he’s finished, and if you kick his face, he won’t protest. What is wanting? That jiva-bhutam mahd-bdho—that living force is wanting. Anyone, any child, can understand that ‘Something is wanting. Therefore thisimportant body is nothing but a lump of matter? Anyone can understand. Everything is explained in the Bhagavad-gita, but people are not serious to understand. That is the difficulty.”

At one point, when a man from the audience came right up to the front of the stage and began to challenge Prabhupada, Prabhupada responded “like a lion,” Racitambara later described. “It was so amazing that from this slumped over, completely weak state, he suddenly looked like the strongest person around. His eyes were full of fire, and he completely smashed this man—and convinced everybody else in the audience. People in the audience were so inspired that one Chinese devotee, Taittiriya, went into the crowd and distributed twenty-seven sets of Prabhupada’s books. Everyone was so fired up after hearing Prabhupada speak so strongly that they were buying the books like anything.”

Finally Prabhupada said, “That’s all. Now chant Hare Krishna.”

Both at the pandal and at the flat, Prabhupada was strong in his criticism of anyone who did not accept and follow Krishna as the Supreme Personality of Godhead. He condemned materialistic civilization, calling it a dog, or anthill, civilization. A dog ran on four legs and a man ran on four wheels, he explained to Kartikeya Mahadevia, Tamal Krishna, Bhavananda, and others gathered in his room one day, but if the man had no spiritual knowledge, he was no better than the dog. “What is the difference between the anthill and the skyscraper building?” he asked. “The ants are living in holes, and we have also made some holes.”

“In Africa we saw big, big anthills—twenty-foot anthills,” Bhavananda interjected.

“If more people come,” Prabhupada said, “I shall describe all this anthill civilization. ‘Health’—nonsense. What health? He’ll be kicked out immediately,” referring to the man’s question from the pandal. “Who is healthy if he is going to die?‘I am so healthy that I am going to die tomorrow? This is their health.”

“Illusion. Almost every one of those questions was about the body,” Tamal Krishna pointed out.

“Krishna says, na hanyate hanyamane sarire” Prabhupada quoted. “That is healthy. When you do not die even though the body is destroyed, that is healthy life. What is this healthy life? The body andeverything are finished. Actually, everything is not finished, but people are kept in that ignorance—‘The body is finished; everything is finished’—but that is not the fact. Krishna very clearly says, na jayate mriyate va kadacin. People do not even question how it is possible. But that is the most important question.”

He also criticized the United Nations World Health Organization. “Rascal, who is healthy? Everyone is going to die. They do not think, ‘Where is health?’ Such foolish things are going on all over the world. So organize something real and spread it, slow but sure.”

“We shouldn’t be impatient to compromise,” Tamal Krishna said, “just to—”

“There’s no question of becoming impatient,” Prabhupada responded. “You have got a diamond. If there is no buyer, that does not mean you have to throw it away.”

“And sell something less.”

“Yes, diamond is diamond. . . . People must know that ‘Here is a diamond. If I want it, I must pay the proper price.’ That I want to establish. Why should India’s culture be lost in this way? I am not a cheap patriot ... I want to give Indian culture to the whole world. I am not going to cheat people, taking Bhagavad-gita and speaking all nonsense. I want to present Bhagavad-gita as it is. That is my mission. Why should I cheat you?”

“We will try to follow your message properly,” Kartikeya said.

“Why should India’s big culture be lost for the matter of these rascal leaders?” Prabhupada continued. “This should be stopped. As Krishna says, catur-varnyam maya srstam guna-karma. There must be ideal brahmans, ideal kshatriyas, ideal vaishyas. That is the Krishna consciousness movement. It is all-inclusive. The economic question? Krishna says, annad bhavanti bhutani—grow food. Practical. When I was traveling, millions of clerks were coming—‘Education. Educated.’ And who is growing food? Then these clerks have to be provided in these pigeonholes and depend on rations. Is that civilization? Throngs of people are coming, just like ants. And when you go to the village areas, all vacant land. No one is interested to produce food. Everyone is interested to live in the city, in these pigeonholes, and go to the cinema,the brothel, the club, and learn how to drink, how to become ‘gentlemen'. Is that civilization? The aim of human life is lost. You do not know why you are going to the office, why you are eating. They are keeping people in an animal mentality, a doggish mentality. We have explained. University education means a doggish mentality. Unless he becomes a dog, there is no food. ‘Give me some food.’ . . . For five hundred posts, three hundred thousand applications.”

“Oh, yes,” Kartikeya agreed. “For five jobs, five thousand people applied.”

“Is that education?” Prabhupada asked. “Better not to be educated. Those who are not educated, they can purchase ten rupees’ worth of potatoes and sit down anywhere. . . . They have no scarcity. And after spending so much money, living at the cost of fathers and mothers, they are unemployed: no job, no food. Then they plan something—Naxalite, this party, that party—or join some political movement and help Indira Gandhi. They are paid to make propaganda.”

“But all that has vanished now,” said Kartikeya. “That plan has failed completely.” Like many other Indians, he was hopeful that with the new election, things would be better.

“Not failed,” Prabhupada corrected. “Another man will come— because unemployment is there. When we were children, we were purchasing mustard oil for eight annas for two and a half kilos . .. now it is selling for thirteen rupees per kilo. Will the change of government bring this thirteen rupees to three annas? Then what is the benefit? It is the same stool, whether this side or that side. People are not going to get any relief by this change of government. So, we are not so concerned about thirteen rupees or three annas or .. . Some way or other, people are getting their things. That’s all right. But the real loss is to remain in animal mentality and forget the aim of life. That is the real loss. Krishna says plainly,

asraddadhanah purusa  
dharmasyasya parantapa  
mam aprapya nivartante  
mrtyu-samsara-vartmani  
\[Gita 9.3\]

‘This Bhagavad-gita that I am speaking, if one is not interested to hear it or to take it, then the result will be that he’ll not get Me.’ ‘So, what is loss if I don’t get You?’ Mrtyu-samsara-vartmani: ‘Then go again to the cycle of birth and death.’ That’s it. That is nature’s law....

“Why this human form of life should be lost in this way? At least try to give this knowledge to the people in general. This is para-upakara. And that is Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s gift. And especially India can do it.bharata-bhumite haila manusya-janma yara  
janma sarthaka kari’ para-upakara

\[“One who has taken his birth as a human being in the land of India (Bharata-varsa) should make his life successful and work for the benefit of all other people.” (Cc Adi 9.41)\]

“The natural tendency of the people here is to be God conscious,” Tamal Krishna said, “but the government is artificially checking. Will this new government be any different?”

“No. The same fools and rascals.”

“So, we have to be very strong in our center here in Bombay.”

“We are for everyone. We are not for any particular nation or any particular person.”

“Our preaching has to be so strong that it will counteract the government’s preaching, the movies, and all these other Kali-yuga things.”

“Oh, yes. All influences. . . . People are in darkness. And the politicians keep them like dogs, hogs, and camels, and take votes from them and become leaders. Nobody protested that I called all men dogs, hogs, and camels. No one came forward that, ‘You are using very strong words.’ Because it’s a fact.”

“They especially liked your idea of American money and Indian culture,” Hridayananda said. “They applauded for that."

“That is my mission,” Prabhupada agreed. “I am doing that. I am bringing money from America. Nobody is paying me. It is not a joke. Ten lakhs of rupees—who else brings?”

“Even big export companies don’t bring so much,” said Gopal Krishna.

“And they will be glad,” Prabhupada predicted. “They have got money, and they are getting culture. I am trying for united nations. That is the real attempt, not this United Nations, all rogues and thieves andcheaters, barking dogs. I am trying for real united nations. . . . Let us cooperate together nicely.”

“Your Bombay project is very impressive,” Hridayananda reported. “We’ve just taken a tour.”

“Therefore I persistently took that place,” Prabhupada said. “Nobody encouraged me. Nobody helped me. I hesitated a little, that ‘If I am persistent to take it, they will not cooperate. It may be failure.’ Still I took it. And only fifty thousand and one lakh of rupees I gave this thief Nair: ‘All right, take it. Come on. Whatever I have got, you take it.’ Still he thought, Oh. I'll get money.”

“He had already played the trick with one man,” Tamal Krishna said.

“Still, I took the risk, that ‘I have no money. If he cheats me, that’s all right, but let me attempt.’”

“Then you installed the Deity as soon as possible.”

“Yes. Immediately, after leaving Akash Ganga. All Krishna’s desire.”

“Everyone is appreciating how wonderful this project is—all of Bombay.”

“So many obstacles, one after another, one after another, one after another.”

“Krishna would not leave.”

“No. That was my request: ‘Please sit down here tight. Then I shall do everything.’”

“Practically Giriraj has not left either,” Pancha Dravida added.

“Yes,” Prabhupada said. “He has not trembled in any circumstance. That is his qualification. That nasty place—hot, mosquitoes. You also lived there. No gentleman can live there . . . rats, mosquitoes, and so much inconvenience. You had no place—sometimes here, sometimes there, sometimes there.”

“You were also so inconvenienced,” Tamal Krishna said to Prabhupada. “You had to move. One time you were living in that—”

“But for me you make good arrangement wherever I live,” Prabhupada noted, “that’s all. But I know how you were living in that nasty hut, full of dirty things, mosquitoes, rats, dripping of water. And Nair is attacking, municipality is attacking.”

“You always said that we were so trained, we would even live on the roadside.”

“Oh, yes. That you are trained,” Prabhupada said with a laugh. “You don’t care for this palace or underneath a tree.”

“Formerly we were living like that as hippies, and now we live like that to serve you.”

“I was living in Radha-Damodar temple. It was not a palace. But before that, I was living in a palace—Keshi Ghat. But this gosai, goswami, called me, that ‘You live here? And I said, ‘All right, Jiva Gosvami’s place. Let me go there?

“Now organize. Make a very good plan that our Bombay temple will be always crowded with thousands of men, and some program must go on.”

“You mentioned the other day that five hundred devotees should always be there,” Tamal Krishna said.

“Oh, yes. We have got room.”

"Jaya Srila Prabhupada!” the devotees exclaimed.

“So enthusiastic. All young men.”

“Our enthusiasm is coming from you, Srila Prabhupada,” Tamal Krishna said.

“I am an old man,” Prabhupada whispered.

But we didn’t see him that way; to our eyes, he was ever fresh.

At the pandal Prabhupada continued his strong preaching— through his books, which were read out loud, and through his and his disciples’ talks. On the second night, Hridayananda gave a preliminary address and Prabhupada spoke mainly on the Bhagavad-gita,

When I invited people to come forward with their questions, the first man asked, “When chanting, you chant the name of Rama as well as Krishna. But I do not see any photograph of Rama here. What is the reason?”

“You do not see, but can you hear?” Prabhupada asked.

“I do not see!” the man insisted.

Prabhupada exploded: “But you do not hear!” And he explained that hearing was the best way to understand what one could not see. “Hearing is also experiencing,” he said. “Why do you want to see? . . . Seeing and hearing are the same thing. Suppose you have a grandfather. Are you seeing him? How do you accept you had a grandfather? That is hearing.”

“No, I saw him also.”

“You did not see your great-grandfather. But how do you know? Hearing is also a process.”

“My question is whether there is distinction between Rama and Krishna.”

“The distinction is that hearing is also a process of acquiring knowledge. Why don’t you accept it? Simply seeing is not acquiring knowledge. There are so many senses, and hearing is the first-class sense for understanding what you cannot see.”

When I asked others to come forward and inquire, Tamal Krishna turned to Prabhupada and said, “I think you scared them away.”

The next man asked, “How can I know the unknown with the known?”

“This is already explained,” Prabhupada replied. “How could you know your great-grandfather? From the parampara system. Your father says, ‘Yes, I had my grandfather.’ So, from the authority of your father you can understand. This is easy process. Evam parampara-praptam imam rajarsayo viduh. You have to hear. Therefore Veda is called sruti. Sruti means you have to hear from the right source. Then you know. That is knowledge. You don’t hear from a cheater. You hear from the right source. Then the knowledge is perfect.”

The third questioner asked, “If a man is highly religious, it is very difficult for him to move in the material world. How should he move with materialistic people?”

“You have to understand your spiritual identification. Because you are fools and rascals, you are thinking, ‘I am this body.’ And Krishna gives instruction in the beginning that you are not this body. Dehino ’smin yatha dehe kaumaram yauvanam jara. Asmin dehe: you are within this body; you are not this body. Krishna is authority; you have to take it. But Krishna is not only simply speaking authoritatively; He is giving practical example. Dehino ’smin yatha dehe kaumaram yauvanam jara. Because the soul is within this body, it is changing. Tatha dehantara-praptir dhiras tatra na muhyati. You have to become dhira, sober, not adhira. There are two classes of men: dhira and adhira. And in order to become a dhira, you have to go to a guru. Tad-vijnanartham sa gurum evabhigacchet. You have to be trained up; then you’ll understand—not so quickly, without being dhilra. Dhiras tatra na muhyati.”
