I saw that Prabhupada could answer any question with clarity and conviction just on the basis of the Bhagavad-gita. And he was practical: if one wanted to be spiritual and move in this world among materialistic people, he had to be trained by guru to become dhira, sober, undisturbed.

The last of several more questions was, “Can you please explain what is our only way out for salvation?”

“Yes,” Prabhupada said. “People are so fallen that they cannot take the life of tapasya. Athato brahma jijnasa. This is the life of tapasya, Tapo divyam putraka yena suddhyet sattvam. Tapasa brahmacaryena yamena niyamena va. So, there is a process of tapasya, but in this age, Kali-yuga, people are so fallen that they cannot undergo all the items of tapasya. It is very difficult. Therefore Chaitanya Mahaprabhu . . . Chaitanya Mahaprabhu did not manufacture. It is mentioned in the shastra that \[one can go back to Godhead\] only by this process:

kaler dosa-nidhe rajann  
asti hy eko mahan gunah  
kirtanad eva krsnasya  
mukta-sangah param vrajet  
\[SB 12.3.51\]

\[“My dear King, although Kali-yuga is an ocean of faults, there is still one good quality about this age: Simply by chanting the Hare Krsna maha-mantra, one can become free from material bondage and be promoted to the transcendental kingdom.”\] This is a special concession to the Kali-yuga, that there are so many faults in this age, but if one sticks to this principle of kirtanad eva krsnasya mukta-sangah param vrajet, he becomes liberated and goes back to home, back to Godhead.”

The gentleman inquired further, “And is it so, that in Srimad-Bhdgavata it is also written that many great men want to be here in Kali-yuga, because it is easier for salvation?”

“Yes. That I am speaking. Krsnasya kirtanad eva mukta-sangah param. Simply by chanting. Therefore we see practically that these Western people, they are not coming from high-class brahman or Vaishnava families, but still, by klrtanad eva krsnasya they are becoming so liberated that they are preaching Krishna consciousness all over the world.”

Every evening at the pandal a prominent guest would give a short introductory talk, and on the third night the chief guest was Justice J. M. Gandhi of the Bombay High Court.

Continuing with the theme of tapasya from the previous night’s program, Prabhupada had Bhavananda read aloud the first two verses and purports of Srimad-Bhagavatam Canto 5, Chapter 5: “Lord Rsabhadeva’s Teachings to His Sons”:

“Lord Rsabhadeva told His sons: My dear boys, of all the living entities who have accepted material bodies in this world, one who has been awarded this human form should not work hard day and night simply for sense gratification, which is available even for dogs and hogs that eat stool. One should engage in penance and austerity to attain the divine position of devotional service. By such activity, one’s heart is purified, and when one attains this position, he attains eternal, blissful life, which is transcendental to material happiness and which continues forever.

“One can attain the path of liberation from material bondage only by rendering service to highly advanced spiritual personalities. . . . For those who are not interested in such activities, who associate with people fond of women and sex, the path to hell is wide open. The mahatmas are equipoised. They do not see any difference between one living entity and another. They are very peaceful and are fully engaged in devotional service. They are devoid of anger, and they work for the benefit of everyone. They do not behave in any abominable way. Such people are known as mahatmas”

Prabhupada spoke briefly and then took questions.

“If God is everywhere,” a man asked, “why is His presence not felt by everybody?”

“Everybody is not intelligent,” Prabhupada replied. “Mostly they are rascals. Manusyanam sahasresu. This is the statement by God that, ‘Out of millions of persons, one tries to become perfect. And out of many millions of perfect persons, one can understand God.’ So, understanding God is not so easy. But if we want to understand, God will help us. That is the point.”

“I don’t think God is opposed to sex,” the next man said. “I have heard many lectures, and it is always stressed as if God is opposed to sex. But I don’t think that’s so.”

“God is never opposed to sex,” Prabhupada responded. “Who said? God said, dharmaviruddho bhutesu kamo 'smi: ‘Sex which is not against the regulative principles of religious life, that I am.’ God never says,

‘Stop sex.’ Otherwise, why is there grihastha ashrama? Ashrama means that there is Krishna consciousness.... So make it ashrama, and follow the rules and regulations of ashrama. Then it is all right. Otherwise, you are bound up by the laws of nature.”

The man then referred to Prabhupada’s purport that Bhavananda had read: “One of your principal statements was that a man goes on the local train, stands there for two hours, reaches his place of business and works there from nine o’clock in the morning to five o’clock in the evening, returns back, has his food and sex and all that. I found many people who have worked very hard, raised children very nicely, and have sex but lead a good life. I don’t think there is anything wrong with that.”

“Yes, if there is no wrong,” Prabhupada said, “it is all right. But this sort of life is not very palatable.”

“Because I find even the dog—”

“If you like that life,” Prabhupada interrupted, “then that is up to you. But I don’t think this is a very nice way of life, to work so hard simply for bread.”

“No, I agree there.”

“Then agreed, agreed. Then why disagree? That’s all right, no more.” And Tamal Krishna called on others.

“Would you agree that God is just a concept?” one man asked. “If you do not, please give a logical reason for that.”

“Why shall I agree that God is only a concept?” Prabhupada asked.

“Because I want it logically.”

“You do not know logic. You have to learn logic.”

“But I still would like you to explain it logically.”

“Yes, but you have to learn how to know it. There is master. Just like you cannot prove logically that without father, there is a child. There cannot be any child without father. Therefore if anyone thinks that without father there can be child, he is an animal; he has no logic.

“But still the question is unanswered. Would you agree that God is just a concept?”

“No, no. There must be father. Just like you see that everything is growing out of this earth. Sarva-yonisu kaunteya sambhavanti murtayah yah. There is mother, and there is child—then where is the father? This is logic. Unless you come to this point, that there is mother, there is child,there must be father, then there is no logic. Without father there cannot be child. Simply mother cannot give birth to a child. This is logic.”

“Thank you.”

“Now chant Hare Krishna.”

Back at Kartikeya Mahadevia’s flat, Prabhupada, Tamal Krishna, and others discussed the previous night’s program.

“It seems like you are giving more stress to science in recent years than previously,” Tamal Krishna suggested.

“That is required for convincing the modernized man,” Prabhupada replied. Then, after a long pause, he said, “The ordinary man’s logic that ‘There is no God; I cannot see,’ that we have defied. There is child, there is mother—there must be father. This is logic, because without father there cannot be child. Three things are required—mother, father, and child. Child means there must be father and mother. Mother is there, the child is born, but where is the father? We know who is the father, what is His name, what are His activities. That is our advancement. And ‘We do not know’ means you are not a respectable, wise chap. You do not know your father’s name. Any respectable man, in the court or anywhere, the father’s name immediately . . . ‘Your name?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘Your father’s name?’ Is it not? If he does not know his father’s name, that means he is not a respectable person. He has no respectable position. Anyone who does not know what is God, he is just like the child who does not know his father’s name. Father must be there. That you do not know—that is your foolishness. Anyone who does not know who is his father, what is God, he is not a respectable man. It may be that you have not seen your father, but you cannot deny that with father you were born. That is no logic. Hmm? Is that logic?”

“They don’t know what the meaning is, what logic is,” Tamal Krishna said.

“Orphan,” Prabhupada continued. “Orphan—does it mean he has no father? He does not know who is his father. But we are not orphans. We are taken care of by our very rich, very wise father, very able father. We are not forlorn orphans. We have got respectability. And we offer our respect to our father. We depend on our father. We are safe. Everyone can become safe. The opportunity is offered. If you don’t take, that is your misfortune. We are offering, ‘Every one of you can becomesafe, safely protected by the father, Krishna. Aham tvam sarva-papebhyo moksa. Why don’t you take advantage?”’

Then Prabhupada said to Hari-sauri, who was about to leave for Australia, “We have got knowledge for understanding the whole philosophy. So try to convince others about this philosophy in Australia. And Krishna will help you more and more. The more you try to convince others about this Krishna consciousness, the more you become enlightened.”

He thought Svarupa Damodara should preach internationally as well. “You should make colorful slides and give presentations like this throughout the world,” he told him, and suggested that he bring Krishna consciousness to Russia. “Russian people like science,” he said, “but you should be accompanied by a cultural group.”

He turned to Sudama, the head of the Vaikuntha Players performing troupe, and told him, “You should go with Svarupa Damodara. Team up together: you make the cultural presentation, and he will speak about the science of Krishna consciousness. Russian people are very enthusiastic about Vedic culture. It’s a science. So this will be a very good combination.”

Prabhupada also said that when the auditorium at Hare Krishna Land was ready—it had been designed by the premier theater designer in Bombay—he wanted the troupe to perform there as well.

Prabhupada very much appreciated Svarupa Damodara’s scientific presentation of Krishna consciousness, and the next night of the pandal he asked him to give the talk and then spoke afterward, but only briefly.

“Ladies and gentlemen,” Prabhupada began, “the very learned, erudite, scholarly speaking by our Dr. Svarupa Damodara Singh must have created some impression in your mind, I am sure. This Krishna consciousness movement is full of scientific knowledge. Jnanam te ’ham sa-vijnanam pravaksyamy anasuyave. Krishna said to Arjuna that ‘I am speaking to you knowledge, jnanam, sa-vijnanam, with scientific understanding.’ So, ‘Why are You speaking to me?’ Jnanam te ’ham sa-vijnanam pravaksyamy anasuyave: ‘Because you are not envious. That is your qualification. You are a very submissive student. Therefore I’ll give you.’ So the dictation is coming from Krishna, as Dr. Svarupa Damodara said.”

“Last night,” he concluded, “we were speaking of the Bhagavata sloka that this life should not be spoiled like hogs and dogs. We must learn how to love Krishna with love and affection and take instruction from Him to make our life successful.” Then he left without taking any questions.

The next evening, Prabhupada did not speak at all, but he listened as two leading cardiologists, Dr. Keshavrao Krishnarao Datey and Dr. S.N. Sharma, each spoke briefly in appreciation of Krishna consciousness. Dr. Datey was a pioneer of cardiology in India and had received the Padma Bhushan award—India’s third-highest civilian honor. He said that heart disease could be eliminated by controlling anxiety and then praised Prabhupada and his movement. And after the doctors’ talks, Svarupa Damodara gave another scientific presentation, with slides.

The following day, at Kartikeya Mahadevia’s flat, Prabhupada spoke about the importance of scientific preaching. “I want that the intelligent men should come and learn this science,” he told us. “That is wanted.

yad yad acarati sresthas  
tat tad evetaro janah  
sa yat pramanam kurute  
Iokas tad anuvartate

These people. Bring important men, important students. Take this opportunity. Give them a nice place so that they may not be uncomfortable. Give them good food.”

“We have a lot of facility,” I offered.

“Then there should not be any scarcity for their comfort. People are trained up to the modern comforts. Therefore I am building such big, big institutions. Otherwise, Radha-Damodar temple is sufficient for me. It is not for me that I want these big, big buildings. I am accustomed to live anywhere. But those who are educated, scientists, they are accustomed—Europeans, Americans—they must be given proper place. That was my guru maharaja’s policy. Not that all of a sudden they should now live on the floor. No, that is not possible. Then they will be disturbed. Give them nice place, nice food, nice instruction. You are all intelligent boys. Do it immediately. Construct another building. That colony should be for first-class Krishna conscious people, to preach.”

Prabhupada told Svarupa Damodara, “On the whole, I very much appreciated your presentation. I thank you very much.”

“Thank you, Srila Prabhupada,” he replied.

“Yesterday there was sufficient crowd,” Prabhupada said, returning to the pandal program.

“There was nice crowd—all respectable men also,” Sridhar said. “Tonight will be bigger.”

“Sunday is always the biggest,” Gargamuni added.

“I find that Bombay people are a little bit more open-minded,” Svarupa Damodara said.

“Oh, yes,” Prabhupada agreed. “Bombay is the best city in India, undoubtedly—from the very beginning—and the richest city. Sixty-three percent of the government revenue is collected from Bombay. Bombay is so rich. Sixty-three percent from Bombay and 37 percent from the rest of India. That is the position. And religiously-minded.”

“Yes,” Svarupa Damodara said. “I find that almost everybody appreciates Srila Prabhupada so much, especially in Bombay. Anybody who knows about Srila Prabhupada, they highly appreciate him, especially these scholars.”

The discussion turned to the reception of Prabhupada’s books in America and how our preaching was strengthened by the devotees’ expertise in so many fields. “Art also,” he said. “Art, literature, science, philosophy, religion . . . everything, strong background.” With such a foundation of knowledge, he assured us—with Svarupa Damodara’s scientific background—there was no need to fear.

“Once this scientific basis is established, then everybody will be finished,” Hari-sauri predicted.

“It is very easy,” Prabhupada said. “There is a superior element—life. On account of that superior element, the inferior element has got meaning. Otherwise, it has no meaning.”

“No one serves a dead body,” Hari-sauri added. “Push it in the ground and let it rot.”

“That superior element you cannot manufacture by combination of these inferior chemicals,” Prabhupada stated.

“It is actually such a clear and simple thing,” Hari-sauri said, “but they become so complicated they can’t understand.”

“They have made it complicated. Insufficient knowledge.”

“They have been misguided, that’s all,” Svarupa Damodara said.

“Misguided, yes. Rascal leaders. Andha yathandhair upaniyamanah \[“the blind leading the blind” (SB 7.5.31)\].”

“We also would have been misguided in this area if we hadn’t met Srila Prabhupada,” Svarupa Damodara said, addressing the devotees.

“I never agreed to be misguided by these rascals,” Prabhupada said. “Perhaps I am the first man who protested against these unauthorized scientists.”

“Oh, yes,” Svarupa Damodara replied. “Very strongly. Everybody is afraid except Srila Prabhupada.” Prabhupada chuckled. “Frankly speaking, I never knew that the problem was this serious before I met Srila Prabhupada. I never thought about this.”

“Therefore I took it so seriously,” Prabhupada said. “Every morning walk, I was asking, ‘Where is the scientist?’ I thought, Here I have got an opportunity to impress that will fructify. That was my aim. Therefore I was bothering you in so many ways.”

“It is your wonderful mercy, Srila Prabhupada.”

“Because I cannot use the technical words and he can do that,” Prabhupada said, referring to Svarupa Damodara, “so he should be trained up.”

One day Prabhupada spotted an Arab in traditional garb in the pandal crowd and asked one of the sannyasis to call the man to the stage and seat him next to him. The man had worry beads in his hand, and Prabhupada asked him, “What is that? What do you do with it?” He replied that he just fiddled with the beads. Prabhupada showed him his japa-mala and said, “We also have something like that, and we chant the names of the Lord and keep count. Your beads are also meant for chanting the name of God, Allah, and keeping count. So, you should chant the name of the Lord. And you shouldn’t just carry the string of beads in the open, because it is sacred; you should keep it carefully. You should get a bead bag like this, so it is not exposed to unclean things.”

It turned out that the man was a chief of police in Kuwait and a member of the royal family. He had come to Bombay for medical treatment, and on his first day out of the hospital he was strolling in the area,saw the big pandal and crowd, and out of curiosity came to see what was going on.

By bringing the man on stage and having him sit with the distinguished guests, Prabhupada demonstrated that Krishna consciousness was open to everyone and could be appreciated by everyone—even Muslims. He even asked the man to speak, but the man had reservations because he was a prominent person from a Muslim country and didn’t want too much publicity. Overcoming his hesitation, however, the man joined in the kirtan, clapping his hands, and told Prabhupada that he liked the movement very much and would return the next day. Prabhupada invited him to come visit him at Mahadevia’s house.

Two days later, the man came with a Kuwaiti friend. Prabhupada told them that Krishna consciousness, God consciousness, was our original consciousness. “Any system of religion which revives this consciousness is first-class religion,” Prabhupada said. “It doesn’t matter whether it is Christian religion or Hindu religion or Muhammadan religion. The system which revives our original consciousness—that ‘I am eternally related with God as part and parcel; my aim of life is go back to home, back to Godhead and to act accordingly’—this is God consciousness.”

“Let me ask you one question,” the man said. “Now, your God is Hare Krishna, and Krishna ...”

“God is one,” Prabhupada stated.

“God is one, that’s right.”

“Your God, my God—there is no difference.”

“God is one.”

“God means the supreme controller,” Prabhupada explained. “Everyone has to accept the supreme controller. So there is no question of ‘your God,’ ‘my God,’ or ‘his God.’”

“So that means,” the man began, “my religion is ...”

“There is no ‘my religion’ also,” Prabhupada clarified. “If God is one, then to know God or to abide by the orders of God is religion. According to the Bhagavata definition, dharmam tu saksad bhagavat-pranitam: Dharma means the orders or the laws given by God. Just like law means the order given by the state. Nobody can manufacture law at home. The state has ordered, ‘Keep to the left’—that is law. You cannot make ‘Keep to the right’—that is not law. Therefore religion means the orderof God. So, we must know what is God and what is His order—then you are religious. Otherwise, there is no religion. If there is no government, then where is the law? There is no question of law. Law means there must be government, and the order given by the government is law. Similarly ...”

“Do you have a book—about your religion—teaching the rules?” the friend asked.

“Oh, yes,” Prabhupada replied. “The Bhagavad-gita, We have got many books—this is the beginning, A-B-C-D. First of all let us learn A-B-C-D; then you go to higher standards.”

“It’s available all over the world,” Bhavananda said. “I don’t think it’s ... Is it available?”

“We can get him a copy. We have extra copies,” said Tamal Krishna.

“It is not available in my country,” the man said.

“Here we have a copy,” Tamal offered.

“We have got our center in Tehran,” Prabhupada said. “We have got many followers in Tehran. The in-charge man, formerly his name was Akhtar. Now I have changed his name—Atreya Rishi. I have got many Muhammadan disciples.

“Actually, sir, I respect your religion, but I would like to read some books,” the man said.

“You will benefit,” Prabhupada said.

“I will take some books with me. I just came from Bombay Hospital after treatment—the doctor allowed me. I’ve been walking like this, and then I came here. This gentleman saw me and offered me the opportunity to meet you.”

Tamal Krishna asked the man if he could stay for our program in the evening, which would run for only about an hour. And the man agreed, “Yes, of course I will.”

“We have also got chanting beads,” Prabhupada said.

“Like ours,” the man said. “Yes. You know, in our religion, actually before I pray I have to put this in, what do you call it, seyara, we call it seyara.”

“We keep these beads in a bag so that they may not touch the dust of the floor,” Prabhupada said.

“Oh, I see. No, I don’t keep it on the floor, I keep it on the seyara because I pray—”

“Just to protect it, because we chant God’s name, so it is not different from God.”

“That’s right.”

“God’s name and God—the same, absolute.nama cintamanih krsnas caitanya-rasa-vigrahahpurnah suddho nitya-mukto 'bhinnatvan nama-naminoh

\[Padma Purdna, quoted as Cc Madhya 17.133\]

\[“The holy name of Krsna is transcendentally blissful. It bestows all spiritual benedictions, for it is Krsna Himself, the reservoir of all pleasure. Krsna’s name is complete, and it is the form of all transcendental mellows. It is not a material name under any condition, and it is no less powerful than Krsna Himself. Since Krsna’s name is not contaminated by the material qualities, there is no question of its being involved with maya. Krsna’s name is always liberated and spiritual; it is never conditioned by the laws of material nature. This is because the name of Krsna and Krsna Himself are identical.”\] There is no difference of quality between God and His name. When you say Allah and Allahu Akbar—as you say—there is no difference.”

“Allahu Akbar,” the man repeated.

“Yes. Allah means ‘the great,’ I think,” Prabhupada said. “‘God is great.’ So in connection with His name, whatever is there, it is great.”

“Yes.”

“I am very glad that you have come. Please try to study the philosophy.” Prabhupada told the devotees to keep the man’s information. Tamal Krishna gave him a pen and paper to write his name and address and asked if we equid visit him in Kuwait sometime.

“Oh, yes. Why not?” the man replied. And his friend also gave his address and telephone number.

“Police department,” the man explained. “Inspector.”

“Inspector of police,” Tamal Krishna said. “So we won’t have any difficulty finding you there.”

“Of course not—you just call,” the man said with a laugh.

“It’s very kind of you to give this address,” Tamal Krishna said.

“Okay, thank you. This is very good opportunity. Hare Krishna.” “Please stay for the program.”

“Yes, I will stay.”

Bhakti Charu Swami later commented, “Just by calling that man to the stage, Prabhupada did a million dollars’ worth of preaching.”

One of the most popular attractions in the pandal was the dramatic performances of the Vaikuntha Players. Lord Chaitanya Himself played in dramas, and Prabhupada had told early devotees in New York about his own experience performing in a drama of Lord Chaitanya’s pastimes:

“Perhaps theatrical performances on stage—drama—were introduced by Lord Chaitanya. But His dramatic performances were limited within the devotees. He would not allow anyone who was not a devotee to take part in the performance. So if we play—train our devotees to present some dramatic performances or movie—I think it will be very successful, because they will play from transcendental sentiment, not for trade purpose. That will come out very successful. Yes. In our childhood we had the occasion of taking part in a drama, Chaitanya lila. I took the part of Advaita, and our friends, others, somebody took the part of Chaitanya, Nityananda, and others.”

The director of the play had been Amritlal Bose, a well-known author and lecturer and one of the main theater producers in Calcutta. “We practiced for more than a year,” Prabhupada said. One of Bose’s main points of training was to get the actors to internalize the feelings of the characters, and he kept telling Prabhupada, “Feel like Advaita Acharya.”

“That drama was so successful,” Prabhupada remembered. “It was unique in Calcutta, because we were not professionals. I saw from the stage a huge gathering, and they were all crying. I was surprised—‘Why these people are crying?’ It was due to training. He had trained us in such a way that we could not understand how we were playing, but the audience, they appreciated so much.”

With Prajapati directing, the Vaikuntha Players performed the Ramayana in two parts, and a piece with dance and music called “The Song of Hanuman.” The performers would come by taxi from Juhu— an hour’s drive—in their elaborate costumes and makeup. They were quite a sight: Prajapati portraying Rama; his wife, Satarupa, Sita; Nanda Kishore, Laksmana; Lohitaksa, Hanuman; Rasajna, Surpanakha; and Lokamangala, Ravana—all riding in the cars. When they arrived the first night, Prabhupada was just leaving. But when he saw them, his face lit up and he beamed a big smile and expressed his happiness to seethem: “Ah! ‘Song of Hanuman’!” The next night, Prabhupada was still speaking when the troupe arrived. They did their street plays, Sudama gave the purports, and then Satarupa danced her Dasa Avatara, though there was a little trouble with the sound system, so the crew had to put the PA mic next to the small tape recorder’s speaker. But she danced beautifully, and the audience loved it—and her. There was also a dance version of the Bhagavad-gita that Prajapati choreographed to 108 Gita verses, which he narrated during the performance.

One morning during their run of shows, I informed the players that an important man, the pious industrialist and philanthropist K.J. Somaiya, had phoned me to say that he was coming and bringing his family for Rama lila, one of the most popular dramas. So in spite of Rasajna, one of the main players, being sick, they did it, without a rehearsal. And unlike the dances, which were performed to prerecorded music, the play required microphones, which created something of an obstacle course of tangled wires on the stage. But this performance too was a success.

Toward the end of the pandal, Prajapati—Rama—still in character, took up a collection. He hadn’t wanted to go back on stage for curtain calls, but Sudama and Achyutananda prevailed upon him to return, and after bows he announced that if there were any Rama bhaktas in the audience, they should come forward and give a donation to install the deity of Rama in Juhu. He collected many rupees, and hundreds of people touched his—Rama’s—feet. “My devotees want to build a temple for Me in Juhu,” he called out, “so please help.”

The morning after one performance, Gopal Krishna told Srila Prabhupada, “The drama was very much appreciated last night. Somaiya watched it with us, and he said he would like to arrange a big program in his house. He liked the drama very much.”

“It has become one of the main attractions,” Lokanath added. “For two nights, after the program, I inquired from the public on the microphone, ‘Did you like this drama?’ and immediately everybody raised their hands: ‘Yes!’”

“They were asking me whether they are professional men,” Prabhupada said. “‘No, no, these are all my disciples.’”

“They’re actually much better than any of the professional men,” Gopal Krishna noted.

“Oh, yes,” Prabhupada confirmed.

Later, Sri Nathaji said, “I remember how powerful the actors and actresses were in the Ramayana performance. The only thing, it surprised me to see Sita as an American lady. I didn’t mind Rama, or Ravana, being American, but I was still in the bodily concept. The important thing was that these actors and actresses were so wonderful in their acting. They really brought out the best of Ramayana, At the end, Prabhupada said that these performers were better than the book. Then he said, ‘When Lord Chaitanya Himself performed His plays five hundred years ago, Sacimata, His own mother, could not recognize Him, her own son.’ Lord Chaitanya, I believe, acted as Laksmi-devi. That’s the power of a strong actor who really puts his consciousness, heart and soul, in the role he plays, and that’s when the Lord Himself assists such an actor to exhibit all the qualities of that person. I observed that, and Prabhupada was extremely happy with these Vaikuntha Players. That was obvious at the end of the play.”

On the last scheduled evening of the pandal, the chief minister of Maharashtra, Shankarrao Bhaurao Chavan, who had helped us obtain the permissions for the temple, was scheduled to give the introductory speech. There had been political upheaval in Maharashtra, and there were daily reports that Chavan’s Congress government could be toppled at any moment. We had been hoping that he would last as the chief minister at least until he spoke at the pandal—and that he would not cancel.

In the end, Chavan was still the chief minister and kept his commitment. “Krishna consciousness is another term for God consciousness, which is the essence of every faith and is the main artery of all religions,” he told the crowd. “In that sense, Krishna consciousness belongs to the world, and the world belongs to Krishna consciousness, because no amount of mixtures of cultures can change the fundamental principles of religions, whichever they may be. The essential principles of all religions enjoin on their devout followers the glorification of God, the Supreme Lord.

“It is in this context that I pay my full quota of deserving tribute to His Divine Grace A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, the illustrious founder of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness. I feel a deep sense of spiritual joy in doing so.

“The philosophy and message of the Bhagavad-gita contain profound values for humanity as a whole. The fratricidal war between the Pandavas and Kauravas, as vividly and heart-throbbingly described in the Mahabharata, should act as a permanent restraint to the world powers who have armed themselves to the teeth with nuclear weapons and warheads which, if used, can destroy the bulk of mankind—and with them would go the civilizations of the world, born out of endless years of human thought, endeavor, action, and sacrifice.

“The true significance of the Bhagavad-gita and its imperative values was never of greater importance than today. The great and indomitable founder of your Society has already published eighty-four books in English on Krishna consciousness and Hindu philosophy and culture, which have also been translated into a great number of international languages. At the same time, the Society has, within just eleven years, established no less than one hundred Radha-Krishna temples across all six continents of the world. These are indeed great achievements.

“The fact that as many as five thousand universities, schools, and public libraries have ordered these books should ensure that Krishna consciousness will be blazoned across all parts of the globe. And the hundred temples built should in the future no doubt keep on radiating the soulful inspiration of the gospel of the Gita to the endless stream of humanity thirsting for spiritual knowledge and wisdom.

“These facts, and that a mammoth cross section of the world’s peoples, belonging to many races, creeds, and nations, are represented in the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, speak eloquently for the vitality and velocity in the better world of God consciousness that exists in the hearts of men behind the crass temptations and selfish involvements generated by impulses and compulsions of this modern materialistic world.

“In this hectic and cantankerous world of today, the first casualty has been the light of spiritual inspiration. Alas, there is darkness at noon. In the Orient and Occident, the problems of life could be lightened and even sweetened if the Krishna consciousness movement heralds the dawn of spiritual enlightenment and happiness.

“I am very glad to learn that the Sri Sri Radha-Rasabihariji temple is fast coming up in Juhu on the very spot where stones were foundindicating the existence of a temple six hundred years ago. That will be another great event in the history of the Society.

“I thank you again for letting me spend these few minutes in an atmosphere of peace and serenity in the company of those spiritually blessed.”

After the chief minister’s talk, I spoke: “We wish to thank the honorable Chief Minister S.B. Chavan for his beautiful talk and understanding of the Krishna consciousness movement. And we are very pleased to inform you that today we received a letter from Russia acknowledging receipt of six of Srila Prabhupada’s books and thanking us very much for sending them.”

After pausing for applause, I continued, “The letter further said that these books will be of great interest to scholars and persons in Russia specializing in Indian thought and culture. So, pursuant to what the honorable chief minister said, this is further proof of the validity of Krishna consciousness, that Krishna consciousness is not a sectarian religious faith. There are so many different faiths and so many fanatical people following them, but Krishna consciousness is a universal science valid in all parts of the world and, actually, all parts of the universe, all different universes, for all different races. And not only all different races, but in all species of life, even among the demigods. The Krishna consciousness movement is all-auspicious for the welfare of every living entity. Therefore we say that Srila Prabhupada is the greatest welfare worker in the whole universe—” Again the audience applauded. “He’s actually giving relief to living entities all over the world, and this relief can be given only by Krishna consciousness—not by any material adjustment. Now we shall ask Srila Prabhupada himself, the real guru of the universe, to speak before this gathering.” And yet again the audience broke into applause.

Achyutananda read a verse and purport from Srimad-Bhagavatam (5.5.3), which stated that although everyone had to earn enough to “keep the body and soul together”—“not more than that nor less than that”— people interested in Krishna consciousness were not interested in other things, or in people who were busy with mundane activities. Rather, he read from Prabhupada’s purport, “A householder should lead such a life that he gets full opportunity to hear and chant. He should worship the Deity at home, observe festivals, invite friends in, and give them prasada”

Srila Prabhupada spoke next, advising the chief minister to tolerate material upheavals and execute his duties—in Krishna consciousness. “The real problem of life,” he said, “is not to adjust things materially, change from one form of government to another form of government. These things are temporary. It will not give relief. And this fighting between one party with another amongst the politicians or the kshatriyas or the administrators, is going on perpetually. That is not a very new thing. But we should not forget our real life. For ruling over to get political predominance, there may be fighting. That is natural. It is going on. Just like the Battle of Kurukshetra—it was a fighting between two sections of the same family, who will rule. So, there was fighting, but at the same time, they did not lose Krishna culture. That is the important point. Similarly, India has got a great culture, background, Vedic culture, or Krishna culture. Vedic culture means Krishna culture, and Krishna culture means Vedic culture. Vedais ca sarvair aham eva vedyam. So to study Veda or Vedanta means to understand Krishna. That is the purpose. Vedais ca sarvair, Veda means ‘knowledge,' and anta means ‘end.' Srila Vyasadeva has given us the Vedanta philosophy. What is the purpose? That is explained in the Bhagavad-gita:

sarvasya caham hrdi-sannivisto  
mattah smrtir jnanam apohanam ca  
vedais ca sarvair aham eva vedyo  
vedanta-krd veda-vid eva caham  
\[Gita 15.15\]

So, we should take care very seriously about this culture of Bhagavad-gita. This is India’s property. This Vedic culture, instruction of Bhagavad-gita, was spoken on the land of Bharata-varsa, although it is not meant for a particular class of people or a particular country. It is meant for everyone—manusyanam sahasresu kascid yatati siddhaye— especially for the human being.

“Our request is that we may fight amongst ourselves for political predominance, but why should we forget our real culture, Vedic culture, Krishna consciousness? That is our request. All important men, leaders of the society, should take this Vedic culture, Krishna consciousness, and not only preach in their own country, but all over the world.”

Prabhupada spoke for another fifteen minutes and concluded, “We have got such vast knowledge for achieving the goal of life. This is India. Why should we neglect? Why should we become so foolish as to forget our real purpose of life and engage in a will-o’-the-wisp struggle for existence, which will never be successful? Why this misconception of life? At least there must be this institution of Krishna consciousness in India so that not only the Indians, but all outside India, they should come and learn what is Krishna consciousness.” The audience clapped in agreement.

“We are trying to develop this institution in Bombay. Bombay is the best city in India, and people are also very advanced, enlightened. So let us combine together and develop this institution for the whole human society. That is our ambition. It is not for any sect or any creed or any particular class of men. Manusyanam sahasresu. It is for the human society, and we have got this opportunity of human body. A Bengali poet sings, hari hari biphale janama gonainu. Manusya-janama paiya, radha-krsna nd bhajiya, janiya suniya visa khainu. ‘My Lord, I have wasted this valuable human form of life because I did not take to Krishna consciousness.’

“If you do not take Krishna consciousness seriously in this human form of life, then you must know that you are drinking poison knowingly. Don’t neglect it. Try to understand. It is based on science, philosophy, shastra, knowledge. It is not a blind faith. And we are prepared to answer you in any way. The method is very simple; even a child can take advantage of it. Not that we are manufacturing. It is sanctioned in the shastra. Kaier dosa-nidhe rajann asti hy eko mahan gunah. This is the statement by Sukadeva Gosvami to Maharaja Pariksit. He describes the faults of this Kali-yuga; it is just like an ocean. But there is one very great advantage, he said. What is that? Kirtanad eva krsnasya mukta-sangah param vrajet. If you chant Hare Krishna maha-mantra, then you become free from all contamination and go back to home, back to Godhead.

“Thank you very much.”

Attendance had been encouraging, so we proposed extending the pandal another week. “Many good classes of people have been coming,” Tamal Krishna told Prabhupada. “The extra cost will not be more than about a thousand rupees, since the main cost is in actually building it, so

Bhavananda Maharaja and myself felt that the devotees could continue the pandal, and you wouldn’t have to attend.”

“Very nice,” Prabhupada approved. “I want it to be possible for you. Why it should be closed? We have so much subject matter for speaking.”

Prabhupada said he would move to his now-ready quarters at Hare Krishna Land. Although he had originally planned to go to Juhu on Monday, when I informed him that the chief minister would be attending the pandal on Tuesday, Rama-navami, he had agreed to go on Wednesday instead.

“I think Surabhi will be quite relieved,” Tamal Krishna said.

Prabhupada was happy with his new quarters. “I think I haven’t got such place to live anywhere in the world,” he said, laughing.

“Especially your own building,” Gargamuni added.

“Los Angeles and New York, big, big cities they are—London, Paris. But nobody can present such a luxurious royal palace.”

Once he had settled in, he reviewed the pandal program with the devotees. “That chief minister spoke very nicely,” he said. He wanted Chavan’s speech transcribed and published in either a magazine or The Hare Krishna Monthly. “Both he and his wife appear to be devotees.”

The Times of India covered both the chief minister’s talk and Prabhupada’s response:

“CHIEF MINISTER LAUDS KRISHNA MOVEMENT

“Krishna consciousness was the essence of every faith and belonged to the world, Maharashtra Chief Minister Mr. S. B. Chavan said at the Third International Hare Krishna Festival at the Cross Maidan in Bombay on Wednesday. Mr. Chavan lauded the work done by Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Founder-Acharya of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness. He said that Swami was responsible for popularizing Krishna consciousness all over the world. Speaking after the chief minister, Swami Prabhupada emphasized the need for scientific understanding of the Bhagavad-gita to solve the problems confronting humanity. ‘When human society is without dharma,’ he said, ‘it becomes animal society.’ The festival, scheduled to end on Tuesday, has been extended another five days.”

Two days later, Prabhupada dictated a letter to the chief minister:

Dear Shri Chavan:

Kindly accept my greetings and extend the same to your good wife. I am so much obliged to you that you have lauded our activities throughout the world. This Krishna consciousness movement is based on deep science of the laws of nature. This human life is a boon to the conditioned soul to understand this science. I do not wish to take much of your valuable time, but I would be very much pleased if persons like you without any political prejudice come and take up this movement seriously and benefit the whole human society with this knowledge.

At least in India, where this knowledge was generated, there must be some institution to know it perfectly and distribute it throughout the world. That will glorify India’s prestige. To broadcast India’s glorification is the duty of every Indian without any political differences.

I wish that you may take some active part in this movement and thus magnify the prestigious position of India.

Thank you very much for coming the other day and speaking so nicely about this Krishna consciousness movement.

Your ever well-wisher,

A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami

When after a few days Prabhupada did not receive a reply, he commented that the chief minister was in a bind: he could not agree to join Prabhupada’s movement, but neither could he refuse—so he was staying silent.

Prabhupada seemed fascinated by Indira Gandhi’s sudden, dramatic downfall, and he had devotees read him headlines and excerpts from newspapers about it. Then, after some time, he commented, “What the fools and rascals are saying—that is newspaper.”

## In Juhu

When I arrived in Juhu, Tamal Krishna wanted Prabhupada to let me know what they had been thinking about Prabhupada’s stay. “Generally, visitors will not come up here, right?” he said. “Now that Giriraj is here, if you can explain to him what the policy should be . ..”

“You explain,” Prabhupada told him.

“Prabhupada said that he will go down once a week to have darshan” Tamal Krishna told me.

“No,” Prabhupada corrected. “I shall go daily in the morning. At seven. And I'll stay there half an hour or more.”

“Guru-puja.”

“Those who are visitors, they can see me there. And for lecturing, on Sunday I shall lecture. You can fix up which time. But Sunday I shall speak from Bhagavatam. This is the general program. And if something special is required, that is another thing. So, what is the use of inviting visitors here?”

“I agree with that policy,” I said.

“What do you think, Dr. Sharma?” Prabhupada asked the eminent cardiac surgeon, who was sitting with us and had been a chief guest at the pandal.

“I agree,” Dr. Sharma replied. “Some very urgent or special thing, then it can be done. Otherwise not.”

“Generally,” Prabhupada continued, “people come to visit: ‘How are you? How you are feeling?’ And it takes half an hour even. What is the use of wasting time like that—‘How are you?’ Everyone knows that I am not feeling well.”

“They can come in the morning,” Tamal Krishna said.

“Yes. If they actually want to see me, I am going there; they can see me. For half an hour, more than half an hour. And for talking ... There is no need of talking, ‘How are you? How you are feeling?’ This is not talking.”

“Instead, they can buy some of your books downstairs,” Gargamuni said.

“This is waste of time,” Prabhupada continued. “At least, I want to stop this, to answer all these things, ‘How are you?”’

“That will conserve a great deal of energy if you don’t have to meet with people,” Tamal Krishna said.

“And balance time saved, I can do work.”

“That’s good,” Tamal Krishna said. “Practically everyone has Sunday as a holiday. So if they want to hear you speak, they are all free to come Sunday.”

“Yes. This is the general program. And if there is something special, that we shall do. I am all right so long I am able to write; I do not stop writing books unless I am not all right. So, generally, arrange likethat, and specifically we shall meet once daily, half an hour to one hour. There is no difficulty. But not continually people coming. That is bad.”

“I agree with that,” I said.

“Actually, people respect that, Srila Prabhupada,” Tamal Krishna added. “It is not unusual that someone should have a program like that. People take advantage of your compassion and mercy. They used to come two or three hours every evening and sit.”

Prabhupada had previously complained to me about people coming and wasting his time, but he had said that if he stopped holding his darshan hours, people would complain, “Oh, Swamiji has become a big man now—he has no time for us.” He had said, “Maybe when I move to my new quarters ...” but clearly, here too, even without his having darshan hours, we would have to make arrangements to keep visitors away so that he could do his work and conserve his energy.

“I think I shall be able to work from today,” Prabhupada said. “Now I have got very nice place, full freedom. So there will be no difficulty.”

I suggested that he need not begin coming at seven in the morning now, that he could hold off for some days if he wanted to rest more and gain strength.

“No, I can go,” he said, “provided the lift is working,” and everyone laughed. “Otherwise, I shall be obliged. What can be done?”

Gargamuni asked Prabhupada if he would be taking his morning walk.

“Walking should be stopped at least for some time. And if I walk, I may walk on the roof.”

“The lift doesn’t go up to the roof, though,” Gargamuni said.

“We can take you by palanquin,” I suggested.

“No, one story I can go,” Prabhupada said. “Not now, but I can go. You are trying so much for my comfort. I do not know whether I shall be able to repay you. Then I shall try my best. It is not possible to repay my debt to you. You are so kind. I can simply pray to Krishna to give His blessings to you so that you may remain very steady in devotional service and preach this cult all over the world. Otherwise, I have no other means. Without your help I could not do anything. You are very much kind. Kindly continue your cooperation. Paropakara. This is the movement for paropakara.”

Prabhupada’s words melted our hearts and made us feel even more obliged to him—that we could never repay our debt.

When Prabhupada asked how the activities were progressing in various places, Dhananjaya reported that everything in Vrindavan was “improving nicely.”

“If you become nice devotee, everything will be improved,” Prabhupada said. “Bhaktya mam abhijanati yavan yas casmi tattvatah. The more you increase your devotional service, the more everything will be increased. Who expected such temple here? Hmm? Nair wanted from me fourteen lakhs. I had no fourteen hundred even. With so much difficulty we collected the money. Bali Mardan sent from New York ten lakhs. Giriraj, you were here from the very beginning? No, at that time you were in Calcutta.”

“I came after about two weeks,” I replied.

“Our Tamal Krishna Maharaja refused to take charge,” Prabhupada continued. “Madhudvisa also. I was a little hopeless. Then Brahmananda encouraged me, ‘I will do it? But then he was silent.

“Nair’s policy was ‘Where he will get this money from? He is a beggar. Fourteen lakhs? Whatever he gives—one, two lakhs—that’s all, swallowed? I told him frankly that ‘I have no so much money. Immediately I can collect four lakhs. I shall give you two lakhs against your amount, and two lakhs I shall spend for construction. Of course, within three years I shall fill up? He thought that whatever comes—two lakhs, one lakh—I would not be able ... I knew that I had no money, but I never thought, I shall not be able to do. That I was confident. So, it’s a great history. So many things happened. It is all Radha-Rasabihari’s lila.”

Prabhupada was confident because of his faith in and surrender to Lord Krishna. As he had explained in a talk in Vrindavan a year earlier, “In Bombay, now the land is worth one crore of rupees. And when I purchased this land I had maybe three or four lakhs. So it was completely speculation, but I was confident that ‘I shall be able to pay. Krishna will give me?”

He turned to Svarupa Damodara: “Now next program—yours. Make a strong party and travel extensively all over the world, amongst the scientists. And whatever amount is required, I shall spend. What do you expect monthly expenditure will be, without any difficulty, for a whole party? How many you want to travel?”

“To start with,” Svarupa Damodara said, “three of us should travel. Three scientists can travel together, and if it is necessary—”

“You are recruiting other scientists also?”

“Yes.”

“Supposing you were recruiting,” Tamal Krishna asked, “how many would you make ideally as a team?”

“About five will be ideal. A bigger group will be too expensive, and sometimes—”

“No, make five,” Prabhupada said.

“Yes, five.”

“Recruit two others and make it at least five, and travel all over the world—all institutions, all universities, all scientists. If you have got commodity, deliver. It is not a bluff, gold manufacturing. It is not that. Actual fact. That day, your presentation was very nice. Any scientist will be convinced by such presentation, learned speeches. So, now at least five men, and estimate what will be the expenditure. I shall arrange. Don’t worry. . . . For expenditure there is no worry. What will be the rough expenditure?”

“It will depend on what part of the world we are traveling,” Svarupa Damodara replied.

“You travel all over the world. Why ‘part of the world’? We are not preaching ‘part.’ Prthivite ache yata nagaradi grama we are concerned. Nothing shall be left over.”

“Tamal Krishna Maharaja can give us some hints how much it costs; he has some experience in traveling.”

“Maybe ten thousand dollars,” Tamal Krishna answered.

“Sanctioned,” Prabhupada stated. “I will give you ten thousand. Do it. . . . This is solid work. Yes. It must be done. Without any hesitation, without any impediment. That will increase the prestige of our movement.”

Although Prabhupada was satisfied with his new quarters, he still had one concern: noise related to his personal staff—he wanted silence so he could focus on his work. He told a story about a husband whose wife’s tinkling bracelets disturbed him. The man took away one bangle, but still, “Tink-tink-tink.” Then he took away another bangle, and again “Tink-tink-tink.” Another bangle, still “Tink-tink-tink.” Not until there was only one remaining bangle was there no “Tink-tink-tink.”

“So remain always one and read books,” he said. “Then there will be no noise. And as soon as you become two, ‘Tink-tink-tink.’ That I don’t want.”

“No, it won’t happen,” Tamal Krishna assured him. “If anyone comes to see me, I’ll go out of the apartment.

“Yes. You can make reception there.”

“At the elevator shaft.”

“Yes. In this way arrange. It should remain always quiet and serene.” “These are your quarters. No one else should come.”

“And we shall arrange for seeing our own men, at a time. That we shall see. But the principle should be silence. Then it will be all right. I will be free to work.”

“Very good. We’ll see to that, Srila Prabhupada.”

The next morning, without notice, Prabhupada came down to the temple room. A few devotees and I hurried to remove his picture from the vyasasana so he could sit, and though many of the devotees were absent, when news spread that Prabhupada was there, they ran to join him.

After the guru-puja, Prabhupada spoke to console the devotees. He said that he was sorry he couldn’t come down more often and that he wanted to cook for them and serve them. On Sunday he would cook a feast and invite them up to his quarters. “I shall come daily to the temple,” he said, “and I shall remain up to eight for our darshan and talks, if there are any. Generally every day it will be done. And on Sunday you can fix up some time. I will speak in the evening. And then Krishna’s desire, as He likes. But for the time being, this arrangement.”

Then Prabhupada spoke about the significance of guru-puja. “What is that verse? Divya-jnana hrde prakasito. Just recite the one before that.”

“Prema-bhakti yaha hoite, avidya vinasa yate," someone said.

“The necessity is prema-bhakti. Prema-bhakti yaha hoite, avidya vinasa yate, divya-jnana. What is that divya-jnana? Divya means transcendental, not material. Tapo divyam. We are combination of matter and spirit. That spirit is divya, transcendental. Apareyam itas tu viddhi me prakrtim para. That is para prakrti, superior. And for understanding that superior identity we require superior knowledge, not ordinary knowledge. Divya-jnana hrde prakasito. This is the duty of the guru, to awaken that divya-jnana. And because the guru enlightens with divya-jnana, he is worshipped. That is required. To those who are inmaya, that divya-jnana is never manifested. They are kept in the darkness of adivya-jnana: ‘I am this body.’ ‘I am Indian,’ ‘I am American,’ ‘I am Hindu,’ ‘I am Muslim’ —this is adivya-jnana. Dehatma-buddhih. Yasyatma-buddhih kunape tri-dhatuke."

He was referring to ^rimad-Bhagavatam 10.84.13:

yasyatma-buddhih kunape tri-dhatuke  
sva-dhih kalatradisu bhauma ijya-dhih  
yat-tirtha-buddhih salile na karhicij  
janesv abhijnesu sa eva go-kharah

“One who identifies this body made of three elements with his self, who considers the by-products of the body to be his kinsmen, who considers his land of birth worshipable, and who goes to a place of pilgrimage simply to take a bath rather than meet men of transcendental knowledge there, is to be considered no better than a cow or an ass.”

“I am not this body,” Prabhupada continued, “so the beginning of divya-jnana is there when we try to understand that ‘I am not this body—I am superior element; I am spirit soul. This body is inferior. So, why should I remain in this inferior knowledge?’ We should not remain in the inferior... Inferior knowledge means darkness. Tamasi ma. The Vedic injunction is, ‘Don’t remain in the inferior knowledge.’ Jyotir gamah: ‘Come to the superior knowledge.’ So we worship the guru because he gives us superior knowledge—not how to eat, how to sleep, how to have sex life and defend. Generally, the political leaders, social leaders, they give this knowledge: how to eat, how to sleep, how to have sex, how to defend. A guru has no business with these things. He gives divya-jnana, superior knowledge. That is required. This human form of life is an opportunity to awaken that: divya-jnana hrde prakasito. And if a person is kept in darkness about that divya-jnana^ if he is simply trained up how to eat, how to sleep, how to have sex, and how to defend, then life will be lost. That is a great loss. Mrtyu-samsara-vartmani. Aprapya mam nivartante mrtyu-samsara-vart-mani \[Gita 9.3\]. It is a very risky life if we do not awaken our divya-jnana. We should always remember this. Very risky life—once again thrown into the waves of birth and death, we do not know where we are going. Very serious. This Krishna consciousness is divya-jnana. It is not ordinary knowledge. Everyone should try to understand this divya-jnana. Daivimprakrtim asritam. Therefore one who is interested in this divya-jnana, he is called daivim prakrtim asritam. From daivi, divya comes, the Sanskrit word—from daivi, divya, adjective.

“So, mahatmanas tu mam partha daivim prakrtim asritah \[Gita 9.13\]. One who has taken to this divya-jnana process, he is mahatma. Mahatma is not made by stamping, for receiving knowledge how to eat, how to sleep, how to have sex. That is not the definition in the shastra. Sa mahatma su-durlabhah.

bahunam janmanam ante  
jnanavan mam prapadyante  
vasudevah sarvam iti  
sa mahatma su-durlabhah

\[“After many births and deaths, he who is actually in knowledge surrenders unto Me, knowing Me to be the cause of all causes and all that is. Such a great soul is very rare.” (Gita 7.19)\] One who has got this divya-jnana—vasudevah sarvam iti—he is mahatma. But that is very, very rare. Otherwise, mahatmas like me, they are loitering in the street. That is their business. So, you should always remember these words, divya-jnana hrde prakasito. And because the spiritual master enlightens with divya-jnana, one feels obliged to him. Yasya prasadad bhaga-vat-prasado yasya prasadan na gatih kuto 'pi. This guru-puja is essential, just as Deity worship is essential—it is not cheap adoration. It is the process of enlightenment, of divya-jnana. Thank you very much.”

Not only did Srila Prabhupada give us his personal association and reassure us of his care; he also taught us how to love and serve him, even in his physical absence.

In his delicate condition, Srila Prabhupada spent most of his time upstairs in his quarters. Most days, he honored his lunch prasada at 1:00, and, for his health, he wanted it exactly on time, and hot. One afternoon Nava Yogendra Swami, who served Prabhupada his prasada and sometimes cooked for him, brought the prasada a few seconds before 1:00, and Prabhupada’s hand was on the bell, poised to ring. Prabhupada smiled and said, “You came on time. How are you?”

When something in the service once went wrong and Prabhupada became angry, Nava Yogendra wasn’t sure how to respond. “Srila

Prabhupada,” he asked, “when you get angry with us, what should we do, how should we feel, what should we think?”

“If the spiritual master is angry with you, you should be pleased,” Prabhupada replied. “It means that he’s attending to you. You should feel happy. You should understand that your spiritual master cares for you. His getting angry with you means he is looking after you. He is concerned about your spiritual progress.”

“When my guru maharaja became angry with me,” he added, “we were pleased. . . . There are so many hundreds and thousands of people in the streets, but no one is looking after them. But if the spiritual master becomes angry with a disciple, that is his mercy on that person. If someone is walking down the street and doing nonsense, no one will check him. So many people are doing so much nonsense, but no one is checking them. But if someone is checked—if a disciple is checked by his spiritual master, this is to his eternal benefit. So many people in the material world are doing all kinds of nonsense. Is there anybody checking them, correcting them? No. They will all go to hell. When the spiritual master gets angry at the disciple, it is the mercy of Krishna on that soul.”

Nava Yogendra reflected on what Prabhupada had told him. “His anger was only for our rectification,” he saw. “In the material world people get angry, but Prabhupada’s anger was not like theirs. He was a pure devotee, and he knew the value of this human life, that this human form is meant for self-realization and we should not waste even a second. We should cultivate Krishna consciousness all the time. If he saw that his disciples were not acting properly, he would get angry for their rectification.”

One of our best friends in Bombay politics was Ratansingh Rajda, who had been a municipal councilor when the standing committee of the municipal corporation had condemned Mhatre’s engineering of the illegal demolition of our temple. Rajda belonged to the same political party as our friend and supporter Sri R. K. Ganatra, the mayor of Bombay, so they were also close. In the recent elections, Mr. Rajda had been elected to parliament from the prestigious Bombay South area, and when I told him that Prabhupada was in Bombay, he was eager to meet him.

A meeting was arranged for the eve of Mr. Rajda’s departure for Delhi, on March 27, at Kartikeya Mahadevia’s flat. Like many other

Indians, Mr. Rajda was hopeful that with Morarji Desai as prime minister, the newly elected government would effect positive change.

On the afternoon of the 27th, I told Prabhupada that when I had informed Mr. Rajda that Prabhupada had agreed to wait to meet him, Mr. Rajda had said, “This is wonderful. I have been pining for his darshan. Now we must have rama-rajya \[a government like Lord Rama’s\]. That is why I must meet your guru maharaja before I go back to Delhi tomorrow.” Mr. Rajda was participating in a big political rally at Shivaji Park, I told Prabhupada, and he had invited me to sit on the dais with him. “But I don’t know if this is a good idea for us,” I said, thinking about the possible ramifications if we were seen as aligned with a particular political party.

“Why not? He is honoring you,” Prabhupada replied.

“Mr. Rajda said that he would ask the organizer that he should speak early in the program so he can be free and come here as early as possible,” I explained. “So he is very serious. I don’t think there will be any delay.”

“He formerly helped us?” asked Tamal Krishna.

“Yes. When Mhatre did that demolition attempt, he was one of the leaders in the corporation, and he fought for us. In fact, today also he asked if there was any trouble, because he is still maintaining his position in the municipal corporation. So I think when he gets back from Delhi in a week, I might bring up some of our little problems.”

I had to leave, but I told Prabhupada that I would return with Mr. Rajda as soon as possible, and when I did, Mr. Rajda told Prabhupada, “I came for your darshan when you were at Walkeshwar last time.”

“At Bhogilal Patel’s,” I added.

“Since then, much water has flowed in the Arabian Sea and the Ganges. For nineteen months I was in jails.”

“Jail?” Prabhupada asked.

“Yes,” he said, and he explained that during Indira Gandhi’s political emergency he and 150,000 others had been imprisoned, including Jayaprakash Narayan and Morarji Desai—“all big leaders and all other workers.” When he was released, he explained, he had run for election in Bombay South and won by “a very comfortable margin.”

“Just now we were at a huge rally at Shivaji Park,” he said, “and when Girirajji told me that you were here, I told him definitely I would like to rush for darshan.”

“This material adjustment,” Prabhupada began. “Just like we felt a little danger under the regime of Indira Gandhi. Now we have another feeling. This is material adjustment. Material adjustment may be temporarily beneficial, but it is not permanently beneficial.”

“Unless there is adhyatmika \[spiritual\] adjustment, there cannot be lasting benefit,” Mr. Rajda accepted.

“The difficulty is that we do not know,” Prabhupada continued. “Just like you take a fish from the water and put it on the land—it will never be happy. Again you throw him in the water, he will feel happy. So, the living entity is different from prakriti \[material nature\]. In Bhagavad-gita it is clearly stated, apareyam itas tu viddhi me prakrtim. These material elements—earth, water, air, fire, ether, mind, intelligence, ego—these are gross and subtle material elements. And the living being, jiva-bhuta, is superior to the inferior material elements. Apareyam itas tu viddhi me prakrtim param. Para prakrti—it is part and parcel of God. Unless we understand this fact, which is very nicely explained in the Bhagavadgita, this material adjustment will never make us happy.”

Although Mr. Rajda followed Prabhupada’s point, he still believed that a significant change would take place as a result of the elections. “As far as this change is concerned,” he stated, “the basic difference is that formerly there was no moral code observed by the rulers.”

But Prabhupada was not satisfied. “It can deteriorate at any moment.”

“That is there,” Mr. Rajda conceded. “But if the rulers have got faith in dharma ...”

“They have no faith. That is the difficulty. They talk of God, talk of religion, but they do not know what is God, what is religion. That is the problem. If we do not know what is the identity of the living entity, then where is the question of religion?”

“No,” Mr. Rajda replied. “The last rulers, most of them were communists; they said that religion is opium. They didn’t believe in religion at all.”

“Therefore they say something, we say something, he says something, you manufacture something. But nobody knows what is reality. That is the difficulty. Unless you know the reality, to suggest something, ‘I suggest it,’ does not mean that it is a solution. This is going on all over the world. Na te viduh svartha-gatim hi visnum durasaya ye bahir-artha-maninah. Bahir-artha. The external, material features—theyare concerned with that. Earth, water, fire, air, mind, intelligence. But they do not know that beyond this, there is another element. Unless you come to that knowledge, there is no question of welfare activities. That knowledge is available in India. India should understand. This is Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s mission. Bharata-bhumite haila manusya-janma yara. Not only Indian, but he must be a human being. Not only human being, but also systematic human society. Of course, we are trying to give this knowledge. These Americans and Europeans, they are taking it. It should be done very systematically, not alone.”

“No, but in spite of that, your efforts have even had effect on the Western world also.”

“Western world knows it is genuine.”

“Genuine, correct.”

“Therefore even a little effort is giving great benefit. But we must know what that effort should be. Everything is there. We must take advantage of it. But we are not taking advantage. We have got good government—very nice. Now you should take advantage of the privileges which are there in India. The Bhagavad-gita is there. If you take direction from the Bhagavad-gita, the whole human society will be benefited. But that you do not do. That is the defect. Even big, big leaders, they profess to be students of Bhagavad-gita, but they do not know what is Bhagavad-gita, although it is clearly stated. Who is the leader in India who does not know Bhagavad-gita? Everyone knows. Even Morarji Desai, when he was to be arrested by Indira’s government, he said ‘Wait. Let me finish my reading of Bhagavad-gita,' is it not?”

“Yes, yes,” Mr. Rajda agreed.

“‘Then you can arrest me.’”

“And in jail also he was studying very minutely.”

“But now,” Prabhupada stated, “he says that ‘\[the political party\] Janata is my God.’ Did he not, recently?”

Mr. Rajda conceded that Morarji had said that, but added that later he had clarified it.

“He’ll swear he is for God: Krishna. He is very clear in his mind.”

“Then why not preach Krishna, God? Why not give the people .. . Why not the government make people God conscious? It is a very simple thing. God personally is explaining how to become God conscious: Man-mana bhava mad-bhakto mad-yaji mam namaskuru. Four things.

Even a child can do it, so why not leaders? Then their example should be followed.

yad yad acarati sresthas  
tat tad evetaro janah  
sa yat pramanam kurute  
Iokas tad anuvartate  
\[Gita 3.21\]

\[“Whatever action a great man performs, common men follow. And whatever standards he sets by exemplary acts, all the world pursues.”\]

“Why not take to this, God consciousness? Do it seriously. Then everything will be all right. They are defying the existence of God and reading Bhagavad-gita, This is the position.... We have got everything in India, and to become God conscious, to establish the Lord’s kingdom, is not at all difficult. But we manufacture our own ideas. We want rama-rajya, but without Rama. Then how rama-rajya will be there? So, those who are leaders of the society, if they take seriously, India can be an ideal state. And you can set an example for the whole world. The whole world will be happy. But we must be very serious about it. That is our Krishna consciousness movement.

“We are trying, but we have no support from the government, from the leaders. We are alone. Now, after twelve years, they have recognized in the United States and London, Germany. Otherwise, twelve years before, I was loitering in the streets of New York. Who was caring for me? Now these boys have joined; they are doing something, they are fighting.”

“Yes,” Mr. Rajda agreed. “They are doing wonderful work.”

“It is the duty of the Indians,” Prabhupada said. “But instead of Indians, I have to collect these young men from foreign countries.”

“We were just talking about it on the way. In India we must take it up.”

“Let there be one institution for training Indian youth for this Krishna consciousness movement.”

“That could be done.”

“You do it, and it will be a wonderful thing. . .. Cooperate with us. It is scientific. Last night our Dr. Svarupa Damodara presented it very scientifically. We can challenge any scientist, any philosopher. If you become serious, if you cooperate with us, this institution can set a great example, not only in India, but to the whole world. You are so kind, youhave come to see me. You have got desire. So let us take it seriously.”

“Yes, sir—correct,” Mr. Rajda agreed.

“It is serious, but nobody has taken it seriously. The Bhagavad-gita is a popular book. Everyone takes the Bhagavad-gita and says, ‘I am a student of Bhagavad-gita' It is a very simple thing, and if the leaders of society set the example, others will follow.”

“Correct,” Mr. Rajda confirmed. “That’s correct. Serious effort should be made. Only lip service will not help. I fully agree, and we shall definitely apply our mind to that. I came into contact with this movement when the small Juhu temple was demolished; at that time Giriraj and some friends came to me for cooperation.”

“You have given a great service,” Prabhupada told him. “Now it is not only not demolished—it is standing there.”

“It is standing,” Mr. Rajda said, “and very nice temple.”

“So, let us take advantage of it and make a perfect institution so that people may utilize.”

Mr. Rajda asked Prabhupada how long he would be in Bombay, and, when Prabhupada said for at least a month, offered that when he returned from Delhi, he would come again and arrange a meeting for Prabhupada with Prime Minister Desai. “That meeting could be arranged any time,” he said. “Whenever it is convenient to you.”

“My life is dedicated for this purpose,” Prabhupada said. “It is convenient for me at any time. Otherwise, I am not keeping good health at the moment. Still, I have come. I am just trying, even up to the last moment of my life, if I can deliver some good to the people—that is my determination.”

Mr. Rajda reaffirmed that he could arrange the meeting with Prime Minister Desai any time and would be in communication with us by telephone.

“So, there is some Krishna’s purpose that you were elected,” Prabhupada concluded.

“It is through His blessings,” Mr. Rajda said.

“Take advantage of His blessings,” Prabhupada told him. “Do some service.”

Six days later, I informed Prabhupada that I had just talked on the phone with Mr. Rajda. “He has already spoken to the prime minister about your meeting,” I told him, “and the prime minister gladly accepted. He is going to arrange for the prime minister to meet you here in Bombay, at Juhu.”

When he heard that Mr. Rajda was coming from Delhi the next morning and departing in the evening, Prabhupada asked me to invite him and his associates for prasada and to meet him.

“He’s coming because he is a leader in the municipal corporation,” I explained, “and tomorrow they are electing the new mayor. I was thinking that we could invite him to stop here on his way to the airport in the evening. Otherwise, he is coming back on the 8th to spend about a week here. But he is very enthusiastic.”

“Very good,” Prabhupada responded. “He is a good boy.”

“He said, ‘I am all out for this movement. I am all out for Swami Prabhupada.’”

“Send him the remark from the chief minister,” Prabhupada said, referring to the Times of India article “Chief Minister Lauds Krishna Movement.” “He’ll so much appreciate. Everyone is appreciating this movement. Gradually, they will appreciate.”

I told Prabhupada that I was thinking of going to Delhi for a few days so Mr. Rajda could introduce me to the pious members of parliament and we could organize a whole group to visit our Krishna-Balaram temple in Vrindavan.

“Do the needful,” Prabhupada said. “Go. At least in India there must be this spiritual institution. The whole world may take advantage. What is this cats’-and-dogs’-race civilization? Is that civilization? Here is civilization—Bhagavad-gita. Basic principles of civilization. India should maintain this. There are so many big universities. A student may or may not go, but the university must be maintained. Because there is no student, therefore university closed—no. This Krishna consciousness institution must be maintained for the benefit of the whole world. Mrtyu-samsara-vartmani. They do not know how nature’s law is working.”

I was struck by how convinced Prabhupada was about the necessity of Krishna consciousness and how he was always preaching, even to us.

Soon thereafter, while Prabhupada was speaking with Tamal Krishna and me, the recording of Yamuna singing “Govinda” began playing—the devotees were greeting the Deities in Their new dress for the day. “Such a nice thing,” Prabhupada said. “Alone in this world I am struggling, and the so-called intelligent persons, they will not come. They have business. Why? If it is actually beneficial to the human society, why I should try alone? I will go on trying as long as I live. There will be no checking. But what kind of intelligent persons there are?. . . We shall go on playing govindam adi-purusam tam aham bhajami. People may hear or not. We don’t mind.”

On April 13 I went up to Prabhupada’s quarters to see Tamal Krishna. We were always mindful not to disturb Prabhupada, so we met in the furthest outside room, where Tamal Krishna had his desk, and spoke in whispers—with two sets of closed doors between us and him. Tamal greeted me with a warm embrace and then asked me to go to the bank to make a deposit.

I hesitated. I am the temple president, I thought. I have so much important work to do that nobody else can do. Why me? Why do I have to go to the bank? Anyone can go to the bank and make a deposit. So I told Tamal, “There are so many devotees who can make a bank deposit, but there are many things that only I can do, so better I do those things and let someone else make the deposit.” Perhaps on some deeper level, based on envy and false ego, I may have been considering, “Who are you to tell me to go to the bank?” We were discussing it all in hushed tones, so as not to disturb Prabhupada.

Suddenly Prabhupada’s bell rang, and Tamal Krishna and I raced around the outside hallway to his room. Especially then, it was a rare treat to be summoned into Prabhupada’s presence.

“Now you have to do so many things,” Prabhupada said to me straight away, chuckling. “Again, another burden. You have to do all these things. So, how is your preaching?” I wasn’t sure exactly what he meant, but he knew that I sometimes felt burdened by management and preferred to preach.

I gave him a report about our recent preaching successes, and he spoke about the mood of a Vaishnava and the mission of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. “If one does not present Bhagavad-gita as it is, then whereis its authority?” he asked. And then, apparently to illustrate his point, he said, “If I say, ‘Giriraj, you go there, to the bank,’ and ‘No, no, I cannot do this; I can do only this,’ then where is my authority?” Then he laughed. “Just see.”

I didn’t think Prabhupada could possibly have heard my exchange with Tamal Krishna; we had been separated by a room and two closed doors. Krishna, I thought, must have inspired him from within. And further, he had pointed out a defect in my mentality, that I was seeing Tamal Krishna independent of him, thinking he was just my godbrother, and that I should have seen him as Prabhupada’s representative, that it was Prabhupada’s order coming to me through him.

I thought of Prabhupada’s opening words: “Now you have to do so many things. Again, another burden. You have to do all these things.” He had spoken with emphasis: “You have to do all these things.” And I understood that if I saw the service as coming from Prabhupada, I wouldn’t feel it a burden.

Two days later, Mr. Rajda came to visit with his wife, daughter, nephew, and two associates. After the customary greetings, Prabhupada showed them some of his most recent publications. “The get-up is wonderfully attractive,” said Mr. Rajda, “and the contents are, no doubt, divine.”

“Srimad-bhagavatam amalam puranam” Prabhupada quoted. “This is the regrettable fact, that we have got in India the real knowledge, and we have locked up that knowledge.”

“We have locked up,” Mr. Rajda agreed. “That is the greatest crime we have committed.”

“Jnana-khala. Sarasvati jnana-khale yatha sati. There is a verse in Srimad-Bhagavatam. Jnana-khale. If you have got some knowledge, you should distribute it. That will glorify you, not that ‘I have got some knowledge; I’ll keep it secret.’ India has got such exalted vast knowledge of spiritual life, and that is locked up. We are imitating the Western dog-dancing. This I wanted to bring to your notice. This will not do any good. Some arrangement should be made that this exalted knowledge of India must be distributed. That I have begun with my humble . . . But I have no cooperation of the authorities. That is most regrettable. Now there is change of government. And Morarji is a very religious person. So why not attempt? At leastkeep an ideal institution. Just like for technical knowledge—if there is a good medical college in any part of the world, people go there without any consideration of nationality or anything. Similarly let there be an ideal institution in India so that the whole world will come and learn. ... “This is Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s mission.
