He declares, bharata-bhumite haila manusya janma yara: ‘Anyone who has taken birth as human being in India (bharata-bhumi)... first of all make your life perfect’—you have got the opportunity, Vedic culture—‘and then distribute the knowledge all over the world for doing good to the whole human society.’ That will glorify the prestige of India. “If you object, ‘India is secular,’ Bhagavad-gita is for every man. There is no question of Hindu, Muslim, Christian, or this or that. No. Krishna says,

dehino 'smin yatha dehe  
kaumaram yauvanam jara  
tatha dehantara-praptir  
dhiras tatra na muhyati

\[“As the embodied soul continuously passes, in this body, from boyhood to youth to old age, the soul similarly passes into another body at death.” (Gita 2.13)\] A child is growing to become a boy; a boy is growing to become a young man; a young man is growing to become an old man. So, what is the question of secular? Everyone grows. Does it mean, when it is spoken in the Bhagavad-gita, it is only meant for the Hindus?”

“It is universal,” Mr. Rajda agreed.

“It is universal—science. It is science. So why this science is kept locked up and distorted by the leaders? If you understand one line of Bhagavad-gita, your life becomes successful.”

Then they came to points of practical cooperation, how Mr. Rajda and the government could help. “You are young man,” Prabhupada said. “You can think it over.”

“With your blessing, I can be sure to be able to do something.”

But Prabhupada also wanted Mr. Rajda to actually go deep in Krishna consciousness. “We have got, at least in Bombay, the most important place in India, this institution. So, come here. Try to understand the philosophy. There is no difficulty.” The way Prabhupada spokecould have been taken that he was speaking in general, not to Mr. Rajda in particular—but he was also addressing Mr. Rajda personally.

Prabhupada asked for prasada to be served to his guests and showed Mr. Rajda a BTG. “Universal,” he said. “We have got recent pictures from our different temples. Just see how they are worshipping. This is in foreign countries. They have got their own religion. Why they should worship Krishna?”

“What is the circulation?” Prabhupada asked Tamal Krishna.

“One million copies per month,” Tamal Krishna replied. “That’s in English only. Then it also is published in Spanish, Portuguese, German, French, Dutch, Japanese, Chinese, Hindi, Bengali, Gujarati, Telugu. Recently we came out with a Hungarian publication.”

“They are following,” Prabhupada said. “I want to make it more speedy, but I have no help. Now, for the time being, these boys are helping me, and the government is driving them away: ‘Get out! Get out!’ Can you not help me in this?... No Indians are coming. I am bringing men and money from there, and government is driving them: ‘Get out!’ This is my position. And if one boy goes back and again comes—ten thousand rupees. In this way I am losing five to six lakhs of rupees per year—for nothing. This is the cooperation of the government.”

“But why is the government driving them out?” Mr. Rajda asked.

“This, your so-called visa.”

“They won’t give us the proper visas so we can stay,” Tamal Krishna clarified.

“Just like I have got in America permanent residence. So, why not give them permanent residence?”

“Correct. But this problem could be settled very easily,” Mr. Rajda said.

“Kindly do that.... That will be a great help immediately.”

“That I’ll do immediately. That’s why I was just inquiring what concrete thing you would like me to do.”

“Immediately kindly help me, that give at least one hundred men permanent residential permission. They are not politicians. They are not interested. They are devotees. Then I can manage these big, big establishments like Bombay, Vrindavan.”

Mr. Rajda asked for a list of Prabhupada’s men who needed visas. “I will arrange immediately,” he promised. Tamal Krishna said he would compile a list. “We’ll do this immediately, and if necessary, I will evenfight with the government. They have got to do it. Only thing is if you can give me some note, what are the hurdles.”

“Bring some paper,” Prabhupada instructed. “Write it. Immediately begin to do this. They are coming from very rich, respectable families. They have not come here to earn money or exploit India. They have no such business. I can guarantee that they will bring money from America and live here—not touch a single paisa of India. Now, suppose there are one hundred Americans, and if I am bringing ten lakhs of rupees per month, then what is the per capita?

“Ten thousand,” I said.

“Kindly help me,” Prabhupada appealed.

“We will think ourselves duty bound,” Mr. Rajda replied. “I feel intensely about it. There is no question about it.”

“And I guarantee that if they take any part in politics, you can drive them away immediately. They have no ... They have given everything. They are not thinking that they are Americans. Sarvopadhi-vinirmuktam tat-paratvena nirmalam. This is the process of bhakti. Sarvopadhi-vinirmuktam. Upadhi \[designation\]. This is upadhi. I am a living being, but I have got some designation, ‘I am Hindu,’ ‘I am Muslim.’ These are designations. Then MP. This is a designation. You are not MP. You are living being, part and parcel of God.”

“Correct.”

“And this designation can be removed at any moment. Indira Gandhi, no more prime minister.”

“Gone in a wink.

“Designation finished. So sarvopadhi-vinirmuktam, when one becomes free from all designation, tat-paratvena nirmalam, simply by Krishna consciousness he becomes purified. Hrsikena hrsikesa-sevanam bhakti. Then bhakti begins.”

Although Prabhupada was taking help from Mr. Rajda as an MP, he wanted him to know that he was not the temporary designation “MP”; he was Krishna’s eternal servant.

brahma-bhutah prasannatma  
na socati na kanksati  
samah sarvesu bhutesu  
mad-bhaktim labhate param

\[“One who is thus transcendentally situated at once realizes the Supreme Brahman and becomes fully joyful. He never laments or desires to have anything. He is equally disposed toward every living entity. In that state he attains pure devotional service unto Me.” (Gita 18.54)\] This is the preliminary condition. As soon as they have become devotees, they have no more designation. This conception is not there: ‘I am American,' ‘I am Indian,' ‘I am Hindu,' 'I am Muslim’—no.”

Tamal Krishna typed out the note and read it aloud: “To Ratan Singh Rajda, Member of Parliament, Bombay. Dear Sri Rajda, We thank you very much for visiting us at Hare Krishna Land and for sympathetically hearing our divine master Srila Prabhupada. His Divine Grace mentioned several difficulties which are impeding his great work, and you have been kind enough to promise to remove these obstacles. (1) Our men are regularly being asked to leave India. How can we manage such important projects when our men are forced to leave? Every year we have to send so many men away from India, and then again we have to bring them back. For every man who comes and goes like this, we have to spend Rs. 10,000, and in this way we are wasting not less than rupees five to six lakhs each year. Our men should be given permanent residence in India. The United States Government granted Srila Prabhupada a permanent residency visa so that he could fulfill his mission in the USA. Similarly, Srila Prabhupada’s foreign disciples should be given permanent residency in India. Srila Prabhupada requires at least one hundred men to remain in India, and he is prepared to bring rupees ten lakhs, foreign exchange, per month just to maintain them. They will not have to seek employment, they are not interested in politics, and they will not touch one paisa locally for their maintenance. Rather, they will bring money. Therefore we request that the government of India should grant permission for at least one hundred of our men. (2) Locally we are being troubled by the municipal corporation. The local councilor is trying to take over ten feet...”

“I am meeting the commissioner on Tuesday,” Mr. Rajda said.

Prabhupada repeated his appeal to Mr. Rajda—and all others—to participate personally in our activities. “I want that at least on the weekend respectable gentlemen come here, live here, try to understand thephilosophy, and if possible render some service,” he said. “That’s all. We have got now nice building. Every room is air-conditioned—not”—he laughed—“that you have to go to the jungle!”

“No, it’s a nice atmosphere,” Mr. Rajda said.

“For us, we can live underneath a tree. But if I would have lived underneath a tree, you would not have come.” Everyone laughed at both the humor and truth of his comment. “Therefore this building is required. So, give them, one each, this magazine, latest edition.”

Mr. Rajda thanked Prabhupada, and Prabhupada thanked him for coming. And Mr. Rajda promised to return.

After his guests had left, Prabhupada said, “So, this opportunity is there, and the leaders are not giving people this opportunity. This is the greatest harmful civilization. They are keeping them in ignorance. Anyway, if people agree to take our guidance, we can change the face of the world. That is a fact. The whole world will be peaceful.”

Conversing with Tamal Krishna the day after meeting Mr. Rajda, Prabhupada said, “I have gone through various stages of life, so I have got full experience of this material world. I don’t want it. That determination is there. Society, family, love, friendship—this nonsense, everything—out! I have tasted. I am no more interested. That is niskin-cana. Finished.”

“Distaste for all worldly things,” Tamal Krishna said.

“That I am realizing, that Krishna pushed, dragged me through all circumstances, that ‘These are useless.’ Niskincanasya bhagavad-bhajanonmukha. That is required. Just like Jagai-Madhai were made to promise, ‘No more.’ ‘Yes, sir, no more.’ ‘Then I accept you. That’s all right.’ And they kept their promise. They became faithful.”

“Actually,” Tamal Krishna said, “you also demand of us that promise: ‘Now whatever you have done, never mind, but no more. Follow these four principles.’ That means if devotees don’t follow, they will not make advancement.”

“They are breaking their promise. Before accepting them, I make them promise, and they promise it. If they break, what can I do? This should be the principle: ‘No more.’ Then he becomes fit. Ara vakya na.”

“Therefore, accepting initiation is a serious matter.”

“Initiation means to seriously take up the ...”

“Vow.”

“And if you make it a fun business, then I become implicated, and you become implicated."

“In what way does the spiritual master become?”

“He accepts the sinful reactions?’

“He does that?”

“It is not an easy job to become a spiritual master. Yes. Then when he is overloaded, he suffers.”

“Krishna transfers the sinful reactions of the disciple unto the spiritual master?”

“Yes. That is the principle. This is aham tvam sarva-papebhyo moksayisyami. ‘You have to take all the sinful reactions? This is the principle. Krishna is God; He can nullify everything. But I am not God. When it is overloaded, I have to suffer. This is the principle, like the Christian idea, that Christ takes.”

“The trouble with the Christians is that they never relieved Christ. They went on sinning. That’s not love.”

“Yes. The principle is that the spiritual master takes all the resultant sinful action, but the disciple also says to himself, ‘Now, stop it. Otherwise, my spiritual master ...’ That is gentleman—not ‘Go on taking our sinful reaction; we will go on with our own business?”

“That’s not loving at all. That is taking advantage.”

“That is cheating. And he is not liberated, because he continues cheating.”

“Frankly, we see some defect is there in Christianity. It’s probably not there on the part of Jesus. He could have given them a way to purify themselves, but they—”

“One chance, that ‘You have accepted me; I take your all sinful reactions? But these rascals continue.”

“His point was that ‘Now you must continue to follow my instructions?”

“Yes. Otherwise, why Ten Commandments? And these rascals took it that ‘I shall not follow any of \[them\]; you take our sinful reaction. It is very good religion?”

“Therefore they say no one is more merciful than Jesus. We are doing anything, but he still forgives us.”

“This is going on. Therefore, according to history, he retired. After the resurrection, he went to Kashmir. ‘It is hopeless.’”

“He didn’t die on the cross.”

“It was not possible to kill him. Such a great personality, representative of God, he was not killed. That is not possible. He made a show that ‘I am killed.’ That is the resurrection. And when you finished your business, then he ...”

“They say that when he got down they rubbed his body with oils.”

“He was a great yogi.”

Tamal Krishna cited one book that stated that Jesus had learned yoga in India.

“We admit,” Prabhupada said. “Guru Maharaja said Jesus was saktyavesa-avatara, empowered incarnation. Therefore, whenever there was question of Jesus, I never disrespected him, never criticized him, because I knew that he is a powerful representative of God. We took it from Guru Maharaja. He said that Christ is saktyavesa-avatara, like Buddha. How can he be otherwise? He sacrificed everything for God. He cannot be an ordinary man.... I have got full respect for Christ and his real disciples. Why not? He said, ‘Thou shalt not kill,’ and they are interpreting killing. This is going on. And they are Christian. Just see how much cheating. It is clearly written, ‘Thou shalt not kill.’ Their only business is killing, and still they are Christian. How much cheating it is. Whatever little success is in our movement, the cause is that I have not tried to cheat. What I heard from Guru Maharaja and scripture, I took honestly. There was no cheating.”

“You pointed that out yesterday when you talked with Mr. Rajda, that it’s an open secret. You are not introducing anything new. You are simply giving the instructions of Bhagavad-gita, and you are not introducing anything on top of those instructions. No interpretation. As it is. That’s the whole problem: These politicians are all reading Bhagavad-gita, but none of them as it is.”

“Therefore I said, ‘Who understands the meaning of one line?”’

“They really think that Morarji is a big religious man. They are very happy to think that their prime minister now is very, very religious.”

“I said that my disciples rise at 3:30 and worship till 9:30. Rajda said that Morarji rises at 3:30 and three hours for ... So I immediately said, ‘They are doing twenty-four hours.’”

“Yes, we don’t engage in politics for the other nineteen hours. Of course, I never would have said anything, but the fact is that this is not the business of one who is eighty-four years old, to be the prime minister. It would be better if he were to take up preaching Bhagavad-gita—you gave that advice to Gandhi—he could do more good then.”

“They take advantage of Bhagavad-gita and do their business.”

One perennial social and political issue that would engage Mr. Rajda and the other members of parliament was the position of the harijans, the untouchables. The anniversary of the death of Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, who had championed the cause of the untouchable castes, fell soon after the elections, and Ksiracora Gopinatha told Prabhupada about a recent article entitled “One Hundred Million Harijans Pick a New Messiah,” featuring a photo of Dr. Ambedkar. Prabhupada asked him to read him the entire text.

I had learned about the harijan issue in The Nectar of Devotion, Chapter 9, under the heading “Touching the Deity”: “In the Visnu-dharmottara there is a statement about touching the lotus feet of the Lord. It is said, ‘Only a person who is initiated as a Vaisnava and is executing devotional service in Krsna consciousness has the right to touch the body of the Deity.’ In India there was agitation during Gandhi’s political movement because the lowborn classes of men like street-sweepers and candalas are prohibited, according to the Vedic system, from entering the temple. Due to their unclean habits they are prohibited, but at the same time they are given other facilities so they may be elevated to the highest grade of devotional service by association with pure devotees. A man born in any family is not barred, but he must be cleansed. That cleansing process must be adopted. Gandhi wanted to make them clean simply by stamping them with a fictitious name, harijana (‘children of God’)...” And Prabhupada himself was purifying and elevating people from all different backgrounds to the position of initiated brahmans and Vaishnavas.

Gopinatha read, “‘As the nation observes this week the death anniversary of Dr. Ambedkar, it behooves our news research to face a challenge for the plight of this downtrodden community. The story of the vast quantity of harijans in this ancient and illustrious land is a miserable story of shame and sorrow, harassment and humiliation, operationand separation, poverty and pity. The harijan problem is not merely a social or religious or economic or political one. It is a complex problem involving many factors. It is, however, the most baffling national problem, posing a great challenge to the leaders, rulers, and people of India.’”

Prabhupada was encouraging and training senior disciples to write letters and articles in response to contemporary news stories, and he asked Tamal Krishna to write a letter to the leader of the harijan movement. “Why not say, ‘We can lead you to the highest perfection of cultural, social, religion’?” he suggested. “They are feeling frustration. Now we can give them the light.”

When Gopinatha pointed out that the article’s author was a professor, K.H.A. Parthan, Prabhupada said, “So write to him, on the basis of

mam hi partha vyapasritya  
ye 'pi syuh papa-yonayah  
striyo vaisyas tatha sudras  
te ’pi yanti param gatim

\[“O son of Prtha, those who take shelter in Me, though they be of lower birth—women, vaisyas (merchants) and sudras (workers)—can attain the supreme destination.” (Gita 9.32)\] According to Bhagavad-gita, we can lead you and make your life successful.”

“One problem I see,” Tamal Krishna said, “is that generally they very much oppose—of course, unrightly so—the designation of sudra. They are sudras, these harijans, but—”

“But it doesn’t matter,” said Prabhupada. “We shall elevate them to go back to Godhead—whatever they may be. Striyo vaisyas tatha sudras. Kim punar brahmanah punya bhakta rajarsayah. Simply denying—‘I am not sudra’—will not help. They must be elevated to the standard of brahman. That we will discuss later. But we have to convince them that ‘This world movement is going on to take the human society to the highest perfection of life. If you join, we can help you to the perfection of life, on the basis of Bhagavad-gita. There is no difficulty. That we can do. If you really want, there is a ...’ We are actually doing it all over the world. Why not here?”

“But the thing is that Dr. Ambedkar is dead now,” said Gopinatha.

“He was the leader of the harijans.”

“Whoever, but they could not do anything, and neither they can do anything now. They do not know how to elevate them. We know. We can help. And we are actually doing it. They are feeling frustration for want of a leader. We are prepared to guide them to the highest perfection of life. The defect was Gandhi started this harijan movement keeping them where they are and at the same time changing by rubber stamp to harijana. That must be failure.”

“Yes,” Tamal Krishna agreed. “Unless you change the inner makeup of a man, he won’t improve. They are thinking that by spending money, by giving a better home, by these things they’ll improve. But we have practically seen in Madras on the beach, these harijans were given some of the better houses, and they immediately did one of two things: either they rented the house to someone else and kept living on the street, which is their nature, or else they turned the house into the street. . . . Unless you actually reform a person, just artificially giving him money or stamping approval won’t change anything. You have to change him. And they have no plan for that. They spent 3,100 crores on the harijans. Can you imagine if they had given you that money, Srila Prabhupada, what you could have done with it?”

“Gandhi has degraded the name of harijana to such a position,” Prabhupada said, “that if somebody says, ‘I am harijan,’ immediately people will hate him, because we know here is a chamar bhangi \[untouchable\], only he has changed the name to harijana."

“That is another thing that we should point out in our letter: What is the actual meaning of harijana? ‘One who serves Hari, or Krishna.’”

“One who has been elevated to the position of associate of Hari. That has to be done. Then it will be first class. That we can do.”

“What is the translation for the word jana?”

“Jana means person. Hari means the Lord. Hari’s man. Like Narada.” “Narada Muni is a harijana?"

“Yes. All devotees.”

Tamal Krishna continued the reading from the harijan article: “‘The only remedy lies in the ending of their subservience to the higher castes and securing for them economic independence.’ But according to the Bhagavatam, a sudra can never be given economic independence. If they want economic independence, they should elevate themselves to the higher caste.”

“They will not become higher caste,” Prabhupada commented. “They do not know how. Economic independence—who is checking? There is no such check anywhere in the world. Just like in Bombay, everyone can do business—so why they cannot do?”

“Because they are not intelligent enough,” Tamal Krishna said.

“Everything requires intelligence. If you haven’t got that intelligence, how can you do it? Nowadays, suppose if you do some business, is there a hindrance that ‘You are low class; you cannot do this business’? No, neither by the government nor the society. You can do it.”

“Look at this next question, Srila Prabhupada. It says ‘Who are these harijans? What is their origin? What sins did they commit?”’

“You answer that.”

“Yeah, we can answer these questions. Yes, they did commit sins. Therefore they are in this position. Everyone is getting what he deserves.”

“Yes. Prakrteh kriyamanani gunaih karmani. Sad-asad-janma-yonisu. Karanam guna-sango 'sya \[The cause is the living entity’s association with the modes of nature\]. This is the science. Now you can rectify—not that you must remain. If you accept Krishna consciousness, even you are born in low-grade caste or family, you can be elevated. What’s done is done. Now we can elevate you from this position. That is in our capacity.”

Tamal Krishna read further: “‘There are no authentic answers to these questions.’”

“There are. Karanam guna-sango 'sya. Read Bhagavad-gita. Karanam guna-sango ‘sya. Here is authentic answer. Why is he saying that? That means you are not in proper leadership. Just explain that if you are infected by cholera disease, germ, you must suffer. That is nature’s law. Similarly, karanam guna-sangah asya sad-asad-yoni-janmasu. Now you can change the karana, the cause. Mam hi partha vyapasritya ye 'pi syuh papa-yonayah. And you can neutralize it. Mam ca avyabhicarena bhakti-yogena yah. Quote this. Everything is there in Bhagavad-gita.

mam ca yo "vyabhicarena bhakti-yogena sevate  
sa gundn samatityaitdn brahma-bhuydya kalpate

\[“One who engages in full devotional service, unfailing in all circumstances, at once transcends the modes of material nature and thus comes to the level of Brahman” (Gita 14.26)\]

"Brahma-bhutah prasannatma na socati. Everything is there. They do not know ‘Why I am in downtrodden condition?’ The answer is there: karanam guna-sango ’sya.”

Tamal Krishna read further: “‘They desire freedom from the age-old shackles of superstition.’”

“Where is the shackle, ‘age-old shackles’?”

“There is nothing keeping them down but their own inability.”

“You are keeping yourself in shackles. If you want to be educated ... Dr. Ambedkar belonged to the harijan community. How did he become a lawyer? Where is the shackle?”

Tamal Krishna read on: “‘According to the constitutional directives, harijans should account for twenty percent of the posts in the government service.’ But first of all they should be qualified. We can use the example that if your father is a high-court justice, does it make you a high-court justice? First you have to be qualified. . . . Then they quote Dr. Ambedkar saying, ‘We will attain self-elevation only if we learn selfhelp, regain self-respect, and gain self-knowledge.’ But what is the self, they don’t know.”

“That we can teach.”

“He says, ‘The surest way for our salvation lies in higher education.’ It says, ‘Here are some measures to be implemented. The caste system should be abolished.’ They are always trying to abolish the caste system.”

“The caste system ... Where is the hindrance in the caste system? If you want to become a brahman, you can become a brahman. Why should it be abolished?”

“Incorrect understanding of it should be abolished.”

“‘This is the definition of becoming a brahman.’ Give this.”

“Samo damas tapah saucam.”

“You have to learn how you can become a brahman. These are the symptoms of becoming a brahman. You develop these symptoms. Who checks you? Practically we are doing all over the world. ... The caste system should not be abolished, but it must be properly established. That is wanted. If you have got any defect in the eye, it is not that the eyeshould be plucked out. But it should be treated and brought into the normal condition. That is wanted. That we admit.”

“Actually, you told Professor Kotovsky that this caste system is existing everywhere, in every society in the world,” Gopinatha added.

“Yes. In the body there is caste system. The head is the brahman, the hand is the kshatriya, the belly is the vaishya, and the leg is the sudra. If there is only a head, that will not help. There must be legs also. But they must be conducted under the guidance of the head. Then it is all right. The leg must work according to the dictation of the head. The hand must work according to the dictation of the head. ‘The caste system should be abolished? What caste system? There is no caste system. Everyone is sudra. Who is a qualified brahman now except one or two in our camp?”

Tamal Krishna read the end of the article: “‘Let harijans be their own pathfinders, and let them lead themselves from darkness to light, from pain to pleasure, and from a living hell to tranquility and joy of life.’”

“You do not know how to do it. Otherwise, you would have done it. You do not know the way. We can teach you. So cooperate with us; we shall fulfill your ambition.”

“I'll have to work on this. It will take a little time to write nicely.”

“We are willing to help them. And we are the only right person who can help them. Nobody knows. If he is serious, let him come and talk with us.”

“Then we can end the letter to him like that.”

“Capture these ideas. Explain it nicely.”

Around that time, Jayaprakash Narayan, a famous Indian freedom fighter, political activist, and social reformer, held a huge gathering, with lakhs of people, in which members of the higher castes, in protest of the artificial dominance of the higher castes over the lower, took off their brahman threads and placed them in a massive bonfire. When Prabhupada was told about the event, he commented, “Good—they admit that they’re all sudras.”

Another new member of parliament to come and meet Prabhupada, at my invitation, was the eminent lawyer Sri Ram Jethmalani. When he arrived, I introduced him: “He is the member of parliament representing this constituency. He recently came from Detroit. He was teaching ata university there while this emergency was going on. He mentioned his idea of helping the slum-dwellers. I showed him the article ‘One Hundred Million Harijans Looking for a New Messiah’ and gave him a copy of the letter Goswami Maharaja \[Tamal Krishna\] wrote. In the meantime, he was busy with other functions, so he didn’t get a chance to go through it. But he is very interested.”

“We can uplift the position of the harijans very easily by this process of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu,” Prabhupada said. “There is a Bengali song, vrajendra-nandana yei. You understand Bengali?”

“No.”

''Vrajendra-nandana yei, saci-suta haila sei means that ‘He who was formerly Vrajendra-nandana, Krishna, Nanda Maharaja’s son, the same person has now come as Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.’ Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s mother’s name was Sacidevi. Therefore He is introduced, ‘The same person who was formerly the son of Nanda Maharaja has come again as the son of Sacidevi.’ Balarama haila nitai, ‘And Balarama has come as Nitai.’ These two brothers, Gaura-Nitai, have started this Hare Krishna movement. What is the purpose of this Hare Krishna movement? Papi-tapi yata chila, hari-nama uddharila. In the Kali-yuga, 99 percent are sinful and suffering. Papi-tapi, Papi means sinful, and tapi means suffering. All of them—papi-tapi yata chila—are delivered simply by this process of Hare Krishna maha-mantra. Papi-tapi yata chila, hari-nama uddharila. Then where is the evidence? Tara saksi jagai madhai, You are a lawyer, so you want witness, evidence.”

“You don’t blame me,” Mr. Jethmalani said, laughing.

Prabhupada laughed as well. “No, it is not blaming,” he said. “It is the fact, the real understanding. Without evidence, without proof, how can a case be established? That’s a good method. He is speaking like a lawyer, that ‘You want evidence, you want witness: See here. Tara saksi jagai madhai! That was five hundred years ago. Now in our Hare Krishna movement you see practically: drunkards, illicit-sex hunters, and so on have become saintly persons. This is the effect of it. And Krishna also says, mam hi partha vyapasritya ye ’pi syuh papa-yo-nayah, It doesn’t matter. Papa-yoni. According to our Vedic system, low class, those who are born in low-grade family, are called papa-yoni. Brahman, kshatriya, vaishya, sudra, lower than that—sudradham,

Kirata-hunandhra-pulinda-pulkasa abhira-sumbha yavanah khasa-dayah. They are called papa-yoni, untouchables. Of course, nowadays these things cannot go on. But these statements are there. Krishna says, ye ’pi syuh papa-yonayah. Anyone born anywhere, te ’pi yanti param gatim \[can attain the supreme destination\]. Mam eva vyapasritya. Krishna consciousness is so nice, everyone can be elevated. So what is this harijan? We can uplift them.”

“Some of these slum-dwellers are not harijans,” Mr. Jethmalani said. “Some of them are Muslims, some of them are—”

“Anyone. You see. My disciples are coming from Christian, Jewish, Muslim, every kind of background.”

“Have Muslims taken to this movement?”

“Oh, yes. Many. One professor, Dr. Amjar, is my disciple; I gave him the name Rama-ranjana. He was Muslim. It is philosophy, science. It is not meant for a particular caste or creed or nation. No. Rather, to accept this creed or accept this process, one is required first to give up his designations. Sarvopadhi-vinirmuktam tat-paratvena nirmalam. That is nirmala. So long as we are covered by this material body, we are not nirmala; we are polluted. So, one has to give up this designated, bodily concept of life. Tanu-manina. These words are given: tanu-manina. So long as one is continuing in the bodily concept of life, it is sinful life, comparatively. This we have to give up, in order to come to the transcendental position. Sarvopadhi-vinirmuktam tat-paratvena nirmalam. Nirmala. Hrsikena hrsikesa-sevanam bhaktir ucyate. When we become nirmala, in our original, pure spiritual life, then bhakti begins.

“In Bhagavad-gita also it is stated,

brahma-bhutah prasannatma  
na socati na kanksati  
samah sarvesu bhutesu  
mad-bhaktim labhate param  
\[Gita 18.54\]

Such a person, brahma-bhuta—aham brahmdsmi, that is the preliminary qualification to become bhakta. These disciples, these devotees, are not thinking that 'I am American,' ‘I am Indian,' ‘I am brahman,' ‘I am...' ? No.”

“How is it that the Bhagavad-gita doesn’t emphasize public service?” Mr. Jethmalani asked. “Why is there no emphasis on public social service?”

“There is no need ” Prabhupada replied. “This is animal conception of life. The dogs also combine together and go bow-bow-bow-bow-bow”—Prabhupada made a barking sound. “A human being also can do like that. Then what is the difference between animals and human beings?”

“But I don’t know that animals serve each other. It is men who do.”

“But what is the use of serving? What can you do? What service you have done? You cannot do anything beyond the laws of nature. Now Indira is in difficulty. What can you do? In one day, everything is finished. The law of nature is so strict. You cannot do anything. You are falsely proud that you want to do something, but it is not possible. Prakrteh kriyamanani gunaih karmani sarvasah. You can do only the service that ‘You are not this body; you are spirit soul. Your business is this.’ This is dharma.”

“But when you see so much physical suffering around—”

“But what you can do? That is my... It is very good to be sympathetic.”

“Is it right to tell the suffering that ‘I am busy, at work for my salvation’?”

“We don’t say like that. We say, ‘Here is the remedy for your suffering: Krishna consciousness. Come to it.’ We don’t say that ‘You suffer.’ We say, ‘Stop your suffering in this way: tyaktva deham punar janma naiti mam eti kaunteya.' We are also trying to stop that suffering. But ordinary people do not know how to stop it. Just like the United Nations. They are united to mitigate the sufferings of the whole human ... What they have done? Simply like barking in that assembly ... Stop suffering. So, you must know first of all how sufferings can be stopped. Then you do this, the needful. Otherwise, what is the use if you do not know the method? Here is duhkhalayam asasvatam \[a place of misery, and temporary\]. I think you have read Bhagavad-gita”

“Oh, yes, but not for—”

“Find out this verse,” Prabhupada said to Tamal Krishna. “Mam upetya kaunteya duhkhalayam . . . napnuvanti mahatmanah samsiddhim paramam gatah. This is real mitigation of suffering. The world is suffering.”

Tamal Krishna read the verse aloud.

“Mam upetya punar janma duhkhalayam asasvatam” Prabhupada said. “So long you have to accept another body, you must suffer. This body means suffering. That Krishna says. Janma-mrtyu-jara-vyadhi-duhkha-dosanudarsanam. Real suffering is here, that you have to take birth, you have to die, you have to suffer from disease and old age. But your position is na hanyate hanyamane sarire. Na jayate na mriyate va kadacit. Your business is not to take birth and die. But why you are suffering? Nobody wants to die; you must die. Nobody wants to become old; you must become. So, you do not know what is suffering and how to mitigate it. And Krishna points out, ‘This is suffering: janma-mrtyu-jara-vyadhi-duhkha-dosanudarsanam.' This is knowledge. Suppose there is a boil, and if you \[Prabhupada made a blowing gesture\]—is that mitigation of suffering, do you think? The surgeon must come and operate and get out the pus and then suffering stops. So, here Krishna recommends, ‘This is mitigation of suffering: Stop your birth, death, old age, and disease? We do not know what is suffering and how to get out. Therefore we have to consult Krishna at every step. Then our life will be ... This is Krishna consciousness. You take instruction from Krishna and try to abide by it. Your sufferings will go. Otherwise,” he chuckled, “simply dog barking will not help.”

“Srila Prabhupada, Tamal Krishna said, “we just received a letter from Pakistan, which I thought you might be interested to hear along with Mr. Jethmalani. It describes some very interesting preaching there. It is just a short paragraph, if I could read it.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada agreed.

“It’s from your disciple Atreya Rishi.”

“Hmm. He went there?”

“Yes, Srila Prabhupada. Srila Prabhupada has a disciple by the name of—”

“He is Muhammadan,” Prabhupada said. “He was Faramarz Attar, so I have given him the name Atreya Rishi. There are many like that. In Iran we have got center, Tehran. We have got many Muhammadan disciples there, prosecuting our method. And he is the head there. Just see. Atreya Rishi. What he has said?”

“Srila Prabhupada sent Atreya Rishi to Pakistan,” Tamal Krishna explained. “He writes, ‘My dear Srila Prabhupada, please accept myhumble obeisances. All glories to you, who are the only guiding light in the world of darkness. India is that holy land in which the Supreme Personality of Godhead Lord Sri Chaitanya appeared and whose inhabitants He instructed to go all over the world and spread the science of love of Godhead. It is in this way that I realize your emphasizing the activities of ISKCON in India after your very successful endeavoring in the West. Pakistan is a nonseparable part of India, and I appreciate your compassion towards them and your desire to help them.’”

“Yes, yes,” Prabhupada said.

“‘In accordance with your desire I went to Karachi and spent two days there. I first visited the marble factory of Mr. Azis Pir Mohammed. This man belongs to the Ismaili sect of Islam, the followers of Aga Khan. His factory is very small, and he and his three brothers manage it. Their primary business is cutting alabaster into vases, tiles, plates, cups, etc., and they sell their products mainly to foreign countries. I made two visits to their factory and preached extensively to Azis, his brother, his friends and workers. They all liked Krishna consciousness. They are intelligent enough to understand, and in due time will be able to follow your instructions seriously. However, they need more association and a devotee to constantly engage them. I did not see fit to ask them for the use of their house as a center yet, but I told them that I would be opening a center in Karachi, and they were happy to hear this. They promised to help in whatever way they could as soon as our men appear on the scene.”’

I mentioned to the guests that I knew that they hadn’t eaten all day, and Mr. Jethmalani asked if this was our standard food—and what our normal dinnertime was.

“The same—rice, dal, chapatis. One o’clock.”

“Were you nonvegetarian before you joined this movement?”

“Yes,” Tamal Krishna answered. “But now I cannot even think of eating anything but Krishna prasada. That is how Prabhupada got us off all nonvegetarian foodstuff. He personally cooked for us, and he made us eat so much that we lost all remembrance of anything but prasada. Then, after we were very nicely fed with prasada, he taught us the chanting of Hare Krishna. And after our being very much pleased with the chanting of Hare Krishna, he would lecture to us on Bhagavad-gita and

Srimad-Bhagavatam. So, every part of us was satisfied—our tongues, our voices, our minds and intelligence, fully satisfied.”

“Your movement does allow householders and professional men like us to be a part of the movement without having to—”

“Actually, we very much eagerly look forward to having persons like yourself taking great part in our movement. It is with great difficulty that someone like Giriraj dasa has to go to the court because we have no one like you.”

“Oh, my great pleasure. Anytime you just tell me when there is a problem in the court, and I'll be there in two minutes.”

“He is a lawyer,” Prabhupada said.

“But can one be in the movement without having to adopt the stricter forms of all this, even at home?” Mr. Jethmalani asked, pursuing his original question.

“Yes, he can participate,” I replied. “If someone is initiated as a disciple, he must follow these four principles very rigidly: no meat-eating, no intoxication, no illicit sex, and no gambling. But the shastra says that you can serve either by giving your whole life, by giving your intelligence, by giving your time, or by giving your words. So, in whatever way possible, anyone can serve Krishna and make more and more progress.”

“Actually, this gentleman who has written this letter from Pakistan is a big businessman,” Tamal Krishna added. “He is the head of a very, very large business consultant firm in Iran. But in his free time he also tries to do a little preaching work.”

“He is a very responsible officer. What is his position?” Prabhupada asked.

“He is the managing director of Arthur Young & Company.”

“It’s a big international firm of chartered accountants,” I added. Then I mentioned, “There was some discussion earlier whether Krishna had an actual existence or whether He is imaginary.”

“Why imaginary?” Prabhupada questioned. “He is in the history, Mahabharata. Mahabharata means the history of greater India.”

“One of the historical pieces of evidence is that if Ramayana was historically earlier than Mahabharata, it is curious that there is no reference in the Mahabharata at all to any other gods of Ramayana,'' Mr. Jethmalani said. “And if it will be the other way around, there is no reference to—”

“But there is reference in Srimad-Bhagavatam about Ramayana” I countered.

“In Srimad-Bhagavatam there is reference of Ramayana. Srimad-Bhagavatam is the last writing of Vyasadeva,” Prabhupada added.

“The last writing may contain, but between the two of them, there is no cross-reference of any kind. Now, a personality like Krishna, when first set up, it must have become a phenomenon at least.”

“But in the Gita Krishna describes His different vibhiltis, opulences, and there He says, ‘I am Rama,’” I said.

“‘Amongst the warriors, I am Rama,’” Prabhupada confirmed. “The reference is there. These very words are there: ‘Amongst the warriors, I am Rama?”

“And it’s also described that the great sages in the forest who were worshipping Rama,” I added, “they wanted to associate with Him in a particular way which was not possible because He was acting as the ideal king, so He said that ‘In My future appearance as Lord Krishna, I will fulfill all your desires?”

“And besides that,” Prabhupada pointed out, “in the Vedic literature, Brahma-samhita, this name Rama is mentioned:

ramadi-murtisu kala-niyamena tisthan  
nanavataram akarod bhuvanesu kintu  
krsnah svayam samabhavat paramah puman yo  
govindam adi-purusam tam aham bhajami  
\[Bs 5.39\]

Krishna is the original God, and Rama is His expansion. Not only Rama— other incarnations. Ramadi-murtisu. Rama, Nrsimha, Varaha—many.”

“Rama comes later according to this,” Mr. Jethmalani ventured.

“There is no question of later or former,” Prabhupada clarified. “These are always existing. And They appear and disappear according to the necessity. Yada yada hi dharmasya glanir bhavati bharata tadat-manam srjamy aham. The murtis are there permanently, and They appear and disappear according to the necessity. Suppose in a case you require the reference to a law. It is not that the law has appeared for the purpose. The law was already there. You have simply to bring it foryour business. Ramadi-murtisu kala-niyamena tisthan nanavataram akarod bhuvanesu kintu krsnah svayam samabhavat paramah. Any sweets?”

“Here,” one of Mr. Jethmalani’s associates said.

“Oh, you have got. Madhurena samapayet. At the end you must take some sweet,” Prabhupada responded, quoting Priti-sandarbha. “Then it will be digested.”

“In U. P. they give you sweets first,” Mr. Jethmalani said.

“First, at the time of taking water even. First they will give sweet and then water,” one of his associates added.

“What is the system in your society? Sweet first or last?” Prabhupada asked.

“In here also, they are given first sweet,” his associate answered.

“Yes, but now everything has become Westernized. We have dessert,” said Mr. Jethmalani.

“In northern India first of all they give sweets,” Prabhupada said. “They eat sweet to their heart’s content. Then, to counteract the sweetness ...”

“The best way to destroy your appetite is to eat sweet first.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada laughed.

“They eat last to digest,” the friend said.

“The sugar produces energy to digest your food,” added Mr. Jethmalani.

“I am very glad that you have taken the prasadam” Prabhupada concluded. “I am pleased. Therefore I wanted that you eat before me. It is a great pleasure.”

“We are also very fortunate to eat before you, sir,” said Mr. Jethmalani.

“Hare Krishna. Jaya,' said Prabhupada as the men washed their hands in his sink.

“Thank you,” I said. “We will have to meet, then.”

“Any time,” Mr. Jethmalani agreed. “You just let me know; whatever, any problems, I am yours.”

“Jaya” said Prabhupada. And after the guests left, he commented, “By feeding, how much one becomes obliged. Any gentleman, give him something. Give him prasadam”

“He ate everything,” Tamal Krishna observed.

“Oh, yes, everything. Very sumptuously, pleasing. They were hungry.” “He hadn’t eaten all day. That’s why Giriraj was insisting he must take.”

“No, you must insist.”

“He said, ‘I am yours.’”

“Handle them very cautiously. He’ll take, certainly. Intelligent boy.”

Tamal Krishna wrote in his diary, “Mr. Jethmalani, the most eminent lawyer of India, was highly impressed. He promised to give all help for Srila Prabhupada’s movement.”

Mr. Rajda continued his efforts to arrange a meeting between Srila Prabhupada and Morarji Desai. When I entered Prabhupada’s room on April 28, he greeted me with, “So, what news?”

“The reason I came up is I’m going to try to phone Mr. Rajda now,” I replied. “And considering that the prime minister may not have that much time . . . Earlier we had discussed that he should come here to meet you, but suppose if we fix up a minimum time of say at least a half hour undisturbed and if he can’t come here, is it possible to arrange it in the city, or we should just insist that...”

“Hmm?”

Tamal Krishna clarified, “He’s suggesting that if the prime minister can’t give that much time, whether you would go to see him?” He turned to me. “Actually, if you give the idea that Prabhupada wants to see him in the early morning hours ...”

“I’m going to,” I said.

“I mean, if he says that that’s not possible—”

“That is not respectful,” Prabhupada said. “Then he does not know how to honor a saintly person and it is useless to meet him. If he has no respect for a saintly person, if he thinks he’s greater than a saintly person, then he’s useless.”

“Then nothing will come of it, anyway,” Tamal Krishna said. “And if we give him this opportunity, that he come in the morning, if he—”

“No, no, apart from that, if he has got that sense, that ‘I am very big man, so everyone should come here,’ he’s useless and we cannot do anything with him. The very beginning is ...”

“On the wrong foot” I said.

“No, he has to come to see you, Srila Prabhupada,” Tamal Krishna said. “There are so many examples in the shastra of great personalities—”

“Chaitanya Mahaprabhu refused even to see, what to speak of going there,” Prabhupada said. “Even big, big kings—Akbar, Mansingh—they used to come to Rupa Gosvami.”

“I agree with you completely,” I said.

“Did he demand like that?” Prabhupada inquired.

“No,” I replied. “When I spoke to Mr. Rajda, I said that the prime minister should come here, and Mr. Rajda agreed. But I just spoke to Gopal, on my way to make the call, and he said that I should ask you about this. ... I was just going to phone, and I mentioned to Gopal Krishna Prabhu that I was going to make this call. I said that the prime minister was going to be coming here and that in the call I wanted to make that very clear so there would be no mistake. And he said that the prime minister might be too busy to come here and that—”

“Gopal said.”

“Yes. So I thought it would be better just to—”

“No, there is no question of...”

“I agree completely. I mean, you’re millions and billions of times greater than anyone, so there’s no question.”

“No, apart from that, if one has no proper respect for a saintly person, he’s a useless man. You cannot have any benefit. Neither can he derive any benefit.”

“Because he’ll think he has nothing to learn, that he is already in the best position.”

“And we don’t require anything from them. But for the whole human society’s welfare, we can suggest to him, ‘Do like this.’ That is our . . . But we don’t require anything from them.”

“I know that. This is your—”

“Of course, sometimes we are in difficulty; we ask them something.”

“But that’s their duty, anyway,” Tamal Krishna said. “Kshatriyas should provide protection for the saintly person.”

“Anyway, our real protector is Krishna,” I said.

“Yes,” Prabhupada confirmed.

“Because we’ve seen so many difficulties. Nobody could see any solution, but—”

“One of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s devotees was ordered to be hanged—Gopinatha Pattanayaka. All the devotees approached Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, thinking that ‘He must... The king will excuse him? He never agreed. ‘Oh, I cannot do that. If he has done something wrong, then let him .. ? Of course, he was saved and protected by Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s good will, but He never agreed. These are some of the examples that... Simply depend on Krishna. But if they are actually respectful, we can ask them. But if it is a difficult job— visayinam sandarsanam atha yosit.”

Prabhupada was referring to a verse quoted by Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, recorded in Sri Caitanya-caritamrta (Madhya 11.8):niskincanasya bhagavad-bhajanonmukhasyaparam param jigamisor bhava-sagarasyasandarsanam visayinam atha yositam caha hanta hanta visa-bhaksanato 'py asadhu

“Alas, for a person who is seriously desiring to cross the material ocean and engage in the transcendental loving service of the Lord without material motives, seeing a materialist engaged in sense gratification or seeing a woman who is similarly interested is more abominable than drinking poison willingly.”

“We cannot keep so strictly,” Prabhupada concluded, “but these are the principles taught by Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.”

The negotiations were going back and forth with Mr. Rajda, who also had to reckon with the prime minister’s brief and sporadic visits to Bombay. But the prime minister was going to be in Bombay for a day, on May 6, and I was eager to hear what Mr. Rajda would have to say about him meeting Srila Prabhupada.

Finally, around midnight on May 5, Mr. Rajda phoned to say that the meeting with Morarji Desai was fixed for seven-thirty the next morning. The prime minister was going to be in Bombay for only one or two days and would be staying at his son’s flat on Marine Drive. Although Prabhupada had said that he would not go to meet the prime minister, I wanted to inform him of the news and take his advice.

It was the middle of the night, and everyone else was asleep. Not knowing what Prabhupada was doing and not wanting to disturb him, I stepped softly through the hallway around to the far entrance to hiswork area and peeked in. Prabhupada was sitting dictating at his marble-topped desk, illuminated by only a small lamp. He looked up and motioned for me to come forward.

I sat on the floor, in front of him. It was just the two of us in the large, dimly lit room—a rare, intimate moment, one of the most intense l'd ever experienced. “Srila Prabhupada,” I said, “I am very sorry to disturb you at this hour, but I just received a phone call from Mr. Rajda.”

“That’s all right,” he said. “Actually, with this sickness I cannot sleep at night. Even if I want to, I cannot sleep. And due to this illness, I cannot eat also. I am such an old man, there is no question of sex life and there is no question of defense either, so I guess I am liberated.”

Of course, I knew that Prabhupada was liberated, not because of bodily circumstances, as he was humbly—and wryly—saying, but because he was in transcendental consciousness. He was always up at night, translating, not because he was sick and couldn’t sleep, but in the mood of service to his guru maharaja and Lord Krishna.

When I told Prabhupada that the prime minister was prepared to meet at his residence the next morning, he explained that he had wanted to see if Morarji would be willing to come and meet him at Hare Krishna Land. “It’s not that I’m proud,” he said, “that I can’t go meet him at his place. But unless his mood is respectful, there is no use.” This was a test of whether the prime minister had the proper attitude. Still, he agreed that Tamal Krishna and I should go ahead and meet him.

In the morning, Tamal Krishna and I prepared to leave well in advance for our meeting with the prime minister. We asked Prabhupada what books we should give him.

"Bhagavad-gita, Krsna book, and Teachings of Lord Caitanya," he replied.

“In Hindi?” I asked.

“No,” Prabhupada said with a frown. “English.”

The plan was that we would drive to Mr. Rajda’s flat, pick him up, and then proceed to meet Morarji Desai on Marine Drive. When we got there, I kept ringing Mr. Rajda’s front doorbell, but there was no response. Finally, after about twenty minutes, he appeared. He said that we would have to wait just five minutes more while he finished dressing and eating.

By the time we reached the apartment on Marine Drive, it was already 7:55, almost half an hour past the time of our appointment. “You are very late,” the prime minister reprimanded us when we arrived. He was already meeting with Murli Deora, the mayor of Bombay, and others, but he said that he would see us for a few minutes. He repeated that he had been waiting since 7:25. We were so embarrassed, we didn’t know what to say. We simply apologized and gave him Prabhupada’s books. He didn’t say much and quickly excused himself to return to his meetings with the others.

When we returned to the temple, we were apprehensive about telling Prabhupada what had taken place. We went up to his quarters, offered our obeisances, and sat on the floor before him.

Prabhupada was eager to hear what had happened. And he was upset when he heard that we had been late. “Very bad,” he said. Morarji Desai was known for his punctuality, he told us, and we had missed a good opportunity by our misbehavior.

When we explained that Mr. Rajda had made us late, Prabhupada asked for a more detailed report. We told him that the main thing Morarji Desai had wanted to know was the reason for our lateness.

“Did you tell him that Mr. Rajda made you late?” he asked.

We shook our heads. Prabhupada became disgusted and said, “Why did you not say that he made you late—that you were on time but he made you late? I know you were thinking that he is our friend and you didn’t want to embarrass him in front of the prime minister, but now the whole thing is spoiled.”

Feeling foolish and ashamed, we hung our heads and remained silent.

Prabhupada reflected for a moment and then said, “Anyway, these men will never change their views.”

Still, trying to salvage some benefit from the meeting, later that day Tamal Krishna and 1 sent the prime minister a letter:

Dear Shri Morarji Desai:

We thank you very much for allowing us to meet you to explain our mission. Our Guru Maharaja His Divine Grace A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada is pushing on this Krishna Conscious movement throughout the world, with great difficulty. But he cannot stop the movement in spite of all difficulties because Krishna wants this movement to go on. As it is stated in the Bhagavad-gita:

ya idam paramam guhyam  
mad-bhaktesv abhidhasyati  
bhaktim mayi param krtva  
mam evaisyaty asamsayah

We are servants of Krishna. Every servant wants to please his master. We are, therefore, requesting you to give our Guru Maharaja the following facilities in India.

In India Srila Prabhupada has very big establishments for the Krishna Consciousness movement in Bombay, in Vrindavan, in Mayapur (District Nadia, West Bengal), and in Hyderabad, and small establishments in Calcutta, Delhi, Ahmedabad, and other places. We invite you to visit at least his Bombay project. To manage these affairs properly he requires assistants. As far as Indians are concerned, they are not practically coming to help our Guru Maharaja. So Srila Prabhupada has to manage these establishments by getting some foreign disciples.

Therefore we have to request you to kindly arrange for assistance for foreign disciples to live in India as permanent residents. In America Srila Prabhupada received permission for permanent residency, along with other Indian members, and he does not require any passport or visa. Similarly, the devotee assistants who are coming to help Srila Prabhupada in India should be allowed to stay as permanent residents without visa problems. Our Guru Maharaja will guarantee that his disciples will never participate in politics or internal affairs of India, and if any discrepancy is found in them, they can be immediately deported. In addition, Srila Prabhupada is getting Rs. 10,00,000/- every month for construction and other expenditures in his different establishments, so these devotees will not touch Indian money, even one paisa.

At the present moment, Srila Prabhupada’s assistants are coming to India and the Government is allowing them three-month visas, with a maximum extension of further three months. In this way after six months his disciples have to go away and then again come back with new visas. This process of going outside India and then coming back costs Rs, 10,000/- for each devotee. In this way our Guru Maharaja is losing about Rs. 5,00,000/- to Rs. 6,00,000/-per year for nothing. And an assistant who is trained up is checked from his prescribed duties and is forced to go away. If the Governmentallows these foreign assistants to stay as permanent residents, as Srila Prabhupada has been allowed in America, then there is no loss for the Government but it will be a great benefit and relief for our Guru Maharaja.

Kindly help our Guru Maharaja to continue this Krishna Consciousness movement to prove to the world that there is God and that the Supreme Personality of Godhead is Krishna. Krsnas tu bhagavan swayam. So kindly immediately favor us with this help and we shall remain thankful to you forever.

Hoping this meets you well.

Yours in the service of the Lord,

Tamal Krishna Goswami, Secretary to His Divine Grace A.C.

Bhaktivedanta Swami

Giriraj das Brahmachary, President ISKCON Bombay

The construction was proceeding well with ECC, but Prabhupada felt that he needed someone strong to deal with them regarding the schedule of payments. He discussed the issue with Tamal Krishna and me and concluded that none of our devotees could do it; we needed an intelligent, reliable, expert, and experienced businessman-friend. We thought Brijratan Mohatta, who over the years had proven himself in all these ways and more, would be ideal.

When Mr. Mohatta came to Juhu to meet Prabhupada, Tamal Krishna asked Prabhupada if we should explain the situation, but Prabhupada said that we were not capable of doing even that; he would explain it to Mr. Mohatta himself.

Mr. Mohatta understood the situation, but he told Prabhupada that if matters were taken out of Surabhi’s hands, Surabhi might feel bad. Prabhupada agreed and decided that Surabhi would remain in charge but be required to submit all ECC’s bills to Mr. Mohatta for approval before any would be paid. Prabhupada himself was managing the funds for the construction.

Mr. Sethi, who was so staunch and had so much faith in Prabhupada that his devotion for him reminded me of Hanuman’s for Lord Rama, loved to chant the holy names, and for years before he met Prabhupada he had been associated with a group called the Radha Madhava Prema

Sudha Sankirtana Mandala. Their guru was based in Vrindavan, and they chanted the Hare Krishna maha-mantra. In Bombay they were all householders—and very devoted. Every Sunday they would have a twelve-hour akhanda-hari-nama-sankirtana—“unbroken,” continuous Hare Krishna kirtan—from six in the morning to six in the evening, followed by two hours of songs from Vraja.

Mr. Sethi had the idea that instead of having the kirtan in one of their devotees’ homes, the group could have it at Hare Krishna Land, along with our temple devotees. So we arranged it in front of the Deities in the small temple, beside the complex, which was nearing completion. Prabhupada was staying just above, in his new quarters, despite the construction not being completely finished and the lift not working. Ill as he was, he would recline or lie down and relish the kirtan, which he could hear coming from below.

Many of the temple devotees left in the heat of the afternoon, but the Mandala people continued chanting. When Mr. Sethi went up to see Prabhupada and told him that there were no devotees in the temple, Prabhupada, displeased, called for me and told me, “Our devotees cannot do like they \[the Mandala group\] do—our devotees can only eat and sleep.” Upendra, who had joined Prabhupada’s team of personal servants, reported that Prabhupada continually praised the group and repeatedly condemned us or lamented, “Why our men cannot do the same thing? They are just eating and sleeping.”

The Mandala devotees wanted to see Prabhupada, to have his audience, but they were too many to come up—and anyway, they had to be in the kirtan. And Prabhupada was too ill to walk down the stairs or meet them all. At one stage they were so eager that they came out of the temple and just stood beneath Prabhupada’s balcony doing kirtan, chanting for him.

Eventually Tamal Krishna and Mr. Sethi helped Prabhupada walk to the balcony, and when he glanced down and smiled upon the Mandala devotees, they welled up with ecstasy and love for him. He stayed for a little while and then went back in, and the group continued their kirtan in the temple.

One highlight came at the end when a female devotee sang, “Jaya radhe jaya radhe radhe, jaya radhe jaya sri radhe. Jaya krishna ...” Later,

Mr. Sethi told us that when Prabhupada was listening to that song, tears of ecstatic love were streaming down his cheeks.

“That kirtan was wonderful,” Prabhupada told me the next day. “We should invite the whole group to stay at Hare Krishna Land. Tell them that we will maintain them. They won’t have to work. All they have to do is continuous kirtan.” The group comprised fifty families, and he said he would build them accommodations and provide all their necessities. He wanted only one thing from them: they should chant Hare Krishna day and night.

I wasn’t sure how to respond, but it seemed that Prabhupada knew that this might take some time. Then he said, “At least our devotees, they should do the twelve-hour kirtan every day, from 6:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m.”

I hesitated. Prabhupada had always emphasized that we had to serve and spread the mission, and in Juhu we were especially busy, finishing the temple and getting it ready to open. I didn’t see how all the devotees could spend twelve hours a day chanting in the temple. “Srila Prabhupada,” I said, “we have so much service to do. How will we be able to do it all?”

“All right,” he said, “then one day a week, on Sunday.”

I immediately agreed, relieved—only one day, twelve hours.

Tamal Krishna later commented to me that Prabhupada had done some transcendental bargaining. If he had begun, “Twelve hours every Sunday,” I might have said, “Oh, that’s too much. Maybe four hours.” But because he had begun with twelve hours a day, seven days a week, when he had arrived at twelve hours, one day a week, I had been relieved: “Oh yes, we can do that.”

So, every Sunday we did twelve hours of continuous kirtan. And it was just as Prabhupada had said when I was in Boston—that by sankirtana all problems would be solved, materially and spiritually. Prabhupada had complete faith in the holy name. He knew that the holy name was Krishna Himself, that if we chanted the holy name, we would be in Krishna’s association, and that He would preserve what we had and provide what we lacked.

As the temple president, I had to deal with many problems. We had to construct the complex, deal with the civic authorities, organize the temple programs, deal with the devotees, and just survive in India, withall the disease and other hardships. Devotees would come to me, and on Monday, Tuesday, and sometimes Wednesday I would deal with the problems. But by Thursday we were getting close to the twelve-hour hari-nama, and I knew—it happened every time, without fail—that all the problems would be solved. Either the problem would solve itself or the devotee would realize that it wasn’t really a problem after all, or we would get some insight or inspiration about how to deal with it. So, beginning Thursday, I would say, “Just give me a few days to think about it,” but I knew that by the time the Sunday kirtan was over, the problem would be solved.

On May 8, the day after Prabhupada left Bombay, I was pleased to write him, “Today we instituted the Sunday continuous kirtan as you instructed before you left, and all the devotees who are participating are experiencing transcendental ecstasy. In addition, the kirtan is attracting many nice people to attend the program. At noon we served prasadam to all the guests and gave them a tour of the new building. We hope to improve the program week by week.”

“Thank you for organizing the all-day Sunday kirtan program,” he replied. “This should be developed very nicely, stressing kirtan and prasadam.”

Bombay was hot and humid, and Prabhupada was looking to regain his health in a better climate. The day after the continuous kirtan—Nrsimha-caturdasi, May 2—Prabhupada decided on Srinagar, in Kashmir, and asked Tamal Krishna to set a date and make all arrangements.

That afternoon, however, Shriman Narayan, the former governor of Gujarat who had so much appreciated—and facilitated—Prabhupada during the Gita conference in Wardha, came to meet him. Seeing how ill Prabhupada was, Shriman Narayan suggested that his health would be improved by going to Rishikesh, on the banks of the Ganges at the foothills of the Himalayas. Jaidayal Dalmia had a bungalow there, he said, and a great deal of influence in the area. He would arrange everything.

As always, Prabhupada took the opportunity to stress the value of Krishna consciousness. “Indians are intelligent,” he said, “but they have sacrificed everything to imitate the Westerners. Our knowledge, we have locked it, and we are trying to imitate.”

“Yes, true,” Shriman Narayan accepted. “Imitation is not good at all. We must keep our originality and ancient culture.”

Prabhupada said that his books were being received “with great praise,” and I added that they had been translated into twenty-three different languages, which impressed Shriman Narayan.

“Within ten years I have already written eighty-four books,” Prabhupada said. “And the daily proceeds from the sales of my books is five to six lakhs. . . . All universities, libraries, professors—they are taking.” He mentioned his devotees’ difficulties with visas for India and their need for permanent residence, and Shriman Narayan promised to speak to Morarji Desai and also to introduce us to Atal Bihari Vajpayee, the new minister of external affairs.

A feast had been prepared for Lord Nrsimha’s appearance day, and at Prabhupada’s insistence Shriman Narayan and his family accepted and relished the prasada. Prabhupada had been suffering from poor appetite and ate later, after the guests had left. He explained that when you gave someone prasada, he would be with you through “thick and thin,” in good times and bad, and said that we should always remember that.

“Immediately contact Jaidayal Dalmia,” he told Tamal Krishna. “He has got a nice house. We will go to Rishikesh immediately.” Prabhupada had never been there and had always wanted to stay by the banks of the Ganges.

“Rishikesh is known to be very good,” Tamal Krishna said. “Ganga is there.”

“We can go there immediately. That is decided. Rishikesh is appealing—to drink Ganges water and take bath in the Ganges.”

“I immediately feel attracted to going there because it’s a holy city,” Tamal Krishna said. “These other places were not so. This Rishikesh is a holy city.”

“It is nearer.”

“Tomorrow I’m going into Bombay city anyway. I’ll make arrangements.”

Four days later, as Tamal Krishna was preparing Prabhupada’s red bag, which Prabhupada always kept with him, for the journey to Rishikesh, Prabhupada told him to bring the photograph of Radha-Rasabihari. “Who can fully understand the relationship of thespiritual master with Krishna?” Tamal Krishna wrote that day in his diary. “Prabhupada had asked Krishna to sit down on this land and had promised Him that he would manage everything. Still, the temple was not yet completed, and Radha-Rasabihari were being kept waiting to be installed in Their beautiful temple. The delay in Their installation was the reason Prabhupada’s demands regarding the construction were so great that sometimes they seemed almost unreasonable. By material standards they might have been, but Prabhupada was building this temple for Krishna. He loved Krishna, and Krishna was being made to wait. When Srila Prabhupada is demanding that Krishna not be made to wait any longer, he is speaking out of love.”

We were all hopeful that in the peaceful, spiritual atmosphere and cool temperatures of Rishikesh and with water from the Ganges, Prabhupada would recover his health. The day after he left, I wrote him, “We hope that Your Divine Grace is enjoying your stay in Rishikesh, and we hope that this letter will find you in improved health with increased appetite.”

“Mr. Mohatta came to Juhu yesterday to discuss our problems with ECC and the other contractors,” I reported. “After hearing the different arguments regarding paying or not paying ECC, Mr. Mohatta suggested that we pay them two or three lakhs now. He said that if we refused to pay anything we would have to expect a delay in the work, so he suggested we make a small payment with a note to ECC that we are still very dissatisfied with the speed of the work and that they should complete and leave so we can settle the final bill. After reading him the contract, it was apparent that all of the terms are in ECC’s favor, but at the same time he said his man would check the bills in the next few days.

“Amongst the conditioned souls Mr. Mohatta is an expert businessman, but you are a pure devotee and you have advised that we pay nothing. We are always ready to stand by your decision, but if you feel that we should take Mr. Mohatta’s advice, then we request you to send us the letter to present to Bank of America instructing them to pay ECC Rs. 2,00,000 against their bill numbers 11 and 12 for January and February. We will present this letter to Bank of America only after receipt of the next inward remittance from abroad.”

Prabhupada agreed to the proposal, but with provisions. “As Mr. Mohatta has recommended, I have enclosed a letter to Bank of America advising them to make payment to ECC for the amount of Rs. 2 lakhs,” he replied. “This letter as well as the other letter advising a transfer of Rs. 6 1/2 lakhs to State Bank of Hyderabad account, should only be presented to Bank of America after they advise you that they have received Guru Kripa Swami’s $100,000.00, and not before. But Mr. Mohatta should be shown all the bills so that he can check them. I am not at all in favor of paying them any more money until the final bill is presented.”

In regard to his health, Prabhupada wrote that yes, it was improving, but only “a very little.”

“The house that we have been given is the best in Rishikesh,” he assured us. “It is very nice, and the climate is much better than Bombay’s. Many persons are coming in the afternoons for darshan.”

Within a week, however, Prabhupada felt like he was soon going to leave his body. At 1:30 a.m. on May 16 he called for Tamal Krishna and said, “As I was telling you, the symptoms are not good. I want to leave immediately for Vrindavan. If I am going to die, then let it be in Vrindavan.”

There weren’t any train reservations available, so Prabhupada went by car with Tamal Krishna and Upendra, with Damodar Pandit driving. When they stopped overnight at the Delhi temple, devotees offered Prabhupada maha-prasada, but after just a taste, he said, “Eating is finished. I prayed to Krishna to be freed from eating and sleeping, and it is happening. I have already given up mating and defending. Now all these material activities are finished.”

On the way out of Delhi, Tamal Krishna noted that Prabhupada seemed content. “You look very happy to be going to Vrindavan,” he said.

“Yes,” Prabhupada confirmed. “Vrindavan is my home, and Bombay is my office.”

When he got to Vrindavan, Prabhupada announced that he had come to leave his body. “If death takes place, let it be here,” he repeated in his arrival address. “There is nothing to be said new. Whatever I have to speak, I have spoken in my books. Now you try to understand it and continue your endeavor. Whether I am present or not presentdoesn’t matter. As Krishna is living eternally, similarly the living being also lives eternally. But kirtir yasya sa jivati: ‘One who has done service to the Lord lives forever.’ So you have been taught to serve Krishna, and with Krishna we’ll live eternally. Our life is eternal. Na hanyate hanyamane sarire. A temporary disappearance of this body, it doesn’t matter. The body is meant for disappearance. Tatha dehantara-praptih. So, live forever by serving Krishna.”

On May 17 I wrote Prabhupada with news of Bombay and also expressed my appreciation and gratitude to him, quoting two verses:

bhavantam evanucaran nirantarah  
prasanta-nihsesa-mano-rathantarah  
kadaham aikantika-nitya-kinkarah  
praharsayisyami sanatha-jivitam

“By serving You constantly, one is freed from all material desires and is completely pacified. When shall I engage as Your permanent eternal servant and always feel joyful to have such a fitting master?” (Stotra-ratna 43, Cc Madhya 1.206)

evam janam nipatitam prabhavahi-kupe  
kamabhikamam anu yah prapatan prasangat  
krtvatmasat surarsina bhagavan grhitah  
so ’ham katham nu visrje tava bhrtya-sevam

“My dear Lord, О Supreme Personality of Godhead, because of my association with material desires, one after another, I was gradually falling into a blind well full of snakes, following the general populace. But Your servant Narada Muni kindly accepted me as his disciple and instructed me how to achieve this transcendental position. Therefore, my first duty is to serve him. How could I leave his service?” (SB 7.9.28)

Two days later, Tamal Krishna wrote in his diary, “Srila Prabhupada received a letter from Giriraj. He offered loving prayers to Srila Prabhupada, especially the prayers from Srimad-Bhagavatam 7.9.28. When Prabhupada receives such letters from Giriraj, he appreciates them very much. He closes his eyes and drinks in every word. He has so much affection for Giriraj because of his faithful service. Giriraj never became fearful even when his life was threatened. He never lefta difficult service, but remained always cool-headed, considering only Prabhupada’s desires and not his own. Ye yatha mam prapadyante, tams tathaiva bhajamy aham.”

Prabhupada called for the movement’s leaders to come to Vrindavan and be with him. He asked that they chant for him, and he made arrangements for his will and other documents and procedures to ensure the smooth and proper running of ISKCON (and the BBT) and safeguard its properties after his departure. Devotees would come to his room in shifts and do kirtan and sometimes read to him.

But even in such a condition, Prabhupada remained focused on Juhu and took action to ensure that the required funds were arriving. On May 18 he wrote Guru Kripa in Japan, “For some reason temples are not sending in as much money as was expected to the BBT. Ramesvara says that he cannot afford to send any money for completing Bombay at this time. Therefore I am hoping it may be possible for you to continue to send $100,000 monthly for finishing the Bombay project.” And he concluded, “I was staying in Rishikesh hoping to improve my health, but instead I have become a little weaker. Now I have come back to my home, Vrindavan. If anything should go wrong, at least I will be here in Vrindavan. Vrindavan is for residence, Bombay is office for organization, and Mayapur is for worship of the Supreme Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.”

Three days later, he wrote to me, in Bombay, “I am very glad to learn that you are getting great spiritual encouragement and strength. Krishna will give you all power. You have persevered throughout all difficulties and have acted as commander of our army there in Bombay and always you remained cool-headed throughout. Remain faithful and Krishna will give you all intelligence and strength how to organize everything very nicely.”

I was encouraged, but I was also extremely anxious about Prabhupada’s condition and wanted to join him and the other leaders. So within a few days I was on a train headed to Vrindavan.

There, two days after Prabhupada wrote to me, he told the devotees, as Tamal Krishna recorded in his diary, “Your love for me will be tested how after my departure you maintain this institution. We have glamor, and people are feeling our weight. This should be maintained. Not like Gaudiya Matha: After Guru Maharaja’s departure, so many ‘acharyas’came up? Later, Tamal Krishna told Satsvarupa that Prabhupada had said, “Your love for me will be shown by how much you cooperate to keep this institution together after I am gone”—the same message.

As Bhakti Charu Swami recalled, “When Srila Prabhupada was in Vrindavan during his last days, Tamal Krishna would read him the letters that devotees wrote to Srila Prabhupada, and His Divine Grace would dictate his replies, and sometimes he would also make comments. One devotee had written that he wanted to offer his longevity to Srila Prabhupada so that he could continue to be with us on this planet. It was a very sweet letter, steeped with emotion. However, Srila Prabhupada reacted in a rather unusual way and commented that our real love for him would be shown by how we cooperate with each other to continue his mission. That incident left a very deep impression in my heart, and I became aware that the best way to show my love for Srila Prabhupada is through my cooperation with the devotees of ISKCON who are serving His Divine Grace so sincerely to continue his mission.”

Prabhupada had made the same point in a letter in 1973: “The test of our actual dedication and sincerity to serve the spiritual master will be in this mutual cooperative spirit to push on this movement and not make factions and deviate.”

When I arrived in Vrindavan, Prabhupada asked me about Bombay, and I helped make the legal and other arrangements he requested. One of his concerns was that ISKCON’s properties should be protected. He brought this up the morning after I arrived, and I reported back to him later that day. “This morning you gave the hint that there might be envious persons coming to take away our properties,” I said, “so in our GBC meeting here we discussed this point. A committee of six of us was made to resolve this. Basically we made a model trust deed, which can be used for all the Indian properties. There may be three trustees for each property. And the basic point of the trust deed is that the property rests with these trustees and they have no right to sell or mortgage or dispose of the property in any way. That is the basic point. And then we have proposed the three trustees for each of the properties.”
