Prabhupada accepted the proposal, but, knowing our inexperience with such matters, especially in India, he wanted the trustees to make an advisory board of local friends—though the trustees would retain final authority.

“This is based on the BBT Trust document that you wrote many years ago,” Ramesvara said, and he read from the document we had drafted: “‘I, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Founder-Acharya of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, disciple of Om Vishnupada 108 Sri Srimad Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Gosvami Maharaja Prabhupada, and we, the members of the Bureau of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, hereby give and transfer the properties and all the property rights incidental thereto, as hereinafter described, to the following persons as trustees in trust for purposes hereinafter stated and to be administered in accordance with the provisions hereinafter set forth? And there are five different trusts. The first one is for Mayapur, and the proposed trustees are Jayapataka Maharaja, Bhavananda Maharaja, and Gopal Krishna. The second one is for Bombay, and the proposed trustees are Tamal Krishna Maharaja, Giriraj, and Gopal Krishna. The third one is for Vrindavan, and the proposed trustees are ...”

As Tamal Krishna wrote in his diary, “Prabhupada was very satisfied and said, ‘Jaya future directors of ISKCON? And later he said, ‘Now I can die peacefully? And he cried.”

Having dealt with the properties, we met the next day to consider the bank accounts. When I entered Prabhupada’s room, I could see that he was in a deep, reflective mood. “When I go to Los Angeles, I am in Vaikuntha,” he said. “When I go to New York, I am in Vaikuntha. Wherever we have got temple, that is Vaikuntha. So why shall I have objection to remaining? Do your duty nicely and see what Krishna desires. Let it be fulfilled. But you do your duty. It is your duty to pray to Krishna as affectionate children, and let Krishna decide. And I have no objection, either way. So, what is next?”

“In continuation of arranging for the properties and other things to be managed ...” I said, and Prabhupada approved suggestions for property trustees. “Then for the bank accounts, the main fund is the ISKCON Mayapur-Vrindavan fixed deposits and savings account. So, we thought that the best thing would be to have a committee to oversee the spending of this money in terms of your desire. We propose that the committee consist of Guru Kripa Maharaja, Ramesvara Maharaja, Jayapataka Maharaja, Tamal Krishna Goswami, Gopal Krishna, and myself.”

“Very good. Approved.... I think you are all competent. Very good selection. Do it.”

“Then the persons who sign the checks, they would do so according to the decision made by the—”

“Committee.”

“Yes.”

“That’s nice.”

“And then the signers would be, in Bombay, Tamal Krishna Goswami, Gopal Krishna, and myself—two out of the three. And then in Los Angeles, jointly, Ramesvara Maharaja and Satsvarupa Maharaja.”

“Very good.”

“Then for the BBT, the idea would be that the principal amount should not be touched, but the interest can be given for loan if absolutely necessary, just as you have been doing. But the idea is that that amount should always be repaid.”

“In principle. But when there is necessity, it should ... be given. Even if by chance it is not paid, don’t mind. Business should not suffer. That’s all.

“Yes.”

“If you can provide, you must, of course, see that our business is done. And then they should try to pay. If they are actually not able to pay, don’t mind. Is that all right?”

“Yes, Prabhupada,” Ramesvara said.

“The principle should be that they should return back. But if by chance they cannot, don’t press. Let them go on with their business. But don’t be lenient.” Everyone laughed at the apparent contradiction.

“They should want to pay, out of duty to you,” Tamal Krishna said.

“Krishna will give them,” Prabhupada said. “You are increasing the book sales. That is Krishna’s favor. Krishna is assuring, ‘Don’t be disturbed about money matters; I’ll pay you.’ But don’t be very loose or extravagant. Every paisa should be spent very cautiously. That is wanted. So, it is all right.”

“So, the signers on this account would be Tamal Krishna, Gopal Krishna, and myself—two out of three,” I said.

“Don’t open many bank accounts. The same signer, one or two of them must sign the ... The accounts may be in your books, but there isno necessity of opening so many accounts and different signers. That is not necessary.”

“Right. So, these are actually the same signers as the Mayapur-Vrindavan Fund. And in some cases . . . There are different accounts distributed in different places that should be—”

“That you can keep in your books, not in the bank.”

“So all the funds can be consolidated in the accounts in Bombay.” “Yes.”

“Then for the BBT money, the decision to give out loans should be unanimously approved by all three of us—Tamal Krishna, Gopal, and myself.”

“Yes.”

“Then the accounts in your personal name. We thought that those funds could be transferred to the Mayapur-Vrindavan Fund, as you suggested, and just keep our own account, how it is spent in terms of your desire.”

“Yes. You can transfer at any moment. Do it very nicely, cool-headed. Mattah smrtir jnanam apohanam ca \[from Krishna come remembrance, knowledge, and forgetfulness\]. We shall be always prepared to take instruction from Krishna. That is best.”

That night, Prabhupada again reflected on his condition: “Bhavau-sadhac chrotra-mano-bhiramat \[“Glorification of the Supreme Lord is the right medicine for the material disease.”\]. You’ll not find any medicine throughout the universe that will benefit you whether you die or live. This is the only medicine. Both ways . . . Death is inevitable; you die today or tomorrow. So, by taking this medicine, if you die, you have the greatest benefit. And if you live, you enjoy. If you die, enjoy; if you live, enjoy. Go on chanting. I am prepared in either way.

“If you send a dhenki \[rice-husking machine\] to heaven, what will it do? The same business. Whether the dhenki is kept here or in heaven, his business is to do that 'Dag, dag, dag, dag.'”

He was assuring us that wherever he went, he would engage in chanting and hearing the glories of the Lord. Kirtan was the best medicine because whether he lived or died, was on earth or in heaven, he would enjoy such chanting and hearing of Krishna’s glories.

“I am very much confident of this medicine,” Prabhupada explained.

“Nobody is prepared to die, but I am prepared to die. That much strength I have got. Generally people do not like to die. But I will be very glad to die if Krishna wants—or to stay with you. I have no objection either way. But I am not afraid of death. That much strength I have got. Why shall I be afraid?

Bhakta-sane vasa \[to live with devotees\]. Such a great opportunity. You are all pure devotees. To live with you and to die while you are chanting—such a great fortune. So there is no question of being afraid of death.”

“Of course, we have our preference,” Tamal Krishna said, referring to the devotees’ ardent desire that Prabhupada remain with them.

“I have no objection. Whatever is His desire.”

Five days later, we approached Srila Prabhupada about his last will and testament. “We drafted a will,” I began, “including the trust for the properties of India and some of the other—”

“Will?” Prabhupada said. “Will—there will be direction that ‘Management should be done like this.’ That’s all. Nobody can say in court case that ‘This temple will be in the charge of this person, this temple ...’”

“We’ve included those points in your brief will. Should I read it? Then we can type it. ‘I, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Founder-Acharya of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, settlor of the Bhaktivedanta Book Trust, and disciple of Om Vishnupada 108 Sri Srimad Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Gosvami Maharaja Prabhupada, presently residing at Sri Krishna-Balaram Mandir in Vrindavan, make this, my last will. 1. The Governing Body Commission, GBC, will be the trustees of the entire International Society for Krishna Consciousness.”

“Instead of ‘trustees,’” Prabhupada said, “‘supreme managers,’ or ‘the ultimate managers’—like that.”

I continued, “'2: Each temple will be a trust property—’”

“Again ‘trust’ word.”

“‘ISKCON property,”’ Gopal Krishna suggested.

“Okay, we can change that wording,” I accepted. ‘“. . . and will be managed by three committee members.’”

“Yes,” Prabhupada confirmed.

‘“The system of management will continue as it is now. There is no need of any change. 3. The property in India will be managed by thefollowing committee members,’” and I read out the names. ‘“The committee members who have herein been designated are appointed for life. In the event of the death or failure to act for any reason of any of the said committee members, a successor committee member or committee members may be appointed by the remaining committee members, provided that the new committee member is an initiated disciple and following strictly all the rules and regulations of ISKCON as detailed in the books of His Divine Grace . . .’” I caught myself, realizing that the will would be in Srila Prabhupada’s name, and then continued ‘“... detailed in my books, and provided that there are never less than three or more than five committee members acting at one time. 4. I have created, developed, and organized the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, and as such, I hereby will that none of the immovable properties in India in the name of ISKCON shall ever be mortgaged, borrowed against—’”

“Why India?” Prabhupada questioned. “Everywhere. Everywhere.”

Ramesvara and Tamal Krishna discussed possible exceptions for outside India, to which Prabhupada agreed, subject to “with the consent of the GBC.”

He said that an inventory should be made of all ISKCON properties and that trustees should be assigned to each of them. “Better not to be sold,” he reaffirmed.

I continued, “‘. . . shall never be mortgaged, borrowed against, sold, transferred, or in any way encumbered, disposed of, or alienated.’”

“This is the Indian properties,” Tamal Krishna clarified.

“‘This direction is irrevocable,”’ I continued. “‘5. I declare, say and confirm that all the properties, both movable and immovable, which stand in my name, including current \[checking\] accounts, saving accounts, and fixed deposits in various banks, are the properties and assets of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, and the heirs and successors of my previous family or anyone claiming through them have no right, claim, or interest in these properties whatsoever, save and except as provided hereinafter....’”

“What should we do about the clause which appoints the executors?” I asked. “They’re responsible to see that the will is carried out.”

“How many executors?” Prabhupada asked.

“I think the lawyer suggested two or three.”

“He suggested not less than three, ” he corrected. “Up to seven or eleven. So I'll give you seven names.” And he agreed to give them after thinking it over.

When we had finished discussing the will, Ramesvara informed Prabhupada about developments in the distribution of his books. “I just received a telegram from America about the book selling,” he said. “It is from our main warehouse in Los Angeles. They report that there has been increase this month over last month. For Back to Godhead the increase has been 70 percent.”

“Hmm!”

“For small books like Perfection of Yoga, it has increased 45 percent; for medium books like Krsna trilogy and Isopanisad, it has increased 45 percent; and for the hardbound books like Bhagavad-gita and Srimad-Bhagavatam, it has doubled—a 200-percent increase.”

“This is very good.”

“That means tripled,” I added. “One-hundred-percent increase is doubled, so 200 percent—

“Tripled,” Tamal Krishna said. “Tripled, the big-book distribution.”

“Very good,” Prabhupada said.

“Simply by your word, Srila Prabhupada, it is happening.”

“Everyone is now wearing these ‘Double If buttons,” Ramesvara said. “The whole movement is simply thinking of doubling book distribution.”

“Yes, that is our real mission,” Prabhupada stated. “Yare dekha tare kaha 'krsna'-upadesa \[“Whomever you meet, tell him the instructions of Krishna”\]. That’s all. This is the opportunity of speaking the words given by Krishna. Krishna Dvaipayana \[Vyasa\] or Krishna are the same. So, that’s all right. Now no more talking.”

“Jaya Srila Prabhupada!” the devotees exclaimed.

Although I didn’t want to leave Srila Prabhupada, I had duties to attend to in Bombay, so around the beginning of June I returned by train. When I got back, I wrote Tamal Krishna, “Everyone is very anxious about Srila Prabhupada’s health. An article headed ‘Srila Prabhupada Seriously Ill' appeared on the front page of The Times of India, and thereafter many concerned sympathizers telephoned thetemple. Amoghalila Prabhu then issued the statement carried under the heading ‘Srila Prabhupada Now Better’ on the third page of The Times of India. Srila Prabhupada is our life and soul, so please inform us if there is any change in his health. We are continuing 24-hour kirtan.”

The first Times of India article had made Prabhupada’s condition sound dire:

“MATHURA, May 31: Swami Bhaktivedanta Prabhupada, organizer of the ‘Hare Krishna’ movement in India and abroad, has been brought to Vrindaban in a serious condition from Rishikesh. Several of his disciples from Mayapur and Delhi ashrams have arrived here.

“The 85-year-old swami has established a temple in Vrindaban.

“The inaugural function of the Sanskrit university built by Swami Prabhupada has been postponed.”

Three days later, another article appeared, quoting Amoghalila: “The health of His Divine Grace A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, ‘although apparently poor, is not critical, and in fact has improved since he left Bombay last month,’ according to a statement issued in Bombay on Thursday by the International Society for Krishna Consciousness.”

After two weeks, I wrote Prabhupada, thanking him for allowing me to come to Vrindavan, expressing my concern about his health, and informing him of people’s responses in Bombay. “We wanted to thank you for calling us to Vrindavan,” I wrote, “though we are all very perturbed by your bodily condition. When we returned to Bombay we found that The Times of India had carried an article about your illness on the front page, and that everyone in the city was experiencing transcendental anxiety for Your Divine Grace. Susheel Asnani was especially upset. He has been reading your books very intently and decided to completely reform his habits according to your direction. He is eager to take initiation from Your Divine Grace and prays that he will have that opportunity. Similarly, Sri K.J. Somaiya was ready to leave for Vrindavan when he read the news. Solicitor Merchant immediately started to pray for your health and mentioned that she has been living just so she could read your translation of the Tenth Canto. In general, the entire population of Bombay has been merged in the ocean ofremembering your merciful pastimes and chanting your transcendental glories. I have sent a newsletter to all the members requesting them to pray to Krishna for your improved health and long life.”

I also shared my own thoughts and reflections—and the recent developments, progress, and plans in Juhu: “From these incidents we have concluded that you are indeed the Supreme Personality of Servitor Godhead. Every functioning organism must have an active living principle. Generally that living force is called the soul, and due to the presence of the soul, the body’s activities develop. When the soul departs, the body is dead. This same process operates in every functioning entity, be it the tiny body of an insect or the gigantic form of the universe. In the ant the living energy is called jiva, and in the universe Krishna.

“We find that while Lord Krishna is the soul of the universe, Your Divine Grace is certainly the soul of this planet. Srimad-Bhagavatam states:

jivan chavo bhagavatanghri-renum  
na jatu martyo ’bhilabheta yas tu (SB 2.3.23)

Only the dust from your lotus feet gives life to this planet.

savau karau no kurute saparyam  
harer lasat-kancana-kankanau va (SB 2.3.21)

Only because you are engaging us in devotional service do we have life. The soul is the living principle in the dead body. Since you are the living principle on this planet, we conclude that you are the soul of this planet. ‘You are the life and soul of all the inhabitants of Vrindavan. So because You have left Vrindavan, all of the servitors of Your lotus feet there are suffering. It is as if the lakes filled with lotus flowers have dried up from the scorching heat of separation from you.’ Without Your Divine Grace this planet is dead. You are like the Supersoul, as Lord Krishna is sarvatma, the soul of all souls. When Lord Krishna expanded Himself as a duplicate set of cowherd boys and calves, all the residents of Vrindavan loved their new ‘sons’ and ‘calves’ more than their original ones. In fact, they loved the new ones just as they loved Krishna. Sukadeva Goswami explains that we love our children, friends, society, etc., because they are all expansions of our selves, but first of all we loveour selves. And why do we love our selves? We love our selves because the self is an expansion of Krishna. Therefore Krishna is the supreme lovable object.

“We think that Your Divine Grace has the same quality as Krishna, that you are the dearmost personality on earth. I am not saying this just because I am your disciple; actually, everyone feels this way. I first had this realization when Mr. Nair sent a prostitute to entice me. She was placing her hands on different places of my body and I was affected by the desire to enjoy. I am such a rascal that I was thinking, ‘Let me enjoy. I know that Krishna will punish me, and I am ready to face that suffering. But let me enjoy now.’ But then I considered, ‘If I do this, Prabhupada will suffer,’ and the thought of you suffering was so painful to me that I rejected my foolish ideas. That was the first time I realized that you are just like sarvatma, more dear to the living entity than the person himself. And now the people of Bombay are experiencing the same phenomenon, that they are more concerned with your life than with their own.

“The activities in Bombay are gaining more and more momentum. The preachers are enrolling more and more members, and we have purchased two more Ambassador cars to facilitate their work. The construction is more and more taking its final shape, and everyone is anticipating the grand opening in October. We met Mr. Mohatta to discuss checking the bills and paying the ECC, and he suggested that we pay ECC Rs. 2 lakhs or Rs. 3 lakhs per month after checking their actual work for that month. He said that the margin of approximately Rs. 10 lakhs that we owe to ECC should be maintained, and that at the end of the work we can ask them to reduce their final bill. We also met the mayor of Bombay, and he has set the mechanism in motion for giving us the ten-foot access area as per their usual rates. He also said that he would give us a concession on municipal taxes for our religious and educational activities, and he requested us to give him a separate application for that. Our committee has also discussed arrangements for the grand-opening ceremony. Surabhi Swami and Gopal Krishna Prabhu will be meeting you in Vrindavan and they will give you any more details that you might want.”

On July 7 I wrote Prabhupada, “As your most unfortunate and foolish servants, we are trying to take your hint to meet regularly as a committee. We say that we are unfortunate because in spite of being in this movement for so many years we have failed to acquire a taste for hearing the message of Vasudeva. And we say that we are foolish because we have accepted this material body, we are inexperienced, and we are foreign. Therefore we are completely dependent on your guidance, and we pray for your mercy:

susrusoh sraddadhanasya  
vasudeva-katha-rucih  
syan mahat-sevaya viprah  
punya-tirtha-nisevanat  
(SB 1.2.16)

“We have discussed amongst ourselves and wish to appraise Your Divine Grace of the following situation:

“We have to spend a further sum of Rs. 58,00,000 by the first week of November in order to complete the project in time. Ramesvara Swami is committed to sending a further sum of Rs. 42,00,000 by the first week of November, and Gopal Krishna Prabhu agreed at Mayapur to raise the balance Rs. 16,00,000. From experience we know that Ramesvara Swami’s final installment of Rs. 6,00,000 may reach late, and Gopal Krishna Prabhu’s Rs. 16,00,000 may take up to two years. Therefore we had to consider how to ensure receiving the Rs. 22,00,000 so that we could open the project in time. Considering the urgency of the situation, we did not want to leave anything to chance. Therefore we decided to request Your Divine Grace to sanction a loan of Rs. 22,00,000 against our deposits at Bank of America, to be given to us as follows:the first week of August  - Rs. 6,00,000the first week of Sept. - Rs. 6,00,000the first week of Oct. - Rs. 6,00,000the first week of Nov. - Rs. 4,00,000

“Ramesvara Swami’s final installment of Rs. 6,00,000 due in November can be used to repay Rs. 6,00,000 of the loan from Bank of America, and we propose that half of his future remittances from January through March also be used to repay the loan. From Aprilwhatever balance remains to be repaid on the loan (about Rs. 4,00,000) can be paid from the local Bombay collections and BBT profits in the intervening months, and as such your valued deposits would be safe. Then the extra money taken from Ramesvara Swami’s December to March remittances could be reimbursed from Gopal Krishna Prabhu’s pledge of Rs. 16,00,000....

“We pray that Your Divine Grace will consider our situation and guide us accordingly.” The letter was signed by Surabhi Swami, Gopal Krishna, Bali Mardan, and me.

Twelve days later I wrote, “I hope that Your Divine Grace is enjoying the Vrindavan atmosphere, filled with peacocks, desire trees, and surabhi cows. You must be experiencing transcendental ecstasy in the association of Krishna, Balarama, the cowherd boys, Srimati Radharani, the gopis, and all the other inhabitants of Vrindavan, pure devotees who are simply absorbed in chanting, hearing, and remembering the glorious pastimes of the Lord.

“Your new Centre for Vedic Culture and Education is manifesting its real form. Surabhi Swami has conceived of such a beautiful plan, and now it is actually taking shape. Most of the marble has already been fixed in the darshan mandapa and courtyard, and work has begun on some of the small domes. Maharaja says that the inside marble work can be completed in two months. The large domes also should be ready for the grand opening, and Surabhi Swami will be checking the progress when he goes to Makrana at the end of the month. Many of the guestrooms are practically finished. Mainly the furnishing work remains, and the decorators are now completing three sample guestrooms. These rooms are so attractive that anyone would be eager to stay in them. We expect that many gentlemen will contribute for such rooms after the project opens, and that the whole world will rush to experience the wonder of Hare Krishna Land. Our regular committee meetings are creating an auspicious atmosphere for opening the project on time....

“We are planting 200 more coconut trees to beautify the land and increase the yield, and we anticipate an additional Rs. 15,000/- per year from the coconuts....

“Jayantilal Mankar is organizing the World Vegetarian Conference in India this year, and he wants to bring all 500 delegates for at least one day for prasada and meetings at Hare Krishna Land. He will alsoencourage the delegates to stay in our guesthouse, and he is giving us a booth at their exhibition at Cross Maidan. He wants to sell your books, make propaganda, and earn.

“Some of our boys have been very successful selling your books to wholesale distributors and retail shops. Some have also arranged with bank managers to sell your books to all of their staff. We also want to contribute to DOUBLE IT!!

“Our Sunday Festival Program is becoming more popular every week. More and more people are coming to relish the sublime mercy of Lord Chaitanya and the holy name. From 4:30 am to 9:00 pm we have a continuous program of kirtan, aratis, lectures, book distribution, prasada distribution, and philosophizing. To accommodate all the guests at the love feast we now have two complete servings in the temple, as well as an exclusive serving on stainless steel, in our special rooms for distinguished guests. While we serve one group, we give the other group a tour of the new building. Many gentlemen immediately volunteer to become members of our society, and some are asking to contribute for guestrooms....

“Whenever we write you we meditate upon your greatness and are overwhelmed. We cannot even begin to imagine your position of transcendental knowledge and bliss. We can only thank you again and again for engaging us in these small services and in writing reports because only in this way we are able to reciprocate in love with the spiritual master, or Servitor Godhead.”

Eight days later, I wrote again: “We are writing in pursuance to our letter of 7-7-77 and in reply to Tamal Krishna Goswami’s letter of 17-7-77. The matter now is very urgent.

“We again wish to request a loan of Rs. 22,00,000 against your fixed deposits. The information given in our letter stands correct, and we need only the loan already requested by us. In the event Ramesvara Swami’s November remittance reaches in time, we will not require your last installment, but whenever his November remittance comes we can use it to repay the loan. Ramesvara Swami also confirmed by telephone that he will send the additional $200,000 after the temple opens for the purpose of repaying the loan. Gopal Krishna Prabhu will be meeting you in Vrindavan to discuss the actual formalities involved in takingthe loan.” The letter was signed by Surabhi Swami, Gopal Krishna, Bali Mardan, and me.

In Vrindavan Prabhupada was hearing reports of increased book distribution and of the devotees’ prayers for his health. He also liked getting our regular Juhu updates. “Srila Prabhupada always keeps you within his heart,” Tamal Krishna wrote me, “and I know how much he appreciates hearing from you as often as you like to write.”

He was still hardly sleeping, in the heat staying up on the roof and translating most nights. But with encouragement from the prayers and positive reports, and care from a local kaviraja, an Ayurvedic doctor, his appetite increased and there was some improvement in his health. And within a few weeks, as unexpectedly as he had announced his decision to go to Vrindavan, he said that he wanted to return to his preaching in the West.

The devotees taking care of Prabhupada were concerned about him traveling, and his doctor was opposed to the idea, proposing that he at least wait until winter, when his body would respond better to his treatment, but Prabhupada was determined to go. His plan was to visit London for Janmashtami and Vyasa-puja; then New York, the Gita Nagari farm in Pennsylvania, and Los Angeles; and then Hawaii, where the pleasant climate would facilitate his work on Srimad-Bhagavatam.

“You will be amazed to know ... that it is almost definite that Srila Prabhupada is coming to the West immediately,” Tamal Krishna wrote Ramesvara on August 22. “Throughout the world, all devotees are praying, ‘My dear Lord Krishna, if You desire, please cure Srila Prabhupada.’ The love of his disciples is the greatest medicine and is having the most wonderful effect on His Divine Grace. Although physically he is in very poor health, he is being kept alive by the love of His devotees. In one letter, Pancha Dravida offered his youth in exchange for Prabhupada’s old age. Upon hearing this, Srila Prabhupada said, ‘I have no old age. We are of the same age. It is not depending on old or young body—the atma has no old age. We are all Vaikuntha men. All new boys—nava-yauvana.’ In all of the letters which are daily received, the devotees are all praying to Prabhupada to please remain with us. Srila Prabhupada said after hearing one of these prayers, ‘I think I will have to stay on your request. Krishna is very kind—He is bhakta-vatsala. So manydevotees are praying, their prayers cannot be frustrated? Although the traveling will be very difficult upon Srila Prabhupada, he is requesting me now daily to take him under any condition to the West.”

Two days later, he wrote me, “By the time you receive this letter Srila Prabhupada should have already left India. I could not inform you earlier of His Divine Grace’s plans, because Srila Prabhupada was thinking to go one day and then not to go the next. It was only three days ago that His Divine Grace actually decided definitely to leave India. His reason is that he feels the change will be good for his health, as will a cooler climate. But most of all he wants to be in his Western temples with the Western disciples, because he feels that this will enthuse him and give him new life. Srila Prabhupada says that he wants to see our society a little stronger, and by his going around the world, even if he does not speak but is simply present, this will make our society stronger and thus it will endure permanently. So now once again you will have to serve His Divine Grace in separation.”

“While he is overseas I request that you write very often,” Tamal Krishna continued, “as Prabhupada is always thinking of Bombay. The other day Srila Prabhupada said, 'I was thinking why I have neglected the West for so long. It is because I had to persist in Bombay.’ Actually, for the last six or seven years Srila Prabhupada’s main work besides translating has been the Bombay temple. So you must keep him continuously informed of all the events and activities, with full descriptions, photographs, and anything else you can send which will allow Srila Prabhupada to see through your eyes.”

One morning Tamal Krishna saw Prabhupada gazing intently at the Deities, and afterward asked him what he was praying. “I was praying to Radha-Gokulananda,” Prabhupada replied, “to please engage me in the service of Sri Sri Radha-Rasabihari.”

A week after receiving Tamal Krishna’s letter, we wrote to Prabhupada, “We are pleased to inform Your Divine Grace that the work is progressing nicely and that the public are anxiously awaiting our grand opening. At this stage we again have to propose that Your Divine Grace loan us Rs. 10,00,000/- from your monies in India, and we, your servants of the Hare Krishna Land Committee, guarantee to repay the loan. We do not want to borrow any money from the

U.S.A., nor do we want Ramesvara Swami to repay any loan for us. We want to take the loan on our own account, and we ourselves pledge to repay it. The reason we want the loan is to ensure that the mission of Hare Krishna Land is successfully fulfilled. We have spent so much money to build Hare Krishna Land because we want to attract the fallen souls to the lotus feet of Krishna. Specifically, we want them to purchase Your Divine Grace’s books and associate with the Supreme Lord and His pure devotees. If the building is incomplete, we will be unable to attract people as we could if it were complete. We wanted to increase the prestige of our movement, but if we open and have to try to function in an unfinished building, we may actually become a laughingstock.

“The reason we want to borrow the money and then repay it over time rather than just finish the building over time is we can save money and trouble by allowing the workers who are already here to continue in the same way that they are now working. Having brought them here, now to send them away would add to the expense of the work, as well as to the problems, so we feel that we would rather allow the work to finish as planned. In the past months we have already undertaken to raise Rs. 3,00,000/ to Rs. 6,00,000/ for the new Deities as well as for equipping and staffing the new restaurant and guesthouse. In other words, we have accepted some financial responsibility for the new project, but we never thought it necessary to mention this particular point.

“In conclusion, we pray that you will consider our plea and cable your decision.”

Prabhupada had been supplying funds for the Juhu construction, and he was emphatic that he would not give more than his specified limit. But as hard as we tried to control the expenditure, we still ended up needing considerably more funds. I was in a dilemma and did not know what to do, so I consulted Tamal Krishna. He said that I was the only one who could get Prabhupada to give the funds and that the best approach was for me to phone him in England. So I did—before our letter could reach him. I apologized to Prabhupada for having to ask for more funds, and I gave my personal guarantee that I would repay the loan.

Prabhupada agreed, and on September 5, at Bhaktivedanta Manor, he drafted a loan agreement:

I, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami, Founder-Acharya of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, am giving a Ioan of Rs. 16,00,000/-(Rupees Sixteen Lacs only) for the purposes of the completion of the Temple and Guest House at Hare Krishna Land, Juhu, Bombay. The Management of ISKCON-Bombay will pay this loan back, with the first payment due on the 30th of November 1977. The loan will be payable over a period of two years in twenty-four equal installments with 10 percent interest charged. As the loan was given in three parts, one in August, one in September, and one in October, 10 percent interest will also be charged for loaning these amounts through November, 1977. The Monthly Installment payable is Rs. 75,533/39 (Rupees Seventy-five thousand, Five Hundred and Thirty-three and thirty-nine Paisa only).

Below the main text of the document were places for each of us to sign—Prabhupada, me, Gopal Krishna, Bali Mardan, and Surabhi Swami. Prabhupada was meticulous in business dealings, even with his disciples, showing us by example how we should deal with money— Krishna’s money—in the material world.

The same day, Tamal Krishna wrote to Svarupa Damodara in America, “Srila Prabhupada is resting very nicely here at Bhaktivedanta Manor, which he said is his nicest house in the world. The atmosphere is wonderful, very serene, and Srila Prabhupada is resting in a way that he was unable to do in India, completely free from any worries. He also very much enjoys the loving association of all his disciples here, to whom he gives darshan every day from 8:30 to 9:15 in the morning in front of Sri Sri Radha-Gokulananda. Srila Prabhupada will be probably coming to the U.S. quite soon, perhaps in a week’s time.”

Away from India, Prabhupada also reflected on his struggles there. “I am doing such a great work,” he said, “and they are suspecting that I have brought some CIA.”

“I just read that news in a Hindi newspaper here,” an Indian devotee said, “that in Nadia they have got themselves a Krishna conscious ashram for CIA, and Bhavananda, he worked in high-portal rank in Vietnam, and all this. The communist people, they are against us. So they are . . . The government should try to encourage our movement, rather than trying to stop it.”

“I have so much disgust that I don’t wish to return to India” Prabhupada stated. “I have got enough people to work here in Europe and America. Why shall I have to protect myself from these obstacles offered by the government? A different energy is lost. They are foolish government servants. Recently they have asked me for an explanation: ‘You have acquired some residential land, so explain, or we shall punish.’ Agricultural land in Mayapur, say about two, three bighas \[about ten acres\], we have made a pavilion for prasadam distribution. What will be produced on two or three bighas land? Say practically, how much rice will be produced? Say about thirty maunds \[around 2,400 pounds\] rice. So, thirty maunds rice—how many people can you feed throughout the whole year? Hmm? And we are preparing thirty maunds of rice every week. Without any production, they are eating ready-made food, three thousand per week. How many people are we feeding? Throughout the whole year? How many?”

“Three thousand per week, fifty-two weeks,” Tamal Krishna replied.

“One hundred and fifty-six thousand,” the Indian devotee said. “So, why does the government not see this, that we’re giving something?”

“I am just speaking, all the government officers are rascals,” Prabhupada said. “They have no common sense. Suppose stopping for a few thousand, not over a hundred, and we’re feeding so many thousands. So, what is the loss there? I am asking explanation. They have stolen . . . Such government men are . . .” Prabhupada made a sound of disgust.

“Their only business is to harass,” Tamal Krishna said. “And take money.”

“Should we protest and fight against them?” the Indian devotee asked.

“How can I protest against them?” Prabhupada said. “It is folly to be wise where ignorance is bliss. So many rascal government servants, and their determination is to put obstacles in the way of this movement. It will be impossible to build. My best energies are lost. They are always putting some obstacles.”

“Like what happened in Juhu,” Tamal Krishna said. “How much energy you had to expend simply for the building of one project. How much? No one in their whole life could have expended as much energy as you spent there.”

“So, considering all these points, from the very beginning, their suspicion and putting obstacles, I have no more desire to return back. It is my heart’s desire—not the least desire to go back to India again.”

“But how can we spread this Krishna consciousness there?” the Indian devotee asked. “In India also we need it.”

“Whatever I have done is done; now do. But I do not wish to return back to be governed by these nasty laws. Most nasty. And now I can live here very comfortably. I can live in America very comfortably. Finished. In India, oh, they have put me into so much uncomfortable position that sometimes I cried. ... By such treatment I have lost my health.” Prabhupada was practically weeping as he spoke.

“Last year what I saw and compared to this—I couldn’t believe the report,” the Indian devotee said.

“I can die in London. . . . Everyone is a rascal, magician. They do not know what is God, what is bhakti, how to perform it. So, cent percent I am disgusted. I do not wish to return to India any more. For the next—next is death. In the morning when I sit down, there are nice devotees chanting Hare Krishna. I have seen. Radha-Gokulananda. If I die in London, that is my great fortune. Why should I return to India, to feel always botheration, anxiety? Whatever I have done, I have given my will and purpose of honor; you try and maintain it. Otherwise, I have no desire—nothing. I have no such sentiment, ‘This is my country, this is my ...’ If I would have been driven by such sentiment, nobody leaves Vrindavan in this condition of life. I have no special love for India. I am not that materialistic, nationalist, or ...”

“It is a pleasure to be here because of the devotion,” Tamal Krishna said. “The devotion is everywhere, in all of these devotees.”

“There are so many nice devotees here. I am so much pleased how the boys and girls are enjoying spiritual life, dancing wonderfully. Here also the Indians are not coming. So why shall I have a special affection for India?”

“The last six or seven years you have labored so hard in India with unbelievable obstacles in each place—in Mayapur, in Bombay, in Hyderabad, in Vrindavan. Everywhere so much opposition. I don’t think the American government ever gave any such opposition.”

“They are civilized. These are nasty, all third-class, fourth-class men. They have no common sense with such motives. Even if we stopped feeding a few hundred men, we’re giving regularly prasadam for so many lakhs of people, and still they’re asking explanation: ‘Why you are ... ?’ Such nasty people are in the government. And they are the heads of the government. How can you expect good behavior from them?”

Tamal Krishna summarized Prabhupada’s journey and stay at Bhaktivedanta Manor in a letter to Hamsaduta: “Srila Prabhupada arrived here in London on the 27th of August. The ride was very difficult, taking eighteen hours due to a six-hour delay caused by the strike in the London airport. However, His Divine Grace tolerated the ride and arrived all right. Srila Prabhupada was so much pleased to be in the West with his Western disciples, and he felt very much enlivened to see them and the wonderful way they are conducting Krishna consciousness here. He also very much enjoys staying at the Manor, which he says is his best house in the world. The atmosphere is very peaceful and restful, and Srila Prabhupada is not at all bothered by any anxiety, as is always the case when he is in India. Just as you are experiencing difficulties in dealing with the Indian government there, Srila Prabhupada has had so many difficulties in his various projects, with the Government in India. Practically they have never been cooperative at any time. So now He is feeling quite relieved by being outside of India. His health, however, has not very much improved.”

And on the same day, he wrote me, “Srila Prabhupada has just undergone a minor surgical operation which seems to have come out successfully. His Divine Grace is resting, but is very, very weak, at least as weak as he was in Vrindavan. Please pray for his recovery and have all the devotees there also do so.”

Meanwhile, Tamal Krishna had been making arrangements for Prabhupada to go to America. But the day after his Vyasa-puja, Prabhupada’s health took a downward turn and he couldn’t even go down to the temple room. Then, the following day, he said, “If I live a few days more, let me see the opening of the Bombay temple. We can wait here, then fly to Bombay. I have worked so hard for it. If I see the opening and then die, it will be a very peaceful death. And if Ilive, I can come back here.” And when Svarupa Damodara arrived from Boston the following day, Prabhupada told him, “I want to return to India, to Bombay.”

Within two days, Prabhupada and his party were on a flight to Bombay. When they landed, Gargamuni, Bali Mardan, Haridas, and I met them on the tarmac with Prabhupada’s car. The immigration and customs procedures were handled right there, and within minutes, Prabhupada was on his way to Hare Krishna Land.

I had told the devotees not to go to the airport for Prabhupada’s landing. There wouldn’t be a greeting, and when his car came through the gates in Juhu, they shouldn’t rush and greet him there either but should stay in the background.

Upon arrival, Prabhupada proceeded straight to his quarters (the elevator was now working) and went right to bed. He called for me, and I came and sat on the floor beside him. He spoke about his time in England and the kirtans there. “They were wonderful,” he said. He also told me that K. J. Somaiya had come to visit him in Vrindavan and upon seeing his bedridden condition, had started to weep. When I asked if the hammering and chiseling and other noises of the construction would disturb him, he replied that it was like music to his ears. He then closed his eyes and lay back to rest.

When Prabhupada awoke toward the end of the day, Tamal Krishna also asked him if the noises were bothering him. “These sounds do not disturb me at all,” Prabhupada said, “because I am thinking that work is being completed. You can note the distinction, how in London I was feeling restless, but not here. It is because I like Bombay. Of all the cities in India, I like it the most.”

When Abhirama told Prabhupada that his Juhu quarters were fit for Indra, the king of heaven, Prabhupada smiled broadly and for a long while. He was beaming, and Abhirama sensed that he was feeling “a little proud and quite happy.”

“You can arrange for one or two men to have kirtan in my room when I sleep,” Prabhupada told him, “so if I die, I can be hearing.”

“Srila Prabhupada,” Abhirama replied, “from my observations, it appears that you just have not become accustomed to old age. You couldlive this way for a very long time, simply lying in bed, preaching to disciples, and seeing different devotees, and we would take care of you?’

“I have no objection,” Prabhupada said. And as Abhirama was massaging his back, he commented, “This massage gives me a little relief. Otherwise, there is no relief.”

“Srila Prabhupada,” Abhirama said, “my giving service to you is giving me relief from my miserable material existence,” and Prabhupada smiled. Abhirama told him that he had read that a sick person could get strength from a healthy person through massage, and Prabhupada nodded yes. “We disciples are ready to give our lives,” Abhirama continued. “Otherwise, we would be wasting them in sense gratification.” And again, Prabhupada agreed.

Prabhupada spent the whole next day in bed. He did not speak and hardly moved. Despite drinking juice, milk, and Complan (a nutritional milkshake), he had no strength. When Tamal Krishna asked him how he was feeling, he said simply, “Crisis.”

The following morning, Prabhupada asked for his japa-mala and kept the beads around his neck all day, even while resting in his bed. During his massage, he fingered the beads and chanted silently.

He had asked for kirtan in his room, but when two devotees who we thought were good singers came and chanted, Prabhupada had them dismissed, saying that their kirtan was dead. Then he had Lokanath come, and he very much appreciated his kirtan. And that night he called for Tamal Krishna and asked him to sit next to his bed and chant japa with him.

Prabhupada’s physical condition seemed to be worsening. The next day, he wanted to try a doctor who had cured the father of one of our neighbors, who was supposed to have been suffering from the same disease, but Tamal Krishna dissuaded him and Prabhupada agreed, saying, “Your advice is always very nice.”

“I said I felt confident Prabhupada would remain to see the temple opening and go to Vrindavan also,” Tamal Krishna wrote in his diary. “This pleased Srila Prabhupada very much, and with great feeling he rubbed my head and said, ‘May your words be blessed. Bless me that I may fix up my mind.’ How can I, who am like stool, bless the pure devotee of the Lord?”

In the morning, Tamal Krishna asked Prabhupada whether he could stay as he was in Juhu for five weeks, until the temple opening.

“If you encourage me,” Prabhupada said, and then added, “The next program is Vrindavan.”

Due to Prabhupada’s poor health, not many visitors were allowed in to see him, but that afternoon the devotees were invited to have his darshan in his quarters. They lined up and were instructed to approach him one by one, pay their obeisances, and then get up and leave without talking to him.

Prabhupada was sitting hunched over and cross-legged behind his desk, holding his knees with his arms as if to prop himself up. He was just skin and bones. “People don’t live that long,” Kanta later remarked. “They die before they get to that point. But Prabhupada just kept going.”

Word spread that Prabhupada was in Bombay. Sridhar Swami arrived from Hyderabad, but Prabhupada wanted him to come only for darshan and not give a report. When Tamal Krishna asked whether he would see any important guests, he said that he would see only Bhogilal Patel and Kartikeya Mahadevia.

Within minutes, as if on cue, Kartikeya showed up, and he and Sridhar went in together. Seeing Prabhupada’s deteriorated condition, Kartikeya was uncharacteristically silent until, at Prabhupada’s request, he described the political climate in India.

Prabhupada asked to be raised up, and he showed an unusual amount of interest in the topic. After hearing Kartikeya’s report, he commented, “They are missing the point. The whole world is. This is the disease of the body. One party is no better than the other. It is stool, one side or the other. What can they do?”

One of Prabhupada’s previously regular visitors was Smriti Warrier, who, at the age of twelve, remained very attached to him. She was accustomed to bringing Prabhupada his breakfast every day and pretty much walking in anytime, but now his staff was not allowing visitors, and although Prabhupada had been in Juhu for days, she had not been able to see him. One evening, she came and they would not let her in. So she just stood there crying.

When Tamal Krishna saw her, he understood the situation and said, “Okay, go ahead.” But he cautioned her, “Be very quiet; he’s taking rest.

Just go in and come out.” Prabhupada was sleeping when she went in, so she simply stood there for a few moments, looking at him. He was lying there, and she saw him calm and peaceful, not feeling pain. So she grasped his feet for a moment and then turned and ran. “I don’t know if I woke him up or not,” she said years later, “but I just grasped his feet and ran out; I just grabbed the mercy. And that was the last time I saw him.”

Although Prabhupada’s visitors were being closely monitored, when a young Muslim who had been helping our Society in Iran came for darshan, Tamal Krishna let him in, thinking that encouraging him might help Atreya Rishi’s program there. But when the man asked Prabhupada whether everything in his books was true and then asserted that there were many incorrect statements, because they did not agree with the Koran, he was ushered out. Tamal Krishna was surprised that such a person had been engaged to translate Prabhupada’s books, and Prabhupada agreed that he should not be permitted to do so.

The following day, Tamal Krishna wheeled Prabhupada out on one of the verandahs, wanting to give him some fresh air and a change of surroundings. But Prabhupada asked to be brought back to his bed after only a minute.

Soon after, I became ill, and I was confined for some days to my small room at the back of the property. From the day I had come to Krishna consciousness, I had never listened to any songs besides those written by the Vaishnava acharyas, but a devotee had recently given me a tape by Mangalananda, and while recuperating on the floor of my room, I decided to listen. One song, “Hidden Worlds,” was about going back to Godhead, and I played it again and again, thinking of Srila Prabhupada.

The song began with a description of what devotees are like, what they do, and what happens to them, what result they get.

Selflessness relieves distress

The gentle rain of happiness

Puts out the burning fire of life

Transports the soul beyond all strife

Past starry night and cruel death

For those who give their living breath

Upon their lips the holy name

In praise of He who came

To them a store of bliss is known

And hidden worlds to them are shown.

Then there was a description of the spiritual abode, the life that is our goal:

Where love supreme fills every eye

Sweet jubilation fills the sky

As dancing milkmaids and cowherd boys

Play in forests green with joys

Of bael and jackfruit lily white

An endless full-moon nectar night

Of dancing magic loving smiles

And gopi damsels' playful wiles

They sport in lotus lakes with He

Whose glances taste of ecstasy.

I was sad that Prabhupada was so sick and might soon be leaving us, but I was also heartened by the thought that he was going back to Godhead—though in one sense he was already there. And I also considered that it was my destination, too. One day I too was destined to join him there.

I knew where Prabhupada was going, and I knew this was my ultimate goal and destination, but I had no idea when I would reach it. I also wondered what would happen after Prabhupada left. I even thought, What will happen to me? He was my savior and protector, and I felt anxious, uneasy, and unsettled about what would happen after his departure. At the same time, as I lay there, I felt ashamed of and disappointed with myself for worrying about myself so much and for having so little faith.

Although Prabhupada was not able to go down to the temple to see Radha-Rasabihari, he daily asked to see Their photo, on which he meditated with love. One morning, after Tamal Krishna had given him his bath and put on his tilak, he held Radha-Rasabihari's picture andchanted the Gayatri mantra, taking ten minutes, longer than usual. Then he asked Tamal Krishna to nail the framed picture to his bedpost so he could always see Their Lordships.

On awaking the next morning, he immediately began talking. “Every living entity is suffering,” he said. “From Brahma down to the ant, there is no happiness.” Then he closed his eyes and fell back asleep. When he woke up again, he said, “Daivi hy esd guna-mayi.”

Tamal Krishna asked him whether he was thinking these things while sleeping.

“Yes,” he replied. “I was dreaming.”

“The whole machine has gone bad,” he told Brahmananda and the other assistants that afternoon. “You cannot expect me to have a young body like yours. It is material. When I was younger, I would always recover. You cannot expect me to live forever. Naturally, I can’t live. It will have to depend on Krishna. If Krishna likes, He can do anything. My request is . . . Somehow or other, I was born in a different community, a different atmosphere. You were born in a different community, a different atmosphere. I have given some idea, and you have taken it, and people have appreciated. It is standard. Now it depends on you how to spread it. The ideas, the plan, I have already written in my books. You have to take the direction and spread it all over the world. The reception is already there. If by Krishna’s grace I survive, I shall certainly help you more and more. You can request Krishna’s blessings to spare me.” When Brahmananda said that Prabhupada’s quarters were very nice and that, in fact, everything in the movement was made for his pleasure, Prabhupada replied, “I cannot take these with me. I am leaving them for you to use.”

When Gargamuni came and described how he was organizing Southeast Asia for “spiritual encyclopedia” sales, Prabhupada said, “A lion in the chase and a lamb at home. May you be blessed by Krishna.” Then he began to cry. “What I can do?” he lamented. “You are doing so much service. I can only pray to Krishna on your behalf.”

Gargamuni replied that he could find no one in the world besides Prabhupada whom he wanted to serve.

Prabhupada smiled and said, “That I could understand. You are not one to serve anyone very easily.”

Later that night, Prabhupada spoke for half an hour. “Material enjoyment is wine, woman, and flesh,” he said. “It is a very dangerous life.” Hearing an airplane overhead, he commented, “Formerly also there were airplanes—floating palaces, lakes, gardens. Kardama Muni did it just to show his wife how great a yogi he was. This 747 is nothing.”

Jayapataka arrived the next day. Prabhupada had been asking about Mayapur, and Jayapataka gave him a full report. But when he asked Prabhupada to sign a legal document in response to a show-cause notice from the West Bengal government, Tamal Krishna explained that Prabhupada had already drafted an affidavit in which he stated that everything in his name belonged to ISKCON and that he was holding it only as a benamidar, a trustee, on behalf of the Society. After he passed away, his last will would take effect. For the time being, Prabhupada wanted nothing more to do with these things.

“Now there is no other way but to make me completely aloof from all management,” Prabhupada confirmed. “There is no expectation of my living. My duration of life is finished. If by Krishna’s grace I survive, that is another thing.” He held up his arm. “Simply a bundle of bones. Whatever I drink is passed out. Now the platform for Krishna consciousness is made. If you work hard, it will succeed more and more. Distribute literatures—that will push on.”

Tamal Krishna wrote in his diary, “Though it was warm, Prabhupada was wrapped with a chaddar. He was slightly shaking all over, there was no color in his face, and his extremities were more swollen than usual. He told Upendra to call everyone in: Brahmananda Swami, Jayapataka Swami, Jasomatinandan, and myself. He asked, ‘So what is to be done as things are going on like this?’ Then he asked Jayapataka, ‘What does your astrologer say? Now you all decide.’ It was obvious that we had to take a new direction in Prabhupada’s care. After some discussion, we decided to take up Ayurvedic treatment again. We must locate the best available vaidya in Bombay. Jasomatinandan Prabhu was dispatched to find him. After consultation, he met with Giriraj, then called Sri K. J. Somaiya, who suggested his own family physician, Ram Gopal Vaidya from Lonavala.”

Early the next afternoon, K.J. Somaiya arrived with the vaidya, who took Prabhupada’s pulse and diagnosed the disease as a problem with the kidneys and liver. He prescribed various things to eat anddrink—sandesh, mosambi (sweet lemon) juice, mung water, barley water, papaya, chiku (sapodilla), raisins, fig water, and Horlicks malted milk—and Ayurvedic medicine.

The devotees were not very happy with the vaidya, who chewed pan while taking Prabhupada’s pulse, and after he left, Tamal Krishna expressed his doubts to Prabhupada, saying that he wanted nothing to do with the man. Because the vaidya spoke only Hindi, Prabhupada had asked Jasomatinandan to be present, and Tamal Krishna said that Jasomatinandan should deal with him.

Prabhupada chided Tamal Krishna, saying that this mood of noncooperation was not good; we should all cooperate and follow the vaidya’s treatment for eight days, knowing that Krishna could act through him. Most vaidyas were like that, he said, but after all, he was sent by Krishna, and if Krishna liked, He could work through him. We should follow whatever he said and try to work cooperatively.

Tamal Krishna pointed out that the vaidya would again be out of town for five days, during which time Prabhupada’s disciples would attend to him.

Prabhupada said that two men should be assigned, so that there wouldn’t be any strain. When Abhirama told him that Kuladri had offered to make sandesh, Prabhupada’s eyes opened wide, and he said, “Yes, have him make,” and when it was ready, he ate some of it, and a few spoonfuls of chiku and papaya.

He seemed hopeful to try the treatment, but the whole night his sleep was disturbed by too much mucus and his inability to move his bowels. He called for Tamal Krishna in the morning and said that the vaidya was no good; his prescription had created many problems. What was to be done? he asked. Tamal Krishna, Abhirama, and Upendra tried various measures to ameliorate the situation, and Prabhupada felt some relief.

There was kirtan in Prabhupada’s room that evening, and, as Abhirama described, “All of us felt the ocean of ecstasy that Srila Prabhupada was floating in.”

After being in Russia for three weeks, Gopal Krishna returned with his report. A book about Hinduism had been published there, including a photo and three pages about Prabhupada and ISKCON. It portrayed us from the typical communist viewpoint of religion, but the maha-mantrawas included. “Thus delivered!” Prabhupada said with approval. And many important libraries had taken large orders of Prabhupada’s books, as had the Indian embassy.

That afternoon, Prabhupada had Tamal Krishna read from Srimad-Bhagavatam. He sat up in bed, put on his reading spectacles, and for the next hour held Radha-Rasabihari’s photo and meditated on Them, occasionally leaning back with his eyes closed, while listening. This was the medicine he wanted.

Tamal Krishna could see how much Prabhupada had relished the reading, how, when listening, he had seemed completely transcendental to thoughts of his body. And subsequently, when Tamal Krishna suggested that he read again, Prabhupada said, “This is the most important thing. Read as much as possible.”

The following day, Prabhupada was completely exhausted. Mucus was filling his whole system, and his legs and hands were swollen. Attending him, Tamal Krishna felt almost hopeless.

Prabhupada asked for caranamrta from the Deities, and in the afternoon the devotees had kirtan and read from Srimad-Bhagavatam. Later, Sri K.J. Somaiya came with Sri Prabhudas Patwari, the governor of Tamil Nadu and a strong advocate for abstinence and moral virtue. They were shocked to see Prabhupada’s condition, and Prabhupada asked them to return the next day.

Prabhupada himself acknowledged that his condition seemed to have gone from bad to worse, but when we went in to see him the next morning, he had, to everyone’s surprise, improved considerably. He had slept soundly through the night and looked well-rested. And the mucus was practically gone.

Prabhupada called for Somaiya and the governor. He spoke to them about ISKCON and asked them to help arrange visas so his foreign disciples could stay in India. They requested that he see the vaidya again, and he said he would do so.

Afterward, he asked Abhirama what he thought. Abhirama did not like the vaidya, but he spoke carefully, expecting that Prabhupada would follow the vaidya anyway. Because the treatment was given in love, Prabhupada would feel some obligation to reciprocate.

Prabhupada told Abhirama that shastra dictated that one should not overlook the advice of a big man. “Governor means favored by Krishna,'' he said. “Governor means big man. No one can become a big man without being blessed by Krishna. You should not ignore the advice of a big man.”

Abhirama considered that there was an instruction for him in what Prabhupada had said. And Prabhupada resumed taking the vaidya's medicine.

As Prabhupada’s illness had worsened, he had gradually put more trust in his personal servants, especially Tamal Krishna. And as Tamal Krishna later remembered, “he gave me the ultimate vote of confidence by letting me hold the key to his desk drawer.” Everyone who served Prabhupada closely knew the importance of that key, which he used to secure his most valuable possessions and which he always kept with him.

One day, Prabhupada asked Tamal Krishna for something that was locked away. But when Tamal Krishna went to retrieve the item, he couldn’t find the key. “I was completely bereft of the desire to live,” Tamal Krishna recalled. At first he didn’t tell Prabhupada what had happened. “I scoured Hare Krishna Land,” he said. “I went everywhere looking for that key, and I had people looking everywhere. But we could not find it. Finally I went to Prabhupada and said, ‘Srila Prabhupada, I have to tell you something.’”

“Yes?” Prabhupada inquired.

“Srila Prabhupada, I lost the key.”

“Call the GBC,” Prabhupada said. “Call the whole GBC here to decide what should be done.”

Oh, God, Tamal Krishna thought. Call the whole GBC? He couldn’t figure any way out of it. Okay, he accepted. I'm just going to call the whole GBC body to Bombay, and when they come they can decide what to do with me.

But just then, when he had almost run out of hope, Tamal Krishna considered, Let me try another key. And sure enough, the other key opened the lock. Like many locks made in India, this one could be opened by more keys than one.

Tamal Krishna ran to Prabhupada. “Srila Prabhupada, I opened it, I opened it!” he announced. He begged for another chance to hold the key, and Prabhupada agreed.

“Now put the key on your brahman thread,” Prabhupada directed, and Tamal Krishna did it. “Don’t ever lose this.”

Prabhupada’s condition was such that he could hardly accomplish even small efforts. When he had to sign a letter to a bank, his hand was so unsteady that Tamal Krishna suggested that he give power of attorney to someone to sign on his behalf. Prabhupada consented and named Tamal Krishna and me.

In the evening, as Prabhupada lay in his bed, Brahmananda and Tamal Krishna recounted to him the history of Hare Krishna Land. Though weak, Prabhupada listened carefully to each word as they described how he had persevered and triumphed over so many obstacles. “That dog,” he interrupted at one point. The devotees did not know what he meant. Was he referring to Nair, or Mhatre? Then he explained that when he had been staying in the company guesthouse next door to Siri Krishna Kapoor in the Juhu Scheme, he would ride each morning in Mr. Kapoor’s car to Juhu Beach, and he had to sit next to Mr. Kapoor’s large German shepherd dog.

As Prabhupada spoke, both Tamal Krishna and Brahmananda realized that even in bed he was still conducting a battle. He was fighting for life so that he could preach for Sri Sri Radha-Rasabihari. As Tamal Krishna was leaving, after offering his obeisances, he exclaimed, “All glories to Krishna’s great soldier!”

The next day, Prabhupada told Tama Krishna, “I am thinking to go to Vrindavan and be treated by my kaviraja there. What do you think?” Tamal Krishna suggested that such a move should be considered by other disciples as well, and Prabhupada asked him to call them immediately.

Tamal Krishna, Brahmananda, Surabhi, Gopal Krishna, Hari-sauri, Upendra, Abhirama, Kuladri, and I sat around Prabhupada’s bed, and Prabhupada asked each devotee to give his view on Prabhupada’s going to Vrindavan. Tamal Krishna spoke in favor of going. He pointed out that even if Prabhupada were to remain in Bombay, in his present condition he would not be able to attend any of the functions. Further,

Prabhupada, the world acharya, was known for his powerful preaching, and it would not be fitting for the public to see him in his present condition. And, he added, Prabhupada could come back later.

Prabhupada listened without comment.

Brahmananda said that Prabhupada should definitely go to Vrindavan.

Hari-sauri said that he felt it was difficult to decide; that it depended on how strongly Prabhupada wanted to stay in Bombay as opposed to doing what was best for his health.

“It is for health,” Prabhupada responded, and Hari-sauri immediately said that he was in favor of Prabhupada’s returning to Vrindavan.

Gopal Krishna disagreed, saying that it would be better if Prabhupada remained in Bombay until after the opening. How could he leave Bombay when so many arrangements had been made and so many important guests had been invited?

Surabhi also favored Prabhupada’s staying, because he wanted him to see the temple opening. If Prabhupada went to Vrindavan, he pointed out, he might not come back.

When it was my turn, I said that in Bombay, with the constant noise from the construction, each day was difficult for Prabhupada and each successive day would be even more difficult. Therefore, I concluded, waiting three weeks would be too risky.

As I spoke, Prabhupada was moving his head in affirmation.

Abhirama spoke in favor of going to Vrindavan, and Upendra said he didn’t know.

For the most part, Prabhupada mainly listened, not expressing any personal preference. Next he wanted to discuss the best course of treatment. His old friend Dr. Ghosh from Allahabad had written, and Tamal Krishna read aloud that Dr. Ghosh advised that Prabhupada should go to Jaslok Hospital, the best in Bombay, for a thorough check-up and treatment.

“So, what is wrong with this proposal?” Prabhupada asked.

Tamal Krishna said that the doctors would probably want to give intravenous feeding.

“What is the use of artificial feeding when there is no digestion?” Prabhupada asked.

Making a point in favor of hospital, Tamal Krishna remarked that although Ayurvedic medical science was perfect, the practitioners had lost the science and now were mostly quacks, whereas allopathic medicine, although imperfect, had many expert practitioners.

Prabhupada conceded the point, and there was more discussion, but in the end he concluded, “Hospital is not a guarantee, but still we take it as up-to-date scientific knowledge. My godbrother Tirtha Maharaja had to undergo all these treatments, and they were very proud that he died with the latest scientific treatment. My guru maharaja, however, did not like it when he was given injections. He objected, ‘Why are you giving?’ Going to a hospital means giving in to the mercy of the material scientists. Whatever they like, they will do. They cannot guarantee, and we cannot be confident. And going to Vrindavan—whatever may happen, let Krishna do it. Hospital is a chance technique. Going to Vrindavan, I have no objection. But now, here, there is a dilemma—I am neither dying nor living.”

When Tamal Krishna questioned whether the Vrindavan kaviraja was any better than the present one in Bombay, Prabhupada replied, “Better or worse, some husband must be there.”

Then Tamal Krishna offered a new argument, that Prabhupada’s staying in Bombay meant a purpose for his living—to see the opening of the temple—whereas his going to Vrindavan was only for dying.

“That is only a sentiment,” Prabhupada said. “Living or dying is not in your hands or mine.”

The devotees understood that Prabhupada had decided, and they were there to support him.

“Vrindavan,” Prabhupada said. “Let’s go.”

“Yes, Prabhupada,” Surabhi agreed.

“But Srila Prabhupada,” Tamal Krishna said, “what about the devotees here? They will not want to be separated from you, but then how will they be able to work on the opening of the temple? I mean, all the devotees, when they hear you are going to Vrindavan, will want to come.”

“Yes, they can come,” Prabhupada replied. “I have no objection.”

Tamal Krishna mentioned that a thousand devotees, from all over the world, might want to come to be with Prabhupada, which would slow down ISKCON’s work. Would that be all right?

Again Prabhupada said, “Yes. I have no objection. They can come. We can accommodate them.”

“But then again,” another devotee suggested, “there may be devotees who feel they can serve you better and please you more if they stay where they are and distribute books.”

Prabhupada replied that devotees could do that also. He was giving them the freedom to choose, according to their individual inspiration and realization.

Was it compulsory for the GBC members to come? Tamal Krishna asked.

Yes, Prabhupada confirmed; it was.

There were no more questions, and the devotees offered their obeisances and left to make preparations for Prabhupada’s moving to Vrindavan. Only Kuladri remained.

“So, Kuladri,” Prabhupada asked, “what do you think?”

“I feel like an intruder,” Kuladri replied. “I shouldn’t even be here. But it seems to me that you are waiting for Krishna to make some decision on whether you stay or go.”

“What?”

“It seems you are waiting for Krishna’s decision. If you are going to wait for Krishna’s decision, you might as well be in Vrindavan.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada said, as he smiled and closed his eyes. “That is very good advice.”

Hari-sauri was dispatched to Vrindavan to get everything ready, but he phoned the next day to inform us that the road from Delhi to Vrindavan was closed, precluding the possibility of flying to Delhi and then driving the rest of the way. .

After some discussion, the devotees decided that Prabhupada should go by train from Bombay. With Mr. Gupta’s help, they booked a compartment in the first-class section on the Deluxe, leaving at 11:00 the next morning. Brahmananda, Bali Mardan, Kuladri, Nayanabhirama, some others, and I were booked in the air-conditioned chair-car class.

I phoned Dr. N. D. Desai and asked him to bring a large car to drive Prabhupada to the train station. I explained to him that Prabhupada was going to Vrindavan to leave his body.

That evening, when Mr. Asnani came with the notary for Prabhupada to execute the power of attorney, I had not yet returned from the city, and despite Tamal Krishna’s urging that he proceed without me, Prabhupada refused to sign the document without my okay.

The terms were clear and straightforward:

1\. I am the Founder-Acharya of International Society for Krishna Consciousness and Settlor/Trustee of the Bhaktivedanta Book Trust and President/Chairman/Trustee of various charitable institutions connected directly or indirectly with International Society for Krishna Consciousness having branches throughout the world.

3\. \[There was no 2.\] As Founder-Acharya for International Society for Krishna Consciousness and Settlor/Trustee of the Bhaktivedanta Book Trust, many properties, immovable and moveable, bank deposits, bank accounts, are in my personal name which in fact are owned by the aforesaid institution and do not personally belong to me.

4\. Due to my old age I am desirous of appointing Joint Attorneys for me and for International Society for Krishna Consciousness and Bhaktivedanta Book Trust in the manner hereinafter appearing.

NOW KNOW YE ALL THESE PRESENTS WITNESS: that I, the said A.C. BHAKTIVEDANTA SWAMI PRABHUPADA, Founder-Acharya of International Society for Krishna Consciousness and Settlor/Trustee of the Bhaktivedanta Book Trust and President/ Chairman/ Trustee of various other charitable trusts in which I am directly or indirectly interested do hereby NOMINATE, CONSTITUTE and APPOINT TAMAL KRISHNA GOSWAMI (Thomas Herzig) and GIRIRAJ DAS BRAHMACHARY (Glenn Teton), my disciples, (hereinafter called “the Joint Attorneys”) as my true and lawful attorneys for me and on my behalf as well as on behalf of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness and the Bhaktivedanta Book Trust to do all or any of the acts, matters and things and to exercise all or any of the powers and authorities hereby conferred upon them ...

I reviewed the document and approved, and Prabhupada signed.

Early the next morning, Prabhupada had to sign a number of letters to the bank. And with those also, although Tamal Krishna had approved them, Prabhupada wanted my consent. Tamal Krishna took itthat Prabhupada was showing us that we must do all important business jointly, together.

Around 9:30 Prabhupada’s assistants escorted him downstairs. Hundreds of devotees were waiting on the ground floor, and they wept when they saw Prabhupada, many for the last time.

Dr. Desai, who had arrived with his big Dodge, was shocked and pained to see Prabhupada’s emaciated state. “Here is the person with whom I fought and argued,” he reflected. “Here is the person who was such a fine debater that he was like a lion who could defeat anyone philosophically.” He was reminded of Krishna’s description in the Bhagavad-gita of a person who withdraws within like a tortoise pulling his limbs into his shell.

Dr. Desai had personally cleaned his car—a first for him—and his wife had arranged silk bedding, flowers, and incense. When Prabhupada came down, devotees were crying, devastated by feelings of imminent separation. Dr. Desai felt like the “cruel” Akrura, who took Krishna from Vrindavan and the gopis. But it was his duty and he knew he had to do it.

Brahmananda sat next to Dr. Desai, with me next to him, and then Tamal Krishna, by the window. Prabhupada was lying on the back seat, with Upendra sitting on the floor next to him.

“Drive very slowly,” Tamal Krishna told Dr. Desai. “The Bombay roads have potholes, and Prabhupada will be uncomfortable if you drive fast. His nerves are pressing on his bones. There is hardly any flesh or fat. He is mainly skin, nerves, and bone, with very little muscle.”

When Dr. Desai slowed down, however, Upendra told him, “Prabhupada wants you to drive faster,” and he picked up speed.

But the moment Dr. Desai hit the accelerator, Tamal Krishna objected. “I told you to drive slowly,” he said. “What are you doing? Slow down.”

“Upendra just told me that Prabhupada wants me to drive fast.”

“No, no, no. Go slowly.”

So Dr. Desai slowed down, but then Upendra said, “Prabhupada says go faster. Why aren’t you going faster?”

Dr. Desai was in a predicament. But he considered that Prabhupada was the person he had to serve, so he sped up again and told Tamal Krishna, “You sort this out with Upendra and allow me just to drive.”

Because of our speed'and early start, we reached Bombay Central thirty-five minutes ahead of the scheduled departure and thought we had arrived with too much time to spare. I had my assistant Rama Tulasi go with Dr. Desai to the stationmaster to get a wheelchair to take Prabhupada from the car to his special cabin on the train.

“Is the Deluxe leaving at 11:00?” Dr. Desai checked with the stationmaster.

“Didn’t you read today’s newspaper?” the man replied. “It’s leaving at 10:30.” The timing had changed that very day.

Dr. Desai looked at his watch and exclaimed, “There are five minutes left! The train is leaving in five minutes!”

“I will pay you anything,” he told the stationmaster, “but hold that train. Don’t let it start until I tell you.”

“What? I’ve never heard such a request.”

“There is a big team coming. A very holy person is going to leave his body in Vrindavan, and he has to be on that train.”

“Leave his body? What do you mean?”

Dr. Desai and Rama Tulasi ran back to the car. “The train is leaving a half-hour early today,” Dr. Desai told me.

“No,” I said. “According to the timetable, it leaves at 11:00.”

“Whatever it says there doesn’t matter. The stationmaster is going to blow his whistle, and the train is going to go.” So we ran to the platform.

Some devotees had come ahead and gotten Prabhupada’s special cabin ready. Unfortunately, it was not an air-conditioned car. We knew that Prabhupada didn’t prefer AC, but in this case he really needed it.

We got Prabhupada into his compartment just minutes before the train was to pull out.

Dr. Desai had not had any food or water since 4:30 that morning, and he was extremely thirsty. He bought a Limca soda from a stand on the platform and was just about to drink it when Upendra rushed up to him and said, “Prabhupada wants to see you.” Dr. Desai left the drink and hurried into the cabin, wondering why Prabhupada was calling him.

“Come closer,” Prabhupada said when Dr. Desai entered.

When Dr. Desai came right up to him, Prabhupada said, “Thank you for driving me.”

Dr. Desai was touched. Prabhupada was about to give up his body, and except for this small service, Dr. Desai felt that he hadn’t done much of anything. He was overwhelmed with the feeling that he must surrender to Prabhupada at that very moment. In front of everyone, he paid full obeisances on the floor, caught hold of Prabhupada’s feet, and put his head on them.

“Don’t touch his feet,” Tamal Krishna told him.

“No,” he said. “This is it. This is the last chance I’ll ever get.” And looking up at Prabhupada, he said, “Prabhupada, I surrender to you. You are my spiritual master.”

Prabhupada put his hand on Dr. Desai’s head and blessed him. With what meager strength he had, he raised himself up a little on one elbow and smiled sweetly.

The train started moving, and one of the devotees alerted Dr. Desai that he had better get off; the next station was quite far. So he reluctantly jumped off, and then he watched the train until the last car disappeared in the distance. With tears in his eyes, he returned to his car and got in. “And lo and behold,” he later recalled, “there was Prabhupada’s garland on the steering wheel. He had not forgotten me. He was so kind and considerate that he left the flower garland he was wearing on the steering wheel. I kept that garland for a long, long time.
