“That was the last time I saw Prabhupada. From 1971 to 1977 I was fighting with him, debating with him, arguing with him. Finally, at the end, I surrendered.”

## Chapter four

Vrindavan— The Final Journey

OCTOBER-DECEMBER 1977

## Back in Vrindavan

WHEN SRILA PRABHUPADA ARRIVED AT THE Mathura station, Brahmananda carried him in his arms from the train to a waiting car. The devotees gathered to greet Prabhupada at the temple were distressed by how much his condition had deteriorated in the month since they had last seen him.

Prabhupada proceeded directly to his sitting room, where a large bed had been set up. He lay still with his eyes closed for some time, surrounded by his senior disciples.

After a long silence, he quoted King Kulasekhara’s prayer,

krsna tvadiya-pada-pankaja-panjarantam  
adyaiva me visatu manasa-raja-hamsah  
prana-prayana-samaye kapha-vata-pittaih  
kanthavarodhana-vidhau smaranam kutas te

“My Lord Krsna, please let me die immediately so that the swan of my mind may be encircled by the stems of Your lotus feet. Otherwise, at the time of my final breath, when my throat is choked up with cough, how will it be possible to think of You?” (Mukunda-mala-stotra 33)

“I was remembering the discussion we had—all of your disciples and you,” Tamal Krishna said, “when we were considering whether we should go to Vrindavan or not—how we were all giving different arguments, one side or the other. Then we all concluded that the best program was to come to Vrindavan. And now I can see it was the right conclusion, because I feel that we are at home. Here it is home. Krishna and Balarama are here.”

Prabhupada indicated his agreement.

When the time came for the temple bell to ring but Prabhupada didn’t hear it, he said, “This is my concern, that such a huge, huge establishment, if not properly, regularly, managed, then everything will be finished.” He had been insisting for years that the temple authorities arrange for the regular ringing of the bell and considered it a test of their management.

“I don’t think that that’s going to happen,” Tamal Krishna responded. “We’re too much indebted to you to allow what you have established to become spoiled.”

“Please see to that.”

“Yes, Srila Prabhupada.”

“In this condition, it is impossible for me.”

“All you should have to do is just think about Krishna and Balarama.”

“Yes. Kindly give me that chance. In this condition, I cannot even move my body on the bed. Only this chance you should give me: Let me die a little peacefully, without any anxiety. I have given in writing everything, whatever you wanted—my will, my executive power, everything. Disaster will happen if you cannot manage it. Hmm?”

“We do not want any disaster to happen,” Tamal Krishna said. “Our only business as your sons and servants is to maintain what you have established. Even if we don’t increase it, if we just can maintain it...”

“Yes.”

“You’ve done so much. Even if it’s just maintained, it will be a great credit. We shall be proud if people will say that ‘These young men are fit sons of their guru maharaja.’ That would be our great pride if people will say that of us, that ‘They were worthy sons of their guru maharaja.’”

“I must thank you that you took me to London and again brought me without any difficulties,” Prabhupada said. “That’s a great credit for you. For that I am thanking you, that in this condition, a bundle of bones, you did it. Krishna will... So, you will have kirtan now?”

“Yes, Prabhupada. I’ll bring the little kartals.”

Later, Tamal Krishna reassured Prabhupada, “The bells are being rung on time, on the hour and the half hour.”

“It is going on?” Prabhupada asked.

“Oh, yes,” Aksayananda, the temple president, assured him. “Everything’s going on nicely.”

“Where is that Dr. Sharma?”

“He’s here,” Tamal Krishna said. “Did that milk give you any mucus, Srila Prabhupada?

“No.”

“That’s good.”

“It is very, very good,” Prabhupada said about the milk.

“Really fresh.”

“Hmm. If I drink this milk twice, morning and evening, I think I can avoid any food.”

“You don’t like fruit juice?”

“I mean to say, I can drink in the meantime, but by simply drinking this milk, I can live healthy. I think so.”

“Saintly persons in the past did adopt that policy. They were living simply on milk. Are you feeling all right?”

“Yes.”

“You are happy to be in Vrindavan, I think. You look very natural, being in Vrindavan, Srila Prabhupada.”

“Hmm,” Prabhupada agreed.

A week later, Prabhupada stopped drinking. He didn’t make any announcement; he just stopped. Previously, he had said that when his father had wanted to leave his body, he had stopped drinking, and that this was a bona fide way to proceed when the time came.

“But Srila Prabhupada,” Upendra told him, “you have to drink. If you don’t drink, you will become dehydrated.”

“Oh, you want me to drink?” Prabhupada replied. “Call the GBC.”

Abhirama informed the GBC members, and they and other senior devotees came into the room. Prabhupada said, “If I want to survive, of course I’ll have to take something. But my survival means so many inconveniences. Therefore I have decided to die peacefully.”

“Everything is in the hands of Krishna,” said Tamal Krishna. And that had been the mood, coming from Prabhupada: everything depends on Krishna. Many times Prabhupada had said that whatever Krishna desired he would accept. If Krishna allowed him to stay, he would stay. And if Krishna wanted him to go, he would go. Previously, a disciple had asked him, “You said that your guru maharaja left early because he was disgusted. Is that the case with you?” And Prabhupada had replied, “No. If Krishna allows me to stay in your association, I will be most happy to stay in your association.”

Now, however, Prabhupada opened his eyes and said, “Krishna wants me to do as I like. The choice is mine. He has given me full freedom.”

This was a different mood, a different answer. And it gave us a glimpse into the intimate reciprocation between Prabhupada and Krishna.

We all went out into the anteroom to discuss our response. “If Krishna has given Prabhupada the choice,” Kirtanananda said, “and if Prabhupada is giving us the choice, then we should ask Prabhupada to stay.”

Everyone agreed: “Yes, we should ask him to stay.”

“But all the GBC men aren’t here,” one of the devotees pointed out.

“Come on,” Brahmananda retorted. “What GBC is going to say that they want Prabhupada to go?”

So, it was unanimously decided: we would go back into Prabhupada’s room and, with Kirtanananda as our spokesman, tell him that we wanted him to stay.

Back in the room, Prabhupada was lying quietly on his bed. As soon as we finished offering obeisances, Kirtanananda broke down, sobbing. He couldn’t speak. Brahmananda, sitting behind him, rubbed his back to soothe him. Then Kirtanananda implored Srila Prabhupada, “If Krishna has given you the choice, then don’t go! We need you!”

“Is this your joint opinion?” Prabhupada asked. “Have you discussed?” “Yes,” Brahmananda said. “We have all met together. We want you to remain and lead the movement and finish the Srimad-Bhagavatam,"

Prabhupada was silent for what seemed like ages. Then he began to yawn and in the same breath said, “All right.” Just like that. And then he added, “This is real affection.”

We were jubilant, within ourselves rejoicing: Prabhupada is going to stay! He's not going to leave us!

After three days, Prabhupada’s younger sister (and godsister), Bhava-tarini-devi-dasi, came from Bengal to be with him. Prabhupada had told us that she was a pure devotee—and she was—and to address her as Pishima, Bengali for “the father’s sister.” She was respected and appreciated for her simple and pure devotion to Lord Krishna and His devotees, and her physical resemblance to Prabhupada endeared her to us even more.

Five days later, when Prabhupada asked for Bhavananda, Upendra told him that Bhavananda was outside with the vaidya. “This is Upendra and Giriraj,” he said. “We’re just with you while they’re talking with the doctor, finding out information.”

“Hmm. Giriraj?”

“Yes, Srila Prabhupada?”

“News from Bombay?”

“The activities are going on. Haridas promised that he would maintain the collections for maintenance, so he’s doing that with the help of one or two other boys. The construction is in the final stages. We had a meeting to discuss the plans for the opening and the management of the new guesthouse and restaurant and theater. I think the plans are very good.... We decided that we want to open around January, so that we can take advantage of the facilities immediately, so that the building doesn’t lie vacant.” We had proposed to open the temple in October, but the work had not progressed enough and devotees wanted to be in Vrindavan with Srila Prabhupada.

“Subhasya sighram” Prabhupada replied, quoting the well-known Sanskrit maxim that auspicious things should be done without delay. “As early as possible.”

“The reason we selected January 8 was because many important devotees, like Yasodanandana Swami, are going out of India for collecting and felt that it would be easier for them to be back by then.”

“No, no. It cannot remain vacant.”

“For the Bombay opening, is it necessary to have those South Indian brahmans?” Tamal Krishna asked. “If Yasodanandana Maharaja knows the ceremonies ...”

“Then why?”

“Guru Kripa Maharaja and others were expressing the feeling that Bombay is not like Vrindavan. In Vrindavan there are so many smarta-brahmans, but Bombay is a very materialistic, modern, Westernized city. Some of our devotees—Achyutananda and one other—had themselves been invited for opening a temple. So it was the common opinion of most of the devotees that, ‘What is the need of hiring these fourteen, fifteen brahmans?’ In Bombay, the people don’t care about this.”

“No.”

“Rather, they may be more impressed to have the Western devotees doing it, and we save so much—”

“Western brahmans.”

“Imported,” I added, and everyone laughed.

“That was my prediction,” Prabhupada said. “As they’re importing ghee and milk, similarly, brahmans also. Go-brahmana-hitaya. That’s a nice proposal.”

“Yasodanandana can do it very nicely,” Hari-sauri said. “He did it expertly in Fiji. And the Indians there were very appreciative that the Western, white brahmans had done the installation. They were telling Vasudeva, ‘Now we must take instructions from these men. They know puja.’”

“That is a good proposal,” Prabhupada agreed.

Tamal Krishna asked, “Would you like it to be opened on your guru maharaja’s disappearance—”

“Any ... as early as possible. But that would be nice, Guru Maharaja’s appearance day.”

“It’s his disappearance day,” Tamal Krishna clarified.

“The disappearance day is on December 29, which is just the time when we want to open,” I said.

“Ah, that’s nice.”

“So, we could begin—”

“We make no such distinction, disappearance and appearance.” “Except in your case,” I said. “We don’t want disappearance.” Prabhupada chuckled. “Jiva va mara va. Because we are going to accept eternity, the appearance and disappearance of this body is not a very important thing. Nitya-lila, eternal life—that is our Krishna consciousness. So, as early as possible. Use as far as possible our men, and we can keep some local brahmans as assistants. If we keep one or two South Indian brahmans, they may take it that we are doing with cooperation. One or two can be kept.... Or local brahmans. You can get local brahmans to assist us. Perform the yajna gorgeously—that’s all. If you can distribute to the important local brahmans some silk cloth and grains, they will come. And let them cook themselves and take prasadam and do that.”

“I think the local brahmans will be very pleased to be connected with the opening of such a big temple,” Hari-sauri said.

“Yes, yes,” Prabhupada agreed.

Ever since Prabhupada had arrived in Vrindavan, we had wanted to pray to Krishna to allow him to remain with us, but as surrenderedservants, we did not want to place demands on Krishna or impose on Him. So we asked Prabhupada if we could pray for his health, and if so, how.

He suggested that we pray, “My dear Lord Krishna, if You so desire, please cure Srila Prabhupada.”

We prayed day and night, sometimes with Prabhupada’s words and sometimes with our own. And I wrote a prayer, which I wanted to read to him.

When I entered his room, Prabhupada was lying on his bed as usual, and I approached Tamal Krishna.

Prabhupada heard me whispering and inquired, “Hmm?”

“Srila Prabhupada,” I said, “I wrote a prayer to Lord Krishna for your health. I was thinking of bringing it to read to you.”

“Oh, yes.”

“My dear Lord Krishna,” I read, “You are known as Yogesvara, the master of all mystic powers. So it is very easy for You to perform the impossible, as You have done many times in the past. By Your merciful glance You restored life to the boys and cows who died by drinking the water of the Yamuna River, which was poisoned by Kaliya. You swallowed a devastating forest fire to protect the inhabitants of Vrindavan. In the rasa dance, You expanded Yourself to be simultaneously present by the side of each gopi And as guru-daksina, You recovered the dead son of Your teacher. When the hunchback maidservant of Kamsa smeared You with sandalwood pulp, You made her straight and beautiful. And as a householder in Dvaraka, You expanded Yourself into sixteen thousand Krishnas and simultaneously satisfied each of Your sixteen thousand wives. When Sudama Brahman offered You chipped rice, You transformed his poor cottage into a beautiful palace suitable for the king of heaven. To satisfy Mother Devaki, You returned her six dead sons from the kingdom of Bali. And to appease the Dvaraka brahman, You also reclaimed his dead sons from Maha-vishnu.

“When Srila Prabhupada sat with seven dollars under a tree in Tompkins Square Park, You transformed that tree into so many regal palaces, and You expanded that seven dollars into millions. When Srila Prabhupada spoke Your message, You turned the mlechchhas and chandalas who heard him into Your devotees. And when Srila Prabhupada went all by himself to sell his Srimad-Bhagavatam sets, You expandedhim into ten thousand loving salesmen who worked day and night without asking any salary, and You expanded his suitcase of books into fifty-five million pieces of literature in twenty-three different languages. And then, when Hare Krishna Land was lost to the demons, You returned it to His Divine Grace.

“From these examples we can understand that for You, the impossible is not difficult. Rather, You have performed so many impossible feats for Your devotees. Therefore, if You desire, please give Srila Prabhupada a new body.”

“Excellent,” Prabhupada said. “Print in Back to Godhead. I am getting a little glimpse—He may agree to your prayer. Yes.”

Prabhupada wanted more than anything to see the opening of the Juhu temple. “If I see the opening and then die, it will be a very peaceful death,” he had said in London. But he knew that his attendance might not be possible.

“Where is Giriraj?” he asked one morning, a few days after hearing me read my prayer.

“Probably at drati, guru-puja,” Tamal Krishna said. “Now there’s a class. Should we call him?”

“No,” Prabhupada said, they shouldn’t, but a few moments later, he said, “I wanted to speak to you all. Therefore I was asking about Giriraj.”

“If by Krishna’s desire,” he began without me, “I do not exist during the Bombay opening ceremony, then the ceremony should be very gorgeously performed, and everyone should be given sumptuous prasadam—whoever comes. Of course, the opening ceremony should be performed as early as possible.”

When I arrived, Prabhupada asked Tamal Krishna to repeat what he had said.

“Prabhupada said that if he does not exist till the Bombay opening, it should be performed very gorgeously,” Tamal Krishna told me. “And everyone should be fed sumptuous prasadam, and it should be celebrated as early as possible.”

“And don’t try to cook all the preparations in the temple,” Prabhupada added. “Order the foodstuffs from a confectioner. Have a good stock and distribute.”

“All of the prasadam, or just sweets?” Tamal Krishna asked

“Sweets. There are many nice sweet suppliers in Bombay. Order them. How do you like this idea?”

“It’s a very good idea, except that we feel that you should personally be present,” I replied.

“That depends on Krishna’s desire. You are trying. I am also trying. Now it is up to Krishna-Balarama’s desire.”

“You are the jewel that will make it all gorgeous, Srila Prabhupada,” Bhagavan said.

“So, I am giving the idea.”

After a short interlude, during which Prabhupada sat up and drank Complan and asked for soft kirtan, he said, “I want association of Vaishnavas. You are all pure Vaishnavas. You have sacrificed everything, material comforts, for Krishna’s sake. That is Vaishnava. Anyabhilasita-sunyam. You have no other desire. You Europeans, Americans, you are born amongst material desires. And when you become free from material desires . . . Therefore you are all Vaishnava, anyabhilasita-sunyam. So you are so merciful.”

“Because you are a paramahamsa, Srila Prabhupada, you are seeing everyone else as surrendered to Krishna,” Jayapataka said. “But only by your mercy, you are forcing us to serve Krishna.”

The next morning, Prabhupada asked, “Baradraj is here?”

“I’m here, Srila Prabhupada,” Baradraj replied.

“You can sing Parama Karuna?"

“Yes, Srila Prabhupada.”

Baradraj took the harmonium, prayed for Prabhupada’s mercy, and began singing. Prabhupada lay with his eyes closed. At intervals he sang along, but so softly that Baradraj could not hear him. Other devotees gathered around them. “Repeat,” Prabhupada requested after Baradraj had sung through the song once, and Baradraj did—several times— after which Prabhupada said, “Thank you.”

That afternoon, when Baradraj began playing the harmonium again, Upendra conveyed the message he had received from Prabhupada: “No harmonium.” So Baradraj proceeded to sing "Gauranga" bolite ha'be without the harmonium. But when Prabhupada asked Upendra who was singing and learned that it was Baradraj, he said, “He can play.

Harmonium will go well here.” He asked to be sat up, and when Baradraj began singing an early melody that he had heard sung only by Srila Prabhupada, Prabhupada began to gently clap in time.

The following night, Prabhupada had a dream in which he saw a Ramanuja vaidya preparing makara-dhvaja medicine. As Tamal Krishna told Prabhupada’s staunch Vraja-vasi friend and supporter Vishwambhar Dayal, known affectionately as Bhagatji, “Prabhupada’s dreams are transcendental, so that means Krishna has given some idea how to get Prabhupada treated.” So, devotees began to search for that Ramanuja kaviraja.

The next day, Prabhupada dictated his purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.13.54. “Discuss Bhagavatam daily as much as possible,” he said. “Everything will be clarified. Because Bhagavata is the essence. Nigama-kalpa-taror galitam phalam. And vyasadeva-krta. Kim va parair. When he was self-realized, Vyasadeva wrote this. Maha-muni-krte. The more we read Srimad-Bhagavatam, the more its knowledge becomes clarified. Each and every verse—transcendental.”

Later in the conversation, I told Prabhupada that I had never met anyone with so many wonderful transcendental qualities. He laughed and said, “It has to be developed. Transcendental qualities are already there. Only when we are without designations do they become manifest. Svayam eva sphuraty adah. Sevonmukhe hi jihvadau svayam eva sphuraty adah. When we become prone to give service to Krishna, it becomes revealed. It is already there. Nothing is imported. Now print books and distribute. Jaya Krishna-Balarama!”

A few days later, Tamal Krishna read Prabhupada a letter he had received from Haridas in Bombay. “Gopal Krishna Prabhu showed me a voucher that ISKCON Bombay owed BBT India Rs. 70,000,” Haridas had written. “When Srila Prabhupada said he wanted to stay with us, I got greatly encouraged and had a desire in my heart to pay back this money for Srila Prabhupada. I have been encouraging all the preachers here at ISKCON Bombay to go out and collect the money to pay off this debt to the BBT. Srila Prabhupada has made all this very easy because of his encouragement to us. Even devotees who have engagements where they are not likely to make a life member are making life members and are collecting money. And even persons not expected to becomemembers are now becoming members. This is all due to the desire in the hearts of the preachers in Bombay to serve Srila Prabhupada. And by his grace, everything is coming very smoothly. This confirmed in our hearts that without Srila Prabhupada, we cannot do any single work in this movement. Srila Prabhupada gives us encouragement just by kindly agreeing to stay with us. So yesterday, on Dasami, we collected over 21,000 rupees and made ten members.”

Prabhupada laughed and said, “Very good.”

“We cannot express in English what we are feeling in our hearts,” Haridas had continued, “but we are all very encouraged to go out and collect for Srila Prabhupada and expand his Life Membership program, and we are all very thankful that he has been merciful.”

“Very encouraging,” Tamal Krishna commented. “This Haridas is transformed. You said that it was due to the mercy of a Vaishnava, Giriraj.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada affirmed. “Tumi ta’ thakura, tomara kukkura, baliya janaha more"—“My dear Vaishnava Thakura, kindly accept me as your dog.”

“Giriraj gave him his association,” Tamal Krishna explained to the other devotees in the room.

“Vaishnava,” Prabhupada added. “Chadiya vaisnava seva, nistar payeche. \[“Without serving a Vaishnava, one cannot be delivered from the material condition of life.”\] Vaishnava’s krpa. Vaishnava is already merciful. Vaishnava means merciful. Krpa-sindhu, ocean of mercy. That is Vaishnava.”

“Last night, Dr. Pathak, the dean of the College of Veterinary, said Srila Prabhupada is a touchstone who can transform everybody,” Svarupa Damodara said.

“This change with Haridas is a miracle,” Pancha Dravida added, knowing that before meeting the devotees in Juhu, Haridas had been a professional thief serving time in prison.

“Bombay is the richest city in India,” Prabhupada said. “And now they are willing to help us. So there will be no scarcity of money. Wherever you’ll go, you’ll get it.”

“That project is so nice, you don’t have to go anywhere,” Tamal Krishna confirmed. “They come to you and give money.”

“Yes,” Svarupa Damodara agreed. “That is Prabhupada’s mercy.”

“It is a long way from this grass hut we used to live in, Srila Prabhupada,” Pancha Dravida said, and the devotees laughed.

“It’s already so famous in Bombay,” Svarupa Damodara added. “Everybody knows—all the taxi drivers. You just say, ‘Hare Krishna Land, Juhu.’ Everybody knows.”

“Gradually the whole world will be sympathetic,” Prabhupada predicted. “Everyone will recognize that we are doing real service.”

The Ramanuja kaviraja arrived the next day from Calcutta. He was a middle-aged Marwari, well-educated and nicely dressed, wearing Ramanuja tilak.

Conversing in Hindi, Prabhupada asked him, “You have makara-dhvaja7.”

“Yes.”

“Please give me some and save me.”

“Definitely you will be saved.”

“In a dream I saw Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu informing me to take makara-dhvaja from the Vaishnava sampradaya.”

“Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was a Vaishnava. He was Lord Krishna’s incarnation (bhagavata-avatara). You are the king of devotees (bhakta-raja) and in His sampradaya.”

“My guru maharaja wanted me to preach. Is the preaching going on nicely?”

“Yes, very nicely.”

“Extensive preaching is going on, but some work is still pending—if you will save me.”

“Only you can do it.”

“We are ready to do it—around the whole world, in every town and village. That is why this problem has come. Look, all these foreign devotees have come. Now it is in your hands, if you will save me.”

“They are doing lots of work in Calcutta, very good preaching. It is happening in foreign countries, and in India it will surely spread.”

“Please cooperate.”

“Surely, we will support.”

“Your name?”

“Damodar Prasad Shastri.”

“As you understand from the dream, Chaitanya Mahaprabhu has given you this chance.”

“This is solely His mercy. A human being can only be an instrument: nimitta-matram bhava savya-sacin” the kaviraja said, quoting Lord Krishna’s instruction to Arjuna: “You, О Savyasaci, can be but an instrument.” (Gita 11.33)

“According to your understanding, you may treat me.”

The kaviraja examined Prabhupada, and they discussed his swelling and other symptoms, which he had been experiencing for months.

“Your whole life you didn’t care for your body,” the kaviraja said.

“I had to accept many disciples,” Prabhupada replied, “so I had to accept their karma.”

The kaviraja took Prabhupada’s pulse, then listened to his chest with a stethoscope. He advised against Prabhupada’s taking makara-dhvaja, explaining that in his condition, any medicine with mercury and arsenic would be poison. He would prescribe other medicines to control Prabhupada’s condition and anticipated that in ten or fifteen days Prabhupada would be much improved. He assured the devotees that Prabhupada would get better because, although his kidneys and liver were weak, his heart was strong. He would first repair the liver and kidneys and then give rasayana, tonic, for building strength.

After the kaviraja left, Prabhupada said, “Take his chart and try to follow. This is the last resort.”

“He seems very hopeful,” Tamal Krishna said. “They all say that your heart is very strong. Therefore, what is the question of dying? Their whole contention is that because the heart is strong, there’s no question of dying. And actually, that agrees with the astrologers. None of the astrologers say you will die now. They all say it’s a difficult time, but they never say that you will die now. They all say that you’ll overcome this.”

“That’s nice.”

“And your disciples all say that you will overcome.”

“So, I shall remain under this kaviraja's treatment. That’s all. Take his chart and strictly follow. I’ll not object; I will follow. Is that all right?

“Yes, Prabhupada,” the devotees replied.

All of us, including Prabhupada, had hoped that the Juhu temple would be ready to open on Rama-vijaya-dasami (Dasara, celebrating Rama’s victory over Ravana), on October 21, and I had informed my parents and invited them to come then for the grand opening—the culmination of my work in India. And they had agreed to come. But with the delays in the construction and with Prabhupada’s ill health, the opening was postponed.

I cabled my parents and told them that the opening had been put off and that I would inform them when a new date was fixed, so they could come then, but they never received my telegram, and I had to rush to Bombay to meet them.

Because the Juhu temple’s guesthouse was not ready, I arranged accommodations for them at the nearby Holiday Inn—the best place in the area, and quite fancy—and I introduced them to my friend Susheel Asnani, who, like my father, was a lawyer. But there was not much for my parents to do, and they felt uncomfortable in the Bombay heat and humidity, so we decided to go to Nepal.

One of our life members in Juhu, Shanta Shamsher Rana, was a member of one of Nepal’s aristocratic families, from which came, by hereditary tradition, the king’s prime ministers, and he supplied me with letters of introduction. In Kathmandu my parents, sister, and I stayed in a large, opulent hotel, The Yak and Yeti, and I would steal out in the early morning to chant and visit holy shrines—including our ISKCON temple. I helped the temple president, Prabhavishnu, by introducing him to people connected with the royal family, assisting him with the Society’s registration and other administrative matters, and working with him on strategies for further progress.

While I was away with my parents, Ramkrishna Bajaj and Shriman Narayan arrived in Vrindavan the day before the opening of their two-day Gita Pratisthan conference and came to see Srila Prabhupada.

“Are you feeling better, Swamiji?” Shriman Narayan began.

“Yes. Little, little,” Prabhupada replied. “Always two attendants are taking care. Otherwise, personally I would not . . . So, Tamal Krishna, who has got those films?”

“I’m going to arrange with Aksayananda Maharaja,” Tamal Krishna replied. “The temple has everything here.”

“Call him.” And to his guests, Prabhupada said, “Just see our activities all over the world.” And then to Tamal Krishna, “Why don’t you show them the South African article?”

“This is a temple we have built there,” Tamal Krishna explained. “We have a big farm there, as well as two temples. This is one of the temples, near Durban. They had fifteen thousand people attending the Janmashtami celebration. Here you see some go-puja.”

“Without culture, people are suffering,” Prabhupada said. “If you want to mitigate their sufferings, give this Gita culture. That is my experience. We have sold this Caitanya-caritamrta even in Russian countries.”

“Here are some of our African publications, Srila Prabhupada,” Tamal Krishna said, “published in Swahili.”

“African, Chinese, Japanese. This is really humanitarian work. We can influence the whole world.”

“What is the latest about the Bombay temple?” Shriman Narayan asked.

“We haven’t heard anything in the last two or three months,” Tamal Krishna said. “This telegram came from the former mayor Ravji Ganatra. He wrote, Tray God to give you long life to spread Indian culture in every nook and corner of the universe.’”

“That is the feeling of everybody,” Mr. Bajaj said.

“Para-upakara” Prabhupada said. “This is the mission of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, para-upakara. Especially those who have taken birth in India,bharata-bhumite haila manusya-janma yara  
janma sarthaka kari’ kara para-upakara

\[“One who has taken his birth as a human being in the land of India (Bharata-varsa) should make his life successful and work for the benefit of all other people.” (Cc Adi 9.41)\] This is Indian culture, para-upakara. Indian culture is not meant for exploiting others. Para-upakara. That is human life, para-upakara. And that is Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s mission. Bharata, especially.”

Two days later, Shriman Narayan and Ramkrishna Bajaj came to meet Prabhupada again. Shriman Narayan said in Hindi that he had explained in the conference that because of ill health Prabhupada could not address them but that he had spread Indian culture, Gita culture, all over the world, in the mood of para-upakara.

“This is Indian culture,” Prabhupada said.

“Indian culture, Gita culture—they are the same,” Shriman Narayan agreed.

“Yes. Yada yada hi dharmasya glanir bhavati. Whenever there are discrepancies in the human society—tadatmanam srjamy aham—at that time Krishna appears. Paritranaya sadhunam vinasaya ca duskrtam. This is the program. And when He comes, the time is fixed. Imam vivasvate yogam proktavan aham avyayam. This system, in Bhagavad-gita, is yoga, bhakti-yoga. Bhakti-yoga is the topmost.

yoginam api sarvesam  
mad-gatenantar-atmana  
sraddhavan bhajate yo mam  
sa me yuktatamo matah

\[Lord Krishna says, “And of all yogis, the one with great faith who always abides in Me, thinks of Me within himself, and renders transcendental loving service to Me—he is the most intimately united with Me in yoga and is the highest of all. That is My opinion.” (Gita 6.47)\] There are many yogas. The aim is to come to the topmost yoga. That is bhaktiyoga. And Krishna says to Arjuna, bhakto ‘si me sakha ceti rahasyam hy etad uttamam. ‘Because you are My bhakta and friend, therefore I am speaking to you the old system, puratanah' No new system. People now introduce new systems. They introduce their own interpretations. No.”

Shriman Narayan told Prabhupada about two Hare Krishna films they had shown at the conference.

“People of the world are hankering after this civilization,” Prabhupada said. “Unfortunately, we are misers. We are not giving them.”

“All that they should get,” Shriman Narayan agreed.

Prabhupada had Tamal Krishna read from the beginning of the fourth chapter of the Bhagavad-gita. And when Tamal Krishna suggested that he read the purport to text 2, Prabhupada approved.

“‘It is clearly stated that the Gita was especially meant for the saintly kings because they were to execute its purpose in ruling over the citizens,’” Tamal Krishna read. ‘“Certainly Bhagavad-gita was never meant for the demoniac persons, who would dissipate its value for no one’s benefit and would devise all types of interpretations according to personalwhims. As soon as the original purpose was scattered by the motives of the unscrupulous commentators, there arose the need to reestablish the disciplic succession. Five thousand years ago it was detected by the Lord Himself that the disciplic succession was broken, and therefore He declared that the purpose of the Gita appeared to be lost. In the same way, at the present moment also there are so many editions of the Gita, but almost all of them are not according to the authorized disciplic succession. There are innumerable interpretations rendered by different mundane scholars, but almost all of them do not accept the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krsna, although they make a good business on the words of Sri Krsna. This spirit is demonic because demons do not believe in God but simply enjoy the property of the Supreme. Since there is a great need of an edition of the Gita in English as it is received by the parampara disciplic succession system, an attempt is made herewith to fulfill this great want. Bhagavad-gita, accepted as it is, is a great boon to humanity. But if it is accepted as a treatise of philosophical speculations, it is simply a waste of time.’”

Shriman Narayan expressed his appreciation for how Prabhupada had presented—and people had accepted—the Bhagavad-gita all over the world. “It is really marvelous how it has happened.”

“They were hankering,” Prabhupada said. “And as soon as they got it, they got life.”

“Yes,” Shriman Narayan agreed. “They got light.”

Prabhupada’s guests asked him in Hindi if they could speak with him alone, and Prabhupada told the devotees, “You can go. They will talk with me something.” But when they went out, the devotees left the tape recorder near Prabhupada running.

“Since I met you yesterday and saw you in this condition,” Mr. Bajaj began, “a few questions appeared in my mind. We don’t know about the relationship between you and God. We don’t know when He may call you back to Him. So, I was wondering, when you are not here, who will take care of such a big establishment that you built? I mean, won’t there be someone who would take your position?”

“They all will do that,” Prabhupada said.

“They will do that. Won’t there be one particular person or a group of about five to ten people who will take your position?”

“Chaitanya Mahaprabhu didn’t say that just one person would be there. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu says, ‘You all become guru. But become gurus the way I am saying you to be. Then the movement will spread around the world.’”

“But Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was alone. And you also are alone.”

“Chaitanya Mahaprabhu said, ‘I don’t have the power; you all come and make me powerful and spread the holy name around the world.’ This is Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s teaching.”

“But what you have done—how many could do that?”

“No, it is a matter of trying. If you try, then you also can do this.”

“But God empowers someone.”

“Yes, God gives the power.”

Just then, Mr. Bajaj realized that the tape recorder was on and called one of the devotees in to turn it off. But after a while, Tamal Krishna could no longer restrain himself and walked into their meeting. Mr. Bajaj and Shriman Narayan seemed a little embarrassed—and frustrated.

After they left, Tamal Krishna asked Prabhupada what they wanted.

“That After you, who will take the leadership?”’ Prabhupada told him. “And I said, All my disciples will take. If you want, you can also take—but if you follow. They are prepared to sacrifice everything, so they’ll take the leadership. I, one, may go away, but there will be hundreds, and they’ll preach. If you want, you can also become a leader. We have no such thing, that ‘Here is leader.’ Anyone who follows the previous leadership, he’s a leader. ‘Indian’—we make no such distinction, ‘Indian,’ ‘European.’”

“They wanted an Indian to be the leader?” Brahmananda asked.

“Yes,” Prabhupada said, laughing. “‘Everyone, all my disciples, they are leaders. As purely as they follow, they become leader. If you want to follow, you can also become a leader—you are Indian—but you don’t want.’ I told them that.”

“They probably wanted to propose somebody who would take over our movement,” Tamal Krishna said.

“Yes. Leaders. All nonsense. Leader means one who has become first-class disciple. He is leader. Evam parampara-praptam. One who is perfectly following. Our instruction is ara nd kariha mane dsd. You know this? Guru-mukha-padma-vakya, cittete kariya aikya, ara nakariha mane asa. Who is leader? To become leader is not very difficult, provided one is prepared to follow the instructions of a bona fide guru.”

“They wanted us to leave the room when they were talking to you. I felt very bad when they told me to leave like that. I don’t like to leave you alone. I get very disturbed. I was standing on the other side of the door. I didn’t like leaving you alone like that. We’re trained to always be with you.”

“Deal with them very carefully,” Prabhupada warned.

“Good reason for you to remain with us, Srila Prabhupada,” Tamal Krishna said. “They won’t do anything while you are present. It’s better that you should remain with us. Then they won’t be able to do anything.”

“Krishna will protect you.”

That day, Citsukhananda brought Srila Prabhupada the latest volume of Srimad-Bhagavatam—Tenth Canto, Part Two. The volume was especially made for Srila Prabhupada, with gold embossing. While Prabhupada looked at the pictures, everyone could see the love in his eyes. And Tamal Krishna remarked, “How much love for Krishna Prabhupada has!”

My parents and I stayed in Nepal for a little over a week, then flew to New Delhi, from where they left for Chicago.

I returned to Vrindavan. When I entered Prabhupada’s room, Tamal Krishna told him, “Giriraj is here.”

“Oh. Giriraj?” he said.

“Yes, Srila Prabhupada,” I replied.

“How is your health?”

He was so kind and compassionate. Practically on his deathbed, he was asking about my health.

“I’m better,” I said. “Improved.”

“What is the news of Nepal?”

“They have a very nice program there. They have a nice house with many rooms—”

“How many rooms?”

“About nine big rooms. And they do street sankirtana every day in the main street, and they distribute literature. The Society is not yet registered there, but I went with Prabhavishnu to a lawyer, and we’ve set up the formalities for getting registered, but the government is presentlyreviewing the registration law, so it might take a few weeks before they accept our case.”

“On the whole, it is favorable, hmm?”

“Oh, yes. There is tremendous scope.”

“Hmm!” Prabhupada approved.

“The royal family is very powerful,” I continued. “They run the whole country, and, of course, they’re Hindus. So, I also went with Prabhavishnu to meet a relative of the Queen Mother, and this lady was very enthusiastic about our activities. I discussed with Prabhavishnu the strategy for how to approach the royal family. It’s a Hindu state. They don’t claim to be secular, like in India, so it is hopeful. And he has one local Nepali boy who has joined, and he’s very nice. There’s so much field for preaching. There’s the royal family, there’s life membership for the business community, there’s sankirtana and book distribution for the general people, and also there are many hippies, so we could recruit devotees from amongst them.”

“The hippies seem to still be very good customers,” Tamal Krishna said, and Prabhupada laughed.

“That’s because Prabhupada is patita-pavana” I said—the deliverer of fallen souls. “And the temple atmosphere is nice. It’s mainly sankirtana—very good atmosphere. They have a nice program. They have a Love Feast program, and many people are coming. I think they can have two or three hundred people coming very soon. And the people are very simple and good natured. Everywhere we went, people would chant Hare Krishna.”

“They recognized the devotees?” Tamal Krishna asked.

“Yes. And they’re not envious. It seems that in India many of the people are a little envious of us, but everywhere we went in Nepal, it seemed that the people were very happy to see us.”

“Have you ever been there, Srila Prabhupada?” Tamal Krishna asked.

“No.”

“You’d like to go sometime?”

“Why not?”

“Okay. We’ll include that on our world parikrama”

“The relative of the Queen Mother whom we met was also asking about people coming who could give good lectures and enthuse everyone.

So I said that you yourself would probably like to come when you’re feeling better. She was really wild about that idea.” Everyone laughed. “I’m sure that they would give you a real royal welcome.”

“It sounds like a very good field,” Tamal Krishna said.

“What about the language?” Trivikrama asked. “Is that a problem?” “No,” I replied. “The educated people speak English. In all the schools they teach English, so all the youngsters speak English in Kathmandu. And then most people in Kathmandu, even if they don’t speak English, they speak Hindi. And there are just a few who speak only Nepali. But Prabhavishnu has arranged for The Perfection of Toga to be translated into Nepali.”

“He sounds like he’s doing very well, Prabhavishnu,” Tamal Krishna said. “Good man.”

“Yes,” I agreed. “He’s very good. So he’s eager to get that in print. Then they’ll be able to distribute literature to everyone without exception.”

“Srila Prabhupada?” Tamal Krishna asked, “Do you remember when Prabhavishnu was here and you told him to go with ‘the courage of an Englishman and the heart of a Bengali mother’? He remembers those words.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada said. “These are the words of a great poet.”

“Giriraj’s parents took him there, Srila Prabhupada, and they made another offer to him.”

“What is that?” Prabhupada asked, and Tamal Krishna laughed.

“My father has increased the fortune, so he was trying to tempt me again,” I said, “but I wasn’t interested. But I think in the end he may give in to Krishna, because ... We were helping Prabhavishnu by giving him dollars, and he would give us rupees. So, we were in a shop, and my mother was making a check that she was going to give to me to give to Prabhavishnu. The owner of the shop thought that the check was for him, and he started making objections. But my father said, ‘No. In our system the husband gives to the wife, and the wife gives to the son, and the son gives to Krishna.’ Everyone laughed.” And the devotees in the room with Prabhupada also laughed.

“Just try to manage,” Prabhupada said.

“I had a very nice dream last night in which Your Divine Grace appeared,” I said after a pause. “You were walking around the premises of the Vrindavan temple, and there were some doll exhibits. You were saying that they should improve the quality of the exhibits, because thiswas their sadhana. I felt that actually you were telling me that I should improve the quality of my service and that this was my sadhana, but to be polite, instead of saying it to me directly, you were pointing to their service. And then you started to speak very directly and boldly, and you quoted the verseamara ajnaya guru hana tara ei desa  
yare dekha tare kaha ‘krsna’-upadesa

\[“Whomever you meet, speak the instructions of Krishna. In this way become a spiritual master and try to deliver everyone in this land.” (Cc Madhya 7.128)\] And you were saying, ‘This is my order, so you do it for me.’ I felt that you were saying that since it was your order and we were doing it for you, even though it was very difficult, it would be successful.”

“Anyway,” Prabhupada said, “there is a beginning in Nepal. Try to implement. What is the rent of the house?”

“It’s about twelve hundred rupees, but that’s less than one thousand Indian rupees, and it’s right on the way to the Pashupatinath temple, which is the biggest temple in Nepal.”

“Hmm. Very famous temple. People go there to see.”

“How is it on the way? Directly on the way?” Tamal Krishna asked.

“There’s a crossroads that all the traffic passes to go to that temple, and our temple is just a few hundred yards from that crossroads. It’s a bungalow. In the compound they’re growing flowers and vegetables. It’s about half an acre, but whatever land they have, they’re using. The owner of the house is a Vaishnava, and his house is next door, called Vishnu Nivas.

“Oh,” Prabhupada said.

“And when he built the second house, he wanted it to be used as a temple, and he called it Bhagavan Nivas.”

“They are taking their prasadam and living there?”

“They have a nice meal in the morning and evening, and in the day the main activity is the chanting party, and around the chanting party they distribute literature.”

After further discussion about the potential and positive points about Nepal, soft kirtan resumed.

I was a bit confused, because Prabhupada had said so many encouraging things about Nepal, including, “Just try to manage” and “Try to implement,” but I knew he wanted me in Bombay. So afterward I asked Tamal Krishna whether when Prabhupada had said those things he had been referring to me personally or to us as a movement, collectively. Tamal Krishna said that he thought Prabhupada meant the movement—not me personally. And that seemed right.

I was getting messages from Gopal Krishna that he wanted me to return to Bombay to help prepare for the temple opening, but I was in a dilemma. I wanted to be dutiful, but I also wanted to stay and be with Srila Prabhupada. I asked Tamal Krishna what I should do, but he was silent; he would not give any indication. I asked him two or three times, but he would not respond. Then I asked Jagadish, and he analyzed the pros and cons of the options, but when I asked him what the conclusion should be, he told me that I would have to decide for myself. I prayed and prayed for guidance—for some indication—and it came in my heart that I should stay on with Srila Prabhupada.

Two days after I spoke with Prabhupada about Nepal, he asked me about the progress in Bombay.

“The construction is going on,” I told him. “And this man Mr. Lord, from England, is getting more active.”

“England?”

“He’s about a fifty-year-old gentleman who was the manager of a big club in London. He had been associating with devotees in London, and they suggested he come to India and help manage our restaurant and guesthouse. He was the aide-de-camp of the viceroy of India when he was a young man, so he knows a little Hindi. He has a very distinguished—”

“Which viceroy?”

“The last, Mountbatten. And he’s very diplomatic in dealing with people. And when he meets with Indians, they immediately respect him, just like in the old days. So, I think he’ll be a very good person to have in the restaurant and guesthouse. People will be happy to meet him. He’s tall, he has a nice British accent, and he’s following our regulative principles. He’s a devotee.”

“I met him at Bhaktivedanta Manor when we were there,” Tamal Krishna added. “He came a couple of times—very nice gentleman. He’sworking without any salary. Simply he asked for a room, and he wants to devote his life.”

“Very good.”

“Real gentleman. He’s more British than any Britisher I’ve ever met.” “Forty years?”

“I think he’s about sixty years old now,” I replied. “When he was a young man of twenty, he was the aide-de-camp of the viceroy. And I think he was also the secretary to the governor of Punjab when it was under the British.”

“He met with Gandhi and all of these other leaders,” Tamal Krishna said.

“Just before I left Bombay, I spoke to Gopal Krishna, and he was arranging for Mahamsa Swami and Mr. Pulla Reddy to meet the president of India to invite him to be the chief guest, because Mr. Pulla Reddy of Hyderabad knows the present president. And then, so far as the publicity for the opening, we felt that we should actually fix up the chief guest first, because if some big person like the president comes, then that will be an important part of the wording of the invitation and the other publicity.”

“So, finishing?” Prabhupada asked.

I described what the state of things had been before I had left with my parents for Nepal: “The building was not finished. The inside of the temple, the theater, the restaurant, the lobby of the guesthouse, and many of the guestrooms will be ready, but the marble work on the domes was behind schedule. When I was there, only 10 or 15 percent of the marble on the three big domes was up, though the three domes at the entrance were almost ready. The three main domes could be finished by the time of the opening, but there will be marble work that will still have to go on.”

“It will never be finished,” Prabhupada said. “When is the date fixed?”

“We fixed the opening for January 1 and will begin the ceremonies on December 29, which is Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati’s disappearance day. The ceremonies will begin a few days before the actual installation of the Deities. Those ceremonies, or yajnas, will begin on Srila Bhaktisiddhanta’s disappearance day, in about six or seven weeks, and a few days later, on January 1, which is the English New Year’s Day and a Sunday, will be the actual installation ceremony, and thousands of people will be coming. We also discussed that there should be veryopulent prasada distribution, and arrangements for receiving people and kirtan and darshan and festival activities.”

“Still work is going on.”

“Yes. Actually, on the date we were planning to open on earlier, Dussehra, nothing was ready, not even the things we were sure would be ready. But I feel that even if some things are not ready this time, most will be. But there has to be some final date; otherwise, it will never end.”

“Brahmans?”

“Before Yasodanandana Swami left, he had written the brahmans that the new date was going to be January 1, and I spoke to Yasodanandana Swami’s assistant, Smara-hari, and he was not sure whether the brahmans had confirmed. He was going to write them today and ask them to confirm that January 1 was all right. But he received a letter from Yasodanandana Swami saying that Yasodanandana Swami would be coming December 26. So he’s definitely planning to be in Juhu in time. And when we postponed the last opening, the brahmans said that whenever we have the opening, they are always ready to come. So it seems that they should be able to come on December 28 or 29 to begin the ceremonies.”

“The brahmans must be fixed first of all.”

“Yes. He said he would write today, and this evening I’ll confirm that he wrote and sent that letter, and then, within a week, we should actually get the confirmation. Otherwise, they are very eager to do this; the only thing would be the date.”

Prabhupada was applying the same strategy for Juhu as he had for the Vrindavan temple opening, which he had explained in his purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam 6.3.25: “Unintelligent people bewildered by the grandeur of Vedic yajnas want to see gorgeous sacrifices performed. They want Vedic mantras chanted and huge amounts of money spent for such ceremonies. Sometimes we have to observe the Vedic ritualistic ceremonies to please such unintelligent men. Recently, when we established a large Krsna-Balarama temple in Vrndavana, we were obliged to have Vedic ceremonies enacted by brahmanas because the inhabitants of Vrndavana, especially the smarta-brahmanas, would not accept Europeans and Americans as bona fide brahmanas. Thus we had to engage brahmanas to perform costly yajnas. In spite of these yajnas,the members of our Society performed sankirtana loudly with mrdangas, and I considered the sankirtana more important than the Vedic ritualistic ceremonies. Both the ceremonies and the sankirtana were going on simultaneously. The ceremonies were meant for persons interested in Vedic rituals for elevation to heavenly planets (jadi-krta-matir madhu-puspitayam), whereas the sankirtana was meant for pure devotees interested in pleasing the Supreme Personality of Godhead. We would simply have performed sankirtana, but then the inhabitants of Vrndavana would not have taken the installation ceremony seriously.”

After seeing Prabhupada, I went to Mathura, accompanied by Bhagatji, to register the Bhaktivedanta Swami Charity Trust. Prabhupada had formed the trust to create good relations among the Gaudiya Vaishnavas, especially the followers of his guru maharaja, and he planned to invest money in its name so that the interest could finance the completion of different projects in Gauda-mandala-bhumi, specifically some of his godbrothers’ projects that they couldn’t complete on their own.

It was hot, and dealing with the Mathura bureaucracy was difficult, but after six hours we returned with the registered document. I left it in Prabhupada’s house and, exhausted, went to rest in my room in the temple guesthouse. I felt completely drained and wanted to forget the whole experience of struggling with the Indian lawyers, courts, rickshaw drivers, and debilitating heat.

After ten minutes or so, I was startled by a banging on my door. There was only one person it could be.

And sure enough, when I opened the door, there was Tamal Krishna— really upset. “You have made such a blunder!” he exclaimed. “Srila Prabhupada is furious. You have registered the ‘Bhaktivedanta Charitable Trust.’ That is not the name of the trust. It is the ‘Bhaktivedanta Swami Charity Trust.’ There could be so many Bhaktivedantas, but there is only one Bhaktivedanta Swami. You blew it.”

“So, what do I have to do?” I asked.

“You have to go to Mathura tomorrow and redo the whole thing—right!”

Aside from feeling chastened by the correction and apprehensive about the trip into Mathura, I felt elated. Over the years, Tamal Krishnaand I had become close friends. His interest was so closely aligned with Prabhupada’s that I just tried to be in harmony with the two of them. In my mind, my relationship with him and my service to Srila Prabhupada went together. But this incident made it clear that the center of our relationship was Srila Prabhupada and that when it came to Prabhupada’s service, Tamal Krishna would not compromise. He wouldn’t be nice to me simply for the sake of our friendship if it was at the expense of Prabhupada’s service. And that made me happy—that our relationship was spiritual, based only on Prabhupada’s service. If I made a mistake that was detrimental to Prabhupada’s service, he would let me know. I had always thought that was the case, but this incident confirmed it.

The next day, Tamal Krishna and I went to Mathura and corrected the name, and when we returned, we informed Prabhupada. “Giriraj and I were just with the registrar,” Tamal Krishna said, “and we made the correction in the name without any difficulty, so now it’s correctly given as ‘Bhaktivedanta Swami Charity Trust.’ I wanted that, because whenever we give money from the trust, I want to make a plaque with your name on it. I thought that would be a nice thing to do, and now your name will be properly given.”

The next evening, Bhagatji came to Prabhupada’s bedside and knelt near his head. “I am suffering like this,” Prabhupada said, “because of the sins of so many disciples.”

“No, Prabhupada,” Bhagatji countered. “It is stated in shastra that by chanting the Hare Krishna mantra even once, one becomes free from all sins—what to speak of these boys; they are always chanting the holy name of Krishna.”

“But Lord Chaitanya warned against accepting large numbers of disciples—unqualified disciples—for this reason.”

In response, Bhagatji insisted that Prabhupada had never accepted unqualified disciples.

Baradraj, who heard this conversation, understood that the whole exchange was meant for the benefit of the devotees, warning them not to commit sins on the strength of chanting, because it would cause suffering to the spiritual master—and when the time came, not to accept large numbers of disciples, especially unqualified ones. He furtherconsidered that Prabhupada had accepted this suffering for our sake, and for the sake of the world, and he resolved to reciprocate by dedicating his full energy to fulfilling Prabhupada’s will, or mission, and sharing Prabhupada’s gifts with others.

Two days later, I went to Delhi to open the trust’s bank account, and the following day I reported to Prabhupada, “Yesterday I spent the day in Delhi and opened an account with the Punjab Bank in the name of Bhaktivedanta Swami Charity Trust. We also gave them a letter that the interest from the ten lakhs sixty thousand should go into that Bhaktivedanta Swami Charity account. And I took the original deed of the new trust and made photocopies and got them notarized. Then I bought a copy of the income-tax act, because there’s some provision that if funds are used to restore an ancient place of worship or a place of worship that is famous in a particular state, then they are exempt from income tax. I think this fits the aims and objects of this new trust, so we should be able to get a tax exemption. Then I spoke to Bombay to see how things were doing, and Gopal Krishna said that everything is going nicely and that he’s coming here in two days. I told him that your condition was very serious and that I wanted to stay here a little longer, and he said that was okay.

“I confirmed with Yasodanandana Swami’s assistant that he sent the letter to the South Indian brahmans to confirm that they can come on the dates we have fixed. We’re waiting for their reply.”

“You can take some brahmans from here,” Prabhupada said. “They’ll chant the Vedic mantras very nicely.”

“We can have these brahmans and also the South Indian brahmans,” I suggested.

“Krishna is giving us all facilities—utilize it,” Prabhupada told Tamal Krishna the next day.

Tamal Krishna spoke about the bank that had opened in our new building at Hare Krishna Land, which Prabhupada wanted as an attraction and a facility for visitors—and as a source of income from rent. “I especially like that bank,” Tamal Krishna said, “because when you come in, in the center of the wall, instead of seeing some old grumpy-look-ing bank president, we see Your Divine Grace’s effulgent picture, andright under your picture—it’s a very big picture—it says, ‘I.O.B. \[Indian Overseas Bank\] Welcomes You.’ It’s very nicely done. And in each of the tellers’ counters, each of the cashiers’ counters, there’s a little picture of Radha-Rasabihari. Yes, it’s very nicely done. People who go there bank with confidence.”

‘And they are getting benefit,” Prabhupada stated.

“Yes. It was the proper bank to have there. And because it’s right on the ground floor, just near the entrance of the gate, people don’t mind coming from the outside. And I’ve noticed that people, after they come and do their banking business, go for darshan.”

“Very good.”

“Maybe our Deities will get known, that people who bank in our bank get more money,” Tamal Krishna said with a laugh. “I think the I.O.B. is thinking like that, that to be connected with the Deity is very auspicious, so they’re accentuating their involvement with ISKCON and Your Divine Grace and Radha-Rasabihari.”

“That’s a fact.”

“We had no idea how that Hare Krishna Land would ever be successful.”

“Yes. It was a jungle.”

“That’s what we were thinking. Why does Prabhupada want us to live in a jungle! So far away. Nothing there but mosquitoes, and so many rats. We thought, Who will come there?"

“When we construct the other building, further down, it will be of use,” Prabhupada said of the gurukula building, a seven-story structure for which Surabhi had submitted plans.

“The godown will be on the ground floor,” Tamal Krishna continued, “and residences and gurukula on the other floors. The only problem is that it’s such a good place that now we can’t get the tenants to move out of those other buildings. They say, ‘Why should we move? Now we have a temple. There’ll be a gurukula. There’s a bank.’ It’s very hard to get them out. Of course, we don’t mind if they stay, if they’re nice.”

“Gradually they’ll become devotees.”

Prabhupada returned to the topic of the Juhu temple opening: “You take four brahmans from South India, four from Vrindavan, and four from Bombay. In this way, make it gorgeous. And Yasodanandana should be head.”

“Very grand event,” Tamal Krishna said. “There is no such project anywhere else in India—or in the world.”

## A Controversy of Service

Lokanath arrived later in the day from his traveling bullock-cart program, having visited holy places throughout India. He told Prabhupada about his travels and the pleasant weather that still prevailed even in North India.

The next day, Prabhupada told his leaders, “I wish that you GBC manage very nicely and consider that I am dead and let me try to travel to all the tirtha-sthanas without any responsibility. If I recover from this malady, I shall come back—and die anyway. What is that? When the dead body is there, bring it to Mayapur or Vrindavan. Bring a little medicine—or no medicine—a little milk, and travel one place to another. And if there is death, what is the lamentation? My age is ripe. In the open air and bullock cart during daytime. You can say civil suicide. Although I am living, consider me dead for the time being. You manage. Nowadays in India there is ample sunshine. So during daytime I shall travel, and nighttime make a camp under a tree. In this way let me travel to all the tirtha-sthanas. I am thinking in this way. What is your opinion?”

“We promise that we’ll manage everything to the best of our ability,” Bhavananda said.

“No, no, you are managing, I know,” Prabhupada responded. “But you are all important men, and unnecessarily you are bound up; you cannot go. Lokanath’s party has got some experience, so let me go. In India the climate is good now. If I recover, it is very good. So, what is the wrong? If I die, then the body will be brought either to Vrindavan or Mayapur. And if I live, it will be a great end of a life. You are all experienced.”

“As much as you have trained us,” Jayapataka said, “that is only how much we are experienced. We don’t want that you be burdened any more with material management problems, but serving your—”

“No, not from that point of view. But what is the use of lying down here?”

“The kaviraja said—”

“Kaviraja may say ...”

“—that your body has got a life of six to ten years and that even a healthy cow, if kept locked up inside a room, will deteriorate?

“Therefore? Prabhupada responded with a chuckle, “I say don’t keep me locked up. You do your duty as I have trained you, and let me be free, and if money is required, Lokanath will come and take and go back again, as he is coming to take books. They have got experience in India. We can go village to village—there arrangement has to be made—but it is to be taken that I am no longer. You manage. If I live, I can come again. I shall be very glad?

“Previously it was mentioned that there was some risk in traveling? Trivikrama said.

“What is that risk? Nowadays there is no risk. What is the risk? Mm?” “Well, from the medical point of view, it’s with the organs or something,” a devotee replied. “I don’t know exactly, but it’s been considered.”

“This is my proposal.”

“That would be after you gain some strength?” Jayapataka asked.

“Free air and free movement—some change. And I can come back again in a year.”

“You will be translating while you’re traveling?”

“No. Yes and no.”

“I think it’s a good idea,” Bhavananda said. “The only factor at this point is not to take any unnecessary risk.”

“No. Freedom. As I think free, so I remain. Then when I am healthy, I shall come back again, either to Mayapur or Vrindavan or Bombay or any other place.

“You would travel by a minibus?” Jayapataka asked.

“That you decide.”

“We’ll all sit down and discuss the different arrangements that have to be made,” Bhavananda said, “plans that have to be made. It’s a very nice idea. Real sannyasa life.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada said. “You have tried doctor, kaviraja, medicine— everything. Everything has failed. Now suppose I am taking the risk of death, what is wrong? When I am dead, within India, you bring the body either to Mayapur or Vrindavan.”

“This kaviraja assures that by taking a little milk frequently during the day ...” Jayapataka said.

“I will take milk. Milk is available everywhere,” Prabhupada said, and everyone laughed. “I shall take a little milk and sleep, that’s all. If I live, that’s all right. If I don’t live, that doesn’t matter.”

“Very nice program,” Bhavananda said. “We can all accompany you at different times of the month.”

“Yes. Not very many, but you can come and go back.”

“Which holy places would you like to visit?” Jayapataka asked.

“India is full of holy places.”

“Krishna Iila, Mahaprabhu Iila.”

“And gradually go to Mayapur.” Prabhupada asked if Tamal Krishna was there, and Bhavananda informed him that he was and that he had heard everything.

“By your going to the holy places, you will purify the holy places,” Jayapataka said.

“There are two things: life or death. So if I die, where is the wrong? If there is death, that is natural.”

“For you, Srila Prabhupada, to be alive or to die is no different, because you are in the transcendental position,” Jayapataka said, “but for us, when you leave the body, we will be bereft of your association. So for us it will be very unfortunate.”

“You live by my words, by my training,” Prabhupada said, and after a pause he asked, “So, you like this idea?”

“I like it,” Hamsaduta said.

“You are very famous,” Jayapataka said. “Wherever you go, there will be crowds of people to have your darshan.”

“So they will see me,” Prabhupada replied. “I have no objection. I want a little milk from them—that’s all. And so far as my presence is required for management, I think I have bequeathed it; you can manage properly. Hmm. It is to be admitted that the so-called medical treatment is a failure.”

“All the doctors say that you defy all medical laws. Sometimes you become very weak, and sometimes you become immediately strong.”

Finally I offered my opinion: “I think this is a good idea. I don’t have any faith in the doctors and their treatments, because they’re notworking, and ultimately it depends on Krishna, and Krishna is everywhere. He can exercise His will in any condition. And, as you said, if you go out and you recover, then it’s very good. And even otherwise, if that is Lord Krishna’s decision, then this is a very glorious way.”

‘All seriously consider this submission,” Prabhupada concluded, “and let me go.”

Later in the day, Bhavananda said to Prabhupada, “We should begin the parikrama in Vrindavan.”

“Yes.”

“Because quite honestly, Srila Prabhupada, I think most of us are very worried. If you go off down the road and send us all back to our different assignments, we would not be able to serve with our full attention, knowing that our beloved father and spiritual guide was in such weak condition. So, if we begin in Vrindavan—we’re all here now—we can see, so that we know what arrangements to make for the future when you want to travel.”

“We heard that Your Divine Grace had a dream that a kaviraja of the Ramanuja-sampradaya would treat you and bring you back to strength,” Jayapataka said, “and this kaviraja says that in a very short time, following his treatment, you would regain your strength. Although he hasn’t got all the medicines yet, within a day or two they’ll all be prepared, and he says within fifteen days you should be quite improved in strength. So far, he seems to have been quite sincere.”

“No, no, he’s sincere. I’ll drink milk. Whatever strength is obtainable, there will be.”

“To follow the same treatment, only while traveling.”

“That’s not part of the treatment,” Tamal Krishna whispered.

“So, we should meet and make a program for going around Vrindavan,” Hamsaduta volunteered.

“Yes.”

“You want to begin tomorrow morning?”

“Yes.”

“If Prabhupada travels in a van, it will be very bumpy,” a devotee said. “He should have a big bus.”

“Bus?” Prabhupada queried.

“A big bus.”

“No, no, bus will not be good. Bullock cart.”

“That is very bumpy,” Jayapataka said.

“Hmm?”

“Your guru maharaja used to have a bullock cart travel from Hoolaghat up to the Chaitanya Matha,” Bhavananda said. “You told me to put a nice mattress down in the back and a cover, and lay down there. You even told me once to go to Calcutta that way. You lay down at night; you go little bit, little bit; and in the morning, when you wake up, you’re in Calcutta.”

“Bullock, you get the cow dung,” Prabhupada added.

“In this part of India it’s very cold now for Your Divine Grace,” Jayapataka said.

“Underneath the tree it is not cold,” Prabhupada countered.

“You sound like you are very determined to go, Srila Prabhupada,” Tamal Krishna said.

“Daytime we are in the sunshine, and camp underneath a tree at night. That has to be arranged.”

Tamal Krishna noted that it was 1:30 and asked Prabhupada if the devotees should take prasada, and Prabhupada said yes. He then suggested that after lunch the devotees would meet and chalk out a program for parikrama and tirtha-yatra. It was concluded that the devotees, including Lokanath, would meet at 4:00. “And then we’ll begin tomorrow. Is that soon enough?”

“Yes.”

Later in the afternoon, Tamal Krishna informed Prabhupada, “We were discussing how to make this parikrama possible, and we’ve concluded that the best thing was, as we had said earlier, to do parikrama around Vrindavan to begin. And for that purpose we sent Lokanath Maharaja and Pancha Dravida Maharaja and Trivikrama Maharaja to get a bullock cart ready.”

“Hired or purchased?” Prabhupada asked.

“For now, just hired, not purchased. Later we can make a more permanent arrangement, and it can be fixed up as nicely as possible. At the same time while we were meeting, the kaviraja also was present. So we inquired from him what he thought about this program, from a medical point of view, of course. Spiritually he is in complete agreement. Butfrom a medical point of view, he said that you would not at all be able to withstand this kind of a trip. He said that in a bullock cart, moving around, bumping on the road, you might not be able to live more than a couple of hours. He’s here now. He wanted to speak to you.”

The kaviraja asked Prabhupada what his thoughts were, and Prabhupada replied, “I am thinking that enduring in this house, day by day, all my energy is being lost. Therefore I want to go for parikrama.”

“Not just one parikrama” the kavirdja responded, “but I will arrange for two. Let your body get some energy first, then I will accompany you. Right now you are not in any condition. The other day during the temple parikrama you were feeling giddy—yesterday only you complained. Please wait for some days and get some strength first, then not only this \[Vrindavan\] parikrama but outside \[Govardhana\] parikrama. Some strength should come. Without strength, the heart will be affected the most. The heart gives energy to the whole body. I will cure your illness. In this condition, you should not go. This is my opinion.”

Prabhupada asked for Lokanath, and the devotees informed him that Lokanath had gone to Mathura to rent the bullock cart. Tamal Krishna said that Lokanath had estimated that going around Vrindavan in the cart would take five to six hours.

“Make an experiment,” Prabhupada said. “Then we shall decide.”

“Does that mean Your Divine Grace will come on the experiment,” Tamal Krishna asked, “or we should go without Your Divine Grace and experiment?”

“To see if the road is very rough and if the road is passable by bullock cart the whole way,” Jayapataka added.

“Bullock cart is not smooth,” Prabhupada said.

“Then how would you propose that we go, Srila Prabhupada?” Tamal Krishna asked.

“Come, let us take the risk.”

“Go anyway—‘Let us take the risk.’”

“As your disciples, we are all neophytes,” Svarupa Damodara said. “We don’t know what is right and what is wrong. But at the same time we feel very hopeful that you’ll get strength slowly and slowly. And this morning you were telling us that you are getting a little strength. So, weare hoping every day that ‘Prabhupada will become even stronger and be with us for many more years? So we are taking advice from kavirajaji that you take milk more and more, day by day, so that you will get stronger. The kaviraja is suggesting that when Your Divine Grace gets stronger, he will go with you on the parikrama”

“So, let us make an experiment in Vrindavan.”

“Shall we do that immediately?” Svarupa Damodara asked.

“Hmm.”

Bhakti Charu explained in Hindi to the kaviraja that Prabhupada wanted to go for parikrama by bullock cart, and then he reported to the devotees, “Shastriji’s saying that Prabhupada shouldn’t do it under any circumstances.”

“Srila Prabhupada,” Bhavananda said, “if we follow the kaviraja’s instructions and advice, then he feels that within fifteen or twenty days you will have strength. To take an unnecessary risk at this time, we have to practically appraise what will be the loss. You have said, ‘If I live or die on this parikrama, it will be glorious,’ but the loss will be that Srimad-Bhagavatam will not be finished, so many works will be unfinished. If it’s just a matter of being a little patient and waiting fifteen more days—only two weeks—then when you have strength, we can all go on the parikrama, and hopefully you’ll be able to gain more strength and finish up all of these works. But I think that the risk now, in terms of the future of the whole world, is too great.”

“Vrindavan parikrama is not a risk,” Prabhupada asserted.

Bhakti Charu translated what Prabhupada had said, and the kavi-raja addressed Prabhupada directly, “You will feel jerks on Vrindavan parikrama. Please postpone it. Observing your bodily machine, I cannot permit you to go on parikrama. My heart doesn’t allow me to give you permission. I wish to take you to Mayapur soon and then world parikrama. With this in mind, please discard the thought of parikrama now.”

“Srila Prabhupada,” Tamal Krishna said, “the other day when you went on parikrama around the temple, you became dizzy just going around the temple four times. That’s when you were even able to sit up in bed a lot more. How is it going to be possible to go for four, five, or six hours, when you couldn’t—”

“Not four, five, six ...”

“That’s how long it takes to go around Vrindavan by bullock cart. It takes three hours walking at a good pace, and it takes at least five or six hours, Lokanath says, by bullock cart. How will you do it? We couldn’t even go a half hour just around this temple.”

“No, I traveled. It takes two hours in the morning.”

“By walking.”

“Yes.”

“But not by bullock cart. That’s when a man walks very quickly—he can do it in two hours. But by bullock cart it will take five hours. You had difficulty even doing a half-hour parikrama around this temple. You became very faint. Do you think that you can go five hours in a row?”

“From Madhava Maharaja’s matha, bring Krishna dasa Babaji,” Prabhupada said, referring to his godbrother. “Then talk.”

“As your humble disciples, we are ready to take up any instruction that you’ve kindly given us,” Svarupa Damodara said, “but at the same time, you have advised us many times that we shouldn’t take unnecessary risks. Just like a few days ago you were quoting a Bengali saying that when you are doubtful, don’t do it. You instructed us.”

“That is material,” Prabhupada replied, and the devotees laughed.

“Can you tell us why you want to go on this parikramd?” Jagadish asked.

“This program seems like suicide,” Tamal Krishna said. “It seems to some of us like it’s suicidal.”

“And this is also suicidal.”

“Now you have to choose which suicide.”

“Ravana will kill, or Rama will kill. Better to be killed by Rama. Eh? That Marica—if he does not go to mislead Sita, he’ll be killed by Ravana; and if he goes and is killed by Rama, then it is better.”

“Just judging the symptoms, which is all we can do, certain symptoms have certainly improved. For instance, you’re passing more urine, stool is coming naturally, and you’re able to drink milk without getting any cough. These things were never there before.”

“That will continue,” Prabhupada said.

“So, if the treatment is continuing, if the treatment is working, why not continue it under the guidance of this kaviraja for some time? Hispoint is this. What I've seen, being your secretary all these months, is that whenever you took milk you would get cough. For the first time I see there’s no cough coming. Another problem: you couldn’t pass urine. Now there’s double the amount of urine. Another thing: you couldn’t pass stool. Now it comes normally; at least it comes without any artificial means. The one thing that has not yet come is strength, and kaviraja is suggesting what you yourself had always said: ‘If I can drink milk, I will get stronger.’ To my feeling, the kaviraja’s treatment has worked. At least the symptoms have been better under his treatment than under any other doctor so far.”

“That will work.”

“Also, Srila Prabhupada is resting better than before,” Svarupa Damodara added.

“Obviously, we’re all conditioned,” Tamal Krishna continued, “and the kavirdja is not claiming not to be a conditioned soul either, but according to him, going on this bullock cart is a suicide. He said within an hour or two hours, the bouncing and jumping of the bullock cart will cause a heart attack. You were having a little heart spasm the other day, just lying in bed two days ago. He says this going in a bullock cart, up and down, within one, two hours, it can cause heart attack. So, as his treatment has been better at least than any other doctor’s, and certain symptoms have improved, why are we giving up his advice? If you say his advice is wrong, then there’s no comment; but all along, his advice seems to have been more accurate than any other doctors that we’ve had. I mean, we who are closely around you, Srila Prabhupada—your servants, secretary—our opinion of him is far superior than our opinion of any of these others. I see that he’s able to take care of one symptom after another somewhat successfully. He’s able to deal with these problems. He can deal with the problem of not enough urine—”

“That I know.”

“He feels quite confident that you can live for six, seven more years, Srila Prabhupada.”

“We also feel very confident,” Svarupa Damodara said.

“Better that you live for six or seven years productively than that you go on this parikrama and die within two hours gloriously,” Tamal

Krishna said. “Why not live for six or seven years and then go on parikramd and die? If the parikrama can always be done, why not put it off for six or seven more years of preaching?”

“You’ve already been glorious,” Svarupa Damodara said, “all over the world. Whether you’re here or outside doesn’t really matter. You’re already glorious.”

“By your presence countless souls will attain devotional service. That’s more glorious,” Jayapataka added.

“But I think I shall be cured,” Prabhupada stated.

“Prabhupada says he thinks he will be cured by the parikrama” Tamal Krishna repeated.
