“Under the circumstances,” Hamsaduta said, “we have to consider whether Prabhupada’s opinion is more or less than the kaviraja’s. That’s what it comes down to.”

“We can’t consider,” Tamal Krishna replied. “Srila Prabhupada has to.” “If Prabhupada says that by going on parikrama he feels he’ll be cured, then how can we continue to place arguments against him?”

“Ultimately, what Prabhupada decides, we will do. As Prabhupada goes on, his disciples also go on.”

The kaviraja said something in Hindi, and Bhakti Charu explained to the devotees, “Shastriji’s saying that Prabhupada shouldn’t talk too much. It’s bad for his heart.”

“We can have kirtan until Krishna dasa comes,” Tamal Krishna suggested.

Hamsaduta led the chanting. I found his kirtans exceptionally beautiful, and I had suggested that we record them. “People always want to use some gadget,” he’d replied. “We have to keep the kirtans in our hearts.”

The debate over whether or not Prabhupada should go on the parikrama continued outside his quarters, couched in the larger question of how we as disciples should serve and relate to him. One group, led by Lokanath and Hamsaduta, felt that we should do just what Prabhupada, as our spiritual master, ordered. We shouldn’t question his order; we should just execute it. Other disciples, most of whom had been attending to Prabhupada’s personal care, felt that Prabhupada’s health would not sustain travel on a bullock cart and that, because he was so emaciated—he had practically no flesh on his bones—it would be very painful for him. Even if the devotees padded the cart with a mattress,it would still be a basic bullock cart, and the roads in Vraja were rough, so the cart’s movement would jostle Prabhupada and he would feel pain. Some devotees feared that he might even give up his body on the way. They did not want him to be subjected to what they foresaw as certain pain—and perhaps death.

I listened closely but without saying anything. I respected and appreciated both groups, and they both had good points. By nature, I was a sympathetic listener, and as each person spoke, I was sympathetic to what he had to say. Personally, I was closer to the devotees who were caring for Srila Prabhupada, so I felt especially sympathetic to their position, but philosophically I wasn’t sure: I didn’t know which side was right or even if I had to align myself with one or the other.

“The controversy and confusion were so palpable and so high,” Baradraj recalled, “that even Satsvarupa, with whom I tried to share my feelings, would not express himself one way or the other. He just remained quiet—neutral. He was reluctant even to express his feelings, because it was so intense. He said he didn’t want to be on either side. So I realized that everyone had their own private feelings and that their private feelings were more important than any public discussions about it.”

Prabhupada had been emphatic. “Let me travel to all the tirtha-sthanas” he had said. And whatever objections devotees had raised against the proposal, he had countered. “One-day experiment,” he had proposed. “Rest assured. I will not die in one day.” When even his kaviraja had predicted that he would not survive more than two hours on the ride, Prabhupada had replied, “But I think I shall be cured.” Still, Tamal Krishna, Bhavananda, Bhakti Charu, Svarupa Damodara, and others felt strongly that the “experiment” would have dire consequences. But how to convince Prabhupada?

So, the controversy continued. When Prabhupada said, “I think I shall be cured,” Hamsaduta and others took it that he was supporting their position. But the other side took it differently: “What does it mean that he is going to be cured? It means that he is going to leave his body and get a spiritual body.” Each party was seeing things in a way that supported its particular point of view.

That evening, Hamsaduta and Baradraj, concerned that some disciples were impeding Prabhupada’s expressed desire to go on parikrama, went to consult Bhagatji, who lived nearby. Baradraj asked him whatwas going on, what he thought. “You need not worry about it,” Bhagatji replied. “Prabhupada will do what he wants.”

After hearing Bhagatji’s response, Baradraj felt relieved. He had perceived that the relationship between Prabhupada and Bhagatji was “extraordinarily intimate.” As he said later, “It was not always in words. A lot of the time it was just in the mood, in the way they were with each other. I saw that Bhagatji had complete and utter love and respect and faith in Srila Prabhupada and that he saw him in his full glory. So after that meeting with Bhagatji, I began to feel the knot of anxiety and concern ease, untie, and I was able to appreciate what I began to see as a pastime, a Iila, as if Prabhupada had created this tension just to allow all these different relationships with his different disciples who were present to blossom.”

When Lokanath returned a few hours later, he went to see Prabhupada.

“So? Where did you go?” Prabhupada asked.

“I went to Mathura. First I went to Vrindavan and looked for the carts. They were not a very good kind; they were made for rough loads. So I went to Mathura and spoke to one farmer. He had a fairly big cart and two strong bullocks. He asked for a hundred rupees. He wouldn’t come down. So ultimately I agreed to a hundred rupees. He will reach tonight at eleven o’clock. I asked him to start immediately, but they have puja—as we have go-puja, they also have oxen puja today—so he will reach only at eleven o’clock, and he will be with us all day tomorrow.”

“So, what do you think?”

“About what?”

“How many carts do you have?”

“I got just one today, for you, and those who serve you can sit beside you in the cart, and the rest can do kirtan around the cart, and the whole unit, bullock cart and sanklrtana group, will move together.”

Prabhupada discussed the logistics of the Vrindavan parikrama with Lokanath and a few other devotees. “Tamal Krishna?” he asked.

“Yes, Srila Prabhupada.”

“Our experiment...”

“It certainly is an experiment. Of course, we always like experiments to be successful.”

Then Bhakti Charu pointed out that Lokanath hadn’t answered Prabhupada’s question. “He asked what you think about this trip,” he said to Lokanath. “You didn’t answer that. You have some experience with bullock carts. What do you think? In this condition, will Srila Prabhupada withstand the trip?”

“How can I answer that?”

“No, you know what condition Prabhupada is in now.” The devotees’ words were polite, but their underlying feelings ran deep and were expressed in their tone.

“Bullock carts are usually very bumpy,” Gopal Krishna said.

“This one has rubber tires,” a devotee said.

“If these roads are not bad, and the cart has tire wheels...” Lokanath began.

“Yes?” Prabhupada asked.

“We’re discussing bumping. There won’t be much bumping in the cart. Also, we always could go slow. If Prabhupada wants to make an experiment, we could make one day—”

“A few hours,” Svarupa Damodara suggested.

“So, where will we go tomorrow, if we go?” Tamal Krishna asked.

“Govardhana?” Prabhupada proposed.

“Yes, Govardhana,” Lokanath agreed.

“That’s very far,” Pancha Dravida said.

“Govardhana will take about six hours to reach,” Tamal Krishna stated.

“No,” Lokanath objected. “How many kilometers is that?”

“Twenty-eight to thirty kilometers.”

“Take five kilometers an hour.”

“That’s six hours to get there.”

“And six hours back,” Pancha Dravida added.

“Six hours to get there, and then three hours around Govardhana: nine hours,” Tamal Krishna calculated.

“And six hours back,” Gopal Krishna pointed out.

“And the bulls might need to rest,” Pancha Dravida said.

“That’s quite a big experiment to make, going to Govardhana the first day, Srila Prabhupada,” Tamal Krishna reasoned. “Do you feel confident that you can travel nine hours in a row on a bullock cart?”

“I am sleeping here,” Prabhupada said.

“But this is not a bullock cart,” Tamal Krishna countered.

“The same thing.”

“It’s the same thing?” Tamal Krishna questioned.

“Srila Prabhupada?” Hamsaduta said. “The main concern of the devotees is whether you will be able to survive such an experiment. But before, you said that you felt that such a parikrama would actually cure you. You said that. Your vision is transcendental, because you are the spiritual master. You’re a pure devotee of Krishna. So if you say that it will cure you and that it will be beneficial for you, then we have to carry that out, whatever you desire. We do not know. We’re just on the mundane platform.”

“One-day experiment,” Prabhupada repeated. “It is for one day?”

“We have hired it for one day,” Lokanath said.

“Rest assured, I will not die in one day.”

“So, we should go to Govardhana?” Hamsaduta asked. “Because tomorrow is Govardhana-puja.”

“Yes. And we shall make our cooking there and ...”

“We should start early,” Lokanath said.

“He has got experience,” Prabhupada said. “Dig the ground and make our foodstuff. Very good picnic.”

“We were planning, if we go to Govardhana, that we would take the prasadam prepared here and bring it there, so that many people can take,” Hamsaduta said.

“I have no objection,” Prabhupada replied.

“Or otherwise, we can make real picnic,” Lokanath suggested. “We could collect some grains there from door to door and cook some kichari there.”

“That will be very nice.”

“You have assured us that in one day you’re not going to die,” Hamsaduta said, “and you want to make this experiment, so we should do it.”

“Oh, yes.”

“We’ll do it, with great enthusiasm. Your Divine Grace is infallible. So if you say that it will help and cure you, then that must be a fact. You’ve never been wrong about anything, Prabhupada, so you must be right this time also.”

“So, let us make the experiment,” Prabhupada decided. “Don’t hesitate. ... As far as possible, take me in a comfortable position. That’s all. As far as possible.”

“Srila Prabhupada, please, may I make a request of you?” Jayapataka asked later. “If you feel any pain or experience any difficulty, then we can bring you back.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada accepted. “I’m not obstinate.” And the devotees laughed.

“We can make nice arrangements,” Pancha Dravida said. “This will purify Govardhana Hill, Srila Prabhupada. Tirthas become purified by the presence of...

“... another tirtha” Lokanath filled in.

“You’re a Vaishnava like Arjuna and Hanuman,” Jagadish told Prabhupada.

“Tomorrow is a great festival,” Prabhupada stated.

“Govardhana-puja festival,” Lokanath added.

“Yes,” Prabhupada said. “We are in Vrindavan and we shall not take part? We must take part.”

Again the devotees discussed logistics: who would accompany Prabhupada, where they would reside, when they would return, and who would stay back to attend to the Govardhana-puja festival at our temple. “So,” Tamal Krishna asked, “after circumambulating Govardhana, we will return to Vrindavan or stay out?”

“Maybe we could stay overnight,” Pancha Dravida suggested.

“When we are out there, we’ll decide,” Lokanath said.

“It will be helpful for the devotees to know, so they can bring something to wrap around them when it gets to be nighttime,” Tamal Krishna pointed out. “It’s not the middle of the summer, you know.... It’s something that should be considered now, not when we get there.”

“The devotees should be prepared to stay overnight there,” Lokanath finally agreed. “Under the trees.”

“We’re supposed to be gosvamis," Hamsaduta said. We have to stay under a tree. A different tree every night.”

“When we were traveling from Vrindavan to Mayapur, we stayed outside many times,” Lokanath remembered. “We’d live under a tree. It’s nice.”

“Yes,” Bhakti Charu said, “but if just one window is open at night, Prabhupada starts feeling cold in spite of the blankets.”

“It will be very cold in the early morning hours,” Svarupa Damodara added.

I was listening intently, hanging on every word. So much was at stake—Prabhupada’s very life—and I still wasn’t sure what I thought. I hoped and prayed that if I had to express an opinion, Srila Prabhupada and Lord Krishna would guide me what to say.

Hamsaduta proposed that Prabhupada could sleep overnight in a van or that they find some place, but Gopal Krishna objected that all the ashrams would be overcrowded for the festival. The cart could be tented over, Lokanath suggested, and it was agreed that he should make a plan for the whole parikrama, with the route and everything pre-arranged.

“Then it is all decided,” Pancha Dravida said.

And Hamsaduta and the devotees performed kirtan as Prabhupada closed his eyes to rest.

When Krishna dasa Babaji Maharaja came that evening, Tamal Krishna announced his arrival with “Jaya Srila Prabhupada!” Babaji Maharaja, Prabhupada had told us, was a paramahamsa, a fully liberated, self-realized soul, always blissful, always absorbed in chanting and hearing Sri Krishna’s holy names.

“Dandavat," Prabhupada greeted him. He told him in Bengali about his plan to go on a bullock cart to Govardhana for Govardhana-puja and asked if he would like to accompany him.

“Yes,” Babaji Maharaja agreed. “On your instruction, I will come along.”

Bhakti Charu said that they would leave at five the next morning, and Prabhupada added that they would be staying overnight.

“Somebody may go and bring his mala-japa, his beads,” Prabhupada told the devotees.

“Where are they?” Hamsaduta asked.

“At Imlitala,” Babaji Maharaja replied. “I can go. I can go and come back.” “You can go in the car,” Prabhupada suggested.

“We’ll take you,” Tamal Krishna told Babaji Maharaja, “and you can get your mala. You’ll stay overnight here.”

“He’ll get his bedding ” Tamal Krishna told Prabhupada.

“His bedding and beading,” Prabhupada quipped, and everyone laughed. He invited Babaji Maharaja to take prasada, then affectionately recited, Sadhu-sanga sadhu-sanga sarva-siddhi—By even a moment’s association with a pure devotee, one can attain all success.

Tamal Krishna and Bhavananda went upstairs to talk, and Hamsaduta led the singing of Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura’s Sri Nama-kirtana. Prabhupada asked that prasada be served, but Bhakti Charu said that he had already arranged Babaji Maharaja’s setting in the other room, so Prabhupada let Maharaja go.

Bhakti Charu had wanted to speak with Babaji Maharaja alone. He told Maharaja all about the arrangements for the parikramd—the difficulty and risk involved, what the kavirdja had advised—and shared his fear that Prabhupada would not survive the journey.

“Then he shouldn’t go,” Babaji Maharaja declared. And after prasada he and Bhakti Charu went back into the other room, just moments before Tamal Krishna and Bhavananda, and Babaji Maharaja told Prabhupada that he had heard everything about the parikrama and did not think Prabhupada should go.

“So, do you all jointly request me not to go?” Prabhupada asked.

"Ji” Babaji Maharaja confirmed.

“I was getting so upset sitting in the room upstairs,” Tamal Krishna said. “Two of the devotees told me this road is so bad that you’re going to be jolted back and forth. The road is terrible. I mean, I just can’t understand, Srila Prabhupada, why it has to be tomorrow that we have to go. If anybody wants you to travel, I do. My whole desire is to take you all over the world. I want to take you on parikrama, but why do we have to go when you’re in this condition? I can’t understand it. It just... I was standing outside. This kaviraja has worked so hard. He’s so much disappointed. He can’t understand why . . . He says that today you’ve taken half a kilo of milk. No mucus has been produced. No stool is being passed. He says that tomorrow he wants to give you a medicine that will begin to build the milk into muscles. He’s going to get you to a point where you can take two kilos of milk a day. And he says that very soon you’ll be able to have the strength to actually do parikrama. So why are we throwing everything out the window, that we must go tomorrow? I cannot understand.”

“All right,” Prabhupada said.

“Jaya Srila Prabhupada!” Bhakti Charu said with a laugh.

“Thank you, Srila Prabhupada,” said Bhavananda.

“I cannot refuse all your request,” Prabhupada conceded.

“And we cannot refuse your request,” Tamal Krishna said. “We will take you all over on tirtha-yatra, to all the places. Just that you should get a little stronger. You’ll be free of all management. You will simply go to tirthas and take darshan of all the Deities in India. And everyone will stay in their respective places. They’ll manage. But we want you to be stronger.”

“All right,” Prabhupada said, and the devotees laughed in happiness. “Are you satisfied?” he asked Bhavananda.

“Now I am, Srila Prabhupada, yes,” Bhavananda replied. “I was in too much anxiety.”

“No, no, I cannot put you in anxiety,” Prabhupada told him. “You have done so much; you have suffered for Mayapur so much. I cannot put you in anxiety. So I shall do what you like.” Prabhupada turned to Babaji Maharaja. “Left hand, right hand,” he said. “I cannot refuse.”

“I’m amazed, Srila Prabhupada,” Tamal Krishna said. “A half kilo of milk you’ve drunk today—no mucus, no stool. And that is wonderful. You could not have done this two weeks ago.”

“Yes,” Bhakti Charu added, “when I told the kaviraja, he got quite amazed.”

“Where is the kaviraja?” Prabhupada asked.

“He’s out again getting medicine,” Tamal Krishna answered. “Adri-dharana says he sits up all night worried about you, thinking, taxing his mind how to give you just what you require.”

“No.”

“Yesterday, when I went to call him at 4:30, I saw him sitting on his bed,” Bhakti Charu said.

“All night,” Tamal Krishna said. “He goes in the jungle four, five hours looking for roots and herbs to give you. He’s so sincere.”

“So many well-wishers,” Prabhupada said, “I cannot refuse. This is not my business. . . . All right. You take Babaji Maharaja. That will be my going.” And the devotees laughed.

“Jaya!” said Babaji Maharaja.

“Yes, the bullock cart will go tomorrow,” Tamal Krishna confirmed.

“Yes,” Prabhupada said.

“To Govardhana.”

“Yes, other devotees can go. I cannot go.”

“No, they’ll go on your behalf, but you will go one day. That we promise you.”

“All right.”

“Our greatest pleasure will be to take you on tirtha-yatra, Srila Prabhupada. We wanted so much to go with you on that.”

“Thank you very much.”

“Actually, Srila Prabhupada, we’re so much attached to you that you practically drive us to madness sometimes. Tonight we were becoming mad.”

“No, no, I shall not do that. Babaji Maharaja, just see how much my devotees love me!”

“Amazing!”

“This Bhavananda recently suffered so much. People used to spit on him. To refuse him .. .” and both Prabhupada and Babaji Maharaja laughed. “So, you will take bath in Radha-kunda on my behalf.”

“We’ll get you better,” Tamal Krishna said, “and you will also be able to take bath there personally. We’ll see you get better.”

“That’s all right.”

“Krishna will make all of our words come true, Srila Prabhupada.”

Prabhupada told Babaji Maharaja, “Kaviraja is working so hard, and to refuse him ...”

“And this kaviraja^ Tamal Krishna said, “we’re fortunate to get this sincere man.”

“Where is kaviraja!"

“He’s out getting more .. . He’s out working, at work.”

Bhavananda asked Adri to see if the kaviraja was available.

“As soon as he comes,” Tamal Krishna told Adri, “he can come and see Prabhupada.”

The next day, Prabhupada again brought up the subject of parikrama. Concerned, Tamal Krishna suggested once more that he wait until he got more strength. “If you get a few days of strength,” he advised. “I have no objection to take you even tomorrow. I just would like to hear what the kaviraja says. I really have a little faith in him. I mean, I haveall faith in you, Srila Prabhupada. I have only a little faith in him, but I don’t want to reject his advice as a doctor. This kaviraja has given sound advice so far.”

“Where he is?”

“We’re just trying to get him here. He went out again to get some more medicine for you. He says now that he’s seen that you took this half kilo of milk, he’s going to start to give a medicine that will make this milk make muscles on your body, because all the muscles have become slackened. He wants to do that so that you’ll have strength. Doing parikrama around the temple is not so bad. Let’s just see what he says. It’s certainly not that difficult. The main thing is, you have to be able to sit up for some time.” Addressing other devotees in the room, Tamal Krishna said, “Prabhupada wants to become enlivened spiritually, by some spiritual activity.” And to Prabhupada he added, “We’ll ask the kaviraja if he thinks we can take you tomorrow for a short parikrama around the temple.”

Reflecting on the recent days’ events, Tamal Krishna said, “Srila Prabhupada, the way you deal with us simply deepens our attachment every moment.”

“It is my duty,” Prabhupada said, and the devotees laughed. “There was a professor in Scottish Churches’ College. When you would say something, he would reply, ‘That’s my ‘juti,’ ‘juti,’ j-u-t-i.” Prabhupada chuckled. “So a student asked, ‘Is that Scottish pronunciation?’” And again the devotees laughed.

## Final Pastimes

The evening concluded nicely for the devotees in the room. We stayed, and there was quiet kirtan as different devotees, including me, massaged different parts of Prabhupada’s body. “The sons are cooperating to serve the father,” Tamal Krishna commented.

As I massaged Srila Prabhupada’s right foot, I felt small particles of dust, which were magnified in my consciousness. I thought, This is the dust of the lotus feet of the pure devotee, I told Tamal Krishna that I felt so whole and complete and satisfied, like never before in my life—and heconveyed the same into Prabhupada’s ear. All the devotees were attracted to Prabhupada, as we hear about all the creatures of Vrindavan being attracted to Krishna or Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, in a beautiful mood of harmony.

That night at around midnight I was awakened on the roof of the gurukula building. “Prabhupada is calling you!” a devotee alerted me. So many thoughts raced through my mind: Was Prabhupada leaving? Was something wrong?

I rushed to Prabhupada’s room, painfully aware that any word he uttered could be his last. When I entered, he was lying in an internal state of consciousness. I offered my obeisances, sat close beside him, and waited in silence.

After a few minutes, he whispered, “Do you think this movement will go on after I leave?”

I was surprised that he had called me in the middle of the night to ask me this, but I replied, “Yes, Srila Prabhupada, as long as the devotees are sincere and go on chanting Hare Krishna and following the regulative principles, the movement will be successful.”

He was silent for a moment. I leaned in, straining to hear. He spoke just one word— “Organization”—paused, and then said, “Organization and intelligence.”

I was startled. Prabhupada’s words were packed with meaning. Yes, I realized, we had to be sincere and chant our sixteen rounds and follow the regulative principles, but we were meant to do more than just maintain our own spiritual lives. We were meant to preach, to expand the movement and increase the number of devotees, and to do that required both organization and intelligence. The endeavor to spread Krishna consciousness in an intelligent, organized way was our service to Srila Prabhupada and Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu—as much as were chanting the holy names and following the regulative principles.

“Is there anything else?” Prabhupada asked—was there anything else I wanted to say? Within my heart I was crying out, “Srila Prabhupada, please stay with us; don’t leave.” My heart was screaming, but I simply said, “No, Srila Prabhupada,” offered my obeisances, and left.

The next day, when Lokanath came to see him, Prabhupada told Tamal Krishna to work with Lokanath to plan a tour.

“Make up a tour?” Tamal Krishna asked. “All right. Very good.”

“Since a long time I have had a desire.”

“Prabhupada’s had this ambition for a long time,” Tamal Krishna told Lokanath.

“Traveling the holy places,” Lokanath said. “So, you’ll be doing it in—?”

“That we can discuss.”

“Lord Balarama did that,” Jayadvaita said. “He went to all the holy places. So, in the same way, you can get a little strength from Krishna and Balarama here in Vrindavan, and then you can go. Lord Balarama was going to all the different places.”

“An advance party will give us a description of the land,” Prabhupada told Lokanath, “and before our going, they’ll make a camp. Small, big— that doesn’t matter. In the morning, the camp is broken, and they go to the next camp with kirtan. And in the meantime, the other camp is ready to receive us. Then, after taking prasadam, they’ll go to the next camp.”

“So, there is a smaller group going in advance, and the bigger group with you stays back.”

“Yes.”

“And the smaller group goes, fixes the place, and informs your party where they are and what kind of arrangement they have made. And when you are satisfied, you leave that place to join the small group, the advance party. Right?”

“And after Prabhupada joins that group, the advance party goes again,” Tamal Krishna said.

“To the next place, to make further arrangements.”

“In this way,” Prabhupada confirmed.

“This kind of program we have done before. Whenever we had a big group traveling, we always sent ahead two, or sometimes four, devotees.”

“We also did that with our Radha-Damodar program,” Tamal Krishna said. “That is the way of traveling—advance booking.”

“And when you go in procession,” Prabhupada instructed, “have kirtan.”

“Yes. That would be nice,” Lokanath agreed.

“Originally, Srila Prabhupada,” Tamal Krishna said, “when we talked of this idea, we were considering going with a few vehicles so thatwe could go to many holy places all over India. I still think that that’s the best idea, and Lokanath agreed with me when we talked about this. Because bullock carts ... Of course, we’re not in a big rush, but if we would like to go to a few places all over India, we can go very comfortably with a few vehicles. You can have the back seat of a vehicle and travel very comfortably.”

“I could see the Volkswagen we have here,” Lokanath said. “It doesn’t have any seats; it’s all flat. It’s kind of a big room, and it already has mattresses.”

“Like that. That’s more convenient for traveling all over India, Srila Prabhupada. I mean, we should be practical also. Otherwise, we’ll spend from one tlrtha to another, just like from here to Ayodhya, oh, three weeks.”

“More. It will take two and a half months.”

“Two and a half months, Srila Prabhupada, just to go from one tirtha-sthana to the next. We don’t have that kind of time. Better that we go in very good caravan of vehicles, comfortable. You will have your own vehicle, your party will have another two or three vehicles, and the advance party can have one vehicle. We have enough cars. Your Divine Grace has a car in Mayapur; we have a car here in Vrindavan; we have one of your cars in Bombay. There are so many vehicles and vans. So we have our choice. We can get very nice vehicles.”

“That will make a very nice impression also,” Jayadvaita said.

“Otherwise,” Tamal Krishna continued, “Svarupa Damodara was mentioning to me that if we were to take you in a bullock cart, people would accuse us of being negligent of you, and it would reflect very badly upon our Society. They would accuse us, how we have taken our spiritual master.”

“They wouldn’t understand these transcendental activities of the Vaishnavas,” Lokanath said.

“You’ve always preached that we should do things in a modern way, just appropriately,” Tamal Krishna said.

“And use for Krishna whatever is available,” Svarupa Damodara added.

“I think if we fix up vehicles very nicely, that will be nice,” Tamal Krishna said. Will that be all right, Srila Prabhupada?”

“Hmm,” Prabhupada agreed.

“And most of the holy places are connected with good roads,” Lokanath said. “During our preaching we also visit holy places—they’reon the way; we pass through them. And if we travel not very fast, with good drivers, it won’t be much inconvenient.”

“I think some scientist should also come with us,” Tamal Krishna added, and the devotees laughed, “In case we meet anyone very intelligent, we need a scientific mind to defeat them. So Svarupa Damodara can come with us?”

“Oh, yes,” Prabhupada accepted.

“And someone to make members,” I said, and the devotees laughed, “in case we meet any rich people.”

“By managing, you can come—everyone,” Prabhupada said.

“Right. If you manage properly, then you can all come,” Tamal Krishna repeated.

“So, do I come with you, Srila Prabhupada?” Lokanath asked.

“You will be the leader,” Prabhupada said.

“I have a vehicle,” Lokanath added. “My party also could travel with us and in the same town do nagara-sankirtana and distribute books all day long?”

“Hmm,” Prabhupada agreed.

“I think that it will make our program complete,” Lokanath concluded. “We have a membership team, we have a scientist visiting the scientists, and our boys will go door to door, house to house, and spread your message.”

“With book distribution and sankirtana,” Tamal Krishna said.

“I think that the Mayapur book distribution team now has some heavy competition,” Bhavananda remarked.

“With Prabhupada’s traveling sankirtana and book distribution,” Lokanath said. “Also, our party is well equipped to do evening programs. There will be a lot of senior devotees, and the advance party could arrange programs and do different big temples or different public meetings.”

“You want that, Srila Prabhupada?” Tamal Krishna asked.

“Hmm,” Prabhupada affirmed.

“But Srila Prabhupada, you shouldn’t overexert yourself.”

“No.”

“We can do the speaking and the kirtans,” Tamal Krishna said to Lokanath and the other devotees. “Prabhupada should be allowed to simply do tirtha-yatra.”

“You’ll be acting through us,” Lokanath said to Prabhupada, “by your mercy.”

“Srila Prabhupada never does anything small,” Jayadvaita said.

“Prabhupada is big,” Lokanath agreed. “He thinks big, and he does big.” “But first get a little more strength, Srila Prabhupada,” Tamal Krishna advised. “That we really request you to do, so that the program becomes successful—not that after two days we have to turn back. When going, we should not turn back.”

“Yes,” Prabhupada said.

“So, let us become prepared properly.”

That evening, Prabhupada indicated that he wanted to pass urine, and because most of the more experienced devotees were not present, Upendra thought I should do it. So I placed the plastic urinal bottle between Prabhupada’s legs, eased his penis into it, and waited—but nothing came. I waited and waited, but nothing came, so I turned to Upendra for guidance, and he indicated that I should take the urinal away.

Although in a way we had not been successful, the experience had been incredible. After that simple, menial service, I felt more purified than if I had offered hundreds of aratis or chanted hundreds of rounds. And I considered that Prabhupada had mercifully given me the opportunity to serve him in this intimate, personal way and experience such divine grace.

At about ten that night, I was sitting alone in front of the temple, and Baradraj approached me. We both agreed that from all visible signs, neither the vaidya nor the medicines had effected any significant improvement in Prabhupada’s condition. Prabhupada was hinting that he would be leaving. And he would show us—as he had showed us so many other things—how to depart from the world. He told us that the only medicine he wanted now was hari-nama, and he wanted all of us to sit down in his room and chant Hare Krishna. Then Hamsaduta, Baradraj, and I went to Prabhupada’s room and chanted japa, while Prabhupada apparently slept.

At 1:30 Prabhupada had severe pain in his left leg. After a while, it subsided, but it returned at 3:00. Prabhupada was moaning from thepain, and the devotees present stopped their kirtan and surrounded the bed. The kaviraja assessed the situation and recommended some procedures that gradually brought relief, and Prabhupada was able to rest again. But the attacks came again at around 6:00, 9:00, noon, and 3:00. Tamal Krishna worried that if the attacks continued, Prabhupada would not be able to remain with us any longer.

In the evening, Prabhupada was feeling better, and when his godbrothers Bon Maharaja and Krishna dasa Babaji Maharaja came for a pre-arranged visit, he greeted them with “Dandavats” and the three conversed in Bengali.

“Infinite mercy is upon you,” Bon Maharaja said. “You have performed immense service that is beyond compare. Our Prabhupada’s \[Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati’s\] immeasurable energy is with you, and that is why you have achieved the impossible. We are linked to the immensely potent Gaura-vani because of your writings.”

“Please bless me before I go,” Prabhupada said.

“As long as you are alive, more of Mahaprabhu’s service and more of \[Srila Bhaktisiddhanta’s\] greatness will be promoted. By the potency of the holy names, you’ve accomplished such great service. And even now your mind is very, very acute and you are able to speak precisely. But one fine day it will happen to all of us; one day we all will have to leave. Still, you are inclined towards hearing hari-nama and spreading news of kirtan—those things are always with you—in Vrindavan dhama. I have one desire: one day when I leave this body, let it be in the dhama, the place of the Lord’s pastimes—that is the best of all.”

“That is why after traveling all over I have returned here.”

“I hear your glories everywhere,” Bon Maharaja said. “Everyone sings your glories. You have accomplished unlimited service.” And he described his experience with the ISKCON devotees and temples in Montreal and Toronto. “What else shall we tell you? You are turning Mahaprabhu’s vani into reality. Through you, Mahaprabhu has done it: Prthivite ache yata nagaradi grama/ sarvatra pracara haibe mora nama—through you, this is materializing.”

“Thank you, Maharaja. What can I do? I am ...”

“Our Prabhupada selected you only.”

“You are always encouraging.”

“If you remember, from the beginning I would tell you that if you know English, then go abroad, go to America. Everything is Bhagavan’s mercy. He has done this work through you.”

“When I printed books, you said that ‘In each of your books there’s a different insight.’”

“Your books are the real contribution. You were able to do so many shastras, and that will remain intact forever, will live forever.”

Prabhupada asked Tamal Krishna to show them the certificate given to the BBT at the Moscow book fair.

“This is a certificate arrived from the Soviet Union,” Tamal Krishna said. “I have the translation. The top wording here says, ‘Books in the service of peace and progress. A diploma for the Bhaktivedanta Book Trust, Bombay, given by the First Moscow International Book Fair Exhibitions and Fairs, General Directorate of International Book Exhibitions and Fairs, USSR.’”

Prabhupada asked devotees to tell about the Soviet universities.

“All Russian universities ordered Prabhupada’s books,” Gopal Krishna said.

Prabhupada said that two volumes of the Tenth Canto of the Bhagavatam had recently been published, and devotees brought the books.

“That’s Bhagavatam, Tenth Canto,” Bon Maharaja said. “That is up to which chapter?”

“This is up to Chapter Twelve,” Jayadvaita said. “And now the thirteenth chapter is also completed.”

“Inside and out, both volumes are superexcellent,” Bon Maharaja admired. “Inside, in Maharaja’s translation, and outside, in your publication, printing, makeup—everything superexcellent. That is the first attraction: when you take the book in your hand, you feel it is something very nicely done. I don’t think in India we can have this type of printing and publication.”

“The work is done in Los Angeles, then printed in Tennessee,” Jayadvaita explained, “and the pictures are printed separately, for the Bhagavatam, Then the pictures are sent to the publisher in pages.”

“Last time, when your press was in New York, they told me that they were shifting it to Los Angeles. About two hundred brahmacharis were working there, they told me.”

“Now it’s in Los Angeles,” Tamal Krishna confirmed.

“Well, it is all Mahaprabhu’s will, and Prabhupada is our ...”

“Have you ever seen our Los Angeles godown? It is like Howrah Station.”

Krishna dasa Babaji and others laughed.

“It’s about two blocks long and about one block high,” a devotee explained.

“Everything is done in a very big way,” Bon Maharaja agreed.

“Because Prabhupada is big, so he needs everything big,” Jayadvaita said.

“Here’s a picture of that book godown in Los Angeles,” Tamal Krishna said, presenting the photo. And one after the other, he showed Bon Maharaja pictures of our temples, Deities, projects, and other activities in Los Angeles, New York, England, Fiji, and around the world.

Later, Bon Maharaja commented how wonderful it was that Prabhupada was in such perfect consciousness, and I had to agree. I was amazed that in the face of excruciating pain and imminent death, he was still preaching, sharing with his godbrother the accomplishments of the movement and his enthusiasm for spreading Krishna consciousness.

The next day, Prabhupada was withdrawn. A little after sunrise, Baradraj saw him lift his hand as if motioning to someone to halt, to wait. It was an enigmatic gesture, and Baradraj was struck by it—he had never seen Prabhupada communicate with anyone who was not visible. But he believed that Prabhupada was responding to something he was seeing, and he imagined that perhaps the Vishnudutas had come.

Around noon Baradraj heard Prabhupada begin to make the sound that people make at the end of life when the soul is about to leave—what Prabhupada called the “gong, gong” sound. But it was more internal, like a hum—mmm, mmm, mmm, and sometimes longer—and he realized that Prabhupada would soon leave. He was simultaneously trying to understand what he was witnessing and what, as a servant, he should do. He remembered that Prabhupada had been saying that he wanted to hear chanting, and so he began singing Jayadeva Gosvami’s prayer to Lord Nrsimhadeva, which Srila Prabhupada had introduced in the early days of the movement as a “prayer for the protection of the spiritual master.”

tava kara-kamala-vare nakham adbhuta-srngam  
dalita-hiranyakasipu-tanu-bhrngam  
kesava dhrta-narahari-rupa jaya jagadisa hare

“O my Lord, Your hands are very beautiful, like the lotus flower, but with Your long nails You have ripped apart the wasp Hiranyakasipu. Unto You, Lord of the universe, do I offer my humble obeisances.”

Kneeling at Prabhupada’s bedside, Baradraj continued for some time—jaya jagadisa hare, jaya jagadisa hare, jaya jagadisa hare—and then he chanted the Hare Krishna mantra for the next hour or so, until the next devotee, Hamsaduta, took over.

The attacks continued at three-hour intervals. The kaviraja came frequently, but Prabhupada took medicine only after Bhakti Charu urged him to do so. In Bengali, Bhakti Charu pleaded, “Srila Prabhupada, please open your mouth. Do you want to take this medicine?” He was persistent, and finally Prabhupada nodded and opened his mouth.

After a few minutes of silence, Prabhupada’s eyes opened slightly, and a faint smile appeared on his lips. He uttered, “Hare Krishna,” turned on his side, and rested.

Outside, Adri-dharana explained that the kaviraja had said that everything was in disarray: the air was pushing on the nerves and causing a great deal of pain, the pulse was low, and one chamber of the heart was not functioning. There was urine in the bladder, but Prabhupada couldn’t pass it. The kaviraja could administer some medicine so that Prabhupada could pass, but there would not be any hope unless the heart improved.

Later, when the kaviraja asked Prabhupada to drink some juice, Prabhupada replied, “Meri kuch iccha nahin”: “I have no desire”—the only sentence he spoke that day.

When the attacks resumed, Prabhupada moved his right arm back and forth in the air, but none of us could understand. We wanted to help him, but we didn’t know what to do.

When the kaviraja confirmed that Prabhupada’s condition was critical, we understood that the end was approaching.

Baradraj wrote in his diary, “Around noon, there came another attack. In deadly silence the kaviraja examined the pulse. Bhakti Charu was standing by with medicine, ready to perform his duty.

“The kaviraja listens to the heart. Checks the pulse again. Looks up with a hopeless face. Shakes his head. No use of medicine. Fear grips my throat. I begin chanting prayers to Lord Nrsimhadeva. Shaking voices respond. We chant loudly. The doctor sits slumped in a chair, with a hopeless blank look. Many are crying. Some are still hopeful. Everyone chants Hare Krishna loudly. Prabhupada moans and waves his hands in unknown mysterious expressions.”

By afternoon, Prabhupada had fallen into an internal state of consciousness, and devotees placed tulasi leaves and Yamuna water by his head. The room resounded with kirtan, and the doors were opened to everyone. The room was packed: young, old, men, women—all were allowed in to be with Prabhupada and express their love.

Several times, Pishima asked, “Prabhupada, have you eaten anything?” but he did not respond. She poured a few drops of Ganges water in his mouth.

Bon Maharaja, Krishna dasa Babaji, Ananda Prabhu, and Prabhupada’s godnephew Narayana Maharaja soon arrived and sat on benches on either side of the bed, observing his consciousness. When Narayana Maharaja spoke in Prabhupada’s ear, Prabhupada did not respond, but when Bhakti Charu told him that Maharaja and others were present, he slowly raised his left hand to his head in salutation and started crying.

Prabhupada’s godbrothers ventured that his attacks were simply the moving of the airs in the body. He was in perfect consciousness, they said; his time for departure had not yet come. After a while, all of them except Ananda Prabhu left, promising to return the minute the devotees called.

The kaviraja said that Prabhupada had only two or three hours left. Pujaris brought tulasi flower garlands from Krishna-Balarama and placed them on the pillow around Prabhupada’s head. The devotees continued chanting and praying—there was nothing else we could do.

When a final attack came, at 3:00 p.m., Prabhupada rubbed his hand quickly back and forth across his heart. Upendra massaged hisheart, Tamal Krishna sat holding his feet, and for the next four hours, Prabhupada was peaceful.

I was at the head of the bed, wishing I could have one last chance to serve Prabhupada in his bodily form. Suddenly he threw back his arm, and I was able to touch his hand and squeeze it gently. He had fulfilled my desire. I was grateful, satisfied, even amidst the overwhelming sorrow.

As Prabhupada’s departure drew closer, the kirtan, led by Baradraj, became more and more intense, sung, as Shaktimata later recalled, “in a kind of unusual chorus of two parts in a way that we never sang before. Some devotees were singing 'Jaya Prabhupada! Jaya Prabhupada!’ while others were chanting the maha-mantra, and somehow the two blended together in the most perfectly beautiful way. We don't sound like this, I thought. This isn’t coming from us. It was like the room had no ceiling, like all the bricks and beams had dissolved and the whole room was open in a direct current to the spiritual world as Krishna’s messengers came for Srila Prabhupada.”

At 7:25 Prabhupada opened his eyes and moved his lips, as if speaking—Hare Krishna. Then his jaw dropped, his complexion darkened, and he went still.

The kaviraja took Prabhupada’s pulse and held a cotton swab to his nostrils. There was no breath.

“Our beloved Srila Prabhupada had departed,” Tamal Krishna wrote in his diary. He had been surrounded by loving disciples chanting the holy names of Krishna, lying peacefully on his bed in Raman Reti, Vrindavan, the sacred land where Krishna and His friends used to sport. His head was pointing toward the Deities of Krishna-Balarama, his forehead decorated with candana and a large tulasi leaf, with photos of Them and Radha-Krishna and pictures of Lord Nrsimhadeva and Prabhupada’s guru maharaja nearby. A volume of Sri Caitanya-caritamrta laid beside his pillow. Holding tulasi in his right hand, he had departed and returned to the lotus feet of Krishna, from whence he had come. It was 7:25 p.m. on Gaura-caturthi-tithi, the fourth day of the light half of the month of Kartik—five minutes after the beginning of amrta-yoga, the most auspicious time of the day.

“Seven twenty-five,” Baradraj wrote in his journal. “Prabhupada enters my heart in a flood of tears. The sun of the world has set. Theshelter of the world has entered Vaikuntha. Hari-nama continues on and on”

The room was filled with crying and wailing. The kirtan was going wild, with devotees chanting Hare Krishna and “Jaya Prabhupada!” Pishima, weeping piteously, went to the foot of Prabhupada’s bed, lifted the chaddar, and placed his feet on her head. Then she took dust from them and smeared it on her head and her eyes. Other devotees followed, clutching Prabhupada’s lotus feet.

Most of the devotees were then asked to leave, and Upenara wiped Prabhupada’s body, decorated it with Vaishnava tilak markings, and dressed him in fresh clothes. Devotees sat Prabhupada up, crossed his legs, and secured him to his palanquin. Bhavananda closed his jaw, which had remained open, and devotees tied it shut with a cloth around his head.

Narayana Maharaja came, garlanded Prabhupada, and discussed with Tamal Krishna and Bhavananda what should be done. Then we carried Prabhupada on his palanquin into the temple amidst the blowing of conch shells and beating of mridangas and kartals. He was brought before each Deity, then around the temple three times, and again before Krishna and Balarama. Then we circumambulated his body four times with kirtan and finally placed the whole palanquin on his vyasasana.

By Prabhupada’s grace, even amidst the overwhelming feeling of sorrow, I was surprised to find myself experiencing a sort of ecstasy.

Narayana Maharaja, Krishna dasa Babaji, Ananda Prabhu, and many of Prabhupada’s disciples led kirtan and prayers throughout the night, while we sat, as we had so often, at Srila Prabhupada’s lotus feet, gazing at his divine form. Narayana Maharaja began with Ye Anilo Prema Dhana, Narottama dasa Thakura’s song for departed Vaishnavas, while Omkara performed drati and devotees offered Prabhupada flowers. Krishna dasa Babaji sang in the middle of the night, and Ananda Prabhu led mangala-arati.

That morning, the residents of Vrindavan awaited their last darshan of the great acharya of the Gaudiya Vaishnavas, who had spread Vrindavan’s glories throughout the world. At 6:30 the goswamis of the seven main temples arrived to escort Prabhupada’s divine form to their respective Deities. He was sitting straight up, legs crossed, wearing hishat and chaddar, in his flower-decorated palanquin, covered with garlands offered by disciples the night before.

Narayana Maharaja led kirtan as we brought Prabhupada into the courtyard, again circumambulated his body four times, and began our procession with uproarious chanting, maha-sankirtana.

Vraja-vasis came out from their homes and shops to watch, standing on steps and balconies and alongside the road, calling out “Jaya Prabhupada!” to honor Vrindavan’s favorite son, most famous saint, and international ambassador. “All these hundreds of people came from nowhere,” Rajasekhara recalled. “I couldn’t figure how everyone had heard about the procession or even how they had heard that Prabhupada had left. I had never seen Vrindavan in such a mood—everyone came out to pay homage. Wherever we went, the rooftops were packed.”

“As we went from one place to the other,” Bhagavata remembered, “people were performing arati, offering flowers, and offering prasada. All of Vrindavan was displaying their love and affection for Srila Prabhupada. Tamal Krishna—along with many of us—was openly weeping.”

As we approached each temple, the head pujari would come out to receive Prabhupada and the kirtan would rise to a crescendo, with Narayana Maharaja singing, “Jaya Madana-mohana! Jaya Radha-Damodar! Jaya Radha-ramana!” glorifying each Deity, and then “Jaya Prabhupada!” Even submerged in an ocean of grief, we devotees also felt proud to be disciples of such an illustrious, exalted, empowered guru.

The parikrama lasted three hours, concluding when we returned to the Krishna-Balaram temple. We brought Prabhupada to the samadhi site, near the front of the property, and Upendra and Bhavananda undressed him, leaving only his kaupina (loincloth), and placed him on banana leaves. First Narayana Maharaja, then Krishna dasa Babaji, and then Ananda Prabhu poured Yamuna water over him, and Tamal Krishna then took the conch shell and, allowing all the devotees to touch it, poured water over Prabhupada’s body many times.

The personal servants dressed Prabhupada in new silks and a new sacred thread. Narayana Maharaja took a tulasi-manjari and with can-dana wrote the samadhi mantra on Prabhupada’s chest. He, Ananda Prabhu, Tamal Krishna, and Bhakti Charu descended the eight feet into the samadhi pit, at the bottom of which lay a pure-white marbleslab. They performed pujas, with Ananda Prabhu chanting the mantras while guiding the movements of Tamal Krishna’s hands. Bhavananda and Upendra lifted Prabhupada into Tamal Krishna’s arms, and they placed him in a sitting position and offered arati. The devotees above, who had been chanting and blowing conch shells, then offered puspanjali, throwing thousands of flowers upon Prabhupada’s form, and, as Prabhupada had instructed, Tamal Krishna kept some to be taken to Mayapur for his puspa-samadhi.

Devotees lowered brass buckets of salt, and we watched as Prabhupada’s form disappeared under the salt being placed around his body, until all we could see was a golden patch that was the top of his head— and then nothing.

As we passed buckets of earth to fill the rest of the samadhi and, with tears in my eyes and my arms trembling I lifted each shovelful of soil, I reflected that this might be the last personal service I offered to Srila Prabhupada’s vapuh.

Narayana Maharaja asked for a long bamboo stick to place above Prabhupada’s head, to mark the place, and after reaching ground level, the devotees built up an area about three feet square above where his body was situated, and the bamboo pole was extracted. Maharaja broke the bamboo pole into three pieces, put one on either side, and tore some of his upper cloth to attach the third piece to the two sides from behind, creating an easel for Prabhupada’s photo. The area was covered with fresh cow dung and then saffron silk, and another saffron cloth was suspended above on four bamboo poles, with colorful cloth flags at each corner. Tulasi plants were placed on either side, and Prabhupada’s preferred photo of himself, chanting japa on the lawn at Bhaktivedanta Manor, was propped on the raised ground. Pradyumna offered the bhoga (prepared by Ayodhyapati and his team) and a full arati, Baradraj led the kirtan, and we all circumambulated four times.

When the cloth covering was removed from the bhoga offering, Tamal Krishna turned to Upendra and said, “Look, Upendra. In his first offering in his samadhi, Srila Prabhupada got his two favorite foods: lugloo and kachoris \[a sweet and a savory\]!”

In a mood of complete and utter surrender, we offered obeisances at Srila Prabhupada’s lotus feet:nama om visnu-padaya krsna-presthaya bhu-tale  
srimate bhaktivedanta-svamin iti namine

“I offer my respectful obeisances unto His Divine Grace A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, who is very dear to Lord Krishna on this earth, having taken shelter at His lotus feet."namas te sarasvate deve gaura-vani-pracarine  
nirvisesa-sunyavadi-pascatya-desa-tarine

“Our respectful obeisances are unto you, О spiritual master, servant of Sarasvati Gosvami. You are kindly preaching the message of Lord Caitanyadeva and delivering the Western countries, which are filled with impersonalism and voidism.”

Srila Prabhupada had instructed us to give a hundred rupees to the main temples in Vrindavan so that after his departure they would do a raja-bhoga offering on his behalf. They brought the maha-prasada to the Krishna-Balaram temple, and from there devotees took it to Bhagatji’s house.

One of the mahants of the Radha-Damodar temple, where Prabhupada had resided before going to America and where he had kept his rooms even after his return, came to Prabhupada’s house with maha-prasada. As I watched, the mahant, Gorachand Goswami, who was blind, started banging his cane on the bricks around the house and exclaimed, “Where is Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada? Swami Maharaja! Swami Maharaja, are you there? I want to see you! Where are you? I know you’re there. Swami Maharaja, I know you are there.” Considering what had been a mixed relationship between Prabhupada and the Radha-Damodar goswamis, I was touched: the caste goswami’s affection for Prabhupada had prevailed.

So many people had joined together in their love and respect for Srila Prabhupada, but even after his departure, the controversy over the Govardhana parikrama continued and the feelings remained strong on both sides. I still couldn’t determine who had been right, and the question persisted in my mind.

My usual practice had been to chant japa in Prabhupada’s rooms when he was out, and the day after he was placed in samadhi I was chanting behind his bed, in a small corner by a bookshelf, when my eyes fell upon the new volume of Srimad-Bhagavatam—Canto Ten, Volume Two—that had been made for Prabhupada with gold embossing. When I opened it, I happened to land upon Chapter Nine: “Mother Yasoda Binds Krsna.” I read a few verses and purports, and then I came to a verse that I felt answered my question:

evam sandarsita hy anga  
harina bhrtya-vasyata  
sva-vasenapi krsnena  
yasyedam sesvaram vase

“O Maharaja Pariksit, this entire universe, with its great, exalted demigods like Lord Siva, Lord Brahma, and Lord Indra, is under the control of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Yet the Supreme Lord has one transcendental attribute: He comes under the control of His devotees. This was now exhibited by Krsna in this pastime.”

The pastime was encapsulated in the previous verse:

sva-matuh svinna-gatraya  
visrasta-kabara-srajah  
drstva parisramam krsnah  
krpayasit sva-bandhane

“Because of Mother Yasoda’s hard labor, her whole body became covered with perspiration, and the flowers and comb were falling from her hair. When child Krsna saw His mother thus fatigued, He became merciful to her and agreed to be bound.”

When I read the verses, I thought, This is what happened. The spiritual master was the transparent medium through which Krishna manifested Himself. Of course, in vraja-bhakti the relationship with Krishna was different—Krishna exhibited nara-lila, humanlike pastimes, in which there was complete intimacy and freedom between the devotees and the Lord, whereas in the relationship between disciple and spiritual master, there was always an element of awe and reverence, and duty. Still, duty was meant to lead to love. Prabhupada had said to Babaji Maharaja, “Just see how much they love me.” And during the incidenta month before, when the disciples had appealed to Prabhupada to stay longer (which meant him drinking) and he had accepted their plea, he had said, “This is real affection.”

When I read the verse, I thought of the two incidents and put them together. In both cases, when the disciples had expressed themselves—“We want you to stay”—Prabhupada had approved, saying, “This is real affection” and “Just see how much my disciples love me.”

All the devotees in the controversy had been acting on the basis of their realization, of their devotion for Prabhupada, and Prabhupada had been drawing out our loving feelings—and encouraging us to go beyond just following his orders. Following the order was a given; there was no question—to follow the order of the spiritual master was a basic principle of spiritual life, and to disobey his order would be an offense against him and the holy name. So it was not a question of disobeying the order of the spiritual master; it was about developing loving feelings for the spiritual master and expressing them to him. Relating the verse to what Prabhupada had done with us, I saw a parallel between the damodara-lila and that principle of spontaneous love. Every night during the month of Damodara, Kartik, we recited the Damodarastaka, including

itidrk sva-lilabhir ananda-kunde  
sva-ghosam nimajjantam akhyapayantam  
tadiyesita-jnesu bhaktair jitatvam  
punah prematas tarn satavrtti vande

“By such pastimes He is drowning the inhabitants of Gokula in pools of ecstasy and revealing to those devotees who are absorbed in knowledge of His supreme majesty and opulence that He is conquered only by devotees whose pure love is imbued with intimacy and is free from all conceptions of awe and reverence. To this Supreme Lord, Sri Damodara, whose belly is bound not with ropes but with His devotee’s pure love, I offer my humble obeisances hundreds and hundreds of times.”

The damodara-lila was meant to show the special power of pure, spontaneous love to conquer the Lord. The Lord came under its control. Similarly, Prabhupada had brought love out from deep within the recesses of our hearts, and then he had reciprocated with us by coming under the control of that love, by agreeing to our loving requests.

“I came to the conclusion that it was just fine the way it was,” Baradraj later told me. “No one was right or wrong; it was all acceptable. In these personal exchanges with Prabhupada, we cannot judge—we cannot fault or praise them. In their reciprocation with Prabhupada, every devotee received a particular gift, a personal gift, an instruction or a lesson from him, in that interplay, which was almost like a dramatic performance. Everyone was affected in a very special and personal intimate way. It was rasa—an exchange of transcendental mellows.”

Prabhupada’s final pastimes had been very deep. Among the disciples around him at the end, it was understood that as the perfect acharya, he had taught us by his own example how to live in Krishna consciousness and then was teaching us how to die in Krishna consciousness. He was showing us how to retire to a holy place and how to be absorbed in hearing the holy names of the Lord. Up until the end, even in his delicate condition, he was trying to push forward the mission and was translating and dictating purports to Srimad-Bhagavatam. And as an important part of that final lesson, he was also bringing us to a more intimate level of exchange where we could express to him our heart’s deepest desires. There were natural boundaries between the disciples and spiritual master, and Prabhupada had always reminded us of those if he felt we were becoming too familiar, but in these final hours he inspired us to reach out and express our love for him and ask him to stay with us.

Soon after Prabhupada left, amidst all the grief and activity, I asked Tamal Krishna whether there was any service I could do. “Not now,” he said. “Later. Why don’t you write an article about Srila Prabhupada and his departure, which we can send to our friends and devotees?”

So, submerged in feelings of deep separation, I began by quoting Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.48.26:

kah panditas tvad aparam saranam samiyad  
bhakta-priya rta-girah suhrdah krta-jnat  
sarvan dadati suhrdo bhajato 'bhikaman  
atmanam apy upacayapacayau na yasya

“Who can surrender to anyone other than Yourself? Who is as dear, truthful, friendly, and grateful as You? You are so perfect and completethat even though You give Yourself to Your devotee, You are still full and perfect. You can satisfy all the desires of Your devotee and even deliver Yourself unto him?

“The Supreme Personality of Godhead, Sri Krishna, is the most beloved personality,” I wrote, “and Srila Prabhupada was just like Him. We loved him as the dearest personality, the life of our soul.

“He came from the spiritual world to tell us of our real life with God, and to show us the kindness of God he passed so many days with us in this miserable world. He was a divine personality. He was not of this world; he was never of this world. He came to show us God. Everything about him was perfect, and his sublime presence demonstrated perfection in every respect. His beautiful body, his sympathetic face, his compassionate glance, his sweet words, his joyful smile, his appreciative eating, his profound voice, his peaceful resting, his ecstatic dancing—all were perfect, from another world. He was everything to us: our mother, father, friend, companion, guide, master, child—life itself. How can we bear being separated from him? How can we tolerate such a loss?

“Now he has left us here to carry on his mission, waiting for the day when we will again be with him and have the chance to serve him personally.

“‘You are the life and soul of the inhabitants of Vrndavana. So because You have left Vrndavana, all the servitors of Your lotus feet there are suffering. It is as if the lake filled with lotus flowers dried up from the scorching heat of separation from You? (The Nectar of Devotion, Ch. 38)

“Now he has given us a grave responsibility—to carry on his movement in separation. He has invested us with his mercy to continue his great work, and we pray that we will be able to accept his divine grace properly. The whole world is feeling his absence, praying for his mercy. He has left a very insufficient vessel to carry that mercy, but still I pray that he will make me fit to carry his divine grace.

“He was with us for so few years; we hardly had a chance to appreciate him. His every moment with us was full of life, but we were so dull we could not appreciate him, and suddenly he was gone. One devotee said that his appearance was like a flash. He came of his own sweet will to deliver us, and of his own accord he left, but future generations will note how his brief presence changed the entire course of history. Iam not elevated enough to think of humanity. Mainly I think only of myself. But I also felt that his appearance was like a flash, so brief, but it completely altered my life.

“Actually, he was like Krishna. Krishna’s complexion is compared to a cloud, His yellow dhoti to lightning, and His merciful pastimes to rainfall. Similarly, Prabhupada appeared with his swarthy complexion, his saffron dhoti, and his loving exchanges, just to enliven our transcendental senses, to remind us of Krishna, as the Supreme Personality of Servitor Godhead.

“When lightning flashes across the sky, the whole world is lighted in all directions. The dark night is illuminated, and we see the entire landscape of fields, trees, houses, roads, persons—everything. In this way his divine presence showed us an entire spiritual realm, giving us a vision of our real life, our real home—a transcendental world with kalpa-vrksa trees, cintamani stones, surabhi cows, and liberated personalities like him, all engaged in pastimes of love with the Supreme Personality of Godhead. His electric presence sent a current through our hearts, and we will never be the same again.

“When lightning flashes across the sky, only a few people may see it, but soon thereafter deep sounds of thunder rumble through the sky, and everyone hears them and feels their vibration. Although only a few may have been fortunate enough to perceive Srila Prabhupada directly, everyone is hearing the thunderous roar of his message—his books, his vani—the big mridanga, the printing press, rolling on, vibrating everywhere. ‘I will never die,’ he said. ‘I will live in my books, and you will utilize.” A sleeping person may miss a flash of lightning, but the sound of thunder will surely awaken him from his slumber. Similarly, although we were so engrossed in nescience that we could hardly realize who Srila Prabhupada was or what he came to show us, the thunderous vibration of his message of love is reverberating, resounding in our hearts.

“After the deep reverberation of thunder, the sky opens up and pours down rain. Similarly, Srila Prabhupada’s rainfall of mercy is showering down upon the fallen souls. He opened our eyes with light and implanted the seeds of bhakti with transcendental sound. Now his rainfall of mercy is showering down upon us, giving water to the devotional creeper and helping it to grow up to his lotus feet.nama om visnu-padaya krsna-presthaya bhu-tale  
srimate bhaktivedanta-svamin iti namine

‘I offer my respectful obeisances unto His Divine Grace A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, who is very dear to Lord Krishna, having taken shelter at His lotus feet.’

“The instructions of the acharya are always accompanied by his mercy, his helping hand. In May, when Srila Prabhupada was thinking of leaving us, he commented, ‘The trouble is, you are all like children.’ When we asked, ‘If the father leaves the children, is that very good?’ he replied, ‘The children will be provided for.’ And now we are experiencing how he is arranging for our care and maintenance, though he is invisible to our eyes. ‘I may be going,’ he had told us, ‘but Guru Maharaja and Bhaktivinoda Thakura are there. I have asked them to kindly take care of all of you, my transcendental children. The grandfather always takes care of the children much better than the father. So do not fear.’

“Actually, when he was with us, we were always afraid that he would leave us. This transcendental anxiety increased our attachment for him even more.

“‘My dear Lord, when we are away from You we become so anxious to see You again, and there is great misery in our lives. But then, when we do see You, there immediately comes the fear of separation. Under the circumstances, both when we see You and when we do not see You, we are subjected to different kinds of tribulation.’ (The Nectar of Devotion, Ch. 33)

“He made us so attached to him that we cannot imagine living without him. Now we have to follow him back to Krishna. He gave us a taste of nectar, and now he has gone away. What remains for us to do? We can only chase after his footprints, shouting “Krishna! Krishna!” Otherwise, what attraction did we have for Krishna? He came to attract us and free us, and now also he has left us to lead us back to Godhead.

“‘As the swan loves to dive into the water amongst the lily flowers and would die if he were taken from the water, so we only wish to be with You. Our limbs are being shrunken and faded because You have been taken away from us.’ (The Nectar of Devotion, Ch. 38)

“When the rain falls, people collect it in pots so that they can later drink and distribute the water to others. In the same way, Srila Prabhupada has made receptacles for his mercy so that others may also drink. He has created Vaishnavas, sannyasis, brahmans, gurus—all for the sake of distributing his mercy.

“Actually, simply by his desire the entire universe is liberated: ‘Whatever a pure devotee wants from his master, Lord Krsna doubtlessly grants because He has no duty other than to fulfill the desire of His devotee. If you desire the deliverance of all living entities within the universe, then all of them can be delivered even without your undergoing the tribulations of sinful activity. . . . Whosever welfare you desire immediately becomes a Vaisnava, and Krsna delivers all Vaisnavas from the reactions of their past sinful activities? (Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, Madhya 15.166-167,169)

“The rainfall of Srila Prabhupada’s mercy is inundating the entire universe. What is the value of our pots? Only to enliven us in devotional service, to free us from material absorption, has he given us so much responsibility for spreading his movement.

“‘I think this is what Krishna desires,’ he told us. ‘I have come to you, but now in this old age I may be going to Vrindavan, and you will be coming there to me, and be trained up, and we will spread this movement all over the world?

“Thank you, Srila Prabhupada. We are eternally yours.”

Four days after Prabhupada’s disappearance—on November 18, Gopastami, the date when Krishna came of age and was given charge of the cows—to fulfill Srila Prabhupada’s desire to go on parikrama and to have his association along the way, the devotees took a small brass deity of him to Govardhana Hill.

We set out after mangala-arati, with Prabhupada present in his small deity form and a large framed photo. The deity was placed in the back seat of his car, between Upendra and Tamal Krishna. Bhavananda, Achyutananda, and a devotee driver sat in the front. Other devotees, including me, followed in a bus.

We went first to Radha-kunda, and Prabhupada’s deity was placed on the sangam, the strip between Radha-kunda and Syama-kunda,where there is a shrine with govardhana-silas. As we performed kirtan, I had the clear realization that the deity and Srila Prabhupada were the same. The deity was actually him—there was no difference. I began to cry, but I was happy—Prabhupada was right there, still with us.

Prabhupada had told Krishna dasa Babaji, “You will take bath in Radha-kunda on my behalf.” And Tamal Krishna had said, “We’ll get you better, Srila Prabhupada, and you will also be able to take bath there personally. Krishna will make our words come true.” And there he was: Achyutananda performed an abhiseka ceremony, and Prabhupada’s golden form was lowered into the cool water of Radha-kunda. Three times he bathed, as we gazed at his body in the water. Then Jayapataka carried Prabhupada on his head and bathed him three times in Syama-kunda. Prabhupada was dried and dressed in new silk cloth, placed on his palanquin, and offered full arati as the devotees chanted, “Jaya Srila Prabhupada!” and then, with kirtan, we circumambulated those two most sacred ponds.

Next we went around Govardhana, where we carried Prabhupada in procession on his beautifully decorated palanquin. “As we circumambulated the mountain,” Tamal Krishna recounted, “no longer did our hearts burn from separation. We were with Prabhupada again. We were so glad to see him riding again on his palanquin, leading us as always, giving us shelter. It was a cool day, and our walking created dust, the whole atmosphere becoming filled with dust. We could only remember Krishna coming home from tending the cows.”

When we got to Govinda-kunda, where Sri Madhavendra Puri had found the Gopala deity and Indra had performed abhiseka to Krishna, we stopped, listened to The Nectar of Instruction, verses nine to eleven, and sprinkled some of the sacred kunda water on Prabhupada’s head.

As we proceeded, the devotees spoke only of Prabhupada, remembering his pastimes and recounting his glories. We especially recalled his two final weeks, which had been so sweet, appreciating how he had given us his last months solely to deepen our love for him. By his mercy, he had simply laid on his bed, week after week, with no other purpose than to attract us. As we wound around the hill on its uneven paths—eight miles, taking us three hours—Tamal Krishna reflected that Prabhupada could have made this journey only in his present eternal form.

Next we drove to beautiful Kusuma-sarovara, where Prabhupada was placed high in a covered garden house and the devotees took pleasure sporting in the water, jumping and frolicking and swimming. Recorded devotional music was broadcast across the kunda, and at one point the Vande ’Ham album began to play. It was an early album that Prabhupada had recorded in around 1968, and I had listened to it—and loved it— when I was a new devotee in the old Boston temple. When I heard the music again, it was just too much: I burst into tears.

That evening we all sat down and relished a feast and then returned to Vrindavan. “Back to home, with Prabhupada,” Tamal Krishna wrote, “weary as we rode in our car. It had been a wonderful outing, because Prabhupada had been present.”

“Considering Srila Prabhupada’s last desire to go around Govardhana,” Lokanath reflected, “his followers, his disciples, did take him—a small brass murti of him—and hundreds and hundreds of devotees and friends and well-wishers went. We were all thinking of Prabhupada, so we were carrying him in our minds and in our hearts. How could Prabhupada not be there? He was very much there.”

After the exhilaration of the outing to Govardhana, during which we had felt Prabhupada’s presence so strongly, I was again beset by deep feelings of separation. I was constantly on the verge of tears, and any slight remembrance of him could set me off. I was also concerned about our future without Prabhupada’s personal presence. What would happen to us individually, as devotees? What would happen to the movement? How would we function? I recalled an exchange almost six years earlier, when we had been living in the chatai hut in Juhu. One of the devotees had mentioned Prabhupada’s ultimately leaving us, and Srimati had responded, “ISKCON without Prabhupada—it’s hard to imagine.”

Looking for solace and guidance in Prabhupada’s books, I came across a section that addressed the disappearance of the spiritual master: Srimad-Bhagavatam 4.28.45-55. Some passages encouraged me that my lamentation over Prabhupada’s departure was justified—some that I could regain his association by serving his instructions. Text 47 stated, “Being now alone and a widow in that forest, the daughter of Vidarbha began to lament, incessantly shedding tears, which soaked her breasts, and crying very loudly.” In his purport, Prabhupada hadwritten, “Figuratively the queen is supposed to be the disciple of the king; thus, when the mortal body of the spiritual master expires, his disciples should cry exactly as the queen cries when the king leaves his body. However, the disciple and spiritual master are never separated, because the spiritual master always keeps company with the disciple as long as the disciple follows strictly the instructions of the spiritual master. This is called the association of vani (words). Physical presence is called vapuh. As long as the spiritual master is physically present, the disciple should serve the physical body of the spiritual master, and when the spiritual master is no longer physically existing, the disciple should serve the instructions of the spiritual master.”

The next verse discussed the chaos, or disorder, that I anticipated might follow Prabhupada’s disappearance. The queen addressed her late husband, “O best of kings, please get up! Get up! Just see this world surrounded by water and infested with rogues and so-called kings. This world is very much afraid, and it is your duty to protect her.” And in the purport, Prabhupada explained, “Whenever an acarya comes, following the superior orders of the Supreme Personality of Godhead or His representative, he establishes the principles of religion, as enunciated in Bhagavad-gita. Religion means abiding by the orders of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Religious principles begin from the time one surrenders to the Supreme Personality of Godhead. It is the dcdrya's duty to spread a bona fide religious system and induce everyone to bow down before the Supreme Lord. One executes the religious principles by rendering devotional service, specifically the nine items like hearing, chanting, and remembering. Unfortunately, when the acarya disappears, rogues and nondevotees take advantage and immediately begin to introduce unauthorized principles in the name of so-called svamis, yogis, philanthropists, welfare workers, and so on.... The main business of human society is to think of the Supreme Personality of Godhead at all times, to become His devotees, to worship the Supreme Lord, and to bow down before Him. The acarya, the authorized representative of the Supreme Lord, establishes these principles, but when he disappears, things once again become disordered. The perfect disciples of the acarya try to relieve the situation by sincerely following the instructions of the spiritual master.”

I was astonished. Srila Prabhupada was telling me exactly what I needed to know: “The perfect disciples of the acarya try to relieve the situation by sincerely following the instructions of the spiritual master.” Still, I had some apprehensions. How would I get detailed guidance from Prabhupada when there was a question regarding which of his instructions to apply in a particular, complex situation? And what would be my qualification to receive such guidance? His answers began in his purport to text 50: “It is the long-standing tradition of the Vedic system that a faithful wife dies along with her husband. This is called saha-marana.... The wife used to enter the fire voluntarily.... \[W\]hen Maharaja Pandu died, he was survived by two wives—Madri and Kunti. The question was whether both should die or one should die. After the death of Maharaja Pandu, his wives settled that one should remain and the other should go. Madri would perish with her husband in the fire, and Kunti would remain to take charge of the five Pandava children....

“This indicates that a devotee’s wife must be prepared to act in such a way. Similarly, a devoted disciple of the spiritual master would rather die with the spiritual master than fail to execute the spiritual master’s mission. As the Supreme Personality of Godhead comes down upon this earth to reestablish the principles of religion, so His representative, the spiritual master, also comes to reestablish religious principles. It is the duty of the disciples to take charge of the mission of the spiritual master and execute it properly. Otherwise the disciple should decide to die along with the spiritual master. In other words, to execute the will of the spiritual master, the disciple should be prepared to lay down his life and abandon all personal considerations.”

The last sentence was my assignment, my challenge: “\[T\]o execute the will of the spiritual master, the disciple should be prepared to lay down his life and abandon all personal considerations.” And the next two purports explained how that detailed guidance would come:

“In His Paramatma feature, Krsna is the old friend of everyone. According to Vedic injunction, Krsna is sitting with the living entity side by side. According to the sruti-mantra (dva suparna sayuja sakhayah), the Lord is sitting within the heart of every living entity as suhrt, the best friend. The Lord is always eager to have the living entity come home, back to Godhead. Sitting with the living entity as witness,the Lord gives him all chances to enjoy himself materially, but whenever there is an opportunity, the Lord gives good counsel and advises the living entity to abandon trying to become happy through material adjustment and instead turn his face toward the Supreme Personality of Godhead and surrender unto Him. When one becomes serious to follow the mission of the spiritual master, his resolution is tantamount to seeing the Supreme Personality of Godhead. As explained before, this means meeting the Supreme Personality of Godhead in the instruction of the spiritual master. This is technically called vani-seva. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura states in his Bhagavad-gita commentary on the verse vyavasayatmika buddhir ekeha kuru-nandana (Bg. 2.41) that one should serve the words of the spiritual master.
